### IN THIS VOLUME ARE CONTAINED THE FOLLOWING,

A twofold Confession of the Waldensians sent to the King of Hungary,
Letters of Augustin of Olomouc, Doctor of Arts and Decrees <note>original: "Decretorum Doctoris"; a doctor of Canon Law</note>, Provost of the Church of Olomouc and Royal Secretary, against the treachery of the Waldensians,
Two letters from the same Doctor to the Royal Majesty concerning the Waldensian Heresy,
The Defense <note>original: "Excusacio"</note> of the Waldensians against the two letters of Doctor Augustin,
Five books by Jacob Ziegler of Landau, Bavaria, against the Waldensian Heresy,

---

->To the leaders of the Christian estate—the Priests, Parish Priests,<-
->Archdeacons, Bishops, and Archbishops:<-
->The Argument and Commendation of the Work.<-

The Waldensians (likewise called <term>Picards</term> <note>original: "Pighardi"; a derogatory term used for the Bohemian Brethren, often associating them with earlier heretical groups</note>) have stirred up for themselves a most wicked heresy with many heads. They despise the veneration and intercession of the glorious Virgin Mary and all the saints; they deny prayers for the dead; they do not believe in Purgatory; and they do not recognize the ecclesiastical order of the priesthood. They cast the adoration of the body and blood of the Lord in the Sacrament as idolatry and deny its truth, blaspheming our God as being made of grass or rye <note>original: "Herbaceum aut Siligineum deum nostrum"; a mocking reference to the Catholic belief that the bread becomes the actual body of Christ</note>. With such a horrible heresy, they besiege Bohemia and Moravia in droves. Daily they tempt and weaken the bordering provinces of Silesia, Poland, and Meissen, as well as the more distant Wallachia, Styria, and Carinthia, with the poison of their heresy. They strive to push these lands outside of Apostolic obedience and faith. 

Finally, this summer, these most wicked thieves have come forth again with a new madness and some "Apology of Theology"—a false title with the author's name suppressed. They act with frauds, snares, and deceits in all things, doing nothing with an open face or honest confession. These most ruinous traitors of the Christian estate come and go through hidden tunnels <note>metaphorical secret networks</note> throughout the Christian dioceses. While the Apostolic pastors believe everything to be secure in the Lord's flock, the bloodthirsty Picard wolves invade, suffocate, and devour the Apostolic people, intending to send them into the bilge-water of the enemies of divinity—into Hell. 

Our present labor is established against these most impure Picard heretics. Therefore, I implore the Priests, Parish Priests, Archdeacons, Bishops, and Archbishops—by their pastoral care, the honor of their mitres <note>original: "insule," referring to the 'infula' or liturgical headband/mitre</note>, and the account they must give for the Lord's flock on the final day of their life and the world—that they graciously receive these labors of ours. Let them desire that this be spread throughout the dioceses, for by this work they will protect the Christian people against a pestilent heresy. And for Christ, they shall most holily preserve His possession, unharmed and whole, against those obscene "little foxes," the Picards, according to their own best conscience.

# IN THIS VOLUME ARE CONTAINED THE FOLLOWING:

A Twofold Confession of the <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval sect that preceded the Reformation; they were often persecuted for rejecting certain Catholic doctrines.</note> sent to the King of Hungary,
The Letters of Augustine of Olomouc—Doctor of Arts and Decrees, Provost of the Church of Olomouc, and Royal Secretary—against the treachery of the Waldensians,
Two Letters by the same Doctor to his Royal Majesty concerning the Heresy of the Waldensians,
The Defense of the Waldensians against the two letters of Doctor Augustine,
Five Books by Jacob Ziegler of Landau, Bavaria, against the Heresy of the Waldensians,

### An Argument and Commendation of the Work to the Leaders of the Christian State: Priests, Pastors, Archdeacons, Bishops, and Archbishops,

The <term>Waldensians</term> and likewise the <term>Picards</term> <note>original: "Pighardi." A term often used dismissively for the Bohemian Brethren, a group related to the Hussite movement.</note> have stirred up for themselves a most wicked, many-headed heresy. They despise the veneration and intercession of the glorious Virgin Mary and all the saints; they deny prayers for the dead; they do not believe in Purgatory; and they do not recognize the ecclesiastical order of the priesthood. They cast the adoration of the body and blood of the Lord in the Sacrament aside as idolatry. They deny its truth, and blasphemously call our God "a god of grass or of rye." <note>This refers to the Waldensian denial of the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist, viewing the bread as merely grain-based food.</note> From such a horrible heresy, they occupy Bohemia and Moravia in great numbers. Every day, they attempt to infect and weaken the bordering provinces—Silesia, Poland, Meissen—and more distant lands like Wallachia, Styria, and Carinthia with the poison of their heresy, striving to push them out from Apostolic obedience and faith.

Finally, this summer, these most wicked thieves came forward again with a new madness: an "Apology of Theology," a title that is a lie and whose author is suppressed. They act through frauds, snares, and deceptions, never doing anything with an open face or honest confession. These most ruinous betrayers of the Christian state go back and forth through Christian dioceses via secret tunnels; while the Apostolic shepherds believe all is secure in the Lord's flock, these bloodthirsty "Picard" wolves invade the Apostolic people, suffocating and devouring them, intending to drag them down into the sinkhole of the enemies of divinity: Gehenna.

Against these most impure Picard heretics, our present labor has been established. Therefore, I implore the Priests, Pastors, Archdeacons, Bishops, and Archbishops—by their pastoral care, by the honor of the pontifical miter, and by the account they must give for the Lord’s flock on the final day of their lives and of the world—to graciously accept these labors of ours. I ask that they desire them to be spread throughout the Dioceses, since by this work they will defend the Christian people against this pestilent heresy. Thus, they shall most holily preserve the possession of Christ against these obscene "Picard" foxes, keeping it unharmed and whole through their own excellent conscience.

# SOLEMN DECLARATION,
<note>original Latin: "PROTESTACIO"</note>

The professors of Divine Wisdom <term>Divine Wisdom: A traditional way of referring to the study of Theology</term>, when they engage in <term>Scholastic</term> <note>Scholasticism was the method of critical thought and dialectical reasoning taught in the universities of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.</note> disputes or write, are accustomed to first ask for indulgence for their own human weakness. They submit their thoughts and the reach of their intellect to the judgment of the Church, considering their words and writings to be valid and true only insofar as the Church has approved them.

Therefore, I, Jacob Ziegler of Landau, Bavaria, following that same Christian modesty and Apostolic tradition, do declare in this solemn manner: that whatever I have conceived and written in my five books against the <term>Pighard</term> heretics <note>The "Pighards" (or Picards) was a term often applied to the Bohemian Brethren, a religious group Ziegler considered to be outside the bounds of Catholic orthodoxy</note>, I submit to the judgment of the Church. And if I have committed any error, whether by a slip of the tongue or a weakness of understanding, I shall most obediently correct the whole of it, just as Mother Church may decree.

<summary>In this formal preface, the scholar Jacob Ziegler submits his work to the authority of the Catholic Church, expressing his willingness to correct any theological errors in his arguments against the Bohemian Brethren.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Ziegler, Bavaria, Pighards, Picards, heresy, Scholasticism, Church authority, preface, declaration</keywords>

It follows the introductory "Protestatio" by Jacob Ziegler, setting the stage for the theological conflict between the institutional Church and this reformist group.</meta>

# OF THE WALDENSIANS,

## THE DEFENSIVE AND SATISFACTORY SPEECH
## OF THE BROTHERS SENT TO KING VLADISLAUS
## IN HUNGARY,

->c<-

Most Illustrious King, our gracious lord and master,
We, oppressed men, humbly subject to your Majesty, though clothed in a contemptible and false name <note>The "false name" refers to "Waldensian" or "Pighard," labels used by their enemies which the Brethren felt did not accurately describe their faith.</note>, offer to your Highness our humble speech, wishing for your lasting health, the increase of every good thing, and the removal of evil in your happy empire. 
We make known to your dignity that in times past a decree from your Grace reached us—not only as a rumor among men, but also proven through its actual implementation against many of us. By this decree, following the accusations of our enemies who unfairly and unjustly judge us with a wicked sentence, you declared us to be evil and impious men, seducers of the ignorant common people, and more harmful through the cunning of the devil than the treacherous race of the Turks <note>The comparison to the Ottoman Turks was the ultimate insult and mark of "outsider" status in 16th-century Europe.</note>. Acquiescing to the slanders of such enemies, you manifested us as such out of your ignorance of our true nature. Finally, you ordered the officials of your greatness to expel us from the cities of your domain, to remove us from magistracies, and to stop our gatherings—in which we pray to God for your good and benefit. You have sought to compel us against our conscience to give up the faith we hold. Furthermore, you ordered that we should be regarded by the priests of both sides <note>Likely referring to both the Roman Catholic and the Utraquist (Hussite) clergy in Bohemia.</note> as nefarious people who, captured by diabolical wickedness, hold wrong and evil views concerning God, the sacraments of the Church, and the communion of the Body and Blood of Christ. Moreover, you publicly commanded in your letters that men should flee from all conversation with us. 

Hearing this ourselves, and many of us having fully experienced it in reality, we fled to God in our prayers, beseeching His mercy that by His kindness, and by the merit and intercession of His most beloved Son, He might preserve you from the shedding of human blood and the sad affliction of those men who strive to please the divine goodness and to emulate His known will. At the same time, we feared thereafter that God might send His anger and fury from on high upon your person and your Kingdom. Lastly, we have also had a great desire, should the opportunity arise, to simply explain the principles and the rule of our religion <note>original Latin: "Archanis," meaning the inner mysteries or foundational secrets of their faith.</note>—for the sake of which we endure various hardships—so that, supported by this help against the accusations of all slanderers, we might always find you a mild and pious King, and so that every cruel and turbulent storm against us in your merciful empire might immediately grow quiet. Therefore, we submissively ask your piety to be heard patiently, by the grace of God’s justice and His mercy, which you yourself continually desire to be given to you by God. For you should not doubt that what we are about to write arises from the sincerity of our hearts; for what we believe in our hearts before God, we now profess with our mouths in such a manner. 

This first we have received with a believing mind as the true faith, in which we have now lived for some time with a stable soul, and in which we have purposed to persevere immovably for the salvation of our souls with free intention. Namely: all the truth of the faith revealed by the Holy Spirit, then placed in the Holy Scriptures by that same Holy Spirit, and collected summarily in the Apostles' Creed; which was likewise preserved in reality by the primitive church, certified by virtues, wonders, sincere doctrine, and also by martyrdom; and finally explained with zeal against heretics by the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the core doctrine of Christ's divinity.</note>, and by Bishop Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, a champion of orthodoxy against Arianism.</note>, and many other teachers of doctrine, as being necessary for the salvation of souls.

<summary>The Bohemian Brethren petition King Vladislaus II, defending themselves against charges of being "worse than Turks" and pleading for an end to their persecution by explaining their adherence to the Bible and the historic Creeds.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the historical and political grievances of the Bohemian Brethren to a formal "Confessio" (Confession of Faith). It aims to demonstrate that their theology is strictly orthodox and aligned with the early Church fathers, specifically regarding the Trinity and the nature of Christ, to counter accusations of heresy.</meta>

# CONFESSION,

which, especially in this age, we confess with equal faith. Living faith is thus the universal foundation of human salvation; this faith is given by the gift of the Holy Spirit and is mainly bestowed by the merit of Christ’s grace. In the church, however, it is announced ministerially <note>The term "ministerially" (ministerialit̄) refers to the role of the clergy as servants or "tools" of God's Word rather than the source of grace themselves.</note> by the voice of the gospel and the word of truth, and is confirmed by way of example through the ecclesiastical sacraments.

## PROFESSION OF FAITH IN THE BLESSED TRINITY,

From this same fountain of faith, we steadfastly believe and confess as long as we breathe: That the Author and Giver of the faith of salvation is Almighty God, one in the substance of the deity, but three in persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; one God, forever blessed. By this faith we believe entirely concerning God the Father, to God the Father, and in God the Father. Concerning God the Father, we believe that He eternally begets His only Son, whom, moved by His mercy, He gave to the world for redemption and salvation; by whose merit the Father alone, according to the purpose of His election, works salvation. We believe in God the Parent by the same faith when we fully acquiesce to His testimony, which fell from heaven concerning His most beloved Son: "This is," He said, "my beloved Son, hear Him" <note>original: "Hic ē: inqt: fili⁹ me⁹ dilect⁹, ipm audite," quoting Matthew 17:5.</note>. This is also what the blessed and forever inviolate Virgin Mary brought forth in harmonious sentiment: "Whatever," she says, "my Son says to you, do" <note>quoting John 2:5.</note>. We also say with equal faith that His true and faithful commands are from God, so that whoever, living in an adult age in faith, should abandon them, will in no way attain salvation in Christ. We believe in God the Father when, knowing Him to be the omnipotent Creator of heaven and earth, we love Him with our heart and keep His commandments in deed according to our knowledge and strength.

## SINCERE FAITH CONCERNING THE INCARNATE WORD,

The Catholic faith <note>In this context, "Catholic" (catholica) is used in its original sense of "universal" or "orthodox," referring to the historic faith of the Apostles rather than the Roman Catholic Church as an institution.</note> which we once received from God makes us believe and profess the same concerning Christ, to Christ the Lord, and in Christ. Concerning Christ, the Eternal Wisdom, we believe He is the true and only God, equal in divinity to the Father and the Holy Spirit—in power, wisdom, and goodness—and that He is eternal life, proceeding from the Father by perpetual generation, through whom we do not doubt He also made the ages. Who, in order to fulfill the promises of the fathers for the salvation of the nations, descended personally from the high heaven; enclosed in the virginal chamber <note>original: "thalamo virginali," a poetic theological term for the womb of Mary.</note>, He was seen on earth in the fullness of time. He was cruelly stretched upon the cross; while Pilate was then presiding in Judea, He breathed out His soul with most pure blood. Taken down from the wood, He was laid in a stone sepulcher; on the third light, He was awakened from a peaceful sleep. Finally, on the fortieth day, under a serene cloud at His side, we believe He reigns, sitting at the right hand of the Father—namely, in that most worthy and noble place—so that all the desire of our heart, as well as the confidence of our hope, may be raised upward into the glory prepared by His blood. He who resides on the throne of grace as a faithful advocate intercedes for those who are to receive the inheritance of glory—His Church, for which He offered Himself to the punishment of death. He does not desert her by grace, power, help, and free gift, which Church He vehemently observed in the days of His flesh. To Him every race of living things—heavenly, earthly, and infernal—is subject by this law: that just as they worship the Father God, so they should worship and venerate the Son with equal glory, equal honor, and similar majesty; and with their own tongue, they should confess to serve and trust Him in glory, namely, on the seat of the Father's majesty. Nor will He ever descend from heaven until the adversity of all nations is subjected under His feet, and finally crushed by eternal damnation. We assent to this Jesus Christ, provided we say that His commands are true and faithful, which obligate us to believe in Him, to trust, and to love Him for the sake of attaining the life of glory. Moreover, we believe *in* Christ when, recognizing Him as our God and Savior, we embrace all His words with full faith, loving Him also with perfect charity and joined in faith and love with His faithful members.

## TRUE FAITH CONCERNING THE HOLY SPIRIT,

Finally, by the power of the same faith, which we have decided to hold until the end, we tenaciously believe concerning the Holy Spirit, to the Holy Spirit, and in the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Holy Spirit, who is...

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Confession of Faith," moving from the description of the Holy Spirit to a detailed definition of the Church and its ministries. It establishes the "Waldensian" (Bohemian Brethren) view of the Church as both a spiritual body of the elect and a visible community of the faithful, emphasizing humility and the "narrow way" of Christ.</meta>

OF THE WALDENSIANS,
A iij

...the one true God with the Father and the only-begotten Word; in this respect alone is He distinct, that He proceeds from both <note>original: "emanat." This refers to the "procession" of the Holy Spirit, a central point of Trinitarian theology.</note>. By the gift of His life-giving, renewing, and reforming faith, everyone arrives at a participation in Christ’s meritorious grace of justification, truth, strength, and perfect salvation. Upon this faith in Christ—which the gates of hell cannot prevail against—the holy Church is founded. In like manner, the Spirit washes, justifies, sanctifies, ordains, governs, gathers, strengthens, and makes fruitful the members of that true faith. Likewise, the divine Scriptures were inspired and are understood by that same Spirit. By Him, the members of the church are united; from Him, the gifts for governing the church proceed; and many other things are perfected by the same Holy Spirit for a life of glory. We believe the Holy Spirit when we fully consent to the divine Scriptures or the apostles of God. We believe *in* the Holy Spirit when, through a clear knowledge of Him and a faith that is not false, we love Him and, together with the members inspired by Him, we preserve all His revealed truths for eternal glory.

### PROFESSION CONCERNING THE HOLY CHURCH,

With that same fullness of formed faith, we believe that the **holy catholic Church**, by reason of its foundation in living faith, is the number of all the elect from the beginning of the world until its consummation. These are they whom God the Father chooses in Christ by His Spirit, justifies, calls, and magnifies in the glory of salvation; outside of this Church, there is no salvation for mankind. Furthermore, by reason of its ministries and its dispensers, we believe the **holy catholic church** to be the congregation of all ministers and the people subjected in obedience, who from the beginning until the end of all time follow the divine will. These, God alone sends, inspired by the Holy Spirit, giving them the word of faith, peace, and reconciliation, so that they may bring forth fruit in the unity of the church of salvation, and that their labor may not be cheated of its health-giving reward. He alone knows their names and their number, for He has written them in the Book of Life. The first church mentioned above <note>The invisible church of the elect.</note> contains no one who is to be damned; the second, however <note>The visible, institutional church.</note>, remains mixed with various people until the time appointed for the final judgment. The "church of the malignant" <note>original: "Ecclesia malignantium," a common medieval term for the community of sinners or the anti-church.</note> encompasses those who have perished from the Evil One, whom the devil sends for the destruction of the world and the testing of the elect.

In this current span of time in which we breathe, all the bitter and sad things that Christ and His apostles prophesied have fallen upon this church in abundance: namely, that those who are unworthy of ecclesiastical honor rule over it by their own power, and that the promises of renewal have already been fulfilled for her. However, we do not arrogate so much to ourselves that we wish to be called the "Catholic Church" ourselves—as if salvation were stored only with us—but rather we labor with anxious diligence to be made partakers of the ecclesiastical truth. Finally, we stand in obedience to her rulers, being subject to them with inward love.

But as for the **evil workers**—whom we have detected to be enemies of the Bride <note>The Church.</note> and her truth—we fear to be subject to them or to obey them in those things which they think, speak, or act against the Law, out of fear of eternal damnation and out of obedience to Christ and His church. For this reason, we patiently bear hardships, mockeries, and slanders for the sake of the salvation of our souls. For unless a holy fear and the horror of hell restrained us, we would embrace the liberty of the world (in which one is permitted to live as one wishes) along with its vanities. But we have preferred to choose the **narrow way**, sad and mocked, which the Redeemer Christ Himself walked, and which His Bride the church (condemned and cast out by the world) followed, tracing His marked footsteps, rather than to taste and follow the momentary charms of the age.

### CONCERNING THE MINISTRIES OF THE CHURCH,

The first and most powerful mystery <note>original: "misterium," here used interchangeably with "ministry."</note> of the catholic church is the Gospel of Christ, which manifests the grace and truth laboriously acquired through the torment of the cross; which grace is given to the elect who are called...

<meta>This page continues the "Confession of Faith" by the Bohemian Brethren (often associated with Waldensian thought). ->CONFESSION,<-

...faith is granted by the Holy Spirit and God the Father for salvation. Next, we acknowledge another necessary ministry of the church of Christ: the word of sound doctrine, in which saving truth is known in the sense of faith. From this knowledge, the life of grace and glory is administered to humans of good desire. Similarly, we declare that the **seven sacraments** are useful to the church of Christ. By these, the fulfillment of God's promises is signified to the believing people; also, entrance into the church of God for preserving unity among those living in glory is administered through them.

## BAPTISM,

Faith given by God leads one to think such things about **Baptism**, the first sacrament: whoever, being of mature age, has obtained faith by hearing the word of God—by which they are reborn and illuminated in the soul and have gained spiritual strength—such a person is bound to be baptized by an outward washing as evidence of the inward purity acquired through faith, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in the unity of the holy church. This profession of ours also extends to children, because by the decree of the apostles (as Dionysius <note>Likely Dionysius the Areopagite, a figure historically credited with writing on the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies.</note> writes), they ought to be baptized. They are to be invited and accustomed to the life of faith following the guidance of Godparents <note>original: "Cõpatrum." These are sponsors or spiritual guardians who assist in the religious upbringing of the child.</note> who are learned in the law of Christ.

## ON CONFIRMATION,

With faith drawn from the divine scriptures, we profess that in the times of the apostles, this was observed: whoever did not receive the promised gifts of the Holy Spirit during the years of puberty would receive them through prayer and the laying on of hands for the **confirmation of faith**. We feel the same regarding infants: whoever, having been baptized, comes to true faith—which they propose to imitate in reality during adversities and insults—for this very reason, so that a new regeneration in their spirit and a life of graces may appear revealed, such a person ought to be led and placed before the Bishop or a priest. Being questioned about the truths of faith, the divine precepts, and at the same time their good will and stable intention and the works of truth, they shall testify by confessing that all these things are so. Such a person is to be confirmed in the hope of the truth attained. Finally, they are to be aided by the prayers of the churches, so that an increase of the gifts of the Holy Spirit for stability and the "warfare of faith" <note>original: "miliciãq[ue] fidei." A common metaphor for the Christian life as a spiritual struggle.</note> may come to them. Lastly, by the laying on of hands to confirm the promises of God and the truth held in the power of the name of the Father and His Word, may the breath of the nurturing Spirit also join them to the society of the church.

## ON THE EUCHARIST,

By that same faith which we have drawn from the ministry of the holy scriptures, we believe and also resonate with our tongue: wherever a worthy priest, with faithful people, according to the sense and intention of Christ and the ordinance of the church, makes prayer with words of this kind—namely, *“This is my body,”* *“This is my blood”*—it is testified that immediately the present bread is the **body of Christ** offered for us in death; similarly, the present wine is His **blood** poured out for the remission of sins. This profession of our faith is confirmed by the words of Christ written by the Evangelists and by Saint Paul. To this profession, let this also be added: this body of Christ and His blood, according to the institution of Christ and also His church, ought to be received under **both species** <note>original: "sub panis viniq[ue] speciebus vtrisq[ue]." This refers to the practice of Utraquism—receiving both the bread and the wine—which was a central demand of the Bohemian Reformation.</note> of bread and wine in commemoration of His death and the shedding of His blood, just as He says: *“Do this in remembrance of me.”* Then, the death of Christ is to be announced by the word of the Gospel along with the good and useful things disposed by His death. Similarly, the hope of the shed blood, as the Apostle testifies: *“As often,”* he says, *“as you eat this bread and drink the cup of the Lord, you will announce the death of the Lord until He comes.”* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:26.</note> Thirdly, for the knowledge of spiritual truth about which John the Evangelist writes, and likewise for the certification of the gift, the taking, the use, and the acceptance of truth through faith in hope, as the Lord says: *“Take and eat; take and drink.”* Fourthly, because of simultaneous use, for from the institution and practice of Christ and the early church, then the priest...

This refers to the words of Jesus at the Last Supper.</note>. Paul also says: *Is the cup of blessing which we bless not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? This emphasizes the communal unity created by the sacrament.</note> Fifth, [it is administered] for the sake of distinguishing the faithful from infidels and the unworthy, and for the excommunication and correction of those who, defiled by the stain of vices, refuse to do penance. Regarding this, just as we fear to change or take away those very things which the Lord Jesus deigned to testify to with his own words, so we also do not dare to add anything that the Institutor of the sacrament did not add. At the same time, we follow the primitive church which, following Christ in poverty and labor, did not violate the simple delivery of the law. Regarding this perfect sacrament, which the Lord instituted out of great grace for the charity and love of the elect, many discords have emerged from human senses, opinions, factions, and additions—so much so that, contrary to the intention of the Lord’s institution, some, seized by madness, commit murders against others. We, however, to avoid the cause of such great evil, take refuge in the faith of Christ, in his words, his intention, and the meaning impressed upon his words; so that what he commanded us to believe, we believe simply, and what he finally mandated, we faithfully perform. Indeed, we do not only believe that the bread, having been received, blessed, and broken, is his body because he testified it to be so—but even if, taking up a stone, he had said it was his body, we would have fully believed it to be so. Because of this simple faith of ours, and because we do not allow ourselves to be led away from it by the opinions of men, we are called heretics. Because of the actual practice to which the word of Christ and the Apostles and the example of his work in that same sacrament invites us—because we act thus and use our whole faith in memory of Christ’s death—we are condemned, judged, imprisoned, and afflicted. For we worship Christ our Redeemer, bound by his prohibition of worldly distraction and by his precept, with the honor and worship worthy of him; we greatly fear to venerate anything else in the same way as him alone, who sits at the right hand of the Father with the Holy Spirit. Therefore, most kind King, may your Serenity know that we do this not out of contumacy nor any contempt, but out of the fear of God and obedience to him. We pray that your Highness may deign to have compassion on us, who are condemned for the faith of Christ. We also hope that God on high, by his grace, may deign to guard and preserve your Dignity from his wrath.

### CONCERNING THE ORDER OF PRIESTHOOD,

By this same faith of ours, we believe that the ordination of priests proceeds from the High Bishop and Great Priest <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the source of all ministerial authority.</note> in heaven, so that in the place of Christ's embassy <note>original: "legacōis chr̃i." The idea that priests act as ambassadors for Christ.</note>, the ministry, evangelization, doctrine, judgment, offering of prayers from men, thanksgivings, and praises to God may be carried out by them. Similarly, let it be done from God toward men, so that the promises of God, held in hope, may be verified by true faith, and that the evil may be kept away from this good by excommunication. Finally, we also confess by faith that those who intend to ordain others are bound to emulate Christ and to fulfill his embassy with a right mind, without respect of persons, and finally free from greedy desire and simony <note>The sin of buying or selling ecclesiastical offices or spiritual things.</note>. By the same faith, we propose that those who are to be promoted to major or minor orders ought to excel other faithful people in a virtuous life in the faith of Christ. For a living faith sanctifies and grants fitness for all duties; it possesses blessing and life. For good...

<header>CONFESSION</header>

Deeds of an honest life are the garment and ornament of a Priest, for the glory of the heavenly Father, the example of the people, and the power of the word. They are also held to possess the more abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit—namely, a more ardent love for Christ, confidence in their own salvation and that of their neighbors, trust in God, uprightness of intention, a sound sense of faith in a good conscience, feet prepared for the gospel of peace <note>original: "p̄paratos pedes in euangeliū pacis." This is a biblical allusion to Ephesians 6:15.</note>, the wisdom of the spirit, knowledge of the divine law, the discernment of spirits, and so forth. Whoever is raised to the priesthood through such an ordination, we profess that such an ordination is a Sacrament, since it is a sign of the truth of the supreme priesthood of Christ Jesus and of his appointment by God the Father, and a form of ministry as the head of his church for burning to God the incense of truth in Christ. For the full advancement of a priest, we approve that three things are necessary: First, the proof of life, faith, and gifts, as well as fidelity in the smaller matters entrusted to them; second, prayers with fasting; and lastly, the granting of power with words fit for this purpose, and the imposition of hands for strengthening.

## ON MARRIAGE,

By faith we attest that Marriage is the legitimate, honest, and decent union of two persons of each sex, male and female, in Christ; a chaste bed, kept with indissolubility. It is a sign of a great truth <note>original: "signum magne veritatis." This refers to the "great mystery" mentioned in Ephesians 5:32 regarding Christ and the Church.</note>, namely the bond of Christ with the Church and with the faithful soul.

## ON THE PENANCE OF THOSE WHO HAVE FALLEN,

From faith we affirm that for a fallen sinner, God—if He has granted a heart contrite and humbled for their vices to one who has true faith in Christ, and if they have repented in soul, intention, and deed from their past vices—such a person, established in truth, if they find a priest skilled in discerning evil from good, whose lips have guarded the knowledge of the divine law, they ought to reveal their crimes to such a priest through confession with a right intention. The priest, presiding in the place of God as a judge and by the right of the law of the Lord in the church, should rightly judge the gravity of the fault so that the sinner may be filled with shame; and being corrected, the sinner may have the counsel of penance for their reformation. Whether loosed or bound by the keys of Christ <note>This refers to the "Power of the Keys" granted to the apostles to forgive or retain sins.</note>, they should humbly obey. We call such a submissive contrition of the heart the sacrament of penance; this is the wood of the truth of grace granted to the penitent. But if a heart weighed down, contrite, and abhorring crimes through faith is lacking, along with a troubled spirit that embraces the will of God, and if confession is joined with a simulated release from fault and satisfaction, we pronounce this to be a vain sign, empty of the grace of Christ.

## EXTREME UNCTION OF THE SICK,

The anointing of the sick contains two things within itself. First, the means of easier access to those who are languishing; in this respect, it is not a sacrament. The second is the thing itself signified by such an anointing, which is granted by God in Christ. For this reason, in right faith, one must especially pray that it be granted to the faithful sufferer according to the precept of the blessed James, who says: *Is any among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will alleviate him; and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him.* <note>James 5:14-15.</note> By the faith of the sick person, the sign of anointing certifies the remission of crimes.

## THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS,

Having held to the faith of the Catholic Church and its truth, from which truth holiness is given to it by proclamation, it now remains to confess with that same firmness of faith concerning the communion of saints. The communion of saints is when the members of the holy church mutually use in common the good, freely given, life-giving, and administrative things granted to all by the grace of God without regret; and according to the grace of the gift of God, they offer themselves for the common [good]...

for the utility of others. It is therefore clear that only the elect <note>In this context, the "elect" refers to those chosen by God for salvation through true faith.</note> are truly sharers in the faith, grace, and justice of the merit of Christ for the glory of eternal salvation. Just as they communicate in the sacraments as evidence of their faith, even if they should fall into deception, the damnation of torment will not seize them. But the wicked—those with an unformed faith—even if they should communicate in truth through sacraments, dignities, public administrations, and customs, so long as they remain devoid of true faith, they participate unworthily as hypocrites. If they follow those in error, they fall into seduction and deception by the same guidance.

### THE REMISSION OF SINS,

By our belief in the grace of Christ, we freely announce that he who communicates with a living faith attains the very truth of the release from vices in Christ. Simultaneously, by participating in the sacraments of the Church, he obtains the dissolution of crimes in that same faith and certainty. If he endures until the end of his life, he will follow this life of grace here with the glorification of the soul in the blessed resurrection at the final time of judgment. Amen.

This, most illustrious King, is the profession of our faith which we hold as catholic <note>The authors use "catholic" in its original sense of "universal" or "true," rather than as a reference to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> in our hearts. It has its foundation in the scriptures of faith. The tedious length of these scriptures and the various preoccupations of your mind do not allow us to bring them all forward here. Indeed, with many arguments from the sacred letters and also with ample reasoning, we have previously composed another writing before this one, similarly detailing the causes of our separation from the Roman Church. However, the weight of your own affairs has distracted your Highness from seeing or reading it. Yet, if your Majesty should have the mind to possess it, we are ready to produce it.

Furthermore, let your Majesty know that the cause of our disagreement is not the outward appearance of religion or superstitious rites, but has been primarily the obstacles to the most holy faith and its ministries. By that catholic faith we are indeed distinguished, so that we may freely carry out the prayers and sacraments ordained by Christ. Therefore, we most humbly pray to be heard by your Royal Clemency, so that you might receive this writing with an equal mind, as if sent by upright and simple men. If in this writing less than what is full and decent has been paid to your honor, your kindness will grant pardon to our ignorance. Also, if you detect any sentiments in this writing that are bitter to your Highness, we hope they may be borne with a mild mind. Although we seek stability and immobility in the true faith, nevertheless, when a more certain truth is acknowledged, it puts to flight execrable obstinacy. We stand ready for human instruction and wish to be taught from the sacred traditions of the Law; we desire to be led to the sound sense of the Christian religion. Neither will such labor toward us seem vain or ungrateful, nor should anyone think us so seized by rash obstinacy that we would not yield to the clear truth. Nor will anyone be able to justly call us heretics; for it is not error in the mind, but obstinacy of the will that makes a heretic. Renouncing all heresy, we devote ourselves daily to correction. Indeed, we do not forge new dogmas or recent additions to the Christian religion against the law of God in order to obtain honor, wealth, dignities, or popular favor. For that behavior does not belong to a true worshiper, but to the heretic himself, who savors neither sound faith nor the true worship of God, but rather seeks earthly and fleeting riches, which he refuses to leave of his own accord at the voice of the Lord. Indeed, he defends them even to the shedding of the blood of many men. But our mind is far different; for not only do we studiously abstain from shedding human blood, but also, by divine command, we patiently cast aside our lives and fleeting riches, praying for our persecutors for the sake of attaining eternal life. At the same time, we remain subject to those established in powers of dignity, we observe what is commanded, and we carry out every just work with a ready mind, blaspheming no one, and striving to have peace and concord with all people.

<meta>This page continues the address to the King (likely Vladislaus II) following the declaration of the Bohemian Brethren’s confession. Having established their theological stance on the sacraments and the remission of sins, they now transition to a humble plea for royal protection and religious tolerance.</meta>

<header>CONFESSION.</header>

Moreover, we earnestly beseech your Grace, for the sake of God and His justice, that with favorable kindness you might look upon us with compassion and not disdain to let us lead a mild and peaceful life under your rule. For we do not cease to pray to God continually for the long-lasting health of your life and for your noble offspring, while we live piously and innocently under your lordship. Even if, persisting with an unshaken mind or a stubborn edict, you do not permit us to inhabit the cities of your principality, we diligently entreat your clemency <note>The Latin *clemencia* refers to the King's mercy or leniency in governance.</note> that your moderation might ensure that the cruelty of our enemies does not dominate any servant of yours. Finally, we pray that for those of ours who have been defeated and kept for a long time in dark prisons, the freedom to go out may be granted by your command. We also vehemently ask that for those bound by the law of surety <note>original: *lege fideiussoria*, referring to a legal bond or bail where someone else guarantees a person's behavior</note>, an interval be granted so they have the opportunity to settle their affairs with their goods unharmed.

Furthermore, we do not believe that the priestly law <note>original: *pontificium ius*; here referring to the ecclesiastical principle that faith should not be coerced</note> is hidden from your dignity—namely, that no one is to be forced into faith. How much more does God require from man that both faith and good works be voluntary? Indeed, it is commonly observed among men that no servant should be kept unless they are voluntary; how much more does the God of liberty demand one who is not coerced by some necessity, but who acquiesces to the truths by the choice of free will <term>free will (liberi arbitrii): the theological concept that humans have the capacity to choose between different possible courses of action independently</term>. Therefore, led by a released judgment toward what we have daily come to know as truer and more certain, we are carried toward that good—not only because we are compelled, but because we are drawn by love for it. We cling to this good with such stability that neither the horror of death, the savage edge of the sword, the harshness of tortures, nor many other things are able to tear us away.

We also intimately ask your Majesty’s command that this be done for our brothers who live under the jurisdiction of lords who hate us: that they be given the freedom to change their location and remain under a more peaceful lordship. If you grant this, God, the giver of all good, will kindly pour peace, concord, and the forgiveness of your sins into your kingdom. For we have no other weapons to protect us other than the innermost desires of our hearts, sent always in our prayers to God, our strong protector, so that by His power He might bend your mind and human spirit toward us—men who are ignominiously affected by insult. Therefore, we hope to be defended and protected by you, a just and pious King, like orphans enduring pressures. In these straits, besides the most pious God, we seek no other than your greatness, nor is it our intent to appeal to anyone else besides your Majesty. Order and permit us, therefore, to live with a calm spirit under your principality, and to emulate the religious and pious worship of the God of heaven in Christ Jesus by the power of the Holy Spirit. For the Lord is present, and behold, with Him is a bountiful reward.

But if you desert us in such great distress and cast us off, or permit us to be afflicted or tortured by our enemies as they wish, what else would remain for us to do or think but to cry out to the Lord sorrowfully in our continuous prayers for defense, protection, and provision without ceasing? We trust in His inexhaustible goodness that, according to His faithful promises, He will not abandon us—men who cling tenaciously to Him and His truth—but will support us with powerful help so that we may be saved.

Furthermore, may God from on high grant your Magnificence an acceptable embracing of this summary <note>original: *compendii*, referring to this shortened statement of their faith</note>. Finally, by His kindness, may He soften your heart to protect a rejected and humbled people. Through such defense, you shall obtain a blessing from God and a fortunate administration of your kingdom—now in the grace of Christ, and at last, in the reward of the righteous, you shall attain the eternal glorification of life. Amen.

# THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS. <note>original: "Errores Valdensium." This title was likely added by a critic or the publisher, as the text that follows is a defense written by the Brethren themselves, who were often labeled "Waldensians" by their opponents.</note>

## THE CONFESSION OF THE BRETHREN SENT TO KING VLADISLAUS 
## IN HUNGARY,

We, the brothers gathered in the name of Christ, send forward our humble submission with a suppliant prayer to the Majesty of your Highness. By this writing of ours, we make it known that your Serenity recently sent letters in your name to this kingdom of Bohemia against us, your faithful subjects, scattered abroad. In these letters, perhaps more harshly than is permitted, you commanded our lords to whom we are subject that we be brought to the city of Prague—specifically on the feast day of Saint John the Apostle—to stand before the Rectors of both estates, namely the spiritual <note>The clergy or ecclesiastical authorities.</note> and the secular. Finally, you strictly ordered these same officials that they should, in the name of your Excellence, force us to abandon our opinions to which we have been accustomed to cling tenaciously. You commanded that we should be made to adopt one of the two parties currently at odds with each other <note>referring to the Utraquists and the Roman Catholics in Bohemia</note> at our own discretion, and finally, being fully instructed and taught, we should join the assembly of those prelates. You commanded us to believe in the manner established according to the rite of the orthodox faith and the sanctions of the holy doctors. Yet, if doing this should seem too little to us, you then openly permitted that we be driven from the Kingdom like condemned robbers and persistent heretics, and that many other evils be inflicted upon us by your aforementioned writings, loosening the reins of their cruelty—things which we pass over out of a desire for love. 

We, indeed, were astonished by the mere rumor among men—for it was not granted to us to read or even see your Majesty’s letters—which flew everywhere. Immediately, the thoughts of our minds were stirred; for we have always known your gentleness and humanity, which you have shown since you began to hold the scepter of this kingdom, and how you have diligently devoted yourself to justice, peace, and tranquility. And so, we judged it least fitting for you now to rage against us with such atrocity. For indeed, we have long since learned by experience that your Highness is accustomed to restrain your subjects more with merciful justice than with severe equity. But because we perceive that your gentleness has now departed from the law of humanity and clemency, we deeply sympathize with your Excellence, since you have preferred to embrace a matter so adverse to your own governance. 

Finally, we wish for this very thing to be weighed by your Majesty; we ask that your Serenity discuss whether it be just or unjust. It has been permitted in your public letters for us to be condemned by you as assassins and heretics, to be driven from our native soil <term>native soil: *natali solo*, referring to the Brethren's deep roots in Bohemia</term> against the law of the land, and for all kinds of mortals to believe and confess that we are infamous. To these charges, no public hearing has ever been properly granted; what seems even more absurd is that no response has been given to the satisfaction or the reasoning of our faith, which we already presented to your Royal Majesty some time ago, as to whether we have believed or felt rightly or impiously according to the Catholic way. Instead, it has been suppressed in silence. We have always been prone and willing to correct not only things wrongly believed but even things impiously felt. But now, who would judge that this dire sentence of condemnation, which has recently been brought against us, ought to be borne by right? Will not everyone instead confess that every single thing of this kind has been acted against us contrary to the law of humanity? 

We know very well from what root all these evils and adversities against us sprout and from where they arise; for our calumniators <note>Those who make false and malicious accusations.</note> keep a diligent watch in this matter. Raging against us with an ancient hatred, they prefer to exterminate and destroy us rather than to correct us. They are truly troublesome accusers who, being abandoned to their own wicked crimes, disturb the merciful soul and mind of your Serenity, so that you might not give the ears of your kindness to us...

They blame malicious accusers for influencing the King's usually merciful nature and suppressing their previous defense of their faith.</summary>

# CONFESSION, AGAINST

We pray greatly that it be made clear, for those empty of all justice and integrity strive to fill every corner of this kingdom with injurious machinations and tumultuous seditions, even unto horrific slaughters. To such people, it should indeed be written more effectively so that they might desist from such undertakings. Furthermore, we wish for it not to be hidden from your Magnificence why we have long since withdrawn from the Roman cohort <note>The "Roman cohort" refers to the Roman Catholic clergy and their supporters.</note>. Indeed, the cursed malignity of the spiritual prelates, authored by the devil—whose chief work is to sow discord and dissension among brothers—compelled us to withdraw from the assembly of the Roman Church. 

These men, raging against one another with blind malevolence and the insolent pride of the powers of darkness, have broken the laws of peace and ecclesiastical love. Destitute of all humanity, they used to provoke one another openly, not only with infamous speech but also with biting writings and insults. For, impudently moved by a certain god-opposing <note>original: *Antithei*. A Greek-derived term meaning "against God" or "adversarial."</note> malignity, they stripped one another of the power of the ecclesiastical keys <note>The authority to forgive or retain sins.</note>, the salvific truth, religious worship, free piety, the orthodox faith, the gift of spiritual graces, and finally, every good work. 

Furthermore, in the preaching chairs of their temples, with a great multitude of people present, they used divine authority, strong reasons, and firm arguments from examples, as well as the structures of the paternal canons and threatening censures, to brand and preach against each other as schismatics, heretics, sacrilegious, false prophets, ravenous wolves, and the beast and prostitute of the Apocalypse <note>References to the Book of Revelation, used here to describe the corruption and perceived evil of their clerical rivals.</note>. Having raged with such insolence, they disturbed the entire Kingdom at that time, to the point where it became necessary for the inhabitants of the same kingdom to fight one another with arms; consequently, a bloody slaughter stained both land and sea, and discord arose. Thus, the peaceful and golden happiness of ancient ages was changed.

Therefore, our predecessors, being greatly desirous of peace and concord, viewing with mournful minds these evils occurring in this kingdom, lamented these anxieties with sad groans. They sought God with assiduous prayer to be merciful and change the state of this Kingdom for the better. Finally, seeing that those who are the leaders and pastors of Christ's church—to whom the word of reconciliation was committed by Christ the true shepherd, that they might evangelize the peace of the church with "beautiful feet" <note>A biblical reference to Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15: "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace."</note>—had so insolently removed it, they began to strongly distrust them. They rightfully withdrew from such prelates, who were falsely infatuated and had neither washed away the shameful insults with which they were obscenely branded nor publicly purged themselves before the common people with sufficient satisfaction. 

And unless tedious length prevents it, we would bring for your Moderation's viewing and reading all the obscene insults of the prelates, the hostile calumnies, and the wicked accusations that they ignominiously vomited at one another, briefly recorded in letters. If you have a desire to have them, we are ready to provide them. These are truly the ones who, contaminated and ruined by their own crimes, strive not only to condemn us but also to unjustly slander us and brand us with heresy before your Majesty. 

We earnestly beseech you, by the grace of God and heaven and justice, that you do not give credit to such trifles of theirs. Indeed, we testify before the living God, who will judge the world in equity, that we have never been found to assert or babble anything heretical or blasphemous, neither against God, nor against the orthodox faith, nor against the Eucharist—the body and blood of Christ—nor finally against the Blessed Virgin, nor at all against the saints of God. If a stubborn opinion cannot be torn away and exploded from you by this confession of ours, and if it displeases you to show favor to our congregation, do this at least for the sake of justice, which every innocent person eagerly invokes: make it so that someone may kindly show you where we have ever spoken or done anything of this kind.

They conclude by testifying to their own orthodoxy regarding the Eucharist, the Virgin Mary, and the saints.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of the Brethren (Waldensians) against accusations of heresy. Having previously criticized the corruption of the Roman clergy, the text now turns to a specific defense of their core beliefs: the Trinity and the nature of the Eucharist (Holy Communion), clarifying their stance on the "Real Presence" of Christ and the role of their own ministers.</meta>

# OF THE WALDENSIANS,

...and should approve anything impious or irreligious concerning the Eucharist of Christ, the immaculate Virgin, and the blessed saints that might have been confessed by us; since we are conscious of none of these accusations with which we are frequently blamed. For indeed, concerning God—God himself—and in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we have rightly believed as being of one simple essence and triune in persons. 

Our Apology, which we sent to your Magnificence long ago, clearly shows this; furthermore, the charitable fulfillment of God’s commandments is a certain and ineffable proof that we hold and follow the orthodox faith, for the sake of which we patiently endure all these hardships and adversities. With equal belief concerning the catholic <note>In this context, "catholic" refers to the "universal" Christian church as described in the ancient creeds, which the Brethren claimed to represent more faithfully than the Roman institution.</note> church and its sacraments—especially concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ—we believe fully. For since a rightly ordained priest has expressed the words of Christ’s testimony, immediately the bread is the true, natural body of Christ, taken from the most chaste Virgin, which was to be surrendered, just as the Living Bread testifies: "This is," he says, "my body which is given for you." Similarly, the wine is the blood of his natural body, which was to be shed for the remission of sins for many. 

And we not only believe and confess the bread to be the natural body and the wine to be the natural blood sacramentally, but we also assert that the bread is likewise a spiritual body and the wine a spiritual blood. At the same time, the opinion of the Apostle Paul supports us in this belief: "The bread," he says, "which we break, is it not the participation in the body of Christ? And the cup which we bless, is it not the communication of the blood of Christ? Since we, though many, are one bread and one body, who participate in one bread and one cup." 

At the same time, we confess that this sacrament, according to Christ’s institution and his command, and finally by the example of the primitive Church, ought to be distributed and received under the twin species of elements <note>original: *sub gemina rerum specie*. This refers to "Communion in both kinds"—giving both the bread and the wine to the laity, a practice the Roman Church had largely restricted to priests at this time.</note>. And this we hold from faith and the necessity of the salvation ordained through the Son of God, because the soul-saving dignity of both truths consists in the substance, which must be represented by the sacrament for the sake of conscience and hope.

Furthermore, since many men by no means deign to accept this profession of our faith as true, rashly scrutinizing the depths of our hearts, they say that we confess with our mouth those things which have never dwelt in our heart. These people indeed bring a manifest injury against us before God, to whom the direction and simplicity of our heart is manifest and open; for our tongue dares to produce nothing other than what our heart has suggested. 

Others then, because we do not receive the sacraments from priests of the Roman ordination, judge us for that reason to be unfaithful. These people are surely ignorant that we have our own priests, by whom we, having been rightly instituted, obtain the sacrament. We indeed reject others <note>The Roman Catholic priests.</note> for this reason: that they minister the sacraments for a purpose other than what Christ intended, just as the works of their ministry, which are against the faith, openly prove. 

Similarly, for this reason we are not believed: because that which was commanded us by Christ the Author to observe, we do only that toward the sacrament; and where less has been commanded, in that we conduct ourselves accordingly. Indeed, the Redeemer of men commanded us to believe, to receive, and to eat, and by that very act to make a memory of his benefits; but to worship the sacramental substance of Christ’s body and blood is no command given to believers. For Christ gave it to the disciples as they reclined to be used, and obeying him, they ate and drank without worship of the same sacrament. 

Furthermore, the Apostles and their successors, walking through the homes of the faithful over a long interval of time and breaking bread, received it with joy. These surely exhibited no such veneration to the sacrament, and those who did so were by no means in error, nor were they called heretics. Rather, they worshiped the personal presence of Christ at the right hand of the Highest Father. For this reason, true worshipers of the divine majesty have been commanded by both Testaments—the Old and the New—to worship Christ, true God and man, not in his sacramental existence, but in his natural and personal subsistence...

## CONFESSION,

...natural body <note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page: that Christ's natural body is at the right hand of God.</note> at the right hand of his Father to be cherished and adored is surely an ancient testimony, which he, the vanquisher of the tempting Satan, remembered. "It is written," he said, "You shall adore the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve." <note>original: "Scriptum est... dominum deum tuum adorabis, & illi soli servies" — Matthew 4:10.</note> Truly, the "chosen vessel" <note>A common title for the Apostle Paul.</note> explains this further, saying that for this reason God also exalted him and gave him a name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is at the right hand of God the Father. The Incarnate Truth <note>Referring to Christ himself.</note> corroborates this very thing, saying that just as men honor the Father, so should they honor the Son. Indeed, no one here venerates the Father as a creature, but as being in heaven, as the prayer issued by Christ testifies: "Our Father," he says, "who art in heaven." The teacher of the Gentiles <note>The Apostle Paul.</note> emulates this in his own way, saying: "I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." Therefore, whoever venerates the Son is doing so with equal honor and worship as they do the Father. We are admonished to do this for a specific reason: although Christ, while living on earth, did not compel men to worship him here as one worthy of honor, he nevertheless desired his glorification with his Father in heaven—which he declared he had before the foundation of the world—so that he might be acknowledged by true worshipers to reside there after his ascension, and be adored there. 

Truly, if any contend that it is otherwise, both Testaments prohibit them from doing so. For there is the ancient prohibition: "You shall not make," says God, "for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of those things that are in heaven, nor on the earth, nor in the waters. You shall not adore them nor worship them." <note>original: "Non facies... sculptile." — Exodus 20:4-5.</note> Furthermore, a new prohibition was spoken by Christ the Lawgiver: "Many will come," he said, "and will say, 'Here is Christ,' or 'There.' Do not believe it, nor go out, nor follow them," <note>original: "Hic est christus aut illic. ne creditis..." — Matthew 24:23.</note> because he is never going to descend personally in his natural substance except for the Judgment. The catholic <note>In the sense of "universal."</note> faith approves this sentiment with these words: "He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, from there he shall come to judge the living and the dead." Therefore, Most Gracious King, it is clear to all that we believe and act no differently than Christ’s commandment admonishes us to believe and act, as the examples of the primitive church confirm.

Moreover, by a similar covenant, O most gracious moderator of this kingdom, we believe—and shall firmly believe until the end of our lives—concerning the most chaste Virgin Mary, that she was chosen by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and full of grace, to the end that she might be the immaculate mother of the Incarnate Word. For in her most chaste womb, the Son of the Most High, true God, united human nature—without the stain of vice—through the work of the <term>nourishing Spirit</term> <note>original: "pneumatis almi," a poetic term for the Holy Spirit.</note> into his one person. In the chaste hall of her womb, true God and man personally dwelt, and from her he came forth into the light of this world. By nursing him, she performed the remaining works of upbringing toward him. This most chosen Virgin, just as she was before the incarnation of the Son of God, so also during that time and afterward until death, never knew a man, but remained integral and chaste in both mind and body in perpetual virginity. 

Indeed, the order of our salvation required this. For just as the deception of perdition was perpetrated in paradise through a virgin <note>Referring to Eve, who was traditionally considered a virgin before the Fall.</note>, so also the restoration of salvation should be consummated in virginity. And finally, just as the <term>first-formed man</term> <note>original: "prothoplastus," referring to Adam.</note> was placed in the garden of delights and fashioned by God alone in innocence and purity, so also it was fitting for the Son of God to assume a sincere nature, set apart from vice and the law of sin. Rightly, for this reason, the Virgin is called most full of grace and sanctified in her nature, so that from her most honorable nature the Supreme Word might put on humanity through a mystic breath, and at the same time dwell in her as if in a most excellent bridal chamber, resting above all mortals. These surely are those "great things" of which she spoke to the elderly Elizabeth: "He who is mighty," she said, "has done great things for me, and holy is his name." <note>The "Magnificat" from Luke 1:49.</note> Finally, just as man fell through disobedience into the penalty of death and various calamities, this Sacred Breath deigned to remain in the woman of virginal modesty. This very thing the Son of God wished to assume from the uncontaminated Virgin, so that he might complete our redemption. For this reason, not only from the faith of the Sacred Scriptures concerning the Mother...

# OF THE WALDENSIANS.

...we are compelled to believe in the integrity of Christ <note>The text likely refers to the "integrity" or perpetual virginity of Mary in relation to Christ's birth.</note>. But we are also bound to hold this very thing by the sense of true faith: that it was impossible for that most glorious mother, on account of the mystery of human redemption, ever to be deprived of her integrity at any time until her death. Regarding the unimpaired Virgin Mary, the divine scriptures also command us to believe what they urge must be believed, and what the children of the church truly believed before now; we also now believe and profess this with equal faith. 

Truly, whatever vain men superstitiously believe to the contrary—against the truth of the faith and the mandates of the Most High—we in no way dare to believe that concerning her, or the saints of God, or other works of piety. Indeed, we believe we satisfy the requirements of a living faith when, believing and thinking of her in this way, we confess her blessedness alongside every faithful nation. We also observe and obey her, especially in that instance where she admonishes us to obey her son, saying: "Whatever he says to you, do it." <note>original: "quodcunq; inquit dixerit vobis, facite" — John 2:5. The Waldensians emphasize Mary's role as one who points toward Christ's authority.</note>

Next, O Magnificent King, receive now our thoughts regarding what we feel concerning the saints of God. We pronounce that person to be a saint who has attained the grace of God through the merit of Christ and the shedding of his innocent blood, as well as the gifts of the favors of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "pneumatis almi" — a Latinized Greek phrasing for the Holy Spirit.</note>—namely, of unfeigned faith, charity, and true hope—and who has persevered in these very virtues until death. Furthermore, we profess from faith that those who have the specific testimony of the divine scriptures are most certainly saints; regarding others, however, there is more hope or opinion than certainty. Therefore, believing in the saints as the truth of the divine scriptures dictates, we—founded upon that truth—honor, love, follow, and emulate the blessed ones of God with fitting worship.

Thus, by this our profession, O most just King, it is evident that we are not heretics, since we have stubbornly held no dogma contrary to Holy Scripture. Nor, finally, have we ever been the inventors or authors of evil things, since all our study and every vigilant effort of ours is to believe and perform whatever the catholic <note>Here, "catholic" is used in its original sense of "universal" or "true" Christian faith, rather than specifically the Roman Catholic Church.</note> faith teaches and the examples of the lovers of God <note>term: <term>philotheorū</term> (from the Greek 'philotheos') refers to those who love God or live a contemplative, godly life.</note> have urged. For this reason, we greatly pray to your Clarity <note>A formal title for the King.</note> that you do not allow our slanderers to rage against us to such an extent that they, by their cruel power, cruelly force us into those very things about which we cannot think rightly—which they claim are divine, but which we judge to be discordant with the truth. 

For Christ the Lord, the author of salvation, compelled no man of free will to accept his soul-saving salvation so that it might be believed; rather, so that he might appear more acceptable, pleasing, and certain to them, he enticed them to believe through miracles and worthy wonders, and likewise through kind and gentle speech. Therefore, the men of this age ought to drive others less toward those things which flesh and blood have devised; for unless something is voluntary, it cannot be stable or firm. 

Moreover, we are not the kind of men who, being stubbornly obstinate, refuse to yield to the soul-saving truth; rather, we have always been found ready for every will of God that has clearly presented itself to us. Indeed, your Majesty can hold this as evident proof regarding us: since in this present distress we strive to practice the recognized truth of Christ, we do not fear to voluntarily offer even this fleeting life to the risk of a dangerous death for the sake of attaining such salvific truth. Surely, if we lived in liberty with a more abundant prospect of Christ's will, we would be found even more ready to fulfill it. 

Therefore, knowing our soul to be such in all these matters, we humbly implore your grace that you might deign to have compassion on us as faithful subjects, and that you do not hasten to deliver us into the dire hands of our enemies. For they, according to the laws of humanity explained in the Gospel of Christ and duly observed by the ancient men of the church, will by no means bring about a reformation for us; rather, they will plot to compel our consciences toward the left <note>In this context, "to the left" implies a path of error or sinister intent.</note> by their cruel force, which pertains very little to salvation. Furthermore, if you will not temper the decree of your mind issued in your letters, nothing else remains for us in such a matter except to turn to the God of piety...

# A TREATISE BY AUGUSTINE OF OLOMOUC, DOCTOR OF ARTS AND DECREES, TO THE LEARNED MASTER JOHN NIGRUS, PHYSICIAN, CONCERNING THE SECT OF THE WALDENSIANS: THE OFFICE OF PREACHING IS NOT PERMITTED TO EVERYONE EVERYWHERE IN THE CHURCH.

While traveling over the bridge <note>original: "Super p̃stannũ" – likely referring to the bridge at Písek or a specific crossing in the region.</note>, when I had stopped in the suburbs and was marveling at the many houses recently built and furnished there, I began to ask one of the bystanders who these people were who had constructed such a numerous structure in so short a time as I could see. He replied to me: "The Waldensian brothers, whom the common people call <term>Pighards</term> <note>A derogatory term used for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren, possibly derived from "Beghards."</note>." Soon my mind turned to you, for our friend Slechta had told me not long ago that you had moved there. I asked if you had also settled there; he nodded and even pointed out a certain house where you lived. At this, as if struck by a bad omen, I began to fear that you also had been devoted to that sect. 

Believe me, when I was soon made more certain of this, I grieved quite vehemently that a man otherwise upright and simple should be entangled and snared, as if by birdlime, in the danger of this infamous heresy, and should have defected from the orthodox religion of Christ to that <insert>false</insert> holiness which that impious common folk puts on. For from the time I knew you in Litomyšl <note>original: "Lytomissl"</note>, I was so drawn by your virtue and that simplicity of mind that whenever mention of you arose, I was never able to pass you by without some honorable remark. This was especially true when I happened upon the books of Saint Jerome <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) and defending orthodoxy.</note> placed on your shelf among other good ecclesiastical authors. For I thought that with him alone as your guide, you would never stumble into those things that usually occur as doubts in the faith. I believed that whatever error might fall upon you—whether by the suggestion of the devil, who is often accustomed to transform himself into an angel of light, or by the persuasion of those wicked men—it would all be ruined by the writings of Jerome. 

After all, you would know through him how many heresies were conquered, how many clouds of error were dispersed as if by a clearer light, and how many enemies of the faith, who were making a noise against the Church with their gathered troops, were scattered and crushed. Yet Jerome, although he possessed the most vivid intellect—being the one who restored both the Old and New Testaments to us—never dared to affirm anything against what the universal Holy Church felt, nor did he strive to introduce anything new through rash presumption, as we see these rude and impious men of your profession doing now. For while they hold nothing except a certain "surface" of the Sacred Scripture, they establish everything according to their own judgment. They rashly define all the most difficult things in the scriptures just "as they come to the mouth" <note>An idiom meaning to speak without thinking or speaking recklessly.</note>. While pretending to imitate the life of the Apostles under the pretext of hospitality, they study nothing but avarice and the amassing of wealth. 

They are like the Scribes and Pharisees: "straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel" <note>original: "culicẽ liquãtes & camelũ glutiẽtes" — a reference to Matthew 23:24, accusing them of hypocrisy.</note>. They despise the magistrates because they are found unfit to hold those offices themselves. They blame friendships and social circles because, being accustomed to rustic labors, they have no knowledge of liberal studies or honorable pleasure. Here someone—not as the satirical poet says of a "troop of Centurions," but from the dregs of the shoemakers or tanners—assumes the office of a preacher. He wanders through every rank and grade, and with a certain censorious brow, he preaches that all things are profane, all things are polluted, and full of deadly poison. He does not notice that by both divine and ecclesiastical prohibition, the office of preaching is granted only to a few...

Augustine argues that the Waldensians are uneducated laypeople who misinterpret scripture and illegitimately claim the right to preach.</summary>
