<meta>This page continues Augustine of Olomouc's polemical letter to the physician John Nigrus. In the previous section, Augustine described encountering a Waldensian community; here, he begins his formal theological argument against their practice of lay preaching and secret meetings, citing papal authority and scripture to defend the established hierarchy of the Church.</meta>

OF THE WALDENSIANS.

...sent. Please read, I pray, what Lucius <note>Refers to Pope Lucius III (reigned 1181–1185), who issued the decree *Ad abolendam*, which excommunicated various heretical groups, including the Waldensians, for preaching without episcopal authority.</note> writes concerning this. "Although," he says, "the desire to understand the divine scriptures and the zeal for encouraging others according to them is not to be reproached but rather commended, nevertheless in this certain laymen appear who are deservedly to be rebuked, because they hold secret assemblies, usurp the office of preaching for themselves, mock the simplicity of priests, and despise the company of those who do not adhere to such things." 

For God is the true light who enlightens every man coming into this world; He hates the works of darkness so much that when He was about to send His apostles into the whole world to preach the gospel to every creature, He commanded them, saying clearly: "What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops." <note>original: "Quod dico vobis in tenebris dicite in lucē. & qđ in aure auditis. sup tecta p̄dicate." — Matthew 10:27.</note> And further: For just as there are many members of the body, yet all do not have the same function, so there are many orders in the Church, but not all have the same office. Because, according to the Apostle: "The Lord gave some to be apostles, some prophets, and others teachers," and so forth. <note>original: "Alios dñs dedit apostolos. alios pphetas. alios aut doctores." — Ephesians 4:11.</note> 

Since, therefore, the order of teachers is, as it were, principal in the Church, no one ought to indifferently usurp for himself the office of preaching. For according to the Apostle: "How shall they preach unless they are sent?" <note>original: "q̃modo p̄dicabūt nisi mittant?" — Romans 10:15.</note> Since this same Paul affirms that he was sent not to baptize but to preach, and Truth itself <note>A common medieval title for Christ.</note> commanded the apostles: "Pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into His harvest." 

But if perhaps someone should shrewdly respond that such people are sent invisibly by God (even if they are not sent visibly by man), since an invisible mission is much worthier than a visible one, and the divine is far better than the human, it can be reasonably answered that since that interior mission is hidden, it is not enough for anyone merely to assert "nakedly" that he himself is sent by God—since any heretic could claim this. Instead, it is necessary that he prove that invisible mission by the performance of a miracle or a special testimony of scripture. 

Hence, when the Lord wanted to send Moses into Egypt to the children of Israel, so that they might believe he was sent by Him, He gave him a sign: that he should turn his rod into a serpent and then restore the rod again. John the Baptist also offered a special testimony of his mission from scripture, saying: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord," as the prophet Isaiah says. <note>original: "Ego vox clamātis in deserto dirigite viā dñio sicut ait Isaias ppheta." — John 1:23; Isaiah 40:3.</note>

You see, my brother, by the testimony of sacred scripture, how blameworthy those are who, in your synagogues and secret assemblies, rashly arrogant to themselves the office of preaching; and chattering in corners, they dread to come forward into the light according to the evangelical precept—daily forging new heresies, having indeed different faces, but their tails tied together <note>A reference to Judges 15:4. In medieval commentary, this symbolized heretics who might differ in their specific errors (different faces) but were united in their intent to destroy the harvest of the Church (tails tied together with torches).</note>. 

Therefore, so that I might, according to my ability, release you from being entangled in these errors and win the soul of a brother from the precipice of sin, I have resolved to write this letter to you, my dear John. I shall touch especially upon those matters in which you seem most to stumble: namely, in the rite of ecclesiastical ceremonies, the administration of orders, the feast days and intercessions of the saints, the pains of purgatory, and the images of the saints. In these matters, I will not follow that customary scholastic manner of debating both sides, but rather that continuous thread and fabric of discourse in which I think you are more often engaged, and which I myself am accustomed to hold more familiar; so that, according to the sentiment of Jerome, the threads of words may run in a simple warp, and the texture of the apostolic speech may grow under a pure weft. Come then, read with an even mind what I have written out of charity.

# IT IS NECESSARY THAT THERE BE HERESIES IN THE CHURCH

Considering how they have been accustomed to arise, and how dangerous, varied, and inconsistent the heresy of the Waldensians is, Paul, the "Vessel of Election" <note>A traditional title for St. Paul, based on Acts 9:15.</note>, considering that the devil would most especially attack the minds of the faithful in those things which belong to faith, said it was necessary for heresies to occur in the church so that those who are faithful might be proven. Hence also in the Gospel, our Savior, when He had said that the Apostles would be sought out by the devil in various ways, turned to Peter and said: "And I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail." For He knew that faith...

<meta>This page continues the polemic of Augustine of Olomouc against the Bohemian Brethren and Waldensians. In the preceding section, he challenged the legitimacy of lay preaching. Here, he shifts his focus to the philosophical and theological dangers of departing from the unified faith of the Roman Church, comparing the splintering of sects to the many heads of the mythical Hydra.</meta>

### SAINT AUGUSTINE AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...is the foundation of all virtues, by which the just man shall live, and through the virtuous performance of his labors, he ought to hope for a heavenly reward and perpetual recompense. Therefore, nothing more destructive can be found for mortal man than when, wandering from the path of faith, he begins to walk through the byways of error and is wrapped in the veils of differing opinions. 

From this, indeed, as many heads of error spring up daily as were once born on that Herculean Hydra <note>The Hydra was a many-headed serpent from Greek mythology; when Hercules cut off one head, two grew back in its place. Augustine uses this as a metaphor for how one heresy leads to many others.</note> in the mythical stories of the Greeks. For what cause should we believe lies beneath the fact that so many new sects have arisen in Bohemia and Moravia? It is because they began to oppose the universal custom of Christ's faithful in the practice of the communion of the most holy body and blood of Christ <note>This refers to the "Utraquist" controversy in Bohemia, where reformers insisted that the laity should receive both the bread and the wine (sub utraque specie) during the Eucharist, contrary to the Catholic practice of the time.</note>. Because of this, we have heard of so many wars perpetrated and see so many sacred places overturned in ruins even to this day. 

Yet now, that fervor has cooled down to such an extent that the things for which they were previously accustomed to fight with all their might are now clearly seen to be held in mockery and contempt. This is because new and even more dangerous heresies have arisen, so that now—by the faith of the gods above!—they cast aside all sacraments. Retaining only the name of "Christian," they wander away from ecclesiastical ritual, as it pleases each one, into the sects of those ancient people. In these calamitous times, nearly as many sects are found as there are heads. 

Minds are now so badly occupied by this zeal that nothing more pleasant can happen to them than to stumble upon some book from which they can introduce a destructive dogma or adapt some small sentence to support their own views, as if bringing it into their own family. Such are the things that Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian advisor to Constantine. His writings against pagan idols were often cited by later reformers to justify the destruction of religious images (iconoclasm).</note> discussed regarding the making of images and the establishing of altars and temples. I greatly fear that, just as they are carried away by a wandering and inconstant religion in these matters, they might cast off the name of Christian and fall into the school of Epicurus (who removed divine providence), or Pythagoras (who called the gods into doubt), or Diagoras (who completely and utterly excluded the gods and providence). 

And from where does this come? It is because, as I said, once an error is admitted, it is difficult to emerge from it. We do not see this in the Italians (though they excel in almost divine genius), nor in the Gauls, Germans, Danes, Spanish, or six hundred other nations, languages, and peoples. For these, sailing under the single banner of the Cross, do not easily fall into the wind of any error. But as the Roman Pontiff, the Vicar of Christ, holds the helm, they all emerge into the single harbor of salvation by the breathing of Christ. 

For this is that ark which once received the clean and the unclean; this is the dragnet filled with every kind of fish, representing the ancient type of the Church, which is gathered from both good and bad in the unity of faith, so that in the final just judgment, it may decree rewards for the good and eternal punishments for the bad. 

Therefore, placed in this world as if in a salt sea, we can promise ourselves nothing from our own merits. Yet men of your profession <note>The "profession" refers to the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren to whom the author is writing.</note> dare to promise this to themselves—not from faith, but from their own good works in which they think they abound. They seem to demand God's justice, not weighing that saying of the Apostle Paul: "Everything that is not of faith is sin." <note>original: "Om̄e q̄d nō ē ex fide, peccatū ē" — Romans 14:23.</note> And again: "Not by the works of justice which we have done, but according to His great mercy He saved us." <note>original: "Nō ex opibꝰ iustitiæ q̄ facimꝰ sed ex magna dei misericordia saluos nos fieri" — Titus 3:5.</note> For the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us. <note>original: "Nō sunt em̄ cōdigne passiones huiꝰ feculi ad futurā gloriā q̄ reuelāda est in nobis." — Romans 8:18.</note> 

But we, living primarily by faith—if we do not boast of our works to God like that Pharisee, yet being conscious of our sins like the Publican—each of us standing afar off says: "God, be merciful to me a sinner." <note>original: "Deus ꝑpicius esto mihi peccatori." — Luke 18:13. Augustine is contrasting the perceived "spiritual pride" of the reformers with the humility of the Catholic faithful.</note> Unless perhaps you say that you have a more proven faith because you strive to perform such good works. Behold, therefore, how like that Pharisee you preach your own righteousnesses, while you point out and despise our works like those of the Publicans, claiming that nothing holy can proceed from us because we are polluted, impious, and sacrilegious—as if God had established the men who rule over us not as fragile men, but as angels and sinless beings. 

But what, I ask, is the quality of your faith? It follows no judgment, but allows each individual to fabricate new opinions daily as they become more clever. One believes that the true God and man are contained under the appearance of bread; another immediately [calls] this...

b. 5.
### AUGUSTINE AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...argues. He even dares to worship a god made of vegetation <note>original: "herbaceumque deum." A derogatory reference to the Waldensian/Hussite view of the Eucharist, implying they worship common bread rather than the literal body of Christ.</note>—oh, unexpiable crime! Oh, intolerable opinion of blasphemous men! To think that the holy, immaculate Faith, kept safe and whole through so many centuries of the most holy and learned men, is now being picked apart by the filthiest shoemakers <note>In the 15th and 16th centuries, "shoemaker" was a common slur used by the educated elite against lay preachers and reformers who lacked formal university training.</note>. That which was held in exceptional worship and veneration by kings and princes is now disregarded by the most foul slaves and called into question once more. Who, I ask, could bear this with a calm mind? Who could hear it with an unoffended ear? 

Saint Jerome says that many monsters have been birthed into the world: we read in the book of Isaiah of Centaurs and Sirens, Owls and Bitterns <note>original: "Onocrotalos," a water bird mentioned in the Vulgate Bible, often interpreted as a pelican or bittern.</note>; Job described the Leviathan and Behemoth in mystical speech. The fables of the poets tell of Cerberus, the Stymphalian birds, the Erymanthian Boar, the Nemean Lion, the Chimera, and the many-headed Hydra. Virgil describes Cacus, and the Spaniards spoke of the three-formed Geryon. Yet no monster so strange can be imagined that this class of men does not now produce. For here you will see Nestorians, Arians, Marcionites, Pelagians, Novatians, and Waldensians—men of whatever infamous and diabolical names once existed. And yet they do not fear to call themselves Christians, even as they break the harmony of that holy name and never cease, with various arguments, to tear the seamless tunic of Christ <note>A common metaphor for the unity of the Church, referring to the garment of Jesus that the Roman soldiers refused to tear at the Crucifixion.</note> with their new inventions.

Yet if they are even slightly corrected for these things, you fly into a rage, you cry out, and you do not fear to openly and constantly assert that they have been unjustly punished. This was recently seen in the case of the one from your school in Olomouc <note>The author's home city in Moravia, a center of Catholic resistance against the Hussite and Brethren movements.</note> who was beaten with rods for his irreverence toward the Most Holy Eucharist. Believe me, that was not cruelty, but piety. You have read of Peter’s "cruelty" toward Ananias and Sapphira, or again, Paul’s toward Elymas, whom he condemned to eternal blindness. Indeed, it is written: *If your brother, or your friend, or the wife in your bosom wishes to turn you away from the truth, let your hand be upon them and shed their blood, and you shall take away the evil from the midst of Israel.* <note>A paraphrase of Deuteronomy 13:6-9, used here to justify the corporal and capital punishment of heretics.</note> Behold how, for the cause of the faith, we are commanded even to shed blood!

It is necessary, therefore, that there be some judge in the Church and an apostolic tribunal that may both instruct those in error and, with just aversion, chastise those who obstinately persevere in heresy. For as Aeneas Silvius <note>Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, who became Pope Pius II (1458–1464). He was a prolific writer and a staunch opponent of the Bohemian reformers.</note> writes most elegantly and truly: "There is no scripture so clear or so fitting that it cannot be twisted into different meanings." All the schisms that have grown from the beginning of the rising Church until now have drawn their origin from the sacred books themselves. 

But God knew this would happen. Therefore, when He gave the Law to the people of Israel through His servant Moses, He described in a clear sequence what should be followed and what should be avoided. Yet, knowing there would be those who would apply discordant meanings to His law, and looking out for future generations, He established a supreme tribunal on earth to which the "greater cases" <note>term: "causas maiores" — a legal concept in Canon Law referring to important matters that can only be judged by the highest authority, usually the Pope.</note> and all doubts concerning the law should be brought. As God says in Deuteronomy: *If you perceive a judgment to be difficult and ambiguous between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and leprosy, and you see that the words of judgment vary within your gates: rise up and go to the place which the Lord your God shall choose. And you shall come to the priests of the Levite race, and to the judge who is there at that time, and you shall ask them, and they shall judge for you the truth of the judgment. And you shall do whatever they say who preside over the place which the Lord has chosen... and you shall not decline to the right hand or the left. But he who acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priest who ministers at that time to the Lord your God, and the decree of the judge, that man shall die, and you shall take away the evil from Israel.* <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 17:8-12.</note> 

In this way, the Lord gave commands to the followers of the Old Testament, so that no one, seduced by his own opinion, could divide the people or introduce foreign religions. Nor did Christ the Lord, the founder of the New Law, the master of truth and the inventor of salvation, omit this supreme refuge of a tribunal. For He chose Peter, and in Peter the other bishops of the Roman See who, after His ascension into heaven...

...that faith is the foundation of all virtues, by which the just man might live, and from which he ought to hope for a heavenly reward and eternal wages for his labors through virtuous action. Therefore, nothing more destructive can be found for a mortal man than when, wandering away from the faith, he begins to walk through the devious paths of error, wrapped in the coverings of conflicting opinions. For from this source, so many "heads" of errors are born daily, just like that Herculean Hydra <note>The multi-headed serpent of Greek mythology; when one head was cut off, two grew back. Augustine uses this to describe how suppressing one heresy often leads to the birth of many more.</note> once said to be reborn in the fables of the Greeks. For what cause should we believe lies beneath the so many new sects that have arisen in Bohemia and Moravia? It is because they began to oppose themselves to the universal custom of Christ's faithful regarding the use of the communion of the sacrosanct body and blood of Christ. Because of this, we have heard of so many wars perpetrated, and we see even to this day the manifest ruins of so many destroyed shrines. 

Yet now, that initial fervor has cooled so much that those things for which they previously used to fight with all their might, they now see held openly in mockery and contempt. New and even more dangerous heresies have arisen, so that now—by the faith of the gods! <note>original: "proh superum fidem!" A classical Latin exclamation of shock or outrage.</note>—they cast away all the sacraments. Retaining only the name of "Christian," they wander away from ecclesiastical ritual into the sects of those ancient people, however it pleases them. In these calamitous times, nearly as many sects are found as there are heads of people. Indeed, the minds of almost everyone are now so badly occupied by this zeal that nothing more pleasant can happen to them than to stumble upon some book from which they can introduce a destructive dogma, or to find some little scrap of a sentence to adapt to their own family of beliefs to prove what they feel. Such are the things that Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author. Augustine suggests the heretics are misusing his writings on idols to justify their own iconoclasm.</note> discussed regarding the making of idols and the establishing of altars and temples. I greatly fear that, just as they are carried away in these and other matters by a wandering and inconstant religion, they might even cast off the name of Christian and fall into the school of Epicurus <note>A philosopher often unfairly characterized as an atheist or purely a materialist in the Middle Ages.</note>, who did away with providence, or Pythagoras, who called the gods into doubt, or Diagoras <note>Known as "the Atheist" of Melos (5th century BC).</note>, who excluded the gods and providence entirely. 

And from where does this come? It is because, as I said, once an error is admitted, it is difficult to emerge from it. We do not see this among the Italians, though they excel in almost divine genius; nor among the French, the Germans, the Danes <note>original: "Dacis." In Renaissance Latin, this typically referred to the people of Denmark.</note>, the Spaniards, and a hundred other nations, languages, and peoples. For these, sailing under the single banner of the Cross, do not easily catch the wind of any error. Instead, as the Roman Pontiff, the Vicar of Christ, has held the tiller, they all emerge into the one harbor of salvation with Christ’s breathing. For this is that Ark <note>A reference to Noah's Ark as a symbol for the Church, containing both "clean and unclean."</note> which once received the clean and the unclean; this is the dragnet <note>original: "sagena." Referring to the parable of the net in Matthew 13:47.</note> filled with every kind of fish, which long ago bore the type of the Church, gathered from the good and the bad in the unity of faith, so that in the final just judgment it might decree rewards for the good and eternal punishments for the bad. 

Therefore, placed in this world as if in a certain sea, we can promise ourselves nothing from our own merits. Yet the men of your profession dare to promise this to themselves—men who seem to demand the justice of God not from faith, but from their own good works in which they think they abound. They do not weigh that saying of the Apostle Paul: *Everything that is not from faith is sin.* <note>Romans 14:23.</note> and again: *Not from the works of justice which we have done, but according to His great mercy He saved us.* <note>Titus 3:5.</note> For the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared to the future glory which shall be revealed in us. But we, living primarily by faith, do not throw our works in God's face like that Pharisee; instead, with the Publican <note>Referring to the parable in Luke 18:9-14. The Pharisee boasted of his deeds, while the Publican (tax collector) asked for mercy.</note>, being conscious of our sins, we each say, standing far off: *God, be merciful to me, a sinner.* 

Unless, perhaps, you say that you have a more proven faith because you strive to make progress with such good works. Behold, then, how you preach your "justices" like that Pharisee, while you despise our works as those of the Publican, asserting that nothing holy can come from us because we are "polluted, impious, and sacrilegious"—as if God had established the men who lead us not as fragile human beings, but as impeccable angels. Truly, I ask you, what kind of faith is yours, which you manufacture daily without any judgment, based on the opinions of every clever person among you? One believes that the true God and man is contained under the appearance of bread; another soon [calls] this idolatry...

...argues. And he contends that this "grassy god" <note>original: "herbaceumque deum." This likely refers to a heretical or simplified view of the Eucharist, or perhaps a derogatory reference to the nature of the elements.</note> is to be worshipped—O inexpiable crime! Who, I ask, could bear this with a calm mind? Who could hear it with an unoffended ear? 

Saint Jerome says that many monsters have been born in the world: we read of Centaurs and Sirens, Owls and Bitterns <note>original: "Onocrotalos" - pelicans or similar birds, often used in medieval bestiaries to symbolize desolation.</note> in Isaiah; Job described Leviathan and Behemoth in mystical speech; the fables of poets tell of Cerberus and the Stymphalian birds, the Erymanthian Boar, the Nemean Lion, the Chimera, and the many-headed Hydra; Virgil describes Cacus, and Spain produced the triple-formed Geryon. Yet if they are corrected even slightly for these things, you become exasperated, you cry out, and you do not fear to assert openly and constantly that those corrected were treated unjustly—as was recently seen in the case of one from your school in Olomouc who was beaten with rods for irreverence toward the most holy Eucharist.

For as Eneas Silvius <note>Enea Silvio Piccolomini (1405–1464), later Pope Pius II, a major intellectual figure of the era.</note> writes most elegantly and truly: "No scripture is so clear or so fitting that it cannot be twisted into different meanings." Therefore, when he gave the law to the people of Israel through his servant Moses, he described in a clear series what should be followed or avoided. Knowing, however, that there would be those who would apply discordant meanings to his law, intending to provide for the future age and place a barrier against heresies, he established a supreme tribunal on earth to which the greater cases and all doubts about the law should be brought.

You shall not decline from their sentence to the right or to the left. # CONFESSION,

...held the vicarate <note>The "vicarate" refers to the office of the Pope acting as the earthly representative or deputy of Christ.</note> and the first place in the church, when He promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven to him, as well as the power of binding and loosing, and finally committed to him the pasturing of the flock, saying: "Feed my sheep" <note>original: "Pasce oves meas."</note>. Why was this? Why was it then necessary for Peter to be made shepherd, to hold the keys of the kingdom, to receive the primacy, and to act as Christ’s vicar, if not to lead back those who wander, instruct the ignorant, strengthen the timid, cast out the obstinate, aid the faithful, and oppose the heretics? If we were all righteous and saw the truth by our own natural wit and followed it, there would be need of neither law nor prince; but because ruinous intellects arise who sow pestilential doctrines and pour out deadly poisons, killing gullible souls, the erection of a supreme tribunal was necessary to judge between "leprosy and leprosy" <note>A biblical metaphor from Deuteronomy 17:8 referring to making difficult legal or moral distinctions.</note>. This is the holy Roman and universal Church, which is the hinge <note>term: hinge (original: "cardo"). The word "cardinal" comes from this concept of the Church being the axis or hinge upon which the faith turns.</note> and head, the law and teacher of all things done in faith. But you, under the prince of darkness, do not cut back any thistles of error or thorns; rather, wherever they spring up, you allow them to grow far and wide daily, and having cast aside the sickle of reason, you support a weak strength and ruinous dogma. Therefore, so that you may more clearly behold the darkness of such errors, I ask that you receive with a calm mind the following account of the origin of the nascent and coalescing faith, recounted from a slightly deeper perspective.

## THE FAITH OF CHRIST WAS FIRST INSTITUTED BY THE APOSTLES AND their successors, and that Altars and Temples, and images of the saints, ought to be lawfully made in the Church,

When Christ the Lord was about to depart from this world, since He had not yet fully built up the newborn faith, He promised that He would shortly send the Paraclete <note>term: Paraclete (original: "paracletum"). A Greek-derived title for the Holy Spirit, meaning Counselor or Advocate.</note>, who would teach all truth and fully suggest what the disciples ought to do. For the Lord had left them an as-yet-imperfect law, which was to be first formed in the hearts of the apostles by the Holy Spirit, and then more fully declared to others through their preaching. For even Peter, as the Lord was ascending—as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 185–253 AD) known for his voluminous writings on theology.</note> proves—observed Jewish rites according to Moses, as one who had not yet thoroughly learned from Jesus how to cross over from the letter of the law to the law of the spirit, as we have learned from the Acts of the Apostles. 

On the following day, as they were traveling and approaching the city, Peter went up to the upper parts to pray around the sixth hour. When he became hungry, he wished to eat, but while they were preparing it, a trance fell upon him. He saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending like a great linen sheet let down by four corners from heaven to earth, in which were all the four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of the heaven. And a voice came to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat." Then he said: "Far be it, Lord; for I have never eaten anything common or unclean." And the voice spoke to him again a second time: "What God has purified, you must not call common"—that is, defiled. 

Note, therefore, how he preferred Jewish rites according to these sayings. Indeed, Peter was still observing what was clean and unclean; furthermore, it is shown from the following vision that he needed to be warned to communicate the words of faith to Cornelius (who was not an Israelite according to the flesh) and those who were with him. For up to that time, he lived as a Jew, holding to Jewish traditions and despising others who were outside the Jewish religion. No differently did Paul reveal this in the epistle he wrote to the Galatians: for before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision, and the rest of the Jews consented to his pretense, so that even Barnabas was led by them into that pretense. 

Behold, therefore, how the law of Christ began to be dispensed not so much by His own institution as by the observation of men and the tradition of the apostles, as soon as the Gospel began to be preached—the Holy Spirit teaching this, whom our Savior sent into the hearts of the apostles as promised. For He says in John: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, He will teach you all truth." For what could He have said to them that they were unable to bear, except that once the foundations were laid...

# ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS.

[He] left many things to be established in the Church for the disciples of salvation and their successors through the Holy Spirit, which are now seen to be introduced and instituted either for the worship of religion or for the observation of ceremonies; all of which, however, are despised by profane men <note>The author refers here to the Waldensians, a medieval Christian movement that advocated for poverty and often rejected the institutional Church’s rituals.</note> as if they were ridiculous. They assert that no temples ought to be built, since we ourselves are the temples of God, and God demands the worship of our heart more than the decoration of temples and walls. These arguments, I confess, have a certain color with which you might deceive an unlearned multitude; but the frivolous and foolish things they say are just as easily destroyed by stronger reasons. We know how much care God once took in the Old Law <note>The "Old Law" refers to the era of the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament before Christ.</note> concerning the construction and building of the temple, and what a selection of wood, stones, gems, tapestries, images, tables, and lampstands He desired in its decoration. Indeed, He wished to have no other architect but Himself, so that all things were constructed as He commanded, with the orders of ministers, Levites, priests, and high priests distributed, along with the ritual of sacrifices, the style of vestments, and the distinction of offerings. Did these things not bear the appearance of pride, and of a certain empty and mime-like vanity and pomp unbecoming of God? Yet, unless these were observed exactly as they were instituted, a present punishment soon followed, even if no one dared to overstep his ministry with a good intention—as we read concerning Dathan, Abiram, and Korah <note>Dathan, Abiram, and Korah were biblical figures who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron and were swallowed by the earth as punishment (Numbers 16).</note>. For when the censers were forged together by God’s command as an everlasting memorial for the children of Israel, it was so that no one who was not of the seed of Aaron should rashly thrust himself into such a ministry. 

And yet, as if all those things were detestable to God and not at all pleasing, the Psalmist David says: "I will not take calves, nor goats from your flocks. For shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats? Since all the wild beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High" <note>original: "vitulos, neq; de gregib⁹ tuis hircos... immola deo sacrificiū laudis." This is a paraphrase of Psalm 50 (Vulgate 49).</note>. These wretched men are ignorant that God commanded this material temple to be built so that He might demand the purity of our heart toward Him there, and that from a visible work He might kindle us toward the admirable beauty of His divinity. 

In the same way now, when the holy Catholic Church establishes temples and altars to Christ the Lord, and has introduced the rites of ceremonies through the Holy Spirit for the ministry of His most sacred body and blood, who of sound mind would dare to rebuke it by right? And because images of the saints are seen there, let no one presume that a cult of idolatry is being introduced. For we do not place them there so that we may worship them, or as if we think some divinity dwells in them—as the ancients once did for Jupiter, Apollo, or Neptune—for we know they are metals, wood, or stones. Rather, we are carried away toward the memory of God and the saints as if by an Archetype <note>term: Archetype (original: "Archetypo"). In this context, it means an original model or a symbolic representation that points the viewer toward the actual holy person in heaven.</note>. By a visible sign, we are repeatedly reminded of the glorious triumph which once-brave athletes of the faith bore away in signal victory. 

I know that you are accustomed to resist this by citing the prophet Baruch, who asserts that such idols were only forged for the luxury of priests; and Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian author; the writer suggests that while Lactantius argued against pagan idols, those arguments do not apply to Christian images.</note>, while still a "neophyte" (new convert) in the faith disputing against the gentiles, confirms that one should not look up to and venerate these playful and fragile figments of fingers, but rather God the creator. All these things would be true if we looked upon those images with such veneration as you imagine. But far be it from us to hand down such a thing—I will not say to do it, but not even to dream of it. For we know—to use the words of the divine Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great (d. 604) famously defended the use of images as the "books of the illiterate."</note>—that it is one thing to adore a picture, and another to learn from the history of the picture what is truly to be adored. For we do not, as Lactantius says, bring ointments, incense, and perfumes to decorated and grand statues, nor do we sacrifice rich and fat victims to them; for we would be fools, and more stupid than stone, wood, or oak. But seeing an image of God or some saint, we glorify God in His saints, and we receive from their signs a certain incitement toward virtue. This is similar to what Sallust <note>Sallust was a Roman historian. This anecdote illustrates that even pagans recognized the power of images to inspire moral behavior.</note> refers to having often heard: that Quintus Maximus, Publius Scipio, and other most famous men of the Roman Republic were accustomed to say that when they looked upon the images of their ancestors, their souls were most vehemently kindled toward virtue—though it was not that wax or that figure itself...

# CONFESSION,

...held the office of vicar <note>original: "vicariatū"</note> and the first place in the Church, when He promised him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the power of binding and loosing, and finally committed the pasturing of the flock to him, saying: "Feed my sheep." Why was this? Because it was then necessary for Peter to become the pastor, to hold the keys of the kingdom, to receive the primacy, and to act as the vicar of Christ, for no other reason than that he might bring back those who wander, instruct the ignorant, strengthen the timid, eliminate the stubborn, help the faithful, and resist heretics. If we were righteous and saw the truth by our own intellect and we all followed it, there would be no need for law or a prince. But because pernicious intellects arise who sow pestiferous doctrines, pour out lethal poisons, and kill credulous souls, the erection of a supreme tribunal was necessary, which would judge "between leprosy and leprosy" <note>original: "inter lepram et lepram" - a biblical idiom from Deuteronomy 17:8 referring to making legal distinctions between different types of cases or difficult disputes.</note>. This tribunal is the Holy Roman and Universal Church, which is the hinge and the head, the law and the teacher of all things done in the faith. 

But you <note>Referring to the Waldensians.</note>, under the prince of darkness, have not cut down any thorns of error or any brambles; instead, you allow them to grow far and wide every day as they arise. Having set aside the scythe of reason, you support a weak and pernicious strength of dogma. Therefore, so that you may be able to see the darkness of such errors more clearly, I ask that you receive with an equal mind the following account of the beginning of the rising and coalescing faith, repeated from a bit earlier.

### THAT THE FAITH OF CHRIST WAS FIRST INSTITUTED BY THE APOSTLES AND THEIR SUCCESSORS, AND THAT ALTARS, TEMPLES, AND THE IMAGES OF THE SAINTS OUGHT LAWFULLY TO BE MADE IN THE CHURCH,

Christ the Lord, about to pass from this world when He had not yet fully built the new faith, promised that He would soon send the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit, from the Greek word for "advocate" or "comforter."</note> who would teach all truth and fully suggest what the disciples ought to do. For the Lord had left them an as-yet imperfect law, which was first to be formed in the hearts of the Apostles by the Holy Spirit, and then more fully declared to others through their preaching. 

For at first, even after the Lord ascended—as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD).</note> proves—Peter observed Judaic rites according to Moses, as one who had not yet learned from Jesus how to transcend from the letter of the law to the law of the spirit, as we learn from the Acts of the Apostles. But on the following day, while they were traveling and approaching the city, Peter went up to the upper parts of the house to pray around the sixth hour. Being hungry, he wished to eat, but while they were preparing the food, a trance fell upon him. He saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending like a great sheet, let down by four corners from heaven to earth, in which were all the four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and the birds of the air. A voice came to him: "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." But he said, "Far be it, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean." And the voice came to him a second time: "What God has purified, do not call common"—that is, profane <note>original: "id est ingnatū"</note>. 

Notice, therefore, how from these words he preferred Judaic rites, since Peter was still observing what was clean and unclean. Indeed, it is shown from the following vision that he needed to be warned to communicate the words of faith to Cornelius (who was not an Israelite according to the flesh) and to those who were with him. For up to that time, he existed as a Jew and lived by Judaic traditions, holding in contempt others who were outside the Jewish religion. 

Nor did Paul reveal it differently in the epistle he wrote to the Galatians; for before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles; but when they arrived, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those of the circumcision; and the other Jews consented to his pretense, so that even Barnabas was led by them into that pretense. Behold, therefore, how the law of Christ began to be dispensed not so much by His own immediate institution as by the observation of men and the tradition of the Apostles, as soon as the preaching of the Gospel began—the Spirit, whom our Savior sent into the hearts of the Apostles as promised, teaching this. For He says in the Gospel of John: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth." For what could He say to them that they were unable to bear, except that once the foundations were laid...

# ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS.

Through the Holy Spirit <note>original: "p s̃pm̃sc̃tm̃," an abbreviation for "per Spiritum Sanctum"</note>, Christ left many things to be instituted in the Church by the disciples of our salvation and their successors. These concern the practice of religious worship or the observation of ceremonies which we see introduced and established today. Nevertheless, all these things are despised as ridiculous by profane men <note>The author refers to the Waldensians, a medieval reform movement that predated the Protestant Reformation and rejected much of the Catholic Church’s physical and hierarchical structure.</note>. They assert that no temples ought to be built, since we ourselves are the Temples of God, and God demands the worship of our hearts more than the decoration of temples and walls. I confess that these arguments have a certain "color" or plausibility with which you might deceive an unlearned crowd. But what they say is so frivolous and foolish that it is easily destroyed by even stronger reasons. We know how much care God once took in the Old Law <note>The Old Testament/Mosaic Law.</note> for the construction and building of the Temple <note>The Temple of Solomon.</note>, and what a selection of wood, stones, gems, tapestries, images, tables, and lampstands He desired for its decoration. He wished to have no other architect but Himself, so that all things were constructed as He commanded, with the ranks of ministers, Levites, priests, and high priests distributed, along with the ritual of sacrifices, the style of vestments, and the distinction of offerings. Did these things not bear the appearance of pride, or some empty and mimetic vanity and pomp unbecoming of God? Yet, unless these things were observed exactly as they were instituted, a swift punishment followed. No one, even with a good heart, dared to overstep the limits of their ministry, as we read concerning Datan, Abiram, and Korah <note>Dathan, Abiram, and Korah were biblical figures who led a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron; according to the Book of Numbers, they were swallowed by the earth as punishment.</note>. > I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. For will I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats? Wretched and ignorant men! We know they are metal, wood, or stone. But by these, as if by an archetype <note>term: Archetype/Original Model. By the visible sign of the glorious triumph which those strongest athletes <note>A common early Christian metaphor for martyrs who "competed" for the faith.</note> once won through a remarkable victory for the faith, we are repeatedly reminded. 

I know that you are accustomed to resist this by citing the prophet Baruch, who asserts that such idols were only forged for the luxury of priests. # ST. AUGUSTINE AGAINST <note>original: "D. AVGVSTINVS CONTRA". This likely refers to a work attributed to Saint Augustine or a dialogue written in his spirit against a dissenting "John."</note>

...thinking they possessed power in themselves, but rather that through the memory of deeds done, that flame of inspiration grows in the hearts of excellent men, and is not calmed until they have matched the virtue, fame, and glory of those who came before. Therefore, you accuse us of idolatry in vain, my John, as you see; in vain do you accuse us of avarice and greed because of the splendor of gold and silver in our churches. You yourselves seem more subject to these very vices which you rebuke; perhaps you abstain from more expensive church buildings and images so that the gold and silver—which we spend lavishly for the honor of God—you might instead pour out to satisfy your own greed. What of the fact that you cast away even the bones and relics of the saints as if they were unclean? You accuse us, who preserve them and display them in churches in linens and small vessels, of being profane and sacrilegious. To you, I respond with no other words than those of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) wrote a famous defense of relics against Vigilantius, which is the source of the arguments used here.</note>. I do not say that we worship and adore the relics of Martyrs—nor indeed the sun and moon, nor Angels, nor Archangels, nor Seraphim, nor any name that is named in the present or the future—lest we serve the creature rather than the creator. But we honor the relics of Martyrs so that we may adore Him whose Martyrs they are; we honor the servants so that the honor given to the servants redounds to the Lord, who said: "He who receives you, receives me." Therefore, are the relics of Peter and Paul unclean? Then the small body of Moses must be unclean, which according to the Hebrew truth <note>original: "hebraicam veritatem," a term Jerome used to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible.</note> was buried by the Lord Himself. And as often as we enter the basilicas of the Apostles and Prophets and all the Martyrs, do we then venerate the temples of idols? Shall the wax candles lit before their tombs be called signs of idolatry? I will say something more, which may strike at the head of the Author <note>Presumably the leader of the Waldensian sect or the "John" being addressed.</note>, and might one day heal his insane brain or else destroy it, lest the image of the soul be overturned by such great sacrileges: Was the Lord's body placed in the tomb also "unclean"? And did the angels who wore white garments provide a watch for a dead and polluted corpse? You see indeed, my John, how many errors follow from the perverse credulity of the simple, and what great blasphemies against God and the saints these "leaders of your synagogues" <note>original: "Archisynagogae," a mocking term for the Waldensian leadership, likening them to the opponents of Christ in the Gospels.</note> babble from their polluted mouths. And yet, still justifying them, you assert they are imitators of Christ and the Apostles; and despising the universal Church, you persist in imitating their dogmas so constantly and pertinaciously.

## CONCERNING PREFECTURES AND ECCLESIASTICAL ORDERS
## WHICH IT IS NOT FITTING FOR LAYMEN, HOWEVER
## GOOD, TO USURP; and that clerics may lawfully
## possess temporal goods, and should be judged rashly by no one.

There are those who attack Ecclesiastical orders especially because Christ, the Master of humility, instituted no ranks of dignity in the Church. They claim He left no symbols of office or prefectures to be administered by His disciples, but commanded them to teach the word of life in all humility and gentleness. They do not notice the words of the Savior reported by the "lowing of the evangelical ox" <note>A poetic reference to the Gospel of Luke, whose traditional symbol is the ox.</note>, where He says to His disciples: "When I sent you without purse or scrip, did you lack anything?" and when they answered "nothing," He added: "But now he who has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a scrip; and he who has not, let him sell his tunic and buy a sword." Therefore, the poverty He commanded in Matthew, He relaxed with the passage of time, as Luke reports. Nor is it likely that He wanted priests and bishops to be some sort of wandering beggars who, void of all honor, would only frequent markets and crowds of men to preach—those whom Peter calls "a chosen race and a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people of His own." Rather, Christ wished to teach them the way of humility so that although they preside over the Christian people, they may in mind and soul consider all worldly things of little value. Let them do nothing arrogantly or insolently, nor permit others to do so. For can humility not exist under honest care for the body or the possession of wealth?

## ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS,

Neither Job nor Zacchaeus <note>In the Gospel of Luke, Zacchaeus was a wealthy tax collector who gave half his wealth to the poor after meeting Jesus.</note>—who as a rich man distributed half of his goods to the poor for Christ’s sake—will be seen as just, if we follow your logic. Indeed, let us see: Do you not also, as you say, who strive to follow Christ’s teaching, renounce everything and follow the poor Christ naked and destitute? I have certainly seen many poor and ragged people of our religion, but few of yours who were not clothed in better garments. Again, I have seen many humble men dressed in gold and purple, while in a lowlier habit I saw some so puffed up that for a slight offense or a few words they would froth over with grand speech and thunder out mere Tragedies. Humility is commanded equally to Kings and Princes, and equally to all who have taken up the warfare of Christ.

Nevertheless, bypassing those others, you rage against Christ’s priests alone, and you examine every one of their works. And—what is forbidden by divine and human law—you even punish the household of Christ, who have deserved poorly, under your own courts and judgments. "It is a crime," says the author, "and a shameless insolence to reduce the sons of Sarah <note>original: "Saræ filios". A reference to the allegory in Galatians 4, where Sarah represents the free Church and Hagar the slave.</note>, who were born of the free woman, to slavery along with the sons of the handmaid." 

This is not your vineyard, nor your plantation, nor your making, but God’s. He perhaps assigned it to Himself as His own title and household, the standard-bearer of His name and the dispenser of heavenly treasures and life-giving graces, having attained the right and power of binding and loosing souls. How preposterously and shamelessly one acts toward God if, when He Himself has appointed them to be your judges, you violently judge them yourselves! 

For these are they who, as soon as you were brought forth into light and life, purified you from original sin—as if from leprosy—in the blessed font of baptism. These are they who perform the other sacraments and impart them to you. These are they who alone have the power of opening and closing heaven to men, and through whose lips the Gospel shines everywhere. 

Render the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and leave the things that are God’s to God. It is surely not permitted for the profane to enter the Holy of Holies, nor for those polluted in the flesh to touch the vessels of the temple. Uzzah <note>original: "Ora". The text likely intends "Oza" (Uzzah), who in 2 Samuel 6 was struck dead by God for touching the Ark of the Covenant to steady it.</note>, daring to support the falling chariot of the Lord, was punished with death. Pharaoh, pressing the people of God into service, was drowned in the Red Sea. Antiochus, enriched by the spoils of the temple—than which no more cruel memory exists—paid the penalty. Pompey, he who is called "the Great," after Jerusalem was captured and the temple polluted with Roman idols and the stabling of horses, lay foully and miserably in the sand on the Egyptian shore with his neck cut off. And Crassus, his colleague, who followed him as a victor and plundered the temple ornaments that Pompey had spared, was overwhelmed by the arrows of the Parthians at Carrhae.

Therefore, the presumption of those who, judging Christ’s priests, rashly define what they will, is unworthy. For the people must be taught and corrected by the priests, not the priests by the people, lest the disciple be above the master. History relates how wisely the Emperor Constantine <note>Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD). This story refers to the Council of Nicaea, where he reportedly burned petitions of grievance against bishops to maintain church unity.</note> acted; when some had gravely accused certain Bishops before him and brought petitions, he neither read them nor permitted others to read them. Instead, he burned them in all humility in the presence of the Bishops, adding that it was not permitted for him to judge those whom the Lord had deigned to choose as His ministers, and whom He had called now "angels of the covenant," now "christs" <note>original: "christos". Here meaning 'anointed ones' rather than Jesus specifically.</note>, now even "gods."

Since Paul, writing to Timothy, also forbids an accusation to be received against a priest or Bishop <note>See 1 Timothy 5:19.</note>—O Christian sentiment of the best prince! For he knew that Bishops, however wicked, are the instruments of the Holy Spirit—not indeed by merit, but by office. Caiaphas would never have prophesied unless he had been the high priest of that year. Consider how Paul, after receiving a blow, called Ananias—that wicked high priest—a "whitewashed wall." He later excused himself, saying he did not know he was the high priest, because he found it written: "You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people." <note>Acts 23:3-5.</note>

Therefore, priests and Bishops are to be honored, observed, and looked up to with all honor and veneration, even the difficult ones <note>original: "disfcholi" (from the Greek 'dyskolos'), meaning harsh, ill-tempered, or hard to please.</note>, because human rashness ought not to despise those whom God willed to put in charge of His ministry. Not all are good, not all are perfect; yet those Bishops and all priests...

<meta>This page continues the defense of the clergy against the Waldensian critique. The previous page argued that even if a priest is personally sinful, his sacramental authority remains intact. ST. AUGUSTINE AGAINST...

...and for this reason, Judges are established over us, not according to their own works (which are sometimes evil) but according to the dignity of their office. For even David, although he was an adulterer and a murderer, when questioned by the prophet, gave sentence against the rich man who had robbed the poor, saying:
> The man who did this deserves to die. <note>original: "Iudicium mortis est viro huic". See 2 Samuel 12:5, where Nathan the prophet confronts King David.</note>
Likewise Solomon, though he worshipped the gods of the gentiles for the love of his many wives, nevertheless the whole people of Israel flocked to his judgments. So too Ahab, although he worshipped Baal, still judged the ten tribes. Many others are found in both the Old and New Testament whose lives were blameworthy, yet their sentences were upheld because they proceeded from the integrity of the judicial order. Wherefore the Lord also says in the Gospel:
> The scribes and the Pharisees sit on the chair of Moses <note>original: "sup cathedrā Mosi sederũt scribæ & pharisei". See Matthew 23:2. This is a classic argument for "ex opere operato," meaning the office is holy even if the person is not.</note>, and so forth.

From this it is clearly evident that evil pastors, while they strike at the crimes of others with a sentence of just examination, harm themselves as long as they care to correct the vices of others without the example of their own amendment. However, they are of benefit to their subjects if those subjects, corrected by their rebuke or restrained by their sentence, learn to change their lives for the better. "You look at Peter," says Saint Jerome, "but consider also Judas; you look up to Stephen, but look also at Nicolaus," <note>Nicolaus was one of the first seven deacons mentioned in Acts 6, but was traditionally (though perhaps inaccurately) accused of founding the heretical Nicolaitans mentioned in Revelation.</note> whom the Lord condemns by his sentence in the Apocalypse. Nor should anyone pride himself on bodily chastity and other virtues, since for every idle word that men speak, they shall give an account. Since even a simple insult against a brother is the guilt of homicide, woe to us! As often as we lust, so often do we commit fornication. "My sword," says the prophet, "is drunk in heaven," <note>original: "Inebriatus est... gladius meus in celo". See Isaiah 34:5.</note> and much more so on the earth, which produces thorns and thistles. The <term>vessel of election</term> <note>original: "vas electionis". A traditional title for the Apostle Paul, referring to Acts 9:15.</note>, in whose mouth Christ resonated, beats his body and subjects it to slavery, and yet he perceives the natural heat of his flesh fighting against his judgment, so that he is forced to cry out:
> Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? <note>original: "miser ego homo quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius". See Romans 7:24.</note>

And do you think Bishops and priests can live without a lapse, beyond reproach? It is a profane opinion and alienated from all reason. An angel sinned in heaven, man in paradise, and Judas from the college of Christ. What wonder if a fragile man, established in whatever office, happens to transgress? I see, however, my dear John <note>Likely referring to a specific Waldensian or Reformist leader, perhaps Jan Hus or an interlocutor named Johannes.</note>, what moves the men of your order, so that their offense against us flourishes so greatly. For these men, since they value nothing in the way of goods except financial gain—which comes to them only through labor, care, and anxiety—cannot endure without envy that such things come to priests who are entirely free from all labor. For this reason, they reproach us with the poverty of Christ and the apostles, because by Christian law all greed, avarice, and luxury are forbidden. I marvel, however, since they are so studious of the apostle Paul, that they have not read this, or rather—as they say—<term>passed over it with a dry foot</term> <note>original: "sicco pede transijsse". A Latin idiom meaning to ignore or skip over something quickly.</note>:
> Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock and does not feed on the milk of the flock? <note>original: "qs plantat vineã, & de fructu eius non sumit...". See 1 Corinthians 9:7.</note>
And again, the same Apostle, when he said that we sow spiritual things so that we may reap their temporal things, and that he who serves the altar should also live from the altar. This they pretend as if it were not the law of Christ, but whatever is said about parsimony and other such things, they twist it all against the clergy and ministers of Christ—as if it were permitted only to you to lend at interest under the hope of humility and virtues, and to pursue the catching of money by every hook. But lest I seem to have let loose the reins of slander against you instead of exhortation, I will check my momentum and proceed to touch upon other things in which you are entangled in equal error.

# ON THE PRAYERS OF THE SAINTS and the Pains of Purgatory,

Now that the greater part of the doubts has been resolved, there remains the rest: to briefly touch upon what is believed in the Church regarding the <term>suffrages</term> <note>original: "suffragijs". These are intercessory prayers or good works offered on behalf of the souls in Purgatory.</note> of the saints and Purgatory. For I know that various disputes are common among many concerning this; we, however, setting aside the testimonies of the doctors of the Church, will confirm our opinion by only two: namely, one from the Old Law and one from the New. Concerning the Old Law, it is read in the books of the Maccabees how Onias the high priest appeared... <note>In 2 Maccabees 15:12, the deceased High Priest Onias appears in a vision to pray for the Jewish people, a key text used to support the intercession of saints.</note>

# THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS,

...to Judas Maccabeus, and showed him Jeremiah the prophet saying: "This is he who prays much for the people and the whole city of Jerusalem" <note>original: "Hic est qui multum orat p populo & vniuersa ciuitate Hierusalem". Reference to 2 Maccabees 15:14, a key text for the intercession of saints.</note>. Furthermore, we read of Paul in the Acts of the Apostles, that when he was in a shipwreck with many others, an angel of the Lord stood by him saying: "Fear not, Paul; behold, God has granted you all those who are in the ship" <note>original: "Ne timeas Paule ecce tibi deus donauit omes q sunt in naui". See Acts 27:24.</note>. From these examples, it is sufficiently clear that the prayers of the saints benefit us toward obtaining forgiveness, and because of them, God sometimes saves the guilty and the sinners. 

But a greater doubt arises concerning the pains of purgatory: whether there is a place for souls stripped of their bodies, and whether almsgiving and other works of piety performed for them in this world benefit them, either by the lessening of guilt or the relaxation of punishment. There are many things which theologians, inspired by God, have both committed to books regarding this matter and left for the common people of the faithful to believe. However, since you reject all sound doctrine, keeping only the naked letter of the law <note>The author is criticizing the Waldensian principle of "Sola Scriptura," or relying only on the Bible while rejecting Church Tradition.</note>, it is my plan to offer only a few points so that we may close this lengthy letter. 

I omit recounting by what reasons theologians demonstrate that Purgatory exists, and that the support and prayers of the living benefit the souls existing there; for that would be a long task, and you are accustomed to accepting nothing beyond the authority of the Law <note>Meaning the Bible.</note>. Consider, therefore, what even the Psalmist says: "The Lord," he says, "leads down to the underworld and brings back" <note>original: "Dominus inqt deducit ad inferos & reducit". See 1 Samuel 2:6, often cited in this context.</note>. And again: "But God will redeem my soul from the hand of the underworld, when he shall have taken me" <note>Psalm 49:15.</note>. It is established, however, that no one is brought back from the hell of the damned. 

Consider also what the history of the Maccabees testifies concerning that Judas, the bravest "Hector" of the Hebrews <note>The author compares the Jewish hero Judas Maccabeus to the Trojan hero Hector to emphasize his bravery.</note>. Judas, that most valiant man, having made a collection, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to be offered at Jerusalem for the sins of the dead, because he considered that those who had fallen asleep with godliness had great grace laid up for them. He adds: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins" <note>original: "Sancta ergo & salubris est cogitatio p defunctis orare vt a peccatis soluant̃". See 2 Maccabees 12:43–46. This is the primary scriptural defense for Purgatory.</note>. 

Unless, perhaps, you also demand testimony from the Apostle? I shall therefore add what he writes to the Philippians: "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth" <note>original: "In nomiē Iesuh omē genu flecti celestiū terrestriū & infernorū". See Philippians 2:10.</note>. It is clear, however, that the malice of the damned is so obstinate that they would by no means bow their knees at the name of Jesus, but would rather tear it apart with blasphemies and a thousand insults. Thus, you are necessarily forced to confess that there is some place in the underworld where the souls of the pious are kept. 

Nor are the opinions of the Gentiles and Heathens lacking to us to strengthen this point. But though I pass over the poets, who used a more licentious style of writing, hear, I beseech you, how "Christianly" Proclus the Platonist <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher. The author is using a pagan philosopher to show that even "natural reason" recognizes Purgatory.</note> and your religious men have written concerning the purification of purgatory. He says: "The places of the underworld, the judicial states beneath the earth, and the rivers which Homer and Plato describe, must not be thought of as vain and fabulous imaginations or merely as bugbears <note>A "terriculamenta" or bugbear is something used to scare children.</note>. Rather, just as many and varied places are distributed according to merit for souls returning to the heavens, so it must be thought that for souls needing punishment and purification, there are places arranged beneath the earth having various flows from the elements surrounding the earth, which flows they have surely called 'rivers'." 

He concludes that there are different orders of demons set over this work: some as avengers, some as chastisers, some as purifiers, and some as judges. It is agreeable that souls there are terrified by the appearance and state of the demons in charge, varying and confused according to their merits and habits, and cut off from the rays of the sun above. 

Behold how consistent with our faith are the things this Platonist brings forward! You, however, holding none of these things in regard, defend the opinion you once conceived—and believe it constantly with an irrevocable error—even when convicted. By Hercules, nothing more ruinous, nothing more alien to true religion can be found than this! But since—to use the words of Saint Jerome—the discourse has sailed out from rocky places, and the fragile boat has proceeded into the deep among hollow rocks and foaming waves, the sails must be spread to the winds; and having waded through the rocks of questions, in the manner of rejoicing sailors, the [conclusion of the] let[ter]... <note>original: "de scopulofis locís enauigauit oratio". Jerome often used this metaphor of a ship to describe the progress of a difficult argument.</note>

...chant must be sung, that whatever he teaches outside the common and universal tradition of the holy church is a pestilential dogma, a ruinous dogma, and produced from the devil's workshop. Though it may present a show of virtues, it is nonetheless poison and a viper-like fascination of heretics, for they are deceived by false opinions. The devil has as many forms as he has images of lies; for just as of old he deceived Adam and Eve when he told them they would be like gods, so he does not cease to deceive you daily. While transformed into an angel of light, he confirms that you shall be like the holiness of the apostles. Therefore, my John, having left behind the profane and ignorant commoners, reintegrate yourself into the holy church. You possess a vivid and flourishing nature, and an intellect easily disposed to act with virtue in all things. You can, therefore, easily grasp this: that nothing is firm and nothing is constant which is discussed in your little assemblies <note>original: "conciliabulis"</note> regarding the faith of Christ. Thus, for the most part, the decrees of those in Litomyšl <note>original: "Lythosmissensiū"</note> are different from those in Přerov <note>original: "Prerouienfiū"</note>, and again, they are far different from those taught among you in Pišťany <note>original: "pstanno"</note>. Our faith, however, just as it consists in the solid foundation of Peter and his successors, is not easily undermined by any tunnels or by the devious twists of errors. Your own virtue compelled me to write these things to you—perhaps slight and even laughable matters, yet they are the invitations of a Christian man, such as they are, to the orthodox faith. I pray, therefore, that you read them in such a way that they please you; that is, so that one currently entangled in vain errors may be led back, as a penitent, to the fold of Christ. Farewell from Buda, on the Wednesday of the Ember Days of the Holy Spirit <note>The Ember Days are four seasonal periods of fasting and prayer in the liturgical calendar. # AUGUSTINE OF OLOMOUC, DOCTOR OF ARTS AND DECREES <note>A title indicating high academic standing in both the liberal arts and canon law.</note> TO JOHANNES NIGER <note>Jan Černý, a famous physician and member of the Unity of the Brethren.</note>, PHYSICIAN, SENDS HEARTY GREETINGS.

How difficult it is to lead a man confirmed in heresy back from his opinion and to have him embrace the precepts of sounder counsel is shown by the *Apology* which you wrote to me. In this, although you promised you would respond to the things written to you, you nevertheless refute or even touch upon very few things. Instead, you merely construct the wrappings of your own opinion. Truly, you bring nothing new to me, my John. I certainly know from which fountain you have drunk these lethal poisons for the soul, and to whose doctor's errors you, a "better" disciple, have subscribed. Yet, by my faith <note>original: "mediuffidius," an old Roman oath to the god of truth.</note>, it wearies me of this ill-advised counsel: that having set aside Augustine, Jerome, and both the elder Origen and Basil, as well as Hilary, Chrysostom, Athanasius, Tertullian, and Lactantius, you preferred to be a follower of a certain impure Jakoubek <note>Iacobellus refers to Jakoubek of Stříbro, a primary successor to Jan Hus in the Bohemian Reformation.</note> recently barking against the Church. You have gone so far that you seem to have preferred the wandering and old-wives' ravings of a certain apostate man—as can be seen—to the Apostolic and Nicene Creeds. But you are deceived if you think a Catholic man is moved by these traps, or that he would cross over to that whitened and cloaked shadow of piety which you impose upon the unlearned common folk. No such crafty attempts of this kind harm us. For as Augustine says: "All enemies of the church, whether blinded by error or depraved by malice, profit her rather than harm her." For if they sometimes receive the power to afflict her bodily, they exercise her patience; if, however, they oppose her by thinking wrongly, they exercise her wisdom. For a question moved by an adversary becomes an occasion for learning. Many things pertaining to the faith, while they are stirred up by the clever restlessness of heretics so that they may be defended, are both considered more diligently, understood more clearly, and preached more urgently. The leaders of heresy were once learned; Arius was learned (as his letters in Cassiodorus show), and many of his followers were most learned. Yet their insane doctrine profited them nothing against the knowledge of piety, nor did the savagery and cruelty of the princes of that time against the orthodox avail, for the truth of that most holy and constant bishop Athanasius conquered, and...

<meta>This page continues the polemical argument of Augustinus Olomucensis against the Bohemian Brethren (referred to here under the broader label of Waldensians). The author is urging his correspondent, Johannes Niger, to return to the Catholic Church, arguing that private interpretation of Scripture leads to the same ruinous heresies and "beastly" superstitions found in antiquity.</meta>

# THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS.

...[the Church] has, up to this very day, thoroughly removed, extinguished, and completely uprooted that pestilential blight which was creeping through all of Italy and the Gallic lands. But you, who boast in the simplicity of the spirit and of the scriptures, what—I ask you—do you bring forward of this kind that you have not unearthed from the condemned dogmas of the ancient arch-heretics? You support yourselves with some portion of the scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments, in the manner of leeches, which are accustomed to always suck the dregs and the tainted part of the blood, while leaving the healthy and whole part behind. Some deny the truth in the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood, <note>This refers to the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist, a major point of contention during the Reformation.</note> arguing that a sacrament is merely a "visible form of invisible grace" and a "sign of a sacred thing." Thus, they judge that only the power <note>original: "virtutem"</note> and not the actual substance of the body and blood of Christ is contained there. When this is preached by many, humanity truly falters: eyes turn away, the brow knits, eyebrows wrinkle, the guts shudder, feet tremble, and the entire soul grows embittered. It should not seem strange that all of nature and all its force and power ought rightly to rise up against such blasphemous and diabolical men.

Arius, because he denied the *homousion* <note>original: "homousion" – a Greek term meaning "of the same substance," referring to the divinity of Christ being equal to the Father.</note>, was struck not only by human but also by divine vengeance; while he was relieving his bowels, his internal organs suddenly burst, and he cast out his unhappy soul in a place worthy of himself and his opinion. We read that the same thing happened to Pope Liberius, who followed that same error. He, too, used to support his error (just as you do yours) with the words of the Gospel: "The Father is greater than I," and "Concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the Son, but the Father," and other such passages, thinking the Son was by no means equal to the Father. And Sabellius, because it was said by the Son, "I and the Father are one," judged it necessary to contract the Father and the Son into a single person. 

Furthermore, whoever believed that those baptized in the spirit could never be tempted by the devil confirmed their opinion with those words of John: "Everyone who is born of God does not have sin, because His seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God" <note>1 John 3:9</note>. And again: "He who is born of God does not sin, but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him." Truly, this is not the fault of the sacred letters that arguments are taken from them by which heretics bolster their errors. Rather, those people are to be rebuked and condemned who, with a depraved mind, pervert things that were rightly said. For if Origen or Arius had perfectly understood the sacred Scripture, they would never have fallen into such childish error, which they were afterwards foolishly forced to defend using the words of both Christ and Plato.

It is worthwhile, therefore, my John, so that no errors arise from the sacred scriptures, that the simple and the learned alike be held within the measure of the laws. They should be restrained from wandering opinions in faith by the one ministerial head of Christ on earth <note>A reference to the Pope.</note>, to whom all ambiguities are to be referred through soul-saving decrees and constitutions. For if faith were to be shaped according to the pleasure and opinion of every individual, we would slide into the worship of irrational and brutish animals, as the ancients did of old. 

Certain Nomads not far from the Tanais <note>The Don River in modern Russia.</note> worshipped the trunks of trees—which many Ruthenians <note>East Slavs</note> and Scythians are said to do even today. The Egyptians worshipped the ox, the cat, and the crocodile. The Thebans worshipped the eagle; the Scythians, the sheep. The Sardians who were in Asia worshipped long-tailed monkeys and apes. The Smyrnians in Phrygia worshipped mice. The Persians worshipped fire and water. Those ancient Romans worshipped individual emotions of the soul, so much so that Scipio—a man otherwise very great—having entered Africa, sacrificed even to Fear and Boldness. 

Why was this so, I ask? Because whatever pleased anyone, this or that was admitted as something to be worshipped everywhere; and as the human race is prone to superstitions, it poured itself unpunished into various forms of religion. So it must also be judged regarding your sect: for while you despise public sacred things contrary to the custom of the fathers and most holy men, you hold the ceremonies of the church in contempt, you do not observe the feast days of the saints, and you refuse to offer tithes and first-fruits. You withhold the customary rites and funeral offerings for your ancestors...
