# AUGUSTINE AGAINST [THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS]

...you drag along, and you mock the statues of the saints, religious incense, and offerings as if they were <term>food sacrificed to idols</term><note>original: "idolothyta." This refers to meat offered to pagan gods, which early Christians were forbidden to eat.</note>. For what else are you doing but doing away with the common consensus of the faithful with frivolous arguments, and impiously undermining holy religion with these "tricks" of yours? The foundations of our religion are not what you imagine them to be. Rather, they are the religious decrees of the most holy Fathers established for the worship of God. Just as it was once permitted for the Apostles to establish certain precepts and laws for the Christian faithful beyond those handed down in the Gospel—which were nevertheless later abolished—so too is it permitted for their successors, and it shall always be permitted, no matter how obstinately you protest, to establish new laws and to abolish old ones according to the quality of the times.

For I ask you—who boast that you follow the apostolic life and discipline in all things—why do you not observe the Sabbath as the Apostles did? Why, according to the Apostolic decree, do you not abstain from blood and the meat of strangled animals? <note>This refers to the "Apostolic Decree" in Acts 15:29, which early Christians eventually stopped following as the Church moved away from Jewish dietary laws.</note> Why are you not also circumcised, since you read that Timothy was circumcised by Paul after the Law had already been given? Why do you not also offer the legal offerings for brothers on the day of purification, as Paul did? 

You will say that Paul did this out of fear of the Jews. Where, then, was his constancy? For when speaking to Timothy, he said: *The Lord has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power.* <note>2 Timothy 1:7</note> And again, when he writes to the Philippians: *In nothing, I say, shall I be ashamed, but with all confidence, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in me, whether by life or by death.* <note>Philippians 1:20</note> 

If your way is right, then you must say: "You erred, O Paul, you erred! The shadow of the Law had passed away in the light of the Gospel, yet you still follow it? Circumcision has ceased, yet you still embrace it? Altars have ceased, yet you still place an offering upon them?" Where were the Waldensian brothers then to draw you away from "profane sacrifice"? Where were <term>Jacobellus</term> <note>Jakoubek of Stříbro (c. 1372–1429), an early Hussite theorist who advocated for communion in "both kinds" (bread and wine).</note> and <term>Lawrence</term> <note>Lawrence of Březová (c. 1370–1437), a Hussite writer and chronicler.</note> to "resist you to your face," just as you once did to Peter? These men must surely be more divinely wise than you, O Paul—wisdom which you, though caught up to the third heaven, could not grasp, and which you, though taught by God, could not attain! 

And where was my "John the Black" <note>original: "Niger meus Ioannes." This refers to Jan Černý, the physician and leader of the Bohemian Brethren to whom this letter is addressed.</note> then, to instruct the Church more fruitfully than Augustine and Jerome, and to unlock the mystical senses and explanations of Holy Scripture? Jerome would never have written against <term>Vigilantius</term> <note>A 4th-century priest who criticized the veneration of relics and saints; Jerome wrote a famously biting polemic against him.</note> if he had read the learned writings of John against the relics of the saints. Nor had Jerome seen <term>Origen</term> <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253) whose views on the spiritual nature of worship were sometimes used by later reformers to argue against physical temples.</note> such that he himself might judge that temples and altars ought to be overturned. Jerome would never have approved of ecclesiastical orders distinguished by such various offices if he had known those religious "shoemakers" and "slaves of the mill" <note>This is a derogatory reference to the humble social origins of many Brethren preachers, who often continued to work manual trades.</note>—men more learned than himself!—practicing their trade in the "mills" of <term>Přerov</term> or <term>Litomyšl</term>. <note>Two major centers of the Bohemian Brethren in Moravia and Bohemia.</note> Likewise, he would never have established the monasteries of Religious and Monks and their different habits to any degree if he had known those things would displease my John.

You see how I recall you to yourself, lest, relying on your own wit, you so inconsiderately condemn the institutes of our ancestors and most learned men. They were full of the Holy Spirit, whose peculiar gift is knowledge, and they discoursed so learnedly in the field of the Scriptures—scriptures which you are scarcely able to understand even with great sweat, and from whose writings you steal everything you have. Yet, regarding other matters, you are accustomed to stop up your ears like "deaf asps." <note>A reference to Psalm 58:4, commonly used to describe heretics who refuse to listen to reason.</note> 

For since you profess the Creed of Jerome which he sent to Pope Damasus, why did you not also submit to this part: *This is the faith which we have learned in the Church; in which, if perhaps something has been set down with too little skill or caution, we desire it to be corrected by you, who hold both the faith and the See of Peter.*? <note>A famous quote from Jerome's "Letter to Damasus," emphasizing papal authority.</note> But this is exactly how you act in all things: you pick out only those things that serve your purpose, while you either suppress or ignore the rest—which is proven to be the peculiar trait of all heretics, past and present. 

How much more wisely do we read that the Pagans—and the Romans especially—acted! They wished for shrines to be in their cities so that, according to the opinion of <term>Thales</term>, <note>Thales of Miletus, an ancient Greek philosopher who taught that "all things are full of gods."</note> the likenesses of the gods might be observed not only by their minds but also by their eyes. Religion was so constant among them that it was considered a sacrilege to repudiate in any part the traditions of the fathers and ancestors introduced not only in the cities, but also in homes and families. They even established by law the manner in which each person should conduct himself in religious matters...

# THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS

...what [religion] ought to contain. Receive, then, some examples of what these laws were: "Approach the gods chastely; bring piety; remove wealth. Let no one have gods separately; let them not worship new or foreign gods privately unless they have been publicly adopted. Let them have temples built by their ancestors. Let them keep the rites of their family and fatherland. Let quarrels be removed from holidays. Let the priests publicly offer certain fruits and certain berries; let there be different priests for different gods, and <term>Pontiffs</term><note>Chief priests in the Roman religious hierarchy.</note> for all, and <term>Flamens</term><note>Specialized priests dedicated to a single specific deity.</note> for each. Let the priests prophesy for the vineyards, the groves, and the safety of the people; let them foresee the anger of the gods and obey them. Let the city, the fields, and the temples be liberated and consecrated; let them expiate lightning and <term>bird-omens</term><note>original: "oscina," referring to birds like ravens or owls whose songs were used by Roman augurs to interpret the will of the gods.</note>. He who steals a sacred thing or something entrusted to a sacred place shall be considered a <term>parricide</term><note>Traditionally one who kills a parent, but used here to denote a most heinous and sacrilegious criminal.</note>. Let vows be paid cautiously. Let there be a limit to the consecration of gold, silver, and ivory. Let private sacrifices remain perpetual. Let the rights of the gods of the underworld be holy."

You see, my dear John, how those pagan Romans took care to obstinately guard their ancestral laws and what diligent care they had for the ancient rites. Even when <term>Pythian Apollo</term><note>The famous oracle at Delphi.</note> was consulted by the Athenians as to which religions they should most especially hold, he issued this oracle: "Those which were in the custom of the ancestors." And indeed, this is proven to be true.

Whenever someone, leaning on his own judgment, turned away from the public and common law of the ancestors, who would not consider him a pernicious citizen? Who would not decide that he should be punished by a more severe law as one who first dared to either infringe upon or despise laws healthily established for the Republic? So it must be thought in religion. For all things have been strengthened toward holiness; all things toward virtue. No one approves of pride, luxury, greed, seditions, homicides, thefts, frauds, or robberies; all detest these in common. The papal constitutions decree nothing that is not known to be either founded on the law of the Gospel or introduced for a legitimate and reasonable cause.

This is so that in such a multitude of peoples, nations, and races—who are not all of the same customs—nothing may be found that does not consult the safety of all, and that restrains the rebellious, bloodthirsty, and violent by this one strictness of laws. But you "good men," while you seek to enjoy your liberty, while you permit impunity for evils, while you pursue everything as it pleases you under a certain shadow of virtue—namely Greed, Hypocrisy, Envy, Hatred, and Emulation—you take care to falsely persuade the simple that you live under the norm of the Apostolic religion. 

Do not all the epistles of the Apostle Paul agree on this: that greed is the service of idols? If it belongs to idols, then it does not belong to Christ. Therefore, throw away this very greed first, good brothers; throw away, I say, the service of idols. Give back to us the money to which you have been enslaved until now! For we—whom you say are held by greed—will soon in turn heartily give you the bones of the saints and relics. 

O foolish and senseless men, to take this pretext of a "new religion" for themselves! To claim that we—who fashion images of God and the saints in their memory, who frequent temples, who preserve the bones of the dead, who hold the memory of saints and men pleasing to God—are the authors of new inventions! These things are not new, my John, but handed down from the Fathers and derived down to us through a series of many centuries. 

If these things displease you, what wonder? For you have grown accustomed to being displeased by all right things. Among you, all things are practiced and believed in a confused, wandering, and uncertain manner, and they arise daily. You fashion for yourselves whatever kind of priesthood you wish, and you hold it as long as you please, and you even set it down. You receive the Sacraments as it suits you. You distort the Holy Scriptures to whatever senses you wish; you tear them apart and brand them with dark interpretations and foul stigmas; and yet you claim for yourselves adoption as sons...

# AUGUSTINE AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

...you do not fear to assert that you are called by God, even though your profession teems with so many evil errors that it undermines the entire sacrament of the Church, not just in part like other heresies, but as a whole. You will soon receive a short work from me in which your errors will be attacked individually and chapter by chapter. In the meantime, I wanted to write these things to you so that you might understand how vehemently I grieve over your perdition and infamy—not, by Hercules <note>original: "hercle," a common humanist exclamation meaning "truly" or "by my faith."</note>, with the cunning of one who slanders, but with the affection of one who feels your suffering. 

And although you yourself write that I have acted with too little consideration, since I have neither sufficiently examined your profession of faith nor found any error in your conduct, and yet did not fear to falsely accuse you of the crime of heresy—and that I ought to have abstained from this kind of writing since you stray neither in the faith of Christ nor in <term>matters of conduct</term><note>original: "agibilibus," referring to practical morality and deeds.</note>, to use your own words—nevertheless, my dear Johannes, you were clearly able to understand from the beginning of that letter of mine why I fell into that suspicion regarding you, and how vehemently I grieved once the matter was fully perceived. Therefore, what you ascribe to ill-considered judgment, I would have thought should rather be attributed to piety, since I have certainly attempted nothing else. 

And now I attempt the same again: both to lead you back from your wandering to the path of truth, and to recall you to the harbor of salvation from the storm-tossed sea of errors. Recognize, therefore, this piety; recognize the counsel of a best friend. Do not let even these somewhat harsh words disturb you, since the Apostle Paul also commands: *Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and doctrine.*

Farewell from Olomouc, on the Wednesday of the <term>Ember Days</term><note>A period of fasting and prayer in the liturgical calendar; these occurred four times a year.</note> of Pentecost <note>original: "Sanctispiritus," of the Holy Spirit.</note>. In the year of Christ, 1501.

->AUGUSTIN OF OLOMOUC, DOCTOR OF ARTS AND<-
->DECREES, TO JOHANNES NIGER PHILICUS, SENDS GREETINGS.<-

I feel, my dear Johannes, that I am accomplishing nothing in trying to recall you. For your opinions drive you so headlong that I have no hope that this ruin of yours can be easily restrained by any reasons. You seem to me—if I may say so with your permission—to have taken on the persona of a certain man in Plutarch <note>Referring to the character Gryllus in Plutarch’s "Moralia," who was turned into a pig by the enchantress Circe.</note> who, while disputing with <term>Ulysses</term><note>The hero of the Odyssey.</note>, could be led by no reasons to return to being a man again from being a pig, into which <term>Circe</term><note>The sorceress of Greek myth.</note> had previously transformed him. 

For even if I am little practiced in the Holy Scriptures, such that I might use their accumulated testimonies against you and recall you to the use of sounder counsel—for I do not yet feel I have <term>washed fingers</term><note>original: "phelotos [perlutos] digitos," a metaphor for being spiritually or intellectually unprepared to handle sacred things.</note> with which I might purely touch the mysteries and secrets of the holy—nevertheless, if you have rightly weighed my writings, you will find that I have brought forward nothing that tastes of any new dogma, nor anything that introduces the invention of some foreign tradition beyond what has been handed down by the most learned and holy men. I have only acted to recall you from the error in which you are ensnared by means of familiar examples, and to lead you, wandering and fasting, back within the unity of the Church if I could do so in any way. 

Furthermore, since you affirm that you follow not only the Apostles, but also Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, and Origen, and the other doctors of the Church, and that you do not dissent from Catholic unity, I pray you allow me to trifle with you again for a few moments to see how truthful you show yourself to be in this, and how far you stray by dissenting not only from them but even from yourself. 

And to begin first with the Apostles: they, as you know, were turned aside by no fear of King or Governor, and were worn down by no bitterness of punishments, but freely preached the word of God in cities, towns, and villages. You, however, stay held within <term>hiding places</term><note>original: "latibula," suggesting dens or secret holes.</note> which you rent for a fee in certain small towns; when you leave your schools, you do not dare to even open your mouths freely. Where, then, is that evangelical liberty of yours, that you should not fear Kings and Governors? Doubtless it is because you fear the secular judgments and the tribunals of the judges. Therefore, the liberty of Christ and of apostolic discipline ceases in you first. 

And to confront you more closely: the Apostles worked in the cities; they cured the sick and the languid, and they raised the dead. What signs does Christ, even the Lord, give to you yourselves?

<meta>This page continues the polemical argument of Augustin Olomucensis against the "Unity of the Brethren" (Waldensians) and their leader Jan Černý. The author shifts from attacking their claim of divine calling to challenging their consistency with the historical Doctors of the Church, specifically focusing on Saint Jerome’s support for Church hierarchy and ritual.</meta>

->### ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS,<-
->c 5.<-

...[He] affirms that the Church would follow the disciples. But since you have never demonstrated these virtues, nor do you demonstrate them now, it necessarily follows—and I believe you will concede this without controversy—that no relics of apostolic power remain in you. Let us pass on, therefore, to those whom you call the <term>Doctors of the Church</term><note>The "Doctors" or "Teachers" of the Church refer to authoritative early Christian theologians like Jerome, Augustine, and Thomas Aquinas.</note>, and let us see if it appears that you hold any consistent dogma even with them. Jerome approves of ecclesiastical orders, monastic discipline, and the ranks of bishops, priests, and <term>Levites</term><note>In early Christian literature, "Levites" was a common term for deacons, drawing a parallel to the assistants in the Old Testament temple.</note>. You and your church should see whether you accept any of these. You laugh at all these things; yet, whoever among you stands out above the rest in authority or the use of speech, you call him whatever you wish—I know not whether a bishop or a deacon, but certainly a priest, or rather an <term>Archisynagogue</term><note>original: "Archisynagogen," a Greek-derived term meaning "ruler of a synagogue." The author uses it mockingly to suggest the Waldensians are more like a Jewish sect than a Christian church.</note> is what you have among you. "Let envy be gone," says Jerome to Pope Damasus:

> Let the ambition of the Roman height recede; I speak with the successor of the fisherman and the disciple of the cross. Following no leader but Christ, I am joined in communion with Your Blessedness, that is, with the Chair of Peter. Upon that rock I know the Church is built. Whoever eats the lamb outside this house is profane. There, the earth being fertile with a rich sod, the purity of the Lord's seed returns a hundredfold; elsewhere, the grain overwhelmed by furrows degenerates into weeds and wild oats. <note>Jerome, Letter 15 to Pope Damasus. The "fisherman" refers to St. Peter.</note>

But you sing me some other songs, fashioning for us many churches in Armenia, Greece, and Prague like a multi-headed <term>Hydra</term><note>A mythological serpent that grew two heads for every one cut off; here it represents the "monstrous" proliferation of different sects.</note>. Is this, I ask you, following Jerome, who says the Church is built upon the unique Roman see as the prince of all others? The same man says again, when he speaks of ceremonies and the use of ecclesiastical vestments:

> What hostility is there against God, I ask, if I wear a cleaner tunic? If a bishop, priest, and deacon, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order proceed in white robes during the administration of the sacrifices? <note>Jerome, *Against the Pelagians* I.29.</note>

Listen here to how well you "agree" with Jerome! You say the rituals of the Roman Church's ceremonies save no one; they contribute nothing to faith, nor to the integrity of life, but rather seem to hinder them. You call the common people "ignoble" for seeking these things, as if they were not seeking goodness in Christ but merely earthly things. But you, forsooth, are the "nobles" who neglect these things! And you are an "excellent teacher" who, contrary to Jerome, prescribes for us that these things should be despised. But if they do not "save" by themselves, should they therefore be cast aside? See now how much you agree with Jerome, to whom you always appeal. 

I know what you will do: you will now reject Jerome, since he is contrary to your opinion, and you will flee to other camps. St. Paul the Apostle will soon be ready for you—lest someone like Jerome, Augustine, Thomas [Aquinas], and other Doctors of the Church deceive you with their ceremonies "through philosophy and empty deceit according to the tradition of men and not according to Christ" <note>A reference to Colossians 2:8.</note>. Now, therefore, feast days will also cease, since for us who believe Christ rose from the dead, there is a perpetual Sabbath. Fasts instituted by the Church will also cease, since "every creature is good and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving" <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 4:4.</note>. Priesthood will cease, and all things at once which are known to have been most religiously instituted either by popes or by the councils of the Holy Fathers, since none of these are found explicitly in the Gospels.

And since mention of Councils has occurred, I will repeat your words which you recently wrote to me, so that I may pierce you with your own weapons and reveal how much you yourself are consistent in your faith. 

> It is clearly evident, you say, that the apostles of Christ governed the Church of God in the beginning of the rising Church through various constitutions and councils according to the necessity of times and things; which, however, were later abolished.

These are your words. Answer me this first: what Council could have been of such power and authority as to infringe upon and abolish apostolic laws and decrees, and presume to decree anew other constitutions to be held in the Church? Tell me again: were not the Councils that abolished the apostolic laws (as you say) the very ones we now [follow] in our Church?

<summary>Augustin Olomucensis mocks the Waldensians for claiming to follow early Church Fathers like Jerome while simultaneously rejecting the hierarchy, vestments, and rituals Jerome defended. He highlights the logical contradictions in Jan Černý's claims regarding the authority of Church Councils.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the polemical address by Augustinus Olomucensis to Jan Černý (Joannes), the leader of the Unity of the Brethren. The author is moving from a critique of their authority to a defense of Church tradition and ritual against the reformers' "Scripture-only" approach.</meta>

# SAINT AUGUSTINE AGAINST...
<meta>catchword: church</meta>

...whether in the ordaining of the clergy or in the other ceremonies we hold, they [the apostles] instituted them. If you grant the first—that they did—then you will be bound to necessarily observe the apostolic decrees, and you and your followers will have to abstain from blood and from what has been strangled. <note>original: "a sanguine & suffocatis." This refers to the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15:29, where the Apostles commanded early Christians to abstain from blood and strangled meat—laws which the author notes the Reformers do not actually follow.</note> If you grant the second—that they did not—then having abandoned those traditions of the elders, you must necessarily agree with us. Or, perhaps you can offer this third option: by what council were your <term>sect</term><note>original: "secta." The author uses this dismissively to distinguish the Unity of the Brethren from the universal Church.</note> and your <term>conventicle</term><note>original: "conciliabulum," a derogatory term for an unauthorized or heretical gathering.</note> induced to follow those rites you observe, after the apostolic decrees were (as you say) abolished? You cast aside the decrees of councils and popes, and through your own little new interpretations of the Scriptures, you prescribe for yourselves a new norm of living, separate from that which is observed by our people. Who were the fathers of that council of yours? How many popes did it have, and in what place did they preside? Unless, perhaps, they were certain fugitives from our side and apostates, who hold the place of popes among you—bankrupts, or those who (as they say) "kicked up their heels" <note>An idiom suggesting rebellious or insolent behavior.</note> with a silent hand.

You feel, my Jan, what sort of thing it is that you attempt to defend with such effort. I bring nothing to you now from the storehouse of the Scriptures, for I am a <term>profane man</term><note>The author likely means he is a layman or "uninitiated" in their specific theological circle, using a modest irony common in Renaissance polemics.</note> and, as the proverb goes, I "worship the threshold from afar." I fight with "thick" <note>plain or common-sense</note> reasons, as you see. But I do not add that pompous ornament of words which you condemn in me—though why you attack it, I do not see. For you seem to imitate the custom of those who (as a certain witty fellow said) often have Boar, Hare, or Thrush placed upon the table, yet they themselves greedily seek out some dull broth or stew or the most sordid scraps, simply because they have many undigested wastes in their stomach and are accustomed to touching nothing except what is common and worn out.

Wisdom is a thing reverend and divine in itself, my Jan, and it does not lack for exotic ornament. Yet it is certain, as <term>Lactantius</term><note>Lactantius (c. 250–325) was an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent Latin style.</note> says, that the truth flows more powerfully into the minds of listeners if it is equipped with its own strength and adorned with the light of oratory. For who would deny that things which are decent in themselves become even more decent if they are adorned? Beware, therefore, of despising the ornament of words, which none but the heartless, the foolish, and those who are utterly "unwashed and bristly of ear" (as the saying goes) are accustomed to despise.

But leaving these things aside, let us touch upon the rest. Since you say that you also agree with Augustine, let us begin the matter again from the start and unweave there the whole history of your profession. First, you set forth the <term>Creed</term><note>original: "symbolum," the Apostles' Creed.</note> according to Jerome, and rightly so; for in that, there is nothing for which you ought to be rebuked. You add that you are free from every stain and contagion of heresy, and that you do not hold any view that seems alien to the tradition of the best and most approved men—Origen, Jerome, and Augustine. You say that you only reject and despise "old wives' superstitions" and the ceremonies of the Roman Church as being useless for salvation, and because you have consumed a great part of your life in these "superfluous" things without perceiving anything health-giving in them.

Hear now, most learned and clever master, what you are saying. First, you concede with us that the apostolic decrees have been abolished, but you observe neither those nor the new ones. You say you imitate the Doctors of the Church, but when you cast aside Roman ceremonies as superstitious, you simultaneously ruin all of their doctrine. To see that this is true, hear what <term>Augustine</term><note>The author quotes a passage often attributed to Augustine (though also found in Basil the Great) regarding the importance of unwritten tradition.</note> first writes against you:

"We have received," he says, "some ecclesiastical institutions in writings, but some we have received through apostolic tradition confirmed by successors in the Ministry; others, indeed, strengthened by custom, which only usage has approved. To these, an equal rite and the same affection of piety is owed. For if we attend to the customs of the Church, it will clearly be established that they were handed down not through the Scriptures, but from the Fathers."

For instance—to begin there—what Scripture taught the faithful to be marked with the sign of the health-giving cross? Or what Scripture commended the words of the long prayer of consecration over the bread and the chalice? We bless the font of baptism; we anoint those we baptize with the oil of unction; we instruct them to renounce Satan and his angels. From where do these and many other things of this sort come, if not from the silent and mystical tradition from the Fathers of the Church...

<summary>Augustin Olomucensis challenges Jan Černý's rejection of Roman ritual, arguing that if the reformers reject unwritten tradition, they must also reject core Christian practices like the sign of the cross and baptismal rites which are not explicitly detailed in Scripture.</summary>

...reside not in the letter, but in the understanding. Otherwise, if we follow the literal letter as Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"; Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> says, we too could compose a new dogma for ourselves, asserting from the Gospel that those who wear shoes and have two tunics should not be received into the church <note>A reference to a literalist reading of Matthew 10:10, used here to mock the "plain" lifestyle of the Waldensians.</note>. 

I wanted to write these things to you again, my dear John, not so much to respond to your letters—which contain struggles against the church lighter than straw—but so that I might warn you again and again that, having left behind the foul error of the Waldensians <note>The "Waldensians" here refers to the Unitas Fratrum or Bohemian Brethren, a pre-Reformation Christian movement that Augustin viewed as heretical.</note>, you might return to the way of truth and raise yourself from the precipice of eternal damnation into the purity of faith. Do this so that you may say with the Psalmist: *Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would have soon dwelt in hell* <note>original: "Nisi quia dominus adiuvit me, paulominus habitasset in inferno anima mea" - Psalm 94:17.</note>, and with Augustine: *I turned to the Lord, and I saw my darkness in which I had been, and the dark abyss in which I had lain, and I said: Woe, woe to my darkness in which I lay, woe to my blindness in which I could not see the light of faith, woe to my past ignorance in which I did not know you, Lord! Of what use to me then was a mind agile through various doctrines, and so many most knotted books unknotted with no help from a human teacher, when I erred so hideously and with sacrilegious foulness in the doctrine of piety?* 

If you do this, you will both consult your own honor among men and provide joy to the angels in heaven over your conversion. Farewell from Buda <note>Modern-day Budapest, then the capital of the Kingdom of Hungary.</note>, on the day of Saint Francis, in the Year of Christ 1501.

### AUGUSTIN OF OLOMOUC, DOCTOR OF CANON LAW, 
### TO THE PHYSICIAN MASTER JOHANNES NIGER, 
### SENDS GREAT GREETINGS.

<margin>d</margin> We have long interrupted our habit of writing, my dear John, and from the field of the scriptures in which we began to be beautifully exercised, we have betaken ourselves to the shade and to leisure. I truly thought, after your heresy began to be so spread abroad that it came forth from its hiding places into the open, that it was no longer necessary to deal with you through scriptures, but according to what Gamaliel <note>A Jewish teacher of the law mentioned in the New Testament.</note>, the teacher of the law, said in the Acts of the Apostles: *If it were of God, it would be in vain for us to struggle and resist you; but if it were of men, the work you were building would collapse of itself* <note>Acts 5:38-39.</note>. 

Therefore, when I saw such freedom of preaching among your men, and that the Gospel—which they themselves call the light—was now thundering everywhere through towns and villages, I thought that you would surely disseminate the standard of apostolic religion beyond the borders of Bohemia and Moravia <note>Regions in the modern Czech Republic where the Unitas Fratrum was most active.</note> to other nations as well, which in your opinion wander far from the law of Christ. I thought you would call men back from idols and images to the worship of the one God by your example. 

Just as the apostles divided the provinces—so that the Parthians fell to Thomas; the Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, and Bactrians to Matthew; the Ethiopians to Bartholomew; the Indians to Andrew; the Scythians to Andrew; the Asians to John; and Pontus, Cappadocia, and Bithynia to Peter, the prince of the apostles—so I thought you also would go out into the regions of the "idolaters" (to use your word) and divide the provinces. In particular, I thought that Laurentius <note>Likely referring to a specific leader of the Brethren whom Augustin finds particularly offensive.</note>, that emasculated and unmanly eunuch—as he is the perfection of the others—would approach the Prince of Priests <note>The Pope.</note> with his assembly of Cardinals, and would preach to the Roman Pontiff himself that the first teachings of our religion are of no value, and that Christ left no visible head in the church to preside over the rest, but that he himself is the head of the church who sits at the right hand of the Father to judge the living and the dead. Likewise, I thought you would teach that ecclesiastical ceremonies were introduced only for pomp and empty boasting, and that idols and the golden and silver shrines of the saints were for avarice and luxury. For so the prophet Baruch says: *Now you will see in Babylon gods of silver and gold, stone and wood, being carried on shoulders* <note>Baruch 6:4.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the polemical letter of Augustin of Olomouc to Johannes Niger (Jan Černý). In the previous page, Augustin warned John to abandon the "errors of the Waldensians" (the Unity of the Brethren) and return to the Catholic Church, mocking their literalist interpretation of Scripture.</meta>

-># THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS<-

<note>original: "ERRORES VALDENSIVM"; Augustin uses the term "Waldensians" to refer to the Unitas Fratrum or Bohemian Brethren, a common tactic to link them to an older, condemned heresy.</note>

...displaying them with fear to the nations; they certainly have golden crowns upon their heads, from which the priests steal gold and silver, and they give it to those appointed from among themselves, and they deck out prostitutes. I used to think that Lawrence <note>original: "Laurentiū"; likely referring to Vavřinec Krasonický, a leading scholar of the Brethren.</note> would preach these and similar things—unless, perhaps, for this reason, since that assembly of yours rejects him because he is neither male nor female. Just as in the past, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus <note>A Roman statesman from the 1st century BC.</note> took away the inheritance from Genucius, a priest of the Great Mother <note>Cybele, whose priests, the Galli, were castrated.</note>, and this was done by the leaders because one who had voluntarily cut himself off and was castrated was neither man nor woman, and thus should not enter into another's inheritance. It was then even prohibited by a decree of the Senate, lest those who were cut off should defile the tribunals with their presence under the pretext of seeking their rights. Furthermore, Quintus Metellus, the urban praetor, made Vetilius lose his case in a testamentary matter for no other reason than that he did not think he should be considered a man. 

Therefore, my dear John, if such a thing happened to Lawrence at Rome, you—who are not castrated but, being a priest, have married a very beautiful wife as I hear—should take up his role. You should fight manfully with men, and leave Germany to brother Luke <note>original: "Lucae"; referring to Luke of Prague, the primary theologian of the Brethren at this time.</note>, France to the Frenchman, and Spain or Sicily to the Bishop of Litomyšl or to Bernard <note>original: "Lytomislensi Episcopo vel Bernardo"; referring to Jan Železný (the "Iron Bishop") and Bernard of Žerotín, powerful Catholic opponents of the Brethren.</note>. 

For, my brother, I did not think that you would dispense the rain of salvation in your little gatherings and villages of Přerov and Pšán <note>original: "Prerouiae & p̃stanne"; villages in Moravia where the Brethren had strongholds.</note>, but rather upon the rooftops and in the light, without any fear, across all nations everywhere. I thought you would lead the sick and the weak back to their former health by the example of the apostles, not with any medicines but by the word alone. 

But now I experience something far different than I had thought. For I see your mouths blocked, your synagogues <note>A derogatory term used by Catholic polemicists for the meeting houses of the Brethren.</note> closed, and that evangelical trumpet has fallen completely silent among you. But it is right that you have appealed to the Masters of Prague and their college <note>Referring to the University of Prague, which often mediated religious disputes in Bohemia.</note>. For these men, without a doubt, will approve of your reasons, subscribe to your opinions, and cause your synagogues to be opened once again, so that what now lies hidden under a bushel may shine upon the lampstand. Then your preachers may again take up the office of preaching from the field, the plow-handle, and the hoe <note>A jab at the Brethren's practice of having laypeople and laborers as ministers.</note>. 

For it does not seem safe to seek this freedom of preaching in Rome, nor to exercise it in the universities of Paris, Bologna, Vienna, and Cracow, or in Olomouc or Brno. For perhaps your "apostolic preachers" would encounter whips or fire. And since the Holy Spirit—who has not yet appeared to them in tongues of fire—has not yet fully confirmed them, they would not be able to endure those things. Perhaps, however, you do not expect the Holy Spirit to appear and confirm you in tongues of fire or the form of a dove, but rather provided with iron and swords. But since these are known to be the instruments of an evil spirit rather than a good one, if you decided to strengthen your cause with these, you would be embracing a deed far removed from the evangelical institution. For Christ promised that He would send fire upon the earth, but He commanded the sword to be returned to its scabbard. 

What, therefore, should I think of this sudden consternation of yours out of fear of expulsion and fire? I pray, my dear John, write to me fully, and relieve me of this care and anxiety. 

Given at Olomouc, on the third Sunday of Advent, in the Year of Christ, 1504.

...consist not in the letters but in the understanding. <note>Augustine is arguing that the "Word of God" is the intended meaning, not just the literal text.</note> Otherwise, as Jerome says, if we follow the letter, we could even compose a new dogma for ourselves to assert from the Gospel that those who wear shoes or have two tunics should not be received into the church. <note>original: "calciati sint & duas tunicas habeant"; a reference to Christ's instructions to the apostles in Matthew 10:10, which Augustine argues shouldn't be taken as a permanent legalistic ban on shoes.</note> Farewell.

I wanted to write these things to you again, my dear John, not so much to respond to your letters—which contain resistances against the Church lighter than straw—but to warn you again and again to leave the foul error of the Waldensians <note>original: "Valdẽfium"; Augustine uses this as a derogatory label for the Unitas Fratrum, linking them to the older, condemned Waldensian heresy.</note> and return to the way of truth. Raise yourself from the precipice of eternal damnation into the purity of faith, so that you may say with the Psalmist: *Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would have almost dwelt in hell* <note>Psalm 94:17</note>; and with Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the author's namesake.</note>: *I turned to the Lord, and I saw my darkness in which I had been, and the dark abyss in which I lay, and I said: Woe, woe to my darkness in which I lay, woe to my blindness in which I could not see the light of faith, woe to my past ignorance in which I did not know you, Lord! What did it profit me then to have a mind agile through various doctrines, and to have many knotted books untied with no help of human teaching, when I erred so deformedly and with sacrilegious filthiness in the doctrine of piety?*

If you do this, you will both look after your honor among men and provide joy to the angels in heaven over your conversion. Farewell from Buda, on the feast of Saint Francis, in the year of Christ 1501.

## AUGUSTINE OF OLOMOUC, DOCTOR OF CANON LAW, SENDS HEARTY GREETINGS TO MASTER JOHN NIGER, PHYSICIAN,

We have for a long time interrupted our established custom of writing, my John, and from the field of the scriptures—in which we began to exercise so beautifully—we have betaken ourselves to the shade and to leisure. I truly thought, since your heresy has now begun to be so widely publicized that it has come out from hiding into the open, that I should no longer deal with you through the scriptures. Rather, I thought of that which Gamaliel, the doctor of the law, said in the Acts of the Apostles: *If it were from God, we would resist you in vain; but if it were from men, the work you build would fall of its own accord.* <note>Acts 5:38–39</note>

And so, when I saw such great freedom of preaching among your men, and the Gospel (or as they call it, the "light") thundering everywhere through the towns and villages, I imagined that you would surely disseminate the norm of the apostolic religion beyond the borders of Bohemia and Moravia to other nations which, in your opinion, wander far from the law of Christ. I thought you would recall men from idols and images to the worship of the one God by your example.

Therefore, just as the apostles divided the provinces among themselves—so that Thomas went to the Parthians, Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, and Bactrians; Matthew to the Ethiopians; Bartholomew to the Indians; Andrew to the Scythians; John to the Asians; and Peter, prince of the apostles, to Pontus, Cappadocia, and Bithynia—so I thought you also would go to the "idolaters" (to use your word) and divide the provinces.

In particular, I thought that Lawrence <note>Vavřinec Krasonický, a prominent scholar of the Unitas Fratrum.</note>—that unmanly and emasculated eunuch, as he is more accomplished than the rest—would approach the Prince of Priests <note>The Pope</note> with his assembly of Cardinals. I thought he would preach to them that, in the opinion of the Roman Pontiff, the first principles of our religion are nothing, and that Christ left no visible head in the Church to preside over the rest. Instead, he would claim that Christ Himself is the head of the church, who sits at the right hand of the Father to judge the living and the dead. Likewise, he would say that ecclesiastical ceremonies were introduced only for pomp and vain boasting, and that the "idols" and the golden and silver shrines of the saints lead only to greed and luxury. For so the prophet Baruch says: *Now you shall see in Babylon gods of silver and gold, and of stone and wood, being carried upon shoulders...* <note>Baruch 6:3</note>

...displaying fear to the nations, they certainly have golden crowns upon their heads, from which the priests subtract gold and silver, and they give from these to prostitutes and adorn harlots. <note>Augustine is likely quoting a passage describing the corruption of false idols or corrupt clergy to set up a comparison with the Brethren's leaders.</note> I thought Lawrence <note>likely referring to a specific preacher of the Brethren</note> would preach these and similar things, unless perhaps that assembly rejected him because he is neither male nor female, just as in the past, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus <note>a Roman statesman</note> took away the inheritance of Genutius, a priest of the Great Mother. <note>The priests of Cybele, the Great Mother, were castrated; Augustine uses this classical allusion to mock the status of the Brethren's ministers.</note> He deemed it unworthy for a leader, who was voluntarily cut off and castrated and was thus neither man nor woman, to enter into another's inheritance. It was thereafter prohibited by a decree of the Senate that those who were "cut off" should not defile the tribunals with their presence under the pretext of seeking legal rights. Furthermore, Quintus Metellus, the urban praetor, caused Vetilius to lose his case in a testamentary matter for no other reason than that he did not believe this man should be counted as a man.

If, therefore, anything of this sort happened to Lawrence at Rome, you, my John—who are not castrated, but being a priest have (as I hear) taken a most beautiful wife—should take up his part. <note>The Unitas Fratrum allowed their clergy to marry, a practice the Catholic Augustine mocks here as a violation of traditional priestly celibacy.</note> And you would contend manfully with men! You would leave Germany to Brother Luke <note>Luke of Prague, a prominent theologian of the Brethren</note>, the Gallic lands to a Gaul, and the Spains with Sicily to the Bishop of Litomyšl or to Bernard. <note>Litomyšl was a major center for the Brethren in Eastern Bohemia.</note> For, my brother, I did not think you would be drinking the rain of salvation in your little assemblies and small towns of Přerov and Prostějov, <note>original: "Prerouiæ & p̄stanne"; two towns in Moravia that were strongholds of the Brethren.</note> but rather upon the rooftops and in the light, without any fear, throughout all nations everywhere. I thought you would be leading the sick and the weak back to their former health by the example of the Apostles, not with any medicines, but by the Word alone.

But now I experience something far different than I had thought. For I see your mouths blocked, your synagogues <note>The term "synagogue" is used here by Augustine as a derogatory name for the Brethren's meeting houses.</note> closed, and that "Gospel trumpet" of yours completely silenced. But it is well that you have appealed to the Masters of Prague and their college. <note>Referring to the University of Prague (the Carolinum).</note> These men, no doubt, approving your reasons, will subscribe to your opinions and cause your synagogues to be opened once again, so that what now lies hidden under a bushel may shine upon a candlestick—and your preachers may again take up the office of preaching from the field, the plow-tail, and the hoe. <note>Augustine is mocking the Brethren for being uneducated peasants rather than trained scholars.</note> For it does not seem safe to seek this freedom of preaching in Rome, nor to exercise it in the universities of Paris, Bologna, Vienna, and Krakow, or at Olomouc or Brno. For perhaps your "Apostolic preachers" would run into whips or fire; and they, not yet fully confirmed by the Holy Spirit (who has not yet appeared to them in tongues of fire), would not be able to endure those things.

Though perhaps you are waiting for the Holy Spirit to appear and confirm you not in tongues of fire or the likeness of a dove, but provided with iron and swords. But since these are known to be the instruments of an evil spirit rather than a good one, if you should decide to strengthen your cause with these, you would be embracing a deed far removed from the Gospel institution. For Christ promised that He would send fire upon the earth, but He commanded the sword to be returned to its sheath. What then I ought to feel regarding this sudden consternation of yours due to the fear of expulsion and fire, I pray you, my John, write to me at length, and relieve me of this care and anxiety.

Given at Olomouc, the third Sunday of Advent, in the year of Christ 1504.

<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication of Augustine of Olomouc’s polemic against the Bohemian Brethren. # TO THE MOST INVINCIBLE AND GLORIOUS PRINCE AND LORD, THE LORD VLADISLAUS, MOST POWERFUL KING OF HUNGARY AND BOHEMIA, AUGUSTINE THE DOCTOR SENDS GREETINGS,

Most Serene King, I recently came across at your Highness’s court a certain *Apology* <note>A formal written defense of one's opinions or conduct.</note> of the Waldensian brothers, whom they commonly call Pighards <note>original: "Pighardos"; a derogatory term used for the Bohemian Brethren, often implying they were foreign heretics.</note>. In this work, they strive to render an account of their faith to you, the most Christian and religious prince, and immediately thereafter, by a deceptive and utterly diabolical trickery, they try to draw Your Majesty into their favor and pull the unlearned populace into their perfidy. I thought at first glance of the work that all the main points of the errors by which this kind of man is held ought to be reviewed there, but that opinion deceived me greatly. For I found in passing that, according to their ruinous custom, they do nothing else but smear the filth of their errors as if with a kind of plaster. And as the saying goes, they "offer bread with one hand, while carrying a stone in the other." Nevertheless, I read this little book, such as it is, to see if perhaps something of that sort might occur that was worthy of reading—something brought down to us from the third heaven by some secret mystery. For these men are believed to have meetings, not like Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome who claimed to receive his laws from a divine nymph.</note> with the nymph Egeria, but with some "God of Flies" <note>original: "Muſcario"; a reference to Beelzebub, the "Lord of the Flies."</note>. 

Truly, I found that they have achieved nothing in this "corpse-like" *Apology* of theirs, except that, like locusts, they have stolen some honey from the beehives of the Doctors of the Church and mixed into it poisons and monkshood <note>original: "Aconita"; a highly poisonous plant often used as a metaphor for deadly heresy.</note> far more destructive—or, to speak more aptly, with pure and clever lies which they drew from their father the devil: they have tried to cloak their heresy. For this profession of faith which they sent to Your Majesty is not their actual faith, as these worthless and detestable men lie about. This is especially true where they affirm that they believe—as they write—in the <term>transubstantiation</term> <note>The Catholic doctrine that the substance of bread and wine changes into the actual Body and Blood of Christ during the Mass.</note> of the bread and wine into the true body of Christ. 

For they think and preach far differently, and have already become accustomed to call us "idolaters" openly and freely in their secret assemblies, because we, kneeling down, show reverence and due worship to this most sacred <term>Viaticum</term> <note>The Eucharist, here referred to as the "provisions for the journey" of salvation.</note> of our salvation, and because we do not shrink from venerating a "wheaten god"—to use their blasphemous words. But fearing that they might be expelled from this Kingdom—where they have grown very strong—by the decree of the most Christian Prince if they were to state clearly what they think, they have by design retreated into these diversions. They do this so that while they assert they feel the same as we do concerning the holy and undivided Trinity, the Eucharist, and the other sacraments of the Church, they might be approved by all and seen to deviate in nothing—so they say everywhere as they spread their talk. This is their cunning; this is their craftiness; this is the trickery of diabolical fraud. 

But to touch upon certain of their lies told under such a color, so that Your Majesty may clearly understand their craftiness: they write that they profess those to be rightly ordained in the church who obtain that gift and office in the church through the ministry of bishops flowing from the High Priest. Here they wish to seem to attribute some authority to the Roman Pontiff—most wicked liars! But let them bring into the open, I pray, that very High Priest whom they keep silent about, so that we too, coming forward, may adore the man. They will surely soon bring forward not Julius II <note>Pope Julius II, reigning at the time of this writing (1503–1513).</note>, but some cobbler of old shoes, or someone among the sedentary laborers <note>original: "Sellulariás"; manual laborers or craftsmen who work sitting down, used here to mock their low social status.</note> croaking something rather ignorantly about the life of Christ and the Apostles. Indeed, their bishops, priests, and deacons are some slaves of the flour mill or sewer-cleaners <note>original: "cloacarios"; literally "men of the sewers."</note> seeking a living by some filthy profit. Truly an "Apostolic Senate" that should discuss the mysteries of faith, decree laws and canons in the Church of God, and propose an "Apostolic Decree" to be embraced by everyone everywhere! What more? I shall add also this:

# ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS,

It is clear what they think concerning the most glorious Mother of God, the Virgin Mary: that her intercessions <note>Intercessions are prayers made by a saint on behalf of another; Augustine argues the Waldensians reject the power of the Virgin's prayers.</note> benefit us nothing before God, and that she is just like any other woman. Therefore, they believe no special cult should be devoted to her, nor any religious veneration, and that the prayers poured out daily to her by Christ’s faithful are in vain and of no value. Because the pious ears of Your Majesty—if they had written this directly—would shrink away and deservedly loathe these blasphemous men, these **wretched little foxes** have found a way here as well to free themselves from this infamy, by asserting that she was untainted and forever a virgin. 

Who denies this? But why, I ask, do you withdraw the honor paid to her in the Church? I am speaking to you, you impure sycophants! Why do you loathe her feast days as if they were profane? Why do you sing no hymn in her honor in your meeting-houses <note>original: "synagogis"; though the word means synagogue, Augustine uses it here as a disparaging term for the Brethren's places of worship.</note>? It seems you judge this most glorious Virgin unworthy of any honor and veneration from such boorish and **donkey-like**—if I may say so—slaves, even though angels serve her, and her Son honors her as a most devoted mother, denying her nothing.

Consider, I pray, most excellent and religious Prince, the ingenuity of the devil and how, transforming himself into an **angel of light**, he frequently ensnares the unwary and plunges them into the abyss of error. I could list many such things, were I not sparing your most patient ears from the things these false teachers slyly and cunningly omit in this confession of theirs. For why do they not add what they think about the fire of purgatory, about the offerings for the dead and the purification rites <note>original: "februis"; a reference to the Roman month of purification, here likely meaning Christian rituals for the souls in purgatory.</note>, about the sacred rites and ceremonies of the Church, and about the intercessions and prayers of the saints in heaven? Here, all of them are as silent as **Seriphian frogs** <note>A classical proverb. The frogs on the island of Seriphos were said to be mute; Augustine implies the Brethren are tactically silent on these controversial topics.</note> and merely mumble, though in their own workshops they are accustomed to preach about these things with a nearly **Stentorian voice** <note>A voice as loud as fifty men, named after Stentor, the Greek herald in the Iliad.</note>. 

For this reason, most excellent and religious Prince, let nothing of these things with which they try to bend Your Majesty move you. Persevere in what you have most holily and religiously decreed against the enemies of the Christian faith; exterminate and crush this college of Satan, and shatter their bold fronts with which they oppose the holy Church of God, lest by their example the souls of the simple be led astray. And lest, to the shame of the Christian name, your kingdoms—because of these lost and blasphemous men—be taunted and defamed by neighboring nations with the crime of heresy. For as our Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso).</note> says no less elegantly than truly:
> An incurable wound must be cut away with the sword, lest the healthy part be infected. <note>original: "Immedicabile vulnus Ense recidendū est ne pars syncera trahāt." A quote from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* regarding the necessity of harsh measures to save the whole.</note>

Thus may the Best and Greatest God establish your throne. May He most happily direct your most auspicious offspring, and after this earthly peak, place you among the heavenly seats of the blessed.
From Buda, the 14th day of the month of November, in the year of the incarnate God, 1506.

->TO THE SAME ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE VLADISLAUS,<-
->AUGUSTINE THE DOCTOR SENDS GREETINGS.<-

I have seen, and seen again, and I confess, not without great disgust, the letters which the perfidious and abject rustic **Pighards** <note>A common derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren.</note> now write to Your Majesty, most illustrious and most Christian King. And with them also a certain **Martha**—not that host of Christ, but a tavern-keeper for the devil. If I wished to respond to these letters, the discipline of my character, the gravity of my mind, and the immense heap of duties with which I am daily occupied would not permit it. Nevertheless, I shall write briefly and without preparation, setting aside all the artistry of speech, and I shall expose the cunning of that damned people in simple words. Attend, I pray, and consider before all other things, most Christian Prince, how craftily they strive in these letters to cover their heresy regarding the **sacrament of Christ’s body and blood**—to omit their other errors. In the first place, they confess that the true body and blood are contained under the species of bread and wine, but immediately, so they are not caught in a lie (because they have preached and do preach...

# AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...because those things <note>Referring to the previous page's discussion on the icons and intercession of saints.</note> ought neither to be venerated nor should honor be shown to them. Again, in bold opposition to what came before, they move forward with wicked testimonies, covering their treachery with disputes and cunning. I pray you, attend to these matters and weigh how the poison of the most ferocious snakes—as I stated in my first writings and letters—could no longer remain hidden in their hearts regarding the ineffable sacrament <note>The "ineffable sacrament" refers to the Eucharist, or Holy Communion.</note>, but in these times it has poured itself out into the light. 

For if they now confess the true body and blood of Christ under the species <note>term: <term>Species</term> refers to the outward appearances of bread and wine that remain after the substance has supposedly changed.</note>, why then do they not venerate that true Christ? Let them be asked in the meantime: Is this the same Christ whom they confess and say is present with us under the sacrament of bread and wine, or is he divided from the one who sits at the right hand of God? If he is the same, why do they not venerate this one just as they do the other? If he is divided, then according to their logic we would posit two Christs: one on earth, contained in the sacrament and to be despised; the other in heaven, honorable, worthy of praise, and chosen. 

But to say and affirm this—not to mention that it is incongruous and full of heresy—is altogether crude and childish. Let Your Highness, I pray, weigh and recognize this. What more should I say when they flatly confess that the body of Christ under the appearance of bread and wine ought not to be venerated? What more should we seek from them? Indeed, we are by no means ignorant of what kind of punishment and vengeance those most wicked **little thieves** have deserved. They are not even worthy to be consumed by the noble element of fire, but rather that their bodies be torn apart and devoured by the most ferocious wild beasts; that dogs should lick their blood in vengeance for the salvation of the body and blood of our Jesus Christ. Thus, by their "merits," even executioners might be compelled to be honored <note>Augustine is suggesting that the act of executing such heretics is so righteous that the executioners themselves deserve honor for it.</note> because these men spurn and despise giving honor to Christ.

## THE DEFENSE OF THE WALDENSIAN BRETHREN AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF DOCTOR AUGUSTINE GIVEN TO THE KING,

Let it be known to all that just as we wrote two letters to the Royal Majesty, we gave in those first letters an account only of the Apostolic and universal faith. In doing so, we addressed that of which they accused us—which was not and is not among us, and we trust in God it shall never be. 

Furthermore, not long ago, Royal letters were sent through the provinces in which they called us heretics and errant ones, claiming that we spoke rebellious words against the Virgin Mary and the saints. They ordered that the Barons—under whose dominion we live—should present us at Prague on the feast day of Saint John for a revocation <note>A formal public retraction of their "heretical" beliefs.</note> of our views. When we learned of this, we wrote again to the Royal Majesty regarding these matters, so that we might not only give an account of our faith, but also of our understanding—especially concerning the body of Christ and other things. 

We made this known according to the scriptures of faith, not only to the Royal Majesty but to everyone in common. These letters were delivered to the town hall in Prague, making known the fit and pure causes of our salvation and upon what foundation our salvation and faith stand. Based on these things, we assign fault to the priests <note>Referring to the Catholic priesthood, whom the Brethren viewed as corrupt or unscriptural.</note>, which is why we do not dare to use them in divine service. We also explained why we do not perform the traditional veneration of the body and blood of Christ, and we gave an account regarding many other articles about which they accused us. We did this to the end that we might—if it were possible—cease those insults and oppressions that have risen against us, so that they might not stir up divine wrath upon themselves and this Kingdom, and so that some measure of peace might be brought to the dissensions in this province. 

In the first letters we sent to the Royal Majesty, we prayed for his grace: that he would be willing to give us a merciful audience, and that he would not permit others to compel us by force to follow their own presumed will. Subsequently, the Royal Majesty gave us an answer through a letter from the noble maiden Martha of Boskovice <note>Martha of Boskovice was a prominent noblewoman and supporter of the Bohemian Brethren who acted as an intermediary.</note>.

## TWO LETTERS OF DOCTOR AUGUSTINE,

instead of a merciful response, he returned that severity which he previously entrusted to the lords. Regarding this matter, we did not know what to say; therefore, we undertook this: to turn our eyes to God in humble prayer and tears, believing fully that He is able to deliver us from all things if He wills. We trust in Him; whatever part He plays, He will lead us to the clarification of His name and justice, and to our salvation. May honor be to His grace for all things forever and ever, Amen. 

We also make it known to all that among the letters of His Royal Majesty <note>Vladislaus II, King of Bohemia and Hungary (reigned 1471–1516).</note> which he wrote and sent to the aforementioned virgin Martha <note>Martha of Boskowitz, a noblewoman and protector of the Bohemian Brethren.</note>, two letters of a certain Doctor Augustine were found, in which he makes himself known by name. He writes back to His Royal Majesty against our two letters, stirring His Royal Majesty to that severity which seems to us entirely against the justice of the law of God and men, urging that His Royal Majesty should not relent in that severity. He reviles us, calling us both "heretics" and "evildoers," and suppressing us with many other hostile words. He ascribes fraud, cunning, and diabolical poison to our simple and innocent writing; he attributes such things to us, doing us an injustice. 

Understanding that his writing can reach many people—who, reading it and not having our satisfaction, will take his writing as true and because of this might stir the wrath of God upon themselves—and fearing that by our silence we might become a cause of that very thing, we have presumed simply to set out his writing piece by piece and respond as much as the Lord God grants by His grace. However, we take care that we will not match him in his reviling and his least-Christian oppression. Furthermore, what we wish to write, we shall do without indignation, "not returning evil for evil" <note>A reference to 1 Peter 3:9.</note> neither to him nor to anyone else; but what necessity compels, we will make known: where he does us injury and writes false testimony against his neighbor, so that his wicked writing may not be taken for truth where and in what ways he harms us. 

At the beginning, we say this: if we knew for certain that His Royal Majesty gave this writing of Doctor Augustine on behalf of his majesty as a response to our writings, we would write to His Royal Majesty. But because no mention is made of this—only that those letters of Doctor Augustine were sent along with the letters of His Royal Majesty—and because that Doctor Augustine himself does not send or write them to us (since no mention is made of this, nor does he demand a response from us), we did not know what should be done. It seemed best to us to write to everyone in common, to whomever his letters might come, so that this response of ours might also follow them. And so that Doctor Augustine writes as follows:

Setting aside the mockeries, blasphemy, and suppressions of that doctor—so that we do not seem like him, "returning evil for evil," and so that we do not exceed the command of God and the tracks of His examples, who "when he was cursed, did not curse in return" <note>original: "cui cum maledicereť non remaledixit," referencing 1 Peter 2:23.</note>—we shall proceed to the point where he touches upon our reputation and the honor which we have before God and men, taking from us that of which the Apostle speaks:

> For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God, and not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God, we have lived in this world. <note>original: "Nam gloria nostra hæc ē testimoniū cōscientiæ nræ q in simplicitate cordis & synceritate dei & nō in sapientia carnali sed in gĩa dei cōuersati sumus in hoc mūdo," quoting 2 Corinthians 1:12.</note>

And God and our own conscience know this simplicity of our heart better. But that man, against the command of God and our salvation, not only judges but also condemns us, and this in such a way as to say we produced that writing in hypocrisy and fraud, and not in truth, to cover our heresy; and that we deceive His Royal Majesty with diabolical fraud, and thus we would lead His Majesty and the simple people into faithlessness <note>term: <term>perfidia</term> (faithlessness/perfidy) was a serious legal and religious charge, implying a total betrayal of the Christian faith.</note> for our own favor, so that we might escape the punishment imposed on us by His Majesty, as he writes further down. But we, before God who knows and judges the secrets of hearts, say that we used no cunning to hide our writing...

They argue that their intentions are simple and sincere, citing Scripture to justify their refusal to respond with similar vitriol.</summary>

<header>THE WALDENSIANS AGAINST [AUGUSTINE]</header>

To the Royal Majesty: we acted, but only because of those causes which were then set before us. Because it was necessary, we gave only an account of the faith of the twelve articles <note>The Apostles' Creed.</note> which we hold in our heart and confess with our mouth. We have at hand a written account of the meaning and faith that we hold regarding salvation. For the sake of explaining the reasons for our separation, we would have gladly made our views known to his Majesty through our writings, had he desired us to send them. However, since his Royal Majesty did not wish to give us any response, we did not presume to send anything further without just cause. From this, let everyone recognize—we pray—that it is not true that "cunning" is ascribed to us here. If such cunning were in us, we surely would have sought to hide many things in another writing to his Majesty. We say this especially because the King has turned against all of us more severely than before, whereas according to the previous writings, his severity should only have reached some of us.

But on the contrary, out of our innocence, we wrote other letters to his Majesty as the time required. Just as in our first letters to his Royal Majesty we were accused of perfidy and error, for this reason we provided him a brief account of our faith, so that we would not cause him boredom with a long text. But when we were again accused by his Royal Majesty of heresy and rebellion concerning certain articles, we were forced by that situation to give a proper account of what we feel regarding these matters. It can be briefly concluded that a great injustice and harm is done to us by that Doctor Augustine <note>Augustine of Olomouc (1467–1513), a prominent humanist and fierce opponent of the Bohemian Brethren.</note> against our good conscience, which we hold before God and take care to maintain among men.

From this it can be much better recognized by anyone that if we were clever hypocrites and pretenders, we could easily cast off the things with which he oppresses us. If we did not have a heart right toward God, we could simply confess and do what others confess and do, even against our conscience. We could act like the Sadducees <note>The authors use the Sadducees as a symbol for people who prioritize social standing and physical comfort over religious conviction.</note>, who, so that they may be held in public honor and so that no one might disturb their life of tranquility and pleasures, hide the errors they hold until they are forced by necessity to make a confession. Truly, since it is within us to defend this innocence according to the confession of God’s will, we submit ourselves to every danger of our possessions and our bodies, even unto death. Therefore, let either Doctor Augustine or anyone else who does not believe our confession and our scripture, believe our works; for every tree is known by its fruits. 

We confess, however, that while we use that simplicity, we nevertheless employ prudence of mind, according to the Savior’s precept where he says: *Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves* <note>Matthew 10:16.</note>, and *beware of men, for they will deliver you up in councils and in their synagogues*. And in another place: *Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they perhaps trample them under their feet, and the dogs turn and tear you to pieces* <note>Matthew 7:6.</note>. Saint Paul also says: *Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time* <note>Colossians 4:5.</note>. Nevertheless, we incline more from that prudence toward simplicity, because we understand simplicity to be more secure before God than that very "prudence" of which Roman craftiness provides us with many examples—by which they have often deceived some of our people.

And as for the charge he imposes on us that we agree with Beelzebub, the god of flies <note>original: "Beelzebub muscarum deo." This is a derogatory reference to the Brethren's worship, comparing them to idolaters.</note>, he does this following the example of his companion, Doctor Henry <note>Heinrich Institoris (c. 1430–1505), the inquisitor and co-author of the "Malleus Maleficarum."</note>, the inquisitor of heretical depravity. This man came to Moravia and Bohemia with apostolic letters and commands, and requested of a certain Baron and several others that he be given the opportunity to confer with us, pretending that he intended to join the fellowship of the Brethren. When some of our people were gathered in a meeting at Olomouc, he embraced them and gave thanks to those who had brought the brethren, saying they had brought such upright men. He called them "most dear," shared a cup with them, and dismissed them in a friendly manner. Behold! Those simple folk thought all was faithful and holy, while in reality, it was cunning and unfaithful. For he noted some by name as if they were arch-heretics and false witnesses, and he printed his little work in great numbers, in which this also is found, that...

They recount a deceptive encounter with the inquisitor Heinrich Institoris, who pretended to be a friend only to later publish attacks against them.</summary>

### TWO LETTERS OF DR. AUGUSTINE <note>This refers to Augustine of Olomouc (1467–1513), a fierce critic of the Bohemian Brethren, not the famous Saint Augustine of Hippo.</note>

...that we should swallow flies and locusts <note>A metaphorical way of saying they are expected to accept trivial or false teachings.</note>, and that this Master <note>Augustine of Olomouc.</note> should prove us to be priests of lies, and that it is from him that we should understand the Scriptures. He has even affirmed this with an oath. Dr. Augustine imposes such things upon us; yet it is no wonder, for the masters and teachers said the same of the Lord Christ: that he had a demon and cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. If they said this to the Father of the household, what will they not say to his servants?

He falsely accuses us, claiming that our confession is not genuine, based on the reasoning that we write one thing about the sacrament of Christ’s body but believe another; that we say one thing and do another; and that we cunningly hide behind such a confession so that we might appear righteous before men. Let it be known to all that we do not write as he imposes upon us. 

He himself writes that the bread and wine, in their natural substance, are transmuted into the body and blood of Christ—into Christ as God and man—so that nothing of the substance of the created bread and wine remains, but only the appearances <note>original: "accidentia," a technical term in medieval philosophy referring to the outward qualities of a thing (like color or taste) that remain even if the inner "substance" changes.</note> are miraculously sustained in a naked state. For such a confession of faith has no foundation in the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, who spoke no word about a "conversion of substance," nor did he say that he would be "under these species," nor "in it," nor "from it," nor "together with it," as many have explained with great scrupulosity and continue to explain today. We do not receive these explanations in place of faith because the words of the Savior do not harmonize with them. 

The Gospel says that the Lord Savior, taking bread into his venerable hands, gave thanks, blessed it, and broke it, and gave it to his disciples; and presenting that bread as his body, he pointed to the bread and said: **This is my body.** Likewise, taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: **Drink from this, all of you**, and giving thanks he said: **This cup is the new testament in my blood**, or, **This is my blood of the new testament, which is poured out for you.** 

And we, believing the words of Christ with such simplicity, have held this and hold it today. We have given such an account based on faith—on that Catholic Christian faith founded in Holy Scripture—and we confess it with our mouths. Whenever a worthy priest, in accordance with the meaning of the Savior and the ordinance of the Holy and Indivisible Trinity, offers prayer with his faithful people and says that word, **"This is my body"** and **"This is my blood,"** immediately the bread present is the body of Christ given unto death, and the wine present is his blood for the redemption of sinners. 

This is the confession of our faith, founded on the words of the Lord. For true testimony of this matter, we have the primitive Church with the entire college of the Apostles, in whose times they called this sacrament "the Lord's Supper," as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: *When you come together into one place, it is not to eat the Lord’s Supper.* Secondly, they called it the "breaking of bread," as in the Acts of the Apostles: *Continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, they ate their food with gladness and simplicity of heart.* And a little earlier: *And they were persevering in the doctrine of the Apostles and in the communication of the breaking of bread and in prayers.* Regarding this same communication of the breaking of bread, the Apostle says: *And the bread which we break, is it not the participation in the body of the Lord?* 

They believed this bread to be not only the body of Christ, but also to remain in its own substance of bread along with its appearances after the consecration, and that the body of Christ is there. This is confessed by him who was caught up into the third heaven <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul and his vision described in 2 Corinthians 12.</note> and received the sacraments; he says: *I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you,* and further on: *As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.* And further: *Whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man prove himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning...*
