<header>THE WALDENSES AGAINST <note>The header likely continues from the previous page: "The Waldenses Against Augustine."</note></header>

...the body of the Lord. From this it is manifest that the early church held this faith and confessed it, and did not err, and yet did not offer "reverence" <note>In this context, "reverence" refers to the ritual adoration or bowing before the physical bread of the Eucharist.</note> to this sacrament. For at that time, following the example of Christ, they received it immediately while sitting, and they did not retain any of it, nor did they carry it out of the house. This institution stood for a long time, as the *Chronicles of Deeds* show, and as the most ancient Greek, Origen—who lived immediately after the times of Christ as a primary Teacher—writes in his third book on Moses <note>original: "super tertiū librū Mosi," referring to Origen’s Homilies on Leviticus.</note>: "Whoever takes this bread of the supper of Christ on the second or third day, his soul shall not be blessed, but defiled." For this reason, when the Gibeonites <note>A group from the Old Testament who deceived the Israelites with moldy bread to secure a treaty.</note> brought old bread to the children of Israel, they were required to carry wood and water, yet they were not heretics, nor were they judged alien to the faith on that account. Yet that doctor <note>Augustine of Olomouc.</note> accuses us, adjudging such an evil to those who believe and act thus.

Furthermore, we say that he does us an injustice in this: that he claims we speak insulting words. We take care to follow the precept of Saint Paul, "Blaspheme no one," unless he considers it blasphemy when we speak and write for the honor of God—concerning God's power and justice, concerning adoration, and other just matters according to the faith of the Scriptures without blasphemy. In the same way, the word "blasphemy" was imputed to the Savior by his adversaries, saying: "You have blasphemed." And yet we will still confess, even in times of necessity, regarding this sacrament of the body and blood of Christ: that he did not give it for "veneration" <note>To be worshipped as an object.</note> so that it might be adored there, since he who sits at the right hand of God in the heavens ought to be adored with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as everyone must confess. Rather, he gave it so that his blessed body might be received by everyone under both species <note>Both the bread and the wine, a key demand of the Bohemian Reformation.</note> in memory of his passion. Whoever acts or receives otherwise does so against the will and ordination of God and in rebellion against the early church; such a person does not hold the right faith, as we have said in our Latin letters.

In this part of his writing, he again does us a notable injury when he perverts the confession of our faith regarding the consecration of priests. For we have given an account not only of ourselves, but of the whole Catholic faith as we understand it: from where the priestly ordination itself, both major and minor, took its first beginning. For it comes not from the Pope, but from Christ—the eternal priest and Bishop separated from sinners, which is his glory. Regarding this matter, we made a confession in our explanation with these words: "We hold by faith that the ordination of priests proceeds in truth from the High Bishop and Great Priest." This is so that the ministry of Christ's embassy, the preaching of doctrine, judgment, and the offering of prayers by men may take place. We hold that the Lord Christ alone—and not the Pope nor anyone else—is the greatest priest and bishop, the pastor and common head of the entire Holy Church.

We have certain authorities for this proof of faith. First is the word of David, through whom God the Father says to the Son with an oath: *You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.* <note>Psalm 110:4.</note> The Apostle, proving this same thing, says of him: *And the others indeed were made many priests, because they were prevented by death from continuing*—just as these [priests] are now—*but he, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood.* And therefore he is able to save eternally those who approach God through him, as he is always living to intercede for us. And again, regarding his bishopric, he says: *Wherefore, holy brothers, sharers in the heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus Christ*—and not Pope Julius <note>A reference to Pope Julius II (reigned 1503–1513).</note> or any other. And again: *We have such a high priest, who sits at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy things.* And again: *For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest: holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; who does not have the daily necessity, as the priests do, to offer sacrifices first for his own sins and then for the people's. For this he did once for all by offering himself.* Otherwise, he would have been forced to die often since the beginning of the world; but now, he has appeared once at the end of the ages to blot out sins by his own sacrifice. But another time he will show himself to all those without sin who expect him for salvation. And Saint Peter did not turn [them] toward himself...

## TWO LETTERS OF ST. AUGUSTINE,

<note>original: "BINAS LITTERAS D. AVGVSTINI" — While the heading mentions Augustine, the text below is a polemical argument against the Papacy using various scriptural citations.</note>

nor did he call upon himself by his own name, but showed that he was leading toward the Lord Christ, saying: "You have now returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls." <note>1 Peter 2:25</note> And that he alone is the head of the holy faith, the Apostle says: "But speaking the truth in charity, let us grow up in him in all things, who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, being compact and connected by every joint of its sub-ministry according to the operation in the measure of every single member, makes the increase of the body" <note>Ephesians 4:15-16</note> and so forth. And not through the Pope; and that He alone is the head of the entire holy Church, [Scripture] says: "And he gave him to be head over the church, which is the body of Christ and his fullness, who fills all in all." <note>Ephesians 1:22-23</note> And we here, along with the Apostle and the primitive church, say and confess that He is the Bishop and Head, but not Pope Julius <note>Likely referring to Pope Julius II or III, depending on the date of the manuscript</note> nor those following him, because He [Christ] spoke of himself that he is the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the true vine, the foundation, and the cornerstone without which no one can do anything; from whose fullness we have all received, and grace for grace, so that all might come to him. And God the Father commanded that all should obey him, and it is he who is able to be present for the universal faith and to any member until the end of the age. Just as he says: "I am with you even unto the consummation of the age." <note>Matthew 28:20</note> And that he is always in the catholic <note>In this context, "catholic" means "universal" rather than specifically Roman Catholic</note> faith, he says: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." <note>Matthew 18:20</note> He is the one whom Saint John saw in the midst of the seven candlesticks, walking, and correcting, and rebuking. And therefore the Apostle says that he may dwell in your hearts through faith; and again: "Christ is in you." Therefore no bishop, neither the Roman nor the Greek nor any other, is the head of the entire holy faith, except Jesus Christ alone; because no one else offered his body and blood for us, being innocent and holy and separated from sinners, and so forth. Nor did anyone else redeem them, nor purge them, nor make them safe. Nor does he [the Pope] cohabit with them in truth and grace, nor does he save them. 

But we say this: that it should be enough for the Roman Pontiff, together with his council, to be a faithful servant of Jesus by following him in a life that is honest, poor, humble, patient, chaste, and abstinent, so that he might show the way to God, teaching Him along with His law, and serving the Gospel and the sacraments so that he might lead the people to Him, just as Saint Peter and Paul and others did. For He [Christ] is the door, and he who does not enter through him is a thief and a robber. Therefore, look around, we ask: who desires these bishops and prelates of the present world? Whose followers are they? Of the honest life of Christ, or of the glory of the world, and the honor of dignity which comes from benefices, riches, and the delights of life? And you will know for certain that the opposite stands in the holy place. 

Keep in mind Saint Peter and Paul, whose successors they claim to be: what did they obtain then in Rome? Was it the seat of Caesar with a triple kingdom <note>A reference to the Papal Tiara, or Triregnum, representing three levels of authority</note>, or the gallows of the cross? Was it the glory of the world, or contempt? Did they serve tables and divide wealth among themselves, or did they more willingly serve the word of God? And there, anyone can recognize according to the holy scriptures whose successor the present Roman High Priest <term>summus pontifex</term> is, and whom he serves. Regarding the office of dignity of the present age and the ancient customs of the Apostles, their elders, and their counselors, read the letters of Francesco Petrarch "Without a Title" <note>original: *sine titulo* — Petrarch’s *Liber sine nomine* was a famous 14th-century critique of the corruption and worldliness of the Papal court in Avignon</note> if you wish, and there you will see their "holiness." 

Let enough be said about these things for now, so that it may be known that we have not judged the Roman High Priest to be our head, nor anyone else, but the blessed Jesus Christ himself. Therefore, we will omit responses to the mockery which the doctor makes of us here. Likewise, we will say briefly: let him allow it, let him look at the beginnings of the primitive church—how many were from the noble, the powerful, the wise, or the learned in these offices, and what kind of living they had? And that should press his lips shut, and also [consider] who brought greater fruit to the Lord. We are not filled with shame for our priests because they labor with their hands, seeking a living for themselves as best they can; for in this way, apostolic doctrine and example [leads] us here.

<header>THE WALDENSIANS AGAINST</header>

...leads, and we see this more gladly than if they were to spend their leisure in taverns, pursuits of lust <note>original: "commercia veneris" — literally 'the trade of Venus,' referring to sexual immorality or prostitution</note>, and vanities, following after usury, sacrilege, and other wickednesses. It was said above that we have given an account of those matters in which they previously accused us. Even in these letters, they never blamed us for crafting rebellious words against the Virgin Mary and the saints of God, but they only accused us of this: that we do not believe in her virginity. 

In the second letters, they first accused us of this, and yet it was not clearly expressed in what matter until Doctor Augustine <note>This likely refers to a contemporary Catholic interlocutor or critic rather than the ancient Church Father, though the Waldensians often engaged with Augustinian theology.</note> said that he was responding to the first letters; he responds nonetheless to the second, where we satisfy those who accuse us, clearing ourselves and writing to the Royal Majesty and to all people how we believe and hold and think concerning the Virgin Mary, and the singular holiness and blessedness with which God made her blessed above all others, and afterwards concerning the veneration that befits her. 

Whoever wishes to know, let him read those letters there and he will know that we do not craft rebellious words against her, but rather those things which belong to the true religion of Christ. For to this end we have confessed that the honor, power, and piety which belong to God alone and to the Lamb <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the Lamb of God.</note>, we attribute to no creature, but to God alone, because he says: "My glory I will not give to another." <note>Isaiah 42:8</note> And "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me," <note>Isaiah 45:23 / Romans 14:11</note> and "The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve," <note>Matthew 4:10 / Deuteronomy 6:13</note> and Baruch says, "It is necessary for you to be adored, O Lord." And David: "Come, let us adore and fall down and weep before the Lord who made us." <note>Psalm 95:6</note> And in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>: "Fear the Lord and give him honor because the hour of his judgment is come, and adore him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the fountains of water." 

And because they in the primitive church gave honor to God alone, and not to the saints and the Virgin, so John says: "Worthy art thou, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power, because thou hast created all things." And again: "And the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and adored him who lives forever and ever." And Saint Paul to the Ephesians: "For this cause I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." And in the Acts of the Apostles: "When he had said these things, kneeling down, he prayed with all of them." 

And God gave us an example of himself: he fell upon his knees to the Father, so that we should expect help from no one except from God, as he says through Joel: "Turn to the Lord your God with all your heart," <note>Joel 2:13</note> and through Hosea he says: "Return, O Israel, to the Lord thy God," <note>Hosea 14:1</note> and through Zechariah: "Turn to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of hosts." 

And concerning the seeking of help, God says again through Isaiah: "If you seek, seek; turn and come." And in the book of Wisdom, Solomon says: "Thou art the Lord who hast power of life and death," and the Lord God said to his disciples: "Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna." And David says: "I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me; my help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." <note>Psalm 121:1-2</note> And again in another psalm: "He that dwells in the aid of the most High, shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven." <note>Psalm 91:1</note> 

The writings of the psalms are full of these testimonies. Even all the saints of the Old and New Testament sought help from God alone, and they did not cry out to saints born of mortal condition to provide help. For David says to the Lord: "When I was in trouble I cried, and he heard me." And again: "With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice to God, and he attended to me." And again: "Great are the mercies to all who invoke thee," and "The Lord is near to all who invoke him in truth." And again: "They invoked the Lord, and he himself heard them." 

But concerning others it says: "They have not called upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear," <note>Psalm 14:4-5</note> just as our people do now regarding the invocation of saints [male] and saints [female]. For there is no other name under heaven given to men for invocation except the name of God alone; because just as no name is given for adoration and the attainment of salvation, nor for believing in it, except the name of our Lord Jesus Christ alone. So...

# TWO LETTERS OF DOCTOR AUGUSTINE,

furthermore, no name has been given for us to call upon or to worship [except Christ], because to him alone were the promises made. For so he says: *Whatever you ask my Father in my name, he will give to you; ask and you will receive* <note>original: "Quicquid pecieritis patrē meum in noīe meo. dabit vobis, petite & accipietis" — John 16:23-24</note>. For this reason, he taught his disciples to pray, saying: *Thus you shall pray: Our Father, who art in heaven.* Thus, honor and glory ought to be shown to God alone, just as Daniel said: *To you, O God of our fathers, I give thanks, and I praise you* <note>original: "tibi deus patrū nostrorū cōfiteor, teqꝫ laudo" — Daniel 2:23</note>. And again, Nebuchadnezzar said: *I praise, and exalt, and glorify the King of heaven.* And that we should sing hymns to him alone, the Psalm says: *Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things.* And Saint Paul says: *I give thanks to my God.* And the Lord Jesus himself says: *I thank you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth.* 

For God ought to be praised in his saints, just as David said: *Praise the Lord in his saints* <note>original: "Laudate dñm in sanctis suis" — Psalm 150:1. While often translated as "sanctuary," the Waldensians here interpret "sanctis" as "holy people" or "saints."</note>. And we do this when we praise God in this Virgin and in other saints, because he gave such grace and such benefits out of his goodness to them, and to us through them. And we do not only praise God in this blessed Virgin, but we also acknowledge her as blessed and happy, and we love her and follow her example as much as we are able. 

But if that Doctor or another were to show from the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the authority of Holy Scripture.</note> that we should show her more—that we should expect help from her, or honor her with the bending of the knee and prayer, or that she intercedes for us, or that God promised he would do all things she asks in his name, or that she stands with her son before God the Father to be a sacrifice before God the Father—well then, let him show this in the Scripture which is inspired by the Holy Spirit. Let him send proof rather than calling us heretics; but he is able to write and curse as he wishes. Yet if he were a private citizen and did not put his hope in the power of the world, but instead had to prove his faith through gentleness and Scripture, we believe he would act more mercifully with others. 

Nor is it true that we believe the Virgin Mary is equal to other women. For we believe that no other virgin conceived a son by the Holy Spirit as she did; indeed, no other woman gave birth and remained a virgin. No other woman is blessed as this Virgin is, and the fruit of no other virgin’s womb is blessed like hers, so that in him all generations might be blessed, and all might receive from his fullness grace upon grace. Indeed, no other is "Full of Grace" <note>original: "gr̄a plena"</note> except her; no other is called "Blessed among all generations" except her alone, and so for the rest. Therefore, we do not hold, nor do we consider her to be entirely like any other woman. 

Nor is it true that we treat the holy days of commemoration of the glorious Virgin Mary as if they were profane; rather, we observe them as is fitting. Nor is it true that we have no songs about her; for we sing many songs about her in the praise of God. From this let God be praised: though that Doctor, in responding to our letters sent to the Royal Majesty, spoke many insults and provocations against us, yet in all that time he found nothing and wrote nothing against us that was an evil thought against the faith of the Scriptures, or any straying opinion that was against the faith and deeds of the primitive Church. 

Instead, he wants us to have placed in our confession things about which Holy Scripture and the Catholic faith are silent, and of which the first Church and those following for a long time knew nothing—matters in which the present error stands. And because, by the help of God, we have now for the most part defended ourselves against the unjust accusations with which he unjustly stained us before the Royal Majesty (following the precept of God’s law and the ancient Church), so too, with God's help, we wish to resist the present points on which we are accused by this Doctor and called heretics. We wish to show what must be held by faith concerning those points, and first concerning Purgatory, about which we believe this: 

Purgatory is twofold. One is here [in this life], the other is in the future age. The first has its foundation in the Holy Scriptures and is certain, in which people purge themselves toward immortal bodies, as the Savior, the apostles, and the primitive Church testified, and those following for a long time practiced well. The second Purgatory is in the other world, and this is uncertain, because Holy Scripture gives no testimony of it. The primitive Church knew nothing of it, nor did those who followed for a long time, and the ancient Doctors do not confirm it, especially regarding its location. But more recently, the new [doctors]...

<meta>This page continues the Waldensian theological argument against the Roman Catholic doctrine of Purgatory. Having established in the previous section that Christ is the sole mediator, the text now contrasts the "modern" scholastic teachings of Thomas Aquinas with the "ancient" authority of Saint Augustine to argue that Purgatory is not a physical place in the afterlife, but a process of spiritual cleansing that happens in this life through Christ.</meta>

# SAINT AUGUSTINE AGAINST...

<note>The header "D AVGVSTINVS CONTRA" likely refers to "Saint Augustine Against [the errors of others]" or is part of a larger title like "Saint Augustine Against the Manichaeans," though the text here uses him to argue against Thomas Aquinas.</note>

Certain people not long ago, such as **Thomas Aquinas**, found a third place in **Hell**. But the ancient doctor **Augustine** felt otherwise, saying: "The place of purgatory is not shown, except that through many examples souls have shown themselves in these places and have been shown in torments." Perhaps they will say from what is closest that all souls are punished in the place where they committed their crimes, since Scripture also says to that effect: *by the things which a man sins, by those same things he is also tortured* <note>original: "p quæ peccat quis p hec & torquetur" — Wisdom 11:16</note>, and another scripture says: *Just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve justice for sanctification* <note>original: "Sicut exhibuistis membra vestra seruire immunditiæ..." — Romans 6:19</note>. 

And so the ancient doctor **Augustine**, along with other ancient doctors, contradicts Thomas. For the earlier ones held that after the resurrection of the Savior, no souls enter Hell except those of the damned. But Thomas "found" two places in Hell: one for the unbaptized <note>referring to the Limbo of Infants</note>, and the other for souls needing to be purged. Let our doctor Augustine reconcile them and show who is more just, and whom we should believe. There are many such matters in which they disagree—more on this elsewhere. For it would be best, in an uncertain matter about which the Scriptures are not only silent but even say the opposite, not to assert anything, according to the opinion of the wise **Seneca**: *Concerning uncertain things you ought not to affirm, but hold an uncertain judgment.*

We will also set down how the earlier "inventors" thought about a second purgatory, since this too is against the faith. That is, they claim that those to whom God gave a place for penance, yet who did not complete that penance, also pass into purgatory. But these affirmers of purgatory send everyone there—and they send them first to where they know they will gain an advantage <note>a critique of the sale of indulgences and paid masses for the dead</note>. They do not wish to make a distinction, nor do they judge for whom they ought to pray, treating the living and the dead the same. Just as among the living they do not know whether they are in a state of grace or damnation, so they do not know regarding the dead. But they confess that souls are in purgatory because **Greed** <note>original: "Auaritia"</note> taught them to say so. 

Other doctors felt better about this, saying that only those who did not satisfy their penance are purged—meaning the penance imposed by priests, such as fasts, vows, prayers, almsgiving, and the like. So that this error of purgatory might be better understood, we will set down the truth of the faith concerning the *certain* purgatory here in this world. First, it is found in the grace of God, the merit of **Jesus Christ**, and the cleansing of the **Holy Spirit** through faith, love, and hope; and especially through the suffering of this world. Then, it occurs through the Word of God, true repentance, works of mercy, and the service of God, as in the receiving of the sacrament and perseverance until death. Sacred scripture bears witness to this. 

First, concerning grace: *I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I will have mercy* <note>original: "miſerebor cui miſertus ſum" — Exodus 33:19 / Romans 9:15</note>. And in another place it says: *I will be propitious to their iniquity, and I will remember their sins no more.* And **Saint Paul** says: *By grace you are saved through faith* <note>original: "gratia enim estis saluati per fidem" — Ephesians 2:8</note>, and of himself alone he says: *By the grace of God I am what I am.* And **Zechariah** says: *There shall be a fountain open to the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem for the washing of the sinner and the unclean.* And Saint Paul: *How much more has the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleansed our conscience from the works of death to serve the living God?* <note>original: "Quanto magis christi..." — Hebrews 9:14</note>. And **Saint John** says: *He himself is the propitiation for our sins.* 

Concerning the Holy Spirit, whom God promised to give as a cleansing over all flesh, the Apostle says: *For we were once foolish,* and so forth. From these things it is manifest that there is no other principal place of a certain purgatory except the Lord Christ, of whom it was rightly said by the angel: *For he himself shall save his people from their sins.* And so Saint Paul says: *Making a purgation of sins, he sits at the right hand of majesty on high.* He is the fountain of water springing up into eternal life—and this happens in the future age because they pass from death to life. Everyone who is to be saved must drink from this fountain full of justice and equity; one must receive it through the love of the grace of his merit...

<meta>This page continues the argument that "Purgatory" is not a physical place of punishment after death, as described by medieval theologians like Thomas Aquinas, but is instead the process of spiritual cleansing through Christ's grace in this life. It uses a series of biblical citations to redefine "purgatory" as the purification of the soul through faith, hope, charity, and repentance.</meta>

### . TWO LETTERS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE .

The grace of the Holy Spirit, who pours out his love into the hearts of the faithful <note>original: "de amore suo transfundit in corda fidelium" — a reference to Romans 5:5</note>, means that by grace alone, through the gift of faith, everyone who is to be saved comes to "purgatory" <note>Here used in its literal sense: a "cleansing" or "purification"</note> through Christ Jesus. As **Saint Paul** says: *A man is not justified by the works of the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ.* And we believe in Christ Jesus so that we may be justified by the faith of Christ and not by the works of the law. Christ says: *Whoever believes in me has eternal life.* And that leper said out of faith: *Lord, if you will, you can make me clean,* and the Lord said: *I will; be clean.* And again: *Thy faith has made thee whole.* And **Saint Peter** says: *Purifying their hearts by faith.* Regarding love, the Lord says to **Mary**: *Many sins are forgiven her.* Regarding charity, **Saint John** says: *Charity covers a multitude of sins* <note>Though attributed here to John, this is found in 1 Peter 4:8</note>; and regarding the obedience of charity, **Saint Peter** says: *Purifying your souls in the obedience of charity.* Regarding hope, the Lord says to the paralytic: *Be of good cheer, son; thy sins are forgiven thee,* and **Saint Paul** says: *Hope does not confound.* Regarding the power of this faith, **Saint Peter** says: *Minister in your faith virtue; and in virtue knowledge; and in knowledge abstinence... if these things be in you,* and so forth. Regarding repentance, God says through the **Prophet**: *The impiety of the impious shall not hurt him in whatever day he shall be converted from his impiety.* And the **Prophet** <note>King David in Psalm 51</note> says: *Sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop and I shall be clean.* Regarding the works of mercy: *Judge not, and you shall not be judged; condemn not, and you shall not be condemned; for with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and with what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again.* And counsel was given to **Nebuchadnezzar** <note>original: "Mabuchodonosor"</note> that he should redeem his sins with alms. Thus, devout and pure prayer with faith cleanses, when there is living faith and a humble heart within it; the example of this is the tax collector and the sinner <note>The parable of the Pharisee and the Publican</note>. But regarding the repentance that cleanses a person founded in Christ by faith, the Lord Jesus says: *I am the vine, you are the branches; he who abides in me and I in him, he bears much fruit.* And another scripture says: *As gold in the furnace,* and so forth. And regarding the Word, God says through **Ezekiel**: *I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness.* And the Lord Jesus says: *Now you are clean because of the word I spoke to you.* And regarding the testimony of baptism which happens together with faith: *He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.* And **Saint Paul** says: *Let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with clean water.* 

We have now a firm hope and our confession: that we are to have our "purgatory" <note>cleansing</note> not in the "third hell" <note>Refers to the place in the afterlife proposed by Thomas Aquinas</note>, but in eternal life. For God says: *He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved.* And with these words, which have strength in themselves, he cleanses the Church here and purges it for the life of glory. Just as God says through **Jeremiah** in the figure of **Judah** and **Jerusalem**: *I will reverse the captivity of Judah and the captivity of Israel... and I will cleanse them from all their iniquity by which they have sinned against me.* **Saint Paul** says: *Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her,* and so forth. This was not to prepare her for hell, but for heaven—into rest after these present labors—because it is certain that only the blessed are the elect of God. God leads them into that justice which we set down above, concerning whom the **Apostle** says: *He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and immaculate in his sight in charity.* And again he says: *Whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified.* 

Thus far we speak of the true and certain Purgatory, and there is no other. In testimony of this, the Lord said there are two ways; two future eternal bodies—one good, the other evil—and that after death there will be no time for earning merit. For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ just as one is found at the moment of death, and grace shall not be earned then. The testimony for this is in the rich man **Dives**, who cried out to **Abraham** and obtained nothing. And the Scripture says: *For the living know they shall die, but the dead know nothing more.*

<meta>This page continues the Waldensian polemic against the doctrine of Purgatory. Having previously argued that purification happens through faith and grace in this life, the author now addresses specific biblical proof-texts used by the Roman Church to support Purgatory, reinterpreting them as referring to earthly trials or dismissing them as non-canonical.</meta>

<header># WALDENSIANS AGAINST [PURGATORY]</header>

...they have no further reward, for the memory of them is given over to oblivion. And a little further on: *Whatever your hand is able to do, do it instantly, for there will be neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld toward which you hasten.* <note>original: "Quodcumque potest facere manus tua... apud inferos" — a citation of Ecclesiastes 9:10, used here to argue that no "work" of purification can happen after death.</note> And **Abraham** said that *between us and you a great gulf is fixed,* because in Hell there is no redemption, and there is only one "underworld" according to the words of the Gospel, *where their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished.* <note>This refers to the Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16) and the description of Gehenna in Mark 9.</note>

Regarding that Scripture of **Saint Paul** where *someone's work burns*, which some bring forward as proof for Purgatory: Let it be known here that the Apostle in this place is not speaking of that which is to come after death, nor do his words agree with that idea. For in death God will not appear in fire, but here <note>on earth</note>, according to the Scripture which says: *The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous men.* <note>original: "Vasa figuli probat fornax" — from Sirach 27:5.</note> Just as many have fallen into sin and were cleansed, so too **Saint Peter** says: *In this you shall rejoice, even if now for a little while you must be saddened by various temptations.* That is the "day of God's testing."

Therefore, whatever priest places faith, love, hope, and the remaining virtues upon the foundation of Christ—he shall remain in the day of visitation. But whoever places hay, wood, or stubble—which is the ministry of the Old Law or the laws of men—the Day of the Lord shall burn this up. For *every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up* and cast into the fire and burned. Yet he who places the law in right faith shall be saved, though it be, as it were, through the trial of fire. <note>The author is reinterpreting 1 Corinthians 3:12-15, arguing the "fire" is the trial of earthly life and the "stubble" is human-made religious traditions.</note>

Thus is the word of the Lord: *Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven men; but the blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this world nor in the world to come.* <note>Matthew 12:31-32.</note> We understand this just as He himself says: *Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.*

Similarly, regarding that passage in **Maccabees**: *It is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead that they may be loosed from sins.* <note>2 Maccabees 12:46. This was the primary text used by the medieval Church to justify prayers for souls in Purgatory.</note> To this we say that this book is placed among those not received by the Church, which are called **Apocrypha**. They also say that the writer added this at the end. Furthermore, according to what **Saint John** says: *If anyone knows his brother is committing a sin not leading to death, let him ask, and life shall be given to the one sinning not unto death. There is a sin leading to death; I do not say that one should pray for that.* <note>1 John 5:16.</note>

As for the **Maccabees** who were slain, God permitted it because they had gifts for idols hidden under their tunics, and they died without repentance. Hence it is written that **Judas** immediately warned them to beware of sins so that such a plague would not touch them; he collected twelve thousand marks <note>The Latin text says "duodeci marchas," likely referring to the drachmae of silver mentioned in 2 Maccabees 12:43.</note> and so on. Yet nothing stands there concerning Purgatory, nor was such a thing ever heard of, but only of Hell and the **Bosom of Abraham**. <note><term>Bosom of Abraham</term>: A Jewish and early Christian concept of the place where the righteous dead waited, distinct from the medieval concept of Purgatory.</note> Nor would it even exist now if **Thomas the monk of Aquino** <note>**Thomas Aquinas** (c. 1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian whose work systematized the doctrine of Purgatory.</note> had not thought this up regarding the underworld.

We must also say this: it is claimed that only those who are "elect" go into Purgatory—those who are on the way of salvation, making confession, but who do not satisfy the counsel of the priest or who die with venial sins. We can show that this is not true in this way: since God has forgiven the greater <note>sins</note>, why would he not grant indulgence for the lesser? Or what of the penitent in the humble day of anguish and tribulation? It is certain in the case of the **Publican**; and from the Gospel, that servant who was about to be cut off prayed to him, saying: *Have patience with me and I will pay you everything.* The Lord, having mercy on that servant, dismissed him and forgave him the debt. <note>Matthew 18:26-27.</note> This is similar to the **Thief** on the cross; when God granted him indulgence for his sins, He did not send him to Purgatory, but with Himself into Paradise.

To this also **Saint Paul** says: *There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh.* For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death. For what was impossible for the Law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, even of sin, condemned sin in the flesh so that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. <note>Romans 8:1-4.</note>

Thus, the "impossibility" of the penitent who cannot satisfy the counsel of the priest does not proceed from the Soul (for the spirit is willing), but from the body, which can no longer live. Therefore, he shall not migrate into Purgatory, but there shall be fulfilled in him what **Saint John** says: *My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not [sin]...*

<meta>This page continues a defense of Waldensian beliefs, specifically transitioning from the biblical proofs for earthly purification to a direct rebuttal of Purgatory as an "invention" used for financial gain. The text shifts from theological scriptural interpretation to a discussion of how the community navigates human laws and church traditions while maintaining their conscience.</meta>

<header># TWO LETTERS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE</header>

...sins. But even if anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. <note>original: "peccatis. sed et si quis peccaverit..." — a citation of 1 John 2:1–2.</note> Thus, it would be a great contempt for His merit and His promise if a "purgatory" were to have more power regarding the cleansing of sin than the blood of Christ, faith, good will, and devoted prayer. For concerning the faith of the weak, **Saint James** says: *the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him.* <note>James 5:15.</note> And this is sufficient for sin when someone does not satisfy the counsel of the priest—if even that is granted to a prayer not written from books but from the living faith of an upright and faithful priest which he offers to God alongside his faithful followers.

It is also against reason that the soul alone should suffer and not the body, since they shall be glorified together, just as **Saint Paul** says: *if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.* <note>2 Timothy 2:12.</note> Furthermore, those whom the Last Judgment finds living could in no way be sent into purgatory. Concerning this, the ancient doctors agreed more consistently when they said that before the Last Judgment, when God appears in fire, the elect of God will be cleansed. This is founded upon the words of **Saint Paul** which we introduced before regarding the "foundation." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:11–15, where Paul speaks of "gold, silver, and precious stones" being tested by fire.</note> And those ancient doctors had not yet granted "possessions" <note>likely referring to the donation of lands and wealth to the church for the sake of souls</note>, nor did they "free souls from hell," until those people arose who, through the invention of the word [Purgatory], began to make a profit from the souls of men—first from the living, then from the dead. This is what we feel regarding purgatory, of which the Teacher **Augustine** made mention, and for which the king's anger is unjustly stirred against us.

He also wishes to know what we believe concerning the ecclesiastical order. Let him and anyone else know that we keep those constitutions <note>established church laws or rules</note> which are an aid to faith, love, hope, and justice, which can be known through faith for the purpose of carrying out God's commands. We do this so that we might more sincerely use them for the end for which the sacraments exist, according to the example of Christ's way of life. And we observe those things which help toward proper veneration and prayer to God, which promote equity, virtue, honor, discipline, and unanimity. We observe these and teach our own people and others to observe them.

And it is not that we despise proper ordination because it was instituted by men, nor do we separate ourselves in that regard to dishonor them. Rather, this is why we act as we do: because in some matters, ordinations, and statutes—even ancient ones—similar truths are not found. It is our conscience and the fear of God that guides us, lest we provoke Him to anger by willingly being the cause of discord or a bad example, and thereby stir the people's anger against us. Therefore, whatever statutes we recognize as not being against justice, we keep them. Even if they were for the most part against justice, if we can still use them in any way toward justice, we use them in a good sense—such as regarding sacred feasts as well as fasts and other such things—so that we might avoid causing offense and strive to maintain peace with all men.

We also confess that in every deception there is some element of equity <note>fairness or rightness</note>, regarding which there is either a variation of interpretation, or of good use, or of order regarding the observation of equity. Therefore, we teach this so that we might give place to equity, and we are cautious and circumspect about other matters for the sake of security and the failures that could arise from them. Having some equitable practices among us, we keep them lest we trip others up. Regarding this, we understand ourselves to be in great straits and in a time of change, so that we may maintain good stewardship not only before God but also before men. For many charge us with inconsistency and changeability, and others are even worse, claiming we use this to hide our hypocrisy. Others suspect us, saying we would not have entered into such a mindset at the first "seduction" <note>referring to their initial break from the Roman Church</note>; these and many other things we must leave to God.

To the second part, we make it known that we do not hold to many constitutions, customs, ordinations, and inventions because they are in error and are a subversion of the faith and equity from which the commands of God descend—such as honor, veneration, proper service, and hope in God—and because these constitutions are a cause of idolatry...

<header>### THE WALDENSIANS IN OPPOSITION</header>

...and of erroneous hope, vain superstition, and the concealment of mortal sin. For evil priests, these things are a cause for their own unworthiness, for the seduction of others away from justice, for greed, and for profiting from sacred things. For the people, however, they lead to robbery <note>original: "latrocinia" — likely referring to the extortion of fees for religious services</note> and the burden of spending more on fine clothing, buildings, and splendor—consuming and devouring resources uselessly. They usurp for themselves and their churches what they ought to spend on the poor and the needy. Therefore, we do not observe many of these things because they create many obstacles to the word of justice, to prayer, and to holy things regarding the true sense of God's law. Because of this, the law of God has fallen into contempt; yet they guard human constitutions and ordinances as diligently as the commandment of God, or even more diligently. What is worse is that through such constitutions they transgress the commands of God, and through them, grace and justice are corrupted among the servants and in the ministry, and they maintain an erroneous faith, which they value highly because it is observed in this way. These and other causes dissuade us from many other constitutions and those [so-called] holy laws, out of fear and observance of God. The ancient and modern [teachers] warn of this, whom we now leave out for the sake of brevity.

Behold now, this learned man finishes his writing against us, in which he has placed no probable or just obstacle, but only insults. In his writing, three things are found: first, he wished—but was unable—to bring a charge of injustice against us; second, he changed certain points of our confession; and third, he accuses us regarding things we did not address at that time because no cause was given to us. If that man understood us to be speaking contrary to the faith in that confession, he certainly would not have remained silent. At the end, when he finishes his letter, he makes the intent of his writing clear: that he does it for the sake of the **Royal Majesty** <note>The King, likely Vladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary.</note> so that he might induce him to expel us, crush us, and drive us out of the provinces. He does not understand what spirit he is of, for it is the spirit of those who killed the holy prophets and resisted the good and the just, thinking they were offering a service to God. They have insinuated themselves with princes and confirmed the impious hands of rulers. If such men do not repent, they must surely fear that the plague of God will come upon them. May God, out of His love, convert him and make him understand what he is attempting, so that by doing penance here, he may obtain grace, and after this, eternal glory.

Regarding his second writing, we wish to respond in this manner: we shall maintain the same approach as in our previous response, leaving aside his insults and the oppressions found in his work. He is among the number of those who follow the ornate style of the Latin language, who rarely speak with modesty; when they praise someone, they do so with solemn words without weighing the truth, or if they revile someone, they do so with excessive insults, depressing them as much as they can, fearing neither God nor men. Therefore, seeing that he writes this letter with the same intent as the previous ones—to betray us to the **Royal Majesty**—and since we are unable to provide information directly to the Royal Majesty (well understanding why and for what reason), it seemed expedient to us, for the reasons we set forth in our earlier letters, to write to everyone in common. Thus, if our writing should come into their hands, our response might arrive at the same time. We shall complete our response with truth and simplicity. But first, the writing of **Doctor Augustine** <note>Augustine of Olomouc (1467–1513), a fierce critic of the Waldensians and the Bohemian Brethren.</note> which he wrote to the Royal Majesty is presented, and it begins thus: In the prologue of his epistle, he indicates that he viewed with "weariness" the letters we wrote to the Royal Majesty, and immediately he becomes insulting toward us. And not only toward us, but also toward the gracious and venerable virgin, the **Virgin Martha**. It seems marvelous to us why our writing causes him such weariness, or why, making excuses, he blames his own business for his inability to respond. It is well known that we sent our letters not to **Doctor Augustine**, but to the **Royal Majesty**. We did not request a response from **Doctor Augustine**; why then did this care fall upon him, that he should become so solicitous for a response, when neither the Royal Majesty nor he himself indicated who should send the reply, so that we might be instructed to whom we ought...

# TO THE TWO LETTERS OF MASTER AUGUSTINE,

In responding, he states the first cause of his writing was to reveal our frauds to the King’s Majesty; we wish to hear him out gladly. Through this writing, he primarily wishes to show that we are contrary to ourselves, but he will achieve nothing. Thus, through this cunning lie, he imposes upon us so that he might stir the King's Majesty to anger; he blows upon the fire <note>original: "exufflat ignem"</note> so that he might command death to boil, just as ointment boils in a bronze pot. Let anyone examine this—namely, his writing—and the reason for our faith, just as we wrote previously regarding his letters: how we believe that the bread is the natural and spiritual blessed body of Jesus Christ. 

But he himself writes that under the substance <term>substance: the essential nature of something, as opposed to its outward appearance</term> of bread and wine, the true body and true blood exist. Through this, he has changed our faith, which is founded upon the words of Christ, just as we convicted him in our first letters. Regarding this other part, he is not afraid to change his tune, claiming against us that we speak and preach that no honor ought to be shown to the body and blood of Christ. Perhaps, out of anger, he could not calmly read through what we wrote in the Latin language to the King’s Majesty. This was the reason we touched upon this: so that we might be freed from all suspicion. We wish to set down the same thing in the Bohemian language <note>original: "Boemica lingua" — referring to Czech</note>, which is interpreted thus: 

Concerning the body and blood of Christ, we believe that after the word is rightly consecrated by the priest, the bread is immediately the true natural body of Christ, taken from the Virgin Mary, which had to be delivered up, just as he says: "This is my body which is given for you" <note>original: "hoc est corpus meum quod per vobis tradetur"</note>. And the wine is the natural blood of that body, which had to be shed for the remission of sins. And we not only believe and confess that the bread is the natural flesh and the wine the natural blessed blood, but that the bread is also simultaneously spiritual flesh, and the wine spiritual blood, which is the unity of the church. As Saint Paul says: "Is not the bread which we break a participation in the body of the Lord?" <note>Refers to 1 Corinthians 10:16</note>. 

We believe that it must be communicated under both species <term>both species: receiving both the bread and the wine during Communion, a practice known as Utraquism</term> according to the command of Christ and the example of the primitive church, out of faith and the necessity of salvation. This was ordained by the Son of God because, under the appearance of both, a dignity for salvation is placed, which must be configured to the conscience and hope through the sacrament. 

But because some do not receive this faith which we have confessed, they rashly discuss us, penetrating into our hearts, and say that we believe one thing and say another. They act unjustly against us before God, who knows us better through our justice, while others judge us because we do not take communion from their priests. But they do not understand why. It is for this reason: because we have our own priests, and at the opportune time, we prepare ourselves and receive from them. We do not dare go to priests who are opposed to us because we cannot think of them in common as messengers of Almighty God, as they perform works contrary to the matters of faith and the order of Scripture. 

For this reason, they do not believe us, because we only do in this sacrament what was commanded by the Son of God. What is not commanded there, we do not do; but we do what is commanded. For instance, to show [ritual] honor and reverence to the body and blood of Jesus Christ was not commanded by the Son of God. Rather, it was commanded to believe and receive, to eat and drink, and to do this in his memory. We are not commanded to show [ritual] honor to this substance of the blessed body of Christ [in the bread], but rather to the substance of the body of Christ which sits at the right hand of the Father. 

The testimony for this is that our Lord Jesus Christ gave it to those who were sitting; and his successors, passing through houses for a long time, broke the bread and received food with a blessing, and they did not perform [ritual] reverence <note>This refers to the practice of genuflecting or adoring the host</note>. Yet, in doing so, they did not err, nor were they heretics. For it is commanded that they should honor Jesus Christ as true God and man, not in the substance of the sacrament itself, but in the corporal substance of God. We have a command for this which the Lord remembered against the tempter: "It is written: the Lord your God you shall adore, and Him only shall you serve." This is the New Testament of which the Apostle says: "Therefore God also has exalted him and given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father." <note>Refers to Philippians 2:9-11</note>

They clarify that they have their own clergy because they believe the established priesthood acts contrary to Scripture.</summary>

...of the Father, and the Lord himself says that all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father. But no one here honors the Father in a created thing, but rather in heaven, saying, *Our Father who art in heaven*. And Saint Paul says: *For this reason I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all paternity in heaven and on earth is named.* <note>Ephesians 3:14-15</note> In this same way, everyone ought to honor the Son; and for that reason, when he was personally here upon the earth, although he was worthy of honor, he did not wish to compel men to adore him. But in heaven he possesses the glory which he had before the ages, and there, after his ascension, he is venerated and confessed. 

For the testimony of firm proof, we have the New and Old Testaments. The Old, when God says through Moses: *You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of those things which are in heaven above, or which are on the earth below, or which are in the waters under the earth. You shall not adore them, nor worship them. For I am the Lord your God.* <note>Exodus 20:4-5</note> Regarding the New, Jesus says: *Then if anyone says to you, "Behold, here is Christ," or "there," do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead into error, if possible, even the elect. Behold, I have told you beforehand. Therefore, if they say to you, "Behold, he is in the desert," do not go out; "Behold, he is in the inner rooms," do not believe it.* <note>Matthew 24:23-26</note> Nor will he descend corporally with his body before the day of judgment. This is proven by the common Christian faith <note>The Apostles' Creed</note> where it says: *He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty. From there he shall come to judge the living and the dead.* 

From this, anyone can understand that the scholar <note>referring to Master Augustine</note> acts precipitously, not understanding our writings, perhaps out of his own anger. For we have a clear distinction regarding the veneration of these things, just as we clearly confessed in the letters we sent to everyone. Let him respond to these points and the sacred testimonies therein. We perpetually believe, as a matter of faith, that the highest work of veneration is the observance of God’s commandments; conversely, the greatest irreverence is disobedience. This is what Samuel said to King Saul: *Does the Lord desire holocausts and victims, and not rather that the voice of the Lord be obeyed? For obedience is better than victims, and to listen is better than to offer the fat of rams; for to resist is like the sin of soothsaying, and to refuse to submit is like the crime of idolatry.* <note>1 Samuel 15:22-23</note> 

Therefore, believing that the bread and wine, according to the word of the Savior, are his body and blood, we obey his commands. Thus we receive and eat under both species <term>both species: receiving both the consecrated bread and the wine, a practice the Waldenses and Hussites insisted upon</term>, and we do this in commemoration of his passion, just as those before us did. Furthermore, by God's command, we venerate the Son of God as true God and man at the right hand of God the Father; and according to his command, we do not believe him to be personally on earth, nor do we expect him from heaven until the final day of judgment. Neither do we receive those who show that same person to be here, nor do we follow them. 

Furthermore, according to his precepts, we receive him in his powerful spiritual majesty through faithful messengers, and we honor him with faithful obedience and subjection. Yet, regarding this commandment, we venerate him in his faithful members <note>the community of believers</note> in whom he dwells through faith and the merit of his conversation with the Father and the Holy Spirit. We love and serve them with works of mercy if they receive him in his word according to his commandments, and we follow them in deed as much as we know how and as far as is possible. In the sacraments of his New Testament of love and justice, we are united to him out of love. 

Therefore, in doing so, we create no impediment for ourselves in the scriptures or deeds. For if we believed the body of Jesus Christ was in the sacrament with the same kind of existence as it has at the right hand of God the Father, it is certain that we would be rebels against the veneration of this body, and even contradictory to ourselves in adoration. But we believe that the bread and wine are the body and blood of Christ in the existence of a blessing <note>original: "existentia benedictionis" — a spiritual rather than physical presence</note> performed solely for reception, use, and memory. Because if our Lord Jesus Christ were to expend his body and blood in the sort of form they now believe it to be under the sacrament, he certainly would not have neglected his...

To this we respond that we do not believe or think as he does, but as the words of faith show, as his interpreter Saint Paul shows, as the works of the primitive Church, the catholic faith, and the precepts of God show. We say further and simply confess that for us there is but one God, one Lord, Jesus Christ, and that he is in the sacrament with his natural body as such, but through a different mode of existence than that at the right hand of God; and we further say that he is also there with spiritual flesh. For it is one thing to say "that Christ is this body," and another thing to say "he exists in this manner." We grant the first, because that Christ is one with this body. But the other we do not "consume" <note>original: "comedimus" — likely used here metaphorically to mean "we do not swallow or accept this doctrine"</note> according to the scripture of faith; we resist it. This is because our Lord Jesus Christ, after his ascension, exists personally with the natural substance of his body. 

But we say that he was not, is not, and will not be [here] until the final judgment, because with that substance of his body he occupies only one place, just as he did here while he was a wayfarer <note>term: "wayfarer" (viator) — a theological term for a human being living on earth, traveling toward eternity</note>. He cannot be multiplied nor bodily elevated. And to show this by the true scripture of the Christian faith, it is first established that God manifested the personal ascension of the natural substance of the body when he spoke to his disciples: *For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me* <note>Matthew 26:11</note>; and *I go to him who sent me.* And he adds the reason, saying: *I go to prepare a place for you. For if I do not go, the Paraclete <note>term: "Paraclete" — the Holy Spirit, the Comforter</note> will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.* 

And who is that Paraclete who ought to remain with them forever? His coming testified to the true departure of which Christ says: *I went out from the Father and came into the world; again, I leave the world and go to the Father.* Again, he departed personally with the substance of his assumed body. For he says in his prayer to the Father: *I am no longer in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to thee.* And again: *Little children, yet a little while I am with you.* And again, by a comparison: *Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they shall fast.* And again: *I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.*

# THE WALDENSIANS AGAINST

...especially since the Lord gave them power over their labors, and with that power, justice, and help, He promised to be with His faithful until the end of the age. And with His faithful members, where two or three are gathered in His name, He promised to be among them spiritually through the participation of His body and blood, and in the sacrament by power, with the testimony of His justice. To this point sounds the voice of the ancient and great teacher, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whom the Waldensians frequently cited to prove their views were "ancient" rather than "heretical."</note>, where he says: "Until the world reaches its end, the Lord is above; but nevertheless, even here with us is the Truth, the Lord. For the body in which He rose must be in one place, but His truth is spread everywhere." <note>original: "Corpus enim in quo resurrexit in uno loco esse oportet, veritas autem eius ubique diffusa est." This is a famous quote from Augustine's Tractates on the Gospel of John.</note>

Thus, from the Holy Scriptures and many other sources, it is certain that the Lord Christ—with His body and blood existing personally in His natural substance—is not here until the end of the age; and because He is in one place, that is, at the right hand of God. <note>The "right hand of God" is a theological term for the position of highest honor and authority in Heaven.</note> He wished to show this clearly beforehand while here in His mortal body: that by existing in one place, He was not in another at the same time. Just as His own word shows when He spoke to His disciples, saying: "Lazarus is dead, and I am glad for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there; but let us go to him." And Martha says: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." 

In the same way, after His resurrection, with His body glorified, He was not in many places at one and the same time, but in one; and at other times, He was in various other places. Just as when He was in Jerusalem, He was not then in Galilee; and when He was in Galilee, having risen from the dead, He was not in the tomb—which even the angels did not lie about when they said: "He has risen, He is not here." <note>The Waldensians are using logic to argue against "Transubstantiation," the belief that Christ’s physical body is present in every piece of bread in every church simultaneously.</note> 

And so, with His substantial assumed body, in which He sits now at the right hand of God, He cannot be multiplied; rather, He remains as only one, whole and true, existing in heaven. He cannot be received corporally <note>physically</note> by faithful souls, but only spiritually. For He said: "If then you see the Son of Man ascending to where He was before? It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life." <note>Quoting John 6:62-63.</note> Therefore, we believe and feel through faith that although Christ is not here with His natural body existing in a physical dwelling, He is nevertheless present spiritually and powerfully in the blessing of truth. Though He has departed in this physical sense, He will not depart from His own, but is everywhere He wills to be, even in infinite places. The truth of this body and blood increases and can be multiplied for every necessity of His faithful and elect. As the Lord says regarding this: "I am with you even to the end of the age," and "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them." And Saint Paul says: "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith." Also: "Do you seek a proof of Him who speaks in me, Christ?" 

Therefore, from faith we thus receive [the sacrament], and we respond to the writings of that teacher <note>Referring back to Augustine of Olomouc, their contemporary opponent.</note> as we did before: that Christ with His body and blood is in a dwelling of blessing, as at the right hand of God, but not in a similar dwelling as in the heavens. <note>The Waldensians argue the "blessing" of the bread is real, but it doesn't "trap" Christ's physical body.</note> Therefore, we ought not to worship Him in the blessing of the sacrament in the same way as we worship His personal essence existing at the right hand of God. And so that it may be even better understood that we do not equate the two, nor substitute one for the other, we have the example of John the Baptist, of whom the Lord said: "And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come." Yet Saint John himself confessed to the priests and Levites that he was not Elijah himself. Thus, these words do not contradict each other; just as that confession of our faith [does not contradict] Augustine. These words are true when understood in a healthy sense: that John was not Elijah personally in substance, but was so in that spiritual being which the Lord changed. Thus John did not contradict the angel who confirmed his conception to Zechariah, saying: "And he will go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah." 

We also take an example from the words of Saint Paul where he writes: "Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink." <note>Quoting 1 Corinthians 10:1-4.</note> Yet no one concedes that these fathers physically ate the cor...

### TWO LETTERS FROM LORD AUGUSTINE <note>This refers to Augustine of Olomouc, a 15th-century critic of the Waldensians, not St. Augustine of Hippo.</note>
<meta>catchword: and</meta>

...[the] body and blood of Christ bodily. Either they were present in their natural substance substantially <note>The author is arguing against the idea that the Old Testament figures physically consumed Christ before He was even born.</note>, because He was not yet incarnate, nor had He given His body into the hands of sinners for death as a preparation for food, nor His blood for drinking, nor had He yet instituted the sacrament of the body and blood. As Saint Paul says to the Hebrews: "The Law, having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never, by those same sacrifices which they offer continually year by year, make those who approach perfect." <note>original: "umbram enim habens lex futurorum bonorum non ipsam imaginem rerum." See Hebrews 10:1.</note> For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. He says further: "They drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ." <note>original: "bibebant autem de spiritali consequente eos petra, petra autem erat christus." See 1 Corinthians 10:4.</note> Certainly, this was not in a bodily figure, but in a spiritual one of what was to come, which He communicates to Himself in the sacrament of the New Testament. And it is so because the sacraments of the New Testament hold a persevering justice, merit, and use in Christ and the Church. Many more examples of this kind could be drawn from Holy Scripture if it did not require long-winded dispute and cause weariness to the reader. Thus we teach, to speak briefly: with God’s help, we do not fear the snares which that "clever hunter" <note>A derogatory reference to their opponent, Augustine of Olomouc, who is "hunting" for heresies.</note> has set for us—as if before the eyes of birds—claiming that we are forced to confess two Christs.

But he himself, along with others who think as he does, ought to fear those very traps. For by confessing that Christ is on earth personally just as He sits at the right hand of the Father, it is they who divide Christ. Contrary to the commandment, they demonstrate this here; for they lead the faithful away from the sense of His spiritual and sacramental existence and reception. Without that principal spiritual Christ, no one can be saved. But we ask for help so that we may more easily recognize the truth and the error, and that the teacher Augustine <note>Augustine of Olomouc.</note> might permit himself to be asked one or two questions regarding the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. Indeed, it is the same question he asks of us, saying: 
> "Is it the same Christ there, whom they say is under the sacrament of bread and wine together with us, as he [the opponent] feels and promises, or is He distinct from the one who sits at the right hand of the Father?" 

Let Him also be asked this along with that question: If it is the same Christ—true God and man, according to his opinion—substantially and naturally in the sacrament and in the faithful priests or other people who receive the sacrament, is that same Christ in the sacrament divided from the Christ here and in the heavens? If He is the same, why do they not venerate and adore the one and same Lord Christ in the human being just as they do in the sacrament and at the right hand of God? Indeed, they ought to do this even more by the precept of faith, because Christ is in a human being in a more worthy manner than in the sacrament. For He is in the sacrament for a time so that people may receive Him with reverence, not just for a time, but forever—as can be said and confirmed by the words of Christ when He says: "He who eats this bread will live forever." <note>original: "qui manducat hunc panem viuet in eternũ." See John 6:58.</note> If He is divided, let him [the opponent] speak only to himself and to others; and as he judges others, let him judge himself. Here it will be necessary to show faith in Christ the Lord.

And where he maintains and recalls the transmutation <term>transmutation: the medieval term for the change of bread and wine into the body and blood (transubstantiation)</term> of the bread and wine into the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be asked whether the bread and wine are transmuted into the *whole person* of our Lord Jesus Christ, or if not into the whole Christ. If he says into the whole—that is, into the Body, Soul, and Divinity—this is impossible and incredible from the very nature of things. For then a creature <note>The bread and wine.</note> would pass and transmute itself into its Creator; a spiritual person into the incomprehensible and omnipotent Spirit of God. This is contrary to the faith of salvation, and no sane mind has dared to think this, unless he presumes to experience it in himself. O, you are still far off if you wish to think this! For neither in the soul nor in the spirit is there anything created worthy of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, it is impossible to think of this transmutation, because earthly and bodily nature—and whatever spirit—are incomprehensibly different from each other, as if without end, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones. For He has already [received] His glorified nature...

<summary>This page presents the Waldensian critique of transubstantiation, arguing that Christ is present spiritually rather than physically in the bread. They challenge their opponent, Augustine of Olomouc, by arguing that if Christ were physically in the bread, He would be "divided" from His body in Heaven, and they question why the Church does not adore Christ within human believers if they believe He is physically present in those who consume the Host.</summary>
