<meta>This page continues the theological defense of the Waldensians against Augustine of Olomouc. The previous page argued that the Old Testament patriarchs participated in Christ spiritually before His incarnation; this page extends that logic to the nature of Christ's presence in the Eucharist, distinguishing between His physical body in Heaven and His spiritual presence on Earth.</meta>

# ->WALDENSIANS AGAINST<-

Especially the Lord [gave] them power over their labors, with which power, justice, and help He promised that He would be with His faithful until the end of the age. And with His faithful members, where two or three are gathered in His name, He promised He would be among them spiritually with the participation of His body and blood, and in the sacrament in power with the testimony of His justice. To this effect sounds the voice of the ancient and great doctor Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whom the Waldensians cite here to support their view that Christ is not physically present in the bread.</note> where he says: "Until the world ends, the Lord is above; but nevertheless, even here with us is the truth, the Lord. For the body in which He rose must be in one place, but His truth is diffused everywhere." <note>original: "donec seculum finiat sursum est dominus. sed tamen etiam hic nobiscum est veritas dominus. Corpus enim in quo resurrexit in uno loco esse oportet, veritas autem eius ubique diffusa est." From Augustine's Tractates on the Gospel of John.</note> And so, from the holy scriptures and many other things, it is certain that the Lord Christ—with His body and blood in natural substance personally existing—is not here until the end of the age; and that He is in one place, which is at the right hand of God. <term>Right hand of God</term> <note>A theological term meaning the place of highest honor and power in Heaven, implying Christ is physically distant from the Earthly realm.</note> This He wished [to show] previously here in His mortal body; He clearly showed that existing in one place, He was not in another at the same time. Just as His speech shows when He spoke to His disciples, saying: "Lazarus is dead, and I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe; but let us go to him." And Martha says: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." <note>See John 11:14-15 and 11:21. The author uses these stories to prove Christ's physical body can only be in one place at a time.</note> So, after the resurrection, with His body glorified, He was not in many places at one and the same time, but in one. And at other times He was in different places: just as when He was in Jerusalem, He was not then in Galilee; and when He was in Galilee, rising from the dead, He was not in the tomb, which the angels did not lie about when they said: "He has risen, He is not here." And so, with His substantial assumed body, which now sits at the right hand of God, He cannot be multiplied; rather, He remains as only one, whole and true, existing in heaven. And He cannot be received corporally by faithful souls, but only spiritually. For He said: "If therefore you shall see the Son of Man ascending where He was before? It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life." <note>original: "si ergo videritis filium hominis ascendentem ubi erat prius. spiritus est qui vivificat caro non prodest quicquam. verba que ego locutus sum vobis. spiritus et vita sunt." See John 6:62-63.</note> Therefore we believe and feel from faith that although Christ is not here with His body in a natural, existing, and corporal dwelling, He is nevertheless present spiritually and powerfully in the blessed truth. For He did not depart from His own with this dwelling, nor will He depart, but He is everywhere He wishes and in infinite places. The truth of this body and blood is increased and can be multiplied for every necessity of His faithful and elect; as the Lord says in this: "I am with you until the end of the age," and "where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." And Saint Paul [says]: "that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith." <note>Ephesians 3:17.</note> Also: "Do you seek a proof of Him who speaks in me, Christ?" Therefore, from faith we so receive and so respond to the writings of that doctor <note>Referring again to Augustine of Olomouc.</note> as before: that Christ with His body and blood is in a dwelling of blessing, as at the right hand of God, but not in a similar dwelling as in the heavens. Therefore we ought not to worship Him in the blessing of the sacrament, which is and ought to be done in the personal essence existing at the right hand of God. And so that it may be even better understood that we do not compare nor substitute one for the other, we have an example in John the Baptist, of whom the Lord said: "And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come." Yet Saint John himself confessed to the priests and Levites that he was not Elijah. Thus, these statements do not contradict one another, just as that confession of our faith [does not contradict] Augustine; nevertheless, the words are true when understood in a healthy sense: that John was not Elijah personally in substance, but was so in that spiritual being which the Lord changed. And so John did not contradict what the angel also confirmed when he revealed his conception to Zechariah, saying: "And he will go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah." <note>Luke 1:17. This is a key Waldensian argument: things can "be" other things spiritually without being them physically.</note> We also take an example of this from the speech of Saint Paul where he writes: "all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink." <note>1 Corinthians 10:1-4.</note> Yet no one concedes that these fathers ate the body...

<summary>This page presents the Waldensian argument that Christ is physically located only in Heaven at the "right hand of God," while being spiritually present on Earth and in the Eucharist. They use the biblical analogy of John the Baptist "being" Elijah in spirit but not in person to explain how the bread "is" Christ's body.</summary>

Having previously cited St. Augustine of Hippo to prove Christ’s physical body is in Heaven, the text now addresses the "snares" set by their contemporary opponent regarding the nature of the Eucharist and the impossibility of a creature (bread) turning into the Creator (God's divinity).</meta>

### ->TWO LETTERS OF LORD AUGUSTINE<-

body and blood of Christ physically. Whether they were substantially in his natural substance, it was because he was not yet incarnate, nor had he given his body into the hands of sinners for death to prepare it as food, nor his blood to be drunk, nor had he yet instituted the sacrament of the body and blood. And Saint Paul, in his letter to the Hebrews, says that the law, having a shadow of the good things to come <note>original: "umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum." A reference to Hebrews 10:1, arguing that Old Testament rituals were only precursors to Christ.</note>, and not the very image of the things, can never, by those same sacrifices which they offer continually year by year, make those who approach perfect. For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ. He says further: they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. <note>1 Corinthians 10:4.</note> Certainly, this was not in a physical way, but as a spiritual figure of what was to come. And so he communicates himself in the sacrament of the New Testament; and this is so because the sacraments of the New Testament have a persisting justice, merit, and use in Christ and the church. Many more examples of this kind could be brought forth from Holy Scripture, if it did not require much dispute and cause weariness to the reader.

To speak briefly, we teach that by God’s help we do not fear the snares <note>original: "pedicas" (shackles or traps).</note> which that clever hunter <note>A derogatory reference to their opponent, Augustine of Olomouc, depicted as a hunter trying to trap them in heresy.</note> has set for us, as if before the eyes of birds, suggesting that we must confess two Christs. On the contrary, he himself, along with others who think as he does, should fear those very traps <note>original: "decipulas." A pun on "disciples" and "snares."</note>: namely, the idea that Christ is on earth personally in the same way he sits at the right hand of the Father. For these people are the ones who divide Christ. And against the commandment, they show him here; by this, they lead the faithful away from the meaning of his spiritual and sacramental existence and reception. Without that principal spiritual Christ, no one can be saved.

But we ask that we might more easily recognize the help toward the knowledge of truth and error, and that the doctor Augustine <note>Augustine of Olomouc.</note> might permit one or two questions to be asked of him concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. This is the same question he asks of us, saying: Is it the same Christ there, whom they say is under the sacrament of bread and wine together with us, as he [Augustine] feels and promises, or is he distinct from the one who sits at the right hand of the Father? Let him also be asked this alongside that question: If it is the same Christ—true God and man—substantially and naturally in the sacrament according to his opinion, and also in the faithful priests or other men who receive the sacrament, is that same Christ in the sacrament divided from the Christ here and in the heavens? If it is the same, why do they not venerate and adore the one and same Lord Christ in the human person just as they do in the sacrament and at the right hand of God? 

And certainly, they ought to do this even more by the precept of faith, because Christ is in a man in a more worthy manner than he is in the sacrament. For he is in the sacrament only for a time, so that men may receive him with reverence—not only for a time, but forever. This can be said and confirmed from the words of Christ where he says: "he who eats this bread shall live forever." <note>John 6:58.</note> If he is divided, let him [Augustine] speak only to himself and others; and as he judges others, let him judge himself. Here it will be necessary to show faith in Christ the Lord.

And where he holds and mentions the transmutation <term>transmutation</term> <note>An early term for what is now called transubstantiation—the belief that the bread and wine change into the actual substance of Christ.</note> of the bread and wine into the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be asked whether the bread and wine are transmuted into the *whole person* of our Lord Jesus Christ, or if not into the whole Christ. If he says "into the whole"—that is, into the body, soul, and divinity—this is impossible and incredible from the very nature of things. For then a creature would pass and transmute itself into its Creator; a spiritual person would change into the incomprehensible and omnipotent Spirit of God. This is further contrary to the faith of salvation, and no sane mind has dared to think this, unless he presumes to experience it in himself. O, you are still far off if you wish to think this! For neither in the soul nor in the spirit is there anything created worthy of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, it is impossible to conceive of this transmutation, because earthly and corporal nature and whatever spirits there are, are incomprehensibly and endlessly different from each other; because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as he has already clarified his nature...

They claim that if Christ were "substantially" in the bread, it would lead to the logical absurdity of a created object turning into the divine Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Waldensian critique of the doctrine of transubstantiation, specifically targeting the logical and theological inconsistencies they see in the Roman Catholic position. They are responding to an opponent (likely Augustine of Olomouc) regarding how the substance of bread could possibly become the substance of Christ's body.</meta>

### VALDENSES CONTRA
### ->THE WALDENSIANS AGAINST [THEIR OPPONENT]<-

...lest it lose [its meaning]; furthermore, it could not change into the uncreated spirit of God, which is a horrible thing to even imagine. Thus, in the end, one would have to agree and say that the bread changes only into the flesh and only into the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, without his soul or his divinity. And if this were true, the substances of the bread and wine would not pass into the "whole Christ" <note>The "Whole Christ" (Latin: *Totus Christus*) refers to the doctrine that Christ is present in the Eucharist in his entirety—body, blood, soul, and divinity.</note>, and this would not happen. For God would not be there, but only a true man; and how this ought to be understood is clear neither from faith nor from any reason. 

But it is certain and true that the bread does not transform itself into only the body, nor the wine into only the blood. For if it were so, by that logic, the "whole Christ" would not be present under the prior substance, but only the body. As it is claimed, the bread is transformed [into body] and the wine into blood only. But if the body were without its natural blood, and the blood were without the body—and what of the water which they put into the chalice at the same time? Into what does that transform? Perhaps it remains as it is. 

All of that thinking is impossible because the true body of the Lord Jesus was formed once by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin from her pure blood and from no other. But here, a body would be made from something else, where it never was in the Virgin's womb nor born from her. It would come to this: that today there would be some "body of the Lord" which did not exist yesterday, and tomorrow there would similarly be something that does not exist today. But we believe that no one has presumed not only to believe this, but even to think it! 

Perhaps you will say that these things join together—this new thing, not born of the body, joins with that body from the Virgin, and with the soul and divinity? These things have not been heard of from the prophets of God nor the apostles! It would mean Jesus was performing a new thing on earth even greater than the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The mystery of God becoming human in Jesus.</note> of the Eternal Word: a mutual joining with the soul in its whole being, and that this one soul, created once, would unite, vivify, and make into one all those bodies multiplied in some thousands of places at the same time.

These things, and many others, came from the fact that they devised such a "substantial transformation." That doctor <note>Referring to the academic opponent.</note>, when he holds this view, is obligated to provide an explanation according to the logic of faith. Furthermore: will this body of our Lord Jesus Christ, made from the substance of the consecrated bread, be mortal or glorified? Perhaps he will say "glorified," and that it sits at the right hand of the Father? But it is not fitting that the thing sitting at the right hand of the Father be that which is expressed, blessed, and consecrated by words according to the sense of the words. For what is made by these words is mortal, and it is changed [into the body] when it is said: "This is my body which is *given* for you," and "this is my blood which is *shed* for many." If this were the case, Christ would still be dying, and blood would still be shed. 

See what they have imagined regarding this transformation—either an abstraction of the "substance" from the <term>accidents</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are the outward qualities of a thing (like the taste and smell of bread) that remain even if the "substance" (the inner reality) changes.</note>, or they will have to devise other words for the transformation. If other words are made, they will do nothing with these [current] words, and it will not be resolved. From this, the problem grows more and more. If the Apostles had held this sense and this faith, and they had kept portions of this sacrament until <term>Good Friday</term> <note>Latin: *magna sexta feria* (the Great Friday).</note> or longer, this is how things would fall: Christ would be simultaneously alive and dead in one body—alive in the reserved sacrament, but dead on the cross at the ninth hour, and later dead in the tomb. And on the day of the Resurrection, he would be simultaneously glorified and mortal—glorified coming out of the tomb, but mortal in the bread. From this it further follows that he would be simultaneously living and not living, dead and not dead, mortal and not mortal, glorified and not glorified. Neither would God, out of all his omnipotence, do such a thing, nor is it possible or fitting. 

And since we have begun: when does this transformation of yours happen? At the beginning of the words, or at the end? Both are irrelevant. It does not happen at the beginning, because without the expression of the form of the words, the transformation does not occur; it happens only when the final word is finished. Let him be questioned, and let him not be silent: what did Christ the Lord command when he said "Take and eat"? "Take and eat, this is my body." And upon what did he point with that word which in Latin is called *hoc* ("this")? Was it upon the body of Christ? No, because it was not yet [his body]...

<summary>The author presents a logical critique of transubstantiation, arguing that the doctrine leads to absurdities, such as Christ being simultaneously dead and alive or the "multiplication" of his body in thousands of places.</summary>

# TWO LETTERS OF DOCTOR AUGUSTINE,

before the pronouncing of the words, and he did not even show [the host] over the bread according to your opinion. For you would rashly contradict it: almost all the "new doctors" <note>This refers to the Scholastic theologians of the medieval universities, whom the Waldensians often viewed as over-complicating the simple faith of the Gospel.</note> are here, and they do not know which way to turn when they find themselves in a tight spot. If they say: "He showed it over the bread, and made this to be received and eaten," you deny this; and yet it was not the body of the Lord; they would remain in this [position]: that the Lord Jesus showed over nothing with these words, "This is my body," and "This is my blood."

And they place many more points here: that nothing is broken, nothing is seen, nothing is heard, nothing is smelled as sweet, although the senses and the smell of men seem to tell them that they smell all of this. And they say this concerning the "inner man" <note>The "inner man" is a concept from St. Paul referring to the spiritual self, used here by the scholastics to explain how one "perceives" the body of Christ despite physical appearances.</note>; certainly among them there is none of these things. This is the Christian faith. Thus they cling more and more to the words of the Savior by which priests transform the bread and wine.

But whether priests rightly say "This is" <term>formally</term> <note>original: *formaliter*; in scholastic logic, this means the priest speaks "in the person of Christ," intending for the words to actually perform the miracle of transformation.</note> or if they only say those words again after Christ <term>materially</term> <note>original: *materialiter*; this suggests the priest is merely quoting or reciting Christ's words as a historical narrative rather than a creative act.</note>; for if they do not speak formally but materially, it will not be transfigured according to the sense of you all. And thus, truly, no living priest can speak in the proper way as Christ did, because then it would not be the body of Christ but the body of the priest, if he said "This is my body" with those same words. These questions are yours, and come from almost all your <term>beehives</term> <note>original: *alvearibus*; a common metaphor for the busy, buzzing schools of scholastic theology.</note> and many others, and sometimes the response given is not "thick" enough <note>meaning the answer is flimsy or lacks substance.</note>. Such meanings are against the manifest faith of the Gospel, unless that doctor explains all these things according to the right sense of faith and reason and shows a firm foundation, and not from mere opinion when he clothes it with faith. We respond to his questions: let that testament be received in itself according to the one sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, and let him not impose upon us the error which you yourselves have made. We hold to the light of the Holy Gospel upon which we can firmly place our salvation. Certainly the Lord Jesus will not deceive us, who spoke the truth—firm, and firmer than heaven and earth. For now, we do not think to say more of these things because we have written enough about this in those letters which we gave publicly to everyone.

And those standing by said to Saint Peter, "Truly you also are one of them, for even your speech makes you manifest." The same could be said to this doctor according to his own writing: that he is similar in spirit to those who adjured the Lord and said, "I adjure you by the living God that you tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God?" And when he had responded, they said, "What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy! What do you think?" All condemned him, because he is guilty of death. To the likeness of these men we lead that Doctor Augustine. Have we deserved [condemnation] by that which we have deduced? Because this is the true faith of Christ, expressed by Christ the Lord in his own words, and so observed and guarded by the Primitive Church. Yet this is an impudent and iniquitous thing: to give a sentence before making a man a defendant. The Old Law judges no one except after the crime has been heard. And in the New Law there is grace and justice; the Lord Jesus, who came not to damn but to save, prohibited judging, and especially condemning. Therefore, by what law, friend Augustine, by what word of God have you justly accused us? But you have received our scripture badly and unfairly, and you have spoken false witness against us as if it were "just" testimony to the Royal Majesty. Now you yourself bring the sentence of what we deserve, and thus you accuse, testify, and judge. Testifying falsely, you conclude that we despise the veneration of Christ where he must be adored at the right hand of God in heaven, according to his precepts, as has been said more fully above. From which things we now understand: let a faithful man have whatever is just against them; he shall deduce nothing against the Roman Church by this. We have an example of this under the communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ under <term>both kinds</term> <note>original: *sub utraque specie*; the practice of giving both the bread and the wine to the laity, a hallmark of the Bohemian and Waldensian reform movements against the Catholic practice of "bread alone" for the laity.</note>, just as it is the faithful and right justice according to the precept of God observed by the apostles and testified to by the ancient doctors, upon which many "new doctors" and even modern ones will agree.

<meta>This page continues the Waldensian defense against Roman Catholic accusations. The previous page discussed the technicalities of the Eucharist and the "form" of the words of consecration. Here, the author shifts to the practical and historical consequences of these theological disputes, specifically mentioning the Council of Basel and the Hussite movement in Bohemia and Moravia.</meta>

<header>THE WALDENSIANS AGAINST [THEIR ACCUSERS]</header>

They concede and agreed in the Council of Basel <note>A church council held between 1431 and 1449 that attempted to address the Hussite wars and church reform.</note>. But the administration [of Communion] under one kind <note>The practice of giving the laity only the bread, withholding the wine, which the Waldensians and Hussites opposed.</note> is not yet established, as pamphlets likely printed in Prague not long ago show; and yet in no way do they consent to that fairness so that they would do the same and not hold the Bohemians <note>Hussites.</note> as heretics. And why is this? Because they would have to hear it objected to them that they themselves err and have erred; but they will do this in no way, but rather they would perpetrate many and great murders and shed much innocent blood, if God were to permit it. So it is also with the Simoniacs <note>Those who buy or sell church offices or spiritual things; named after Simon Magus.</note>. Is this not the first and greatest heresy, in which they make profit in almost all spiritual matters? They have great prohibitions and severe punishments against this, yet what do they care if someone prohibits it—those who have brought upon this church this horrendous sin of Simoniacal depravity, in which they cause scandal without end day after day. And those priests living in concubinage and the publicans <note>original: *publicani*; used here to mean those who are notoriously sinful or corrupt tax-gatherers of the church.</note> who ought to be deposed from office by their very duty, since it is forbidden for anyone to hear their masses. And many such things are manifest which prove that they err greatly, yet in no way do they confess their sin and do penance. And if Žižka <note>original: *Zircka*; referring to Jan Žižka (c. 1360–1424), the famous one-eyed Hussite general. The author uses a wordplay on "threshing" (trituraffet) with Žižka's name or his "threshing-sleds" (war wagons).</note> with his threshing-sleds had not threshed the Bohemians and Moravians, Communion under both kinds <note>Giving both the bread and the wine to the laity.</note> would have had no place to this day. Regarding this, we who do not hold the opinion that we should answer to the power of the world, but stand in patience alone and testify by our poor confession—certainly we shall not be justified among them. We do not even expect that we would want to triumph; only that we might avoid manifest evil and lay hold of manifest equity, and from there reach blessedness in love here and in the future eternal glory in the life to come. To which may the one God lead us, one in the essence of divinity and triple in persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, blessed forever with all who love the truth and his law. Amen.

Whoever, moreover, desires further instruction according to a sound understanding of Holy Scripture concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, it would greatly benefit them to read the treatise which the ancient Bohemians wrote long ago in the hope of God, the foundation of good and holy men, against their adversaries—and this with invincible testimonies of the law of God. It begins: "To the honor in equity to the sacrament of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ." Their adversaries could not resist these Bohemians' testimonies and reasons, and so they stirred up the power of the world against them through Holy Scripture. Thus some perished in reputation by the mandate of King George <note>George of Poděbrady (reigned 1458–1471), the "Hussite King" of Bohemia, who was often caught between the Pope and his own Hussite subjects.</note>, upon whom many evils came, and upon his sons, and upon all his kingdom by the permission of God as a true vengeance for innocent blood. But they, for the sake of justice, offered up their bodies with patience, confirming themselves as both victors and followers of Christ; they became a merit and obtained a crown from the Lord. Hence it is easily understood that those who suffer for the sake of equity are always closer to the fairness of faith and that narrow way which leads to life, than those who, because of it, disturb others according to their own opinion. But now, that which the Bohemians destroyed in the old time, the moderns are suddenly building up again: such as images, high-priced chests <note>Referring to ornate reliquaries or altarpieces.</note>, organs, and other ecclesiastical things superfluous to happiness. Under these things the people do not conform themselves through virtues, but sins and iniquities increase. If they would look upon such things, they would have mercy on us and give us a place among them. Also, we necessarily make this known here as elsewhere; although God first made this known to us out of his mercy so that we might recognize the deception of the Roman Church from the common salvation—and that it is not what it says it is—yet many of the better people also helped greatly by what they held and felt regarding it, and by their writings...

He contrasts the military defense of the Hussites under Jan Žižka with the Waldensians' "patient" suffering, while lamenting the return of ornate church traditions like images and organs.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as an "Epilogue" to the Waldensian defense, transitioning from the previous page's discussion on the Council of Basel and the corruption of the Simoniacs to a series of citations from respected Catholic authorities who also criticized the moral decay of the Church hierarchy.</meta>

# AFTERWORD OF THE WALDENSIANS,

...left behind after them. Therefore, no prudent person ought to blame us as if we alone had devised these things from ourselves; rather, they were prepared and shown to everyone in common—and to us as well—by those very men. Let us briefly mention one or two of them.

First, **Bernard** <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential French abbot and mystic.</note> says: "Woe to this generation from the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy! <note>original: *hypocrisis*</note> Yet, if it should even be called hypocrisy, which now, because of its abundance, cannot be hidden, and because of its impudence, does not seek to be. Today, a putrid rot creeps through the entire body of the Church, and the wider it spreads, the more desperate it becomes; and it is more dangerous precisely because it is internal. For if an obvious enemy, a heretic, were to rise up, he would be cast out and wither away. If it were a violent enemy, one might perhaps hide from him. But now, whom shall she cast out? Or from whom shall she hide herself? All are friends and all are enemies; all are companions and all are adversaries; all are members of the household, and none are peacemakers. All are neighbors, yet all seek their own interests. They are ministers of Christ, yet they serve the Antichrist. They walk about honored by the goods of the Lord, though they do not offer honor to the Lord.

From this comes that whorish <note>original: *meretricius*</note> splendor you see every day, the theatrical dress, the royal trappings. From this comes the gold on the bridles, saddles, and spurs—and the spurs shine more brightly than the altars! From this come the splendid tables, the foods and the cups; from this come the carousals and drunkenness; from this the lute, the lyre, and the flute; from this the overflowing wine-presses and full storehouses, bursting with everything. From this come the jars of spiced wine and the bulging purses. It is for such things that they wish to be—and are—the provosts of churches, deans, archdeacons, bishops, and archdeacon-bishops. For these offices are not granted for merit, but for that 'business that walks in darkness.' <note>A reference to Psalm 91:6, often used to describe secret corruption.</note> It was predicted long ago, and now the time of fulfillment has arrived.

'Behold, in peace is my bitterness most bitter.' <note>original: *Ecce in pace amaritudo mea amarissima*; a quote from Isaiah 38:17.</note> It was bitter before in the death of the Martyrs; bitterer afterward in the conflict with heretics; it is most bitter now in the conduct of those of the household. She cannot put them to flight, nor flee from them, so much have they prevailed and multiplied beyond number. The wound of the Church is internal and incurable, and therefore in peace is her bitterness most bitter. But in what peace? There is peace and there is not peace: peace from the pagans, and peace from the heretics, but certainly not from the children. This is the voice of one mourning in this time: 'I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me.' <note>Isaiah 1:2.</note> They have despised and defiled me by their shameful life, by their shameful profit, by their shameful commerce, and finally by that 'business that walks in darkness.' What remains is for the 'noonday devil' <note>original: *demonium meridianum*; a medieval term for a particularly insidious spiritual trial or the height of ecclesiastical corruption.</note> to appear from the midst, to seduce those who still remain in Christ, staying in their simplicity—if indeed he has already swallowed the rivers of the wise and the torrents of the powerful, and is confident that the Jordan may flow into his mouth—that is, the simple and humble who are in the Church."

Likewise, in his 22nd sermon [on the Song of Songs], he says: "Let the clerics fear, let the ministers of the church fear, who in the lands of the saints which they possess perform such iniquitous deeds. They are not at all content with the stipends that should suffice them; instead, they impiously and easily keep for themselves the surplus with which the needy should be sustained, and they do not fear to consume the food of the poor for the uses of their own pride and luxury. Truly, they sin with a double iniquity: for they both plunder the property of others and abuse sacred things for their own vanities and filthiness. Therefore, pride has held them so that they are not humbled, but they rule because of their pride along with the proud devil and his angels." Thus says Bernard on the *Song of Songs*.

Furthermore, concerning this matter, **Franciscus Petrarcha** <note>Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet and humanist.</note> in his *Letters Without Title* <note>original: *Epistolis sine titulo*; a collection of letters in which Petrarch criticized the Papal Court at Avignon.</note> writes to his beloved friend: "And what do you still do? Are you stuck or not stuck? But you are held and you struggle and snatch; I think this is rather the case, for I prefer to suspect force rather than laziness. Sluggishness is not your way; you have a burning genius, a fiery mind, and a noble impulse. But what are these things if the impediment is stronger than the virtue? Great force is blunted when opposed by a greater force; all things succumb to necessity. That Babylon <note>Petrarch's name for Avignon, comparing the Papal exile there to the Babylonian Captivity of the Israelites.</note> dragged you there; she detains you. It is hard, but it must be borne. Such is the nature of the place: every good thing is lost there, but first of all, liberty; then, in order, peace, joy, hope, faith, and charity—vast losses of the soul..."

Having previously quoted St. Bernard, the text now transitions into the vivid, stinging rhetoric of Francesco Petrarch—though he is not named here, the "Rhodani" (Rhone) and "Babylon" references identify this as his *Liber sine nomine* (Book Without a Name). # AFTERWORD OF THE WALDENSIANS,

...but in the kingdom of greed, nothing is counted as a loss provided that the money is safe. There, hope for a future life is treated as a hollow story, and everything told about the underworld is dismissed as fables. The resurrection of the flesh, the end of the world, and Christ coming for judgment are held as mere trifles <note>original: *nenias*—often referring to children's songs or nonsense.</note>. Truth there is madness, abstinence is seen as boorishness, and modesty is a great disgrace. In short, the license to sin is called magnanimity and extraordinary liberty. The more polluted a life is, the more illustrious it is considered; the more crimes one commits, the more glory one gains. A good name is cheaper than common mud, and a reputation for merit is the least of concerns.

You have here, as much as was possible in so few words, an expressed state of that "holy" city—which you read about not only in these letters today, but see written daily on the foreheads of those men. No pen and no talent could equal the description of their lives. Furthermore, as I said, the first thing one loses there is liberty. As soon as anyone crosses that threshold, he immediately ceases to be his own master. The place permits him neither to rest nor to leave, but tosses him about and wears him down in fruitless labor. Divine mercy rescues only a few from that law, so that they might love Jerusalem and hate Babylon.

This is the hope I have left for you. Otherwise, I would believe your affairs were finished, seeing you submerged and stuck in such tenacious and deep filth. Meanwhile, I attribute your long stay there not to your will or judgment, but to necessity and fortune; and I willingly excuse the delays that I otherwise vehemently hate. For if there was perhaps some fault in your going there, in the delay itself there is no longer fault, but rather the punishment and purgation of that fault. 

But since many have often learned much in prison, what forbids you also from learning something in those chains that will make you forever wiser? Some things are learned in no better way than through their opposites. Therefore, those who teach the mathematical arts, if the mind of a student seems at times poorly capable of grasping the truth, are accustomed to propose false things; while the mind shrinks back from these, it may flee toward what is truer. 

You, too, have always been accustomed to devote your efforts to both religion and honesty. One of these raises the longing soul to the sight of Him of whom the Psalmist says: *Seek his face always* <note>Psalm 105:4</note>. The other has a "face" which, if it could be seen with the eyes—as **Plato** says—would inflame the soul with marvelous loves <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, suggesting that if Virtue could be seen physically, it would be irresistibly beautiful.</note>; yet it is no less to be loved when discerned by the mind. 

If you think you still lack anything for the full knowledge of either, turn all your study toward their opposites. Prick up your ears, fix your eyes, and direct your mind. Do you wish to know the beauty of God? See how great is the obscenity of His enemies. Nor are those who inhabit Babylon to be sought from afar; every street swarms with these worms. Do you wish to recognize the form and grace of honesty? Contemplate the foulness of the vices, the pattern of which you will see before your eyes wherever you look. By hating these, you may become more loving of both God and virtue at once. 

Rejoice, at least, in having such a "teacher of virtues" through opposites; rejoice, I say, and boast that you have found something useful. Babylon, the enemy of the good and the host and asylum of the wicked, the worst of all things, situated on the wild banks of the **Rhone** <note>original: *Rhodani*. This refers to Avignon, the seat of the Papacy from 1309–1377, which Petrarch famously called the "Babylon of the West."</note>. Shall I call her the famous or the infamous whore who has committed fornication with the kings of the earth? You are indeed that very one whom the Evangelist saw in the spirit <note>A reference to the Whore of Babylon in Revelation 17.</note>; you are that same one, I say, and no other, *sitting upon many waters*. 

This is true whether you take it literally, as you are encircled by three rivers, or figuratively, by the crowd of mortals and riches upon which you sit, wanton and secure, unmindful of eternal things. Or, as he who saw the vision explained: the waters are the peoples, nations, and languages over which the whore sits. Recognize your own attire: *a woman clothed in purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold, and precious stones, and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of the abomination and uncleanness of her fornication*. 

Do you not recognize yourself, Babylon? Unless perhaps an error is made because it was written on her forehead: *Babylon the Great*. You, however, are "Babylon the Small"—small, certainly, in the circuit of your walls, but in your vices, in the ambition of your great ones, and in the heap of all evils, you are not merely great, but the greatest; you are immense. And certainly what follows fits you alone and no other: *Babylon, the mother of fornications and the unholy mother of the abominations of the earth*, giving birth to the worst offspring. For whatever is abominable anywhere on earth, whatever fornications...

It encourages the reader to learn the value of virtue by witnessing the absolute corruption of its opposite.</summary>

# AFTERWORD OF THE WALDENSIANS,

...it comes forth from you, and since you are always giving birth, your womb is always swelling, pregnant, and full of such things. If you still try to hide it, hear the rest: *And I saw,* he says, *the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.* <note>Revelation 17:6</note> Why are you silent? Either show us another who is drunk with this blood, or else deny, if you can, that you are this drunken one. For the vision of the Evangelist and Apostle must be true; if he, seeing you in the spirit, wondered with great admiration, how much more are we overwhelmed with wonder who see you plainly with our own eyes. From all your fornications, of which all the nations and kings of the earth have drunk, and from all your abominations, what do you expect? Except that which the same John says:

> Babylon the great has fallen and has become a dwelling place of demons. <note>Revelation 18:2</note>

The things that follow are well known; you have truly become such a place already. For how much better than a demon is a lost man of desperate wickedness? Truly, you have become a kingdom of demons, who rule in you by their arts though they wear a human likeness. But you, my friend, hear with that same Apostle another voice from heaven saying:

> Come out of her, my people, so that you do not participate in her crimes and do not receive her plagues; for her sins have reached even unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give to her in torment and grief. Because she says in her heart: "I sit as a Queen, I am no widow, and I shall see no grief." Therefore, in one day her plagues shall come: death, and grief, and famine, and she shall be burned with fire; for strong is the God who will judge her. <note>Revelation 18:4-8</note>

Hear all these things, and whatever else the Apostle has there; hear and flee, if there is any way out, lest the iniquities of Babylon—of which there is no limit, no number, no measure, and no calculation—crush your innocence in the ruin of the guilty. I say nothing of the inheritance of <term>Simony</term> <note>The sin of buying or selling church offices or spiritual things, named after Simon Magus.</note> and the rest. Whoever wishes to know more, let him read the letter to its end. He says again in another letter:

If I wished to commit to the pen everything my mind carries regarding the state of this western Babylon—of which I become an unwilling citizen so often by fate, or more truly, by sin—I fear, father, that I would only increase my pain with lamentations and interrupt your most holy cares and most beautiful occupations with untimely and unchangeable complaints. In short: know that not only this pen, but not even a <note>original: *Ciceronianum*—referring to the eloquence of the Roman orator Cicero.</note> Ciceronian pen could equal the reality. Whatever you have read about Assyrian or Egyptian Babylon, whatever of the four labyrinths, whatever, finally, of the threshold of Avernus <note>The entrance to the Underworld in Roman mythology.</note> and the Tartarean forests and sulfurous swamps—compared to this hell, those are mere fables. Here is the tower-building and terrifying Nimrod; here is the quivered Semiramis; here is the inexorable Minos; here is Rhadamanthus; here is Cerberus <note>The three-headed dog guarding the underworld.</note> consuming all. Here is Pasiphae under the bull, and the "mixed breed," as Virgil says, "the two-formed Minotaur"—that is, the monuments of unspeakable lust. Here, finally, you see whatever is confused, whatever is black, and whatever is horrible anywhere on earth or in fiction.

O friend, you were always happy in your virtues, but now you are even happier in your absence. Do you think this is the same city you once saw? It is far different and far unlike it. It was indeed once the worst of all, and at that time most foul. But now this is not a city, but a house of ghosts and spirits, and to put it briefly, a sinkhole of all crimes and disgraces. It is that "hell of the living" noted by the mouth of David <note>A reference to the Psalms of King David.</note> long before it was founded or known. In that and in his other letters he writes many things to that effect, and those books are common in all lands.

The end. Friday of Epiphany. In the year of our Lord 1507.

<meta>The previous page concluded a fierce "Epilogue" written by the Waldensians (a proto-Protestant group), which used the poetry of Petrarch to denounce the Roman Church as the "Babylon" of the Apocalypse. # AGAINST THE EPILOGUE OF THE WALDENSIANS,
## BY JACOB ZIEGLER OF LANDAU, BAVARIA: AN
## IMPROVISED REFUTATION OF THE PIGHARDS’
## APPENDIX COROLLARY

The Pighards <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians, likely derived from "Picards."</note> wrote an unofficial addition to their work, a kind of appendix, in which they speak their own views—and indeed most foul ones—concerning Christian and apostolic obedience into the ears of the Christian people, using our own terminology. Lest we leave such a pestilential suspicion in the minds of the faithful—as if they had learned to cast aside Christian obedience based on the opinions of those within our own house—we have wished to send forth this present defense against them immediately, outside the regular order of the formal work we have conceived against them.

The Pighards refer us to their booklets concerning the "Chalice" <note>The "Chalice" refers to Utraquism, the belief that the laity should receive both the bread and the wine (the cup) during Communion, a central demand of the Bohemian Reformation.</note>, claiming that regarding the Sacrament of the Altar, they believe along with us according to the true rule of faith. They claim they differ from us only regarding the use of the Sacrament under both species <note>original: "sub utraque specie," meaning both bread and wine.</note>. Very well; for the virtue and truth of the Sacrament that must be believed, he who reads either side reads both, for we are clearly of a similar faith. Therefore, the Pighard has appealed to their booklets on the chalice in vain, as if seeking a better faith, while mocking Catholics as if we held views foreign to the faith.

They mention certain good and holy men; but since the holiness that comes through the confession of truth cannot err, let the Pighards be the first to follow the holiness of the Old Bohemians <note>Refers to the earlier generations of the Hussite movement in Bohemia.</note> in order to receive a better faith. Why do they, in good conscience, go against that holiness and the invincible reasons of that faith? It is as if they say these things only to the face and to tickle the ears of others, while in their inner sense they acknowledge neither that holiness nor those invincible reasons. Let them cease to hold us in suspense regarding such things which their predecessors first completed. The Pighards do not truly recognize those Bohemians, for they themselves were not Pighards. We, however, because they fell away from the body of the Christian Commonwealth—in which alone it is necessary for men to be saved—deny that those Bohemians were holy, according to a most just and certain judgment. Finally, we confess that their defeated arguments ought to have been abandoned—arguments which the Pighards have not yet conquered themselves, yet think they should not follow.

We find it difficult to believe that King George <note>George of Poděbrady (reigned 1458–1471), the "Hussite King" of Bohemia, who was often in conflict with the Papacy.</note> held certain schismatics in chains or even killed them for the sake of the faith, since he himself was part of the rebellion. Yet if the Pighards speak truly in this, what did the King do that was so unjust if he cut away the plague? For those who defect from the Apostolic religion are no less guilty of treason <note>original: "maiestatis," or lèse-majesté.</note> than those who defect from the state; it is by right of law that they are punished with the capital penalty. As for the great evils which the Pighards say befell King George and his children in vengeance for "innocent blood," these seem to me to be mere nonsense. King George was from the family of the Barons Kuna of Kunštát <note>The noble House of Kunštát, George’s ancestral line.</note>; though his family was primarily honored for the nobility and antiquity of its lineage, rivaling the noblest and oldest of Bohemia and Moravia, it was nonetheless a private family, owing nothing more to the Kingdom than other families did. Yet the favor of Fortune was present—the Fortune, I say, of Him who grants kingdoms—and it brought it to pass that Baron George Kuna of Kunštát was first chosen by common consent as regent over his equals, and then created King. And to this day, his family alone is the one that produces kings from among its ranks; while other families remained within the nobility of their ancestors, the Kuna of Kunštát alone send forth perpetual Princes to posterity. Let the Pighards call these the "evils" that befell Prince George and his...

He specifically addresses the legacy of the Hussite King George of Poděbrady, refuting claims that the king's family was cursed for shedding "innocent blood."</summary>

# AN IMPROVISED REFUTATION,

things that have happened to posterity. Let it be, then, that a certain bitter misfortune cast the head of King George <note>George of Poděbrady (reigned 1458–1471), the "Hussite King" of Bohemia, who was excommunicated by the Pope.</note> and his children into a struggle of fortune. This resulted from the instability of mortal affairs, so that we need not seek suspicious causes for it: it was a game played with him just as it is played with all kings and peoples. "All things happen equally to all," says Ecclesiastes: "to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who offers sacrifice and the one who despises the victims. As is the good man, so is the sinner; as is the man who swears a false oath, so is the one who fears an oath." <note>original: "vniuerſa æque eueniūt... vt q verū deierat." A paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 9:2.</note> But let the Pighards return and contend entirely that Prince George suffered many evils because of an offense against God. In that case, it was because he himself was among the schismatics. There is no truth to the word that he made a crime for himself out of his Christian confession. Rather, since he was found guilty before God on the side of the schismatics—which side he defended most obstinately—he reaped the material of his own evils from that side where he laid down this mortal life. Therefore, the Pighards act with deceit toward the Christian people when they arrange all these things so that we ought to believe that the King’s downfall proceeded from the fact that he defended apostolic obedience against the schismatics.

It grieves the Pighards that the Bohemians are again seeking out and cleansing the old ruins and the tombs of their ancestors, and raising up new houses for the saints. Therefore, Pighard: are you not yet saturated with the evils of your province? Do you wish that whatever was once torn down through the banditry of a single man should remain torn down forever? Indeed, you desire that even this remaining splendor of the fatherland be given over to ruins, so that there may be nothing illustrious in the kingdom to convict your countryside of its filth. You wish the face of Bohemia and Moravia to be more deformed than the wastes of the Tartars <note>A reference to the Mongol/Turkic tribes, used here as a metaphor for total desolation.</note>. You were once insane; now, lest you admit that it was madness, do you pretend it was a plan for the province? You envy God and his beloved saints everything that is contributed to divine service today, just as your accomplices once plundered it. As if you were the masters of nature, you wish to owe no argument of a grateful heart to God from any of your fortunes. But this is done under the guise of piety, while in truth it stems from deep avarice. You turn all the elements and what is born in them into your own pockets; you think whatever is dedicated to divine service is superfluous, as if now, regarding the entire divine law, nothing is necessary for salvation beyond what a Pighard has decreed. As if the Tabernacle of Moses, with all its ornament in the purest gold, silver, bronze, clothing, and every precious stone, were superfluous. As if the Temple of Solomon, with all its majesty, were superfluous—which he consecrated, which Christ defended against profaners, and which He called His house a house of prayer. As if the sacrifice of righteous Abel were superfluous, who sacrificed the most select lamb from the select flocks. It is a great thing; it ought to be venerated by the great affections of Christians with all our strength and with all the sublime majesty of sacred things. And cursed is the Pighard along with Cain the fratricide, who broods entirely over the profits of the earth and envies all his things to the honor of God and the saints. Nor does he grant a place for a chapel from all his fields, so that he might perform his religion in some pure place; instead, under the same roof, he carries out his shoemaker's frauds, <note>Ziegler uses the phrase "Sutrinæ fraudes" (shoemaker's tricks) to mock the humble, working-class background of many Waldensian preachers.</note> keeps his mistress, and performs his "sacred" rites.

The Pighards pray that a place be given to them among the schismatics. Truly, Pighard, if you agreed with them in faith, they would not claim you for themselves, yet you would be of their party. Now, because you do not agree, you claim them for yourself; you are a false brother to them. Finally, you do not agree with them on the most important point; and if you could alone achieve what you conceive for the overturning of the Catholic faith, you would not want the schismatics as allies. But contend that you desire to concede to them for the sake of some other plan or mere charity. Therefore, it was not right for you to depart from them crosswise in faith, appearance, gait, and all manners. But you did depart. And by the entire institution of your life, you bear witness that you have nothing in common with them regarding daily social life.

Here they wish to protect their perfidy under the cover of divine revelation and the ecclesiastical writers. Indeed, every school of heretics is accustomed to boast of divine revelation as a support for their errors, but the faith of their words remained only within their speech. They cite the holy ecclesiastical writer Bernard... <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic.</note>

He further attacks the group for their opposition to rebuilding Catholic churches, accusing them of greed and comparing their lack of ritual dignity to the "shoemaker's tricks" of unlearned men.</summary>

Having argued that the downfall of King George of Poděbrady was a result of his schism, Ziegler now addresses the Pighards' attempt to use the writings of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux to justify their separation from the Roman Catholic Church.</meta>

### AGAINST THE EPILOGUE OF THE WALDENSIANS,

The Pighards <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren, often associated by their enemies with the Waldensians.</note> call upon us, though they certainly deny the faith to all things apostolic. But look here, you Pighard. For a long time, you have portrayed yourself to the Royal Majesty as one who supports your faith by the primitive church <note>The early Christian church of the first centuries, which many reformers sought to emulate.</note> and the teachers of that time, so that you might cast out all recent men—along with that "whore of the Apocalypse" <note>A reference to the Whore of Babylon from the Book of Revelation, a common polemical label for the Roman Church among reformers.</note>—from the Lord’s portion. Now, having forgotten your own prescription, you bring forward this Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential Cistercian monk and mystic.</note>, whom you do not actually believe to be a saint—that is, a friend of the truth—nor do you call him such. I wonder, then, how he rightfully earns credit for faith in your eyes now. For the sake of condemning the priesthood and the church of the recent age, you have brought him in. 

So be it, bring him in; but you know which side wins by better faith. Since we ought to pierce each other in turn using only the handlers of the apostolic faith, you should confess that Saint Bernard—whom you called the author of your defection from the apostolic faith second only to God—is a Catholic. Indeed, you know it is contrary to the reason of a Catholic man to be judged "apostolic" by only one part of his writings. If Saint Bernard does not agree with the apostolic rule in all things, you should not believe him based on a single point; nor should you urge us to accept him as an authority of great weight in deciding apostolic matters. But he does agree—therefore you rightly appeal to him, and we legitimately stand by him. I say: you have appealed to Saint Bernard, and you shall stand by the saint regarding the whole matter. He himself shall sit as the arbitrary judge of our dispute to decide between the faith of both sides. 

You say, Pighard, that you recognized that "seduction" of the Roman Church (which makes itself the head of the apostolic faith) through the author Bernard. Read out the decree! You have none. Therefore, you both deceive and lead the Christian people astray under his name. I shall go more directly against you and that lie of yours. Saint Bernard confesses that he is a member of the head, which is the Roman Pontiff; he calls the Roman Pontiff the bridegroom, the vicar, and the prince of the universal church—whom you, as an enemy, abandon, deny, and betray. Hear his decree. In Letter 189, to the Supreme Pontiff Innocent <note>Pope Innocent II, reigned 1130–1143.</note>, he decrees thus:

> But you, O successor of Peter, shall judge whether he who attacks Peter's faith ought to have refuge at the See of Peter. You, I say, friend of the bridegroom, will provide a way to free the bride from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.

And in Letter 190:

> It is necessary that all dangers and emerging scandals in the kingdom of God be referred to your Apostleship, and especially those which concern the faith. For I judge it most fitting that the damages to faith be repaired in that place where faith cannot feel a defect. For this is the prerogative of this See. To which other was it ever said: "I have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith fail not"? Therefore, what follows is required of Peter’s successor: "And thou, being once converted, confirm thy brethren." <note>original: "Ego rogaui p te Petre... cōfirma fratres tuos." Quoting Luke 22:32.</note> Now is the necessary time, most loving father, for you to recognize your primacy. Show your zeal and honor your ministry. In this, you plainly fulfill the role of Peter, whose seat you hold.

And in Letter 237 to Pope Eugenius <note>Pope Eugenius III, a former student of Bernard.</note>:

> He says: the place in which you stand is holy ground; it is the place of Peter; it is the place of the Prince of the Apostles where his feet have stood. It is the place of him whom the Lord appointed master of his house and prince of all his possessions.

And in Letter 242: "Indeed, this greatest grief has reached even me, though I am the least of all, because it is the greatest, and because since it belongs to the head, it cannot fail to belong to the body, of which I am a member." Finally, everywhere he writes to archbishops, bishops, and abbots, he denies the order and power of none. Nowhere did he ever say or feel that bishops should be released from the one Supreme Pontiff, or the Christian people from their own bishops. He inveighed <note>Spoke or wrote with great hostility.</note> against the vices of priests, and today one should inveigh against the vices that are committed in every state of life. But we do not defect from the commonwealth for that reason. Both the Prophets and Christ inveighed against the priests of the Old Law, but Christ and the Prophets did not, for that reason, defect from the ordinary priesthood of the Synagogue. While detesting the vices, they followed the authority. You detest both the vice and the authority, and you have made that saying true in yourself: "Upon those who fear the falling ruin, the snow shall fall." <note>original: "Qui timent ruinā. irruet sup eos nix." A proverb suggesting that by fearing one disaster, they invite another.</note> But hear also our judge's confession against your crime, regarding the retention of the ecclesiastical priesthood; in Letter 195 he says:

Having previously discussed the history of the Bohemian schism, he now turns to theological authorities—specifically Saint Bernard of Clairvaux—to dismantle the Pighards' claim that a sinful clergy loses its spiritual authority.</meta>

### EXTEMPORANEOUS REFUTATION,

Read Saint Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and one of the most influential churchmen of the Middle Ages.</note> regarding that Arnold of Brescia <note>original: "Arnoldū de Brixia"; Arnold of Brescia was a 12th-century reformer and student of Abelard who challenged the temporal power of the Church and was eventually executed as a heretic.</note>, a man of your own views. You will see a man aptly rising up against the clergy, relying on military tyranny, rising up against the bishops themselves, and everywhere venting his rage against the entire ecclesiastical order. Regarding the holiness of the priesthood, however, Bernard says in his *Sermon to the Clerics*, in the twenty-ninth chapter: <note>original: "sermone ad clericos capite ip̄ius xxix"</note> "We do not accuse the whole body, but neither can we excuse the whole body; the Lord has left many thousands for Himself. Otherwise, unless their justice excused us, and the Lord of Sabaoth had left us that holy seed, we would have long ago been overturned like Sodom, and perished just like Gomorrah."

Regarding those who desert priestly authority, he says again in his *Sermons on the Song of Songs* (Sermon 66): "Truly, now, because they do not recognize the Church, it is no wonder if they disparage the orders of the Church, if they do not receive its institutes, if they despise the sacraments, and if they do not obey the commands." They say: "Apostolic men, archbishops, bishops, and priests are sinners; and because of this, they are fit neither for giving nor receiving the sacraments." But they claim these two things—being a bishop and being a sinner—can never be reconciled. This is false. Caiaphas was a bishop <note>In this context, Ziegler uses "bishop" (episcopus) to mean "high priest," following the Latin Vulgate's terminology.</note>, and yet what a sinner he was, he who dictated the sentence of death against the Lord! If you deny he was a bishop, the testimony of John will argue against you, for he records that he even prophesied as a testimony of his high priesthood. Judas was an apostle; and although he was greedy and wicked, he was chosen by the Lord. Do you doubt the apostleship of the man whom the Lord chose? "Did I not," He said, "choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" You hear that the same man was a chosen apostle and yet turned out to be a devil; and yet you deny that a man can be a bishop if he is a sinner? 

The scribes and Pharisees sat upon the chair of Moses <note>A reference to Matthew 23:2, where Jesus instructs his followers to obey the religious leaders because of the office they hold, even if they are hypocrites.</note>, and those who did not obey them as bishops were guilty of disobedience even against the Lord Himself, who commanded and said, "Do what they say." It is plain: though they were scribes, though they were Pharisees—that is, though they were the greatest of sinners—nevertheless, because of the Chair of Moses, that which He also said pertained no less to them: "He who hears you, hears me; and he who despises you, despises me." 

Here, you most lying Pighard, you might explain how you have rightfully and holily cast out the ecclesiastical order and that primary chair of the apostolic faith, according to the authority of Saint Bernard! But also in his *Sermons on the Song of Songs* (Sermon 64, and likewise 65, and again 66), Bernard aptly mentions, refutes, and condemns you and your errors by name, so that we might suspect the "Pighards" had already begun back then. But you have skipped over all those things, and you have snatched them from our sight so that you might not be made better by the faith, nor that we might catch you in your voluntary errors and your defiled conscience. 

You say in another place: <insert> That you are this "chosen nursery" of God for the Church, in which the apostolic and primitive faith lives again today. </insert> But Saint Bernard shows you to be a liar with these words: "They call themselves the Church, but they contradict Him who says: 'A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.'" <note>A reference to Matthew 5:14. Ziegler is arguing that the true Church must be visible and universal, not a secret sect.</note> Is it so, then? Do you believe that the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which became a mountain and filled the world, is now shut up in your caves? We must not linger even here; the very opinion shrinks from being made public, content with its own whisper. The Church has, and always will have, its full inheritance from Christ, and its possession to the ends of the earth. Rather, those who attempt to take that inheritance away from Christ withdraw themselves from this great inheritance. 

Against these dogs and pigs of yours, Pighard, by whom you have defiled the entire Christian state, Saint Bernard disputes thus: "What shall we do with these most malignant foxes so that they may be caught? They prefer to harm rather than to conquer, and they do not even wish to appear, but rather to creep." All heretics have always had one intention: to hunt for glory from the singularity of their knowledge. This specific malice is more malignant and deceitful than other heresies; it feeds on the losses of others, being nearly negligent of its own glory. I believe it is learned from the examples of the ancients, who were unable to escape destruction but were immediately caught. It is a cautious new kind of wickedness to work the "mystery of iniquity" <note>A phrase from 2 Thessalonians 2:7, often associated with the Antichrist or secret subversion of the faith.</note> all the more freely because it is more hidden. Finally, they have declared—as it is said—they have fixed for themselves a hiding place, a wicked speech for themselves: "Swear, forswear, but do not betray the secret." <note>original: "iura piura secretum perdere noli"; This was a common medieval saying attributed to heretical groups like the Waldensians, suggesting they were permitted to lie to outsiders to protect their sect.</note> Indeed, in other matters, they refuse to swear at all, so as not to have held to anything, because of that passage in the Gospel: "Do not swear at all, neither by heaven nor by earth," and so forth. Oh, you fools and slow of heart! Filled plainly with a Pharisaic spirit, straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel! You refuse to swear...

<meta>This page continues Jacob Ziegler’s polemic against the "Pighards" (a derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians). Having established the authority of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux in the previous page, Ziegler now addresses the sect's secrecy, their rejection of Purgatory, and their selective use of the Gospels to justify their behavior.</meta>

# AGAINST THE EPILOGUE OF THE WALDENSIANS,

It is permitted, and it is even permitted to commit perjury. Or is it only in this one matter that both are allowed? From what place in the Gospels do you bring forth this exception for me—the Gospels of which you falsely boast you omit not even an iota? It is clear that you both superstitiously observe the prohibition of oaths and wickedly presume the right to perjury. O, what perversity! That which was advised as a caution—namely, not to swear—these people observe so contentiously as if it were a mandatory command; yet that which is sanctioned by unshakeable law—namely, that one must not commit perjury—they dispense with at their own will as if it were a matter of indifference.

"No," they say, "but let us not make the mystery public," <note>The Waldensians were often accused of keeping their true doctrines secret from outsiders to avoid persecution.</note> as if it were not the glory of God to reveal the word. Do they envy the glory of God? I believe rather that they are ashamed to disclose their secrets, knowing them to be inglorious. For they are said to perform unspeakable and obscene acts in secret—indeed, even the hindquarters of foxes stink. But I remain silent on what they would deny; let them respond to what is manifest. Do they, according to the Gospel, take care not to "give what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine"? <note>Matthew 7:6</note> To use this defense is to openly admit they are not of the Church, for all who are of the Church cease to be dogs and swine. Without exception, they believe that whatever their "thing" is must be withdrawn from all who are not of their sect. However, even if they feel this, they will not answer, lest they be made manifest—which they flee by every means, though they shall not escape.

Answer me, O man, you who know more than is proper and yet are more foolish than can be expressed: Is this mystery you hide of God, or is it not? If it is of God, why do you not disclose it to His glory? For it is the glory of God to reveal the word. <note>original: "gloria dei reuelare sermonē"; This is a rhetorical inversion of Proverbs 25:2, which usually states it is God's glory to *conceal* a matter. Ziegler/Bernard argues that for the Gospel, the "glory" lies in its revelation to the world.</note> If it is not of God, why do you have faith in that which is not His, unless it is because you are a heretic? Therefore, let them either disclose God's secret for God's glory, or let them deny it is a mystery of God and stop denying they are heretics. Or certainly, let them confess themselves to be manifest enemies of the glory of God, since they refuse to make public what they know would be to His glory.

The truth of Scripture stands: "It is the glory of kings to conceal a word; it is the glory of God to reveal the speech." You do not wish to reveal it; therefore, you do not wish to glorify God. But perhaps you do not receive this Scripture. So it is: they profess themselves to be the followers of the Gospel alone—and the only true followers at that. Let them answer the Gospel: "What I say to you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in the ear, preach upon the housetops." <note>Matthew 10:27</note> It is no longer permitted to remain silent and keep secret that which God commands to be made public. Why is your Gospel hidden? I suspect yours is not the Gospel of Paul, for he confesses that his is not hidden. "And if," he says, "my Gospel is hidden, it is hidden to those who perish." <note>2 Corinthians 4:3</note> See if he might be speaking of you, among whom the Gospel is found hidden. What is more fitting than that you should perish?

Or perhaps you do not even receive Paul? I have heard this regarding some of you, for you do not all agree with one another in all things, even if you all dissent from us. But truly, the words, writings, and traditions of those who were bodily present with the Savior are received by all of you—unless I am mistaken—as having the equal authority of the Gospel. Did those apostles keep the Gospel hidden? Did they, for that reason, remain silent about the weakness of the flesh, the horrors of death, or the ignominy of the Cross? Indeed, "their sound has gone out into all the earth." <note>Psalm 19:4 / Romans 10:18</note> Where is this apostolic fame and life you boast of? They cry out; you whisper. They are in public; you are in a corner. They fly like clouds; you hide in darkness and in subterranean houses.

Pighard <note>term: "Pighard"; a derogatory nickname for the Bohemian Brethren, possibly derived from "Picards," referring to their perceived foreign or heretical origins.</note>, you deny the Purgatory of souls. Certainly, you deny this against the faith of Saint Bernard, who refutes you on this error with these words: "They do not believe that a purgatorial fire remains after death, but that the soul, once released from the body, passes immediately either to rest or to damnation." Let them ask Him who said that there is a certain sin that will be forgiven neither in this world nor in the future, why He said this if no remission or purging of sin remains in the future. <note>Matthew 12:32; a standard Catholic proof-text for Purgatory.</note>

Pighard, you boast of a "narrow, sad, and mocked path" following the footsteps of the ancient Church, but in another place you are much more swollen with pride regarding the merits and constancy of the martyrs who gave up both life and possessions for the confession of Christ. You count yourself among them; but hear from Saint Bernard how you boast falsely of this as well. For he rebukes your distracted mind with these words: "Many other evils have been persuaded to this foolish and senseless person by spirits of error speaking lies in hypocrisy, but it is not necessary to respond to all... for as far as these people are concerned, they are neither convinced by reasons, because they do not understand, nor corrected by authorities, because they do not receive them."

He also uses the authority of Saint Bernard to defend the existence of Purgatory and dismiss the sect's claims to apostolic poverty and martyrdom.</summary>
