<meta>This page continues Ziegler’s attack on the Waldensians (referred to here as "Pighards"). He moves from discussing their secrecy to describing their stubbornness in the face of death and the various authorities—St. Bernard and Petrarch—they claim as supporters.</meta>

# AGAINST THE EPILOGUE OF THE WALDENSIANS,

They are not swayed by persuasion because they are perverted; this has been proven. They choose to die rather than be converted. Their end is destruction; a final fire awaits them. Indeed, a prefigurement of their deeds appeared in the story of Samson, in the burning tails of the foxes. <note>original: "facto Sanson ex succēsis vulpiū caudis" — a reference to Judges 15:4, where Samson ties torches to foxes' tails; here, the foxes represent the heretics spreading fire.</note> Many of the faithful, having laid hands on some of them, dragged them into the midst of the crowd. Questioned regarding their faith, since they were held under suspicion, they denied everything entirely in their usual manner. However, when examined by the ordeal of water, <note>A medieval judicial test where the accused was thrown into water; if they floated, it was believed the water (a pure element) "rejected" them, proving guilt.</note> they were found to be liars. Since they could not deny it—being caught out by the water refusing to receive them—it was as if they took the bit between their teeth; they did not so much confess their impiety as miserably and freely *profess* it. They publicly asserted their own "piety," and for its sake, they were ready to undergo death—and no less ready to inflict it on those standing by. 

And so the people, rushing upon them, gave these heretics "martyrs" of their own perfidy. We approve of the zeal of the people, but we do not advise the act itself, because faith should be persuaded, not imposed. Nevertheless, they would undoubtedly be better coerced by the sword <note>original: "gladio" — referring to the "power of the sword" held by the state or magistrate to punish crime, based on Romans 13:4.</note>—namely, the sword of him who carries it for a reason—rather than being permitted to drag many others into their error; for that ruler is the minister of God, an avenger of wrath against those who do evil.

Some wondered how they were led to death not only patiently but even joyfully, as it seemed. But such people fail to notice how great the power of the Devil is—not only over the bodies of men but even over the hearts he has once been permitted to possess. Is it not a greater thing for a man to lay hands upon himself than to willingly suffer it from another? We have frequently experienced the Devil's power to do this in many who have either drowned or hanged themselves; after all, Judas hanged himself, undoubtedly at the Devil's instigation. I, however, consider it a greater and more admirable thing that the Devil could have put it into his heart to betray the Lord than to hang himself. 

Therefore, the constancy of the Martyrs and the stubbornness of these people have nothing in common. In the Martyrs, it is piety that works a contempt for death; in these people, it is hardness of heart. Perhaps the Prophet spoke with the voice of a Martyr, saying: *Their heart is curdled like milk; but I have meditated on your law.* <note>Psalm 119:70. The Latin "Coagulatū est sicut lac cor eorū" suggests a heart that has become thickened or insensitive to truth.</note> For although the punishment seemed the same, the intention was far different: the heretic's heart was hardening against the Lord, while the Martyr's was meditating on the law of the Lord. Since this is the case, there is no need, as I said, to waste many words against men who are most foolish and obstinate; it is enough that they have been made known so that they may be avoided.

I do not bring forward Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a prominent Cistercian monk and mystic often cited by both Catholics and later reformers.</note> as our witness regarding the veneration of saints, the truth of the Sacrament of the Eucharist, or his most holy faith—even though he condemns you and your perfidy by name. Do not ever dare to say again that you learned the "seduction of the Roman Church" from the teachings of Bernard, that most Christian Doctor. Truly, he is our witness, and through his very writings against you and your heresy, he has most clearly proven you to be a most lying trifler.

I come now to Francesco Petrarch, <note>The famous Italian poet and humanist (1304–1374).</note> by whom you say you have been warned, Pighard, and from whom you would draw your betrayal of the Apostolic Church. Who, then, is Petrarch among the commentators on the Apostolic faith, or how great is he among the interpreters of Divine Law? For his sake, Pighard, you would order the Gospel, the Apostles, Dionysius, Jerome, Augustine, and all the most ancient commentators to move out of the way? Is your eye evil because the Christian confession is good? I say this: if you were not a most deceptive colluder but stood by your own promises, you would never start anything now, nor would you fix any defense for your perfidy, unless you had received it from Christ, from the Apostles, from the first-fruits of the Church, and from the sacred writers of that time. 

You would have no more use for Petrarch today than any other interpreter of the Apostolic faith who was far removed from that century—the only century from which you pretend to recall your faith. Petrarch was a poet and an orator; in testimony of his profession, he received the laurel at Rome, on the Capitol, in the year 1341. <note>original: "anno a nr̅a etate clxx" — Ziegler is calculating years from his own time or a specific era; the historical date was 1341.</note> Following his own profession, he felt and wrote many things not according to the discipline of an Apostolic commentator or even a Christian man, but rather in the arrogant manner of the gentiles <note>i.e., the pagan classical authors Petrarch emulated.</note>. Nor do I speak now of the "Whore of the Apocalypse," <note>original: "meretrice apocalypsis" — the Whore of Babylon from the Book of Revelation, a common trope heretics used to describe the Roman Church.</note> which no one ever turned against the Apostolic confession unless he was also a heretic. Truly, he stubbornly called the Gauls and all other Christians outside of Italy "barbarians" under a single name...

<meta>This page continues Ziegler’s polemic against the Waldensians (referred to here as "Pighards"). He is specifically addressing the Waldensians’ use of the poet Petrarch to support their arguments, dismissing Petrarch as an unsuitable authority for theological matters and recontextualizing Petrarch's criticisms of the Papacy.</meta>

# AGAINST THE EPILOGUE OF THE WALDENSIANS,

...calls most clearly. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a thought about how the opponent interprets a source.</note> I say that this is a matter of an endless Jewish genealogy and purely pagan boasting. Indeed, the nations care about such things. But in Christ, as the divine Paul says: **"As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ; there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus."** <note>original: "quicũqꝫ baptisati estis christũ induistis..." — a quotation from Galatians 3:27-28.</note> Therefore, we who have been equally received into the one body of Christ—Italians, Spaniards, French, and Germans—who live by the same laws of the Gospel, share the same citizenship and kinship. Christ is not "barbarian" in this part, nor "Latin" in that part; the **Christian Commonwealth** <note>original: "resp. Christiana" — Respublica Christiana, the medieval concept of a unified Christian society.</note> is one and the same, and ecclesiastical laws are not different for Scythians than they are for Latins. Rather, whatever you call Christ, whether Latin or barbarian, we are all equally Christians throughout the whole world. 

Petrarch should have understood this even from the histories of the nations. Whenever the Greeks, and later the Romans, led colonies of citizens into any lands—Spain, Gaul, England, Dacia, Pannonia, Mysia, Syria, Africa, and all of Asia—none there were considered "barbarians." Whether they were Greeks or Romans, both the fathers and their descendants were all under the same law. Petrarch, out of a poorly affected mind, tries to strip this right from Christians. Therefore, neither by his profession nor—what is most important—by his spirit and Christian modesty, should Petrarch sit as an arbiter and author of the faith in a Christian seat. 

Every matter is either confirmed or weakened by the authorities of its own profession: poetry by poets, oratory by orators, history by histories, and all related matters by those within the same field. "Physicians handle what belongs to physicians; craftsmen handle their tools." <note>A common Latin proverb: "Quod medicorum est, promittunt medici; tractant fabrilia fabri."</note> Therefore, the ecclesiastical faith should not be sought from any writers except ecclesiastical ones when there is a dispute over the outcome. 

But here, Pigharde, <note>A derogatory term for the Waldensians, often confused with "Picards."</note> the weightier writers of apostolic doctrine seem to you to be too much for you to dare to bring them forward. For that reason, you summon anyone from anywhere to be witnesses to your perfidy. If you succeed in being granted this license, you could go anywhere. Now you will call upon grammarians as the authors of your faith after God; you will appoint physicians as judges, but also musicians, and finally, without selection, anyone who is ill-disposed toward Christian matters. I say: you, who are acting in this way, who have abandoned the legitimate ecclesiastical writers as judges and think anyone else is suitable for you—anyone who has spoken out against Christian affairs—you will call as witnesses for the same cause of perfidy both the Manicheans and the Arians, and all heretics, Turks, and Saracens. Finally, you would call those most ancient profaners and enemies of Christ and the Church: **Lucian, Hierocles, Celsus, and Porphyry.** <note>Four of the most famous pagan critics of Christianity in late antiquity.</note> For they, distinguished in their opposition to the apostolic faith, barked out every foul thing according to your own stomach's taste. 

You have your answer, Pigharde, as to why we do not allow you this whim of yours—dragging a Christian poet into the decision-making for the Catholic faith. This is not because we deny that Petrarch was a Christian, but so that you do not suddenly introduce him to us as a sufficiently suitable arbiter of the faith. I say, we forbid your deceits by way of a poet, so that you might learn once and for all whom you ought to call upon and whose authority you must stand by when disputing Christian matters. Do not try now with a poet what you hope might be allowed in other cases. 

But do not think, Pigharde, that we say these things as a preface to dodge the issue. I also come to the passage which you have produced here from Petrarch. First, I say this: if you read this passage as if Petrarch suggests and desires that you cast off apostolic obedience, you are lying against the author himself. He wrote these things at that time when the Roman Popes of French name had transferred the Apostolic See to Gaul [France]. <note>Ziegler refers to the "Avignon Papacy" (1309–1376), often called the "Babylonian Captivity of the Church."</note> They had been away from the Roman Church for seventy years, to the great detriment of both the Church and the city [Rome]. Nor were they following holiness, for they were yielding to "flesh and blood" and were striving to place profit ahead of religion or against the Gospel for the sake of their own nation. Christ said, **"He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me."** Therefore, so that the Roman Pontiff might return again to the city of Rome, his legitimate seat, Petrarch wrote such things to the most powerful men and to the Pope himself, while simultaneously reproaching **Avignon**, <note>original: "Auinionis" — Avignon.</note> which is a city of Gaul on the river Rhône...

He is specifically debunking their claim that Francesco Petrarch and Saint Bernard of Clairvaux supported their rejection of the Roman Papacy. ### AN EXTEMPORANEOUS REFUTATION,

...in that age, the residence of the supreme pontiffs <note>Refers to the Avignon Papacy (1309–1376), a period when the Popes resided in France rather than Rome.</note>. Because he most consistently condemned that place—both here and in many other passages—as an adulterous church in opposition to the city of Rome, the rightful spouse. Yet you, Pighard <note>A derogatory term for a member of the Waldensian sect.</note>, exclude the meaning that serves you and present everything as if he wrote against obedience to the Roman Church, and indeed, as if he recognized the seduction of the Roman Church away from common salvation. You boast that you have used the authors Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a prominent mystic and Church reformer.</note> and Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the Italian poet and scholar often critical of the Avignon Papacy.</note> there, but you lie so grossly that it can certainly be felt. 

Regarding Saint Bernard, we have seen—and Francesco Petrarch as well—that they purely and faithfully confess that the Roman Church and its pontiffs hold the supreme leadership over the entire Christian world. From many testimonies, we bring forward these few: in the *Letters of Old Age* <note>original: "Seniliū epľaꝝ" — Petrarch's *Rerum Senilium Libri*.</note>, Book 7, to Urban V, the Supreme Pontiff, he says: "The more distinguished place was deliberately chosen so that where the head of the bridle <note>A metaphor for the seat of government or control.</note> had been, there the seat of the heavenly empire might be on earth, founded on solid faith and humble holiness, and bound together by the sacred blood of the apostles and martyrs; human presumption ought not to change this divine work." Again, he says: "All the others have their own spouses, subjects indeed to you alone but presiding over their own churches; but that one <note>The Roman Church.</note> has none but you. Thus, while you are supreme in the rest, in the city of Rome you are the sole pontiff and sole spouse." And again: "Therefore, the most famous, the highest, the very peak of the Catholic faith wavers, and you, the supreme watchman of the house of Israel and the sentinel of the Lord's tower, sit on the bank of the Rhone <note>The river flowing through Avignon, where the Papacy was then located.</note>."

Furthermore, in the first letter of the ninth book, Petrarch also vehemently congratulates the Christian world that the Apostolic See had been established in Rome once again. It would be an infinite task to transcribe all the testimonies on that point, since this is Petrarch’s sole and perpetual confession regarding the power of the Roman Pontiff and the universal veneration of his diocese. You have read all these things, Pighard, but though you understand them well, you pretend as if you understand nothing. You knowingly and willingly steal the true face of things from our eyes, trusting in your tricks. You think to yourself: "Until they shake out my first lies, I will find others with which to hold the foolish common people." 

I wonder if you are not ashamed of your lies and your fraud. You have cast out the Roman Church—by what authors? You lie by the gods! Indeed, you have made yourself unworthy of God by your perfidy and lies. Bernard and Petrarch? I say you lie! For they think the opposite of you. They say and do everything for the sake of obedience; you say and do everything against obedience. You pretend to follow this Scripture for both of them, and yet you do not follow it—if you take it according to their opinion, you would not kick away Apostolic obedience as they did not, whereas you do kick it away. By imposing your own meaning on the words of our authors, you adorn your own treachery. Therefore, you do not follow them in their meaning, but you lie against the authors themselves, whom you have found in the midst of ecclesiastical obedience, and yet you have produced and adorned them as if they were conscious accomplices in your most harmful betrayal. 

Finally, I come to the passage you transcribed here from Petrarch against the Church, Pighard—namely, that Petrarch mentioned that **"Whore"** from the Apocalypse of John <note>original: "meretrici illiꝰ ex apocalypsi" — the Whore of Babylon, a figure in Revelation often used in medieval polemics to symbolize corruption.</note>. This one thing pleases you above all else, and by it you clearly betray your malevolence. For what Petrarch asserted regarding Avignon in Gaul <note>France.</note>, you, for the sake of strengthening your perfidy, interpret against the entire universal Church, contrary to the author’s meaning. For that reason, I wish to dispute a little on that very passage of the Apocalypse and extract his error, which now titillates you and from which you paint a "stork's beak" <note>A gesture of mockery, essentially saying Pighard is mocking the Church behind its back.</note> at the Church's back from your proud chapter. 

I say this again about Petrarch: he grieved that the Roman See was held among the Gauls, and as a true Christian man, he demanded by prayer that the Roman Pontiff remain at his legitimate Church and not wander as a pilgrim in Gaul. This was most just. However, because he did not approach the matter with a free mind—nor was he moved by the Roman cause alone, but rather by a private hatred for the French name—he descended into the business already corrupted. Therefore, he was led not by the modesty that the law and the nature of the business required, but was carried away by that loathing of his, born of a stomach offended by the Gauls. Nothing was so remote or so foreign that it could not occur to him to drag it in here, provided it was fierce. Thus he found for himself that **"Whore"** of the Apocalypse, and from that he uttered more things against the faithful Christians of Gaul than a right mind according to God could excuse. In which place, if Petrarch was an interpreter of the Holy Scriptures...

# AGAINST THE CONCLUSION OF THE WALDENSIANS,

...let him show other monuments of such a profession from which we might believe he <note>Referring to Petrarch.</note> was an interpreter of the sacred law, and let us see how this passage appropriately depends on the previous explanation and appropriately draws a later sense from itself. This is the law of interpretation, and this is what the sacred canon of Scriptures demands: lest the heavenly mystery be thrust out according to anyone’s whim into arbitrary explanations—just as Aesop's fables <note>original: "æſopianæ fabellæ"</note> are usually adapted to daily and randomly occurring speech. 

If, however, he never labored in such a task nor was professed in it, let him name at least one of the ecclesiastical writers currently in the record whom he followed in this passage. But if he followed no Catholic writer, he will be shown most vain, since you <note>Ziegler addresses his opponent, the Waldensian "Pighard."</note> have transcribed the present passage against the opinion of the elders and above your own capacity, for the sake of fulfilling a temporary contention, into a contradictory sense. Therefore, you were unable to translate the whole passage, in all its clauses and phrases, to your perverse contention.

He [Petrarch] says that Avignon is that Babylon and the harlot <note>original: "meretricē"</note> which John describes in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. I demand here from Petrarch the faith of the ancestors for such a sense; surely, if that very Avignon is Babylon and the harlot, then once the prophecy is fulfilled according to history, it will not signify above all other impieties: idolatry, heresy, Muhammad, or the Antichrist. Thus, would all those impurities of impiety and perfidy be outside the curse in the eyes of Almighty God? For certainly those have fornicated in the past and fornicate today, and in the final time they will fornicate most foully under the Antichrist from God, with the kings and peoples of the earth. 

Or if he places Avignon among the remaining seats of impiety: because those who then presided over Avignon were the supreme pontiffs of the Christian world, and the kings and peoples of that time of the Christian name believed according to the rule of the Apostles which they had received at Rome—which the city of Rome had guarded from ancient centuries and the tradition of the elders, and which today the entire Christian world confesses without changing a single article—therefore, both in that time and our own, not only Avignon but the entire Christian world would be equally defamed by this "harlot." 

But Petrarch indeed frees his own century from all infamy of perfidy, because in his works he everywhere asserts the Catholic—that is, our—dogma, and stands as a witness to the Apostolic faith throughout the whole Christian world. But our own century against the infamy of perfidy—which you, Pighard <note>A derogatory term for the Waldensians, often associated with the "Pickards" or Taborites of Bohemia.</note>, rouse again against the Christian people at this time—we defend, God being favorable, in our five books which we have established against your insanity. 

Thus, there is no cause, Pighard, for either you or Petrarch to adapt this harlot, her fornications, these names of blasphemy, or this cup full of abominations—he for Avignon, you for the whole Christian world—to unload your untimely contention. And regarding you, Pighard, I am not surprised, for you have now set aside both the face and the conscience of a Christian man. But I must strongly demand this of Petrarch: Petrarch, did you think it the act of a Christian man to cast off conscience and the truth of things so far? To speak without measure? To reproach your brother, the son of your mother, so cruelly? 

The French <note>original: "Galli"</note>, as we see even today, are a most illustrious portion of the Christian name, redeemed by the blood of Christ just as much as the Italians themselves; second to none in religion and piety toward God. In their civil institution—not to call them the most refined—they are certainly neither Scythians <note>original: "Scythæ" — an ancient nomadic people used here as a synonym for "uncivilized barbarians."</note> nor descended from Scythians. And to embrace all things, they are in no way hated by God as much as you make them hated because of your untimely contention. Fear the judgment of God, Petrarch, for you do not agree with Christ as long as you walk more proudly than the rest of the members of Christ throughout the world; you make the remaining members of the Church unworthy of yourself and your nation. You cast the Harlot of the Apocalypse against the French. I have said once that those pontiffs of the French name acted in no way holily, but neither did they act so atrociously that you should so headlong...

# EXTEMPORANEOUS REFUTATION

...prophecy, and upon the servants of the devil, the members of the Antichrist: which <note>The prophecy of the Whore of Babylon in the Book of Revelation.</note> was written against those who, as long as they are on this earth, fight against divinity with all their crimes and finally with a false religion against God; you would apply this to the Popes of the French name, and upon Avignon, their seat. Since you also granted this to the Supreme Pontiff: that the Roman Pontiff is the father and head not of one, but of the Universal Church; and that his seat is in whatever place in the Christian world he chooses to remain. Indeed, you felt this way when writing to the Supreme Pontiff Urban V in the seventh book of your *Letters of Old Age* <note>original: "ſeniliū Epiſtolarū libro ſeptimo"</note>. Do you dare now, therefore, Petrarch, to curse whatever the Pontiff pleases to do, as soon as it is done, as the harlot of the Apocalypse? 

But just as those things oppose one another, so thereafter you will get stuck in the final exposition, such as that line: "Do you not know yourself, Babylon?" <note>Petrarch often addressed Avignon as the new Babylon in his poems.</note> or finally that: "Why are you silent? Either show another city drunk with this blood, or deny if you can that you yourself are this drunken one." 

I, Avignon, say: "I know myself. In faith I am Christian—a sinner indeed on earth, but one for whose sake Christ descended from heaven and left the sacraments behind on earth." I point out to you the city of the devil and its rulers—the Neros, Domitians, Decii, Valerians, Diocletians, and Maximians <note>These were Roman Emperors known for persecuting early Christians.</note>—the arena of the heathens, the theaters, and in this day the Turk, the Saracen, and the Tartar <note>Ziegler refers to the Ottoman Empire and other non-Christian powers of his time.</note>. I show those to you as being drunk on the blood of martyrs. 

The vision of the Evangelist <note>St. John, the author of Revelation.</note> is true; I add further, it is not fragmented, but continuous, consistent with itself, and harmonious. If, therefore, Petrarch, you have taken upon yourself some interpretation regarding the prophecy of the Evangelist, it must be true, perpetual, and self-consistent. Here you begin—magnificently indeed, according to your own temper—but you ask the final things of me, Avignon, as an adversary, and by no means innocently. For by this trick, where I might confess no crime against my innocence, you have left a great suspicion in the mind of the listener, that they might believe it is a consciousness of guilt that prevents me from speaking. 

Why do you not settle both sides by your own skill? Make a trial, so that we may see from a consistent exposition that these were not monstrosities from which you fell into these views. I, Avignon, deny that I am drunk with the blood of martyrs. You there, Petrarch, assist your own distorted exposition. Recount which innocents I have killed for the confession of Christ; from whom I have extorted life for the denial of Christ; how many and how great the martyrs were that I sent by my own hand to Christ. I send you not to remote histories, but to your own age. I myself pray you: do not fail against the adversary of your cause. But you know nothing of these things, and you produce nothing. How much greater, therefore, for your reputation—since you were not going to prove such bloody cruelty against martyrs of Christ among the most Christian French—if you had left that part of the harlot of the Apocalypse untouched.

# AGAINST THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS AND
## TO THE MOST REVEREND FATHER AND LORD IN CHRIST, LORD STANISLAUS, BISHOP OF OLOMOUC, THE FIRST BOOK OF THE DISPUTATION AGAINST THE HERETICAL WALDENSIANS BY JACOB ZIEGLER OF LANDAU, BAVARIA.

When, this past year, I followed the noble Lord, Lord Heinrich Kuna of Kunštát, into Moravia, I exchanged the bustle of the city and the sweet company of my best friends for my current solitude. Those circumstances, which might have caused others to regret the change, gave me the material to immerse myself further into my related studies. Here, therefore, when I had begun to pore over certain distinguished writers one after another—now theologians, now philosophers, now any of the more humane letters—I also pursued mathematical studies somewhat more attentively. There, I constructed several remarkable works with great labor and time. I was just about to move on to that armillary sphere of Claudius Ptolemy—which he called a *Meteoroscopium* <note>original: "Meteoroscopiū"; an ancient instrument used to determine the positions of celestial bodies.</note>—a most noble and rare instrument from which he derived almost all the numbers of his cosmographic work.

Suddenly, in the midst of this work, another task <note>Ziegler makes a pun here on the Latin "negotio" (business or trouble) and "negotium" (a task/work).</note> arose which had such weight with me that I relaxed a little from the aforementioned studies (which I was pursuing for pleasure and a certain indulgence of the mind) to turn myself to this new matter with all my strength. One or two men of that superstition, whom the common people call the "Waldensian Brothers," <note>Also known as the Bohemian Brethren or *Unitas Fratrum*.</note> used to come to our people either for friendship or business. One of them was accustomed to boast that he had learned better things about the Waldensian religion through "divine instinct." This was intolerable to Christian ears: to hear divine inspiration boasted of from that side which, in so many things and finally in the whole faith, disagrees with Christian institutions. 

Another man, who showed a singular benevolence toward me, judged—since he thought I was someone of importance—that I might easily cross over to their faith and abandon Roman obedience. I laughed; I held him in the same regard as one who might say, "Since you are wise, strip off the person and put on the beast." Indeed, as many as they are in number, they all come from the rustic and base common folk, among whom the knowledge of any more honorable institution is as much neglected as it is ignored. If any more learned person were to flee to them, he would be the only deserter from among our people and the only one there with understanding. 

From that time, I began to inquire more diligently into what the persuasion of those men might be, that they would dare to rebel against the most holy Apostolic authority, in which the sublimity of kings, the judgment of the most clear-sighted minds, and finally the whole Christian world agrees. I was not fooled into thinking that these plebeian men—shut in among domestic filth, sedentary and rustic labors, and that obscure corner of the world from which they come—could bring forth anything better than the judgment and consensus of the world. 

First, therefore, around last October, I happened upon a certain little book of theirs, written in the Latin language under the title of *Confession and Apology*. Later, another work came into my hands which responds to two letters of Doctor Augustin, the royal secretary <note>Augustin Käsenbrot (1467–1513), a prominent humanist and secretary to King Vladislaus II, who wrote against the Bohemian Brethren.</note>. Since it was issued in their vernacular language, in order to understand it, I was forced to hire a man—the best I could find in this neighborhood—who could translate it into Latin for me with as much faithfulness as possible. There was enough in their prologues to see how bitterly they strike the consciences of the unlearned. Whatever belongs to Christian innocence and purity according to the testimony of the Gospel—which ought only to apply to the most holy men—they have seized all of this for their own side with a most impudent lie. They act as if, whether the Royal power takes action against them or a disputation convicts them by their own scripture, they are the ones in whom these and similar oracles are fulfilled.

# FIRST BOOK OF THE CONFESSION,
->G ij<-

“They will lay their hands upon you, dragging you before kings and governors, and they will put some of you to death; and you will be hated by all men.” <note>original: "vobis manus suas trahentes..." Ziegler is quoting Luke 21:12–17, applying the warnings of Christ regarding the apostles to the current ecclesiastical struggle.</note> Let those very men be the saints of ancient patience who, through fame and infamy, through all fortunes, and finally by the very blood of true martyrs, recall those ancient examples. Finally, whatever deserved punishment may befall the sacrilegious, let it be exactly what the Savior and Lord Christ predicted so many centuries ago: “They will cast you out of the synagogues; but the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God. And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father, nor me.” <note>original: "absque synagogis facient vos..." A quote from John 16:2–3.</note> 

That lying impudence of theirs was helped—I know not whether I should call it chance, or design, or both—by the fact that the most clement King <note>Likely referring to King Vladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary, or his successor Louis II, who dealt with the Bohemian Reformation.</note> had decreed four years ago to heal this plague or to remove it entirely. And although he had gladdened a great part of Europe with these most pious efforts, suddenly everything vanished. Now, therefore, after such a holy expectation has frustrated all those who think well of the Christian cause, those victors in impiety wrinkle their noses at us <note>original: "nasum in nos rugant"; a Latin idiom for sneering or mocking.</note>. By this act, they present a most terrible and dangerous example to the simplicity of believers: because an attempt was once made to repress the guilty, if they were later less repressed, the impious boast that God stood by his own, and that God shook the King's will in another direction so that he would not defile his hands in their persecution. 

When in truth—if a private citizen may nonetheless speculate on public deeds—they were saved by no other means than the patronage of certain men who were either once allies of that impiety or are certainly today its defenders. These men receive the most ample returns from them and fear that deserted estates will remain empty—estates which they are accustomed to having that class of men plow across great tracts of land. 

Therefore, when I saw the public conscience languishing with such a destructive seduction of the weak, I attempted to offer my private labor to the public, focusing on whatever cause I had discovered underlying the "Waldensians" <note>original: "Valdesium".</note>. Thus, when I most diligently laid out all their ways before my eyes—the beginning of the work, the means, and the end—and when I weighed their consistencies and contradictions, I found the "hinge" or the supreme point of the entire cause to proceed from this: once they have become embittered against the ecclesiastical order, they believe everything consists of the fictions of priests. 

They claim that priests, using religion as an opportunity, make a mockery of kings, princes, republics, and every rank—the simple and the sharp-minded alike. Once they had opened this window for themselves, and once they had cast themselves out of ecclesiastical veneration, they were free to forge any harmful thing according to the lust of their minds. They were, in effect, their own masters; there was no one left to restrain them as they raged through their conceived impiety. Finally, whatever pestilential doctrine they introduced would be believed as "pure" among those who had already been primed by prefaces claiming that the Gospel prophecies regarding patience were fulfilled in them. On the other hand, anything would be considered "impure" which proceeded from that side where they had placed fictions, mockeries, human decrees, and even avarice, shameful profit, or any sacrilegious deed. 

And this is a sufficiently effective trick for those who are not very perceptive regarding such crafts. Among the more clever, however, they stick in the same mud—for instance, regarding **Intercessions for the dead**. <note>original: "Suffragia per mortuis".</note> We accept these; they remove them entirely. If there is anything in the Scriptures by whose authority we are moved, they stay silent. They ignore it, or—what is worse—they erase it. They make the cause appear to be about envy and nothing but profit. And while they themselves are primarily guilty of reckless handling of the Scripture, they "forget" this and obtain an appearance of equity against us before ungodly judges, based on naked avarice. 

Yet, they ought to have guarded the will of the sacred canon with the highest piety above all else; afterwards, if any evil had crept in under its occasion, it was necessary to amend that in the second place and cut it back to the quick, so that while they wish to seem to avoid vices, they are not also found to be contrary to divine decrees. I thought the <term>cacotechnas</term> <note>From the Greek *kakotechnia*: malicious tricks, fraudulent arts, or bad craftsmanship.</note> of those men ought to be investigated in a fuller disputation, so that in those very things by which they think they earn trust, we might deserve greater trust—we, among whom the antiquity of perpetual succession remains, continued from Christ and the apostles down to us. If any human error...

# AGAINST THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS AND

If any fiction were underlying it, it would have erupted long ago. Kings and princes would have long ago cast off their ill-persuaded veneration <note>The author suggests that if the Catholic faith were a lie, rulers would have stopped honoring the Pope centuries ago.</note> so that they would no longer yield in dignity to the present Vicar of Christ <note>The Pope.</note> and submit themselves even to his feet—a dignity to which that rebellion of the Waldensians does not even bow its head. In all things, finally, by which they labor to stir our stomachs, they are found to be such that in the secret depths of their work they are by no means found to be the kind of people they showed themselves to be on the surface; for the truth is found to be more tightly bound by their lies. 

Thus, whatever Scriptures they took up to construct their errors, they would corrupt by twisting them to their own private sense; other parts they would erase more freely. In their entire work, finally, they find no testimony that would voluntarily support their opinion. At this certain point, if these men wished to be esteemed as highly as they desire, they would be destined for greatness. But they have forgotten a necessary thing, in my judgment: that after those examples of the martyrs which they seemed to have undergone, they should consequently have testified that they would not corrupt the testimonies of the Scriptures, nor hide them, nor twist contrary passages into a foreign sense, or even erase them entirely. And I believe they did not forget this, but rather wondered how they could dare to promise that which they were most certainly going to violate. Since, therefore, I find them exposed on this side, we shall overthrow all their pretenses and all their superstition with a far easier dispute. 

“For such are false apostles,” says Saint Paul, “deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ. And no wonder: for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. It is no great thing, therefore, if his ministers are transformed as ministers of justice, whose end shall be according to their works.” <note>original: "pseudo apostoli sunt... oparíj subdoli..." A quote from 2 Corinthians 11:13–15.</note> 

Since it was necessary for this labor of ours to go out into public from its very first birth, and it could not endure to be better shaped over a longer time, I thought it fitting that whatever it lacked in refinement should be confirmed by public authority. Indeed, I did not dare to appeal to the Royal Majesty for this, either because our insignificance dreaded the royal height, or because those Waldensians had attacked the teacher Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western theology.</note> precisely because he had attempted to write against them in the ears of the prince. We wished to remove from them this occasion for slander, and also the fear of royal power, so that they might not complain that we dared to move against them only by the power of arms, and not by the conscience of truth. Nor should they complain as if, following the example of a previous time, we were attempting to make them "saints" again <note>Ziegler refers to how persecution often led to the sect being viewed as martyrs by their followers.</note>—especially since I understood they would rather enjoy their little rustic possessions in silence under a pretense of confession than risk the glory of their preserved faith (as they would have it believed) for any sort of immortality.

For these and many other equally opportune and necessary causes, our work comes to you, most Reverend Prelate. <note>Refers to the Bishop of Olomouc in Moravia, Stanislav Turzo (served 1497–1540).</note> For if it is not permitted to build and raise even the tiniest chapel throughout the diocese without your knowledge, then if any work concerning the Christian religion—of which you are the father and prince throughout Moravia—were to depend on it, and which ought to reach the people subject to you, it should also be established by us. I thought it the most correct counsel that your sacred and episcopal authority should be established before I sent it out. For indeed, outside of you, there is no other whom such care would touch by legitimate right, concerning which the Prophet said: “Son of man, I have given you as a watchman for the house of Israel; and you shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me. If I say to the wicked, ‘You shall die the death,’ and you do not announce it to him, nor speak so that he may turn from his impious way and live, that impious man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it to the impious man and he is not converted from his impiety and his impious way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.” <note>original: "fílí homínis speculatofẽ te dedí..." A quotation from Ezekiel 3:17–19.</note> 

In this matter, most Reverend Prelate, I desire this present dispute to be established by no other than your censorship, and thus, as you judge it worthy, to produce it openly for the overthrowing of the adversaries and the confirmation of our own people—since otherwise I see that I have exposed their position as so naked, weak, and prepared for mere trickery, that there the reader's desire for a full satisfaction will be easily met by the overflowing abundance of the facts...

<meta>This page continues Jacob Ziegler’s polemical defense of the Catholic faith against the Waldensians. Having previously justified his choice of audience and tone, he now moves to a direct critique of the specific written confessions submitted by the Waldensians to the Hungarian royalty, accusing them of using deceptive language to hide their true beliefs.</meta>

# THE BOOK OF CONFESSIONS, BOOK ONE

...so that I could not be accused of any fault. Our cause, however, I have prepared with such a constant conscience on the opposite side that I have pursued individual points most diligently, lest I leave anything "lame" or incomplete through which the truth we must establish might be endangered by us. Having used the pure canon of the Holy Scriptures to investigate the cause of both our sides, I have called upon ecclesiastical commentators in no great number, thinking I would act more appropriately by addressing them now where they had not yet summoned us; specifically, it was not right to rise higher than they had provoked. But if this work proceeds and they speak ill of these writings of ours, then I will think the time has come to confirm all and singular of our points from a deeper treatment, in which all the most learned interpreters of the sacred letters agree.

Thus we have stated the reason for our work, against whom it is directed, and for what causes it was undertaken. Now the time calls us to engage hand-to-hand <note>original: "pede conferentes" — a military metaphor for close-quarters combat</note> and, in a dense debate, to clear ourselves against those Waldensians <note>A medieval and Reformation-era Christian movement that was often declared heretical by the Catholic Church for its rejection of certain dogmas and its emphasis on lay preaching.</note>. And since exactly two of their short works have come into our hands, following, as I believe, the nature of the matter itself, I wished first for the nature of their faith to be established between us before I descended to those things they answer to the teacher Augustine; since these Waldensians themselves have more than once referred to their own confession. I have therefore taken into my hands that which they published under such a title: *An Apologetic and Satisfactory Prayer of the Brothers sent to King Vladislaus in Hungary* <note>Vladislaus II (1456–1516), King of Bohemia and Hungary, to whom the Waldensians (specifically the Bohemian Brethren) sent several defenses of their faith to avoid persecution.</note>. Which indeed, if it were such as they promised it would be from these words:

> We have been with great desire, if the opportunity presented itself, to simply reveal the reason and rule regarding the secrets of our religion, for the sake of which we endure various hardships,

and a little later:

> For you should not doubt that each thing we are about to write will arise from the equity of the heart; for what we believe in our heart before God, that same thing we now confess with our mouth in such a manner:

In which, if it were truly such a document, we would not labor further in searching out what is already plain. But when they were brought into hatred before His Royal Majesty on account of a new superstition, and they then feared that all the most grave punishments were being prepared for them, they devised a document of such a type that they fashioned themselves to appear as similar to us as possible in that apology; although they had nonetheless resolved by a silent vow to remain exactly as they were. Therefore, just as at that time they were not of the same mind openly as they were at home, so they did not compose their confession with the same meaning for the public as they did in private. 

And if indeed in every business the masters of the craft better understand the internal workings of that art, it is not difficult to detect the present deceptions. For just as practitioners of the gymnasia <note>original: "gymnaste" — here referring to trained athletes or wrestlers</note> know all the strikes by name, whether delivered by the point or the edge, and know when one thing is shown as a feint while another is guarded against in the art of wrestling; so a man who has been instructed from childhood under teachers in the reading of history, by the examples of the most serious men—men who at home, abroad, in war, and in peace through the most ample magistracies, exercised by sharpness of genius and long experience of affairs, have known most subtly how to simulate and dissimulate such plans, to show one thing and be far from it elsewhere—one who is practiced in the writings of such men discovers the rustic commentaries of those Waldensians with minimal effort. These works, in the end, they attempted more through ignorance of affairs than they were actually able to perfect. 

We have read the apologies; we have seen the instructions and preparations which the ancients presented to kings and rulers of provinces—and also in the schools <note>original: "gymnasijs"</note> of the most fertile philosophy and all secular erudition—to be understood concerning the nature of the apostolic faith; works most absolute, naturally, in all wisdom and all constant truth. Did that confession of the Waldensians achieve anything like that? Indeed, before the ear of which learned man does it not blush? I do not wish to say that they joined Latin words together with difficulty, so often do they mix in barbarisms <note>Words or expressions that are not considered "pure" or classical Latin, often used by Ziegler to mock the Waldensians' lack of formal education.</note>; for although the investigation of truth does not depend on that, let them at least be ashamed that they have not attained the minimum of skill when they are so confident about the greatest things. I wish, however, to scrutinize their sentiments. Certainly, from this side, nothing is more meager in their confession, nothing drier; it is weak and bloodless, barer than bare, entirely slippery, entirely focused on its feet, and placed only in flight. If our ancestors—those most circumspect men who observed the nascent Christian religion either for the sake of civil tranquility or for the exploration of philosophy and sublime things—had been eluded by similar ravings, where would those Waldensians find the Christian world today?

<meta>This page continues Jacob Ziegler’s polemical attack on the Waldensians. # AGAINST THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS AND...

...they were, upon whom those who had come forth from their hoes <note>original: "de Sarculis" — likely a derogatory reference to the Waldensians' rustic or peasant origins, as a *sarculum* is a weeding tool or hoe.</note> might so impudently impose. Truly, lest we seem to speak such things of them out of thin air, let us take an example from their own distinguished "apology." They write: "We have had a great desire to open the reason and the rule of the secrets of our religion," and again, "that which we believe in our heart, we now profess with our mouth in such a manner." What, then, are those discovered secrets of theirs that we do not know? Whatever they are able to think or write rightly concerning God, the most blessed Trinity, heavenly matters, and all the most serious things, we can show that these were born among our own people with the greatest fertility and expanded by the highest erudition. They are *ours*, and they were ours before we even knew there would be Waldensians. If we hold these things in common, why do they keep thrusting them forward as if they were "secrets"? Furthermore, regarding those points in which we are secure and Catholic, and in which they alone have sinned—the cause of their various "distresses," as they call them, and the infamy of their new heresy—why do they sustain these? If they find that the reasons for which they suffer these various distresses are admittedly different from our own, why then have they so carefully fashioned their present confession to resemble our faith? It follows that they do not profess with their mouths in the same way they believe in their hearts. Let us grant them this: that what they believe, they profess in such a manner. If we examine that confession in the manner of more learned works, we find nothing secret, nothing beyond the common and worn-out phrases used by any simple person. They will surely be guilty of a shaky faith before his Royal Majesty; indeed, they stumble headlong into that common proverb: *a liar ought to have a good memory* <note>original: "mendacem memorem esse"</note>. For the secrets they promise here, they testify in another place to have not provided, which is a supreme insult to the Royal Majesty.

"We leave it," they say, "to the judgment of all men, whether if we had been clever—as **Doctor Augustine** <note>This refers to Augustinus Olomucensis (Augustin Käsebrot), a scholar and official in Moravia and Hungary who was a fierce opponent of the Waldensians.</note> charges us—we could have hidden many things which we have confessed more simply in those letters given to the King." By admitting they *could* have hidden much, they have not yet confessed everything. In the following passage, however, they say something much more fitting: *Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine* <note>original: "nolite sanctum dare canibus, & nolite pijcere margaritas ante porcos" — Matthew 7:6.</note>, and *conduct yourselves prudently toward those who are outside.* If indeed they are not going to give what is holy to dogs, nor pearls to swine, what "secrets" do they expect the King to find here? Indeed, they are leading everyone by the nose. Because of these things, I think the King will be ungrateful, the nobility ungrateful, and most ungrateful of all, Doctor Augustine, because they do not agree with such a "true," "pure," and "simple" confession.

I certainly confess of myself that I saw everything was in flight; though saying nothing of their purpose, they wished to seem to say everything. I decided entirely to follow them, so that I might pull them back into a certain confessed station of faith. Therefore, so that I might dispatch my task more quickly, I did not wish to examine everything in their prologue, by which they prepare their case for the Royal Majesty using arguments from their adversaries, from their own persons, and from the terror of divine provocation. These things are commonplace, used by anyone to introduce their cause as best they can. I did not want to pursue all of them, as these are common speeches used equally by the good and the wicked. For this reason, they bring very little strength to a cause, and least of all when the cause itself is found to be wicked. Indeed, the best speech is a righteous life. Furthermore, this is no new example; the Church has often heard the impure, the filthy, the impious, the sacrilegious, and heretics speak their defense in words of innocence. For nothing is easier for a harmful man than to emulate the appearance of virtue through a good speech, by which the worst crimes have often been defended. Therefore, in such a place, one must look not only at the entrance but at everything that exists everywhere in such matters, from which we may finally detect if they are righteous members of the household with whom such things would be appropriate among the sons of the family. But at last, let us hear what is offered.

->Under the heading: Confession of the faith of the blessed Trinity, it says:<-

> By whose merit the Father alone works salvation according to the purpose of his election,

<meta>This page continues Jacob Ziegler’s polemical attack on the Waldensians. Having previously argued that the Waldensians stole their "secret" doctrines from the Catholic Church, he now begins a line-by-line critique of their specific theological phrasing, accusing them of either distorting Scripture or lacking the proper reverence in their terminology.</meta>

# BOOK ONE OF THE CONFESSIONS,

The Savior says of himself: **"Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it; for whatever he does, these things the Son also does in like manner."** <note>original: "Amē amē dico vobis nō p̄t fili⁹ a se facere qc̄q̄..." — quoting John 5:19.</note> Yet they <note>The Waldensians</note> press or constrain the meaning too much. For Aurelius Augustine, in the thirteenth book of *On the Trinity*, speaks much more balancedly on this same sense; he says that all things—the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of them both—work equally and in concord, yet we are justified in the blood of Christ and reconciled to God through the death of his Son. This also accords with the prophets and the **Apostle** <note>In this context, "the Apostle" always refers to St. Paul.</note>. Isaiah says of Him as the liberator: **"Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth,"** and again, **"truly he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows; he was wounded for our iniquities and bruised for our sins."** <note>Quoting Isaiah 16:1 and 53:4-5.</note> The Apostle, moreover, says: **"He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, so that he might redeem those who were under the law and that we might receive the adoption of sons."** <note>Quoting Philippians 2:8 and Galatians 4:5.</note>

In the following chapter they say: **"with his most pure blood he exhaled his soul,"** <note>original: "cum sanguine purissimo animā exhalauit"</note> using the word "exhaled" <note>original: "exhalauit" — Ziegler finds this term too weak or undignified for Christ's voluntary sacrifice.</note> which is cast down and entirely foreign to the person of Christ; especially since Christ expressed his own release with a term more fitting and worthy of himself. He said: **"I lay down my life, that I may take it up again. No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have the power to lay it down, and I have the power to take it up again."** <note>Quoting John 10:17-18.</note> Therefore, if Saint Jerome rightly believed that the **Apocalypse of John** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> contained as many mysteries as it did words—indeed, that multiple meanings lay hidden in every single word—then surely we believe by a far more powerful argument that individual mysteries lie hidden in every single word of the Savior. Finally, when speaking a parable about a certain rich man, He immediately used a different word for the same thing; God said to him: **"Fool, this night they will require your soul of you; then whose will those things be which you have prepared?"** <note>Quoting Luke 12:20.</note> For this reason, we should by no means dare to corrupt such great mysteries with hastily conceived words. Consequently, they say:

**"His Church, for which he offered himself,"** etc. I would not dispute this point with those whose piety toward the Roman observance was well-attested, but since these men are **Waldensians** <note>term: Waldensians — A medieval Christian movement that preceded the Reformation; they were often accused of heresy for rejecting the institutional Church's authority and ceremonies.</note> who utterly reject ecclesiastical ceremonies, they rightly make us suspicious that some fraud may lie beneath. They may think they have followed the example of Christ in this, and where we think they are speaking simply, that is precisely where they stand most ready for battle. Therefore, if our suspicion is true, and they are deceiving us here, let them know that Christ observed the Church which existed then. According to its custom, as Luke writes, after the days of Mary's purification were fulfilled according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the law of the Lord: **"Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord"**) and to offer a sacrifice according to what was said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. For this Church of the "new grace" did not exist before Christ died on the cross and one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and the Church was born with its sevenfold sacraments from the side of the sleeping heavenly Adam <note>Ziegler uses a classic theological metaphor: just as Eve was born from the side of the sleeping Adam, the Church was born from the side of the "New Adam" (Christ) as he "slept" in death on the cross.</note>. Therefore, let those Waldensians take more diligent care, lest—while they are ignorant today of those legitimate things which Christ observed, and yet equally despise the apostolic institution which first began after the Ascension and indeed after the death of Christ—they be utterly convicted of remaining without any observance of the Church at all. They subjoin:

**"To whom every kind of living thing,"** and so forth, up to the point: **"Finally, let him be crushed by eternal damnation."** In transcribing this passage from the Apostle somewhat too freely, they have, through ignorance, cast out almost all of its true meaning. The Apostle said: **"As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."** <note>Quoting Romans 14:11.</note> The Apostle tempered these words so that, because he understood that this future confession would be made with different emotions in the **elect** and the **reprobate** <note>term: elect and reprobate — The "elect" are those chosen by God for salvation; the "reprobate" are those rejected or destined for damnation.</note>, he also chose words which, by his power, would apply to both. Indeed, the confession of the Saints is of the kind the Savior showed: **"Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent."** But the confession of the reprobate is that "worm" and the stinging of foolish repentance, concerning which the Savior says again: **"and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn."**

# AGAINST THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS AND...

**"and they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty."** <note>original: "et videbūt filiū hoīs venientē in nubibus cœli..." — quoting Matthew 24:30.</note> And Zechariah says: **"and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as with a mourning for an only son, and they shall grieve over him as one is accustomed to grieve at the death of a firstborn."** <note>Quoting Zechariah 12:10.</note> But those Waldensians were by no means discerning enough <note>original: "emuncti" — literally "clean-nosed," a Latin idiom for being sharp-witted or having good judgment.</note> to perceive such things. Worship and veneration—which surely proceed only from that piety of souls called <term>theosebeia</term> <note>A Greek term meaning "godly-worship" or "reverence for God."</note>—they attributed equally to the impious and the elect, although they should have been warned by their own words not to conceive such a thing.

For they say: **"Nor will he ever descend from heaven unless the adversity of all nations is crushed and subjected."** <note>original: "Neqȝ cœlo inqūt aliqn̄ deſcēſurū..."</note> If, therefore, there is "adversity" here or in Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, there will be no worship and veneration; for if they were to worship and venerate him, there would be no "adversity." Furthermore, Simeon says of the Son of God and the Virgin: **"Behold, this child is set for the fall and the resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted."** <note>Quoting Luke 2:34.</note> Even the unclean spirits, when they saw Jesus, fell down before him and cried out, saying, **"You are the Son of God,"** <note>Quoting Luke 4:41.</note> but let no one dare to say this was done out of worship and veneration. For what difference would there be between the merit of such a confession from Peter, the prince of the Apostles—who said the same: **"You are the Christ, the Son of the living God"**—and that of the unclean spirits? Therefore, let no one dare to think the demons did these things out of piety, but rather out of fear of Christ’s judgment and power; hence that cry of theirs: **"I adjure you by God, do not torment me!"** <note>Quoting Mark 5:7.</note>

Thus, Christ discerns a different meaning between the two. Christ invites the Apostles to confession by his question, and to the one confessing <note>Peter</note> he says: **"Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven."** But he rebuked the demons who confessed of their own accord and would not let them speak, because they were then (and are today) so far removed from the worship and veneration of the Divinity. Indeed, that most impure demon even dared to tempt Christ, the Lord of all, regarding his own adoration, saying: **"All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me."** <note>Quoting Matthew 4:9.</note>

Furthermore, let us move from demons to men: by what law are **Sabellius** or **Arius** <note>Two of the most famous early Christian heretics. Sabellius (3rd century) taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were just three names for one person; Arius (4th century) taught that the Son was a created being, not eternal God.</note> subjected so that they might worship and venerate the Son and the Holy Spirit with equal honor and similar majesty as they do the Father? Sabellius does not admit a Trinity of persons, but believes the Father, Son, and Spirit are "empty names" without distinct reality. Arius creates "levels" in the Divinity and blasphemously calls the Son and the Holy Spirit "creatures." His slogan was: **"there was [a time] when he was not,"** <note>original: "erat qn̄ nō erat" — the defining phrase of Arianism, denying the Son's co-eternity with the Father.</note> and that there was eternity with the Father when the Son did not exist. They did not worship or venerate the Son and the Holy Spirit as God.

The Waldensians make themselves even more "pious" through their deceptions: as long as they lived, they set before themselves Jesus, the Son of God and the Virgin, as "a sign that shall be contradicted." If they now confess in Gehenna by compulsion what they denied on earth of their own will, what does this have to do with piety? Both the demons and the high priests who were his crucifiers, looking upon him whom they pierced, now confess and tremble.

I have lingered longer on this point not so much because of the error itself, but to expose the remarkable ignorance of the Waldensians, so that they might recognize themselves. They so easily arrogant to themselves the handling of Sacred Scripture, yet they are barely able to remain consistent in the meaning of the words they adopt. For just as with every art, so too Theology has its own character of speaking; unless this is guarded, it distinguishes—more quickly than anything else—those who descend to practice the arts based on a teacher’s skill versus those who do so out of their own [misplaced] confidence.

Finally, regarding this little verse: **"that he will never descend from heaven,"** and what follows—I do not know if they said this innocently. I do know that in another booklet they try to press us very hard with this same testimony, saying: *If Christ is not to descend from heaven before the "adversity of the nations" is crushed under his feet, then the Christian faith preaches in vain that Christ becomes present daily in the Sacrament of the Altar.* <note>The "Sacrament of the Altar" refers to the Eucharist/Mass. The Waldensians are using the doctrine of the Second Coming to argue against the Real Presence of Christ in the bread and wine.</note> But we shall explore how much weight this holds in the fifth book; for now, let us descend to the next points. We do not wish hereafter to examine every single one of their words, by which they everywhere restrict their meanings so that, while appearing to speak of everyone in general, they are actually speaking only of themselves with a hidden sense. In which matter, having phrased their words in a certain way...

He specifically attacks their argument that Christ cannot be present in the Eucharist if he is not scheduled to "descend" from heaven until the end of time.</summary>

# CONFESSIONS, BOOK ONE

...perpetually they use terms like "living faith," "vigorous faith," "formed faith" <note>Scholastic theology distinguished between "unformed faith" (mere belief) and "formed faith" (faith animated by love or charity).</note> and other things of that sort, in which deception they even hang entire chapters—as with their profession on the Holy Church, part of which we have already examined, as well as on the ministries of the church, and finally all their doctrines—down to this most recent point where we are joined in the love of faith with its faithful members. For if they receive us as faithful members and we participate equally with them in the mysteries, then we are not those of whom they said in another place: **"Do not give what is holy to dogs"** <note>original: "Nolite ſctm̃ dare canib⁹" — quoting Matthew 7:6.</note> and **"conduct yourselves prudently toward those who are outside,"** <note>original: "cõuerfamini prudẽter ad eos qꝫ foris ſunt" — quoting Colossians 4:5.</note> because if they keep that saying about dogs and swine fixed upon us, we are not, by their agreement, those faithful members who rightly believe in Christ just as they do. We have not wished, as I said, to follow their hiding places one by one, for the speech would never find an end; so full are they of a crafty nature and so rich in it. I shall consider myself to have triumphed enough on this part if we leave it witnessed that they have not mocked us. We shall now descend to those matters where they offer us manifest poisons from a full cup.

Under the heading of "True Faith in the Holy Spirit," they write thus: **"Regarding the Holy Spirit, we believe that he is one true God with the Father and the only-begotten Word, differing only in this: that he emanates from both."** Let those who say the Holy Spirit is "diverse" from the Father and the Son confess that they have committed a manifest blasphemy. If they do not confess to having committed it, let them defend it, and we shall know what they think about the most blessed Trinity—just as in other matters they present themselves under a cloak of innocence while feeling no less [error]. That is to say, they feel along with Arius, Donatus, Eunomius, Eudoxus, and Macedonius <note>A list of ancient heretics: Arius denied Christ's full divinity; Macedonius denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit; Eunomius and Eudoxus were radical Arians.</note>, all whose sacrileges these Waldensians revive. They feel in opposition to the Council of Nicaea, Athanasius, Hilary, Didymus, Ambrose, and Augustine; indeed, even against the Gospel and the Apostles, against the whole Church and the entire Christian school in which those Waldensians have chosen to do battle. To these Waldensians, the most foul heretics were more pleasing than Christian purity—whose pestilential errors (as everyone knows) Christian discipline cast down with the most profound disputations. Christian discipline both preaches and confesses that the Holy Spirit is <term>homousion</term> <note>From the Greek "homoousios," meaning "of the same substance" or "consubstantial." This was the key term of the Nicene Creed to describe the shared essence of the Trinity.</note> with the Father and the Son. 

Go on in your impiety, you Waldensians! Is this how you treat this truth of the faith? As you yourselves attested in the rest of your prologue: revealed by the Holy Spirit, placed in the Holy Scriptures by that same Spirit, collected summarily in the Apostles' Creed, and simultaneously guarded by the primitive Church in reality, certified by virtues, wonders, sincere dogma, and martyrdom—and finally explained with zeal against the heretics at the Council of Nicaea by the bishop Athanasius and many other teachers? Now, having restored heretics who are not Christians today, do you so seduce "Royal Innocence" <note>Likely a reference to the King of Bohemia, to whom many such polemics were addressed, or a general appeal to a sovereign.</note> that he might believe you have found there the true truth of the faith from the Holy Spirit? A truth confirmed by the Holy Scriptures, the Apostles, the martyrs, the councils, and the ecclesiastical commentators? Is this how you bring back Arius, Eudoxus, Donatus, Eunomius, and Macedonius—those abominable heads of error—to a most Christian Prince and his whole Christian people, under the memory of apostolic and martyr-like sanctity? 

But let us hear this foul-smelling impiety. They say: **"The Holy Spirit is one true God with the Father and the only-begotten Word."** This part is indeed good and according to Christian piety. But then: **"differing only in this."** This "differing" <note>original: "diuerſus"</note> is the evil they speak according to the school of heretics. It is pleasing here to consider their cunning, as they draw two colors from a single brush at once: black from white, mixing the poison of heretics with Christian sincerity. Now, if the Spirit is one true God with the Father and the Son, remove that word "diverse." If you confess him to be "diverse," remove that "one true God." But the Holy Spirit is one true God with the Father and the Son; for John writes in his epistle: **"There are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one."** <note>This is the "Johannine Comma" (1 John 5:7), a verse often used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance to prove the Trinity, though it is not found in the earliest Greek manuscripts.</note> He said "one" and "they are." They are "one" according to essence, which is the same God. They "are" [plural] according to the distinction of persons. According to the sense of this mystery, the Savior had also said: **"I and the Father are one."** Finally, in...

# AGAINST THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS

...we read in the same canonical [letter]: **"God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God and God in him,"** <note>original: "Deus charitas est & q̃ manet in charitate in deo manet & deus in eo" — 1 John 4:16.</note> and again, **"If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him."** <note>original: "Si q's diligit mū dū, nõ ē charitas p̃ris in eo" — 1 John 2:15.</note> It is necessary, therefore, that the love of the Father be as great as the wisdom and truth of the Father. Now, Christ is Wisdom and Truth equal to the Father, because he said, **"I and the Father are one."** <note>John 10:30.</note> Therefore, Love [the Holy Spirit] shall also be equal. For if the love of the Father were less than his wisdom and truth, then wisdom and truth would be loved by the Father less than they are. Thus, so that all things in God are not the highest, absolute, and perfect, [one must admit] that wisdom is equal to the Father. Therefore, the Holy Spirit, the love of the Father, shall be equal in all things because of the most absolute <term>simplicity|The theological doctrine that God is not "made of parts" but is a single, unified essence.</term> which exists in the essence of God. The reason for this unity of essence in divine matters is a lack of distinction into which diversity cannot fall. Therefore, as for those who think the Holy Spirit ought to be called "different" from the Father and the Son, a distinction immediately follows them, and from distinction, plurality—so that the Trinity would no longer be one God in essence. Furthermore, diversity is only accepted according to a specific form; for example, as this may be wood and that may be stone, diversity is not taken from the "matter" (which is the same for all in material things) but from the "form." Therefore, by "form," the Holy Spirit would be diverse from the Father and the Son if indeed he is called "diverse." In that case, the Holy Spirit would no longer be *what* he is, but would be *something because of* this form. To be "something because of" another already signifies a composition <note>In Scholastic logic, if God were "composed" of different parts or forms, He would not be the "First Cause."</note>; or, if that form by which he were diverse were called "accidental," and since the foundation of an "accident" is not the form of a thing but its matter, we would thus be forced to attribute "matter" to God as well. We, however, have shown before that three persons are one essence, the highest simplicity, and must be so believed to be God. Therefore, the Catholic and Christian confession—which those Waldensians flee from, attack, and damn—neither knows nor confesses anything "diverse" in the divine nature.

Under the heading of their "holy profession" concerning the Church, they say this: "In this cycle of time in which we breathe, all the bitter and sad things that Christ and his apostles prophesied have fallen upon this Church in heaps—namely, that those who are unworthy of ecclesiastical honor dominate it by their own power." We are prompted at this point to engage in a longer dispute; but since we reserve ourselves for another work of theirs, and presently only inquire into what they might freely grant us regarding the established confession, I thought I should apply myself not to the whole matter but to a small part, as much as their words require. If, therefore, these bitter and sad things have fallen upon the present Church because of those who are unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, I do not see who are more unworthy than those priestly [figures] whom those Waldensians look up to—drawn from every lowliest wool-worker and butcher—who usurp the priestly order for themselves out of a lust for power, without [proper] ordination or legitimate anointing, and outside of any delegated authority. Consider them most certainly bound to the **rebellion of Korah against Moses and Aaron.** <note>Korah led a revolt against Moses and Aaron's exclusive right to the priesthood; the earth swallowed him as punishment (Numbers 16).</note> They administer the sacraments of the Church with new rites contrary to the institutions of the Fathers. They have done away with the Divine Office—established by the apostles, guarded by the holy Fathers, and derived inviolably down to us—and have condemned it in favor of human fictions. They have put forward pestilential opinions against the most present decrees of the sacred canon, while boastfully lying that they observe it and that we violate it—both claims being equally false. These "priestlings," whom those Waldensians have caused to rise from the crowd to perform sacred rites with the same votes by which they might designate some other infamous person to guard a prison, have long since cast away the oracles of the Holy Spirit, being outside the lot of the legitimate priesthood. **"And you have cast out,"** it says, **"the priests of the Lord, the sons of Aaron and the Levites, and you have made for yourselves priests like all the peoples of the lands. Whoever comes and initiates his hand with a bullock, with oxen, and seven rams, becomes a priest of those who are not lords. But our Lord is God, whom we do not abandon, and the priests who minister to the Lord are from the sons of Aaron, and the Levites are in their order. They also offer burnt offerings to the Lord every single day, morning and evening, and incense prepared according to the precepts of the Law; and the bread is set out upon a most clean table; and with us is the golden lampstand and its lamp, so that it may be lit always at evening."** <note>original: "eiectis inqt sacerdotes dñi filios Aaron atq̃ leuitas..." — quoting 2 Chronicles 13:9-11.</note> We...
