# ON TRUE RELIGION,

Vacuna <note>The Roman goddess of leisure or rural rest.</note>, Stercutius <note>The Roman god of dung and fertilization.</note>, and Fever earned altars; from the stable to the Palace, from birth to the grave, from phlegm to urine, the Romans came to venerate individual gods for every purpose. Then came the philosophers who, either out of flattery for the powerful or for the sake of "Philosophy" (as they called it), mixed the reception of the gods with things mortal and immortal to cover their tracks. Heaven—the most holy seat of God toward which all mortality bows, and which Christ commanded should not be profaned by any oath—they filled with the filthiest fables of boys, girls, marriages, prayers, and bridesmaids. In this, the Poets sinned most of all. This was furthered by the insanity of individual provinces and the zeal of individual empires, for they established their borders by nothing more strongly than by a diversity of religions. Hence the altars of Busiris <note>A mythical king of Egypt who sacrificed foreigners.</note> in Egypt; hence the Colchian sacrifices. They established these, I suppose, so that they might keep strangers away from their borders. Finally, even the responses of demons confirmed this error, by which men were held fast as if they were worshiping true gods who knew the future—beings who could forewarn them of whatever they themselves had decreed regarding trembling mortality, for both public and private benefit. And so, they were worshiped as the true masters of our lives in every outcome, whether to procure better things or to ward off the worse. By these things *they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened* <note>Romans 1:21.</note> until, according to the prophecies of the saints, the One desired by all nations should come, and Christ should be born into the world. He was the one who would bring the pure vein of that true and original religion—which had been maintained with difficulty in the one nation of the Jews—into the light for all nations, spreading it everywhere from the rising of the sun to its setting, and who would finally extinguish all idolatry.

But even this was attacked not long after by the fraud of him who seduced Eve. Not indeed by idolatry—for in that kind of error, the devil had been defeated and bound for a time, he who had even tempted Christ with idolatry—but rather he lay in wait for the purity of the apostolic preaching with sacrilegious opinions and sects of perdition. He prepared for himself teachers with "itching ears" for lies, whom the Lord knows how to reserve for torture on the day of judgment; but especially those who walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness and despise authority. Bold and self-pleasing, they do not fear to introduce blasphemous sects. Sent by this devil, Sabellius, Arius, and Donatus took up a fight concerning the Divinity. From this same source, Manichaeus <note>Founder of Manichaeism.</note> posited two principles of things, Good and Evil, and believed the flesh of Christ was a mere phantom. The Cataphrygians <note>A name for the Montanists, a prophetic movement from Phrygia.</note> preached that the promise of the Holy Spirit was fulfilled not in the Apostles, but in Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, one hundred and thirty years after the passion of Christ. Novatus attacked the penance of the lapsed; Helvidius attacked the virginity of Mary, the Mother of the Lord; Vigilantius attacked the veneration of the saints; and the monk Pelagius attacked free will. Muhammad <note>original: "Maumettes"</note>—than whom no one has approached more closely to the impiety of the Antichrist—claimed the consummation of all prophecy for himself. 

The cause of such great errors for each person was manifold. The Syrians, Parthians, Persians, Arabs, and Egyptians—from whom the Manicheans, Sabellians, Arians, and Saracens emerged—were never truly faithful to the Roman Empire, and thus they were not faithful to Christ either, since they thought nothing concerning Roman authority ought to be received by them. The Greeks mixed the opinions of their own philosophers with our dogmas; in their very schools they had learned to always follow "novelties," and thus they thought religion should be as free as philosophy, in which individuals drew their own disciples. Furthermore, because the Latins sought every kind of erudition from the Greeks, they disdained having the Roman Pontiffs as the sole arbiters of religion. This situation spurred Arius onward, so that that small Alexandrian spark caught the whole world on fire with its conflagration. It also stirred up Nestorius and Eutyches, whom the Emperors and Patriarchs of Constantinople...

# ON SELECTION, BOOK TWO,

...as if they were opposing the faith of the Western churches with the two golden calves of Jeroboam <note>A reference to 1 Kings 12:28, where King Jeroboam set up golden calves to divert worship away from Jerusalem; the author uses this as a metaphor for the Greek Church's split from Rome.</note>. Since they were puffed up by the majesty of their city and the presence of the emperors, those patriarchs, intruding themselves, contended that just as the seat of the empire had been moved, so too the keys of the faith and the power of Saint Peter had been transferred to their own Constantinople. Thus, relying on insolence and force of arms, they were always inventing something new or reviving something old to show themselves as adversaries to the Latins. They finally mocked Roman authority by claiming that faith ought to be sought from the place where the apostles had first traveled. 

Truly trifling men! As if they had not corrupted what they had received from the apostles, and as if the current dispute were about the apostles and not about Arius <note>Arius was a 4th-century priest in Alexandria whose teachings led to Arianism, a major early Christian heresy that the author associates with the East.</note>. If the Greeks were to be considered superior defenders of the faith simply because the apostles set out from among them, then for that very same reason the Latins should be held as by far the most powerful defenders of the apostolic faith. For the whole world knows that we read of the apostles never departing from the Romans, but rather leaving other places to settle among the Romans, establishing themselves there, confirming the testament of faith, depositing it there, and finally sealing it with their own blood. 

But God, weary of such great impieties, finally restrained the most proud Greeks—who were irrevocable and incurable—with barbarian captivity <note>A reference to the Fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, viewed by Western writers of this era as divine punishment.</note>. The West, however, after the guest Arius and the citizen Pelagius <note>Pelagius was a British monk whose "Pelagian" heresy regarding free will and grace was a major Western controversy.</note>, produced from itself no further notable rebellions or plagues that might spread to the masses. Instead, it has always remained most devoted to the footsteps of the Roman See and remains so today—except for this Bohemia, and except for those **Rustic Waldensians** <note>The Waldensians and the Bohemians (Hussites) were pre-Reformation movements that challenged Papal authority.</note> who think they see more than all of Europe sees. They are certainly all the more insane and less worthy of pardon before God because they defected without any nearby example to follow, because they revived matters anciently condemned by the judgment of councils, and because they stirred up a new heresy for themselves from smoldering embers. 

Amidst all these religions or errors of the whole world, everyone has looked for this one thing: happiness resulting from piety. For when each person believed, according to their own rite, that they were holily worshiping whatever divine power there might be through sacred acts and devotions, they hoped that as a consequence—by the merit of their rightly undertaken piety—everything desirable they had conceived in their prayers would come to pass. And so, by the common consensus of all peoples, all ages, and all religions, happiness is sought through piety. 

Finally, if the immortality of our souls is understood to be transferred to that place where the Divinity dwells—whom they thought they had holily worshiped and to whose will they had adapted themselves—peoples have looked to religious discipline to ensure their souls are received into that immortality. It ought not to seem a vain thing, that which we see believed by the natural judgment of all. For the counselor of such great persuasion was the **conscience**. Although man was disturbed by sin, the conscience—made in the likeness of God—alone remained pure and clear in its seat as the incorrupt judge of our actions, pointing out these and all more useful things, just as the Apostle writes: 

*For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, they are a law unto themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts meanwhile accusing or even defending one another, on the day when God shall judge the secrets of men* <note>Romans 2:14-16.</note>. 

Therefore, since such a great prize as happiness is sought in our final times through religion—and not just any religion, but the one most true out of all—no religion should ever be pursued rashly. Plato considered himself fortunate because he was a Greek; and not just any Greek, but born an Athenian. This is nothing: he was no closer to heaven for it. Even a man born among the Scythians <note>A nomadic people of Central Asia, often used as a symbol for the most "uncivilized" barbarians.</note> is fortunate if he is born there into the true religion. For here the judgment concerns eternal things, not fleeting ones like nobility, one's native land, ancestral splendor, or possessions. For the longer we hold these things, the further they slip away, the more foreign they become, and the closer they approach...

# ON TRUE RELIGION,

to a lord unknown to us, closer even to the loss of the grave, unfaithful in these matters; yet in these shared lives, if we look ahead with such great care, calling together friends and advisors so that we may find those with whom we might live blessedly tomorrow, how much greater care ought we to take in providing for that which, after all these unfaithful things, will receive us with perpetual faith? For either by true piety we are led into liberty and the most luminous seats, or by impiety into the foulest prison and shadows smelling of the flesh of the wicked. We ought to pass this care happily from boy to youth, from youth to man, and from man to old man; we must turn this over in our minds and keep it before our eyes whether we are being born, growing up, or growing old. If we are foolish in this, or if we wander from this goal <note>The author uses the Latin word "meta," referring to the turning post in a Roman racecourse, symbolizing the ultimate aim of life.</note> toward false religion, we are more miserable than even the most despised little beasts. 

Indeed, I need not mention the more noble beasts, which God proposed to us to be looked upon for a certain superior character: the lion, the bear, the boar, the horse, and the bull. Nor need I invoke the small birds ennobled by a fuller soul, a more lively agility, and a beauty prepared for every grace, as if by a miraculous breath into the air. God brought all these things forth into fitting and common elements. He gave them the most pleasant forests, green grass, and sweetly running waters—which capture even the most delicate men with their pleasure—as homes. These animals, roaming through every abundance and security, today inhabit the earth in these delights, just as the first man <note>A reference to Adam in the Garden of Eden.</note> would have if he had remained within the commandment. They live so powerfully by their own right that if we ever capture them, their liberty immediately avenges itself upon us. It is not enough that they are provided with food for free, but they are subject to man even down to their dung; indeed, there are even those whose dung is sent across the seas, and though it was furthest from the mouths of the beasts themselves, we apply this flow and madness to the human mouth. 

I do not wish to call man more miserable than only these beasts, but even than the slithering creatures of the earth, who, condemned to the common elements, live without a complete soul or full senses, and are almost lifeless. Behold, they are born from the womb into security and liberty, and they find food everywhere. Just as they do not know how to prepare it by plan (since reason is denied to them), so nature, serving them in all things, casts food before them wherever their animal instinct leads. 

But although from their first birth they do not come forth fresh to the heat and cold just like humans, nature could have hardened the faces of humans—though smooth and tender—against wind, rain, heat, and cold, so that we are more quickly offended by the rest of our bodies under clothing than by our faces in the open air. We consider that irrational animals, whether born with bristles, shaggy hair, and feathers, or smooth, are born far more hardened against all injuries of the sky, so that neither cold twists them nor heat dissolves them. If they are affected by any pain at all, we suspect it is only light, as if something happening to them in a dream. 

For indeed we feel this in the human body: how often we are worn down by bitter or sharp passions—from hunger, thirst, fever, or a wound. Yet there, as often as imagination <note>original: "Imaginatio"</note> is absent and we turn our mind elsewhere, we forget all pain; the pain seems to be gone. Or we think of ourselves as affected as if in a sleep, or as if regarding someone else's body, until we return to thought. How much more obscure and deep then will the passions be in brutes! Indeed, nature has raised brutes into such a state of painlessness <note>The author uses "indolentiam" to mean a physiological lack of suffering, rather than laziness.</note>. For whether they have that sense and imagination, whether they are happy or less so, whether they have or lack, whether they are strong or worn down by disease, they do not know the outcome of either event equally. They enjoy present things with an indiscriminate disposition. Neither hope, nor fear, nor pain, nor joy delays their impulse; they are always the same. Finally, they meet death without the fear of death; whether they fail from the established goal of nature, it is more truly extinguished than...

->J. 5.<-

the soul is driven out. Whether hunting spears pierce them, or the briefest moment kills them, no account of their past life remains for them; they are entirely whatever they were, and they possess entirely whatever they had. For man, all things turn out quite the opposite. That life-giving air which receives us from the womb torments us; we are born immediately into the bonds of the cradle.

Our childhood is not spent in peace; at every moment we tremble before "flogging teachers" <note>original: "Plagosos pedagogos," a phrase famously used by the Roman poet Horace to describe his harsh tutor Orbilius.</note>. We enter adulthood, and there we are exhausted by commands, military service, trades, and the worry of seeking a living. Even if we are very wealthy, a poorly mannered wife torments us, or children are born—another source of care. Then there is the quarrelsome neighbor, ambition, stolen honors, and the slander of others. These things sometimes seize our minds so violently that a pleasing wife, sweet children, splendid houses, the most delightful estates, well-prepared dinners, gold, and purple cloth cannot pull those instruments of torture from us; rather, all those things with which we had made ourselves happy are dragged into a state of weariness. 

Even if our glory has overcome all envy and we are worshipped next to Kings, it is there first that "the giants groan under the waters and those who dwell with them" <note>original: "gigantes gemunt sub aquis," a reference to Job 26:5, often used in this period to describe the internal suffering of the proud or the damned</note>. These things, in our first heat of passion, seem pleasant to us like a sea to those about to sail; but after we have entered deeper and the nausea and the churning sea reveal themselves, then we desire in vain to have called back our course. Finally, our imagination and the suspicion of better things make these matters more bitter; the memory of who we were occurs to us, and tranquility occurs to us. We see a modest sufficiency and an "honored mediocrity" <note>original: "Honorata mediocritas," a reference to the classical ideal of the "Golden Mean," or living a balanced life without excess or poverty.</note> which, suspended before our eyes in the midst of our cares, we view like a safe shore upon which we always strive to cast ourselves, but never can. 

This difficulty is why so many tyrants and princes, living at every moment in the public hatred of the human race and in desperation of safety, were able to lay down their lives sooner than their administration. Death finds all these torments of our mind—death, which is terrible even from the mere expectation of it. It is uncertain, after all, in what manner or what kind it will occur; for many have been found killed by beasts in the deep or in vast solitudes, far from any human comfort. Others, cut open by the most grievous wounds, have met their end too suddenly; others still, tested throughout their whole body by insurmountable punishments, have provided a spectacle for the most cruel tyrants and entire theaters to satisfy a bloodthirsty pleasure. 

Hence the cruelties of Thrace, the bronze furnaces of Phalaris <note>original: "camini Phalaridis," referring to the Brazen Bull, an ancient torture device in which victims were roasted alive.</note>, and the Sicilian butcheries—almost as many in number as the Kings. Through the Roman arena, through gladiators, through beasts, through the "little horses" <term>Equuleos: a rack or timber frame used to stretch the body during torture</term>, "scorpions" <note>a type of knotted, stinging whip</note>, and white-hot iron plates, death has carried countless mortals out of this light through tortures unexplored by previous ages—horrors never to be mourned enough for the atrocity of their savage punishments. 

To these torments are added domestic misfortunes: a tyrant lying intestate <note>dying without a legal will</note> plundering our fortunes, a most tender wife, and infant children who, before they can even understand their calamity by age, are cast out from their flourishing and most rightful wealth into unmerited poverty or sold into slavery. As we stand here, the thought of how these things might happen torments us more heavily than prison itself, more savagely than the tortures themselves. From these torments of mind and body, if we also depart toward "Gehenna" <term>gehennam: a term for the place of eternal punishment or Hell</term> for our crimes or because of a false religion we have contracted, nothing will be more miserable than this knot of a Man. Because of this, Saint Jerome <note>original: "Diuus Hieronymus," a prominent 4th-century scholar and Father of the Church.</note>, when he was explaining the terror of the Divine Judgment that is to come upon our final times and upon the age, thought the beasts were happy because they were not born into the terror of eternal damnation. 

It seems, therefore, that the prayer we have undertaken consequently demands that we inquire into what things judgment and choice consist, so that we may find that chaste, holy, and God-pleasing way...

### AGAINST THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS AND...

<margin>1</margin>By God, the ruler of all, who alone possesses eternity and alone bestows happiness: let us distinguish the established [true religion] from false religion. We believe, therefore, that true religion ought to be viewed from no more just beginning than from the integrity of its precepts and the purity of its sacred worship. For indeed, all mortals have understood that all mortality depends upon the one God. Therefore, just as we were not born of ourselves, so we are not happy by ourselves; from God the Creator we both exist and are made happy; no other can provide this. 

From God alone the Creator, from that Ancient of Days <note>original: "antiquo dierum," a biblical title for God from the Book of Daniel.</note>, we ought to expect whatever happiness we shall have in the future. God is Father, God is good; veneration befits God as Father, and goodness and purity befit God as the Good. The heaven is pure, the elements are pure; whatever God has made is very good, and there is no vice in goodness. From that one and only God, whom we all know as Father, our warnings and precepts, our piety and holiness, and our purifications must be sought. He alone who created us knows how we came forth and how we ought to return. He alone knows what worship and what veneration befit Him. 

Therefore, we believe that pure religion consists where we are taught to worship that God as Father, to follow goodness, purity, and holiness; where divine oracles, confirmed by manifest wonders and most fitting signs from heaven in the prophets through whom the God of all things has spoken, have added the most certain authority to this religion. 

From this, then, the Gentiles err; hence we do not admit the worship of elements or the veneration of demons even into the suspicion of true religion. For although they had known the Father, the Creator of all, they did not worship Him as God, but as fugitives from Him, they turned themselves to the empty elements of this world. While they judged the world to be divine because they thought it incomprehensible, they ought rather to have judged the incomprehensible Lord of the world to be divine, and to have worshipped that eternal Mind which gives life to all things rather than the things that receive life from it. 

Nor, finally, was that superstition originally taken up for a good reason. But since an older religion existed—one that worshipped that God by whose help they had recently been liberated from the flood—and the memory of that divine miracle and benefit remained, and there remained fathers who taught better things. Having despised both God’s benefits and the holy reverence of the fathers, and having trampled upon piety on both sides, they invented idolatry for themselves through the pride and disobedience of their minds. This was, in its very institution, irrational. They believed divinity was scattered into elementary portions; why not rather believe in absolute divinity in its entirety than in parts? Or if in parts, why did they not rather choose to worship plants, shrubs, trees, cattle, and reptiles, where—because of the addition of the elements of which they are composed—they found a fourfold portion in each individual thing, rather than a simple one as in the elements? 

But perhaps it was because of this secret that the Egyptians worshipped onions and garlic, crocodiles, the dog, and the bull Apis <note>original: "bouem Apidem," the sacred bull of ancient Egyptian religion.</note>? Perhaps because of this secret the Greeks and Latins received men among the gods? And so, what deputy administrator held together this machine of the universe, who had made it, and who had extended it into the immense, before Jupiter <note>The Roman king of the gods.</note>, the "true heir," took up the government? What right, indeed, did he have to heaven? Perhaps the previous ruler was not governing conveniently, or had negligently distributed the turns of summer and winter, so that a successor had to be sent? Who was that world-builder so weak that he would yield the helm so easily to a stranger? Was heaven empty of an inhabitant? We read nothing in the monuments of the Gentiles about celestial citizens before King Jupiter, the father of things and gods. What did Jupiter deserve so much that he was the first to lead a colony from the earth into heaven? That Jupiter is a recent thing; his offspring, whom the songs of the poets have brought forth for us from Jupiter and with whom they have filled the heaven, are even more recent. These are childish things...

# CONFESSIONS BOOK ONE,

These things are not at all worthy of the wisest Greeks—who invented such things to be celebrated for the sake of their own fame—nor of the most serious Romans who accepted them. Or, if by the name of Jupiter they understood not that theatrical character, but the eternal mind, the true creator of the universe, then they committed an inexpiable crime. For they were able to profane that most holy majesty and incomprehensible omnipotence under the name of a single, most shameless man, by whose adulteries all things were defiled. Would that they had at least refrained from this, so that they might not have elevated the many crimes of a worldly Jupiter—as many as the impulses of his lust <note>original: "nerui mentulæ," a graphic reference to Jupiter's sexual vigor in myth</note>—to the status of divine power through myths, histories, and poems. Under that one name, they produced Jupiter as the father of gods and men, along with all the other gods, notable for thefts, robberies, secret debaucheries, envy, and sickness of body and mind, making them more lecherous in their infamous limbs than any brothel.

Thus, no standard for a more innocent life could be expected from such a religion. All things were permitted, provided they had learned from history that their gods did the same. They saw it in paintings; they considered holy the things the heavenly ones had "played" at. From this arose that example from the *Eunuchus* by Terence <note>Publius Terentius Afer was a Roman playwright; his play "The Eunuch" was frequently cited by Christian authors like Augustine to show how pagan theater corrupted youth.</note>:

> A young girl sits in a chamber looking up at a certain painted panel where this picture was: how they say Jupiter once sent a golden shower into the lap of Danaë. I myself also began to gaze at it, and because he had already played a similar game long ago, my mind rejoiced all the more that a god had turned himself into a man and had come secretly through another's rules, a trick played on the woman through the skylight. And what a god! He who shakes the highest temples of heaven with his thunder. Should I, a mere manikin <note>original: "homuntio," a diminutive meaning a "little man" or "puny human."</note>, not do the same?

With these gods as authors and teachers, they were imbued—I do not say with a more contented life—but with all the crimes that we even blush to hear and shudder at. No discipline by which a civil state might live honorably was to be found in this kind of religion. Only civil laws—that is, terror alone and no conscience—restrained embezzlement, robberies, the denial of deposits, and betrayed faith. Truly, men held a better sense of honor than their gods did. 

But the true God, who has been adored by pious minds from the beginning and will be adored to the end, never ceased to condemn such insane impiety with evident punishment. For immediately from the invention of idolatry, He condemned it with the confusion of languages. This same idolatry He avenged with great slaughters during the forty years in the desert against the people of Israel—whom He had uniquely chosen for His own worship as citizens of divine laws, leaving the others behind. He avenged it through the cycle of hunger, the sword, and slavery to neighboring Canaan, Moab, Midian, the Philistines, Amalek, Ammon, the Syrians, and finally the Assyrians and Chaldeans, even to the destruction of their own homes. The divine oracles, through the divinely inspired prophets, refuted this idolatry on every page of the sacred law: *All the gods of the nations are demons, but our Lord made the heavens* <note>Psalm 96:5</note>. *Confounded be all they that serve graven images, and that glory in their idols* <note>Psalm 97:7</note>.

Men of the Christian religion, whose talents were exercised through all philosophy and pagan religion—men like *Origen Adamantius*, *Quintus Septimius Tertullian*, *Eusebius of Caesarea*, *Lactantius Firmianus*, *Aurelius Augustine*, and many others whose works have either perished or remained among the Greeks—fought against these errors with the most steadfast arguments. They did not use arguments drawn only from our own beliefs (which would have had less strength against an adversary), but finding the religion of the pagans to be weak in itself, they conquered it using the pagans' own defenders—their philosophers and the theologians of their mysteries. Indeed, even the philosophers of the pagans themselves despised such religion. *Socrates*, for this very reason, laid down his life by hemlock in the prison of the Athenians.

<meta>The previous page established a critique of pagan myths, arguing that the Roman and Greek gods were often characterized by immorality. This page continues that argument by showing how even the greatest ancient philosophers and Roman leaders recognized the emptiness or political utility of their own religion, before transitioning into an examination of Judaism and the prophecies of the Messiah.</meta>

### AGAINST THE ERRORS OF THE WALDENSIANS AND... <note>original: "CONTRA ERRORES VALDENSIVM ET"</note>

Plato—led either by the fate of his master <note>Socrates, who was executed for "impiety" against the state gods</note> or by the public customs of the Athenians—followed their sacred rites even against his will. Aristotle, Plato’s student, when he too fell under suspicion of scorning the gods, withdrew to Chalcis, declaring that he did so "lest the Athenians sin a second time against philosophy." Oenomaus <note>a Cynic philosopher</note> wrote a specific book on the falsity of oracles. That famous Platonist Porphyry, the bitterest enemy of the Christian faith and a defender of paganism, when he could not deny that his own gods were liars, blamed the cause on a certain "more pressing arrangement of fate." Numa Pompilius, who first established sacred rites for the Romans, contained the reasons, connections, and mixtures of natural things under the guise of sacred mysteries and the assumed names of the gods. When these books of his were accidentally dug up under the consuls and read in the Senate—and the origins of the Roman ceremonies were read there—the Senate decreed those books should be abolished. They did this so that, if the meager reality of the matter became public, the religion might not begin to be held in contempt. For the Senate thought that a Republic could hardly stand without religion—that is, without a "terror of the heavenly powers." And yet, the things shown in those books were not so great that they could defend themselves by their own excellence. Therefore, they preferred the Roman people to have a religion weakened by public error rather than no religion at all. 

Because of these very flaws, paganism was as easily brought to an end under the preaching of the Apostles as it had been recklessly accepted in the beginning through the terror of princes or private lust. Thus, within the span of a single human life—from the Parthians through the Syrians, from the Greeks through the Latins into Spain, from Egypt to the Scythians, from Gaul into Africa, through governors' palaces, through military camps, and through the schools of worldly wisdom—an innumerable multitude of Gentiles, having come to despise their ancestral religion, received a faith unheard of in prior centuries under the confession of one man, and him a crucified one. This paganism, which collapsed entirely throughout the Roman world under Emperor Theodosius <note>Theodosius I (reigned 379–395 AD) made Nicene Christianity the official state religion of the Roman Empire</note>, has lain ignored for eleven hundred years. Because of this, no one will look to that worship of the Gentile gods for either piety or, ultimately, true happiness. 

Now, let us inquire into the cause of the religion of the Jews, lest perhaps it is that very religion which holds the true worship of God and true piety. Just as that religion was discovered, so the faith of those who received Christ Jesus as the Messiah <note>translated from the Hebrew-derived "Messiam"</note> will show whether it was adopted well or otherwise. For we observe the original adoration equally from the same Holy Scriptures, whose author is God. We use them and are taught to adore the same God and to venerate His precepts. We are equally ignorant of the "fornication" of idols <note>a biblical metaphor for idolatry</note>. We confess one Father, the creator of all. The law and ceremonies of this religion are more aptly confirmed from heaven than anyone would suspect them to be humanly established. But even Christ our Savior, whom the Jews denied, decreed in their favor, saying:

> "We worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews." <note>John 4:22</note>

Up to this point, no one should condemn the Jews for error or impiety. But since the Law, the Prophets, and the entire faith of the fathers was in expectation of a single Messiah, according to this or a similar prophecy:

> "The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations." <note>Genesis 49:10</note>

Isaiah also says:

> "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel," <note>Isaiah 7:14</note>

and again:

> "And a branch shall go out from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from his root, and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and goodness, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him." <note>Isaiah 11:1–3</note>

But they also signaled the time of his arrival. The holy patriarch Jacob showed that neither the kings nor the legitimate leaders of the Jewish people would cease until the Messiah came. Moreover, the prophet Daniel defined the arrival of the Messiah even by the number of years:

> "But you, pay attention to the word," he said, "and understand the vision: seventy weeks are shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, so that transgression may be finished, and sin may reach an end, and iniquity may be abolished, and [justice may be] led in—" <note>Daniel 9:24</note>

### SECOND BOOK OF THE CHOSEN [WORKS],

[...so that] eternal justice may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed. <note>This is a quotation from the "Seventy Weeks" prophecy in Daniel 9:24.</note> Know therefore and understand: from the going forth of the word that Jerusalem should be built again, until Christ the leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and the street and the walls shall be built again in a time of distress. And after sixty-two weeks, Christ shall be slain, and it shall not be his people who will deny him. <note>The author is interpreting the Latin Vulgate's rendering of Daniel 9:25-26, which historically was used to calculate the exact timing of the Messiah's arrival.</note> And so, after the Kings—according to the prophecy of Jacob—had at last ceased under the Babylonian captivity, and after the return from Babylon, the succession from the tribe of Judah administered the commonwealth of the people of Israel no longer under the title of Kings but of leaders. <note>The author refers to the "Scepter of Judah" prophecy from Genesis 49:10, suggesting the right to rule shifted forms but remained with the tribe until Christ.</note> This administration finally collapsed in the civil war between the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. <note>Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II were Hasmonean princes whose infighting led to Roman intervention by Pompey the Great in 63 BCE.</note> And when Herod, the son of Antipater—a foreigner—usurped the administration and the liberty obtained from the Romans by precarious right, finally, at that time, the seventy weeks of Daniel—that is, four hundred and ninety years from his prophecy—expired. Christ, promised in the Law, was born in Bethlehem of Judah. This Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among the Jews by the virtues, wonders, and signs which God did through him in their midst—him, delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, they killed by the hands of the lawless, fixing him to a cross. From this point, they have fallen away from true piety for fifteen hundred years. <note>The mention of "fifteen hundred years" suggests this manuscript was written in the late 15th or 16th century.</note> Prophecies of this infidelity finally came forth; for he was to be the expectation not of the Jews [alone], but of the nations, according to what God had said earlier to Abraham: "Because I have made you the father of many nations, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed," and that word of Daniel: "And it shall not be his people who will deny him." And so, the Jews have distorted the manifest prophecies signifying this Messiah with various evasions. But as to why they erred so blindly, I see no greater causes than that the promises of the Old Law are all temporal. <note>The author argues that because the Old Testament often promised physical land or prosperity, the readers became "blind" to spiritual fulfillments.</note> Therefore, because they expected the Messiah to be a temporal lord, they referred all prophecies to the prosperity of the wicked. At that time, however, when Christ appeared in the flesh, they were serving in the greatest bondage; and when they saw him to be humbler than their opinion [expected]—men who stirred up nothing but impious things—they could be moved by no sanctity of such a great prophecy, nor by any of his miracles, to receive this Messiah promised in the Law. The lust for reigning clung to their minds; steeped in old suspicions, they desired nothing more grandly from the Messiah than the liberty of their fatherland, nor did they wish to see any other Messiah than a liberator of the country. This hatred toward Herod, and this fear in which they were held toward the Romans, demanded [a solution]; there was no greater or more urgent wish in their prayers then than to shake off the unjust lord Herod and the dreaded Romans. They perceived no such hope in this Christ—especially since he had even ordered taxes to be paid, saying: "Render those things which are Caesar’s to Caesar, and those which are God’s to God." Finally, therefore, stirred by envy against him and fixing him to a cross, they were thereafter especially scandalized by him, as if they should have [never] had a crucified Messiah. Therefore, passing over this true Messiah and fashioning another for themselves according to their own ambition, they have looked for another Messiah appearing nowhere for fifteen hundred years. In which case, if in other predictions as well oracles are accustomed to result in an unexpected outcome, why is it so strange if something similar happened to the Jews in the prophecies concerning Christ? Anciently, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 CE), a Jewish-Roman historian.</note> testifies, there was an oracle: "There shall come forth from the East those who will gain mastery over things." The Jews, perhaps applying the great scope of this oracle to themselves, openly revolted from the impious Roman empire in the final times of Nero. There, Titus Vespasian was sent against them; whom, when the Syrian legions had appointed as Emperor and lord of the entire Roman world, the oracle—mocking the vanity of the Jews—amidst the profaned, burned, and cut-down Temple, amidst the city [now] their common tomb, amidst famine and sword, amidst innumerable sales of bodies and slaughters, found its way in Vespasian from the truth...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jewish history and prophecy. <header>ON TRUE RELIGION</header>

found in this sense, the angel in the Book of Judges says of Samson: *he himself shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines* <note>original: "ipſe incipiet liberare Iſrael de manu philiſtinorũ"</note>. Did not his father, Manoah, believe he was conceiving a leadership and an army, so that—in the manner of the ancient judges—the son to be born might also save the people? And yet, as a private citizen and by his own strength, he fulfilled the faith of the oracle through unexpected deeds.

Thus, finally, all predictions—when we interpret them by human judgment before they occur—their meaning is accepted only through suspicion and conjectures; in the end, they turn out in a way we did not think. As the angel rightly said through Daniel: *But you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book until the appointed time; many shall pass through and knowledge shall be manifold* <note>original: "Tu aut̃ Daniel claude ſermones & ſigna librum vſqꝫ ad tẽpus ſtatutũ"</note>. This is because prophets are not read in the same way as history; prophecy first becomes history after the fact.

For a similar reason, the Jews were deceived concerning the prophecies about Christ, being too confident in themselves. While they had conceived with vain credulity that the Messiah would be a warrior, more fortunate than David himself or Solomon himself, they found him not at all in the number of kings, but of prophets, in the thinness and meager state of all things.

But if they had diligently looked around at all things they had concerning him in the prophets, they could not have been so terribly misled. For it was necessary for both kings and leaders to have ceased at the advent of Christ. Moreover, the words we cited above from Daniel signify not at all a royal administration, but prophetic instruction and the training of souls, so that, as he says: *transgression may be finished, and sin may come to an end, and iniquity may be wiped out, and eternal justice may be brought in* <note>original: "vt cõſummat̃ p̃uaricatio & finem accipiat peccatũ. & deleat̃ iniqtas & adducat̃ iuſtitia ſempiterna"</note>. In that sense, God also said through Moses: *I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers similar to you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him; but whoever will not hear his words which he shall speak in my name, I shall be the avenger.* This was to be the way of life for the Messiah, toward whom the patriarchs, the law, and the prophets have looked since the beginning of the world.

Indeed, so that it might be manifest that this did not happen by chance outside of the prophets and the figurative predictions of the law—that is, that we might know it as the divine counsel—the patriarch Jacob says: *He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape* <note>original: "lauabit in vino ſtolam ſuam & in ſanguine vuæ palliũ ſuum"</note>. Daniel, however, says: *And after sixty-two weeks, Christ shall be slain* <note>original: "et poſt hebdomades ſexaginta duas occidet̃ chriſtus"</note>. In the figure of this <term>Passion|From the Latin 'passio', meaning suffering; specifically the physical and spiritual suffering of Christ leading up to his death.</term>, Isaac is led by his father to the sacrifice. This suffering for the reconciliation of the human race is shown beforehand in the Paschal lamb, which the people of the Jews killed at the departure from Egypt. By its blood, sprinkled in the form of a cross upon the doorposts, they were returned safe from the destroying angel.

Concerning his suffering, Isaiah seems to weave not so much a prophecy as a history: *He has no form nor comeliness; and we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, and we desired him: despised and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity; and his face was as it were hidden and despised, wherefore we esteemed him not. Truly he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows, and we thought him as it were a leper, and as one struck by God and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins; the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, every one has turned aside into his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because it was his own will, and he opened not his mouth: he shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter, and shall be dumb as a lamb before his shearer, and he shall not open his mouth. He was taken away from distress and from judgment: who shall declare his generation? because he is cut off out of the land of the living: for the wickedness of my people have I struck him. And he shall give the ungodly for his burial, and the rich for his death: because he has done no iniquity, neither was there deceit in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity: if he shall lay down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand. For that which his soul has labored, he shall see and be satisfied. In his knowledge shall this my just servant justify...* <note>This long passage is a translation of Isaiah 53, often called the "Suffering Servant" prophecy, which Christians historically interpreted as a detailed description of the crucifixion.</note>

<summary>This page argues that the Jewish people misinterpreted messianic prophecies by expecting a political king, failing to realize that scripture—specifically the writings of Daniel, Moses, and Isaiah—pointed toward a spiritual leader who would save through suffering and sacrifice.</summary>

# THE SELECTION: BOOK TWO

...my many servants, and he himself will bear their iniquities; therefore I will distribute to him many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he delivered his soul unto death, and was counted among the wicked; he himself bore the sins of many and prayed for the transgressors. <note>original: "ſeruos meos multos, & iniqtates eorū ipſe portabit..." quoting the prophecy of the "Suffering Servant" from Isaiah 53:11-12</note> Therefore, the holy fathers looked back at the condition of the human race, the stain of sin, and the offense against God which they had inherited from the disobedience of our first parent <note>Adam</note> through the lineage of the flesh. They expected the Messiah to reconcile this—the redeemer and mediator between God and man—not so that they might recover earthly happiness, but eternal life. This is why it is written: *so that transgression may be finished, and sin may reach an end, and iniquity may be wiped away, and everlasting justice may be brought in.* <note>original: "vt cōſummet̃ puaricatio & finem accipiat peccatū..." from Daniel 9:24</note>

Let us consider for ourselves how much it would belong to the divine goodness—which wishes to do good to men who deserve it for their virtue—if God offered nothing but earthly things through blessings such as these: *Blessed shall you be in the city, and blessed in the field; blessed shall be the fruit of your womb, and the fruit of your ground, and the fruit of your cattle, the herds of your oxen, and the folds of your sheep; blessed shall be your barns, and blessed your leftovers; you shall be blessed coming in and going out. The Lord will grant that your enemies who rise up against you shall fall in your sight; they shall come against you by one way and flee from your face by seven.* <note>The author is quoting the material blessings of the Law from Deuteronomy 28</note> *The Lord will send a blessing upon your storehouses and upon all the works of your hands, and he will bless you in the land which you receive. The Lord will raise you up for himself as a holy people, as he swore to you, if you keep the mandates of the Lord your God and walk in his ways. And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord has been called upon you, and they shall fear you. The Lord will make you abound in all good things: in the fruit of your womb, the fruit of your cattle, and the fruit of your land, which the Lord swore to your fathers to give you. He will open his best treasure, the heavens, to give rain to your land in its season, and he will bless all the works of your hands. And you shall lend to many nations, and you yourself shall borrow from none. The Lord your God will make you the head and not the tail, and you shall always be above and not below, if only you listen to the mandates of the Lord your God which I command you today, and keep and do them, and do not turn aside from them to the right or to the left, nor follow foreign gods nor worship them.*

What were they to have after death? For they are nowhere promised heavenly rewards for their good deeds. The holy patriarch Jacob says: *I will go down to my son in the underworld, mourning.* <note>original: "deſcēdam ad filium meum lugens ad inferos" from Genesis 37:35. The term "inferos" refers to the dwelling place of the dead, rather than a place of punishment.</note> And Job says: *Who would grant me this, that you might protect me in the underworld and hide me until your anger passes, and appoint a time for me in which you would remember me?* <note>original: "vt in inferno ptegas me..." from Job 14:13</note> There, the holy ones were hidden from the beginning of the world until the wrath of God should pass, until the appointed time came so that God might remember the reconciliation to be made through the Messiah. This was the true liberation and restoration to original liberty, which later generations incorrectly shifted to mean earthly kingdoms and political revolts.

But if they were not expecting heavenly promises under the images and likenesses of earthly things, then why did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob follow their God everywhere as pilgrims, exiled from their native soil? Why were Moses and Aaron—despite their great holiness—not admitted into the land flowing with milk and honey? Why did Elijah, Elisha, and all the prophets, and even the sons of the prophets, search for another promise while living in the very land of promise? Isaiah, filled with longing, cries out so ardently: *O that you would rend the heavens and come down!* <note>Isaiah 64:1</note> and earlier he had prayed: *Send the lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.* <note>Isaiah 16:1</note> All of these lived in contempt of their present circumstances, though they surely deserved to be most happy and wealthy for their innocent lives. But they reached out for better things, as Isaiah mentions: *Eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you.* <note>Isaiah 64:4</note> Yet concerning the present goods of this life, David says: *But as for me, my feet were almost moved; they almost slipped...* <note>original: "mei aut pene moti ſunt pedes pene" from Psalm 73:2</note>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the true goal of the patriarchs was spiritual rather than earthly. Having established that the Messiah’s mission was to reconcile humanity to God, the author now contrasts the worldly peace of sinners with the physical suffering of the saints, ultimately arguing that the historical plight of the Jewish people is divine punishment for rejecting Christ.</meta>

-># ON TRUE RELIGION<-

...my steps had nearly slipped, for I was envious of the wicked when I saw the prosperity of sinners. <note>original: "effuſi ſunt greſſus mei, quia zelaui ſuper iniquos pacem peccatorũ videns" — a paraphrase of Psalm 73:2-3</note> The royal prophet <note>King David</note> almost questioned God’s administration when he saw a peace among sinners that he did not see among righteous men. Of the righteous, he says in another place: *Many are the tribulations of the saints, and from them all the Lord has delivered them.* Indeed, they were pulled apart, enduring mockings and floggings, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they went about in sheepskins and goatskins, being in want, distressed, and afflicted—men of whom the world was not worthy. <note>The author is quoting Hebrews 11:36-38, which describes the suffering of biblical heroes of faith.</note> They wandered in deserts, on mountains, in dens, and in caves of the earth; and all these, though approved by the testimony of their faith, did not receive the promise, for God provided something better for us.

This was their hope and promise, these were their riches and wealth: to be delivered from the bite of death and to return to that place from which they had fallen through our first parent <note>Adam</note>. To them, the expulsion of Adam from Paradise was their "Egypt"—their exile and captivity. Restoration to original innocence was their "Promised Land," for the sake of which they sought another land beyond the physical land of promise. 

The Jews, however, denied this Liberator when he appeared on earth at the time predicted by the prophets. Though he performed everything the prophets foretold he would do in the flesh, and though he explained the very meaning of those prophecies through the complete history of his own actions, they rejected him before the faces of Pilate and Herod because of the humility of his coming. From this point, they fell away from salvation and from the fatherly piety of God. As with all the prophets, it had been predicted that they would deny him. Because of this sacrilege, they now pay the price in a most wretched servitude, so bitter that in no monuments or history can a nation be found like the Jewish people—so utterly ignorant of all salvation. Thus, to the Gentiles—whom the Jews once called "the uncircumcised," meaning total impurity—the lot is today reversed. The Jews have truly become our <term>purgamenta</term> <note>original: "pipſemata viliſſimaqƶ purgamenta" — meaning the lowest refuse or dregs of society</note>. 

Nor is it a secret that this atrocious and long-lasting captivity happened to the Jews because of this Jesus Christ, the Messiah, whom they denied and continue to deny today, and whose unjust condemnation they called down upon themselves, saying: *His blood be upon us and upon our children.* At that time, when they were inciting so many seditions for the sake of claiming liberty, defending ancestral laws, and protecting the sanctity of the Temple—leading finally to the open war in which they were cut off—they refused to receive the images and statues of the Roman Emperors. I say that at that time, they stood as firm in the worship of the one God as they ever had. They had no public sin other than this sacrilege which they committed against Christ, the Holy of Holies. 

Therefore, if these people, fighting for their country and laws, were not helped by God according to the old examples—such as when they fought for the preservation of piety under the Judges, the Kings, or the Maccabean leaders with the manifest presence of God and miracles from heaven—it is telling. If they were not helped according to all the blessings that were supposed to come to them while they remained in the veneration of the one true God, they might complain that God had perhaps forgotten the covenant he struck with the people of Israel. But if it is a sin to say that, then they are clearly subject today to all these curses:

> If you will not hear me, nor do all my commandments, but despise my laws and contemn my judgments, so that you do not do those things which are appointed by me and bring my covenant to nothing, I also will do these things to you: I will visit you quickly with poverty and burning heat, which shall waste your eyes and consume your souls. I will make your sanctuaries a wilderness, and I will no longer receive your sweetest odors. I will destroy your land, and your enemies shall be astonished at it when they are the inhabitants thereof. And I will scatter you among the Gentiles, and I will draw out a sword after you, and your land shall be a desert and your cities destroyed. Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths all the days of her desolation. <note>A translation of Leviticus 26:14-34, detailing the divine punishments for breaking the Mosaic covenant.</note>

With uncertain fortunes and certain unhappiness, he is suspended by continuous slanders in every time and place.

Lastly, we come to the **Christians**, who, having rejected either Jewish institutes or the filth of the heathens, have begun to know the one true God under Christ and the apostles, according to the teaching of the Law and the Prophets. Since this is that religion from which true piety toward God and the sole happiness of souls arises—which we have been seeking for so long—it must be held as the one way God desires to meet religious minds. We believe this, lest by the pursuit of human faction or opinion, by which all things in the world are corrupted and depart into uncertain and doubtful parts...

So that we are not suspected of believing in such a way <note>The author is likely responding to critics who claim Christians believe without evidence or logical foundation.</note>, I wish to assert this most necessary matter as a certain faith with at least a few proofs. Regarding the authority and innocence of the entire law upon which the **Christian faith** relies, it is not necessary for me to bring forward more evidence at present than what we have said before. This shall suffice: that the Christian faith was destined to emerge from the Jewish succession. 

From this succession, the Jews themselves have fallen away and were therefore neglected by God, according to that passage from **Isaiah**: *Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; listen with your ears to the law of your God, you people of Gomorrah! "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?" says the Lord. "I am full; I do not want the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fed beasts, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you come before my sight, who required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Offer sacrifice in vain no longer; your incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure the <term>New Moons</term> <note>original: "Neomenias" — the Jewish festival marking the beginning of the lunar month</note>, the <term>Sabbath</term>, and your other festivities. Your assemblies are wicked; my soul hates your New Moons and your solemnities; they have become a burden to me, and I am weary of bearing them. When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayers, I will not listen. For your hands are full of blood."* <note>original: Isaiah 1:10–15</note>

From that true piety, I say, the Jews became <term>Transgressors</term> <note>original: "Preuaricatores" — literally those who "plow a crooked furrow," used here for those who deviate from the true path of faith</note>, giving the Gentiles the opportunity, through their own perfidy, to be called in their place by God’s mercy into the true recognition of heavenly secrets. God predicted this would happen, again through **Isaiah**: *I will lead your seed from the East and gather you from the West; I will say to the North, "Give them up," and to the South, "Do not withhold them." Bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the ends of the earth—everyone who calls upon my name. I have created him for my glory and I have made him.* <note>original: Isaiah 43:5–7</note> 

Regarding the transgressing people, however, he says: *Lead forth the blind people who yet have eyes, and the deaf who yet have ears.* <note>original: Isaiah 43:8</note> And through **Malachi**: *For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations; and in every place, a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name, for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts.* <note>original: Malachi 1:11</note> 

**Christ** also says in the Gospel: *I tell you, many shall come from the East and the West and shall sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into the outer darkness.* <note>original: Matthew 8:11–12</note> Because of these things, the **Apostles** finally declared to the Jews: *It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first. But since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. Seeing, therefore, that this <term>Divine Worship</term> <note>original: "theosebiā" — from the Greek meaning "piety" or "worship of God"</note> was to be transferred to the nations in this way—witnessed many centuries beforehand by the Prophets and later at the end of time by the very success of events—we have rightly received it as the only most holy faith, sent from heaven. For God told us these things before they happened so that we would believe when they came to pass. 

Afterward, the Apostles—whom **Jesus Christ**, the author of life, had chosen for the task of announcing this work—carried it out with such miraculous effort for the recognition of the nations that we can perceive nothing in all this success of preaching other than a divine course. In the beginning, the leaders themselves, the Apostles, approached this not persuaded by human ingenuity but illuminated from heaven. **Paul**, the interpreter of this word, was called back from heaven while he was a persecutor. He was caught up to the **third heaven** <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, describing a mystical ascent into the presence of God.</note>, where, instructed by divine mastery, he heard the secret words of this sacrament which no human is permitted to speak. Hence, in his letter to the **Galatians**, he says: *For I did not receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ.* <note>original: Galatians 1:12</note> For this reason, out of a full conscience of so great a matter, he said: *I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him...* <note>original: 2 Timothy 1:12</note>

...preserve until that day. From this illustration of truth, **Peter** also wrote to the churches: *For we did not follow cleverly devised fables <note>original: "indoctas fabulas"</note> when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.* Finally, **John** also says in his Canonical Epistle: *That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked at and our hands have touched concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested, and we have seen it and testify to it, and we announce to you the eternal life which was with the Father and appeared to us.* 

Strengthened by this testimony of divinity, they descended to preach to the whole world. Nature itself was stunned by the magnitude and frequency of the miracles that followed the apostles to bolster their preaching. Everyone, from the seats of religion and Philosophy, rose to meet the messengers of this new salvation. Yet, despite the authority by which the whole world judged the Apostles to be like gods, they sought nothing for their own glory, but only for God's. It certainly would have been easy, given the greatness of their works, to claim such a thing for themselves among those suspended minds—human weakness might have persuaded them to do so, just as **Simon Magus** <note>A practitioner of magic mentioned in the Book of Acts who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.</note> and **Menander** <note>A 1st-century Gnostic teacher and student of Simon Magus.</note> preached themselves. 

But the Apostles possessed a consciousness of divine things that restrained them. Thus, they were so far from seeking worldly glory that they even suffered insults for Christ gladly. Therefore, they are found to have never said or done anything simply to please the people, the wise, the emperors, or the Kings. They preached things that were entirely harsh—unheard of and unexpected in previous centuries—in which you will find nothing composed for human flattery or to gain belief more easily. And what you might wonder at more: they did not hesitate to begin such an arduous business centered on one man, and he a crucified one. Such was the consciousness of the truth. 

They asserted that this man was God and born as a man on earth without a Father; that there are three in heaven—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—a Trinity in simplicity, one essence and one God. They taught that all mortals are held liable to death under the guilt of that sin which the first parent <note>Referring to Adam and the concept of Original Sin.</note> committed, and are held under the death of one man, **Jesus Christ**, who was crucified; a man who appeared in that corner of Palestine as an ignoble figure, whom Roman laws had condemned, and whom the Jews, in a harmonious conspiracy throughout the Roman provinces, attacked as one impious toward divinity. Yet, just as the apostles preached, they testified that the human race must be restored to life through the torment of that God and man. 

This was the most difficult point to admit. Consider our progenitors and ancestors, whose integrity, virtue, and hardships for the Republic were commended, believed, and accepted through images, statues, and **apotheosis** <term>apotheosis</term> <note>The process of a human being being officially recognized as a god, common in Ancient Rome for emperors and heroes.</note> by citizens and foreigners alike. It was demanded that their descendants and posterity—contrary to paternal love, a feeling even barbarians hold—should strip them of every merit. Because the stain of the human race's original sin was not expiated in them, they were believed to be no different than a **Typhon** or an **Antaeus** <note>Giants from Greek mythology who rebelled against the gods.</note>, or any other impious being fighting against Divinity; they were believed to be devoid of all happiness and to endure eternal darkness in another life. 

Finally, it was not enough for them to admit such difficult principles under any vow of living; they even discouraged all things otherwise allowed: they demanded patience in injury, the forgetting of insults suffered, the rejection of even honorable pleasures—in short, the repudiation of every allure of life. They taught contempt for impious magistrates and Kingdoms (which mortals lead the list of good things), and to trample underfoot wife, children, the splendor of family, ancestral possessions, relatives, and kin; to endure prison, chains, tortures, and condemnations before tribunals <note>The 'p' with a crossbar here functions as an abbreviation for 'pro' or 'per'</note> for the sake of earning Christ, and for the sake of happiness in...

# ON THE TRUE RELIGION,

explored things which **no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man** <note>original: "nec oculus vidit nec audiuit auris et ī cor hoīs nō ascēdit"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9</note> as they commanded. All those things were foreign; the intellect was certainly incapable of such great matters. Therefore, so that such arduous things might be sown in the minds of men, the most present divinity—the Author and Arbiter—was at hand. **Moses** was himself the institutor of the old law. He was commended by God with so many miracles and portents among unbelieving minds. Finally, under the benefit of the liberation of Israel from the harshest servitude, and under the promise of happy things, he nevertheless with difficulty retained so small a people behind him. The **Jews**, who carried their law and ancestral holiness through the **Chaldeans**, **Medes**, **Persians**, and **Macedonians**, were to be esteemed by all and known through many centuries. Yet, at the very time of the Gospel preaching, they had occupied **Greece**, **Italy**, **Africa**, and the **Roman provinces** in excessive numbers; they had finally obtained the privileges of the Roman majesty in a great number of free cities. They spoke against **Christ** throughout all the provinces. Yet, neither the holiness of their laws, nor the custom of many years, nor the common civility everywhere, nor the zeal of false detraction, were able to move them to achieve anything like their own law—otherwise holy—in being spread abroad.

The **Apostles**, aided by no single such advantage nor by all of them together—indeed, through all disadvantages, through the **scandal of the cross** <term>scandal of the cross<gloss>From the Greek 'skandalon' (stumbling block); the idea that a crucified man being God was offensive to both Jews and Gentiles.</gloss></term>, through novelty, through the severity of the Gospel law, and penetrating every corner of the world through such remote promises—brought the world into the conviction of their preaching. They did not win over just any simple people who had no choice, but they prepared **confessors of the truth** among the most powerful in the courts of princes, among the military camps, and the **gymnasia** <note>Ancient centers for both physical training and philosophical debate.</note>. Neither the pride of the great, nor the knowledge of things possessed by the **Philosophers**, could stand in the way of them accepting the **foolishness of the cross** <note>original: "stultitiā crucis"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 1:18-25</note>. 

Clearly, the blood of Christ, poured out for the redemption of the human race, was so boiling over, and the **Holy Spirit** was urging. Apostolic miracles provided testimony. The conscience also, heavily depressed in prior centuries as if by an internal weight, was awakened at the preaching of the Gospel and recognized again its own kindred ray of a better life. Above all other things, they were victorious through constancy and a confession even unto blood—a fortitude which the Apostles had received more intimately from the Holy Spirit when **the place in which they were gathered was moved, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence** <note>original: "repleti sunt omnes sp̄ūsancto. & loquebantur verbū dei cū fiducia"; citing Acts 4:31</note>. The Gospel dispensation would surely have been weak if the Apostles had not defended it unto blood; after the truth of the word and the virtues performed, this was the third and perhaps greatest witness by which the Gospel mystery might prevail. The world would believe that whatever the authors did not protect to the end, even to the shedding of blood, had been undertaken rashly. This portion of the propagating faith made mortals astonished; it purified the unbelieving, so that they might consider that Christian philosophy was not in vain, nor were the promises of eternal things in vain, for the sake of which they lost earthly things with such an easy sacrifice. 

All these things look toward this: to affirm that if ever any philosophy or religion more holy, brought down by great beginnings and divine decrees, was increased and preserved in the world, the **Christian religion** is that very one. Aided by no human help, by celestial counsel alone, it precedes all others or incomparably surpasses them, so that no other should be received through which it is necessary for us to be saved and to pursue true innocence and happiness. For **he who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned** <note>original: "qui em̄ crediderit et baptifatus fuerit saluus erit, q̄ vero nō credide rit, cōdemnabit"; citing Mark 16:16</note>. For **this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent** <note>original: "hec est em̄ vita æterna vt cognoscāt te vnum verum deū & quē misisti iēsūm christū"; citing John 17:3</note>; **nor is there any other name under heaven given to men in which it is necessary for us to be saved** <note>original: "neq; aliud nomē est sub cœlo datū hoībus in quo oporteat nos saluos fieri"; citing Acts 4:12</note>. 

But the **heretics** interrupt this confession; those who know the name of Christ the Savior and the Apostles by mouth only, and relying on such a light argument—as if all things thereafter ought to be Christian and Apostolic—claim Christian purity for themselves alone. Not content to be admitted even as a part, they instead wish to seem to have brought back every point of sincere piety by condemning the apostolic confessors.

### CHOICE WORKS, BOOK TWO,

And the minds of men, infected by pestiferous preaching and as if by a wrongly assumed persuasion of pious faith, under the feigned name of true religion, always find it harder to be corrected from impiety due to long-standing error and the consensus of the many. But many great arguments show that teachers of this kind are heretics—that is, enemies of apostolic doctrine. The first point is this: apostolic preaching was heard and received before those men came forward who stirred up seditions in the Church regarding dogmas not heard before. They were not **Catholics**; for the faith of the apostles alone was called **Catholic** (that is, universal), not because the whole world received it at that time, but because it went out into the world through the harmonious **Creed** <note>original: "symbolo"; referring to the Apostles' Creed</note> of the apostles. Therefore, though heretics may boast of being apostolic, we know that the Church was called a **virgin** during the seventy years following Christ’s ascension <note>A common early Christian motif, notably from the historian Hegesippus, suggesting the Church remained "pure" until the last Apostle died</note>. This was not because wicked men did not exist even then, but because there was no place for them to pour out their poisons everywhere, so great was the apostolic care and authority. At that time, they conceived lies more truly than they uttered them; the living voice of the apostles was less accessible and less vulnerable to corrupters than for them to be able to twist the doctrine into a bad sense through slanders. The apostles themselves were present as immediate defenders of their own meanings.

After these men were taken from human affairs and Christian doctrine began to be committed to writing, then, with the reins loosened, they leaped upon the nuances <note>original: "apices"; literally the "horns" or small strokes of the letters, implying they scrutinized and twisted every tiny detail</note> of the Gospels and Epistles. Ravening wolves entered in secret—as **Paul** had predicted—men speaking perverse things to lead away disciples after themselves. **Peter** also said: *and there shall be among you lying teachers who shall bring in chosen sects of perdition, and they deny the God who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.* <note>2 Peter 2:1</note> They are rebels who would admit no one giving good advice, for whom no holiness, learning, or reverence seemed sufficient; instead, they everywhere seize upon that act of **Zedekiah** the false prophet—who struck **Micah**, the prophet of the Lord, on the cheek—against churchmen, saying: *Has the spirit of the Lord then left me and spoken to you?* <note>1 Kings 22:24</note> And so, if any have introduced new sects and falsely boasted that the purity of faith is with them, they came at a later time than the apostles. It is necessary either that they exclude the Apostles from the pursuit of true salvation, or they themselves are excluded.

But how are they not excluded, whom the apostles, by a prophetic spirit, forewarned us to avoid? If we do not consider the **Ebionites**, **Cerinthus**, **Arius**, **Manicheans**, and six hundred other masters of novelties to be those whom the apostles stripped of authority by their Pastoral power, let others show who else introduced unusual doctrines beyond what ecclesiastical ears were accustomed to hear. Behold, **Simon Magus**, having been baptized under false pretenses <note>original: "subiurato baptismate"</note>, returns to the profane worship of the creature. His profession is not the Catholic faith, for the apostles preached before they knew Simon; finally, as soon as they began to know him, they condemned him. The **Ebionites**, among many unspeakable things, confess Christ to be a mere man born in the human manner. Their opinion is not the Catholic faith; the Apostles were known before the Ebionites, who raised themselves up most notably under the Emperor **Trajan**. Here, if the Ebionites are right, then the Gospel of **Luke**—that is, the preaching of **Paul**—will be false. Luke writes: *And a voice came from Heaven: You are my beloved son, in you I am well pleased. And he himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph.* <note>Luke 3:22-23</note> Behold, he is called "Son" by the Father from Heaven! They seize upon this, but wrongly; and as if the Evangelist had placed the word "supposed" there by chance, they pass over it... when certainly he intended to signify that he was called the son of Joseph not by right of birth, but according to the opinion of his fellow citizens.
