### ON THE TRUE RELIGION

...the opinion of the Evangelist, the father will think. Or if he thinks truly, and the scripture is not to be moved, nevertheless the **Ebionites** <note>A Jewish-Christian movement that emphasized Jewish law and viewed Jesus as the natural son of Mary and Joseph</note> preach that Christ was born of human seed; they must necessarily seek another [father] besides Joseph, whom neither the neighborhood then knew, nor the Gospels mention, nor the **Ebionites** ever heard of. **Cerinthus** <note>An early Gnostic-leaning teacher who, according to tradition, was a contemporary of the Apostle John</note> was first heard of seventy years after the ascension of Christ. That which **Cerinthus** stirs up is not the Catholic (that is, Christian) preaching, or else the apostles are not Christians. We certainly heard one thing from the apostles, and another from **Cerinthus**. **Cerinthus** assigned an earthly kingdom to God—to Christ with the saints on earth. He defined it as consisting of drinking bouts, the play of girls, and bodily delights, according to the measure of his own gluttony. 

He is moved neither by the opinion of Christ nor of the apostles who had preceded him. Christ had said to the **Sadducees**: *You err, not knowing the scriptures nor the power of God. For in the Resurrection they shall neither marry nor be given in marriage, but shall be as the angels of God in heaven* <note>Matthew 22:29-30</note>. **Cerinthus** is a delirious head; for if he is true, there will then be mere brothels—or, if they be legitimate marriages, the **Sadducees** would therefore still press Christ further regarding the resurrection of the dead and concerning the one wife of seven brothers. I will add further what impiety overflows upon **Cerinthus**: Christ, the very wisdom of God, still labors, sweats, and sticks fast in doubt, not finding what he should answer to the **Sadducees**. 

But **Paul** said: *The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit* <note>Romans 14:17</note>. Finally, who endowed with a sounder brain would not understand how much it shrinks from that age—in the sight of the divinity, the holy angels, and all the continent—to practice shameful allurements, which we here hide out of shame from a more reverent witness [such as] Paul. Finally, all such things as have ever been called heresies, however much they may flatter themselves regarding the truth, have been found to be things that the apostles (from whom alone, as we say so often, the **Catholic**, that is, the saving faith, derives) were ignorant of; which the fathers and the emulators and successors of the apostolic dogma examined in gathered disputations, and afterwards condemned by synodal decrees. 

Finally, the heretical fraud is opened up by the manner of their treatment of the scriptures. For they were corrupting the faith of their predecessors by no true things, but by slanders and captures of words—nay, even by halved and corrupted little sentences. Just as the bees [gather] honey and the spider [gathers] poison from one flower, so the **Heretics** began to take the material of their errors from the sacred writings. This, however, is accustomed to happen where, as the blessed **Hilary** <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading Latin theologian known for his defense of the Trinity</note> says: *The understanding of things is not expected from the words, but is imposed upon the words; it is not brought back [from the text] but is brought to it; and it forces that to be contained in the words which it presumed was to be understood before the reading.* 

The **Manicheans** <note>Followers of Mani who taught a radical dualism between spirit and matter</note>, once imagining for themselves that the humanity of Christ was not true but fictitious—not truly having suffered but having seemed to suffer—since they have no sense of the sacred scripture that might help them, they stir up suspicions to confirm such a pernicious opinion. *Behold,* they say, *contrary to the nature of a solid body, he remains fasting for forty days; he walks high upon the liquid element; and when about to be cast headlong from the brow of a hill, he suddenly escapes invisibly.* With such and many more lying deceptions they burden God so that they themselves may be held as true. Nor do they care to look into the matter more closely; too many evident testimonies would occur by which their own vanity would lie detected. Content, therefore, to say something lest they should say nothing at all, they no longer act so that they might eventually yield to sacred scripture, but so that the same might serve their lust. Leaving behind all the more pressing points as if they existed nowhere, they drive the unlearned crowd to believe that this alone which they offer was found. The most impure **Manicheans** were able to find that Christ—who did such things through which he came into such wicked suspicion—did not do so without the example of many whose mortal bodies no one calls into doubt. **Elijah** in his strength...

### SELECTION, BOOK TWO
h. 6

...[with the magni]tude of so little bread, [Elijah] sustains forty days of labor on his journey, and though shaken by his wandering through a vast wilderness, his little fasting body does not fail. He does not collapse but arrives at the mountain of God. Moses, in a twice-forty-day fast, awaits the law of the divinity for the Synagogue before the "Senate of God" <note>A metaphorical reference to the divine presence on Mount Sinai</note>. Peter walks upon the same waters together with the Savior; that he sinks is not the fault of his body, but of his distrust. The door of Lot disappears from the eyes of the sinners <note>A reference to the angels blinding the men of Sodom to protect Lot’s house in Genesis 19</note>. Elisha strikes [the Syrians] with blindness—or more truly, if the Latin language would allow the term, with "un-seeing" <note>original: "avidentia"; the author is likely coining a term to describe a state of being unable to perceive what is right in front of one</note>. The Syrian attendants feel neither where they stand nor where they enter; the Prophet himself is the leader of the mindless men for whose capture they had been sent. It must be that Moses, Elijah, Peter, the chaste threshold of Lot, Dothan, and Samaria were present there for these same miracles; otherwise, they were nothing but images, or fictions, or tricks, or phantasms, or all of them together. If the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualistic religious movement that often viewed the physical world as evil and Christ’s body as an illusion (Docetism)</note> cry out here, let them admit that Christ the Savior—in whom fictions and lies cannot fall, since he is truth itself—performed these same miracles in the true nature of the flesh. 

Just as Arius, in order to assert that the divinity of the Son was less than the Father, raises such great impiety from a small phrase; he finds so little: *Because the Father is greater than me* <note>John 14:28</note>. As if he held the whole law by this little sentence, he poured out a new faith into Christian ears as if it were the true apostolic one. However, if this phrase—"because the Father is greater than me"—were found in the Law and the Prophets before Christ was born in the flesh (when only one nature was recognized in him), with what great congratulation and what great bruising of the true faith would he have thought he had found it! But now, after the Son of God emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in human habit <note>Philippians 2:7</note>, such a sentence as "the Father is greater than me" has come forth. Who would not understand the malice of **Arius** <note>A 4th-century priest who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father</note>? What seemed so provable to him that he would transfer to the divine nature that which had only been spoken concerning the human nature? 

Truly, no pardon shall erase this impiety. He was able to read that *the Father is greater than me*, but he was also able to read that *I and the Father are one* <note>John 10:30</note>. He was able to read: *He did not think it robbery to be equal to God* <note>Philippians 2:6</note>; and that, I say, he could read: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing* <note>John 1:1-3</note>. If, therefore, the Word was in the beginning with God, that Word will not be "after the beginning." That which was in the beginning is uncreated. But if, as Arius blasphemes, "there was [a time] when he was not," then because he began so that he might exist, he was not in the beginning. Furthermore, if all things were made through this Word and without him nothing was made, then by this reasoning the Son must be uncreated; or if he were created, then the Word was made through the Word itself so that all things might be made through him. If it were otherwise, then all things were not made through him—but the Evangelist testifies that all things were made through him.

This was Arius; such was his persuasion. This is how he read the sacred letters. It was not so that he might become better or more instructed in piety, but lest he be forced to abandon in public shame what he had once defended. And so, by calumnies, traps, dissimulation of obvious things, and by halved—and therefore corrupted—little sentences, he forced the words and even the accents of Holy Scripture to his own will. He desired it to be believed that he had restored Christian piety to Apostolic integrity, as if it had previously lain corrupted, collapsed, and utterly ignored.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;No one should wonder how 
the sacred letters could be open to such great errors of heretics. For that fault does not happen from the inconstancy of the Sacred Canon (which is most certain in itself), but by the depravity of evil men. For just as *to the pure all things are pure*, so to the impure and unfaithful, both their mind and conscience are polluted <note>Titus 1:15</note>.

### ON TRUE RELIGION
<meta>catchword: each</meta>

Nothing in the world is so pure—as we see with written bonds, securities, and hand-written deeds <note>The author uses legal terms like "syngrapha" and "chirographa" to compare the Bible to a legal contract</note> composed in simple terms—that they do not remains holy, safe, and inviolate among honest and right-holding natures. However, for those who are wicked and greedy for injuries, no matter how much they are hedged in or deliberated down to the smallest detail <note>original: "apiculos examussim," referring to the tiny strokes of a pen or a mason's level</note>, they still think "handles" are left behind. Thus, what was sufficiently guarded is found to be scarcely guarded at all, so that the malevolent might break in or pick a lawsuit. In this same manner, heretics have mocked the simplicity and virtue of the sacred scriptures, corrupting their sincerity in many ways, but especially through these two most famous methods:

**One**, because they break off segments <note>original: "commata," referring to short phrases or clauses</note> from the plain body of a complete sentence, and having extracted them, they impose their own meaning—distorted from the truth—clothing a profane error in a sacred garment. An example is that word of the Apostle: **"Let each remain in the calling in which he was called."** <note>1 Corinthians 7:20</note> We see that if this little verse is lifted out of the scope of the whole speech, it becomes a supporter of a very ruinous error. You hear the apostolic words used nakedly to seem to favor the idolater, the Saracen, the Turk, the Manichaean, the **Waldensians** <note>A medieval spiritual movement (the Poor Men of Lyon) often targeted by the Church as heretical for their views on poverty and authority</note>, and all blasphemers. For if anyone should call them back, rebuke them, or show them the ruin of their error, they would defend themselves under the guise of the apostolic voice: "for let each remain in the calling in which he was called."

But let us restore the captive sentence to its place; let us see the origin from which it began and from where it descended. Then its wicked use and the fraud of those lost men will be uncovered, and it will be proved to say something entirely different. For this passage of Saint Paul did not begin there so that he might presently discuss the differences between the merits of religions. Rather, he was responding to the Corinthians who were consulting him about continence and the marriage bond, having this specific point in question: if a faithful man or woman had an unfaithful partner, whether that union should be considered legitimate. The Teacher of the Gentiles <note>A traditional title for the Apostle Paul</note> responded: "If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her; and if any faithful woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss the husband." In the series of that dispute, he says, **"let each remain in the calling in which he was called."** You are bound to a wife? Do not seek a release. You are released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do take a wife, you have not sinned. For in whatever calling someone was called, let him remain in it. You see the fraud of the previous interpretation; you see how foreign it was to the Apostle not only to say, but even to think such a thing as to suggest that the nations who are ignorant of God were in some "calling of salvation" outside of Christ.

**The second way** sacred scripture is corrupted by heretical fraud is if something written in one place—which is explained and perfected by another—is nevertheless brought forward as if it were understood in isolation. Take the example I previously brought forward regarding **Arius** <note>A 4th-century priest who taught that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father</note>, who claimed: **"Because the Father is greater than I."** <note>John 14:28</note> It is as if he had not read, **"I and the Father are one."** <note>John 10:30</note> Thus, breaking into the divinity with his own treachery, he did not abstain from saying the divine nature of the Son was posterior to the Father. But if he had compared one sense to the other, he would have found that the whole faith concerning Christ confesses a double nature in Him: so that according to this assumed nature from the Virgin, the Son is less than the Father; but according to that by which He is the Only-Begotten in the bosom of the Father, He may say, "I and the Father are one."

The Apostle Paul writes: **"Food does not commend us to God,"** and **"whether we eat, we eat to the Lord; whether we fast, we fast to the Lord."** This sense is used as if it did not look toward another decree of the divine Paul upon which it depends and is perfected—for instance: **"Obey those set over you and be subject to them, for they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls."** <note>Hebrews 13:17</note> As if the former sense were not drawn into a certain place by this latter one! In this way, some wicked man, seeking to satisfy his own gluttony, abusing every liberty for whatever outcome, might rail against the **fasts** <note>original: "ieiunia," the prescribed periods of abstinence in the Church calendar</note> which the leaders of the Church established, and condemn them as superstitious to a simple listener because of a poorly received sentence. Yet if he joined one sense to the other, then both the vain illusion and the virtue and moderation of that saying—"food does not commend us to God"—would be clear to everyone.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE SELECTION

...would extend itself, it would catch the meaning at once. In this way, heretics use the canonical scriptures, as they themselves preach; they satisfy the ears of the simple with a "knowledge of the law." In this way, they recall the apostolic faith, but they do so only to collect an appearance of testimonies in word alone, so that they might defend their impiety under the memory of the scriptures. They are known to have provided examples not of that Christian simplicity which they all profess with one breath, but of full malevolence. For the Holy Spirit will flee from the deceitful. Through this well-worn pursuit of all heretics, those **Waldenses** <note>The Waldenses or Vaudois were a group that predated the Reformation, emphasizing poverty and the Bible, but often viewed as heretical by the Catholic Church for rejecting Church authority.</note> also impose upon the Christian church in our century. By a similar method among their impious neighbors, extracting sayings from the sacred canon, and relying on these strengths and these subtleties, they once wrote to the Royal Majesty: <insert>[ This, O most illustrious King, is the profession of our faith which we hold in our hearts as Catholic, and which has its foundation in the scriptures of faith ]</insert> I ask, will it be the Catholic faith of the Waldensians if I learn that the Apostles preached it? It will have its foundation in the scriptures of faith if this is how they handle the scriptures! As we have just said, our method will be to detect their treachery. We will prove Christian innocence not by ears, but with the conscience of the listeners as judge. We will press testimony with testimony; we will place articles against articles. I will arrange their opinions in order; I will place the defense of so great a cause before the judgment of the soul and the witness of the mind.

But there is still something I must demand from those Waldenses at the beginning: it has been found that those Waldenses receive no ecclesiastical writers <note>The author refers here to the Church Fathers, the early influential theologians of the Church.</note>. For if they have called upon either **Dionysius**, or **Origen**, or **Augustine** (whom alone, as I remember, they summoned), it was not out of devotion for them. Rather, they produce such great men of holiness and learning only to the shame of our people. I suspect they would have accepted them, had they not been found contrary to their conspiracy. Indeed, the face of our men <note>meaning the orthodox Catholic writers</note> seemed too heavy for those sacrilegious ones to endure. For those things which they are always giving birth to in secret are by no means helpful to put to the test. For everything that is rebuked is made manifest by the light, and everything that is made manifest is light. The Waldenses were unable to bear this light of the doctors of the church and the councils. For when they explained in their confession by what things they received a proven faith, among the rest, they made mention of only one council: the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the core creed of Christianity.</note>.

Thus, according to them, the **Council of Constantinople** against **Macedonius** and **Eudoxus** (the followers of Arius), the **Council of Ephesus** against **Nestorius**, the **Council of Chalcedon** against **Eutyches**, and the other **Council of Constantinople** against **Theodore** were not legitimate. And the fathers who attended in such great numbers were believed to be less faithful to the churches, and less Catholic than those presiding over the Council of Nicaea. Therefore, was **Arius** alone impious? Should only Arius have been condemned? Should they tolerate—and neither shake out nor banish from the confession of the faithful—such pestilential men and such ruined heresies as **Macedonius** and **Eudoxus** (branches of Arius who entirely exclude the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son), **Nestorius** (who posits two persons, as if there were two distinct existences in Christ), **Eutyches** (who denies two natures, as if the humanity in Christ were passed away), and **Theodore** (who asserted that the always-glorious Virgin Mary should be called not the Mother of God <note>original: "dei matrem," referring to the title Theotokos</note>, but only the mother of a man)? Was it not the duty of ecclesiastical censors to banish them? Therefore, the reason our Waldenses do not receive those councils is because they do not receive what they know was determined there against heretical wickedness. Thus, by the insane judgment of the Waldenses, the heretics remain safe—and nothing more pleasing could happen to the devil's followers. I would like, however, to observe what is in the secret of the Waldenses, for whom all things are most contaminated before the ecclesiastical decrees please them. We know it is impossible for them to be supporters of such great impieties unless they are also aware of them. For this reason, the Catholic writers seemed to be of less authority among the Waldenses, and finally, the consciences of the councils seemed worse.

-># ON TRUE RELIGION<-

The authors of these errors—men like **Arius**, **Macedonius**, **Nestorius**, and **Eutyches** <note>These were major figures in early Christian history whose teachings on the nature of God and Christ were condemned as heresies by the Great Councils of the Church.</note>—were defiled heads of falsehood. I believe they were eventually moved by the shame of their own infamy, or perhaps they shuddered at the example of what awaited them. Yet our "Apostolic" **Waldensians** <note>A medieval movement that emphasized poverty and the Bible; the author uses the term "Apostolic" sarcastically here to mock their claim of following the original Apostles.</note> make themselves deeply suspect; indeed, by their every action, they have embraced not an apostolic life, but a full and sacrilegious imitation of those earlier heretics. The **Severians** <note>Followers of Severus of Antioch, though here the author attributes to them the rejection of the Old Testament and the Resurrection.</note> do not accept the Old Testament or the resurrection; **Apelles** the elder even accuses the Prophets of lying. Truly, these men are the liars themselves! For what was the motive for both groups, except that fewer scriptures might remain by which their errors could be challenged? Finally, what kind of Gospel can we believe they truly receive, since they boast of it? How mangled and truncated it must be, since they have erased so many testimonies of the Old Law as if they were forged. How implausibly they then denied the resurrection, which they knew **Christ** had proved against the **Sadducees**! Do those who do not believe Christ regarding the resurrection believe in Christ at all? With what wicked eyes have they endured those chapters of the Gospels in which Christ himself is recorded to have risen, unless they have erased these as well, laboring even today to keep Christ in a sealed tomb? They are worse than the **Jews**, who, by saying he was stolen from the tomb—even if they speak falsely of a "theft"—at least admit that the one they were guarding was not found. 

However, we shall prove, with this Severian as judge, that it was not by theft but by his own power that he left the tomb vacant. For how, considering the number of disciples and the strength required to break in, the obstruction and sealing of the tomb, and the need to carry away a body (which, being bloodless and dead, would require greater effort to move), could they have deceived such a numerous guard, as if they had all fallen into such a deep sleep at the same time by some coordinated effort? But suppose they did sleep. How, while sleeping, did they perceive that the thieves were the disciples? Yet it was well known from the neighborhood that they were disciples. Why did they not later drag those convicted of breaking into the tomb before the tribunals for such an infamous crime? The Jews would surely have sought capital punishment for the disciples according to **Roman laws**; they were never going to be more just toward Christ and his followers than that. Do you see, **Severian**, how many things here turn back upon themselves? Do you see that it was not by human effort that he was removed from the tomb, in which the Jews confess he was not found? And yet you, with a hardened brow, walking through the middle of the Gospels, dare to deny the resurrection? What will you answer to the **Epistles of Paul**, in which he proved the resurrection so many times with such profound arguments? Or do you perhaps not even read these in your own books? The **Ebionites** <note>An early Jewish-Christian sect that insisted on the necessity of following Jewish law and rejected the writings of St. Paul.</note> reject these same Epistles of Paul as if they themselves knew deeper things. Thus, this single body of Epistles seemed to them insufficient to occupy their time. 

The **Jews**, **Turks**, and **Saracens** <note>The author groups together non-Christian religions of the time, including Muslims (Turks and Saracens).</note>, though they hold other books and even philosophical ones, do not know the Gospel; this one book of all books is thought by them to wander entirely from the path. Our **Waldensians** have followed in their footsteps—they who are the only ones in this century to have "rescued" a truth they claim was wandering from all lands. They have cast out from themselves all ecclesiastical writers. I believe they wished to make an abbreviation, so that they might be less hindered by the number of writings and arrive more quickly at the end of knowledge. But if this is the plan, and if the Christian state can stand without the internal interpretation of the Law, why then did the Church after Christ have need of the **Apostles**? For what is **Paul**, what is **Peter**, **James**, and **John**, if not interpreters of the Gospel? If the number of writers ought to have stopped with them, then who are those workers who are sent into the **Lord's vineyard** <note>A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard from Matthew 20.</note> at the first, second, third, tenth, and last hour of the day? Does this parable not signify the course and administration of the present Church? Surely, then, have those writers found nothing useful from their contemplation of the Law for the instruction of the people? Certainly they have, and because they labored well, the Lord decrees this reward: he gives them a daily denarius for their labor—that is, eternal happiness. To others who, with the talents entrusted to them...

### SECOND BOOK OF THE CHOICE
L ij

...earned more from others. He says: **"Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord."** <note>Original: "Euge serue bone & fidelis..." quoting the Parable of the Talents from Matthew 25:21.</note> Therefore, those who were considered good stewards of the Lord’s household—who lived in such a way that they dispensed Apostolic doctrine to the ears of the faithful—transmitted this stewardship to posterity through their writings. 

What madness it is for the Heretics to prepare such an unjust rejection of those monuments! For it was necessary that not only the first founder be sent, but also that wise administrators be sent for the future—or shall we say the Church was poorly provided for? What of those same **Waldensians**, <note>The Waldensians were a medieval spiritual movement that emphasized poverty and lay preaching, often rejecting the authority and "learnedness" of the Catholic hierarchy.</note> who so lightly condemned all holiness (which they find burdensome)? They do not cease to make themselves teachers and to comment daily on new things to overthrow our traditions. 

But who does not understand how foolish that opinion is? It is a view that could only be conceived and originated by rustic cobblers <note>Original: "fellularijs" (likely a variation of *sutilariis*). The author is using a common class-based slur against the Waldensians, who were often stereotyped as uneducated shoemakers.</note> involved in the filthiest trades. One asks the priests about the law; the Apostles were rebuked by the Savior because they did not understand the parables. Those same Apostles command a **Bishop** to devote himself to wisdom and meditation on the **Scriptures**. 

Did the later generations of most burning intellects listen to their Apostolic mentors in vain, finding nothing healthy to pass down to their subordinates? Was no one found in so many centuries who, through martyrdom or holiness of life, earned faith and successfully worked at explaining and understanding them? If so, the Church would be more barren than the Synagogue <note>A traditional term in this period for the Jewish religious community, here used in a comparative polemic.</note>, having produced no one of its own to respond to the Lord’s inquiry in the manner and merit of **Isaiah**: **"Here I am, send me."** <note>Isaiah 6:8.</note> 

But there *were* those who wrote the most profound commentaries and explained the law with the fullest erudition. If those Waldensians do not treat these works like dung <note>Original: "stercoratione."</note>, yet they do not cease to babble their own suddenly thought-up trifles in their assemblies to the applause of their own people, then they are knowingly and willingly rushing headlong toward the ruin of their souls. 

But it is worth hearing the persuasion by which they are carried away into such an unjust estimation. They take the power of speaking of the most learned men—and that art of knowing how to say everything appropriately—and they turn it into a crime. Because of this eloquence, they hold the Catholic faith suspect. Now, if that is the case, whoever from now on does not speak "rustically"—that is, in a disorganized way where neither "head nor foot" matches the form—will be considered more suspicious. 

This madness would first begin in the courts of **Princes**. In the royal chancelleries, no one wants to write the principal edicts except in the most refined language. Eloquence persuades the courts, the forums, the assemblies of illustrious men, and civil gatherings. Indeed, whether in legal briefs, accusations, defenses, reports, or decrees, everyone strives to prepare their case with the most suitable speech according to their ability. 

Will our "Pagans" <note>The author sarcastically calls the uncultured Waldensians "pagans" or "country-dwellers" (*pagani* originally referred to rural people).</note> interfere with royal edicts, concessions, and immunities? Will those who reject **Ecclesiastical Doctors** because of the splendor of their speech also rescind so many legal judgments, so many royal decrees, and the acts of the **Senate**? Among the noble-born and those of urban refinement, faith in speech would not exist if it were not for the "rustic" style—even though in every other piece of furniture or clothing, their habits are more serene, more splendid, and more composed than what is found in rustic negligence and filth. 

Should speech alone be uncultivated, filthy, unwashed, and unrefined—something that brings no honor and betrays faith? Should we endure that through which the rustic commoners (whose wide-mouthed gaping is often narrowed by their own verbose words) are laughed at by all people? But while they take up the habit of making men "learned" from a worse example, let us take up the cause of retaining those same men for a better one. For even if this were a good thing and the other an evil, we should not look at the eloquence, but at the facts themselves. That is to say: as for the Waldensian, who maintains so many sacrilegious opinions, would he be considered any less impure whether he speaks with total lack of skill (as he certainly does) or with the most eloquent...

# ON TRUE RELIGION,

...spreads his own piety through the minds of the unwise, his own rudeness will not make a Christian into a heretic, nor will a Christian’s eloquence make a heretic. We read the **Gospels**; these certainly offer simplicity, yet no one who has **Paul** in his heart fails to understand what power is in them, what energy <note>Original: "energia," referring to the spiritual "working" or "power" of the text.</note> and growth of the divine ray, how much they instill themselves, and how much they take root. **Christ our Savior**, as much as he was humble in the flesh, appeared so powerful in word to the Jews; he never allowed the effect of his preaching to be weak or listless. But he also poured that power into his disciples: **"I will give you,"** he said, **"a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict."** <note>A reference to Luke 21:15.</note> For how much money would the most eloquent **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was the most famous orator of ancient Rome, often used as the standard for perfect Latin style.</note> have redeemed such effectiveness of the word from his teachers—if this were a matter of human faculty? In the Roman forum, Cicero alone reigned; the disciples of Christ reigned in the whole world. The most divine **Paul** filled everything from **Syria** to **Illyricum** <note>A Roman province in the Balkans; Paul mentions this mission in Romans 15:19.</note> with the Gospel. He is called the **"Trumpet of the Gospel"** <note>Original: "tuba Euangelij."</note> because of the force of his words and sentences; it would take too long for this time to bring you even a few passages from **Jerome** and **Augustine** <note>Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine were two of the "Ecclesiastical Doctors" or foundational scholars of the early Church.</note> concerning his eloquence. 

But even the **False Apostles** acknowledged the power of his Epistles. For he records their words to the **Corinthians**: **"Lest I should seem to terrify you by my Epistles; for his Epistles, they say, are weighty and powerful, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible. Let such a one think this: that as we are in word by Epistles, such will we be also in deed when present."** <note>Quoting 2 Corinthians 10:9–11.</note> What do those **Waldensians** have to say to me here? Will they detract from the Gospel? Will they detract from the Apostle? Since that strength of speech and power of persuasion is found even in that simplicity of the Gospel and the Apostle, will they find some flaw that would make the faith of truth less certain? 

The Gospel and the Apostle must necessarily displease those whom the **Ecclesiastical Doctors** <note>The "Doctors" or "Teachers" refers to the highly educated theologians of the Church hierarchy whom the Waldensians rejected.</note> displease. Let those who accuse the Ecclesiastical Orators of being guilty of deceitful persuasion claim that everything there consists of human persuasion. But is this not the height of wickedness? For when they sensed that in reading our teachers there was a faculty for persuading toward better things—by which they seemed likely to be reformed or to set aside the obstinacy of their minds—they recoiled as if attacked by a **magical song**. Thus, they do not cease thereafter to compare the most brilliant minds, the holiest men, the most learned works, and the most steadfast Christian philosophy to fables and fictions; they claim it is held in high regard only as much as eloquent men could achieve through enticement and the corruption of words. 

But if, by a reversal of judgment, they themselves were to be put on trial by us, and those things which did not sufficiently please them in our works were found in their own—along with other most serious matters—I would drag them to the tribunal. I would bring forth the **abjuration of the Christian name**, the **baptism repeated in unspeakable ways** <note>This likely refers to Anabaptism or the Waldensian rejection of Catholic baptism in favor of their own rites.</note>, and the **stiff and unbending necks** of those worst of two-legged creatures toward the sacrament of Christ's body, and all their crimes. With what confidence in their deeds will they think themselves superior? Will I not, with the same faith, expose all their things as not merely "fictions" (which we know is the lightest of their crimes), but as most deadly **sacrileges**? Whatever they might say there in their own defense could also be said for us. Either they have bound themselves by a guarantee to be most truthful if they accuse anything of the Christian state, and we are most vain if we accuse their impiety; or, if they bring forth any depraved opinion, it is "faith from heaven," but when our people write Catholic truth, they claim the faith was sought from a "wicked tongue." Will we not, by this reasoning, have prepared an endless lawsuit for ourselves? Will not this stubborn contention find no end? Therefore, let us call the whole cause back to the beginning: namely, **what** someone says, not **how** he says it...

...let us look at the facts; for it is the matter, not the speech, that creates a flaw. Therefore, no one’s writing should be rejected unless error, falsehood, fraud, impiety, or anything else repugnant to the **Canon** <term>Canon: The official list of books recognized as genuine Holy Scripture.</term> of the scriptures is charged against it. This is the hinge upon which the distinction between a Christian and a **Waldensian** <term>Waldensian: A member of a medieval spiritual movement that emphasized poverty and often rejected the formal authority of the Catholic Church.</term> shall henceforth be decided. For if a scripture is not accepted simply because it does not suit our will, or because it opposes something more urgently than we can push away—as one who thinks this should not happen and thinks so justly—what faith will finally remain in our own legal documents? Would not every peasant who serves for a portion of the crops deny them? If it were permitted for anyone to deny whatever seemed difficult to endure, what scripture or what notebooks in our courts and business dealings would sufficiently protect our good faith? By what witnesses, finally, would slanderers be settled? 

When the Christian faith was being established, there were the books of the Philosophers, there was the assertion of the heathens, there was Jewish absurdity, and shortly thereafter, there were the perverse dogmas of the Heretics. Did the Fathers of the primitive church—whose heirs those Waldensians falsely claim to be—did those Fathers, I say, ever condemn any books useless to Christian piety with such "rustic" ignorance, using only a single cry, such as: "they are fictions," "they are honeyed words," or "do not read them"? No; for it was not enough to strip away faith in things—otherwise false—with such a small word. Instead, they joined "foot to foot and hand to hand" <note>A metaphor for close-quarters combat, signifying rigorous, point-by-point intellectual debate.</note> and did not condemn them until they had conquered them with the fullest reasons. Unless these false dogmas had been struck out by the most well-tested judgments, who could have persuaded perverse men (who always desire to hear something new) to destroy so many books of old superstition? Out of such an immense number of volumes of perverse dogma, we find that scarcely a very few survive today. 

Let our Waldensians do the same regarding the books of both Testaments that do not please them; let us experience the same regarding **Ignatius, Dionysius, Origen, Eusebius, Ambrose, Jerome,** and **Augustine**, and all who are numbered among the learned. As strongly as they prove them to be false, so strongly will we concede to their sect. As long as they do not do this—and cannot do it—we judge it insane to believe them in such a great matter over the witnesses themselves. Let them cease speaking ill of writers of better reputation, who have remained untainted for so many centuries and cannot be shaken by this foulness of the most sluggish common folk. 

It is worth noting that the Church doctors never allowed anyone—whether heathen or Heretic—to write anything against Christian discipline with impunity without unravelling it and exposing it in the open. We see with what sharpness **Didymus, Hilary,** or **Augustine** wrote against the **Arians** <note>Arians: Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, distinct from and subordinate to God the Father.</note>, or **Origen** against **Celsus** <note>Celsus: A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and fierce opponent of early Christianity.</note>, and the rest of the Churchmen against the rest of the faithless. If our men could be so despised, or if the heathens and heretics could be so powerful, why do they mutter in secret? Why do they not oppose genius with genius? Clearly, they were found to be weaker, and the cause of the faithless was too unjust to dare to encounter the sharpness of our men. Just as thefts are safer when they are hidden rather than defended, so a defiled doctrine—for which it was not at all helpful to be rubbed raw too often—withdrew itself rather than descend into battle. Therefore, because this is the reason why the most illustrious geniuses were not admitted among the ancients or among the heretics of our time, I shall henceforth have little fear if I bring forward some of the most proven men, so that they may dare to impudently accuse their authority to the detriment of truth, as is their custom.

# OF TRUE RELIGION

...piety may be spread through the minds of the unwise. Neither will a heretic’s lack of polish make him a Christian, nor will a Christian’s eloquence make him a heretic. We read the **Gospels** <note>original: "Euangelia"</note>; they certainly exhibit simplicity, yet no one who has the mind of **Paul** <note>original: "Paulum"</note> fails to understand the power within them, the energy, and the vitality of the divine ray—how much they penetrate and settle within the soul. Our Savior **Christ** <note>original: "Christus"</note>, though humble in the flesh, appeared powerful in word to the Jews; He never allowed the effect of His preaching to be weak or stagnant. Rather, He poured that same power into His disciples, saying: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict." <note>A reference to the Gospel of Luke 21:15.</note>

With how much money would the most eloquent **Cicero** <term>Cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator whose style was considered the gold standard of Latin eloquence.</term> have bought such effectiveness of word from his teachers, if this were a matter of human skill? Cicero reigned only in the Roman forum, but the disciples of Christ reigned throughout the entire world. Even the **False Apostles** <note>original: "Pseudo Apostoli"</note> acknowledged the power of his **Letters** <note>original: "Epistolarum"</note>. # THE SELECTION, BOOK TWO

Let us consider that it is the substance, not the speech, that is at fault. Therefore, no one’s writing should be discarded until it is charged with error, falsehood, fraud, impiety, or anything else repugnant to the **Canon of the Scriptures** <note>original: "Canone scripturarū"</note>. Upon this hinge, the distinction between a Christian and a **Waldensian** <term>Waldensians: A medieval religious movement founded by Peter Waldo that emphasized poverty and lay preaching; they were often in conflict with the Catholic Church over issues of authority and tradition.</term> shall henceforth be decided. For if a writing is not received simply because it does not suit our will, or because it attacks a matter more urgently than we can repel, what faith would finally remain in our own rational legal documents? Would not every peasant <note>original: "rusticus"</note> who owes service from a portion of his harvests deny them? If anyone were permitted to deny whatever they found difficult to endure, what scripture or what legal documents in our courts and businesses would sufficiently protect good faith? By what witnesses, finally, would accusers settle their disputes?

When the Christian faith was being established, there were the books of the **Philosophers**, there was the assertion of the **Gentiles**, there was **Jewish** absurdity, and shortly thereafter, the perverse dogmas of the **Heretics**. Did the Fathers of the primitive church—whose heirs those Waldensians falsely claim to be—did those Fathers, I say, condemn any books useless to Christian piety with such unrefined ignorance and with only a single word, saying, for instance: "they are fictions," "they are honeyed words," "do not read them"? No; nor was it enough to strip faith from matters—otherwise false—with such a small word. Rather, they joined foot to foot and hand to hand <note>original: "pedem pedi, manum ad manum," a metaphor for close-quarters intellectual combat</note>. They did not condemn until they had conquered them with the fullest reasoning. 

Unless these false dogmas had been wiped out by the most thoroughly tested judgments, who could have persuaded perverse men—always desiring to hear something new—to destroy so many books of old superstition? From such an immense number of volumes of perverse dogma, we find that scarcely a very few survive today. Let our Waldensians do the same regarding the books of both Testaments which do not please them; let us see them try this with **Ignatius**, **Dionysius**, **Origen**, **Eusebius**, **Ambrose**, **Jerome**, and **Augustine** <term>This list comprises key early Christian theologians and historians (the "Church Fathers") whose writings shaped orthodox doctrine.</term>, and all those who are numbered among the learned. If they can strongly prove them to be false, we will just as strongly concede to their sect. While they do not do this—and indeed cannot do it—we consider it insane to believe them in such a great matter based only on their own testimony; let them cease slandering writers of better reputation. These writers have remained untarnished for so many centuries and cannot be shaken by the filth of this most sluggish rabble. 

One may observe that the Doctors of the Church never allowed anyone, whether **Pagan** <note>original: "ethnicum"</note> or **Heretic**, to write anything against Christian discipline with impunity without unweaving it, without pouring it out into the light. We see with what sharpness **Didymus**, **Hilary**, or **Augustine** wrote against the **Arians** <term>Arians: Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; this was the primary heresy addressed by the Council of Nicaea.</term>, or **Origen** against **Celsus** <term>Celsus: A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of Christianity.</term>, and the rest of the churchmen against the remaining faithless ones. Here, if our opponents could be so despised, or if the Pagans and Heretics could be so powerful, why do they mutter in the shadows? Why do they not oppose genius with genius? 

Evidently, they were found to be too weak, and the cause of the faithless too unjust to dare to meet the sharpness of our men. Just as thefts are safer when they are hidden than when they are defended, so a violated doctrine <note>original: "constuprata doctrina"</note>, which it by no means suited to be rubbed raw again, withdrew itself rather than descend into battle. Therefore, this is the reason why the most illustrious geniuses were not admitted among the heretics of old, nor among those of our time. I shall have little fear hereafter if I bring forward certain of the most approved men, so that they might dare to impudently accuse them—as they usually do—to the loss of truth. # ON THE TRUE RELIGION,

treating the matter with a front of mere evasion and vain elusion. Regarding the inner strength of religion, they disguise and corrupt its true sinews <note>original: "ipsius neruos"</note>, and much more wickedly deny them. There remains for us a final argument to be made toward the same end, where we surely make God himself the witness or judge of such a great matter. For the heretics have never been made illustrious by any miracles from heaven in any age; no saints have come forth from among them, and they have performed no miracles on earth. They have left no miraculous powers <note>original: "virtutes," referring here to the power of relics or post-mortem miracles</note> at their bodies after death. All these things have followed the confessors of Christian piety in abundance, not only in the beginning but in all subsequent centuries. This is the most urgent reason why heretical depravity must be condemned and Christian piety asserted. For the religion beloved by God will stand firm there, where God has willed to honor it so through his saints. For "signs," as the Gospel testifies, "will follow those who believe," and the Apostle Paul says that the faith of his stewardship consists of "signs, wonders, and powers." This matter was in the hands of the Apostles and the faithful of Christ like a military token <term>military token: original "militaris tessera," a password or tablet used by Roman soldiers to identify one another</term> by which they distinguished themselves from false brothers. Thus Paul writes to the Corinthians: "Some have become puffed up, as if I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power."

Even the man born blind in the Gospel of John convicts the truly blind Jews with no greater argument, nor does he allege the holiness of Christ with anything more than the power of the miracle: "In this is the marvel," he said, "that you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does His will, He hears him. Since the world began, it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind. Unless this man were from God, he could do nothing." Christ also, from these same powers, suggests the divinity of his own person to the Jews: "If you do not want to believe me," he said, "believe the deeds, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I am in the Father." Furthermore, the Jews lie condemned by no more powerful witness than these same miracles; for thus He says again: "If I had not done among them the works which no one else did, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father." 

Therefore, on account of such great testimonies—because God does not hear sinners, but hears those whom He acknowledges as His friends and no longer servants, and whom He predicted would perform even greater miracles than He did—let no one hereafter call into doubt the faith taught by the friends of God, which they confirmed from heaven by the testimony of miracles, and for which the monuments and most perfect decrees still exist. Otherwise, by this ray of holiness, all the mists of every error are dispelled into nothingness, as if by a serene sky. In this clarity, all heretics are abandoned as one, for they have been so far removed from miracles that one often reads of miracles being performed *against* them. Moreover, a great part of those who were the authors of these errors lived so poorly that they were a public infamy; they were hardly worthy of being trusted with a heavenly miracle. 

Notable among these: first of all, **Simon Magus** <note>A biblical figure (Acts 8) who attempted to buy the power of the Holy Spirit; traditionally regarded as the first heretic</note> traveled the world with Helena, a most notorious prostitute. **Montanus** took the insane women **Prisca and Maximilla** as partners in his error. The intolerable arrogance of **Paul of Samosata** was a source of disgust even to the pagans. **Novatus** stirred up his heresy out of a most wicked ambition. **Cerinthus** dared to promise in the eternal rewards the same pleasures he practiced here in the body. **Arius** sent his most contaminated soul down into the sewers <note>original: "sub soricas," likely a reference to the tradition that Arius died of a violent bowel discharge in a public latrine</note>. But it is pleasing to relate such a horrendous judgment of God from the most holy **Athanasius**. He, in his first book *Against the Heretics*, writes thus of Arius: "Arius himself, since he was the leader of the heresy and a foster-child of **Eusebius**..."

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that heresy lacks divine validation. Having previously asserted that true religion is marked by miracles, he now uses the historical example of the heresiarch Arius’s ignominious death to contrast the "wretched" end of heretics with the enduring power of the Church. He then applies this critique to the Waldensians of his own day, arguing that their lack of miraculous signs and their threat to civil order prove their illegitimacy.</meta>

# BOOK TWO OF THE CHOICE,

[...the Euse]bians, having been called to Constantine Augustus and required to state his faith in writing, the crafty man wrote, properly hiding his words of impiety; like the devil himself, he disguised the simple words of the Scriptures as they are written. Then, when the blessed Constantine <note>The text reads "Constantius," but the context of Arius and Alexander of Constantinople confirms it refers to the Emperor Constantine the Great.</note> said: "If you have nothing else in your mind, give truth as your witness; for the Lord takes vengeance on the perjurer." The wretched man swore he had nothing else, nor that he had ever said or felt anything besides what had been written. And immediately upon leaving, as if he were already paying the penalty, he fell headlong and burst open in the middle <note>This describes the famous graphic death of Arius in a public latrine, which contemporary orthodox writers viewed as divine judgment.</note>.

And a little later [the author] says again: because the end of Arius was not accidental, it is therefore not unworthy of being remembered. For the Eusebians <note>original: "Eusebiani," the followers of Eusebius of Nicomedia, who supported Arius.</note> were threatening to introduce him into the Church. Alexander, the Bishop of Constantinople, was opposing them. Arius was confident in the threats of Eusebius—it was, moreover, the Sabbath—and he expected to be brought in the following day. There was thus a great struggle; they were threatening, and Alexander prayed, but the Lord, having become judge, decided against the guilty. For the sun had not yet set when, having been drawn to a place of necessity <note>A euphemism for a latrine.</note>, he fell there.

And he was immediately deprived of both things—namely, fellowship and life. The heretics lived in a bad state and departed into a bad state, inclined toward seditions, dissensions, and public discord. They came forward, growing powerful through a merely human faction, either through the delusional negligence of princes or through approaching, confessed treachery; they died having deserved poorly of both human and divine affairs. Finally, their treachery, which was once rashly taken up by mortals, could just as easily later perish from memory. If these were ever true heretics, where did that promise of the Savior satisfy them: "Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age"?

This testimony of true piety—that is, of miracles—at once leaves destitute all heretics, and so also our Waldensians. They exist by no merits of their own, by no heavenly favor, but by diabolical persuasion, public negligence, and their own dissimulation regarding the chalice <note>This refers to the controversy over Utraquism, the practice of giving both bread and wine to the laity, which was a central demand of the Waldensians and Hussites.</note>. They entered secretly from the nursery of the devil—that is, from rebellion—unto the damnation of souls and the overthrow of the fatherland. Those men cared little for the chalice then. They thought it mattered little to them whatever monster might be born in the whole Kingdom, which the Apostolic faith would now hear with grief; and those who did not rule themselves well by religion had come to such a point of madness that they would admit every foulness rather than Christian honesty, which they had once begun to hate. Everything was considered pious as long as it was not Christian. Thus they rejoiced in every novelty. The neglect born of hatred had led them into this, and they did not understand that they were preparing as many swords against the public state as they had stirred up discordant religions. "Scepter and love: these two do not suffer a companion" <note>A variation of a classical proverb meaning that power and affection—or here, unified rule and religious pluralism—cannot coexist.</note>. Nay, indeed, a diverse religion is the most powerful force of all for throwing kingdoms and peoples into confusion. Even those enrolled under one body of citizenship and under the same laws, but poorly in agreement concerning religion, have so many times stirred up for themselves the most deadly civil seditions, almost wearing away what was once a most flourishing Republic.

But let the Waldensians alone be the most negligent of all in their superstition, those who do not rage into a different religion. Thus pernicious heresy began under the brawling of others, so that it is believed to have arisen not by divine calling nor by the predictions of the ancient saints. But if it relies on a holier conscience before God, certainly the evidence has not been lacking by which it might be approved from heaven. O, how we once feared lest some leader <term>Archimandrita: a Greek term for the head of a monastery or a high-ranking cleric</term> of the Waldensians might come forth with those well-known examples from the Acts of the Apostles, and in so brief a moment of an hour draw so many thousands of our people to himself. Most recently, while they were cast into prison for the infamy of heretical depravity and bore chains through all the guards, at no time did Christianity turn so pale, fearing lest, after the ancient example of the Apostles, those Waldensians...

But afterwards they were restored to safety, I confess; and—as we shall one day feel to our great public misfortune—they were restored to quiet again. I suppose so that the fish might feed more abundantly from a place of corpses, grow faster, and become tastier and more salable. Such a man, and of such greatness, undertook an embassy on behalf of the Waldensians out of "piety," just when they had already despaired of their God. Even today his voice is heard saying that it matters nothing to him what monster of a man plows the earth, provided they build well and cultivate the fields diligently. A "Christian" sentiment indeed! But one that tastes of the Waldensian of yesterday.

Will anyone who cherishes every race of men without distinction also receive robbers and highwaymen, provided they offer him some use? Another is guilty of high treason <term>reus maieftatis: the crime of "injured majesty" or treason against the state</term>; he is proscribed by the laws, forbidden water and fire <note>original: "interdictum aqua & igni"; a Roman legal formula for exile and the loss of civil rights</note>, and banned from the province. If this man desires a place, a garrison, and wants to harass his neighbors with raids, to take plunder, and to avenge his condemnation—and offers to let us share in the loot—shall we receive this public enemy, this outlawed traitor? I think that as much as our safety is dear to us, and as much as it does not profit us to betray the public trust, so much will we dread making a private profit from a public enemy. 

This is the fault of men: that they receive those who despise God and men—despisers who do not cease to disturb this great kingdom, the Church of the Heavenly Father, and who even desire to overturn it in their prayers. They are guilty of high treason against heaven, proscribed from all holiness. Forbidden from the divine mysteries, they prey upon the unrefined common folk and lead them captive into the snares of error; prodigal of the common peace, they sharpen their rage as if they are about to fight at the next opportunity. Although such steep offenses are committed by this sacrilegious assembly against God and men, we think it does not yet concern us, nor that consciences are defiled by it. ...to their patrons. Let them nevertheless remember from where they were saved, and from where they ought to have been saved. Let them congratulate themselves and report it to their glory that they have emulated the examples of the ancients—that they have equaled or even surpassed Cain <note>original: "Chayn"</note> the fratricide in the zeal of tilling the field. For whatever the generous nobility desires to cast out from every corner, that man considers cast out for his own use; there, by whatever wind they have been driven, they are received. 

Would that the most pious King had then heard the Christian cause as closely as his own piety dictates! Would that he had chosen to decide by conscience and not by indulgence! For now, through the fault of a few, the entire nobility and every rank of the kingdom comes under accusation among Christian nations; they think that this is a common stain, which is certainly the fault of very few. For in that abundance of the primary nobility, scarcely one, and then perhaps another—scarcely, I say, have the Waldensians themselves filled a four-horse chariot to carry them. It is a suspicion regarding these "new men" <term>novi homines: a term for those who have recently risen to status but lack ancestral tradition</term> that they would never have yielded to this foulness if they had received generous souls from their ancestors. But how can a foreigner discern this? 

But so much for these matters. Such Waldensians, therefore, found in all their institutions, shall by no means be admitted into the true piety of any religion—which we now seek as the one pure and chaste thing ordered by God the author for mortals. Rather, we shall show that they are its most bitter enemies, and that they have taken up a most wicked fight against the Apostolic confession with every kind of heretical impiety. It seemed necessary to us, therefore, to bring forth these and all things we have established against them more expressly from a new beginning, and to descend to the dispute which they published against Doctor Augustine, the Royal Secretary <note>Augustine Käsebrot, a prominent humanist scholar and official</note>. We shall nonetheless remember, where the place demands, their old confession which we examined in the first book. Finally, we shall mention as a sort of finishing touch <term>corolario: a supplementary gift or deduction</term> another booklet which they themselves gave to the Royal Majesty and which came to us only in these recent days; this is so that we do not seem to have knowingly passed over anything that might seem stronger to us, or to be accused of deliberately ignoring it. 

I would first obtain this one thing from them: if, in the translation of their writing, they think a word has not been rendered for word because of my lack of experience with a foreign tongue <note>original: "iexpietiā [inexperientia] peregrinæ linguæ"</note>, I have nonetheless taken care lest their booklet be rendered more hateful or worse. Let them not be angry there, but rather forgive the translator for this deed, if they wish to be forgiven by us for the fact that they have, in many places, most wickedly corrupted the Holy Scriptures, the oracles of the Holy Spirit.

->**THE WALDENSIANS**<-

It has been said quite often that we have given an account up to that point: "and the saints did not cry out to the holy ones so that help might be made." I believe it is demanded of us why we begin chiefly from the prayers to the saints, and not from the prologue, nor from the chapter on the priesthood or the sacrament of the altar. Indeed, the prologue had to be examined in many places where those little foxes—under the guise of simplicity, or more truly, those most rapacious wolves of the Christian flock under sheep's clothing—have attempted to insinuate themselves into the unwary. Truly, as we have stated once before, a speech of that kind cannot be conveniently or sufficiently related for the sake of faith until the inner workings of the work, which usually follow such beginnings, are weighed. For the reliability of the principles is seen from these things alone. For who shall prevent us—whom they regard as most harmful—from gathering all such festive things in our favor following their example? Or what is lacking on our part that our commendation should be less in the ears of their people than theirs is in the ears of ours?

I believe he did this so that the fish might feed more bountifully on the place of corpses, grow faster, and become tastier and more sellable. Such a man, and of such "piety," took up an embassy for the Waldensians just when they had despaired of their God. Even today his voice is heard saying that it matters nothing to him by what "monster" of a man he plows the earth, provided they build well and work the field diligently. 

A "Christian" sentiment indeed! But one that tastes of the Waldensians of yesterday. For now, it seems we can honestly support any monsters of men, any who are publicly dangerous, provided they serve our private uses. Since we hold heavenly things as either distant fables or secondary to all other matters, let us at least look at the fairness of such an opinion in civil business: if someone fostered every kind of person without distinction, would he also receive robbers and highwaymen into his home if they were of use to him? Or suppose another is guilty of treason <term>maiestatis: the crime of "lèse-majesté" or treason against the sovereign</term>, proscribed by the laws, forbidden "water and fire" <note>original: "interdictum aqua & igni" — a Roman legal formula for total banishment and loss of civil rights.</note>, and banished from the province. I think that as much as our safety is dear to us, and as much as it does not profit us to betray the public trust, so much will we dread making a private profit from a public enemy. 

This is the fault of men who receive those who despise both God and men. These are despisers who never cease to disturb this great kingdom, the heavenly church of the Father; they even desire to overturn it. They are guilty of treason against heaven, proscribed from all holiness. Forbidden from the divine mysteries, they prey upon the unrefined commoners and lead them captive into the snares of error. Wasteful of common harmony, they sharpen their rage as if they are about to fight at the next opportunity. Since such downward paths are made by this sacrilegious band against God and men, we still think it is none of our business and that our consciences are not defiled by it. And so that common saying comes back to us: "Infamy matters not, so long as the coins are safe." <note>original: "infamia saluis nūuis" — likely a variation of the Latin proverb "lucri bonus est odor ex re qualibet" (the smell of profit is good, whatever the source).</note> Thus we little men, fit for the coffin <note>original: "capulares homuntiones" — literally "coffin-bound little men," a term for the elderly or those near death.</note>, understand nothing holy or honorable unless it threatens immediate punishment. We are negligent of what is right so long as the laws do not stand in our way. Therefore, because we are so unteachable and forgetful of heavenly things, let those "excellent" patrons enjoy their country-dwellers; let the Waldensian country-dwellers enjoy them in turn.

For whatever the generous nobility desires to cast out from every corner, he thinks is cast out for his own use; there, wherever they are swept by the wind, they are received. 

Would that the most pious King <note>Likely Vladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary (reigned 1471–1516).</note>, as great as his piety is, had then heard the Christian cause more closely! Would that he had willed to decide according to conscience rather than indulgence. It seemed necessary to us, therefore, to bring forth more clearly from a new beginning these matters and all that we have instituted against them, and to descend into the dispute they issued against **Doctor Augustine, the Royal Secretary.** <note>Augustine Käsebrot (1467–1513), also known as Augustinus Moravus, a prominent humanist and opponent of the Bohemian Brethren/Waldensians.</note>

I will ask one thing of them first: if, in the translation of their scripture, they think I have not rendered it word for word due to the difficulty of a foreign language <note>The Waldensians wrote in Czech; the author is translating their works into Latin to refute them.</note>. I have taken care, however, lest their booklet—already hateful—be rendered more hateful or worse. Let them not be angry on that account, but rather forgive the translator for this deed, especially if they wish to be forgiven by us for the fact that they have, in many places, wretchedly corrupted the Holy Scriptures—the oracles of the Holy Spirit.

...ought to prevail. There, if they do not wish to risk our innocence based on such a lightly asserted moment, let them consider what they themselves ought to hope for at a foreign Judgment from those "masks of innocence" which they strive to spread before our eyes. Therefore, the reliability of the present matters will be sought from a comparison of the things that usually follow, which we shall do diligently, so that we may return from the inner treatment of the entire business to the prologues, the epilogues, and all those things which I had previously suspended for that reason. However, those chapters concerning the **Priesthood** and the **Sacrament of the Altar** are reserved for later books, each of which we have assigned to these individual matters. For we think it more practical that whatever must be said for these things against the **Waldensian** impiety be discussed in one place in a continuous treatment. For these reasons, we begin our work with the adoration of God and the veneration of the saints.

The first thing they deign for us to know from their decrees is that they conceive no rebellious opinion against the stainless Virgin Mary; they claim to believe all things that are thought to be learned from the rule of faith and the institutes of the ancients. They refer the nature of these beliefs to another pamphlet of theirs given to the **Royal Majesty** <note>Referring to the petition sent by the Waldensians to King Vladislaus II in 1503.</note>. Because we obtained this in recent days, we have, for this and many other reasons, worked to have it published alongside this labor of ours. Something resembling Christian piety might have been thought spoken there, if they had persevered as they began. But when it came to the point where she <note>The Virgin Mary</note> ought to be called upon in the prayers of wretched mortality, so that she might hope to be a most faithful patroness for the common people devoted to her before her only-begotten son and the common Father, here they cast aside every appearance of piety into a sacrilegious despair regarding the Virgin's advocacy. Not sustaining the heavy mask of piety which they had briefly put on, they suddenly returned to the natural character of their own perfidy. Thus, for this crime—no matter how much they henceforth boast of a "non-rebellious opinion"—they seem to think more highly of Paul than of the **Quran** <note>original: "Alchoranum"</note>. Indeed, even **Muhammad** <note>original: "Maumettes"</note> never wished to disparage the most holy Virgin regarding her virginal birth, receiving nothing more regarding her veneration than the **Waldensian** does. 

There, when our "heathen" <note>The author uses "ethnicus" (heathen/pagan) as a derogatory term for his opponent</note> saw he needed testimonies from a somewhat deeper source, he pushes the matter so far as to dare condemn the Christian people of headlong **idolatry** <note>original: "idolatriæ"</note>, because the Christian people venerate the most blessed Mother of God and all the heavenly saints with pious devotion. By these patrons and helpers, the people hope to be commended to God, toward whom the conscience of fleshly stain—abstaining with most religious humility—does not dare to lift its eyes. Finally, he uses the Holy Scriptures to prove this point no less through fraud and distortion than he wickedly provokes his error into an injury and contempt of the most deserving heavenly spirits before God. If they had acted sincerely and according to the nature of the business, they ought to have produced at the beginning whether we do not adore God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit at all; or if we do adore them, whether we adore them improperly, against the divine command and the institutes of the saints. If we erred there, they might seem to use their present testimonies against us rightly, which they have cited in such great number from a blind fight that they might persuade even the unwilling that they have learned the sacred letters. Then, when we venerate men who are saints and happily received by God, they should have said if we venerate the most chosen citizens of God with the same honor and adoration as God, through the same worship and honor, and with prayers uttered under the same form of words. If they had detected an error there as well, they would likewise seem to use their present testimonies against us correctly. But because it is not with the same worship as God, nor with equal...

-># THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK TWO #<-

...we honor with veneration the heavenly powers and most blessed souls; they should have more clearly declared there—since our mysteries are not clandestine but rather too manifest for them to be able to ignore—how we worshiped them. They should have shown that this worship (even if it is lower than <term>divine worship</term> <note>original: "theosebia"</note>) is permitted to us by the testimony of the Scriptures and the institutes of the Fathers. If they had followed us there, they would have dragged us to those rocks of your idolatry. Now they confuse everything, claiming we do what we do not even think of doing. Thus they dispute, preaching to the simple-minded as if God and the saints were, in our practice, subject to an indiscriminate law—as if the majesty of God were shared equally on both sides in a promiscuous adoration. 

It was not a matter of dealing with the most abstruse and remote questions of the Law, where if one's intellect failed, pardon might be granted due to the difficulty. Rather, it was a matter to be sought from the common practice of men, in which no one can fail unless they wish to be a slanderer. Therefore, between their ill-will—with which alone they have equipped themselves to take up the fight against the Church of God—and the truth of the matter, they falter. Where it was most necessary to speak, they are most silent; they get stuck exactly where the matter most needed to be pressed. 

Thus, the cause of both sides is revealed: their wickedness is exposed, as is the innocence of our people, which they have left untouched here. Therefore, it emerges that we wish to touch upon what they themselves did not want to: to review once more, from the start and with the authority of the Scriptures, what they use to build their slander and what we rightly defend with full freedom of expression and without any dissimulation.

The main point of the **Waldensian** accusation against the Catholic is that the Saints can offer no patronage for mortals before God. Because we confess the intercession of the Saints and invoke them through our prayers, they return to their highest claim: that we do not worship rightly. From this sacrilege of theirs, they desire to bring a charge of impiety against us. To better arrange the matter for the pleasure of their own ears and the flattery of their preconceived opinions, they did not shrink from penetrating—through such a wicked decree concerning God's saints—into infamous insults that are due only to the idols of the gentiles. 

Wishing to clarify this purely, we shall conveniently begin with the types of adoration. All adoration is of three kinds: **latria**, **dulia**, and **idolatry**. 
*   **Latria** <note>original: "latria"</note> is the worship of the one true God; they support this with many testimonies, and we support it with even one on behalf of all: *Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God, and Him only shalt thou serve* <note>Deuteronomy 6:4</note>, or that word of Peter in the Acts: *and there is salvation in no other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved* <note>Acts 4:12</note>. 
*   **Dulia** <note>original: "dulia"</note> is the intellectual worship of an angelic creature or one translated from earth to heaven. By this, we always venerate and adore the **Blessed Virgin Mary**, the angelic spirits, the Apostles of God, and all the saints. 

In this, the **Waldensian** errs the whole way and is openly unjust toward us. It is as if he has passed over it with a malignant silence because it is nowhere found in the Scriptures; for if he had confessed it with even one testimony, his ill-will would have been immediately betrayed. Now, because he pretends not to know such a thing—even though this worship of the saints among us is too manifest for us to be able to deny it, and too pious for us to want to—he rushes into the case based on our actual practice. He acts as if we venerate the saints with the same honor as God (that is, with **latria**), which would be to admit manifest idolatry. But to speak only half-truths with this cleverness, to keep the true hinge of the matter secret, and to cast our actions into something they are not, is to corrupt the case. Whether this is fitting for a good conscience, which desires to appear to handle the assumed business from faith and according to the truth of the Scriptures, let the **Waldensian** see to it. Certainly, no good man approves. 

Now, let us bring back into the light what they have foolishly passed over as if they were the only ones who read the Holy Scriptures. Thus **Job** says: *If there be an angel speaking for him, one among thousands, to announce the man's righteousness, He will have mercy on him and say: Deliver him, that he may not descend into corruption; I have found a way to be merciful to him. His flesh is consumed by punishments; let him return to the days of his youth. He will pray to God, and He will be favorable to him; and he shall see His face with joy, and He will render to man his justice.* <note>Job 33:23-26</note> Furthermore, **Zechariah**...
