# ON THE VENERATION OF SAINTS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

the angel of the Lord answered and said: 
> Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry? This is now the seventieth year,
<note>original: "Domine exercituũ uſq; quo tu nõ miſereberis Iheruſalem..." — quoting Zechariah 1:12</note>

and the Lord answered the angel who spoke in me with good words, consoling words. Idolatry is the worship that is owed to God alone transferred to a creature. God everywhere prohibits this, condemns it when it is admitted, and finally punishes it. To crush this kind of adoration, God says these or similar things: 
> I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to carved images.
<note>original: "gloriã meam alteri non dabo..." — quoting Isaiah 42:8</note>

With these and similar testimonies, our Waldensians aptly cavil against us. Yet through Moses he says: 
> You shall not go after the gods of all the nations.
<note>original: "non ibitis poſt deos cunctarũ gentiũ" — quoting Deuteronomy 6:14</note>

Beware lest you ever forget the Covenant of the Lord your God which he made with you, and make for yourself a carved likeness of things which the Lord has prohibited from being made. We are as far removed from this idolatry—into which that distinguished Waldensian wishes to cast us—as he himself is a sacrilegious man for not venerating the saints. We see, after all, the form of this triple adoration in earthly kingdoms. In any kingdom whatsoever, there are two levels: the Royal Majesty, who is the head of all, and the Friends of the Kingdom, who are privy to secrets and partakers of counsels. We honor both in their own ways, so that we may be permitted to transfer divine matters into human ones for as long as we are discussing this. To the King are owed divine honors and the worship of <term>latria</term> <note>latria: the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone</note>. We make the King the one who commands all things from himself, bestowing, preserving, and condemning as the one powerful over all things. With words of this kind we greet him: 
> If I have found favor in your eyes, O King, and if it pleases you, give me my life for which I ask, and my people for whom I pray.
<note>original: "Si inueni gratiã in oculis tuis o Rex..." — quoting Esther 7:3</note>

To the friend of the king, if we want his help, we also show great honors, yet they are inferior to the royal honors; that is, we exhibit the veneration of <term>dulia</term> <note>dulia: the honor or veneration given to a saint or an angel, distinct from the worship of God</note>. We acknowledge this person as one who dispenses all things, obtaining the royal favor and offering it to this person, or denying it to that one. Finally, we bow ourselves to him with words of this kind: "I pray that you speak to the King, for he can deny you nothing." We see how closely human things are related to heavenly ones. The honor of the purple-clad official <note>The "purple-clad" refers to high-ranking advisors or courtiers, mirroring the "princes" of the Church or saints</note> flows back to the king, for the royal power is seen in his friends. He who disdains them—and whoever treats proconsuls, legates, governors, provincial rulers, or commanders of camps with contempt—has offended against the Majesty. If he escapes punishment, so that he does not by the same act also offend the prince, he brings the prince into suspicion of neglecting his own republic and his own people. 

But does God likewise cast away his saints? Shall we think the blessed are so servile that they can obtain nothing, and are only admitted with difficulty past the first threshold? No. Indeed, if you did not have these purple-clad ones, you would not exist today. Therefore, because you do not have the saints, you do not have God; rather, you have him angry with you. Now, if someone else, neglecting the king, should worship any of the friends or citizens, having betrayed his oath to the king—raising up an idol for himself against his lord—certainly he also raises a rebellion, commits something similar to idolatry, and will be considered a most base deserter. Let this be an example from our republic for the heavenly one. Let the Waldensians defend themselves, those who do not listen to the heavenly counselors of whom the Savior says: 
> You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
<note>original: "Sedebitis & vos ſup ſedes duodecim..." — quoting Matthew 19:28</note>

Those senators of the divine Secret <note>The "divine Secret" refers to God's private council or inner mysteries</note>. But lest we seem to play with analogies and draw out the discourse in a popular fashion, let us also show openly from the Scriptures that it is not beneficial to despise the friends of God. The messengers of David sent to Hanun, king of the children of Ammon, were treated with insult, and David pursued that insolent king with the destruction of his kingdom. Does God not avenge the seditions of the children of Israel against Moses for his own sake? The children of Israel demanded a king for themselves in the ears of Samuel, and as if they were falling away from God, so the Lord confessed that he himself was despised. Christ the Savior says: 
> He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward, and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward. Therefore, he who venerates a saint in the name of a saint shall receive a saint’s reward, that is, he shall receive Christ.
<note>original: "qui recipit Prophetã in nomine Prophetæ..." — quoting Matthew 10:41</note>

Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of my brothers, you did it to me. And in another place: 
> See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for I say to you...
<note>original: "videte ne cõtemnatis vnũ ex his puſillis..." — quoting Matthew 18:10</note>

# THE WALDENSES: BOOK TWO

...for their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.
<note>original: "angeli eorum in cœlis ſemp vident fatiem Patris mei" — quoting Matthew 18:10</note>
Listen, you Waldensian—you who, with a wrinkled nose <note>A classical Latin idiom (*crispante naso*) expressing scorn or disdain.</note>, pass by the honor of the saint, this "little one" whom you despise. If it is forbidden to look down upon a mortal because of the dignity of their guardian angel, how much more is it forbidden for you to despise the angels themselves and all the most blessed spirits? But because you despise them with your head held high, what remains for you except that the saint should shake the dust from his feet against you? What mercy can you finally expect when you hear: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did not do it for one of these least ones, you did not do it for me," and "these shall go into eternal punishment." 
<note>original: "Amen dico vobis q̃ diu non fœciſtis vni de minimis his..." — quoting Matthew 25:40-46</note>
This is clearly because of the guilt of those who now dishonor the friends of God who have been received into heaven. They treat them as being in a worse condition than the ambassadors of David, or than Moses and Samuel; they clearly consider them mere foot-servants to whom God grants so little reverence that they may never approach Him, never pray for those devoted to them, and never entreat or obtain favors. 

Yet they surely possess before God a most ample right and the highest power of administration. This is according to the truth: 
> "But doing the truth in charity, let us grow up in Him through all things, who is the head, Christ: from whom the whole body, being compacted and fitly joined together by every joint of the sub-administration, according to the operation in the measure of every part, makes increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in charity."
<note>original: "veritatem aūt faciẽtes in charitate creſcamus..." — quoting Ephesians 4:15-16</note>

Unless, perhaps, the Waldensian says that this was spoken only concerning the governance of the Church Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians currently alive on earth, as opposed to the "Church Triumphant" in heaven.</note>. If that is so, then the Celestial Hierarchy is not related to the hierarchy of the present Church, and there will not be that "bond of the one body of Christ through every joint of sub-administration" which Paul describes. Nor would Saint Paul remain in the same order in the heavens that he held here in the Church; rather, he would be assigned a higher or lower place based on merit. Both thoughts are iniquitous. Therefore, in his own order, the Apostle who then presided over the Church in such an illustrious place and with such accurate vigils, presides today and offers patronage today. Otherwise, he would be a deserter of his office, excluded and sent into the idle sluggishness of the apostles, rejoicing only in his own happiness. This would bring back to us that pagan and rejected dogma of Epicurus: 
<note>The Greek philosopher Epicurus was often (rightly or wrongly) characterized by medieval theologians as teaching that the gods are indifferent to human affairs.</note>
the belief that the heavenly beings are blessed only because they do not involve themselves in our governance. 

But Paul is no different than all the saints, since they all live as blessed ones under one concordant institution. Our Church would be thought more sluggish, and sustain as many losses, as many instances of being forgotten and neglected as it sees saints sent there to heaven—contrary to that passage in Maccabees concerning Onias, who stretched out his hands to pray 
<margin>pray</margin>
for all the people of the Jews. This same Onias testified: 
> "This is a lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel; this is he who prays much for the people and for the entire holy city: Jeremiah, the prophet of God."
<note>original: "hic eſt fratrum Amator... Hieremias ppheta dei" — quoting 2 Maccabees 15:12-14</note>

Furthermore, the saints have the benefit of illuminating others, as the same Paul says: 
> "To me, the least of all the saints, is this grace given, to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all men as to what is the dispensation of the mystery which has been hidden from eternity in God who created all things."
<note>original: "Mihi aūt om̄ium ſanctorū minimo..." — quoting Ephesians 3:8-9</note>

Afterwards, they have power before God to find favor, just as the angel said to Tobias: 
> "When you prayed with tears, and buried the dead, and left your dinner, and hid the dead in your house by day and buried them by night, I offered your prayer to the Lord."
<note>original: "Ego obtuli orationẽ tuam dn̄o" — quoting Tobit 12:12</note>

And to Cornelius the angel said: "Your prayers and your alms have ascended for a memorial in the sight of God." The holy prophet Daniel explains this triple power and these duties of the celestial orders in human affairs through profound and equally astounding mysteries, using these words: 
> "Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that you set your heart to understand, to afflict yourself in the sight of your God, your words have been heard: and I am come for your words. But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me one and twenty days: and behold Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there by the King..."
<note>original: "noli timere Daniel... Michael vnus de principibus primis venit in adiutoriū meū" — quoting Daniel 10:12-13</note>

# ON THE VENERATION OF THE SAINTS, AGAINST [THE WALDENSES]

...of the Persians, and again: "Do you not know why I have come to you? And now I will return to fight against the prince of the Persians; for when I went out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming." And again: "At that time Michael shall rise, the great prince who stands for the children of your people."
<note>The author is quoting Daniel 10:20 and 12:1 to show that angels act as "princes" or protectors for specific nations and peoples.</note>
The devil in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 12:10</note> is called the accuser of our brothers and servants. Certainly, God is the judge of all flesh, before whom the accuser lays his charge. In that place, if God recounts our faults against the accuser, justice itself demands—and the representation of the judgment requires—that He should recognize our merits through a patron <note>Latin: *patronum*—a legal advocate or protector in the Roman sense</note> in turn. This patron is one who either prays away our faults or commends our merits. For where an accuser is mentioned, a defender is also mentioned, for a judgment is not a matter for only one side. 

But you say, "Our justice commends us." I say, "Our sin accuses us." What more is brought in by an accuser? We find an accuser in the Apocalypse, but we find patrons in the books of Job, Zechariah, Tobit, Daniel, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Maccabees, so that no one henceforth may be ignorant that there are intercessions from those in heaven. 

There remain many more things from the Holy Scriptures to be explained regarding this matter of the intercession of the saints. But since they <note>The Waldensian opponents</note> demand from us the very things we were already intending to say, let us henceforth act as their teacher. Following in their footsteps, let us gather whatever arguments they have left scattered against us. They say they communicate the honor due to God alone to no creature; well and good, for that is also our opinion. But they speak as if we adore the saints of God in the place of God—that is, with the veneration of *latria*.
<note>original: "latria veneratione" — *Latria* is the technical theological term for the supreme worship due to God alone, as opposed to *dulia*, the honor given to saints.</note> 
And in this vice—that is, by the simulation of truth—they continually sin. 

To respond to many such claims of theirs at once: if they had wished to be fair evaluators of this question, they ought first to have shown by admitted arguments that we worship the saints with the same honor as God. Once they had extracted that from us, they could finally rise up against us for such a crime. But now, what do they do but seek traps in naked words? They know we give honor to the saints, but they say nothing of what kind of honor it is, or in what way it is restricted. Instead, they simply criminalize the fact that we provide honor to the saints at all. They want it to be understood by the unlearned as if we venerate as many immense, eternal creators and saviors as there are saints. 

If they had thoroughly examined the matter according to its nature, their entire effort would be recognized as proceeding from a stubborn faction. Now, so that they might sustain this effort in their hatred of us for a longer time, they grasp at an opportunity not from our actual meaning, but only from small marks and syllables. 
<note>original: "solis apiculis & syllabis" — *Apiculis* refers to the tiny strokes or flourishes in writing, suggesting the opponents are nitpicking at letters rather than understanding the spirit of the law.</note> 
They simulate and dissimulate everything; they prolong the dispute and do not focus on what we actually do. For what we do seems too robust for them to accuse; instead, they criminalize what they most desire us to do—out of envy toward us and a desire for their own favor. Greedy for contention, they invented a sin for themselves before it even occurred, which they now force us to defend. They want to throw a "blurriness of the eyes" <note>original: "ophthalmiam"—a medical term for eye inflammation, used here metaphorically for spiritual blindness</note> before our eyes, and they want nothing to be considered fair unless they themselves have told us it is fair. 

But we cannot be guilty of whatever a slanderer wishes, and we have now said enough for our own justice. Therefore, let them seek some other guilty party who would commit such an outrage for them to fight against. We—lest they be mistaken—are not that party. We have sufficiently explained the difference we make between the veneration of God and that of the saints. They have stopped up their ears to those explanations like the "deaf adder" of the charm, lest they admit saner thoughts. 
<note>A reference to Psalm 58:4-5 regarding those who refuse to listen to reason.</note> 

I say again: they seek a dispute of their own accord. The next point to which they call us is: "I will not give my glory to another." 
<note>quoting Isaiah 42:8</note> 
I do not know what I shall do here; they have given a halved testimony and suppressed what follows: "nor my praise to carved images." 
<note>original: "et laudem meam ſculptilibus"</note> 
Let us, therefore, of our own accord, recount something regarding this "carved image"—what it is, how it is detested in the Holy Scriptures, and at what time the calumny was first stirred up against us because of it. I fear they will say we have begun a narrative that is tedious and beside the point; yet if we remain silent and neglect this "carved image" as if it produced nothing against us, I fear they will say we did not dare to touch upon our "foulest crime." For this is the "carved image" because of which they everywhere tear us apart as impure idolaters...

<meta>This page continues the author's polemic against the Waldensians. Having previously established the biblical precedent for the intercession of angels and saints, the author now turns to a specific point of contention: the use of religious images (sculptures). He argues against the Waldensian claim that any "carved image" is inherently an idol, distinguishing between pagan worship and Christian veneration.</meta>

# THE WALDENSES: BOOK TWO

They present their strongest argument—or rather, what they call our crime—in a clumsy manner. Nor do they realize that they have acted without deceit, though it is their habit to dare nothing except through ambushes. For it was to be hoped that such a thing could be overlooked by an incautious person. If this happened, they would draw our perpetual infamy from that unwise silence, and leave us defeated by a tiny word, as if by a very short dagger or a hidden blade. Therefore, it seemed better to fail at the beginning than at the end; it seemed better to remember my duty than their gold. Let them blame what they will; this is not the start, for it began right from our first page why I ought to displease them.

In the beginning, they want it to be believed that a **carved image** <note>original: *sculptile*</note> is never mentioned without the addition of "idolatry," because they hold that these types of nouns are of a nature that they cannot exist alone without a corresponding counterpart—just as God is not called "Creator" if no "creature" exists. But this word is outside the nature of a meaning that depends on another. Indeed, among the Greeks and Latins, there were innumerable carved, molded, and painted images by the greatest artists; there were statues of all kinds and monuments placed by the decree of noble cities for men who had served the Republic well. Even in those pagan times, no one worshipped the Curii or the Scipiones <note>Famous heroes of the Roman Republic</note>—all most deserving men—because of their statues. Even today, traces of ancient honor and diligence remain throughout old cities; in short, entire monuments survive. The same crafts exist among us; they produce their works in great numbers, yet no Christian prostrates himself before them; we observe nothing in them deeper than the craftsmanship itself. It is known, therefore, that there are carved images without idolatry.

Finally, there has been idolatry without carved images. The Persians had temples empty of idols, and they worshipped their fire or the sun (their kinsman) without an image. You see, therefore, that our sculpture does not necessarily provoke idolatry, just as your lack of sculpture does not attest to piety. Thus, such a great matter should have been handled more carefully. For now, if you have only played with appearances, the rule returns to childish declamations: "A foreigner may not climb the wall; a foreigner climbed the wall during a siege and repelled the enemy; he is summoned for a capital crime." Here, if you do not follow the internal intent of the law, you will certainly condemn one who served the Republic well, simply because of the letter of the law. 

So it is with the carved image: if you stick only to the word, the image of the **Savior**, of the **glorious Virgin Mary**, of **Peter and all the apostles** will be the same to you as a statue of Capitoline Jupiter, of Juno Moneta, of Apollo, and the whole cohort of gods. You, who have dared to usurp for the purpose of condemning the memory of the heavenly beings what the Prophet said about statues honored under the name of some impure demon—"I will not give my praise to carved images"—will you dare to defile the **Crucifix** just as you would a dark statue of Pluto? 

Now, Christians, keep watch over the statues of the Crucifix placed on public roads! A Waldensian is passing by; he looks askance, thinking of throwing I know not what filth; he spits equally upon the image of Christ and the statue of bloodthirsty Mars. This is their "piety"; these are the hidden depths of their wicked opinion, from which they labor to stir up a charge against the Christian people regarding a mere sculpture. We receive the Gospel, read and heard, with such holy affection; we reverently study the apostolic writers, the masters of piety; we bow down and worship the one and triune God, the Lord of all, according to the voices of the prophets—and yet we are blasphemed as if we were going to mute idols! 

A crime has been invented which, had it not been forged against us in the synagogue of the treacherous <note>The author likely refers to the Jewish community or a metaphorical assembly of heretics</note>, would exist nowhere. Thus, through the ill-will of others, we now endure the hatred attached to idolatry—a charge so steep that we do not think it would even be admitted in Tartarus <note>The pagan underworld, used here to mean the deepest hell</note>. For that madness of mortals long ago ceased by the merit of Christ. And these accusers are not from the middle of Turkey, nor from farthest Scythia <note>Regions considered "pagan" or "barbarian" by the author's audience</note>, who might have been ignorant of our institutions due to being foreigners; but they are those Waldenses born among us, who read, see, hear, perceive, and feel what we do...

# ON THE VENERATION OF SAINTS AGAINST...

<note>original: "DE SANCTORVM VENERATIONE CONTRA"</note>
...of the Persians, and again: "Do you not know why I have come to you? And now I shall return to fight against the prince of the Persians; for when I went out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming." And again: "At that time Michael shall rise, the great prince who stands for the children of your people." In the <term>Apocalypse</term><note>The Book of Revelation</note>, the devil is called the accuser of our brothers and servants; certainly, however, God is the judge of all flesh, before whom the accuser lays his charges. There, if God reviews our failings through an accuser, justice itself demands—and the very representation of Judgment requires—that our merits be known in turn through patrons who might either plead against our failings or commend our merits. For where an accuser is mentioned, a defender is also mentioned, for a judgment does not belong to only one side. 

But you say, "Our own justice commends us." I say, "Our own sin accuses us." Why is an accuser brought in at all? We find the accuser in the <term>Apocalypse</term>, but we find patrons in Job, Zechariah, Tobit, Daniel, the Acts of the Apostles, and the books of the Maccabees, so that no one may henceforth be ignorant that there are intercessions of the heavenly beings. 

There remain more things to be explained from the Holy Scriptures on this matter of the intercession of the saints. But since they themselves, by their own words, demand from us the very things we were already willing to say, let us henceforth deal with their <term>pedagogue</term><note>likely referring to a specific leader of the Reformation, such as Calvin or Luther</note>, and following in the footsteps of whatever they have left scattered against us, let us gather them up. They say they communicate the honor due to God alone to no creature; that is well and good, and it supports our own view. But they speak as if we worship the saints of God in the place of God—that is, with the veneration of <term>latria</term><note>A Greek term used in theology to describe the supreme worship due to God alone, as opposed to "dulia," the honor given to saints.</note>. 

And they continually sin by this fault—that is, by the simulation of truth—where, to respond once and for all to many such claims of theirs: If they had wished to be fair evaluators of this question, they ought first to have shown by confessed proofs that we worship the saints with the same honor as God. Only after they had extracted that from us should they have risen against us for such a crime. Now, however, what are they doing but seeking traps in naked words? They know we give honor to the saints, but they do not mention what kind of honor, nor how it is restricted. Instead, they charge that we provide honor to the saints at all, and they want the unlearned to take it as if we worship as many immense, eternal creators and saviors as there are saints. 

If they had cleared this matter up according to its true nature, one could already detect that their entire effort proceeds from a stubborn faction. Now, so that they might sustain it longer to breed hatred against us, they catch at no substance of the argument but only at tiny points and syllables. They simulate everything and dissimulate; they have nourished the dispute, and they charge us not with what we actually do (for that seems too robust for them to accuse), but with what they most desire us to do for the sake of their own favor and our envy. Eager for contention, they found a sin for themselves before it was even committed, which they now force us to defend. They want a <term>cloudiness</term><note>original: "opthalmiam," literally an eye disease or inflammation</note> cast over our eyes; they want nothing to be considered fair unless it is what they themselves have told us is fair. 

But we cannot be guilty just because some accuser wishes it, and we have now said enough for our justice. Therefore, let them seek another culprit for themselves who would commit such a sacrilege against whom they might fight. As for us—lest they be mistaken—we are not those people. We have explained enough and more than enough what distinction we make between the veneration of God and that of the saints. If they have stopped up their ears to those things like the deaf adder, so as not to admit saner views, I say again: they seek a dispute of their own accord. 

The next point to which they call us is "I will not give my glory to another." I do not know what they are doing here; they have spoken a halved testimony and suppressed what follows: "nor my praise to carved images." Let us therefore review of our own accord something regarding this "carved image"—what it is, how it is detested in the sacred letters, and at what time. The calumny against us was first stirred up from this. What terrible things the <term>Waldensians</term><note>original: "Valdeſes," a proto-Protestant group founded by Peter Waldo in the 12th century.</note> also conceive against us from this, I fear they are about to say. We have begun a long narrative, but we are silent now and neglect this "carved image" as if it produced nothing against us here. I fear they may say we did not dare to touch our "foul crime," for this is the "carved image" because of which they tear us apart everywhere as impure idolaters; but because...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK TWO

They explain their most serious support—or rather, their crime—not inaptly. Nor do they understand that they have done this without deceit, as is their custom to dare nothing except by treachery. For it was to be hoped that this might be overlooked by one who is insufficiently cautious. If that were to happen, they would derive our perpetual infamy from that imprudent silence, and they would leave us as if dispatched by a tiny word, like a very short dagger or a stealthy blade. Therefore, it seemed better to fail at the first rather than the latter; it seemed better to remember my duty to their ears. Let them, therefore, find fault with what they will; this is not the beginning, but it begins immediately from our first page why I should be displeasing to them.

At the start, they want it to be a settled matter that a <term>graven image</term><note>original: "sculptile"; a carved or sculpted work, often used in the context of the Ten Commandments' prohibition of "graven images."</note> is never mentioned without the addition of "Idolatry," as if these nouns were of such a nature that they cannot exist alone without a corresponding other—just as God is not called "Creator" if no creature exists. But this word is contrary to the nature of a meaning that depends on another. Indeed, among the Greeks and Latins, there were innumerable carved, molded, and painted images of the greatest artists; there were statues of all kinds and monuments of men who deserved well of the Republic, placed by the decree of distinguished cities. No one, even in that <term>pagan era</term><note>original: "gentilitate"</note>, adored the <term>Curii</term><note>A famous Roman family of the Republic, known for their austerity and virtue.</note> or all the <term>Scipios</term><note>The Scipio family, famous Roman generals who defeated Carthage.</note>—men most deserving of honor—simply because of their statues. Today, traces of that ancient honor and diligence still stand throughout ancient cities—entire monuments, in fact. The same crafts remain with us, and they produce their works in great number; yet no Christian falls down before them. We observe nothing in these works deeper than the craftsmanship itself. It is known, therefore, that there are graven images without idolatry.

Furthermore, there was idolatry without any graven image: the Persians had temples empty of idols, and they worshipped their fire, or the sun related to it, without an image. Thus you see that our "graven image" does not necessarily provoke idolatry, just as your lack of a graven image does not attest to piety. Therefore, so great a matter ought to have been handled more diligently. Now, unless you have played only at the surface, you return to childish declamations: "The law is that a foreigner shall not climb the wall; a foreigner climbed the wall during an assault, he repelled the enemy, and he is called to face the death penalty." Here, if you do not follow the inner meaning of the law, you will certainly condemn a man who deserved well of the Republic, contrary to the laws' intent.

So it is regarding a graven image: if you stick only to the word, the image of the Savior, of the glorious Virgin Mary, of Peter and all the Apostles, will be for you exactly the same as an idol of <term>Capitoline Jupiter</term><note>The primary deity of the Roman state, worshipped on the Capitoline Hill.</note>, of <term>Juno Moneta</term>, of Apollo, and the whole cohort of gods. You, who have dared to usurp for the purpose of condemning the memory of the heavenly beings that which the Prophet said about statues honored under the name of any impure demon—saying, "I will not give my praise to graven images"<note>A reference to Isaiah 42:8: "I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images."</note>—will you dare to defile the crucifix just as you would a dark statue of <term>Pluto</term><note>The Roman god of the underworld.</note>?

Now, Christians, keep watch over the statues of the crucifix located in public ways: a Waldensian is passing by! He looks askance; he is thinking of throwing I know not what filth, and how he might spit upon the image of Christ as if it were a statue of bloodthirsty Mars. This is their "piety"; these are the hidden depths of their wicked opinion, from which they labor to stir up a charge against the Christian people regarding a mere carved work.

We receive the Gospel, read and heard, with such holy affection; we study the apostolic commentators and teachers of piety with reverence; we adore the one and triune God, bowing down before the Lord of all things alone according to the prophetic words—and yet we are blasphemed as if we were going to mute idols! A crime has been invented which, had it not been forged against us in the <term>Synagogue of the perfidious</term><note>An anti-Jewish polemical phrase often used by medieval writers to suggest that heresy was "inspired" by those outside the Church.</note>, would exist nowhere. Thus, out of the ill-will of others, we now endure the hatred of "idolatry," as much as we believe would not even be admitted by <term>Tartarus</term><note>In Greek and Roman mythology, the deepest abyss of the underworld; here used as a synonym for Hell.</note> itself. For that madness of mortals long ago ceased by the merit of Christ. And these accusers are neither from the midst of the Turks, nor from farthest <term>Scythia</term><note>An ancient region in Eurasia, used here to denote a remote, "uncivilized" land.</note>, who might have been able to be ignorant of our institutions because of their foreignness. Rather, they are those Waldensians born among us, who read, see, hear, perceive, and feel our ways.

-># ON THE VENERATION OF SAINTS AGAINST<-

...those who know our affairs as well as we do are hurling such a horrendous accusation against us. It is the height of impudence that they do this in Christian ears, where no one—through the conscience of their own deeds—is unaware that these men have fabricated pure lies for the sake of the extreme pleasure they take in their hatred. By this one unrestrained license, let us finally learn how much they loathe us and how fatal they might one day be to us. Today, while their affairs are still weak, they have abstained from no curse so foul to us or so deadly to themselves—if only they were not dealing with the indifferent. What they have produced at this time would never have come forth had not a mind inflamed by a capital hatred boiled over prematurely against all things hated and tainted, finding it difficult to remain silent. But by what reason could they treat anything anywhere with deliberation, they who have never undertaken anything with deliberation or from good authors? For just as with all their other errors, they followed the imitation of heretics rather than the Scriptures or the institutions of the saints; thus, they borrowed this view regarding images from the <term>Greek insanity</term><note>The author is referring to the Byzantine Iconoclast movement, which sought to ban and destroy religious images.</note>. 

Philippicus of Constantinople, about seven hundred and fifty years ago, having killed his Emperor Justinian and occupied the Eastern Empire through a violated oath, sent certain "articles of his perfidy" to Rome so that the <term>Vicar of Peter and Christ</term><note>The Pope.</note> might subscribe to them. This Roman Pontiff not only did not confirm those articles but even condemned them as manifest heresy. Thereupon the Emperor, seized by rage to show his disdain for the Roman Pontiff and to add some strength to his perfidy through royal license, ordered the images of the <term>Fathers</term><note>The bishops and theologians of the early Church Councils.</note>—who had been present at those most established Councils (which hold authority next to the Gospel) against Arius, Macedonius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Theodore—to be scraped from the walls of the Temple of Saint Sophia in Constantinople. 

And this the treacherous <term>Greekling</term><note>original: "graeculus"; a diminutive, often derogatory term used by Latin writers to characterize Greeks as untrustworthy or trivial.</note> did so that no memory of the faith might survive in painting, which had been preached with such orthodox authority by those leaders. This was the reason why, seven hundred and thirty years after the Apostolic preaching, the Greeks first "noticed" this issue. Having been alerted by this recent contention, they "sniffed out" an <term>Apostolic sentiment</term><note>The author is being sarcastic here, suggesting the Iconoclasts falsely claimed their views were based on the original teachings of the Apostles.</note> regarding images under the presidency of Philippicus. Our Waldensians now defend this view, which had lain dormant for a long time, bringing it forward again as if it were Apostolic. In this one thing, however, I admit they are more "pious" than Philippicus: he erased the assembly of the Council of Nicaea along with the rest, while the Waldensians—though they erase everything else—wish to appear as if they approve of the Council of Nicaea. 

But let us look at the case against the Greeks and the Waldensians. Let us see if the Waldensian might finally wish to return to us, just as the Greeks, overcome by conscience, have returned so many times. Let us explain the truth of the matter which was noticed so late, and by no law except through sedition by a murderous and infidel emperor. 

And indeed, they have innumerable testimonies about "carved works" scattered throughout the whole Law. Moses, the greatest of all, says: "You shall not make for yourself a <term>graven image</term><note>original: "sculptile"; a carved or sculpted work.</note> nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or what is on the earth below, or of those things that are in the waters under the earth; you shall not adore them nor worship them." Again, in Deuteronomy: "You saw no likeness on the day the Lord spoke to you in Horeb from the midst of the fire, lest perhaps being deceived you should make for yourselves a carved likeness or an image of male or female, the likeness of any beasts that are upon the earth, or of birds flying under heaven, or of reptiles that move on the earth, or of fish that dwell in the waters under the earth. Lest perhaps, lifting your eyes to heaven, you see the sun and the moon and all the stars of heaven, and being deceived by error, you adore and worship them." 

Let these testimonies from among all of them be enough for us to decide the present matter. Here it must be seen entirely at what time and to whom the prophets spoke such things. Moses was instructing the people in the veneration and discipline of the worship of the one God at a time when the whole world was violently, as it were...

### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK TWO

...bound by the chains of the evil one, with maddened minds, they wallowed incurably in idolatry. At that time, when Israel had recently departed from Egypt, the idols of the Egyptians still resided in their souls; they had prostrated themselves before these as if they were true gods due to Egyptian corruption. At that time, humanity had not yet been assumed by divinity <note>This refers to the Incarnation—the belief that God became man in Jesus Christ.</note> such that the divine nature could be represented by any image. Back then, whatever form was expressed—since it was entirely inappropriate—was believed by corrupt minds, devoid of all higher thought, to be the true form of God; for precious philosophy <note>The author uses "precious philosophy" sarcastically or to mean "true wisdom" was rare in the world at that time.</note> was scarce in the world. Thus, it was only with difficulty and through successive generations across the ages that it was received and continued. 

This was also a <term>stiff-necked people</term><note>original: "populus duræ ceruicis," a common biblical description of the Israelites in Exodus.</note> whom no presence of God, no power of miracles, no deaths, no benefits, and not even the most holy prophet Moses could soften into spontaneous piety, so that they might leave behind what they had once learned poorly under servitude. This was that hard people who, because of their lack of teachability, extorted a <term>bill of divorce</term><note>A reference to Matthew 19:8, where Jesus explains that Moses permitted divorce only because of the people's "hardness of heart," not as an original divine law.</note> contrary to natural law—even, if one may say so, against the will of God. This was the people for whom, on account of their promptness toward idolatry, it was not even permitted to know the location of Moses' grave; for those who committed fornication with the <term>Bronze Serpent</term><note>A reference to Numbers 21:8 and 2 Kings 18:4. Moses made a bronze serpent for healing, but the Israelites later began to worship it as an idol.</note>, what injury against God might they not have committed regarding the small body of Moses? 

To this people, so inclined toward every superstition, the prophet forbade not only things that were prohibited, but absolutely everything. No opportunity at all was to be left to those who could worship the smallest things, the most filthy things: oxen, crocodiles, serpents, the ibis, and <term>Anubis the barker</term><note>Anubis was the jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead; "the barker" was a common Roman literary trope used to mock the god's animal head.</note>. Those who had said to a golden calf, "These are your gods, O Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt," had to be bound by the strictest commands. Truly, were images to be permitted to those who prostituted themselves under every high tree and under every leafy tree? 

Therefore, it was not the fault of the images themselves, but the vice of treacherous men that was the cause for this craft of making images being so severely prohibited. For if images were condemned by their own nature and not because of the occasion for sin, Moses would have committed a sin when he fashioned the Bronze Serpent, or when he later preserved it (for the people were destined to commit fornication with it). It would also be a sin to know anyone's burial place, since it was necessary for Moses' tomb to be unknown to the Jews. Furthermore, if it is a sin to make an image of a living thing, it would be a greater sin for God to create the souls of men, or to make beasts, the Sun, the Moon, and all the host of heaven—for it was on account of these things that the idolaters worshipped those mute images. 

But only the *use* of the thing comes under accusation. The proof of this is that whenever Moses commanded such a thing, he almost never failed to add the condition: *that you should not worship them, nor adore them.* Take away that fear from Moses; receive the children of Israel into your faith and promise on their behalf that they will not go toward idols, and that they will not be stiff-necked and uncircumcised of heart—and then Judea will have more than one craft of painting and sculpting. For why was no such caution regarding an image given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob? Clearly, the occasion for sin was absent. 

If the Christian people—the most certain heirs of the faith of the Patriarchs—remain in unshaken piety in the worship of the one God, whom no height, no depth, nor any creature can turn away so that they might say to a creature what those people said to the calf—"You are my God, you are my Redeemer"—what reason was there to so obstinately forbid images to those who, out of a free conscience, would preserve what is right more holily than another would out of a command? 

Take away the fear of superstition, and images will return. The same God who said through Moses, "You shall not make for yourself a carved image in the likeness of male or female," also said to Moses: "You shall also make two **Cherubim** of beaten gold on both sides of the oracle." Finally, Solomon later erected that same likeness in the Holy of Holies. But he also made various paintings on the walls, and he placed the **Sea** <note>The "Brazen Sea," a large basin used for ritual washing in Solomon's Temple.</note> upon cast figures of animals; finally, there were two rows of engraved sculptures that were cast, and they stood upon twelve oxen. And there were also carved basins...

->ON THE ADORATION OF THE SAINTS AGAINST...<-

Consider the sculptures between the joints and the moldings, the lions, the oxen, and the Cherubim. To you, with your "wedge" <note>The author likely refers to a "wedge" (cuneus) as a metaphorical tool of logical division or a polemical instrument used to split apart the Church's traditions.</note>—you who just a moment ago so destructively ambushed us regarding the issue of sculptures—what do you say here? Or have you not yet heard that God commanded beaten <term>Cherubim</term> <note>original: "ductiles cherubin," referring to the golden figures on the Ark of the Covenant</note> to be made, and that Solomon, without any fear of violating religion, filled the temple with images? Do you dare to blame these authors? It would be more righteous for us to be blamed together with them than to be acquitted with you. You do not dare. God, who commanded these things, is greater than you; Moses and Solomon, who made these things, are greater than you can summon into the hatred of sculpture. Let this slander vanish, and having been acquitted by these authors, let us leave the courtroom.

Let us return to what I said at the beginning: it is the *reason* for false worship <note>original: "falsi cultus materiā"</note> that is forbidden, not the image itself. Therefore, we receive the likenesses of the saints back again as safe. Christ expressed his own face upon a cloth <note>A reference to the "Image of Edessa" or the "Veil of Veronica."</note>; it is not permitted for us to cast away such great relics received from the hands of the Savior. We do not think it a sin to retain what it was not a sin to have expressed. And even if a thousand faces are derived from this <term>Archetype</term> <note>The "original" or first model from which copies are made.</note> into the world, the religious memory of Christ is commended in many, just as it was in the blessed Berenice <note>A name often associated with Saint Veronica in early Christian traditions.</note>. Thus, we proceed from the Cherubim to Berenice, from Berenice to the whole Crucifix, from this to the glorious Virgin, then to the Apostles, from the Apostles to the Martyrs and to all of God's elect, and from the elect back to the Cherubim of the Tabernacle and the Holy of Holies of the Christians.

To whom is this displeasing? Who will claim this is not received from the authority of the Scriptures? Let him say exactly what we are sinning in. Has a Waldensian ever seen a Christian before an image of the Crucified—we grant him the judgment here—does he dare to say the Christian is "forgetful of the living God" and focused on nothing but a "mute image"? Or does the Christian not rather adore the Son of God, whom he calls back into his memory from this figure? Has a Waldensian ever seen a Christian lying before the memorial of a martyr? We give the Waldensian the choice: let him say clearly what he thinks a Christian is praying. For he cannot be ignorant of our ways, even as he slanders us now. But what does he believe a Christian prays? Does he believe it is something like this: "Lawrence the Martyr, creator and ruler of the world, you alone can do all things in heaven and on earth, you alone are my liberator and savior"? 

For it was in this manner that the idolaters prayed—about whom the Prophet said, "Let all be confounded who adore sculptures and who trust in their idols"—they adored their own gods. They attributed the nature of God to a creature, and whatever benefits they held from divine mercy, they credited to their idols as the only true authors. Do you dare, then, to affirm that a Christian, having rejected or ignored God, adores any saint with such wicked vows? Do you dare? We shall all recognize this as a lying slander. You do not dare? Then cease to blame what we do not do, by your own confession. 

But if we pray like this: "Lawrence the Martyr, through the merit of your passion, intercede with God for me, a sinner"—what crime is this, I ask? How do we here provoke the saints to the injury of God? Or do we do anything foreign to the examples of Scripture? The children of Israel pray to Samuel: "Do not cease to cry out to the Lord our God for us," and it follows that "Samuel cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him." Regarding this kind of "adoring" <note>In this context, the author uses "adorandi" in the broader sense of veneration or petition, rather than the worship due to God alone (latria).</note> the saints, we shall speak more copiously a little later. 

We are only showing this now: we do not bow to mute images, nor again to the memory of Baal, Astarte, Dagon, or Ashtoreth <note>original: "Baalim Astaroth Dagon Afterthen," referring to various Canaanite and Philistine deities mentioned in the Old Testament.</note>, regarding whom the Prophet says "all the gods of the nations are demons," whom no one can salute without injury to God. We do not bow to the deserting angel, the Devil, which is the greatest iniquity and a denial of God the Most High. Instead, we bow toward the Memories of the saints. And we do not bring these saints forward as if they were other gods to replace the one God; rather, we venerate them as the inseparable friends of that true God. Because of their intercession for miserable mortals, they are most powerful; and because of their kindness toward us, they are most willing.

# SECOND BOOK ON THE WALDENSIANS

Whoever decides—based on a twisted reading of Scripture—that the saints should not be honored, commits an unpardonable insult against those holy ones. These <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval and Reformation-era movement that criticized many Catholic practices, including the veneration of saints and images.</note> use the same scriptural passages intended to strike down the devil to instead attack us. By casting the saints into the same lot as impure demons, such a person can have no part with the saints themselves; for he excludes from divine fellowship and all honor those whom he treats with the same testimonies used against the devil. He will find his own lot with the devil first, as he thrusts those most worthy citizens of heaven into a state of "demonic" contempt before God and men. 

Now, let neither the saints be subjected to contempt, nor Christians to slander, through images or through Scriptures twisted into a foreign meaning. The Scriptures do not intend this; indeed, they resist the idea that what is meant for the devil and his accomplices should be hurled by an impure Waldensian against the most choice saints of God. We place statues of the saints in a holy manner, causing no injury to the Divinity. We do so only as a memory of virtue and as an incentive for endurance <note>original: "tolerantiæ incitamentum"</note> for both the learned and the unlearned alike. 

After all, who does not know how wandering and unstable human thoughts are when the senses are idle? Give them a task; provide a picture for the eye, and the wandering thought will be fixed there. If a shameful image is presented, suddenly dishonest movements will arise in the soul or even the whole body. Consider us while we are meditating or praying: here, where we set nothing religious before ourselves, there is no time when our senses fly more through empty space. But set before yourself a <term>crucifix</term>, or the Virgin anxious beneath the cross, or the passion of a martyr; there the thought will be fixed, and the soul will conceive holy affections. 

Present to me here your soul, empty of every visual form, and I, in turn, will present the soul of a Christian affected by an image; we shall see which one we believe has progressed more ardently in contemplation. This use of images is, therefore, for both learned and unlearned Christians, just as the use of Scripture is for the learned. He who would take away images from the human race should also take away letters, for the use of both is the same. Nothing different—or perhaps even less—is seen in an image than in letters. Indeed, painting is "chaster" than writing; you were never able to spread your treachery through this visual art, but you were able to do so through writing. For many centuries now, no one has painted or sculpted an "idol," yet books are full of heretical treachery. We learn of the worship of idolatry and its materials from sacred and secular books alike, not from images. These points regarding the "envy of sculpture" should satisfy a modest mind, for the opponents themselves are impatient of delay and continually call us to other matters.

They contend, based on the rite of the primitive Church, that it was handed down that we should grant honor to no saints, but to God alone. They say this without testimony, recently dreaming up such things among their rustic little assemblies. We know it was more modestly handed down that they should give to God that highest veneration <note>Often referred to in theology as "latria," the worship due to God alone.</note> which can be deferred to no creature by any right without the sin of idolatry; yet they did not allow the saints to lie unhonored for that reason, but always religiously cherished them with the honor due to them. We do not bring this forward as a sudden thought of our own, but confirm it with suitable witnesses. 

<term>Pope Pius</term> <note>Pope Pius I, who reigned in the mid-2nd century.</note>, in the 130th year after the passion of Christ, under the Emperor Antoninus Verus, dedicated a temple in memory of the divine <term>Pudentiana</term> <note>Saint Pudentiana, a legendary early Roman martyr.</note>. Who would believe that a most holy man—living in that era of ecclesiastical severity and apostolic zeal which flourished in that Church—would have started this as something new from himself, rather than following a custom received from antiquity? Even if he had done it as something new, it would still be for our time an example from the ancient Church, from which we learn that the primitive Church did grant honor to the saints. 

Consider <term>Eusebius Pamphili</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note>: if you ask about his age, he lived under Diocletian, Maximian, Maximinus, Maxentius, and Licinius—those most savage persecutors of the Christian cause—and he witnessed the sweat, the lashes, and the iron grates of the martyrs with his own eyes. If you ask about his learning, he was chief among the most learned churchmen. If you ask about his faith, he himself, as part of the assembly of the <term>Council of Nicaea</term>, consented to that Nicene faith which you profess, by the command of the three hundred Fathers...

# ON THE ADORATION OF SAINTS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...[the truth] is confirmed by his own mouth. That **Nicene Creed** <note>The defining statement of Christian belief established in 325 AD.</note> is confirmed by the fathers. **Eusebius of Caesarea**, the bishop, in the thirteenth book of *The Gospel Preparation*, says: "These things we do daily; we who are soldiers of true piety, honoring the friends of God, also approach their monuments and make vows to them as to holy men, by whose intercession we profess to be helped in no small way before God." **Constantine the Great**, who first restored peace to the Church of God, constructed countless temples in Rome and Constantinople in memory of the apostles and martyrs. Furthermore, the mystical recitation of the names of the saints who have died piously in Christ has been celebrated among the mysteries of the altar—during the consecration of the most divine sacrament of Christ’s body—ever since the time of the apostles. The holy **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian whose writings on the "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> is a witness to this in the third chapter of his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. We refer most pious minds and seekers of truth to that work, and not to this Waldensian, for whom reading Dionysius is a crime.

However, having been convicted of lying so often, and found to deny what we find written everywhere, it would be well if the Waldensian would finally "pull back his horns," stop barking at his betters, and defer to his own conscience. Or, if he entirely desired to contend, he should produce something that might seem like a just argument. As it is, he is entirely occupied with nothing but veiling people's eyes and leading them about with tricks.

For consider how much weight this passage holds: *For this reason I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ* <note>original: "huius rei gratia flecto genua mea ad Patrem domini noſtri ieſu chriſti." A quote from Ephesians 3:14.</note>. Let us play a bit with the Waldensian using an example of his own wickedness: let us argue against him that Paul never adored Christ our Lord, because he said here that he bowed his knees to God the Father. Do they not currently impose this kind of trap on us, insisting we believe that Paul did nothing more than what he wrote here? This argument is so inherently weak that we hardly wish to refute it. For Paul, who so often commends himself to the prayers of the faithful who were still in the flesh, why—given his confidence—would he not have commended himself to the faithful who are now blessed with Christ? But the apostolic institution, as we have just said and will explain more fully hereafter, has always venerated the saints.

But let us see what other "long train" <note>original: "Syrma." Referring to the long, trailing robe of a tragic actor; used here metaphorically for a long-winded or dramatic argument.</note> they are pulling now. They say Christ gave us an example: he fell on his knees before the Father so that we should expect help from no one else. At this point, we must demand an account of the Waldensian’s own faith; for he who does nothing at all outside the specific example of Christ creates the suspicion that he does not adore Christ himself—or if he does, by what right? For he would be guilty of violating Christ's example, since Christ never adored himself. The overly bold Waldensian ought to have bypassed Christ; he ought to expect help from no one but the heavenly Father. 

We hold—no, we do not hold him yet—but certainly we hold his rustic wickedness. It becomes manifest to everyone in what ways they abuse the scriptures with words of suspicion. This is their perpetual sin against us and the piety of the faith. Look! By the same trap, without changing a word, we return the argument to the Waldensian: that it is not permitted for him to adore Christ, since by Christ's own example he taught that help should be expected from no one other than the heavenly Father. 

Therefore, would the Father and the Son distrust each other? Would he who honors the Son not also honor the Father? Would whatever veneration one now pays the Son be snatched away from the Father, resulting in a madness where heavenly things are treated like earthly rivalries? If it is a crime even to think this—and the Waldensians also feel that they holily honor the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son—then first, let them admit they corrupted the scripture which they twisted against us. Second, let them permit the same indulgence to us: let them loosen the "reins" of this scripture from the Father to the saints, just as they loosened them from the Father to the Son. For in both cases, what we do, we do justly by the authority of other scriptures. I say it again and again: We do not venerate the saints as if we do not know God. We implore the saints, not as if they are going to bestow some "stolen" benefit without God's knowledge; rather, we greet them as messengers of good news...

->## THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK TWO<-

...we pray to these messengers <note>original: "legatos"—referring here to the saints as ambassadors or intermediaries</note> that they may entreat for that which we expect as help from God alone, who is the sole giver and benefactor over all things, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit. In this consists pure prayer. You, I know not whether by greater pride or sacrilege, burst into the secret of the heavenly inner chamber. Those holy princes, the dispensers of all heavenly grace and benefit—of whom the Savior said: **"Well done, good and faithful servant; I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord"**—you despise them in your perverse chapter as if you yourself had come from above the saints. As much as is in your power, you strip and despoil them of all authority and honor. In that venerable council <note>the assembly of saints in heaven</note>, you have recognized no one as fit to whom you might safely entrust yourself and your vow. You alone, most stained with earthly filth, claim to be the interpreter of your own many affairs before the purest Divinity. This is intolerable impiety; it is the condemned pride of a diabolical art and a contempt for heavenly things, ruinous to no head so much as your own, with the most bitter detriment.

We, being more modest and mindful of our fragility, by no means use such impudent shamelessness when we determine our position. If any saints on earth pleased God and held God's power for sudden works of healing for the benefit of mortals, they cannot become absent to those mortals now that they are blessed and stripped of mortality. We now honor these as messengers of our vows. To them, as most faithful patrons—following the example of **Cornelius** and **Tobit** <note>Cornelius (Acts 10) and Tobit (from the Book of Tobit) are cited as men whose prayers and alms were brought before God by angelic/holy messengers</note>—we holy and devotedly entrust ourselves and our concerns. We know that they possess merits before God through which they may be heard; we know that we possess offenses because of which we, in religious humility, abstain from petitioning God in our own name. Thus, we honor the saints for the honor of God, and we adore God in the saints. No injury is done to anyone there; we feel that this is done rightly and orderly among us and in the heavenly realms. 

This Christian institution—even if it were proven by no scriptures (as the most lying Waldensians pretend there are none to be found, though we have produced many very relevant and manifest ones)—ought nevertheless to have been proven by the very discipline of nature. For a person is most hateful who thinks that everything is owed to him by his own merit. Therefore, let them no longer slander us in either way: saying "If you venerate the saints, you do not know God," or "If you know God, you must ignore the saints." Understand us well: we adore God alone in the highest degree; we expect all things from Him alone as the source; but through the merits of the saints, we invite, deserve, and bind that same God to us. This is a pure confession; here you have the whole of what you drag into an accusation. 

But let not this rustic childishness slander us too wickedly, for it bypasses the honor of the saints by using the example of Christ. Christ was the Son of God, God from God, of whom it is written: **"He set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber, exulted like a giant to run his course; his going out is from the highest heaven, and his circuit even to its summit, nor is there anyone who can hide himself from his heat."** <note>A quotation from Psalm 19 (Psalm 18 in the Vulgate), traditionally interpreted by medieval theologians as a prophecy of Christ's incarnation and majesty.</note> It was Christ whose most holy soul, already from the beginning of its creation, was exalted above all thrones and reclined in the very bosom of the Divinity. This was Christ, whom the angels could not contain within their orders, but leading him as victor above all sublimity named in heaven, they frequently cried out: **"In your splendor and your beauty, press on, proceed prosperously, and reign."** <note>A quote from Psalm 45 (44 in the Vulgate), used here to describe Christ's divine glory.</note> Would He—who approached the Divinity as God himself, above all angelic orders, and who was heard because of His reverence, a priest forever according to the order of **Melchizedek**—stand in need of the intercession of a lower power and merit? Was it that Christ, whose day **Abraham** wished to see, and he saw it and was glad—was He to be adored through **Abraham**, **Isaac**, and **Jacob**? 

Represent yourself as Christ, you Waldensian, and then by your own right you will need neither angels nor any saints at all! But truly, how great is your forgetfulness, or to what point has your lust for slandering driven you, that you find such a clever argument? Unless Christ invoked the Father, so that if we now yield to your sharp wit, you would compel us to neither adore the Son nor the Holy Spirit properly from now on...

# ON THE VENERATION OF THE SAINTS AGAINST...

...consequently, they claim that saints did not cry out to other saints to seek help from them. However, we say that the canon of the scriptures is full of examples where the holy pray for the ignorance of leaders and the people. Therefore, it happens that those who have introduced errors by protecting things that are "lame and mangled" <note>likely a reference to incomplete or distorted interpretations of the Bible</note>, stealing all complete things from the eyes of readers, stir up for themselves—and for those who follow them—the damnation destined for those who defraud the sacred scripture.

But before I go deeper, I want us to agree on which "saints" they claim did not cry out to other saints. If they mean those who, having now conquered death, reign with Christ in heaven, it is a certain fact and not in question that they now intercede <note>original: "inuocẽt"—meaning they are called upon or act as intercessors</note>, though they once cried out in prayer that they might eventually reach that heavenly state. Therefore, they must mean those "saints" who exist in this mortal life under the laws and promises made from heaven. We use the term "saints" not only for those famous for miracles and the purity of their lives, but for all members of the former Synagogue <note>the Jewish people of the Old Testament</note> and today’s Church. 

This is according to the word of Moses: **"You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness over the eyes for the dead, because you are a holy people to the Lord your God"** <note>Deuteronomy 14:1-2</note>. From this perspective, those rebels said to Moses and Aaron: **"Let it suffice you, for all the multitude is holy, and the Lord is among them; why do you lift yourselves up above the people of the Lord?"** <note>Numbers 16:3</note>. Peter also, in his Canonical Epistle to the faithful of Christ, says: **"You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition"** <note>1 Peter 2:9</note>. 

These saints everywhere prayed to and through other saints. The leaders and the whole congregation cried out to Jeremiah: **"Let our prayer fall in your sight, and pray for us to the Lord your God for all these remnants"** <note>Jeremiah 42:2</note>. And the Prophet responds: **"Behold, I pray to the Lord your God."** And it follows from the person of God: **"I am now appeased concerning the evil I have done to you."** Following this example, we also pray in this manner: *Remember, O Virgin Mother, when you stand in the sight of God, to speak good things for us, and that he may turn away his indignation from us.* 

Daniel also prays to God through the merit of other saints. He says: **"Do not take away your mercy from us for the sake of Abraham your beloved, and Isaac your servant, and Israel your holy one"** <note>Daniel 3:35, from the Song of the Three Children</note>. Our prayer is similar: *We beseech you, O Lord, that we may be helped by the merits and prayers of your saints, so that what our fragility does not obtain may be granted to us by the prayer of those who were found just before you.* 

Furthermore, regarding the sin of the golden calf, the Lord said: **"Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them and that I may destroy them."** There Moses prays: **"Let your anger cease and be appeased over the wickedness of your people; remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel your servants."** And it follows: **"And the Lord was appeased, so that he did not do the evil he had spoken against his people"** <note>Exodus 32:10-14</note>. Our prayer follows this: *Protect, O Lord, your people, and preserve them with a perpetual defense as they trust in the patronage of your apostles.*

Moses was a faithful servant in all the house of God, with whom God spoke face to face as a friend to a friend. Nevertheless, he does not presume to pray for the sin of the people before God based on his own holiness or familiarity, but rather based on the merit of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Church specifically observes this in her prayers: *Almighty eternal God, who perceive that we are not worthy to entreat your majesty as is fitting, grant that your saints, whom you can worthily hear, may supplicate for our sins.* And to the Blessed Virgin: *We beseech you, O Lord, forgive the offenses of your servants, so that we who are unable to please you by our own acts may be saved by the intercession of the mother of your Son, our Lord.*

Here, you Waldensian <note>original: "valdésis"</note>, go ahead and accuse the institution of the Church! Charge her with doing something foreign to the example of the scriptures! This is how we venerate the saints, and God through the saints. We are taught this by the divinely inspired scriptures, which you either do not know, or you steal, or you deny, and most harmfully corrupt. This is what James commands us to do according to the most ancient apostolic institution: **"Confess your sins to one another..."** <note>James 5:16</note>.

-># BOOK TWO ON THE WALDENSIANS<-

...your sins and pray for one another that you may be saved; for the constant prayer of a righteous person is very powerful. Elijah was a man like us, subject to suffering, and he prayed with a prayer that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months; and again he prayed, and heaven gave rain and the earth gave its fruit. <note>These verses are from James 5:16–18, a central text for the author's argument on the efficacy of intercessory prayer.</note> All the people of Israel prayed there, and there were certainly seven thousand men in that place whom God preserved for himself, whose knees had not bowed before Baal; yet they prayed in vain until they prayed alongside Elijah. <note>referencing 1 Kings 19:18; the author implies that the prayers of the "righteous" Elijah were the key to God's response.</note> I have introduced this passage from the Epistle of James all the more willingly so that I might bring to light the voluntary and blind contention of the Waldensians. For in the following discussion regarding the funeral rites of the dead and regarding purgatory, they have excerpted that small part of the passage: *The prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up* <note>James 5:15</note>. They did this because they thought it worked against us, as if the next part did not immediately follow: *The constant prayer of a righteous person is very powerful, and pray for one another that you may be saved.* Thus, they suppressed the part that made their case weaker. 

O blind and wretched man! The Prophet cries out: *Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord* <note>Psalm 19:12</note>. Was it not enough for you to tremble at the divine examination for your own ignorances, but must you also, with a lost conscience—as if you were stirring up a dispute over a "peasant’s leaky roof" <note>original: "Rustico stillicidio"—a legal or proverbial metaphor for a trivial neighborly dispute</note> rather than over faith and piety toward God and the saints—willingly and knowingly defend a perverse dogma born from the lust of a depraved mind? For if you used your conscience in any way, you ought to have followed the Scriptures, not twisted them to impose your own meaning upon them. 

Now, regarding the worship of the one God, as if you had caught us in the guilt of "gentile foolishness," <note>referencing pagan idolatry</note> you stir up six hundred passages; every time we testify that we worship God rightly according to the precept of Scripture, you repeat, as if nothing had been said: "Worship God!" And when, after this point has been held against you or slipped away, you ought to have moved down to the cause of the saints and overcome error through the Scriptures, you instead made them say what they did not mean when they would not say what you wanted. As if everything depended on a single word, you harp on it again and again and persist in the same thing: "Worship one God," pretending that you have discovered this alone in the whole matter. You pretend, with your lying conscience, that there are no witnesses to the veneration of the saints—so many and so manifest—as if you wished they had never existed. 

Even demons tremble and fall down defeated at the tombs of the saints, confessing by their relics how much the souls of the elect can do in heaven. <note>Relics were often used in exorcisms during this period; the author argues that the power of the saints is proven by the reaction of evil spirits.</note> You have not learned this example from your father, but instead, you insanely leap from the body to the spirit, and from the spirit back to the body, raving in an insult to both alike. For not only the blessed spirits, but the souls of all the dead (to use the words of Eusebius Pamphilus <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Church historian and theologian</note> from the twelfth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*) possess a certain power by which they help human affairs after death; for this is the true opinion. But this cannot be proved except by lengthy reasoning. However, one ought to believe such words because they have been handed down by men of great antiquity; credit must also be given to those who have confirmed these things to be so by their laws. 

Certainly, the Jews contend that it was handed down this way concerning Jeremiah, and the Book of Maccabees recorded that he was seen after death praying for the people. <note>referencing 2 Maccabees 15:14, where the deceased prophet Jeremiah appears in a vision.</note> So great a man as Eusebius, to whom the entire library of the Greeks was known, meets our Waldensians head-on in many notable ways: first, he asserts that one must not disagree with the ancient men (whom those Waldensians reject from their plow-handles <note>original: "de stiua sua"—suggesting the Waldensians are unlearned farmers or peasants</note> like rambling old women at their chores); second, he confesses the patronage of souls; and third, he affirms the faith of the Book of Maccabees, which they thereafter cast out from the number of sacred books as if it were useless. In these Scriptures, we find intercessions from heaven to earth, from earth to the underworld <note>original: "tartarum"—the Greek term for the deep abyss of the dead</note>. But perhaps I have seemed to say something incredible: "from earth to the underworld." Yet that is how the matter stands, and the Gospel testifies to it. *I beg you therefore, father Abraham,* says the rich man at the feast, *that you would send...* <note>Luke 16:27, the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus.</note>

If he means those who now, having conquered death, reign with Christ in heaven, it is a certain matter and does not even come into question that they now invoke God; yet they once cried out in order to lay hold of that state. Therefore, they must mean those saints who, existing in this mortality under the laws and promises made by heaven, are called "saints"—not only those who shone with miracles and a confessed innocence of life, but even the members of the whole Synagogue <note>The author uses "Synagogue" here to refer to the Old Testament community of believers.</note> of old and the Church of today are considered saints. Daniel prays to God through the merit of other saints. Our prayer is similar: *We beseech You, O Lord, that we may be aided by the merits and prayers of Your saints, so that what our fragility does not obtain may be granted to us by the prayer of those who were found righteous before You.*

Our prayer is similar: *Protect, O Lord, Your people, and preserve them with perpetual defense as they trust in the patronage of Your apostles.*

Moses was a faithful servant in the whole house of God, with whom God spoke face to face as a friend to a friend. Yet he did not presume to pray for the sin of the people based on his own holiness or familiarity with God, but rather by the merit of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Church specifically observes this, for she prays: *Almighty and eternal God, who perceives that we are not worthy to plead with Your majesty as is fitting, grant that Your saints, whom You can worthily hear, may supplicate for our sins.* And to the Blessed Virgin: *Forgive, we beseech You, O Lord, the faults of Your servants, so that we who are unable to please You by our own acts may be saved by the intercession of the Mother of Your Son, our Lord.*

Yet we thus adore the saints and God through the saints according to the divinely inspired scriptures—which you both ignore, and steal, and deny, and even more harmfully corrupt. We are taught that we must do this according to the most ancient apostolic institution. James commands: *Confess your sins to one another...*
