->### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK TWO<-

...your **sins and pray for one another that you may be saved; for the constant prayer of a righteous man avails much.** <note>original: "peccata vestra & orate p̄ inuicē vt saluemini multū em̄ valet depræcatio iuſti affidua"; see James 5:16.</note> **Elijah was a man like us, subject to suffering, and he prayed with prayer that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth gave its fruit.** <note>James 5:17-18.</note> All the people of Israel prayed there, and there were certainly among them seven thousand men whom God preserved for himself, whose knees had not bowed before Baal. Yet they prayed in vain until they prayed with Elijah's help. I have introduced this passage from the Epistle of James <note>The author refers to James as "Jacob," following the Latin *Iacobus*.</note> more willingly so that I might bring to light the willful and blind contention of the Waldensians. <note>The Waldensians were a medieval sect that preceded the Reformation; they were often accused of rejecting church traditions and the intercession of saints.</note>

For in the following discussion regarding the funerals of the dead and <term>purgatory</term> <note>The state or place of purification for souls after death.</note>, they transcribed that part of the passage: **The prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up**; because they thought it would work against us, they excerpted it as if there did not follow immediately after: **the constant prayer of a righteous man avails much**, and **pray for one another that you may be saved**. Thus they suppressed the text, making it say less for their own purpose. 

O blind man! O wretched man! The Prophet cries out: **Cleanse me from my secret faults, O Lord**; <note>Psalm 19:12.</note> was it not enough for you to tremble at the divine judgment for your ignorances? But moreover, with a ruined conscience—as if you were raising a dispute over a *rustic roof-drip* <note>original: "Ruſtico ſtillicidio"; a legal metaphor referring to minor property disputes between neighbors, implying the Waldensians treat high theology like petty litigation.</note> against a neighbor, rather than about faith and piety toward God and the saints—so willingly and knowingly you defend a perverse dogma out of the lust of a depraved mind. For if you used your conscience in any way, you would not impose your own meaning upon the Scriptures; it was necessary to follow them, not to pervert them. 

Now, regarding the worship of the one God—as if you had found someone guilty of pagan folly—you stir up six hundred passages; whenever we testify that we worship God rightly according to the precept of Scripture, just as often, as if nothing had been said, you groan out: "Worship God!" And when, after that point was held by you or escaped from us, you ought to have descended to the cause of the saints and overcome error through the Scriptures, here, when they did not say what you wanted, you made them say what they did not intend. And as if everything hung upon one single word, you hammer it repeatedly and stand firm upon it: "Worship the one God!" 

Pretending that you have discovered this alone in the whole matter, you pretend, with your lying conscience, that so many and such manifest witnesses for the <term>veneration</term> <note>The practice of honoring saints as holy examples and intercessors, distinct from the worship given to God alone.</note> of saints do not exist, just as you wish they never had. The demons tremble and fall down defeated at the tombs of the saints, confessing by means of the relics how much the souls of the elect are able to do in heaven. You did not learn this example from your father; instead, insanely leaping from body to spirit and from spirit back to body, you rage in insult against both. 

Since not only the blessed spirits, but the souls of all the dead—to use the words of Eusebius Pamphilus <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and bishop.</note> from the thirteenth book of *The Preparation for the Gospel*: **possess a certain power by which they help human affairs after death; for this opinion is true.** But unless it is proved by lengthy reasonings, one ought to believe such discourses because they have been handed down by men of great antiquity. Therefore, one must also believe those who confirmed by laws that these things are so. Certainly, the Jews contend that this was handed down concerning Jeremiah, and the Book of Maccabees <note>2 Maccabees 15:12–16, where the deceased High Priest Onias and the prophet Jeremiah appear in a vision to pray for the Jews.</note> reported that he himself was seen after death praying for the people. 

So great a man was Eusebius, to whom the entire library of the Greeks was known, who meets our Waldensians so notably in many respects: first, he asserts that one must not dissent from the ancient men, whom the Waldensians nevertheless reject in their stubbornness as if they were senile old women; second, he confesses the protection of souls. Third, he builds faith upon the Book of Maccabees, which they subsequently cast out from the number of sacred books as if it were useless. In these scriptures, we find intercessions from heaven to earth, and even from earth to the underworld <note>original: "tartarum"; referring to the place of the dead.</note>. But perhaps I seemed to have said something incredible regarding intercession "from earth to the underworld." But so it is, and the Gospel testifies to it: **"I beg you therefore, father Abraham," says the rich man at the feast, "that you would send..."** <note>Referring to the parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16:27.</note>

He uses the examples of Elijah, Eusebius, and the Book of Maccabees to argue that the souls of the departed have the power to aid the living and that this tradition is rooted in ancient history.</summary>

-># ON THE VENERATION OF SAINTS AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]<-

**"I have five brothers in my father's house; send him to testify to them, so that they do not also come into this place of torments."** <note>original: "Lazarum in domū patris mei habeo em̃ quinqꝫ fratres, vt teſteꞭ illis ne et ipſi veniant in hunc locū tormentorū"; This refers to the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus in Luke 16:27-28.</note> We hear intercession being made even in hell, yet they deny that it exists in heaven? This would mean the damned surpass the saints in the desire and the will to do good for their own. But they say: "He prayed, but he was not heard." Quite right, and this actually serves our cause, as this is already a mark of merit between the two groups. For what is not owed to a judged enemy, God does not deny to His elect; furthermore, he was asking for something unjust, which I shall explain more clearly in other places. But stand back! Come here, Christian people, lest—just as the snail <note>original: "climaca"; likely referring to a snail or slug (*limax*) which retracts its feelers/horns when touched.</note> pulls in its extended horns at every touch—so this snake, who is about to perish, might leap back into its den upon seeing us.

**"They have not called upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear,"** <note>Psalm 13:4-5 in the Vulgate; Psalm 14 in modern translations.</note> just as they do now regarding the holy men and women. He has come forth! Break out and surround him! Let us turn the dragon over on the pavement and count its spots; let us extract the poison with which he has now attempted to infect the saints and the Christian people. But so that this may be more firmly witnessed, the entire Psalm must be repeated: **"The fool has said in his heart: there is no God. They are corrupt and have become abominable in their ways; there is none who does good, no, not even one. The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any who understand or seek God. They have all turned aside; they have together become useless; there is none who does good, no, not even one. Their throat is an open sepulcher; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully; the poison of vipers is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and unhappiness are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known; there is no fear of God before their eyes. Will they not all know, those who work iniquity, who devour my people as they eat bread? They have not called upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear, for the Lord is in the generation of the righteous. You have confounded the counsel of the poor man because the Lord is his hope. Who shall give the salvation of Israel out of Zion? When the Lord turns away the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall be glad."**

This Psalm was written against idolaters and Jews who deny Christ, according to what John says in his <term>Canonical Epistle</term> <note>The General or Catholic Epistles of the New Testament.</note>: **"Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father; he who confesses the Son has the Father also."** <note>1 John 2:23.</note> And Saint Paul, in the **Epistle to the Romans**, interprets this Psalm generally regarding the human race, which was occupied with such pursuits of error before it was redeemed through the Son.

This argument of the Psalm, defined by the Apostles, has been twisted today by those men in their great madness to fulfill their insanity and defile the Christian faith. They do this so that whatever filth was once committed against God through idolatry might today return through the same thread among the faithful of Christ. And just as they previously attacked us with traps regarding carved images, so now, by the same feigned art—as if they were doing something else—they seek our throats again with hostile and infested souls. They contract the whole business here into one single opinion: namely, that since those people are "suspended" by the saints <note>The author uses "suspended" to mean relying on or looking toward the saints for help.</note>, they do not adore God. Therefore, that curse follows them: **"there they trembled with fear where there was no fear."** Thus they pronounce punishment upon us before they have proved us to be deserving of it. Certainly, they now rage against us in their eighth distorted passage, and they have not yet proved that we are "outside of God." Indeed, we have stood firm, and we are with God—a fact they willfully refuse to know. We have made this clear through the evidence of the Scriptures, so that it is necessary for them to know it hereafter. And even if we receive no other fruit from this than their own salvation, we shall nevertheless seize this most ample reward: that they will not dare, after this, to spread their lying "innocence" and "religion" among the common people as they used to do. They may dare, perhaps, but they will be rejected as the foulest deserters of the <term>orthodox faith</term> <note>Meaning "correct belief" or the established teachings of the Church.</note> and as pestilential schemers against our salvation. Indeed, the Christian people [will reject] their arts, their perfidy, and their wicked deeds—these defections meditated under this appearance of a "new superstition" and these overthrows of those who think rightly—as this work of ours suggests.

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK TWO

He will take more diligent care in the future, perceiving henceforth how deadly they are going to be to us. Even in their small number, they do not restrain themselves from breathing out a savage hatred against us. They act as if they were our conquerors, or as if they had seized us like Syrian slaves for sale with chalked feet. <note>original: "Syros gypsatis pedibus venales"; In Roman slave markets, foreign-born slaves were often displayed with their feet whitened with gypsum to distinguish them to buyers. The author implies the Waldensians treat Catholics like low-status captives.</note> They show no honor to any high rank or nobility, nor to any provinces or cities that have ever venerated the glorious Virgin and the Saints. They strike us openly in the face, subjecting us to every kind of servile shame. In the hearing of the most illustrious Prince, and before the very eyes of Hungary, Bohemia, and Moravia, these defiant men hurl their insults. 

The most pious King spoke regarding this crime of their lack of veneration for the Virgin Mary and the Saints of God:

> The fool has said in his heart: there is no God. Their throat is an open sepulcher; they have acted deceitfully with their tongues; the venom of asps is under their lips. Their feet are swift to shed blood. The nobles of the most powerful kingdoms are corrupted and have become abominable in their pursuits. They have all turned aside and together have become useless; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Destruction and misery are in their ways. There is no fear of God before their eyes, those who devour my people like a piece of bread. They have not called upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear. <note>This is a composite quotation of Psalm 14 (Psalm 13 in the Vulgate), which the author uses to characterize the Waldensians as morally and spiritually bankrupt.</note>

The cause of such great divine punishment is that you, who are worshippers of the glorious Virgin and the Saints, have confounded the counsel of the poor Waldensian <note>The Waldensians often called themselves "The Poor of Lyon."</note> because his hope is in God alone. You wished to compel him to venerate the heavenly powers; then, considering the times they are currently bringing forth, they behave as if they were declaring war. Thus they apply the rest of the Psalm to themselves:

> When the Lord shall have turned away the captivity of His people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall be glad. <note>Psalm 14:7.</note>

They call this very obedience to the King "captivity"; they pray against it and threaten rebellion. This is what they conceive, and this is what will first break out if they are able to rely on public negligence or their own strength. 

But they call me violent, saying I stir this matter more deeply than I ought. I admit I move it more deeply than they would like, but far less than I should. I say this from my conscience: my strength fails me, and the atrocity of their will—which they have raised against us here—overcomes my speech. Let us consider the matter of the Psalm they have heaped upon us; nothing more grave could be found against the Christian name than that which is attributed to every unspeakable and hateful superstition, namely that it should be applied to us:

> The fool said in his heart: there is no God.

The Turk does not struggle with us over such a great deposit of faith. The Turk is fairer to us than the Waldensian. <note>A common rhetorical strategy in the 16th century was to claim that "heretics" were worse than the "infidel" Turks.</note> He does not fight us regarding God, but regarding the Prophet <note>original: "p̃pheta"; referring to Muhammad.</note>; nor does he so greatly reproach Christ, provided we accept Muhammad along with Christ. But these people, with their pestilential "Waldensian piety" regarding our devotion to the Virgin Mary and the Saints, claim we are "without God," that we are everything impure and foul, and everything subject to God's curse. For they even condemn those concerning the Chalice <note>original: "calice"; Likely referring to the Utraquists, a moderate Hussite faction in Bohemia/Moravia who insisted on the lay chalice. The author suggests the Waldensians even look down on their fellow dissidents.</note>—whom they sometimes wish to call their best friends—by the same standard. Since the Church of Olomouc <note>original: "Olomucensis"; Olomouc was a major bishopric in Moravia and a center of Catholic counter-reform efforts.</note> has a somewhat fuller catalog of saints, they ought to have pitied their companions; but now, wherever they are free from danger, they care nothing for them. 

But when the royal punishment presses them, these most vile fugitives want those others to be their partners in dissent so that they may shake the kingdom more violently. Like bats, they fly now to one side and now to the other, prevaricating to stir up public evil. If we drag these deceits and this danger of ours out of the corner and into the open arena, are we being violent? Not at all. For they themselves have brought this upon themselves: "they have not called upon the Lord." We did not impose this on them. Such a thing could not be said against us without the authority of those above. Take away "The fool said in his heart," take away the rest, and there is no longer a place for that verse "They have not called upon the Lord"—truly, to the great laughter of their own, and the bitterness of ours...

...they found in their mockery; they did not call upon the Lord. It certainly cannot follow unless from what preceded: remove the crime and the punishment ceases. With such blasphemies against us, Waldensian, you consider our patience to be folly. For although in your prologue you claimed you would be an emulator of that saying, "Do not return evil for evil," that you would not paint words, nor deceive the King, nor lead the people to you with diabolical deceits—having promised to be open in those things desired of you—and although in the work itself you were not going to stand by one or all of these promises; nevertheless, from this stage-setting, like a fowler who traps thrushes under a cloth <note>original: "sub panno auceps turdos"; a metaphor for a hunter using a concealed net or cloth to catch birds, suggesting the Waldensians are using a "cloak" of piety to trap the souls of the common people.</note>, you labor to detain us so that we suspect no evil lurking beneath. From this crafty service, we might hope for something harmless from your puppet, who later was surely going to strike with a stone. 

I compel you, nobles: see whom you are nurturing for yourselves! Learn from one **Žižka** <note>Jan Žižka (c. 1360–1424) was a famous Czech general and Hussite leader. Though the Waldensians and Hussites were different groups, Catholic polemicists often grouped them together as a single revolutionary threat to social order.</note> what awaits public safety. You nurture as many Žižkas today as there are heads of Waldensians—whether you who are in that faction or you who tolerate them. Since you lead pure blood worthy of your lineage, consider that your ancestors were not such as these. Emulate both their piety and prudence; among them, this filth and internal evil could neither take root, nor be retained, nor finally even be known at all. 

They are not obscurely insane; they even now meditate on seditions. Long ago you became vile to them; long ago they wrote against the Royal Majesty and against you—to whom they have now for the third time given an account of their faith. <note>original: "fidei rationem nunc tertium dederunt"; likely referring to the various "Confessions of Faith" that the Bohemian Brethren/Waldensians submitted to King Vladislaus II between 1503 and 1508 to prove their orthodoxy.</note> According to their "serpentine prudence," they believed they should not give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine. Long ago they considered you as outsiders to themselves, using that apostolic phrase for their own benefit: *Behave prudently toward those who are outside.* <note>A reference to Colossians 4:5. The author is incensed that the Waldensians view the established Church and the nobility as "outsiders" or "dogs."</note> They confess that they have nothing in common with the desire of your souls. 

They remain, however, only as long as the fear of the King has power over them; they remain in their duty until the time for which they sigh arrives: *When the Lord has turned away the captivity of His people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall be glad.* <note>A quote from Psalm 14:7/53:6, used here to suggest the Waldensians are waiting for a moment of political weakness to revolt.</note> Meanwhile, they profane us as dogs and swine, and "prudently" turn toward us who are "outside." Every Christian estate is blasphemed as impure, contaminated, and defiled. The most holy Roman Pontiff, his apostolic assembly, all the majesty of the Christian name in every kingdom, and even your most pious King Vladislaus and all his nobility—to whom they have now for the third time sent the **whitewash** of their confession—are considered dogs and swine, unworthy to grasp the inner workings of the Waldensians. 

There remain—I do not say mysteries, but sacrileges—which only the Waldensians should hear from the **Cave of the Sibyl** <note>The Sibyl was a legendary prophetess in Roman myth; her cave at Cumae was a place of occult secrets. The author is accusing the Waldensians of practicing "pagan" or "occult" secrecy rather than Christian openness.</note> or inspect from her leaves. In this manner were the Heretics who, because of a peculiar knowledge they falsely arrogated to themselves alone, called themselves **Gnostics**—a proud name even if it had been given to heaven. Following this example, the Waldensian **Simoniacs** <note>Followers of Simon Magus, often associated with the sin of buying church offices, but used here as a general slur for heretics who pervert the faith.</note> spoke of certain ineffable things among themselves which, due to their power, could neither be written nor spoken. For they asserted that whoever perceived them in his mind would be driven out of his wits and lose all his senses. In truth, such things were of the sort that could be established by no author but a sorcerer, and could be tolerated by no chaste ears because of their obscenity. Thus, their secrets remained so out of necessity, because they dreaded public judgment due to their filthiness. 

Christ admitted us to the Gospel which had been hidden for ages; the Apostles gave us their preaching; the sublime commentators of the Church communicated the expositions of the Law and the Gospel. In this age, those things are considered nothing; they are thought profane, trampled by swine and dogs, compared to those things which the **rustic Waldensian** envies us for from his **plow**. ...found upon closer inspection: whatever we may finally think of it, it is certainly judged so divine by him that he commands the divine scriptures be removed from their place before he lets it go; the Christian world would sooner yield than submit to this sacrilege. They sharpen their minds for dissension, and they lead away whomever they can as external accomplices. Through their influence—which is all they are capable of today—they train raw minds with such curses, just as they once intended to train them with arms. But I might be laughed at there by the prudent. They might throw that line at me: "What if the sky should fall now?" <note>original: "quid si nunc coelum ruat"; a classical proverb meaning to worry about impossible or unlikely disasters.</note> Let this be my folly, if it means guarding against the rocks before the shipwreck; let me be foolish for now, so that those who know nothing may seem wise. Yet let them not be ignorant of this: it is our ancient custom to be wise only after the fact. But let that pass; let them yield to the judgment of the powerful.

I will press on with this business privately; I will examine within myself, in silence, the rest of what these **vipers** <note>original: "hi colubri"; a common derogatory term for heretics in medieval polemics, suggesting they hiss poisonous doctrines.</note> hiss out under this verse. For now, as if they had conquered and were carrying off the final prize of the contest, they depart with a bitter curse tossed at us, leaping away at an inopportune moment. They "did not invoke the Lord," and because of this crime, we trembled—in their opinion—with "fear where there was no fear." <note>A reference to Psalm 14:5 / 53:5.</note> But we have clearly shown many times that we do adore God. In doing so, we follow the examples of the ancients so holily, while they themselves have abandoned those same examples to their own harm. But because we speak to the ungrateful, who think what is said has not been said, let me be forgiven if I dwell on the same point so often; I cannot allow them to overcome me by sheer numbers. It is not fitting for a proponent of the truth to be rare, when defenders of error wish to be so famous. Let them hear it then, even if they are unwilling; let our diligence conquer their stubbornness. Let them finally, in some way, admit into their ears what they have not yet admitted of their own will: we do invoke the Lord.

Take an example of this that is not obscure, nor is it a newly conceived idea for the sake of maintaining grace. The ecclesiastical books of the night and day offices are full of witnesses. There, in all the **prayers** and **collects** <term>Collect: A short, structured prayer used in the Catholic liturgy that "collects" the intentions of the people.</term>, it is placed before your ungrateful eyes how the Church adores God in this way:

> Grant, merciful God, protection to our frailty, so that we who celebrate the memory of your holy **Mother** <note>Referring to the Virgin Mary.</note> may rise from our iniquities through the help of her intercession.
<note>original: "Cõcede misericors deus fragilitati nostræ presidiũ vt qui sancte tue genitricis memoriã agimus intercessionis eius auxilio a nris iniqtatibus refurgamus."</note>

What will you say is foreign to piety here? What is similar to someone who does not invoke God? What is similar to admitting idolatry? For indeed, the prayer is made to God through the merit of another. And God Himself confesses that He took up the people of Israel through the merit of no one but the Patriarchs; for He says thus through **Isaiah**: *And you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham my friend, in whom I have taken hold of you.* <note>Reference to Isaiah 41:8-9.</note> Prick up your ears at this example, Waldensian! If you judged our ways to be wicked, why did you not bring it out into the public? You would have stirred up shame in us. You would have reviewed every one of our points to the last detail. You would have disputed those things, and the neighbors would have understood that you were not pursuing a blind suit, a suit without a name. But then you fled. No one believes you; but let us grant that you did flee. Therefore, later: if you are going to return to us, stand firm here. Press us here. Fight this knot. You will never better your case unless you overturn our firmest foundations. 

But how does it happen that all those who harass others through slander are the kind of people who shouldn't have to be fought with great effort from afar, but could be held by their own defenses—or rather, their own weapons? That is to say, they are liars; they are vain; they are contrary to themselves; they are forgetful of their own words; they are exposed and full of holes. Unless, of course, they resort to evasion. Look at those ancient heretics: **Arius**, **Sabellius**, **Nestorius**, **Eutyches** <note>These were leaders of major early Christian heresies regarding the nature of the Trinity and Christ: Arianism (denying Christ's divinity), Sabellianism (denying the distinction of the persons of the Trinity), Nestorianism (over-emphasizing the distinction between Christ's human and divine natures), and Eutychianism (denying Christ's human nature).</note>. They were men who were very clever, both by their own wit and by their advocate, the devil. Yet how frivolous they were found to be, how weak in their own fortifications! They are not obscurely insane; they are even now meditating on seditions. Long ago you became vile to them; long ago they wrote against the Royal Majesty and against you—to whom they have now for the third time given an account of their faith—against your very selves. Long ago they considered you "outsiders" to themselves, for which they have usurped that word of the Apostle for their own benefit:
> **Behave wisely toward those who are outside.** <note>original: "conuersamini prudenter ad eos qui foris sunt"; Colossians 4:5.</note>

The most holy Roman Pontiff and his apostolic assembly, the majesty of every kingdom of the Christian name, and even the most pious King **Vladislaus** <note>Vladislaus II (1456–1516), King of Bohemia and Hungary, who faced significant pressure from various religious factions during his reign.</note> and all his nobility—to whom they have now for the third time sent the "whitewash" of their confession—are considered dogs and swine, judged unworthy to perceive the inner workings of the Waldensians.

There remain—I do not say mysteries, but sacrileges—which only the Waldensians are permitted to hear from the **Cave of the Sibyl**, <note>A reference to the Cumaean Sibyl of classical mythology who delivered prophecies from a cave; used here to suggest the Waldensian teachings are pagan or occult rather than Christian.</note> and which they alone should inspect from the leaves. For they asserted that whoever perceived them would be driven from his mind and exceed all his senses. When in truth, such things were established by no author but a Magician; by none could they be tolerated by chaste ears because of their obscenity. Thus these secrets remained hidden out of necessity, because they shuddered at public judgment on account of their filthiness.

You will never have better success in your cause unless our strongest defenses are captured.

## ON THE VENERATION OF SAINTS AGAINST THE [WALDENSIANS] ##

Since he could not use God to refute the truth, he turned away from there and worked to cover himself by stitching together rags from everywhere, piece by piece, just to create a superficial appearance of truth. In this way, our Waldensian, when he accused the Christian of bowing down at the memorials of the saints—where he should have recognized from what vows we truly venerate the saints if he had investigated the matter fully—instead abstains from that and fabricates a case out of his own whim. Wherever he sees just two words together—for example, "God" and "adore"—he collects them, caring little for their internal meaning, provided they paint a superficial face on his argument. 

Thus prepared, he comes forth from his new heresy into public view. He is like someone who, happening upon an armed traveler in a deep forest, rashly judges him a robber out of a fearful disposition, without exploring the man's intent, simply because of the location and the weapons. Similarly, the Waldensian, seeing a Christian in a posture of veneration toward the saints, wickedly curses him as an idolater without judgment of the fact and without mercy, shouting that "he did not call upon the Lord." If there is any punishment destined by God for idolaters—namely, that "they trembled with fear where there was no fear"—he thrusts this upon Christian piety out of sheer resentment. 

And could he be ignorant that not every act of adoration besides that offered to God falls into the crime of idolatry? He surely reads of **dulia** <note>original: "duliam"; a theological term for the honor or veneration given to saints and angels, distinguished from "latria," which is the worship due to God alone.</note>—that is, veneration—celebrated both openly and frequently in the Scriptures, entirely beyond the reach of any blame. This is seen in many places, such as in the **Second Book of Kings** <note>In the historical Vulgate Bible, the books of 1 and 2 Samuel were titled 1 and 2 Kings; this reference corresponds to 2 Samuel 14:4.</note>, when the woman of Tekoa entered to the King, "fell before him upon the earth and adored him," and said, "Save me, O King." A little later, "Joab, falling upon his face to the earth, adored and blessed the King." And in another place concerning Ahimaaz: "Hail, King," and he "adored the King before him, prone upon the earth," saying, "Blessed be the Lord your God." 

If our Waldensian shows the same nose <note>A Latin idiom (original: "eundem nasum") for a mocking or critical attitude.</note> toward these passages as he does toward us and the present writing, he will be forced to hurl many injustices there. First, that the Scripture either remained silent or did not disapprove of a bad example; second, that those who offered these greetings committed an injury against the Divine by "adoring"; and finally, that the Prophet David permitted a rivalry in himself like one who, having seized divine honors for himself, led the whole human race into idolatry. Because it is a sin to say these things, and because those men preserve their innocence, it follows that there is a **middle form of adoration** <note>original: "media adoration"; a form of reverence that is higher than common courtesy but lower than divine worship.</note> below **latria** <note>original: "latriam"; the highest form of worship reserved for God.</note>. 

Because the Waldensian ignores this, he is surely guilty, since he condemns what is innocent. Those who understand this distinction will be innocent, as they have piously transferred the example of the Scripture and the King to heavenly things. He will be the guilty one who, out of mere whim, perverts what has been taken from such great authority. 

But I ask, Waldensian, what then is that phrase: "they trembled with fear where there was no fear"? What is that fear? Or who are those trembling? Tell us more clearly, for we long to hear. But you are silent. Truly, we shall track down the secret of your mind without you. You said, "they did not call upon the Lord," and immediately added, "there they trembled with fear." Therefore, you have twisted against us that very curse which the Lord, through Moses, calls down upon idolaters: "If you will not hear the voice of the Lord your God... the Lord shall deliver you to fall before your enemies; you shall go out one way against them and flee seven ways." 

But what were they doing, those about whom these things were written? "They walked according to the rite of the gentiles," as the **Fourth Book of Kings** <note>In the Vulgate, this refers to 2 Kings 17:8-16.</note> records, "whom the Lord had consumed in the sight of the children of Israel. And they built for themselves high places in all their cities; they made for themselves statues and groves on every high hill and under every leafy tree, and there they burned incense upon the altars in the manner of the gentiles whom the Lord had removed from before them. They made for themselves two molten calves and groves, and they adored all the host of heaven." But in what way did they adore? "I will go after my lovers who give..."

"my bread and my waters, and my wool and my flax, and my drink" <note>This is a reference to the Book of Hosea 2:5, where the unfaithful Israelites attribute their basic necessities to false idols (their "lovers") rather than to God.</note> — those worshipers of demons and elements truly did not call upon God. They attributed divine blessings to impure demons. As we have shown from Hosea, since they received these gifts from such sources, a divine vengeance deservedly followed them because of the crime of their unfaithfulness and ingratitude. "There they trembled with fear where there was no fear," <note>A quote from Psalm 14:5 or 53:5, often used to describe the irrational terror of the wicked.</note> and "you shall go out by one way and flee by seven." <note>Deuteronomy 28:25; a biblical curse for disobedience.</note>

Here, because the Waldensian has transferred such a steep impiety—plucked from a different context—onto a different person, to him a Christian is the same as a worshiper of demons. To him, a Saint in heaven is the same as an impure demon from hell. Let the Waldensian, that destructive defamer of the Christian name, say: who are they in the entire Christian world who tremble due to the crime of impiety alongside their saints and the Virgin Mary? 

You may not know distant histories, but your own neighborhood holds a deep peace on all sides; we pray to God that you may be allowed to hold it for a long time. Consider the Hungarians, who are most devoted to the glorious Virgin. I do not see them trembling before the Turk <note>The Ottoman Empire, the primary military threat to Christian Europe at the time.</note>, whom they have as a perpetual enemy. The Turk—whom neither the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, nor the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, nor the Aegean and Ionian seas, nor that great and most populous Asian Chersonese <note>The Anatolian Peninsula</note>, nor so many famous islands, nor the whole of Greece could block—is held back by the terror of the Hungarian name. It powerfully keeps this most proud victor of so many kingdoms and peoples from its borders. 

Their veneration of the holy men and women and the glorious Virgin Mary is no obstacle to them before God. Indeed, helped by her alone, they are capable of so much. But I hear you well: if they were to go to ruin—may the most powerful King Vladislaus <note>Vladislaus II (1456–1516), King of Hungary, Bohemia, and Croatia.</note>, after God, turn that omen back upon your own head!—if the affairs of the Hungarians suffered any loss, you would shrink into your corner, you would exult among your accomplices, and you would play out a song of the kind the Scriptures record concerning Pharaoh or Sisera <note>Biblical enemies of Israel whose defeats were celebrated with songs of victory.</note> over the public calamity. You would mockingly say: "they did not call upon the Lord, here they trembled with fear," just as our Hungarians do regarding the holy men and women and even the Virgin Mary. 

But the affairs of the Hungarians flourish. The worshiper of the saints and the Virgin lives happily, and despite your wishes, he shall live happily henceforth. Indeed, what just occurred to me is this: the Kingdom of Poland has in these years endured heavy calamities from the Vlach <note>People from Wallachia (modern-day Romania).</note> and the Tatar <note>Turco-Mongol nomadic people known for raids into Eastern Europe.</note>, yet the Poles have a most holy temple of the glorious Virgin in Częstochowa <note>original: "Czefthochou"; refers to the Jasna Góra Monastery in Poland, home of the Black Madonna icon.</note>, of most celebrated fame even among foreigners. Here, as I recall, they insult the German Kingdom, and in the midst of public grief, it is enough for them to indulge their hostile spirit, to pursue the slain with such mockery. Whether people are returning from slaughter or being carried off into barbarian captivity, you [Waldensians] pursue them with this cursed bitterness: "you trembled with fear from the veneration of saints where there had been no fear from the piety of God." 

Thus, whatever sin is committed either through human imprudence (as against the Vlach) or through the rebellion of a subject (as against the Tatar), the saints in heaven are punished for it. Crossing over earthly faults, the Waldensian imposes this on heaven so that he may disparage how things are going poorly on earth. But we have said enough against the Waldensians, those haters of the Christian cause. From just one little verse, we have drawn out the desire of their hearts which they conceive against our private and public interests. 

And yet they do not stop there; instead, by involving themselves against the heavenly and eternally blessed spirits, they open a foul mouth full of horrifying sacrilege in contempt of the saints, which is far more deadly. First, because these sacrilegious Waldensians have adapted the prophetic voices—with which God strikes and curses impure demons—to the rejection of the saints. Second, because under the same reproach they intended for us, they simultaneously seize upon all the saints whose deeds they rebuke under our institutions. They make the saints incur all the testimonies of lying boasting which they wanted us to incur. They cast at them: "they did not call upon the Lord," and they thrust upon them this curse: "there they trembled with fear..."

### WALDENSIANS BOOK TWO ###

...under the guise of the memory of the saints, you reproach us as if it were our own infamy. You act just as Sennacherib did <note>Sennacherib was an ancient King of Assyria who laid siege to Jerusalem and famously mocked the God of Israel.</note>, writing blasphemies against the Most High God and insulting King Hezekiah, the King of kings, with words such as these: "Just as the gods of the other nations were not able to deliver their people, so the God of Hezekiah will not be able to rescue his people from this hand." 

In the same blasphemous way, you treat the Virgin Mary—the mother of both God and man to the Christian people, she who is exalted above the choirs of angels, and after whose Son the heavenly orders see nothing higher or more powerful in heaven. You cast her, who was pre-elected by God, against us today as a reproach, as if she were some pagan idol. You speak with the voice of that impious King, as if she were the idols Baalym and Astaroth <note>Baal and Astarte were ancient Canaanite deities frequently cited in the Bible as false gods or idols.</note>. You claim that the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, the children of Ammon, and the Philistines offered nothing for their suppliants in the sight of God, just as their idol-worshipping followers provoked the Lord to anger with the works of their hands by failing to invoke him, thereby stirring up divine vengeance upon themselves. 

Thus, you claim the saints and the Virgin Mary are worth nothing before divine mercy; you claim that those who venerate them do not invoke the Lord, and because they are seized by heavenly indignation, they now "flee with their saints and the Virgin Mary." Therefore, just as Sennacherib compared the true God to demonic gods, you do not shudder to compare the Mother of the only-begotten Son in heaven and on earth, Jesus Christ—and all the saints, those spirits most closely joined to God in whom the Trinity dwells and walks—with your polluted mouth to impure demons, those enemies banished from all heavenly grace. 

You have wrung this argument, Waldensian, until it bleeds <note>original: "Emunxisti... ad sanguinem." A reference to Proverbs 30:33, suggesting that pushing an argument too far produces strife or perversion, like wringing a nose until it bleeds.</note>. Now, God rebukes us for your opinion regarding his glorious Virgin Mother Mary, just as he rebuked the Jews for the superstition of the nations: "You have left me and worshipped foreign gods; therefore I will not add to your deliverance. Go and invoke the gods you have chosen; let them deliver you in your time of anguish." 

Thus, you would sooner mix heaven with hell <note>original: "tartaro," referring to Tartarus, the deepest abyss of the underworld.</note> than spare us from your madness, or show any ecclesiastical wisdom, or holily set aside what you have wickedly conceived. We find that you take the same offense at the sacred Virgin that others took at Astarte of the Sidonians; the same offense at Peter and Paul and all the saints that others took at Astaroth, at Baalym, and at all the host of heaven. If we scatter flowers upon the altars of the saints, you think we have "passed our son through the fire" <note>An ancient idiom for child sacrifice to the god Moloch.</note>. 

If the Ark of the Old Testament were to be placed in a temple dedicated to the glorious Virgin, and if any image of her were religiously placed there, you believe that by your blasphemy it ought to be found with broken limbs—just like the idol of Dagon of the Philistines was found shattered. You think the Divinity is so impatient with the memory of the Virgin and his own mother, and that he treats her with such contempt, as if she were an enemy of the Divinity rather than one of God's most chosen. 

You consider yourself insulted if a friend, with whom you thought you had influence, does not admit you when you are praying for someone else. Why then should the Virgin Mary—who is most closely joined to God—not obtain through her reverence and maternal right from her most loving Son, that which you hope to obtain through mere human friendship? You, who are filthy and stained, make yourself a patron to God for your own desires without any intermediary. Yet you will not allow the chaste and pure Virgin—blessed without end like the morning star and standing nearest to the divine throne—to be a patroness before God?

Be silent, you impure man! Cut off, bite back, and suppress your blasphemous tongue. Such are your deceits, which we have said elsewhere we would pluck like wool. We have finally looked inside; we have seen the "masked plays" <note>original: "personata ludicra," referring to deceptive or theatrical performances.</note> with which you were maddening us through your prologues and this confession of yours. We find your tongue suspended to the injury of God, the saints, and men—not just with your fingers [in writing] but with an impure mind and a stinging tongue. Those doctors of old, Henry and Augustine <note>Likely referring to Henry of Lausanne (an early heresiarch) and St. Augustine of Hippo.</note>, saw the same thing once. They rightly said that caterpillars and wasps—and not even the scarab beetle—are your gods. That is to say: a stinging God suits stinging men. But whether you swallow that same...

I suggest, however, that you soothe him. Thus he might be more favorable to you despite the sting. But you, most religious prelate, exercising your priestly authority against this blasphemy of the Waldensians—who derive the same crime from the honor of the saints as they do from the worship of demons—spread out this page of theirs, just as King Hezekiah once did regarding Sennacherib <note>In 2 Kings 19, King Hezekiah took a blasphemous letter from the Assyrian King Sennacherib and "spread it out before the Lord" in the Temple to ask for divine intervention.</note>, in the eyes of Almighty God. Perhaps now God, having been appeased, might prohibit from heaven such great errors for His people, which could not be prohibited from an earthly height up to the present day. Let them fall into the hands of Elisha; let them fall into priestly rebuke. For it is written: *And it shall come to pass, that him that escapeth the sword of Hazael shall Jehu slay: and him that escapeth from the sword of Jehu shall Elisha slay* <note>original: "erit quicũq̃ fugerit gladiũ Azachel occidet eum Iehu & quicũq̃ fugerit gladium Iehu interficiet eum Heliseus"; a reference to 1 Kings 19:17 regarding divine judgment on the unfaithful.</note>. May the Lord crush him swiftly under the feet of His saints.

->THE WALDENSIAN,<-

For there is no other name under heaven given to men in which we must be saved <note>A quote from Acts 4:12, used here by the Waldensian to argue that only Jesus, not the saints, can save.</note>. In this way, let us praise God in the saints and the Virgin Mary, because He gave such grace and such benefits to them out of His goodness, and to us through them. We call her blessed and happy, and we love and follow her according to our ability.

**[The Author responds:]**
They prescribe from this place how far we ought to recognize the saints. Therefore, regarding those who have been or are today of such greatness by divine grace, who would not celebrate them unless they were either a Jew or a pagan worse than that? Therefore, let the Waldensian understand that this is not sufficient piety: to confess the saints in this manner, which no one except the extremely impious can deny. For if the Waldensian believes he is doing well in this part, let him not immediately grow proud as if he were fully apostolic in the rest. Even the demons confess as much! From afar, the demon beholds the grace of the saints and gnashes his teeth. You see, therefore, that you still stand within the boundary of the demon and have not yet reached the Catholic position. 

But lest you complain that we do not know or that we neglect that part of the praise of the saints, listen. Regarding the glorious Virgin, we pray thus: *Holy and immaculate virginity, I know not with what praises to extol thee, for Him whom the heavens could not contain, thou didst bear in thy womb.* <note>original: "Sancta & immaculata virginitas q̃bus te laudibus efferam nescio..." This is a traditional Catholic responsory used in the Office of the Virgin Mary.</note> Likewise: *Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, blessed art thou among women.* <note>original: "Aue gratia plena dñs tecũ benedicta tu inter mulieres"</note> Furthermore, concerning the saints: *These are the holy men whom the Lord chose in unfeigned love and gave to them eternal glory.* And likewise: *The saints through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought justice, and obtained promises.* <note>original: "Sancti per fidem vicerũt regna opati sunt iustitiam adepti sunt repromissiões"; a reference to Hebrews 11:33.</note> 

But where you do not also rise with us from this proclamation of the saints so that you might also make them advocates, here you fail, as we have shown before. There, I say, you remain within the boundary of the devil, who likewise does not deign to make them patrons. Just as he himself does not do it, you likewise act as if you do not need their patronage. Just as the devil—your father who persuaded you of these things—is unable to have or to hope for the same. 

But what is this that you say: "and God gave such grace to them and to us through them"? Do you not by this saying allude to the patronage of the heavenly ones? Indeed, you seem to admit that the saints, through their merits, benefit the faithful. We have elicited this one thing from you, then: that it is not permitted for you to be a listless and ungrateful dissembler toward such great benefactors through whom we participate in divine grace. Let us hope you will give this voice to any saint: "Make me a sharer in your merits; through these, keep me commended to God in my final moments." What more is required of you by the apostolic rule? By such a small voice, you would already feel like a Christian. And certainly, as we said before, you see better things in the secret of your heart, yet to satisfy your hatred for our people, you defend the worse path. Because of this, I see that I must not labor so much to teach you the apostolic institutions as to make it open that you, of your own accord, have refused to follow them, having scorned them.

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK TWO: THE WALDENSIAN

### That if a Doctor or others should show from the law that we should exhibit more, up to that point; but if he ought to prove his faith with gentleness and through scripture, we believe he would act more mercifully toward others.

They demand many things here all at once. I was waiting, however, to see if they would find fault with any of our practices in such great number, and if they would declare it based on the present evidence. You act in this way, they say, yet Scripture teaches that it is not permitted to act so. Otherwise, it is the custom that he who brings a charge must also prove it; and unless he settles the matter, he should fall under the same penalty he seeks for the accused, being held to the law of retaliation <note>The "lex talionis" or law of retaliation: the principle that a false accuser should suffer the same punishment they intended for the accused.</note>. If this were not provided for, there would be no end to false accusations. In this, the Waldensian now sins against us; he abuses us at his own whim and fabricates a crime where nothing exists that even looks like a fault, except what he, as an adversary, intends. From this, he draws a suspicion of evil-doing, as if nothing could be upright once the Waldensian accuser has called it wicked. This is how the matter is handled: whatever he thrusts upon us, it should have been enough to have thrust it back at our adversary, provided we give an account of our actions. Therefore, we have yielded to his impudence even beyond custom.

We move forward voluntarily, and in the preceding sections, we have shown quite clearly, based on the sense of divine law, that seeking help from the saints, honoring them with kneeling, and greeting them with prayer is rightfully done by us. But I ask you: if there had been no law for us in this matter, would we therefore owe nothing to the inhabitants of heaven out of consideration for our own nature? On a solemn feast day, I go out in public in cleaner clothing to honor a saint; I abstain from my trade and from making profit. How is it that this is a sin if I do it outside of a specific commandment? You yourself voluntarily grant so much honor and a feast day to your married daughter. No one argues against it. We bend the knee to a friend of the supreme King; you demand Scripture for it, yet you bow at every harsh word to your own stern master or even just the prefect of a house. We, too, ask for some prophetic precedent for your action. Behold, what is not provided for in books is preserved by human discipline <note>The author argues that social etiquette and respect for authority are "human disciplines" that everyone follows without needing a Bible verse; therefore, religious "etiquette" toward saints should be treated similarly.</note>. Stand before him with your head covered and your knee stiff like a shapeless log; the next thing is that he will rebuke your stubborn rudeness with his fist, interpreting it as contempt, even though you perhaps sinned only out of peasant-like cloddishness. Shall the observation of the heavenly beings, therefore, be sought only from Scripture, and not also from the refined integrity of a noble mind? The whole Christian world stands as a witness of a better discipline to you; because you act not from reason but from hateful stubbornness, you not only fail to follow it but, moreover, you accuse it of being wicked. Believe one who is not under oath but tells the truth: that consensus of a more honorable institution will find you guilty—even without Scripture—of an offense against God and the saints.

Furthermore, you persist in asking whether God promised that He would do everything that we ask in the name of the most pure and select Virgin Mary, Mother of God. First, I do not know—since you say "everything"—what exactly you mean by "everything." Do you suspect that we ask her for things like inflicting injuries, taking revenge, the vain pomp of the world, fleeting riches, and all the wicked things that can be irrationally desired out of lust, and that we wish to obtain these from God through her? If you suspect that, you are clearly mocking us. For who would not understand that these are not the prayers of a sane man—to wish to ask for such things from heaven? Rather, we seek the remission of sins, the purification of souls, contempt for the present world, a ray of divine grace, a course of this life that is pleasing to God, a happy end, and all things that look toward this goal; we ask for these with effect from the most glorious Virgin, and we hope without doubt that these are provided to us from God through her. God promised us that He would do this, not only through the intercession <term>intercessio: the act of praying to God on behalf of another</term> of the Virgin and His mother, but also through that of His saints of lesser merit. When God is about to forgive the sin of Abimelech, He commands him to go to the patriarch Abraham; for thus the Scripture has it: *And God said to him: Now therefore restore the man his wife; for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live* <note>original: "nūc ergo redde viro suo vxorē. et orabit p te qa ppheta ē. et viues"; quoting Genesis 20:7.</note>. Then it follows that when Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech and his wife and his maidservants. And in an earlier place, when Lot prayed for the little city of Segor <note>Segor is the Vulgate name for the biblical city of Zoar, where Lot fled during the destruction of Sodom.</note>, the Lord said to him: *Behold also in this I have heard thy prayers, not to destroy the city for which thou hast spoken* <note>original: "ecce etiā i h? suscepi pces tuas vt nō subuertā vrbē p q locūt? es"; quoting Genesis 19:21.</note>. In Job also we read, after the Lord had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite...

# ON THE VENERATION OF SAINTS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

"My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends, because you have not spoken what is right before me as my servant Job has. Therefore, take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job and offer burnt offerings for yourselves; but my servant Job shall pray for you. I will accept his face <note>original: *faciem eius suscipiam*. A biblical idiom meaning "I will show him favor" or "I will accept his person."</note>, so that your folly may not be imputed to you." And it follows: "And the Lord accepted the face of Job; the Lord also turned toward the repentance of Job when he prayed for his friends." <note>These verses are from Job 42:7–10.</note> Those saints <note>referring to Job and the patriarchs</note> were still pilgrims <note><term>viatores</term>: literally "wayfarers," a theological term for human beings still living on earth, traveling toward their heavenly home.</note>; yet, unless they pray, the sins of others are not forgiven. All the spiritual gifts <note>original: *charismata*</note> of the heavenly saints are more perfect, through which they are more pleasing so that they may be heard. Therefore, the same reason that existed with God then—that he would not forgive sinners unless the saints prayed—remains now. Why should he wish to forgive our stubbornness if we neglect, or rather despise, those saints who have passed from us and are accepted by God in the heavens?

The reason for this divine decree has come down to us and is most well-known: "for the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers." <note>Psalm 34:15 or 1 Peter 3:12.</note> Therefore, if you pray to God without the support of the saints, you will necessarily be judged by the merit of the Patriarchs and the heavenly citizens. And like a Pharisee, you would have to untangle that Rule of John the Apostle, in which he so constantly decrees that "everyone who says he is without sin is a liar." <note>1 John 1:8.</note> Let us leave that aside; be whatever you are, whether in your own judgment or ours. If you do not hope to obtain from God everything that you holily ask for, you sin through distrust, despairing of divine goodness. If you do hope to obtain everything, it is in that same place where God promised he would do all things for you as he does for the saints. Therefore, we do not entrust our vows to the saints in vain. Do not think of these as mere dreams, and do not wonder any longer at our "superstition," as you attack it, which is in truth a piety attested by the Scriptures.

If we believe that the Son denies nothing to his most holy mother in heaven, the Church, because of that faith, ardently prays: *Hear us, for the Son honors you by denying you nothing.* Then, turning to Christ: *Save us, O Jesus, for whom the Virgin Mother prays to you.* For the sake of this reasoning of our practice, you would have done better to abstain from this quibbling, even if she herself stands with her Son before the Father so that she may be an offering <note>original: *hostia*</note> before God. To be sure, wicked men quibble at this point—men to whom nothing in heaven or earth has seemed so venerable that they would not attack it with their insults—against that image which bears the name "of Mercy." <note>Likely referring to the *Schutzmantelmadonna* or "Virgin of Mercy," an image of Mary sheltering the faithful under her cloak, which was often criticized by reformers.</note>

And so they deceive us, as if we, led astray by the simplicity of some Anthropomorphite <note><term>Anthropomorphite</term>: one who attributes human physical form or emotions to God or spiritual beings.</note>, were imagining these physical things as existing in the heavens. In truth, just as those heavenly things cannot be spoken of except in a human way, so they cannot be represented except through human figures. If he finds fault with us for this, let him likewise find fault with the prophetic visions: let him strike out a great part of Ezekiel, the forms of the four animals, and the "wheel within a wheel"; let him cast out the Apocalypse of John; let him explode the Acts of the Apostles, since in the vision of Stephen they say Christ "stood," though we confess him to "sit" at the right hand of the Father. Let them rail again against the Apocalypse because it signifies that Christ now walks even more freely, saying: *these follow the Lamb wherever he goes.* <note>Revelation 14:4.</note>

But in truth, whatever is attributed to such spiritual things must be accepted not according to physical positions and shapes, but in mystical ways. These things could not be offered to the capacity of human senses except in a human manner. But those men are ignorant of the power of the scriptures, or they are carried away by a deliberate ill-will, so that they fear to violate nothing so holy that they might not pluck from it some material for their ill-omened envy against us. Thus they rail against the image of the most pious Virgin Mother of Mercy which the Church has received. Whether they were previously ignorant of the example of Scripture by which this could be supported, let them now learn that it could be taken from prophetic similarities; or if they did know, I would warn these ungrateful men not to pretend from now on that they do not know. If, therefore, the Christian people devoutly [receive] the glorious Virgin, full of mercies, and the representation of her intercession from such an image...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK TWO

...expressed. Was it immediately necessary to confess that the same person was also a sacrifice? <note>original: *hostiam*. In this context, the author is mocking the Waldensian logic that for someone to be an intercessor, they must also be a sacrificial victim, like Christ.</note> O blindness! O obstinacy! As if the angel of Tobias <note>referring to the Archangel Raphael in the Book of Tobit</note>, when he commended the works of mercy of that holy man to God; as if that angel of whom we spoke at the beginning from the Book of Job, who is one among a thousand who prays to God for our guilt; or as if the priest who prays at the altar on earth for the people, could not intercede for them before God unless they also became sacrifices. 

But I see what I am doing. We have been stuck on this question for a long time, laboring much to show that the Waldensian accepts the intercessions of the saints, and we doubt whether we have yet persuaded this "stiff neck." <note>A biblical idiom for stubbornness.</note> Truly, I acknowledge my imprudence; it is by our own fault that we do not succeed, since we have attempted to persuade a Waldensian outside of his own Waldensian context. Therefore, let us admit him into the council; let us ask his opinion on what he decrees concerning such a great matter. And so, in his first confession to the Royal Majesty <note>likely referring to King Vladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary</note>, he says in these words:

> For we do not cease to pray assiduously to God for the long-lasting safety of your life and your noble offspring, living piously and innocently under your dominion.

You, Waldensian—you who then wanted it to be believed that you lived so piously and innocently, whom we later discovered living far more impurely and harmfully—you, who mock the saints: when you intercede for the king, are you going to be a sacrifice or not? Whatever you answer for your own cause there, you have answered for ours. Have you made yourself a sacrifice? The Virgin Mary is of an infinitely higher rank than a Waldensian, so that the same would apply to her. Have you *not* made yourself a sacrifice? Then we slip away from your trap; you urge us in vain to make the Queen of Heaven a sacrifice in order for her to intercede. 

But we wish to ask your opinion on the whole matter of advocacy. Are there intercessions, or are there not? You write in favor of both, but which do you actually confess? For you cannot be truthful in both. Are there intercessions? Then later, having trampled the Scriptures, denied the authority of the Holy Spirit, despised the Catholic saints, and harassed so many priests by tossing them about in both directions, you have most wickedly abolished them. You have most wickedly contended that the most Blessed Virgin in heaven cannot do what you—a shameless "Synagogue" <note>A derogatory term used here to describe the Waldensian community as an assembly of heretics.</note> and a professed enemy of heavenly and Christian things—have made yourself able to do on earth. 

Are there *no* intercessions? Then those things were mere lies which you then offered as truths to the most indulgent King; they were naked incantations with which you then demented the vigorous nobility and the entire state of the kingdom. Truly, my saying was correct: that you only study this confession so that you may speak with our words, while living by your own customs. Why then do you not cease? Why do you not strike out what you once so poorly feigned? Return to your true self. Or do you not think it enough to have once mocked us in a childish way with empty colors, unless you continue to mock us as long as this writing remains? 

But let us consider the fraud which they openly admit in the words of that sentence. They say: "But if a doctor or another should show from the Law, and the rest—" <note>The author is analyzing a conditional "if-then" statement from a Waldensian text.</note> Let us consider, I say, the sharpness of that Waldensian, lest we think him to be pure and manifest toward us in any part. He begins the sentence with a conditional clause; however, that type of speech never allows the sense to settle in itself, but always demands another joined clause to complete the thought. For example: "If you do well," and immediately another is joined, such as "you will receive a reward." The Waldensians have subtracted this kind of concluding phrase from their sentence. For after saying, "If a doctor or another should show that such things ought to be done toward the saints," one of two things should have immediately followed to complete the thought: either "then we wish to concede to his opinion," or "then we wish to rise up further." He could not opportunely confess either. Not the first, for he never thinks of being wise like a Christian; and not the second, for that would have betrayed his great malice, where he would have said he would spare neither himself nor the witness of truth. Thus, with the speech hanging, he exited into something else in this manner: "If a doctor or another should show that such things ought to be done toward the saints... let it be that Scripture shows this..." I ask, who of sound mind ever spoke thus?

### ON THE VENERATION OF SAINTS: AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...it was, unless perhaps it was a peasant from your own countryside, or someone else with no right but pure slander, rising up against the innocent and laboring to lead their ears astray with such trickery and verbal snares. Therefore you say: "Let scripture show this." To which I reply: Scripture has shown it, and we have brought forth testimonies of this matter in many ways—and in even greater numbers, had it not been necessary to look toward the end of this speech. Therefore, you have the canonical scriptures against you; what will you do next? Will you follow them? Or do you leave us here and turn back to something else, lest someone call you a heretic?

If Doctor Augustine <note>referring to the author himself, Augustine of Olomouc, writing in the third person</note> has called you a heretic, do not be angry. He has inflicted no injury upon you, nor anything foreign to your condition. You yourself spoke your opinion on this matter in your first confession, freely using these words: *“For we do not forge new dogmas or recent inventions of the Christian religion against the law of God.”* And a little later: *“Since indeed that very thing is not the mark of a man who is a true worshiper, but of a heretic himself, who understands neither sound faith nor the true worship of God.”* And since more things in that vein follow there, you were even then charging us with that same crime. 

At that time, however, we had nothing in hand with which we could dispute somewhat more evidently against one another. Therefore, it did not seem entirely possible then to dispel the suspicion of such a heresy from ourselves; everything was in a state of expectation and preparation. Thus, we have waited until now. Now, therefore, having found a better opportunity as expected, we convict you by the very same means by which you previously made us suspects. We shall continue to convict you with equal success, and we have proven by the very words of your testimony that you have waged an impious fight against God, against the saints, and against Catholics. By the law of retaliation, you now fall into the infamy which you intended for us through false slander.

Finally, there is something else that marks you as a heretic. You write in that same confession these words: *“Likewise setting forth the causes of our departure from the Roman Church.”* You, therefore, who so wickedly and boastfully confess that you have made a split from the Roman Church—whether you are addressed in Latin or in Greek, you are the same. Your cause loses nothing; you are the same thing you have made yourself. You have made yourself a "departer" <note>original: *discessor*. The author is playing on the etymology of "schismatic" (from Greek) and "discessor" (Latin) to show they mean the same thing.</note>. 

The purity of the Latin language uses that word less often, but it commonly uses "schismatic" or "heretic." If, therefore, a learned man avoids an unusual word and replaces it with the common one from the Greek, I do not want you to be angry; he takes it from your own words, and he does so by right. By that same right, I could also call you a "Pharisee" from the idiom of the Hebrew tongue, which signifies "departer" or "separated" even more expressively. You are a heretic and a Pharisee. The three languages which the Lord dedicated on his cross <note>referring to the Titulus Crucis, written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin</note> show you, as a "departer" in every way, to be a transgressor of the Gospel. Perhaps you brought this name upon yourself by that departure; Doctor Augustine did not impose it. 

Greetings, then, "departer." Greetings, heretic. Under these names, do you now hope to be rich in Christ? Or if you dodge the word "departure," you flee in vain. A more Latin term could not have been used; you never were truly "Latin." <note>The author implies that by leaving the Roman Church, the Waldensian has lost his claim to the Latin/Western Christian identity.</note> You went out from the Church; she did not go out from you. The Church endures in continuous succession for over one thousand five hundred years; you are a sudden thing. You departed recently. Today you are what your father or your most remote ancestor was not. 

You have arisen as a heretic more pestilent than all the rest. Some were impious only toward the divinity; some toward the power of Christ; some toward the glory of the Virgin Mary; others toward the ashes of the saints; others toward the purgation of souls. There were those who did not believe in the sacrament of the altar <note>The Eucharist</note>; many did not receive the ecclesiastical scriptures. Almost every individual defended an individual error. You, more harmful than all of them, have bound everyone together from one head with the same thread. You recall, restore, and defend all these things equally. You are impious not just in one article; you have prescribed nothing certain or defined for yourself. Only one thing is certain for you: disobedience, rebellion, and obstinacy. In this one head you conspire; from this you begin all wicked deeds without number and without limit. You yourself do not even know all your own betrayals...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK SECOND

...fashions his doctrine separately from a mad chapter, and as each man errs most, so is he most selected by you for the merit of rebellion. Therefore, that you have defected from the common Christian commonwealth in this way is by your own merit. If, just as a master calls his fugitive slave—without fault—by all disgraceful names: thief, evildoer, traitor, deserter; so the Church and every Christian, by their own right and by your own confession, calls you treacherous schismatics <term>schismatics: people who create a division or "schism" in the Church, separating from its authority</term> and heretics. 

Then there is this point: "What if he were a private citizen and did not hope in the power of the world?" If Doctor Augustine <note>The author, Augustine of Olomouc, often refers to himself in the third person</note> were a private teacher, what would you have done to him, secretly or openly? There you fall silent, and you break off the expected speech with your usual sharpness. Even if you growl fiercely, you flee under that proverb: *Thoughts are not subject to customs duties* <note>original: "Cogitationes ad portorium non debent" — a legal maxim meaning that one cannot be punished for thoughts alone, only actions</note>. But look at me: I am a private man, to such an extent that not even all my own household knows me by name; finish the rest of your speech regarding my person. Do not be afraid; in private you will be out of danger. But I understand the same thing myself: and for that reason I am more merciful toward you, lest at some point you fulfill upon me with iron or Aconite <note>Aconite: a deadly poisonous plant, often called monkshood, used historically for assassinations</note> that which you did not dare against Doctor Augustine. 

You add that if faith had to be proven by gentleness and scripture, it would be a "dislocated limb," neither fitting what came before nor what follows. For it follows: "We believe that he would act more gently with others." To what purpose is this, I ask? Is it from your gadflies and wasps—that you learn the scriptures under a single master in a three-day game? Have you been so well-taught there? No one else speaks thus; you believe that whoever has not been perfected by that sacred teacher of yours does not understand. 

But look, now for the fourth time you sin with the same craftiness and the same vice. For after you have set your path, you suddenly stifle it at the beginning and start something else; having begun something in your mind against us and then thinking it safe to stop, you show only from the goal what you wanted to run toward. You do this so that you may both have said it, and yet leave yourself the freedom to deny having said it. By this art, so often and so presently, you play against Doctor Augustine [saying]: "If he had to prove his faith with gentleness and scripture." You pretend this for one reason: because you now accuse yourself. You claim he cannot [prove it] by his style of speech nor by his knowledge of the scriptures. 

I, however, shall show—when by this labor of ours I cause to be made public the letters of that doctor which he wrote to a certain **John Black** <note>original: "Ioannem Nigri" — likely referring to Jan Černý, a prominent leader of the Unity of the Brethren/Waldensians</note>—that in these letters, contrary to what you accuse here, he explains both very kindly and learnedly what the error of the Waldensians is. A modest mind, which defends its errors truly out of error and not out of stubbornness, could have been abundantly recalled by those letters. But not every beast is driven by every goad. A spirited horse leaps into a jump at a light prick; a dull ox is barely moved even by a ring in its nose.

Nor is it true that we believe the Virgin is equal to other women, [and so on] up to the point: "nor is it true that we have no song about her, for we sing many songs about her in the praise of God."

It is not a question between me and you how glorious you believe the Virgin to be. In denying the patronage <term>patronage: the protective power and intercession of a saint on behalf of a believer</term> of the Virgin and the saints, you have been entirely focused on this: you have shown that you feel no better in these matters than a Heathen. You have summoned us to a contest on that point; there we stood against you. We have convicted you of being impious and a meddler, corrupter, and perverter of the sacred scriptures. You are held by this crime of your impiety; begin there, so that you may think like an Apostle. For as to believing the glorious Virgin is such and so great: how does this relate to the integrity of faith? 

We have shown before that more is owed. If you stand only at this step, what is this great piety of yours? Where is the holiness of the glorious Virgin? Even the powers of Hell <note>original: "tartareis Potestatibus"</note> confess her holiness to be great; was no more than that believed by you? Furthermore, you deny she will be an intercessor <term>intercessor: someone who prays to God on behalf of another</term> to be entreated for your salvation before Almighty God, just as the infernal spirits cannot hope for it; finally, you do not even believe...
