### WALDENSIANS BOOK THREE
### ON PURGATORY AND SUFFRAGES FOR THE DEAD, BOOK THREE,
<term>Suffrages: prayers, masses, or pious acts offered by the living on behalf of the souls in Purgatory to lessen their suffering.</term>

<margin>*e*</margin> For this let God be praised, as if that doctor <note>The "doctor" refers to the author himself, Augustine of Olomouc, writing in the third person or referring to his own arguments.</note> were responding up to that point and first concerning **Purgatory**, about which we believe thus:

They complain at the outset that they have been received poorly and in unworthy ways by Doctor Augustine; would that they complained justly! For a just complaint cannot proceed except from a just faith. Indeed, Doctor Augustine would even desire that a *just* Waldensian—that is, a Christian—might complain in this way about his own disparagement. But now, it seems to more impartial observers that nothing can be justly complained of in reality, except that the Waldensian was then abusing his own judgment, his speech, and the ears of men. However, after the matter came to judgment, he was found to feel quite differently than what he pretended to be in words.

The chief way they wanted to be believed innocent was by acting as if they had never felt anything against the law of God and the ancient church. Thus, since they agree in nothing with the present church, they contend among those unskilled in history as if whatever they themselves observe had been retrieved from the **primitive church**. <term>Primitive Church: the early Christian community of the first few centuries, which the Waldensians claimed to be restoring in its "pure" form.</term> Regarding this, I especially wonder—and all learned men wonder—since they are new, or rather the newest of sects, from where they have found out about these ancient customs? For what is to be retrieved from the law of God is sufficiently explained to all; but what is to be brought back from ancient observation must be remembered either from the commentaries of those who lived then or from the writers of the daily acts of that time.

They have put forward none of these. They only mention the bare names of **Dionysius** and **Athanasius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite and St. Athanasius, two foundational figures of early Christian theology whom the Waldensians often cited to claim antiquity for their beliefs.</note>, or they speak of a point where the matter is not in contention, and yet they say they are calling back the faith of these men. We, however, thought they would say something like: "The memory of the saints is not to be venerated," and that on this matter Dionysius writes in these words: "The Purgatory of souls is not to be confessed," or that Athanasius says something to this effect. They do none of these things.

We, however, have neglected nothing of such things up to now. If it concerned the law of God, we brought forward the law; if of ancient observation, we cited one of the ancient writers on the point; we confirmed present things from present evidence. Since, therefore, they could boast of nothing else than the bare names of the ancients—whom they boasted were champions they had not yet even seen, and whom they wanted to be believed as their own from afar—these very fathers have nonetheless joined *our* camp and fought with the greatest effort against them. The Waldensians deserved this, or even more, for their lying pretense, which is why Doctor Augustine accuses them.

They mention later the "modesty" they used in writing back. They often do the same in their apologies <term>Apologies: formal written defenses of one's opinions or conduct, particularly in a religious context.</term>; it is tiresome to remember, and the text is ready for all to read. They perhaps want to appear to have been modest, though in reality they never were. They could only appear modest to someone very simple who only notices when fists are flying. but to any more sharp-sighted person, the truth is now sufficiently indicated. To such a person, it is plainly visible how they have vexed heavenly and earthly things alike with every kind of insult; how they have atrociously cut off most powerful kingdoms, from the highest to the lowest, from our saints and the Virgin Mary.

Since, therefore, they were going to do everything through deceit, evil arts, and feigned innocence, it was my judgment that whoever would eventually care about these things and want to untangle their crafty minds should have made an agreement with them: that they should not bring forward any writing which they themselves had previously denied. For it was bound to happen that whatever witnesses they agreed upon would not testify to the things the Waldensians pretended they would; thus, the Waldensians would be shamed for open lying and heresy. For it cannot be that the primary men whom the Waldensian had accepted as apostolic <note>original: "apostolicos"</note> could be held as true and apostolic if they had actually thought the opposite of what the Waldensian claims.

# ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

...we will establish from the truth the faith concerning a certain purgatory here in this world. Before we descend into the dispute, we must explain what is being debated regarding Purgatory between the Catholic and the Waldensian—namely, in what points our adversary agrees with us and in what he dissents. It is necessary to know, therefore, that after souls are stripped of the body, three conditions entirely await them: either they are immediately blessed upon leaving the body, or they are immediately damned—regarding these two, no dispute arises between us. Or, the souls themselves are sent from the body into the pains of Purgatory, where the stains of earthly corruption, which they neglected to put away through full penance here, are washed away; once these are purged, they are finally received into the blessed seats. It is regarding this Purgatory that we are currently disputing against the Waldensian.

He is found now to admit this, now to deny it; now to concede it to the **ancient doctors** <note>The "Doctors" or "Fathers" of the Church: influential early Christian theologians whose writings established orthodox doctrine.</note>, now to resist them; now to prove it, and now again to argue against the same proofs. Finally, while he wavers for a long time between both sides, he ends up concluding that there is no Purgatory after this life; yet in this, he is neither certain nor consistent with himself. For at one moment he claims the ancient fathers felt this way, and at another that they did not. Truly, he repeatedly says they felt contrary to themselves and the scriptures.

Therefore, he persists in this alone: that whatever guilt we who are living have laid down here, that alone is set aside. Beyond that, nothing is to be hoped for from divine indulgence. We also confess that **satisfaction** <note>The performance of penance to repair the harm caused by sin.</note> in this world is both most acceptable to God and by far the most fruitful for us. However, for one who has deferred this or not sufficiently fulfilled it, and yet died in the unity of the Church—that is, in the communion of the sacraments—to treat him, because of a **venial** <note>A lesser, pardonable sin that does not result in complete separation from God's grace.</note> fault, as if he were the devil, Herod, or Judas, and thrust him into outer, unending darkness, would be to act entirely against divine clemency. For whatever God had forgiven through penance or released from the weight of punishment, we would be calling back into the category of a criminal act through our own lack of mercy.

Here, therefore, the apostolic truth opposes the Waldensian; in this, we do not agree with the heretic. Here, asserting divine mercy, we restore it to human frailty. To achieve this, following the order to which they themselves call us, we proceed against them thus: They say there is a twofold Purgatory, but that the second one is uncertain and unattested by sacred scripture, and that neither the Church nor the Doctors knew of it for a long time.

I ask you, Waldensian: how many years will you stretch that "long time"? I hope you will grant six hundred years—that is, the time from the Apostles to the age of the great **Pope Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory I (r. 590–604), known as Gregory the Great, who was pivotal in formalizing the doctrine of Purgatory.</note>, a span during which almost the entire flower of the most learned men flourished. It is not irrelevant that such a point is established between us, and that you define by a certain time those Doctors whose faith you pretend to emulate. For you will not deny those same men to us, to whose faith you have presently bound yourself.

Based on that condition, I now say that you are lying about all these things. You have brought forward no such Doctors; you have corrupted these scriptures on this matter, erased those, and bypassed others. For when you said the ancient Doctors do not confirm this, it was all too clearly false. Therefore, you restrict your opinion by that [ <insert> principally concerning the location </insert> ]. Because of this "location," which you wished to remain unestablished, you turn against the whole cause and say there is no purging of souls after death. And since there are some of our own who differ even regarding the location, you ought to have inquired further regarding the location—whether they had found it according to the opinion of the ancients or against it. There, concerning the location, which alone was then in your speech, you fail, and you accuse our people as if they had devised an unheard-of thing concerning the entire purging of souls, which the ancient Church and the saints of that time did not know. This, however, is a deception of the sort that a traveler might report to me as a punishment which, before this time, the Kings inflicted on the Waldensians for their treachery—either a prison or...

He challenges the Waldensian claim that Purgatory was a late invention, citing the era from the Apostles to Pope Gregory the Great.</summary>

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE

...should keep silent about the name, let another come who remembers the prison; I would contend that this man is false, not only regarding the location but regarding the entire punishment of the Waldensians <note>The author is likely referring to a specific historical account or witness whose testimony he disputes</note>, telling tales unknown to previous reports. The Waldensians now practice this trick on us: the authority of the ancient fathers is too heavy for them and too well-attested in the world for them to openly disagree with it without great ill-will. Therefore, when they encountered the **Modern Doctor, Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a "modern" scholastic theologian compared to the earlier Church Fathers.</note>, they found in his works a place for Purgatory—though he was neither the first nor the only one to speak of it. Thinking this man a convenient target for their insults, they return under his name to attack all the ancients in a similar way. They falsely charge that whatever the Church feels today on this matter is an error derived from this author, while the ancients are ignored.

And they want this to seem attested by **Aurelius Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note>, because he said the location of Purgatory was not clearly demonstrated. Since it is well-established by many examples that souls were tormented, they use this to rail against Thomas Aquinas, as if he were the first who dared to establish a specific location for Purgatory, contrary to what the ancients believed—namely, that after the Lord’s resurrection, no souls enter the Underworld except those of the damned. 

O insane heads, you Waldensians! As if Saint Augustine, when he said souls are tormented but did not show the place, thought they were tormented nowhere! For surely that which is tormented nowhere is not tormented at all. He understood there was a place, but whether he should call it "this way" or "that way," he remained silent at that time. But why does the Waldensian labor so? He wishes to turn us away from the established cause. For the question now at hand is whether souls, stripped of their bodies, are purged for penance that was not fully satisfied. This is the main point; let us hold to this. 

Look, here is the faith of Aurelius Augustine for you. Do you accept it? You certainly pretend to. Here, then, is the purgation of souls established by an ancient doctor, just as you desire, witnessed by the ancient Church in which the holy Augustine wrote, and outside of which he never felt anything. You have offered him to us of your own accord without being asked. I ask you then, Waldensian: what do you think Saint Thomas felt regarding the torments of souls? Surely, the same as Aurelius Augustine. For he who spoke of "Purgatory"—or, if you prefer, a "place of torment"—said it because he also understood that souls are tormented somewhere. For "Purgatory" draws its name from the act <term>purgation</term><note>The process of cleansing or purifying.</note> which is carried out there. 

Finally, his own books are witnesses to his faith; I appeal to them. He is therefore not opposed to Aurelius Augustine. He did not devise anything new out of greed or for profit—charges you heap upon this holy man with impudent lies, even now when he has overcome mortality and reigns happily with Christ. The Church of our time has received nothing new or unknown to the ancient institutions from this same Saint Thomas. Rather, it is proven that she has retained this rule of faith from the time of Saint Augustine down to us, and from the time of the Apostles down to Saint Augustine; and so, through the same Aurelius Augustine, from the Apostles down to us again. 

But you, mixing falsehoods with truths without end, have labored to throw a labyrinth in the way of the Doctor, the Royal Secretary <note>A reference to the author's own professional status or perhaps a high-ranking contemporary official</note>, and finally to mock the ecclesiastical commentators by the same act regarding the faith, urging him with your mockery to harmonize those who disagree. But you do this out of your own ill-will, for Catholics throughout the whole world agree more harmoniously in the Apostolic rule than any one of you agrees with your own peculiar leader. 

But let us return to where we digressed. I said the Waldensians strive to lead us, the unwary, in a different direction. This is so: turning away from the purgation of souls—which is the single nerve of the entire discourse—they labor to dodge the issue by quibbling over the one word "Purgatory." These shifty men claim that Saint Thomas said more than the ancient doctors by using this one word, dragging the matter into this sort of reasoning: "Thomas Aquinas found Purgatory; this is not found in the ancient doctor Augustine; therefore..."

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Waldensians use logical fallacies to deny the existence of Purgatory. The author, Augustine of Olomouc, is specifically defending the "Modern Doctor" Thomas Aquinas against the charge that he invented a "place" for Purgatory that the ancient Church Fathers did not recognize.</meta>

# ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

...finds in his own [writings], therefore Purgatory does not exist. This is a crude <term>syllogism</term><note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises. The author calls it "rustic" to imply it is unrefined or simplistic.</note>, yet one borrowed from devilish cunning. But let us expose the fallacy. Thus, the conclusion does not follow from what they have assumed: they begin their discussion with the <term>material word</term><note>original: "materiali voce"; referring to the actual sounds or letters of the word "Purgatory" rather than the concept it represents.</note> "Purgatory," and from this they infer something about its meaning. In this way, they vary the sense back and forth through an equivocation of the word. For since the word "Purgatory" is not actually found in the writings of **Aurelius Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note>, if you incautiously grant that "it is not there," they immediately infer that "therefore, Purgatory does not exist." This now carries the following sense: "therefore, that state of souls needing purification, which is the subject of the present dispute, does not exist." Furthermore, based on this deceptive use of the word "Purgatory"—which they accuse **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> of usurping for his own use—they condemn the entire Church and the Doctors. They previously seemed to cite these same Doctors as accepted authorities, yet now they condemn them regarding this point of faith. Thus, by creeping in through the snares of a single word, they secretly undermine the entire Apostolic institution as if it were a recent and novel invention.

Therefore, if they commit such intolerable fraud from such a tiny little word, let us hereafter show them something of the deed of **Hercules against Antaeus** <note>In Greek mythology, Hercules defeated the giant Antaeus by holding him aloft, because Antaeus drew strength from touching the earth. The author wants to "suspend" his opponents in the air of logic so they cannot "touch ground" with their word-games.</note>: let us hold these men suspended regarding the *purification* of souls; let us not allow them to return again to the word "Purgatory," through which they escape and evade by quibbling. However, if they truly desired to be taught and to perceive the truth, there was no reason for them to seize upon this word so greedily. For since they seemed to have accepted this saying of Saint Augustine—or at least they argue against one point using another from him—they must have noticed that in that same place, souls were shown to be in specific locations and torments. From the torments, it follows that one must confess there is a *purification*; from the locations, one must confess a *Purgatory*. For what else is the word itself, according to its <term>etymology</term>, but a place in which purification happens? Since souls are not just "anywhere," in whatever certain place they showed themselves, in that same place they were also tormented, and that is a "purgatorial place." If the Waldensian does not grant this, he is forced to grant something else: that souls suffer "nowhere," even though those who must be purified exist "somewhere."

Therefore, **Aurelius Augustine** confesses this place of Purgatory just as much as **Thomas** does. It is true that Augustine did not speak definitively about *which* place it was among all possibilities—because "you hear the sound of the spirit, but you know not whence it comes or whither it goes"—but Saint Thomas (whom the Waldensians mock for saying Purgatory is the "third place" in the underworld) did not merely speak of it out of all options. For God’s judgment is not confined to this or that location. However, because every creature is contained by space, a location necessarily either circumscribes or defines it. By this necessity, whatever has been judged—even if not specifically sentenced *to* a location—nonetheless cannot pay its penalties except *in* a location. Just as a man who is proscribed <note>original: "proscriptus"; a person declared an outlaw or condemned.</note> is such even if he has not been deported; nevertheless, in whatever single place he may be, he pays the penalty of his proscription, and that place is for him a "proscriptive place." **Adam** in Paradise was tormented by the conscience of his transgressed commandment. All the most atrocious human passions feed upon and consume the soul even in the midst of exulting companionship, or amid relaxed banquets, games, and jokes. And yet, the companion reclining at your side does not perceive this "place of torment." A person with a fever, even when placed in a warm bath, shakes with cold. The force of the disease burns within, and if you submerge the same man in ice-cold water, he still burns. These are human torments; they do not torture because of one specifically appointed place, but neither do they torture *outside* of a place. By this same law, whoever is blessed is blessed in every place. The soul of **Christ** during the three days was blessed in the underworld. The **Fathers in Limbo** <note>The "Limbus Patrum," where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ.</note> were happy immediately upon the new ray of divinity. But the demons present there, who grieved at this "bite of hell," were unhappy. In those same lower parts of the earth, the thief from the cross rejoiced in...

### THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK THREE
->O iiij<-

...Christ, where **Judas** was tormented by his recent damnation, while **Saint Paul**, being then in the flesh, was blessed when he was caught up into heaven. <note>original: "raperetur in coelum"; referring to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where Paul describes being caught up to the third heaven.</note> The Angel of **Tobit**, while setting out on his journey and returning, was blessed in heaven. <note>A reference to the Archangel Raphael in the Book of Tobit, who assisted Tobias while remaining in the presence of God.</note> Conversely, wherever the evil angel is, that place is his own hell for him, as we read in **Job**: "On a certain day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, **Satan** was also present among them." <note>Job 1:6.</note> And in the third book of Kings: "I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left." <note>1 Kings 22:19 (referred to as 3 Kings in the Vulgate Bible).</note> Then, a spirit came forward and stood before the Lord. Both good and evil angels stand together before God; in the same place, the latter are damned and the former are blessed. Some are in hell, others in heaven.

Hell is everywhere the enemy of God is found—the now-judged devil—and where the members of the **Antichrist** are: **Annas**, **Caiaphas**, and **Pilate**. <note>High priests and the Roman governor involved in the trial and crucifixion of Jesus.</note> Hell is in that dark air into which the demons have been cast; as much of that air as surrounds the whole world, so great is hell. Wherever demons are, they are simultaneously in their own fire. The fire of hell was in that herd of pigs that rushed headlong into the sea, as mentioned in the Gospel. <note>The miracle of the Gadarene swine, where demons called "Legion" entered pigs.</note> Possessed men contain within themselves as many torments of <term>Gehenna</term> <note>A biblical term for hell or a place of fiery torment.</note> as there are demons within them; they are tortured by their own hidden fire, the sensation of which never reaches the possessed person.

Hell is within you, Waldensian, as long as you blaspheme the saints and the **Virgin Mary**, as long as you deny that souls are purified after death, as long as you corrupt the Scriptures into a perverse meaning, and as long as—out of a lying imitation of the ancient church—you insidiously fight back against the whole Church. Within you, with every instrument of infernal punishment, is that "ancient, twisting serpent" whose organ of treachery you provide yourself to be; he who said, "I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets." <note>1 Kings 22:22.</note>

For this reason, just as the blessed are in heaven wherever they may be, and the damned are in hell in every place, so by divine decree, souls to be purified depart—whether to a part of hell (for those perhaps more foul and needing sharper cleansing), or to the caves of the earth, or to the liquid elements, individually or in groups, commanded or uncommanded. This is their receptacle and the "place of purgatory." Regarding these locations, whether one has shown no definite place or just one specific place, neither is wrong; each spoke according to what the current discourse required.

But after the Waldensians have caviled about purgatory, they then "rhetoricize"—that is, they anticipate what they expect us to say with a certain singular artifice, like so: "They might say that souls are purged where they committed their crimes." Then these foolish men further admit that such a statement of ours is confirmed by Scripture, namely: "By what things a man sins, by these he is also tormented," <note>Wisdom of Solomon 11:16.</note> and that other quote from **Saint Paul**. Although those scriptures do not say what they think regarding purgatory, yet because they think they do, we therefore accept them just as if they said it directly. For at least according to their own opinion, they confirm our faith. Therefore, let them either have kept silent before, or if they brought them out, let them later refute them or follow them. They do neither; in both ways, they sin against their own conscience.

It was not necessary for our cause to show that they used these scriptures poorly, especially where they introduced them to support our case. But we do not need false patronage, since we can better confirm our own cause ourselves, nor can we silently pass over their ignorance. "Listen here, then, Waldensian: where is the mention of a 'place' here?" For it says, "by what things one sins." If you define this by place, perhaps the soul of **Judas** wanders to this day around those places where he plotted his betrayal and around the noose. Another sinner, however, perhaps runs from the farthest West all the way to the **Mesopotamians**...

# ON THE ADORATION OF THE SAINTS AGAINST

...traversing land and sea after death to return and gather one’s own punishments. It is ridiculous to suspect such a thing: as if we or the Scriptures believe that such things happen in this way, or that no simpler meaning—more obvious to the mind, if you have any—was seen, such as the one we now propose from an example. A soul needing to be purged would prefer to have performed a fruitful, life-giving penance here, rather than having ignorantly delayed it until after death. Therefore, the soul has its own sin for which it is tortured. Oh, with infinite prayers it wishes never to have committed such a thing or to have paid for it here on earth! Now, it is tormented by the very thing through which it sinned. **Herod** killed the **Innocents** to crush **Christ**. <note>Herod the Great, who ordered the "Massacre of the Innocents" in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16-18).</note> Do you not think he is presently tormented by the conscience of that infanticide for which he suffers such heavy punishment? Surely; that is therefore his own "worm" that eats away at him, through which he is tortured—the recollection of the deed he committed. <note>The "worm that never dies" is a traditional biblical metaphor for the gnawing conscience of the damned, based on Mark 9:48 and Isaiah 66:24.</note> He grieves inwardly, thinking to himself: "Oh, why did I ever come into the purple? <note>The "purple" refers to royal status and power.</note> Oh, why did I ever commit this slaughter out of a lust for reigning?" The torturer is that very penance for his deed, that worm of memory that never forgets the crime; it rages all the more fiercely because he sees that from a temporal offense he has brought upon himself punishment for infinite ages upon infinite ages. This is what is meant by: "by what things a man sins, by the same he is also tormented." <note>A paraphrase of Wisdom 11:16.</note> For while we are certain about the truth of **Purgatory**, we do not wish it to seem confirmed by Scriptures that are foreign to the purpose; we do not allow such a thing to be done for us, just as we blame you whenever you do the like for yourself.

As for that Scripture: "As you yielded your bodies to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now yield your members to serve justice unto sanctification," <note>Romans 6:19.</note> if we remember where our discourse began—namely, concerning Purgatory in the next life—do we understand that this Scripture has absolutely nothing to do with the present matter? **Saint Paul**, in the place where he said these things, was exhorting the faithful **Romans** so that they might turn what they had spent on the loss of salvation before their calling toward the procurement of salvation through the new light of the **Gospel**. To put it in a single word—and one that a **Waldensian** <note>The Waldensians (or Vaudois) were a medieval sect that preceded the Reformation, often criticized by Catholic authors for their "uneducated" readings of the Bible.</note> would be glad to hear—I will summarize the meaning: Paul is speaking of our chastening and purging from the vices of the flesh, which we will accomplish at no time or place more fruitfully or more acceptably to God than in this flesh and this life. Saint Paul makes no mention at all here of the future state of souls. We show in this place the lack of familiarity of those Waldensians with the **Holy Scriptures**; they have so little taste for even moderate understanding that they cannot distinguish even the most remote things, which do not even have the appearance of relating to the matter.

After this, the author returns a second time to **Saint Thomas** and Purgatory. Having now testified to us—unwillingly—concerning the Scriptures, they labor again to wrest this from that holy doctor. <note>Referring to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Dominican theologian.</note> The cause of such great offense is that he found two places in Hell: one for unbaptized children, and another for souls needing to be purged. <note>Aquinas discussed the *Limbus Puerorum* (Limbo of Infants) and Purgatory as distinct states.</note> But, O Christian people, you ought to understand the bitterness of those Waldensians, who rise up against Saint Thomas alone, and in a matter that he was not the only modern to speak of, nor was he the most recent to "find" it—rather, it is something he repeats from the primitive church. Therefore, as they mention in their Prologue, there was a **Doctor Heinrich**, an inquisitor of heretical depravity, who spoke of "locusts and wasps" <note>original: "brucis et vespis"; likely a metaphor for heretics consuming the "garden" of the Church.</note> against them—against those who, like dogs and pigs, have raved against every Christian estate. Since it did not seem enough to them to vent some of their own hatred against him (as men would have taken this one way or another), they chose to attack this **Thomas Aquinas**, a man of the Order of **Saint Dominic**, who by his learning and holiness challenges the most ancient of fathers. The reason is the man’s distinguished fame; an injury to one man would reach too many—namely, all those who deeply and firmly love him.

Thus they now call Saint Thomas into accusation. <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and theologian whose "Summa Theologica" defined much of Catholic doctrine.</note> Thus they blaspheme that whatever he felt regarding Purgatory, he did not derive from Scripture but from a desire for "hunting" wealth.

But listen, you—a common hater of saints and men alike! In that impious **Synagogue** of yours (for I do not put forward our Church, which you consider to be nothing), in that **Synagogue of Satan**, how many ranks do you make? <note>original: "Synagoga Sathanæ." A polemical term used by the author to disparage the Waldensian assembly, referencing Revelation 2:9.</note> You might rightly make three: of the **perfect**, the **progressing**, and the **lost**. But perhaps you do not have this last one; for you have no "lost" person who would deny a deposit, sign false documents, or corrupt wills. You claim no one would abjure a will while the church and the judges’ benches tremble at such cursed imprecations. You have no such person; indeed, you count them among the "perfect."

Let these remaining two ranks stay, then. You do not make these ranks according to the merits of each as the Church does: for instance, that your little "sacrificer" be among the **perfect**, and another—whomever among your accomplices you do not yet deem worthy of the priesthood—be among the **progressing**. Just as in one republic there is a place for a senator and a place for a commoner, a place for the free-born and a place for the slave—not separated by the streets or districts of the city, but living mixed together while distinguished by their legal conditions—so in your one "Synagogue" there is a place for the perfect and a place for the progressing.

Furthermore, this "progressing" member of yours studies (as you boast) abstinence; he avoids every enticement of a dissolute life; he makes everything he handles difficult for himself. Why does he do this? So that he may be **purged**, as you say, for the immortal body. If, therefore, you call a place where one prays an **oratory**, and where one works an **operatory**, and where one washes a **lavatory**, then why—when this man of yours abstains from both permitted and unpermitted things in order to be purged—will you not call this a **Purgatory**? <note>The author is using a linguistic argument: if other places are named after the actions performed there (praying/orare, working/operari), then a state of purging (purgare) should logically be called Purgatory.</note>

Therefore, to return to the business at hand: just as you make different places according to merit within one Synagogue, and just as you name a place where something is done by a word related to that action, so did Saint Thomas—and the Church long before he became "Thomas"—establish different places in the Afterlife for these diverse kinds (namely, for a soul needing to be purged and another that is damned), according to what is done there. Thus he called this place (or "rank" or "path," if you prefer) **Purgatory**, and the other **Damnatary**, or truly **Hell** by its proper name.

For you must not understand these as if they were separated by physical walls, like some triple stable where you might shut up sheep, oxen, and pigs separately. For such a crude opinion, I would consider you a true rustic of the stable! Those "places" are the degrees of divine judgment by which God punishes some in this way, some in that way, and others in another. And as we have said elsewhere: because we can only conceive of things happening physically, we use physical modes and figures to bring them to the understanding of others.

Unless you were wicked and insidiously defending your betrayal of the Apostolic Church, you would never—after those very points you seemed to have admitted regarding the purgation of souls—contend so captiously against one man regarding the locations of the Afterlife and Purgatory. But let us rise higher into the matter and consider if similar distinctions are found in other spiritual things, for which Saint Thomas is now being summoned to court. Christ says of the distinction of heavenly grace: **"In my Father's house there are many dwelling places."** <note>original: "In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt." (John 14:2).</note> Saint Paul, explaining that passage, says: **"There is one glory of the sun, another of the moon, and another of the stars; for star differs from star in glory."** <note>original: "alia est claritas Solis. alia Lunæ . alia stellarum." (1 Corinthians 15:41).</note> By this allegory, he signaled to the Corinthians that in the Resurrection...

The demon, at that very moment he fell from heaven, was seized by the fire of hell according to that word of Peter: *God did not spare the angels who sinned, but delivered them to the chains of hell, dragged into Tartarus to be tormented, to be reserved for judgment.* <note>original: "deus angelis peccatib⁹ nõ peperit ſed rudetibus inferni detractos in tartarũ. tradidit cruciãdos. in iudicium referuari" from 2 Peter 2:4.</note> Yet these same demons cry out to Christ so often: "What have we to do with you, Jesus? Have you come here to torment us before the time?" <note>Matthew 8:29</note> What is this, that the demons, already tormented, pray not to be tormented? Is it not that which is found in Luke, that they begged him not to command them to go into the abyss? <note>Luke 8:31</note> The evil spirits feared being cast out of the habitation of men, where, even amidst their torments, they derive a supreme pleasure from their hatred toward us, if they might occupy, infest, or ruin us through impure actions. If they were excluded from this activity—if they were thrust into that place which they are to inhabit after the final day—they would consider themselves tormented further or most vehemently. We see, therefore, that there are different mansions even among the damned, and now the demons who are tormented fear to be tormented further. 

Finally, "hell" is never spoken of as a single place in the Scriptures, even as the Waldensians presently contend against **Saint Thomas**. There is the hell of which the Savior speaks: *And these shall go into eternal fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.* <note>Matthew 25:46 and 13:42</note> There is the hell into which the Patriarchs Jacob and Job said they would descend, which the Savior more mercifully calls **Abraham’s Bosom**, <note>A theological concept describing the place where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for the Messiah.</note> in which Lazarus the beggar was seen by the rich feaster. This was "Hell" because of the privation of divine enjoyment; it was **Limbo** <term>Limbus: derived from the Latin for "edge" or "border," referring to a state of the afterlife for those who did not deserve damnation but could not enter Heaven before Christ's redemption.</term> because the fathers, resting in the faith of Abraham and the promise they had received, were waiting for their approaching liberation. 

We ask: for what fault do unregenerate children <note>Unbaptized infants</note> descend into Hell? For original sin. Therefore, those children committed no actual sin; they are not guilty of the divine rebuke: *I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink; I was a stranger and you did not invite me in; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison and you did not visit me.* <note>Matthew 25:42-43</note> Over them, therefore, he will not speak the sentence: *Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels.* Would you thrust them into those atrocious flames in which the devil, the prince of all perdition and seduction, is tormented? In which **Judas**, **Herod**, **Nero**, **Domitian**, **Decius**, and **Diocletian**—who all attempted to tear down heaven and took up manifest battle against divinity—are tormented? Will you send them to that same place? They have not deserved it. Therefore, there must be degrees of damnation between innocent children and the most wicked criminals, just as Christ, through the voice of Abraham, says to the rich man that a great chaos exists between him and Lazarus. 

I throw this problem at you, Waldensian: refute this first, and then return to your attack on **Saint Thomas**. For to accuse with naked words—to say "Thomas said this," but to keep silent about *why* he said it and fail to touch upon his reasons—nothing is easier than that; any fool can do it. Why do you not try to demolish the house from the foundation rather than shaking it from the roof? 

However, regarding the third place of souls to be purged <note>Purgatory</note>: if indeed they are relegated by divine judgment so that they may be redeemed soon after, as **Saint Augustine** said in the book *On True and False Penance*: "This fire, even if it is not eternal, is nevertheless marvelously grave." Now, we have sufficiently asserted that this "third place"—which the Waldensians reject as if it were a fable—exists in the present and previous discourse of **Saint Thomas**, because it differs in the degree of punishment from that by which the eternally damned are punished. And these degrees, by human ways of speaking...

# WALDENSIANS BOOK THREE,
### 8. 6.

Scripture speaks of places and mansions according to custom; if these places displease our heretic, let him begin from the final points—that is, the reasons—and by refuting them, arrive at the beginnings. Then he may rightly judge from the head whether he approves or disapproves, and he might be purified if, as Seneca <note>original: "Seneca"</note> rebukes us, we bring forth unexamined and premature judgments upon so great a matter. But how would those evildoers spare the present things, for whom no antiquity is to be revered or worthy enough to be spared? For this impurity of men even charges that the earlier inventors of purgatory felt contrary to the faith. 

But hey, you! If you admit there were earlier inventors of purgatory, why did you just now quibble against Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian. The author is pointing out a contradiction in the Waldensian argument.</note> as if he were its first author? Because if those ancients themselves felt against the faith in that matter, why did you call yourself back to the primitive church and its ancient doctors to assert your views on purgatory? Indeed, you who today—as you lyingly boast—recall the faith of the ancient church: where did you find it outside of the ancients? What else are you doing but simulating and dissimulating regarding all sounder things? Here you are so much in your own element, where you must feel treacherously. For as often as you simulate the face of one who feels rightly, you immediately forget what was to be shown to you; as often as you dissimulate the affection of a perverse opinion, you immediately slide back into yourself; its memory is perpetual for you. 

Thus you vacillate between this and that so you may remain safe under error. You, however, with your impure mouth; you, with your **rakes and hoes**; <note>The author uses agricultural tools as a derogatory metaphor for the Waldensians' lack of formal education, as many were laypeople or farmers.</note> you, with your caterpillars and wasps of teachers, do you accuse most enlightened men—whom the schools of the gentiles and all human erudition have admired, whose life and faith towards God were attested by miracles—do you accuse them of being finders or followers of lies and old wives' tales, now thundering insanely from the master of lies? Do you call those instruments of the Holy Spirit—the spirit of truth—the followers of lies? Do you "correct" them according to your own impurity? 

Digest first, evildoer, what we brought forth above, and then return to us—that is, the Church. Say this is against the faith; claim that we assert what we ourselves do not know. Digest, therefore, the present things and extricate yourself while there is leisure; we will immediately make greater business for you. A little later you will hear more evident things; I speak of those men of apostolic times and signs, at whose names you would be forced to gasp. To refute them, you must first be refuted, for you have never received the faith of salvation from Christ and the apostles. 

But after these most troublesome wasps have left this sting of false opinion concerning Purgatory in the apostolic writers and in those with whom they had previously agreed, they return to us again and object: how can the Church send all souls equally into purgatory, and since she cannot discern for whom she ought and for whom she ought not to pray, does she make no distinction here so that she may make a larger profit from the funeral rites of all? 

But I say the Waldensians lie first in this: that the Church, having no conscience of her own, prays for all without selection and only for the sake of profit. For she does not pray for those who died in confessed mortal sin, such as those who committed suicide. She does not pray after death for heretics. I make even this Waldensian a witness, who, unless he returns to the unity of the Church while living, no Christian priest will be willing to pray for him when dead. For if his kin care to redeem a sacred place for him to hide the infamy, even if the Church were to be filled with riches, he will not obtain a burial place; <note>The author argues that the Church refuses burial and prayers to unrepentant heretics and suicides, refuting the claim that the Church's primary motivation is money.</note> for they are cut off, and nothing remains for them in the communion of Christ and the Church. They are members touched by blight, cut off from the whole body, which have now withered away from the sacred fire. 

The Church leaves them to be tormented forever with evil spirits like you and with the "Jewish crucifiers"—since that Waldensian holds the saints of God and His holy Church in such contempt as they held Christ. But there are members who died in the communion of Christ and the Church under the remission of sins in the confession of the true faith; concerning them, we have a certain hope from faith that they are not destined for eternal punishments.

# AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS] CONCERNING THE PURGATORY OF SOULS

Finally, we hope that through the merit of Christ, the saints, and the present church on their behalf—for the infirmities and inconveniences of life and the most urgent necessity of death—God, through His mercy, has received these in satisfaction of full penance. Whence we believe more readily that they are admitted immediately from the threshold of death into the blessed seats, rather than ordered into purgatory. Because, however, we must not inquire into divine judgments, we pray for them lest they be neglected through supine presumption. We are certain that even if they are holy, the sacrifice of the altar cannot be deprived of its efficacy; otherwise, this mystery is offered to no one privately, but to all standing in the union of the church, according to which each person, by their own merit, makes themselves a participant in it before the heavenly Father. 

But let our words cease; let us hear about such a great matter—and one in which you, Waldensian, so foully defame the church regarding greed—let us hear? I speak of Saint Augustine: learn there first about the **suffrages** <term>suffrages: prayers, petitions, or pious acts offered on behalf of others, particularly to aid souls in Purgatory</term> for the dead, which you pretend are recent inventions. Learn that from the time of Saint Augustine—so that I may call upon nothing more ancient—that is, for one thousand and one hundred years, they have been celebrated in the church. Learn that it was then believed that proper funeral rites profit the dead toward the absolution of guilt. He, therefore, in the book *On Care to be Had for the Dead* <note>original: "de cura p mortuis"</note> writes thus: 

*A certain way of life is acquired while living in this body so that these things might help the deceased. And through this, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by those things which were religiously done for them after the body [death].* 

But listen, I beseech you—you who shortly hereafter are going to deny the books of the Maccabees, you who falsely claim that ecclesiastical ceremonies were devised in a moneylender's shop <note>This refers to the Waldensian accusation that the Church invented rituals for profit.</note>—listen to how much faith is owed to both, and believe also that Saint Augustine will say something truer than you, Waldensian. *In the books of the Maccabees*, he says, *we read of a sacrifice offered for the dead. But even if it were read nowhere at all in the ancient scriptures, the authority of this custom [of the church] is not small, where in the prayers of the priest which are poured out to the Lord God at His altar, the commendation of the dead also has its place. Since these things are so, should we not think that [help] reaches the dead for whom we take care, unless we solemnly supplicate for them through the sacrifices of either the altar, or of prayers and alms?* 

Prick up your ears, Waldensian—how long they are!—for now we shall be liberated through Saint Augustine from that which you reproach us for: that we pray for everyone equally. Therefore he adds: *although they [the prayers] do not benefit all for whom they are made, but only those who, while they lived, prepared themselves so that they might be benefited. But because we do not discern who they are, it is necessary to do these things for all the reborn [baptized], so that none of those to whom these benefits can and should reach are passed over.* 

Is this scripture far-fetched for us, or have we misleadingly translated it here while it was looking elsewhere? Or has it not rather answered for us in the most direct words to every thread of your question? Say here that Saint Augustine lied for profit or asserted what he did not know, so that you, heretic, might seem truthful. Understand, therefore, that you stir up against yourself that same hatred which you previously wished to stir up against Saint Thomas and against us by your accusation. You perceive that whatever you have blathered against the present church, just as much has been blathered against Saint Augustine and the most ancient Catholics from whom he received this, and whom we shall yet bring forward. You perceive that whatever of your perfidy you bring forth in the future, leave it as confessed among the Christian people that it was by no means brought forth from the church—as you lyingly boast and by the authority of the ancients—but rather brought forth incited by diabolical seduction and heretical stubbornness. 

But what is this so great "greed of priests"—I ask—through which the suffrages for the dead were undertaken? It is demanded of no one that they be done sumptuously. Whether you perform the funeral rites more sparingly or more lavishly is your own judgment. However, out of desire for our dearest loved ones <note>original: "pignorum", literally "pledges" or "tokens," often used affectionately for children or family members</note>, we gladly do these things more opulently, ready to do more if we were able to help them into heaven with our own hands, but we simply cannot do so much. This final duty of ours in funeral rites we can perform; we rejoice only to show as much to those preceding us as we hope will be shown to us by those following us. Sometimes our means dictate the limit of the service.

He argues that while rituals vary in cost, they are acts of love and duty toward the deceased rather than a clerical racket.</summary>

### THE THIRD BOOK AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...not a desire; such great expense did not arise from the greed of the priest—and perhaps he is indeed most greedy—but it began from my own piety. I do not wish to lose the fruit of this piety because of someone else's vice. You, who think whatever expense is made for divine matters is lost; you, who envy your money being given to another and thus abandon piety; you, who more seriously commit the very greed in yourself that you accuse in another—why are you tortured by another’s expense? Natural law teaches us this, and we know this to be pious through faith. You might consider it pious if you were to carry out your parents, brothers, wife, and children to the place of the skull <note>original: "in caluariã", referring to the cemetery or place of burial</note> for free, like a decaying beast of burden. If you forget them faster than the taste of a piglet at a banquet, you might consider this "apostolic." But if you truly believed it to be apostolic, you should have recalled them to their innocence where they strayed, not taken it away. Because you have taken it away, the greed of our people there—as you say—does not excuse your faithlessness. In other cases, you pay exactly what you owe and inquire no further than your coin: whether it is received with an open or curved hand, whether for a frugal, prodigal, or entirely stingy use, the fruit comes only from the debt of the work; nothing more depends on you. So too does apostolic faith demand of you: whatever you currently deny is not lost by the agreement of the contract if good men use it well. The faith stands by itself; it is not weakened by the occasion of anyone’s wicked use. You must pay directly whatever the faith says is owed. 

As Saint Paul reminds the Philippians, many preached Christ, though not all from good will, but some for one reason and others for another. There were those who preached so that they would not be in want. Do you not then believe the Gospel—which you certainly do—but rather what Saint Paul says? For he says that as long as Christ is announced in every way, whether by opportunity or by truth, it is good. Others gave alms, as the Gospel records, with a sounding trumpet <note>A reference to Matthew 6:2, regarding hypocrites who seek public praise</note> for mere ostentation. Should we therefore condemn almsgiving because some have used it badly? Now, if we were to cast out everything that men use badly, we would have to drive this world away from us, since idolaters worshipped it to the insult of God. We would have to condemn that other sex <note>A common medieval trope referring to women as a source of temptation</note> which causes us so much trouble, and we would have to cut off whichever limb we sin with. Indeed, you, Waldensian, should even abstain from bread, since it nourishes you to rage longer against Christ, his saints, and his church.

->**THE WALDENSIAN,**<-

First in the grace of God and the merit of Jesus Christ, even until that place where *their worm will not die and the fire will not be extinguished.* <note>Mark 9:48, describing the eternal punishment of Hell</note>

Our Waldensian uses many words on a settled matter, and as if all things were against him, he sweats and labors so, pouring himself into a fight where his adversary willingly agrees. He merely lashes at the winds, so that spectators might think he is contributing much to the matter. In truth, however, he stirs up nothing but the wind in this fight. For we have shown before—concerning the purgation of souls which is completed in this life according to every type we have received from the fathers, prophets, Apostles, and all saints—that nothing has yet come into contention with the Waldensian, for on this point we both concede to each other. Therefore, lest he be puffed up as if he were bringing forward unknown things, let him know and assume that even on this matter he would err. Something more robust than this foolish arrogance, this arrogant foolishness, could have been brought forward by us regarding this opinion. For we confess that we ought to do both, according to that saying: *turn away from evil and do good.* <note>Psalm 34:14</note> We know that conversion from evil—this purgation, I say—comes from no other source than the grace of God, and from this we must not be sluggish, but rather be found practiced in every good work according to our vow and ability. And we know this. Otherwise, we would strike out this phrase: *and do good.* But where we have neglected this and placed our light under a bushel, and depart from this body only in the grace of God—we who are not yet purged of our negligences and earthly stains—we cannot be received into heaven; yet, because we communicate with Christ, we cannot be damned. Therefore, what middle ground remains for us?

## CONCERNING THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

What if we deny purgatory after death? At that point, you drop your ears, you long-eared face; <note>original: "aurita facies," a rhetorical jab comparing the opponent to a donkey</note> here, little donkey, you resist where you ought to have leaned in with the rest. You slip away into another matter. You are eloquent in that which no one denies; you are wordy and acting as a "know-it-all" regarding things no one asks for; finally, you conclude that you have found nothing better. But, good God, how "cold" <note>meaning weak or unconvincing</note> they are here, how many things are twisted! Many things are summoned, almost none are appropriate; clearly they act in this way because they strive to fill the page, caring nothing for truth, provided they say a lot, appearing to press the business among the simple, to insist on their work where they repeat many things. Thus they dare to wander away from the adversary, otherwise turning their backs. We also could have called forth several passages as markers of their folly into our midst. But what pertains to proving the ignorance of another, especially here where they act foolishly not at our risk, but at the risk of religion?

We will take up only a few points upon which they leap at us and where the strength <note>original: "neruus," literally the "nerve" or "sinew" of the argument</note> of the business is driven. Not far from the beginning, where they spoke of the **grace of Christ** <note>original: "gracia Christi"</note> and the **cleansing of the Holy Spirit** <note>original: "emundatione spirituſſancti"</note>, they later bring in an indirect inference: *Therefore there is no other place of purgatory outside of Christ.* But let us meanwhile snatch this speech from their mouths; although true in its own way, it is now not spoken sincerely. Let us throw back at them something of their own ill-will: "There is no other place of purgatory outside of Christ." You agree? Therefore, we shall not admit that the sufferings of this world, nor works of mercy, nor penance and satisfaction of every kind, nor the remaining things you do regarding a "present" purgatory, are species of the purgation of souls. For you say that what you have said thus far concerning Christ and the Holy Spirit is the only purgatory.

Thus, I, who was regenerated in the grace of Christ as a boy, will now as an old man hang supine from that same grace, doing no work of my own? You say this, O one who hastens too much, desiring an adversary too much! I say that same thing to you, **Waldensian** <note>original: "valdenſis," referring to the followers of Peter Waldo, a proto-Protestant movement</note>: you rush too much against us. Just as you do not think yourself restricted so that you may escape into other arguments, so think of us as not restricted when we find a way to assert that purgatory after this life. But you desire us to be restricted. Well, since it pleases you so—but not now; rather later, after we have spoken about the purgatory after this life and shall say more hereafter, you will be more immediately refuted.

But I will go directly against you. If there is no place of purification outside the grace of regeneration <note>referring to Baptism</note>, what will you establish for those who have made this grace void? Will you give them nothing left from which they may rise again? They wish to return to the prophetic voice: *I do not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that he be converted and live.* They wish to return to this and be purged anew. Now, it is not possible for them to be regenerated again; they must necessarily flee to other purifications, namely the **sacrament of penance** <note>original: "ſacramentū pœnitenciæ"</note> and **satisfaction**, and they will reduce the body to servitude. There, therefore, they will find those later purifications which you have now insanely excluded for the sake of our one "purgatory." 

Truly, we confess that these purifications do not happen outside the grace of Christ (by which alone we are able to do what we can, for He said, *My grace is sufficient for you*). But this is a different gift from the grace of regeneration by which alone you strengthened us. And by this wit of yours, you often sin against us, so that you circumscribe things freely spoken and arrange them as captives for your own use. Suppose I said you err regarding the **Patronage of the Saints**; here you infer against me: "Therefore no other error will be charged against us." There, by that tiny phrase "no other," you corrupt my whole meaning and lie about what was said, which in truth was not said. For I did not exclude your remaining errors just because I mentioned only one. So also you corrupt the present scriptures; when they have commemorated only one kind of grace, you infer: "therefore there is no other principal place of a certain purgatory." But this is a crime of violated scripture, upon which you cast chains, as it were, through your contrived fraud, and you force it to say what they certainly do not say according to the mind of the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Sanctiſpūs"</note>. In this fraud, finally, you are much occupied throughout this chapter, so that you might have that [point] of yours...

### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE

...let us now confirm our hope and firm confession that we shall have a Purgatory in the "third hell" <note>The author uses "hell" (infernus) as a general term for the afterlife beneath heaven, divided into the hell of the damned, Limbo, and Purgatory.</note>; and why shouldn’t I? If you wanted to deny this by right, you ought to have brought forward scriptures that defined the modes of purgation by a certain number. If Purgatory after death were excluded from those, you would be right to conclude as you do; but now you conclude this only from a lust for contention. By your own judgment, you set a number, and that which you had found through our—indeed, the apostolic—faith, you corrupt, erase, and bypass, as I will show shortly; it was necessary that what was written be treated as unwritten. You add, *Not so that one might be prepared for hell, but prepared for heaven,* <note>The author is quoting his Waldensian opponent here.</note> and you quibble over the word "hell" as if we were saying this is the same receptacle into which the damned are cast. We, however, call "hell" every place of the soul stripped of its body which it occupies during that delay in which it is prohibited from the divine vision, concerning which we have spoken fully in the preceding sections. Souls to be purged are sent to this kind of hell so that they are not truly sent into the hell into which sinners descend like lead, and therefore so that they may truly be prepared for heaven. 

Wherefore, while you think us harsh, you yourself are obstinately cruel; for when a place remained for wretched souls to redeem the penance they had lost here, you—because of a fixable stain for which they nevertheless cannot be received into heaven—dismiss them into outer darkness without a middle ground, without indulgence, and with purgation denied. You move to another point and attack Purgatory from there; you say there are two future bodies that will be perpetual, one good and the other evil. We say the same, but before this body comes—that is, is resurrected to meet its Lord sitting in judgment—meanwhile the souls are purged. Their bodies will not then rise from some "third grade" (as if we were saying such a thing, which you now falsely attribute to us), but rather from the other state—that is, the state of the blessed. 

As for your claim that there is no "time for earning merit" after death: surely the "sow may teach Minerva!" <note>original: "sus Minervam," a classical Latin proverb used when an ignorant person attempts to teach an expert.</note> Who among our people does not know that, unless he is not yet "washed by the bronze"? <note>A metaphor for someone who is uneducated or uninitiated into common knowledge.</note> We have said that souls are *purged*; who said they *earn merit*? Do "being purged" and "earning merit" necessarily follow one another? Finally, while discussing souls to be purged, you use the example of the rich man feasting <note>original: "diuite epulone," referring to the Parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16.</note>—that is, the state of the damned—and you jump from one thing to another. You mix everything up, striving for nothing except to speak from a spirit of contention rather than conscience. Why do you not stay within the subject? 

But listen, heretical wickedness: someone commits a capital offense against a prince. If he is caught while the offense is still fresh, he is put into prison with no hope of dissolving the crime; such is that rich man who feasted, about whom we have no disagreement. But if he were to wipe away the offense itself by some new service, that service could be so remarkable that it pays off the whole offense and he returns to full favor. This describes those who, from this mortality, immediately become blessed from being a sinner by the merit of their life. Finally, if no such service of his intervened, but he prostrated himself at the prince's knees and prayed for mercy, and the prince’s clemency is moved, he is given over to a temporary prison for punishment. Truly, he earns nothing there; nothing is remitted by his own merit; he depends entirely on the prince and pays as much of the penalty as the prince deems sufficient. If such a person is tortured for a long time by the discomfort of the prison, at whatever time he is finally sent out free, he will never say he was received by his own merit, but by the indulgence of the prince. 

This is the state of souls to be purged. Let the impudence of the Waldensians no longer object to us that we place "merit" in the future age where we place Purgatory. Let that barbarity finally get a scent of the matter and not mix these things with those, whereby it may rage more hatefully against the Christian faith.

The passage which they presently bring forward and distort so that it does not seem to support the assertion of Purgatory is taken from the First Epistle of Saint Paul...

### ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...to the Corinthians. There is a certain passage which I know they have corrupted, and I point it out. However, before I descend into arguments against them, I shall write out the passage in its entirety; then, I shall set forth what the ecclesiastical commentators feel regarding it. Only then shall I begin my attack against them. **According to the grace of God which is given to me, as a wise architect, I have laid the foundation. Another, however, builds upon it; but let every man take heed how he builds upon it. For no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. Now if any man builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, every man's work shall be made manifest; for the day of the Lord shall declare it, because it shall be revealed in fire; and the fire shall try every man's work, of what sort it is. If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man's work shall burn, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.** <note>The author is quoting 1 Corinthians 3:10–15, a cornerstone text for the Catholic doctrine of Purgatory.</note> The holy doctors refer this passage equally to the Purgation that happens here through the fire of tribulation, or elsewhere through Purgatory. According to this, Saint Augustine is cited in the marginal gloss: *He who thinks upon the things of the world, how he may please the world, his work is not consumed. But this work is burned because those things possessed with love do not perish without grief.* <note>original: "qui cogitat quæ mundi sunt quomodo placeat mundo..."</note> Saint Gregory also says regarding the same passage: *Although this can be understood regarding the fire of present tribulation, nevertheless, if anyone takes it to mean the fire of the future Purgatory, it must be carefully weighed; for he said that man could be saved through fire not because he builds iron, brass, or lead upon this foundation—that is, greater and therefore harder and more stubborn sins—but because he builds wood, hay, and straw—that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which the fire easily consumes.* <note>original: "ignis futuri Purgatorij... lignū fœnum & stipulā"</note> Indeed, Saint Augustine shows which sins he considers "minimal" in his book *On True and False Repentance*; for there are certain sins which are mortal, and through repentance they become venial <term>venial sins: minor sins that do not destroy the relationship with God but require purification</term>, yet they are not immediately healed. And again, in the same place concerning this healing, he says: *But if one so converted lives his life and does not die, we do not however promise that he escapes all punishment; for he who deferred the fruit of conversion to another age must first be purged by the fire of purgation. This fire, even if it is not eternal, is nevertheless marvelously severe.* Saint Thomas [Aquinas], moreover, in his *Fourth Scriptum*, says this regarding the degree of venial sins: *The graver a sin is, the more difficult it is to purge. Among venial sins, one is found graver than another, the diversity of which is signified by wood, hay, and straw.*

We leave it now as a testament from these doctors that this passage of Saint Paul signifies the purgation of souls, which is to be perfected not only in the course of this life but also in the future fire of Purgatory. Therefore, our case being established, let us now descend to the Waldensian. He now attributes this as a fault to the Christian faith: that it extends this passage of Saint Paul to the fire of a future Purgatory in another age. It is worth the effort, then, to hear men who belong to the plow-handle and the field <note>The author is mocking the Waldensians as uneducated peasants (the "plow-handle") who presume to argue theology with "Doctors of the Church."</note> intrude themselves so boldly against the teachers of the Church. Therefore, you who seem to yourself a "know-it-all" <note>original: "sciolus," meaning one with a superficial smattering of knowledge.</note> and so often strike at us with our own tools, you ought to have proven that your own sense is true and ours is counterfeit by the testimony of some very ancient authority. For by what other evidence are you true, and another—who feels otherwise—false? But now you speak without a witness; you fail yourself most miserably in that most urgent passage which, for either your sake or ours, most strongly confirms or overthrows the matter. I say, therefore, by my own right, that you have feigned, substituted, and adulterated these things for yourself. Your exposition is adulterous; Paul does not recognize it. But let us look at these things more closely. You say the Apostle does not speak of purgation to be done after death and that his words do not agree on this. I demand some witness of your opinion from the ancients. You produce none; and yet there was...

-># THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE<-

In this matter, apart from witnesses, you should not differ at all based on your own judgment alone. I, however, shall show you to be a mere trifler <note>original: "nugatorem," meaning one who talks nonsense or trifles with serious matters</note> regarding the witness of Saint Ambrose. And I bring him forward to you as the one among all others because you seem to me to have alluded to his meaning through certain words. For he himself would give this understanding: that by "gold, silver, and precious stones" is meant **good doctrine**; while by "wood, hay, and stubble," he explained that **evil, crooked, and frivolous doctrine** is signified. 

Such is what you say: "Whosoever among the Priests place faith, love, hope, and the rest of the virtues upon the foundation of Christ, he shall remain in the day of visitation; and whosoever place wood, hay, stubble—that is, the ministry of the **Old Law** <term>The "Old Law" refers to the Mosaic Law of the Old Testament, which the author's opponent argues is what Paul meant by "stubble."</term> or the **law of men**—the day of the Lord shall burn this." Therefore, since I have caught you alluding to the exposition of Saint Ambrose, I shall use this witness against you. 

Thus you say: "The Apostle does not speak of that which is to come after death." On this point, Ambrose goes against you. He says: **"Evil doctrine will appear to all in the fire; for now it deceives some."** You perceive that Paul is aptly explained as speaking of that which is to come after this life. But also a little later, Ambrose says: **"He shows that he will be saved, but will suffer the pains of fire, so that he may be saved by being purged through fire, and not like the faithless who are tortured in eternal fire forever."** No one doubts that the fire of the faithless is after this life. If Ambrose said that those who build wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation of Christ are to be purged by that same fire, differing only in this—that they will not be tortured by eternal fire like the faithless—then the Apostle was indeed speaking of that which happens to a man after this life for the **purgation of sins** <term>purgatione peccatorum: the cleansing or washing away of the "stain" of sins before entering heaven.</term>

As **Aurelius Augustine** also says: **"He must first be cleansed by the fire of purgation who has put off the fruit of conversion until another world."** <note>original: "prius purgandus est igne purgationis qui in aliud seculum distulit fructum conversionis."</note> This fire, even if it is not eternal, is nevertheless wonderfully grievous. Therefore, by the authority of both Ambrose and Augustine, we have refuted your claim—as if the Apostle in this place were not speaking of that which is to come after death, and as if his words did not accord with this sense.

Afterward, you subjoin the cause of your error: because "God will not appear in fire at death." Let us see if the Apostle said that God would appear in fire. His own words are these: **"Every man’s work shall be made manifest; for the day of the Lord shall declare it, because it shall be revealed in fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work, of what sort it is."** 

Behold your "critical sharpness" by which you reject the doctors of the Church! See your **rustic ignorance**, you who have not yet even caught the scent of the order of the words! It is an ignorance worthy of the whip, which would not be forgiven even in schoolboys. The Apostle did not say "God shall be revealed in fire," but **"the work shall be revealed in fire."** The fire shall test what sort each man’s work is. There, in the fire, the work that will remain and the work that will not remain shall be revealed; it is not God who shall be revealed. 

Ambrose is again my witness to this matter. He says: **"Evil doctrine will appear to all in the fire."** He did not say "God will appear to all in the fire." You then add, from that "divine genius" of yours, what you understand by wood, hay, and stubble: namely, the ministry of the Old Law or the law of men, which the day of the Lord shall burn. How much more correctly does **Origen** explain this passage in his *Fourteenth Homily on Leviticus*! He says: **"The nature of sin is like the material which is consumed by fire, which the Apostle Paul says is built up by sinners who build wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation of Christ."** 

Finally, all ecclesiastical commentators explain this passage regarding the general state of believers. Only Ambrose—as I recall—thought that one specific state out of all was sufficient for him as an example for this passage: namely, those who conduct themselves well or wrongly in the ministry of preaching after having accepted the foundation of Christ. He, therefore, speaks only of evil, crooked, and frivolous doctrine. These are understood in the same sense as the "evil workmen," "mercenaries," and "evil and negligent servants" in the Gospels and in the voice of the Lord...
