## ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...through the ministry and word of God, they serve their own hopes of gain, pleasure, and glory. But you twist this meaning from the divine Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), a Doctor of the Church whose writings were often debated in the Reformation era.</note> and have invented trifles for yourself, as if you had retrieved them from a Catholic source, and thus you hold these things out to us in place of the truth. You explain it according to your own whim: but let us see if the Apostle <note>Referring to Saint Paul.</note> considered the ministry of the **Old Law** <term>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament. The author's opponent argued that "stubble" meant following Jewish rituals.</term> or the law of men to be such light matters that he would wish to categorize them as wood, hay, and stubble. Elsewhere, speaking of those who are jealous for the Old Law, he says: *O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you that you should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ has been portrayed and crucified among you?* And again: *You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth? Consent to no one; this persuasion is not from Him who calls you.* 

Regarding the seducers who had led the Galatians into the observance of the Old Law, he says: *He who troubles you will bear his judgment, whoever he may be;* and again: *I wish those who upset you would even cut themselves off.* <note>original: "vtinam abscindantur," a reference to Galatians 5:12, where Paul uses a harsh metaphor for those insisting on circumcision.</note> Let us ask now: if any either taught or received the observance of the Old Law, would the Apostle have wanted them to remain upon the foundation of Christ? Never. For this reason, he calls back the seduced Galatians, whom he says have failed so gravely that they have "portrayed Christ a second time." Therefore, they did not bring upon themselves wood, hay, and stubble, but rather the guilt of those who crucify Christ. 

Furthermore, concerning the law of men, Peter says in his Canonical Epistle: *But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be lying teachers among you, who will bring in destructive sects and deny the Lord who bought them, bringing swift destruction upon themselves.* Behold! The Apostle decrees even more severely against them and casts them outside the foundation of Christ, so that they can no longer build wood, hay, and stubble upon it. Thus, since they are condemned and ejected outside the foundation of Christ by the sentence of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the final part of that passage—**he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire**—does not apply to them. 

This clause of the entire circuit certainly applies to those who build wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation of Christ according to the Apostle's meaning. Therefore, observers of the Old Law and the laws of men are not understood by "wood, hay, and stubble," as the Waldensian <note>A follower of the Waldensians, a medieval movement that preceded the Reformation and was deemed heretical by the Catholic Church for rejecting certain sacraments and Church authority.</note> believes. Thus, our position remains intact: that this passage is understood to refer to the state of **venial sins** <term>Minor sins that do not break a person's relationship with God entirely, but require purification.</term>, as we have brought forth from Catholic writers. It remains unshaken that the holy doctors have canonically explained this passage as referring not only to the penance of the present life, but also to that future fire of Purgatory.

->**THE WALDENSIAN,**<-

Likewise, regarding that passage in **Maccabees** <note>2 Maccabees 12:46: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead." This is a primary proof-text for Purgatory.</note> stating that *it is a holy and wholesome thought*, and so on... except that Thomas Aquinas <note>The influential 13th-century theologian and philosopher.</note> would have thought this was in Hell. We have shown before that those Waldensians have both stolen the Canon of the Scriptures by theft and corrupted it with lies, saying on the same page that Catholic commentators are now true, then false. Therefore, enticed by this license and confident that it would proceed with impunity, they have become bolder by their previous example. Now they begin to condemn entire books. They think themselves "true" if they keep silent, but they overturn and erase whatever might have convicted them of their error. 

How much better would they have been as "true" men if they had perceived those things which could have been defended while keeping these books safe? They present to us a bit of the seduction of the **Sadducees** <note>A Jewish sect at the time of Jesus that rejected the idea of the resurrection and the afterlife.</note>, who, to be safer in their errors, received nothing of the Old Testament except the five books of Moses, thinking these alone were suitable for them since they could not be openly convicted therein regarding the error of the resurrection. These Waldensians present to us something of Jewish obstinacy, as they themselves do not receive the books in which the presence of the Savior is taught. They wish to keep the dispute hanging, which would otherwise be ended. The Waldensians also deny the books of Maccabees, because...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE,

Regarding the present question, since they have very openly appeared to reject **Suffrages for the dead** <term>Prayers, alms, or Masses offered for the benefit of souls in Purgatory.</term>, we were about to hurl a most direct spear into their heresy, but they simply say, "I do not accept it." If this "I do not accept it" <note>original: "non recipio"</note> were such a certain oath, it would be the best defense in battle—as if one could simply say "I do not accept" to avoid spears, deaths, or wounds. Truly, however, the outcome depends on the strength and the hand of the adversary. Therefore, we would be fools if we waited for them to accept their chains voluntarily. Thus, we march against them—but let those military metaphors cease. We shall try something milder from the shadows with our Waldensian; let us see if, just as a sick man is compelled by a physician, a heretic might be led by an orthodox believer to take the bitter medicine even against his will. 

First, it is certain that they would never have moved from this position unless it had most directly refuted their pestilential opinion. Since the sense of this passage is so manifest that it does not allow itself to be twisted in a different direction, <margin>p</margin> they have found a deceptive substitute—an inversion they often use—to expunge it entirely. These falsifiers of the Sacred Scriptures have said above that a second **Purgatory** <term>A place of purification for souls who die in a state of grace but still require cleansing from venial sins before entering Heaven.</term> is "uncertain" because the Holy Scriptures give no testimony of it. Doubtless, by this art of yours, it will remain forever "uncertain"; by this fraud of yours, the Scriptures themselves will never give testimony. For if you find things that do not suit you, you consider them unfit and expunge them. 

In this, you truly act out the fable of the man who was to be hanged; because he had obtained from a foolish judge the right to be strangled by whatever tree he pleased, he could not find a single willow in the whole world by which he wished to hang. Through this trickery, he escaped unharmed and continues to evade his punishment to this day. You play a similar game with us: if you do not find testimony that suits your wish, you say it does not exist; if you do find it, you contend it is not of the quality you desire, and thus you lead the argument according to your own whim. 

You had promised us in that confession <margin>[Perhaps a reference to the Waldensian Confession of Faith: "We wish to be taught human learning from the traditions of the sacred law..."]</margin> and many things that follow there. I hold you to this: show your faith! Follow Aurelius **Augustine**, **Gregory**, the **Apostle** in his letter to the Corinthians, and now the **Maccabees**. But if these were nothing but mere lies, then the present witnesses do not please you. You seek others who say what no one but a heretic would say. Thus, once you come to the heart of the matter, you call the Doctors of the Church "false," you corrupt the Apostle, and you expunge the Maccabees. What others will ever be enough for you hereafter, you who think these men are nothing? 

You say, however, that the **Book of Maccabees** is **Apocryphal** <term>From the Greek for "hidden." In this context, the Waldensians used the term to mean "non-canonical" or "unreliable," whereas the author defends them as "Deuterocanonical" or secondary but holy books.</term> and numbered among the books not received by the Church. If you now understand "Apocryphal" to mean that which the Church does not receive, then I judge you by your own mouth, you wicked servant! Nothing will be more rightly termed "Apocryphal" in this time than this heresy of yours. The holy Doctors do not know it; the Apostle and the Book of the Maccabees do not know it; the whole Church of all time does not know it. 

But let us leave aside what falls by its own weight, which we have often held up against you, and return to the discourse we began. We shall speak, then, of the Apocrypha. There is more than one kind of Apocrypha. There are those which the Church condemns entirely, such as the books of heretics. But there are others which the Church receives as holy—those which Saint **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), the translator of the Vulgate Bible. His "Galeatus Prologus" or "Helmeted Preface" discussed which books were canonical.</note> mentions in his "Helmeted Preface": the Book of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and the Books of the Maccabees. 

You cast this book out from the **Hagiographa** <term>Literally "Holy Writings," often used to refer to the third section of the Hebrew Bible or, more broadly, to sacred canonical texts.</term>, but for what fault? Is it because it is merely "Apocryphal," or because it is also "false"? If it is because it is Apocryphal, you must explain the reason for the name, and from that, you will perceive the justice of the cause. For they were called "Apocryphal" because they were written at a time when the certain succession of the Prophets had ceased; this happened mostly after the **Return from Babylon** <note>The return of the Jews from the Babylonian Captivity in the 6th century BCE.</note>. Because these books were written out of a devoted and spontaneous zeal rather than by a divine movement, they were not recognized by those few who, inspired by the Divine Spirit, were alone permitted to consecrate the canonically received books.

# ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST <note>The header is incomplete in the original, continuing from the previous page's "Against the Waldensians."</note>

So you say, "I am free to receive or reject them." By no means. If the authors derive their meanings from the canonical scriptures and the acceptance of them, they receive such strength from these sources that you cannot condemn the one without the other. It is like someone who tells you something from the Gospel; although he is not a Prophet or an Apostle, if you call him a liar, you have called the Gospel a lie at the same time. Furthermore, if that book were **Apocryphal**, it should be avoided for that reason alone. Not just in one instance, especially after an "insoluble knot" <note>An idiom for a particularly difficult or impossible problem.</note> had arisen, but it would have been necessary to avoid the rest as well. 

Certainly, in the previous sections, when you were already out of your own danger, **Ecclesiasticus** <term>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach, a book of the Old Testament included in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but considered apocryphal by Protestants.</term> pleased you abundantly. Here, "the furnace proves the potter's vessels, and the temptation of tribulation proves just men." <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiasticus 27:5.</note> At that time, it did not hurt your judgment that it was "Apocryphal," nor did you believe the Church did not receive it. It pleased you then because you wanted to use it against us. 

Then, let me call upon the highest authority. Why do you, with such excessive stubbornness, call these books only "Apocrypha"? In other places, **St. Jerome** <term>A 4th-century scholar and Church Father best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</term> also calls them **Hagiographa** <term>From Greek, meaning "Holy Writings."</term>—by which name they also refer to the Psalter, the books of Solomon, Daniel, Chronicles, Ezra, and Esther; which seven books no one has denied except those who have also lost their faith. If, therefore, the divine Jerome called them both "Apocrypha" and "Hagiographa," he certainly meant they were to be denied by no one except those who are contentious and deserters of Christian piety. 

Thus you ruin yourself too much; you could have found this out. You were able to snatch the word "Apocrypha" from the mouth of the divine Jerome. You could also have found "Hagiographa." Why did you not also pick up that term? But from that first word, envy had to be stirred up; a word of middle and twofold meaning lay open to the injury of your malice. It pleased your "nose" <note>A Latin idiom suggesting a sense of irony or mockery.</note> so that you might cast shame (as you think) upon the Christian cause. Thus, you hold onto an ambiguous word for the sake of deception, which the divine Jerome uttered simply. 

For the word is indeed Greek, and it means **hidden**. Many people keep many excellent things with them which they do not wish to be known; therefore, they are "Apocrypha." I speak of many learned men; they keep all their more distinguished short works in secret with themselves. This is not from a vice of the books, but because of their excellence, on account of which they forbid them to the public; thus they are "Apocrypha." A master of a household keeps the private account of his life secret with his companion of the bedchamber <note>His wife.</note>; they decide between themselves a time of abstaining or some other holy example. This law, remaining hidden between them, is "Apocryphal"—not indeed as something to be blamed, but as something not to be made public. 

In the same way, the Church has received those five books which the divine Jerome mentions in his **Prologus Galeatus** <term>The "Helmeted Preface," Jerome's famous introduction to the Books of Kings in the Latin Vulgate, where he discusses the biblical canon.</term> as being full of holy examples and teachings, which she is accustomed to use for the instruction and imitation of virtue. No fault is given to them because of that name; but because the books of heretics are also usually removed entirely from public sight lest they undermine and corrupt the faith of the simple, for this reason they too are most truly called "Apocrypha." 

Therefore, to say it all in one word: whatever you keep in secret with yourself, whether it is innocent but you have prepared it only for your own use, or whether it is harmful and you do not wish its vice to reach many people—we call both by the single name "Apocrypha." You, however, keep silent about the better sense of the word, and stir up envy against us concerning those **Hagiographa** by using its worse meaning. 

In such matters, you should take nothing away from the faith of the **Book of Maccabees** <note>The Books of the Maccabees contain the primary scriptural defense for the practice of praying for the dead.</note> even if it were "Apocryphal." But perhaps you are going to accuse the same book of being false. Do you then dare to thrust this upon the divine Jerome—a man of the most watchful faith and the sharpest champion against every error? Do you dare to say that this man translated false things and gave the purity of Christianity doctrines that are alien to true piety? You will dare, perhaps, if you call the book false; for even if you believe it to be true, you would still condemn it to smear it with that color. You will contend, therefore, that you are wiser than Jerome alone—a man who was so great that even among the most learned men everywhere today, hardly one in a hundred has attained a tenth of a portion of Jerome's learning. I shall remain silent as to whether I should even admit a drop of learning from you, a **barbarian** born and raised in the filthiest filth.

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE
<meta>catchword: p. s. [the next page begins with "proxima"]</meta>

But you have caught a whiff of something from your grubs and wasps <note>original: "brucis veſpiſq;"—a metaphor for stinging or corrupting ideas</note> that you think surpasses Jerome’s judgment! Go ahead then, stand up like a man! Produce your Greek sources; show us the passages that would make him blush. Rise above your simple state and bring forth something an educated person could listen to with a straight face. 

But let us get down to the immediate facts: you say that the five books called **Apocryphal** <term>Apocrypha: From the Greek for "hidden," these are books like Tobit or Maccabees which the author argues are part of the Christian Bible even if they were not in the Hebrew Bible.</term> are not accepted by the Church. On this point, you are lying through your teeth. Listen to what **Jerome** says on this matter; in his *Prologue to Tobit*, he writes: "The book of **Tobit**, which the Hebrews cut out from the catalog of divine scriptures and relegated to those they call **Hagiographa**" <term>Hagiographa: Literally "holy writings." In this context, the author uses it to mean sacred books that are read by the Church for edification, even if debated by scholars.</term>. And in the *Prologue to Judith*: "**Judith** is read among the Hagiographa." And later: "But because the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church.</note> is said to have counted this book in the number of the Holy Scriptures, I have yielded to your request [to translate it]." Likewise, in another Prologue: "Although the books of the **Maccabees** are not in the Canon of the Hebrews, they are nonetheless noted by the Church among the histories of the divine volumes." 

What more do we need to bring your lies to light, you most wicked of two-legged creatures? You said that according to one passage in Jerome, they were apocryphal. Why did you not mention the many other places where this same teacher called them **Hagiographa** and said they were received by the Church? Consider this, you who occasionally ask to be taught better—consider, I say, your shameless face! For you do not actually wish to be taught, but under this veil of ignorance, you desire to slander the right faith. You care nothing for following those who could teach you; instead, you study only how to hold onto your ruinous opinions. You bring up the ancient Fathers to our faces—men distant from our own age—as if they were a fabrication made up by your neighbors who know nothing beyond their own years. Otherwise, your argument is cold. For you do not actually observe the ancients; you deny them. You read the most recent authors, whom you openly criticize, in secret—not so that you might become a better person, but so that you might be better equipped to defend your treachery <note>original: "pfidiā" (perfidy), meaning a break from the true faith.</note>. If you find anything suitable for slander, or anything prone to being overturned or depraved, that is what pleases you in them. You receive all those things there. You would not prefer the ancients over the moderns, yet suddenly they become "Catholic" and "Apostolic" to you for this purpose. Thus, what you are doing against us now, you want us to believe you have done since the **Early Church**.

Return to your senses! You will find that you have only recently accepted someone because you thought he was suitable for plucking words from **Paul**, twisting them to be contrary to the Christian religion. Have we not already shown that you have raved with false interpretations? Think and understand: you have been caught in a theft. If you were not evil, you ought to have followed the ancients in everything once you pointed them out to us. If you wanted Jerome to be followed when he called a book "Apocryphal" in one way, you should have followed him in the rest. You should have begun to call those same books both **Hagiographa** and "received by the Church." Finally, unless you were wicked, you should have conceded to the **Council of Nicaea**—the council from which you pretended to draw your faith in that first confession of yours—that these are not "Apocryphal" (by which name you wish to imply they are condemned). You should not think that such a Holy Synod would have received them into the number of the divine scriptures if they were. 

Therefore, just as with the other books, the most ancient writers remembered the book of **Maccabees**. **Saint Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian and philosopher.</note>, in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, mentions certain dappled horses and armed attendants. Tell me, where else besides the book of Maccabees did he get these "armed attendants"? For there it is written: "A horse appeared to them, having a terrible rider adorned with the best trappings; he rushed violently and struck Heliodorus with his forefeet. He who sat upon the horse seemed to have golden armor," and more that follows <note>A reference to 2 Maccabees 3:25-26, describing a divine intervention to protect the Temple treasury.</note>. But later writers also mention it: **Eusebius of Caesarea**, **Rufinus** the priest of the Church of Aquileia in his *Explanation of the Creed*, **Aurelius Augustine**, and our **Jerome** again and again—as does the universal Church. 

The **Waldensian** is the only heretic for whom this book is of little use, because it acts as a guide against their treachery; thus he tries to pull it away by fraud. It was more celebrated in everyone's mouth than he could lie about not having found it. They are able to deny it, and having been excluded from his other crimes, he is found trying to strip the book of its authority—but neither...

<meta>Continuing the defense of the deuterocanonical books (which the author calls Hagiographa), this page focuses on the linguistic nuance of the word "Apocrypha." The author argues that "Apocrypha" simply means "hidden" and does not necessarily imply that a book is false or heretical, accusing his opponent of using the term's negative connotations to undermine the authority of books like Maccabees and Sirach.</meta>

### ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS, AGAINST...

Therefore, you say, "It is free for me to either receive or reject them." Not at all. If indeed the authors derive their meanings from the canonical scriptures and their accepted interpretations, they receive strength from these sources so that you cannot condemn one without the other. It is just like someone who tells you a story from the Gospel; even if he is not a Prophet or an Apostle, if you say he is lying, you have at the same time called the Gospel a lie. Furthermore, if a book was "Apocryphal," <term>Apocrypha: From the Greek 'apokryphos', meaning 'hidden.' While it later came to mean 'non-canonical' or 'false,' the author here argues for its original meaning of 'set apart' or 'private.'</term> it should not be shunned merely because of that name. Not only in one instance—and there, after an insoluble knot had been tied—but it was necessary to be cautious about the others as well. 

Certainly, in what came before, when you were outside of your own danger, the book of **Ecclesiasticus** <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note> pleased you well enough. Here: "the furnace proves the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation proves just men" <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiasticus 27:5.</note>. At that time, it did not hinder your judgment that it was Apocryphal, or that you believed the Church did not receive it. It pleased you because you wished to use it against us; but then, as if to make a final appeal, you stubbornly insist on calling them only "Apocryphal." 

In other places, **Jerome** also calls these **Hagiographa** <term>Hagiographa: 'Holy writings.' Jerome used this term for books like the Psalms and Proverbs, but here the author uses it to defend the status of the 'Deuterocanonical' books.</term>—by which name they also refer to the Psalter, the books of Solomon, Daniel, Chronicles, Ezra, and Esther. No one has denied these seven books unless they have also lost their faith. If, therefore, the divine Jerome called them both Apocryphal and Hagiographa, he certainly said this so that they should be denied by no one, except by someone who is contentious and a deserter of Christian piety. 

Thus you betray yourself too much; you were able to find the word. You were able to snatch the word "Apocryphal" from the mouth of the divine Jerome. You were also able to find "Hagiographa." Why did you not take that up as well? But you intended to stir up hatred by using the first word; a word of double meaning lay open to the injury of your malice. It pleased your arrogance <note>original: "In naso tuo," literally "in your nose," a Latin idiom for turning up one's nose or showing disdain.</note> to cast what you consider shame upon the Christian cause. Thus you cling to a deceptive and ambiguous word which the divine Jerome uttered quite simply. 

In truth, it is a Greek word and it means **hidden**. Many people keep many excellent things with them which they do not wish to be known; these are therefore "Apocrypha." Many—I am speaking of the learned—keep all their most distinguished short works in secret; this is not due to a vice in the books, but because of their excellence, for which reason they forbid them from the public. They are, therefore, "Apocrypha." A head of a household keeps the private plan of his life with his spouse; they decide between themselves a time for abstaining or for some other holy example. This "hidden law" remaining between them is "apocryphal"—not indeed as something to be blamed, but as something not to be made public. 

In the same way, the Church received those five books which the divine Jerome mentions in his **Helmeted Prologue** <term>Helmeted Prologue: (Latin: *Prologus Galeatus*) Jerome's famous preface to the books of Kings, which served as a "helmeted" defense of his translation against critics.</term> as being full of holy examples and doctrine, and she is accustomed to use them for the instruction and imitation of virtue. No fault can yet be assigned there based on the name alone; however, because the books of heretics are also usually removed entirely from public view—lest they undermine and corrupt the faith of the simple—they too are most truly called "Apocrypha." 

Therefore, to say everything in one word: whatever you keep in secret with yourself, whether it is innocent but prepared for your use alone, or whether it is harmful and you do not wish its vice to reach many people, we call both by the single name "Apocrypha." You, however, keep silent about the better meaning of the word, and stir up hatred against those **Hagiographa** by focusing on its worse sense. For such reasons, you should not take away any faith from the book of **Maccabees** <note>Two books of the Old Testament detailing the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid Empire.</note> even if it were "Apocryphal." 

But perhaps you are going to accuse it of being false? Do you dare to thrust this upon the divine Jerome, a man of the most clear-sighted faith and the fiercest champion against all error? Do you dare to say that he passed down falsehoods and served up doctrines foreign to true piety to Christian purity? Perhaps you will dare, if indeed you call the book false; for even if you think it is true, you still condemn it by smearing it with that color. You will contend, then, that you are wiser than Jerome alone? Jerome was so great that among the most learned men everywhere today, hardly one in a hundred has achieved a tenth part of Jerome's erudition. I will say nothing of you—a barbarian born and raised in the filthiest dregs—even being allowed a drop of it.

# WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE

But have you sniffed out something from your gadflies and wasps <note>The author uses "wasps" as a metaphor for irritating or stinging heretical arguments.</note> that surpasses the judgment of **Jerome**?

### ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST THE HERETICS

In that matter, however, he persists, and moving to a higher pitch he says: "But the writer added this at the end." If you did not sit there in your little assembly <note>original: "conciliabulo." The author uses this word dismissively to describe a non-sanctioned or heretical gathering.</note> where you sweated over this place and where you cooked up these lies, perhaps someone among your accomplices from a remote corner—or even from the very threshold—suddenly thought of this and threw it out into the common talk. I say this: if you could produce such a claim from any Catholic—not just any man from the countryside, but one from the ancient Church—then you would have something. 

But what is this new "clemency," or rather, what great forgetfulness of yours, that you did not name such a person, to our shame? Too often, when a necessary point must be proven, you lack the evidence—unless you also have some more recent author here whom you read in secret but were afraid to bring forward. Indeed, you were right to be afraid; for whichever of the recent authors you might call upon by name, you would immediately grant them a degree of faith, and by that same faith you would have to stand with us against them in turn. Thus, you could no longer accuse them of corrupting everything from the **Apostolic rule**, and you would finally have to confess that the truth remains sincere in the Church even today. 

However, because this was placed at the end of the chapter, you carry on as if you would not have suspected it to be a forgery had you found it in the beginning or the middle. This is a very weak suspicion. For not only the ends, but all parts of a work are equally marked by churchmen with **obeluses** and **asterisks**. <term>Obelus and Asterisk: Marks used by ancient scholars like Origen and Jerome; the obelus (−) indicated a passage suspected of being a later addition, while the asterisk (*) marked text found in original sources like the Hebrew Bible but missing in the Greek translation.</term> Furthermore, in the earliest times, there was a continuous flow of text in books, especially historical ones. It was not, as you think, divided by chapters; therefore, you should not look for any end other than the end of the work itself. 

How much more skillfully did our interpreters of the **Sacred Scriptures** exercise this kind of textual judgment! If they found anything extra in the common editions that was not in the original books, they would say: "This was added from this or that source," perhaps from **Aquila** or **Theodotion** <note>Early translators of the Old Testament into Greek whose work was often compared to the standard Septuagint version.</note>, or "It is not found in the Hebrew," or "It is not in the **Septuagint**," <term>Septuagint: The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament used by the early Church.</term> and they would mark it with an obelus. If they found something missing, they would show that it was present in the Hebrew or the Septuagint and add what was lacking, marking it with an asterisk. 

But the **Waldensian**, that mere **ape of Catholics** <note>original: "Simius catholicorum." A common medieval insult suggesting the heretic mimics Catholic scholarship without understanding it.</note>, could only imitate this small bit of their scholarship by saying: "The writer added this at the end." Yet they have produced neither the author of the saying, nor any place where it is missing in the most ancient Latin and Greek manuscripts. This was beyond their mental sharpness; there, their rustic effort failed. They cannot yet move this book as if it were **Apocryphal** or unreceived, nor can they move the verse as if it were a forgery. 

If they wish to move such a thing in good faith, we have proposed a standard, like that of a carpenter, based on the testimonies of the ancients, according to which they should proceed in carving such things out. For to allow the writings of the ancients to be moved recklessly at any whim or for any cause would, in the end, expose them to the injury of the most wicked and ignorant alike. Then, the truth would no longer be considered for itself, but according to the lust of each person; all faith in writers would be weakened, and the Truth would remain safe and certain in no book. 

But let us grant for a moment that they had fully proven this passage—"It is a holy and wholesome thought," and the rest—to be entirely a forgery. Nevertheless, their treachery is still refuted by the whole passage. For thus it is written:

> But the most valiant **Judas** <note>Judas Maccabeus, the Jewish leader of the revolt against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BC.</note> exhorted the people to keep themselves without sin, seeing before their eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who were struck down. And making a gathering, he sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to **Jerusalem** to offer a sacrifice for the sins of the dead, thinking well and religiously concerning the **resurrection**. For unless he hoped that those who had fallen would rise again, it would seem superfluous and vain to pray for the dead. And because he considered that those who had fallen asleep with godliness had great grace laid up for them. It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the deceased, that they may be loosed from sins.

Recall to memory here, you Waldensian, the subject upon which we are disputing: certainly, it is regarding the **purgation of souls** after this life and regarding the prayers offered for the dead. You have lyingly charged that these were recently invented out of the greed of the present Church, outside the faith of the ancients. You have here a witness who...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE

...by your madness, let him prove Judas Maccabeus to us. God attested to his piety and faith from heaven with frequent miracles, for he could not have been acceptable to God except through his piety. Look at Maccabeus: he sends silver to Jerusalem as a sacrifice for the sins of the dead, believing it is not a hollow thing to pray for the deceased. What more do you have with which to resist, claiming that sacrifice for the dead ought not to be performed, and that those who do it have recently invented the practice out of greed? Therefore, does not that verse—"It is a holy and wholesome thought," and the rest of it <note>original: "Sancta & salubris." This refers to 2 Maccabees 12:46: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."</note>—agree with the previous sentence in its related meaning? What excuse do you have, then, to reject it as if it were a forgery or a stranger to this passage? Confess your evasion, you Waldensian, and do not accuse us of violating the Scriptures, a crime committed only by your side. 

Then, to argue for the damnation of those slain soldiers, you bring in the words of the Apostle John: "There is a sin unto death" <note>1 John 5:16</note>, and what follows. Before I speak to you from this passage regarding the present matter, I rightfully call out your treachery. In the previous chapter, which dealt with the prayers <term>suffrages: intercessory prayers or works offered by the living for the benefit of the souls in Purgatory</term> of the saints, you pretended that you could find no place in the entire Bible where you believed intercessions were supported. Now, after something else had to be done—when a lie of a different kind needed to be constructed—you conveniently found that same Bible and led it captive to veil your falsehood. You blocked it when it wanted to come forward of its own right to testify to the truth against you. 

But let us return to the point. You say these slain men committed a "sin unto death." What, then, is a sin unto death for which we ought not to pray? It is final despair, hatred of one's brother, and the attacking of known truth. A sin unto death is one that is not admitted through human frailty and which the prayer of the righteous does not purge <note>This refers to the Catholic doctrine that while "venial" or "frail" sins can be cleansed after death, "mortal" sins involving a total rejection of God cannot.</note>. May God have mercy on me, for I do not lie. Your sin, Waldensian, is "unto death," for you—out of your own willful hatred for your neighbor and not out of ignorance (that is, a slip of human frailty)—both stir up and defend a many-headed, pestilent heresy. I confront you at every turn, pointing out things you have willfully passed over and things right before your eyes that you refused to see. I show you the very points from which such errors should either never have been adopted or should finally be set aside by a humble and good conscience. 

But you persist in your madness; you exercise your hatred against us at too great a cost—the loss of your own salvation. Furthermore, your efforts are in vain. You will never destroy the Church that you now attack, for not even the Antichrist will be able to tear it down, though you may cause it great suffering for a time. Therefore, if you were to move from hatred to slaughter against us, as you might one day: we would die in body, but you would go in soul to Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. Take this passing thought from me regarding the "sin unto death"; though I am not your enemy, listen carefully to this stern yet healthy warning. 

The sin of those fallen soldiers was not of that kind; they sinned only out of greed. I admit that greed is a capital sin, but it is one committed through human weakness and does not directly oppose divine grace. Zacchaeus and Matthew, both tax collectors, earned forgiveness for that sin, whereas the Jews who denied the miracles of Christ died in their sins. Those soldiers of Judas Maccabeus sinned from greed; therefore, there was hope for their forgiveness. For this reason, it is written of the survivors: "And so they all blessed the just judgment of the Lord, who had made the hidden things manifest" <note>2 Maccabees 12:41. In the story, the soldiers were found with idols/votive offerings taken from Jamnia, which was considered the "sin" for which they died.</note>; and so, turning to prayer, they begged that what had been done might be consigned to oblivion. 

To make your argument seem more believable—for you saw it was likely we would say they repented of their sins while wounded at the very end of their lives—you try to get ahead of us and shut our mouths by claiming they died without repentance. You certainly did not find this written anywhere; you assert that it is not written here as easily as you deny what is written elsewhere. But because you saw that the "sin unto death" on its own would not look like a reason to mention it here, you added the claim that "they died without repentance." Since you add this from your own mind and without a witness, I shall reply with the same or better faith from my own: they died in a state of repentance.

...in that, however, it consists, he moves higher and says that the scribe added this at the end. If this is so, where did you sit in that little assembly of yours? Where did you sweat over this place? Where did you concoct these lies? If you did not get this from some accomplice in a remote corner or from someone who suddenly threw this thought into the community from the threshold, then I ask: if you have this from some Catholic—not just some peasant from the countryside, but one you might bring forward from the ancient Church—then what is this "new mercy" of yours? Or rather, what great forgetfulness is yours that you have not named such a person, to our real shame? 

Yet, too often in proving a necessary point, you are found wanting, unless you also have here some of the more recent authors whom you read in secret. But you feared to bring them forward; and rightly would you fear, for whichever of the more recent ones you called by name, you would immediately grant them credit. Based on that credit, you would in turn have to stand with us regarding them. Thus, you could no longer charge that they have corrupted everything from the Apostolic rule; you would have to confess, finally, that the sincere truth remains in the Church even today. 

Truly, because this was placed at the end of the chapter, you carry on as if you would not have been equally suspicious of it being a forgery <note>original: "suppositicium"</note> had you found it at the beginning or in the middle. This is a very weak suspicion. For not only the ends, but all parts of a work are marked equally by churchmen with <term>obelisks and asterisks: symbols used by ancient scholars like Origen and Jerome; an asterisk (*) marked text found in the Hebrew but missing in the Greek, while an obelisk († or ÷) marked text that seemed doubtful or extra</term>. Furthermore, in the earliest times, there was a continuous flow of books, especially historical ones. They were not, as you think, divided by chapters; because of this, you should not look for any other end than the end of the work itself. 

How much more skillfully did our interpreters of the Sacred Scriptures exercise such judgment over books! If they found anything more in the common editions than in the original books, they would say: "this was added from this or that source"—for example, from Aquila or from Theodotion <note>Aquila of Sinope and Theodotion were famous 2nd-century translators of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note>—"it is not found in the Hebrew, nor in the Septuagint" <note>The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. And they would mark it with an obelisk. If they read something less, they would show that there was more to be had in the Hebrew or the Septuagint, and they would add what was missing, marking it with an asterisk. 

The Waldensian, however, that monkey of the Catholics, could only imitate this tiny bit of such scholarly judgment: they say that the scribe "added this at the end." Yet they have produced neither the author of this statement nor any place where it is not found in the most ancient Latin and Greek copies. This was beyond their sharpest wits; there, their rustic attempt struck a dead end. Therefore, they shall not yet remove the book as if it were <term>apocryphal: books of the Bible that are of disputed authority or not included in the Hebrew canon</term> or not received; they shall not yet remove the verse as if it were a forgery. 

If they wish to move such a thing in good faith, we have proposed the "carpenter’s rule" of the testimony of the ancients, according to which they should proceed in carving out such things. For to allow the writings of the ancients to be removed recklessly for whatever whim or cause would, in the end, expose them to injury by the most wicked and ignorant alike. Then, truth would be judged not by itself, but by the lust of any person; all trust in writers would be weakened, and truth would remain safe and certain in no book. 

But let us grant for a moment that they had fully proven this place—"It is a holy and wholesome thought," and the rest of it—to be a forgery. Their treachery would nonetheless be refuted by the whole passage. For thus it is written: 

> "But the most valiant Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves without sin, seeing before their eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who were overthrown. And making a gathering, he sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem to be offered as a sacrifice for the sins of the dead, thinking well and religiously concerning the resurrection. For if he had not hoped that they that were slain should rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and vain to pray for the dead. And because he considered that they who had fallen asleep with godliness had great grace laid up for them. It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the deceased, that they may be loosed from sins." <note>2 Maccabees 12:42-46</note>

Recall here to your memory, you Waldensian, the matter upon which we are debating: certainly, the purging of souls after this life and the <term>suffrages: prayers or pious acts performed to help souls in Purgatory</term> for the dead. You have falsely charged that these were recently invented out of the greed of the present Church, outside the faith of the ancients. You have your witness...

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK THREE

Let your madness be refuted before us by Judas Maccabeus, whose piety and faith God attested to from heaven with frequent miracles; for he could not have been accepted by God except through his piety. Behold, for the sins of the dead, this Maccabeus sent silver to Jerusalem for a sacrifice, believing it was not in vain to pray for the dead. What more do you have to struggle against? Why do you say that sacrifice for the dead should not be performed, and that those who do so have newly devised this out of greed? Therefore, that verse—*It is a holy and wholesome thought* <note>original: "Sancta & salubris", referring to 2 Maccabees 12:46: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."</note>—and the rest of it, does it not agree with the preceding passage and the related sentiment? What grounds do you have to object against it as if it were a forgery or a stranger to this place? Confess, Waldensian, your own evasiveness, and do not charge us with violating the scriptures—a crime committed only by your side. 

Then, to argue for the damnation of those slain soldiers, you bring in that passage from John the Apostle: *There is a sin unto death* <note>original: "Est peccatum ad mortem", from 1 John 5:16</note> and what follows. Before I speak to you from this passage regarding the present matter, I rightly demand an explanation for your bad faith. For in the previous chapter, which dealt with the <term>suffrages</term> <note>The "suffrages of the saints" refer to intercessory prayers or works offered on behalf of the souls in Purgatory.</note> of the saints, you pretended that you could find no place in the entire Bible where intercessions might be believed. Now, after you needed to do something else—namely, to construct a different kind of lie—you conveniently found this passage. You lead it away captive to veil your lie, though you previously prohibited it from coming to testify to the truth against you, as was its right. 

But let us return to our point. You say these slain men committed a "sin unto death." What, then, is a <term>sin unto death</term> for which we ought not to pray? It is final despair, hatred of one’s brother, and the attacking of the recognized truth. A sin unto death is one that is not admitted through human frailty, and thus it is not cleansed by the prayer of the righteous. So may God have mercy on me, for I do not lie: your sin, Waldensian, is "unto death." You have fallen into it not from ignorance (that is, human frailty), but from your willful hatred of your neighbor; you both stir up and defend a pestilent heresy with many heads. 

I meet you everywhere, pointing out things you have intentionally passed over—things which were right in front of you and which you could have touched with your finger but refused to see. I show you these things so that you might either never have taken up such errors, or finally lay them aside with a modest and good conscience. But you persist in your madness; at a far too great a stake—that is, the loss of your own salvation—you exercise your hatred against us, and otherwise in vain. You will never destroy the Church which you now attack, for even the Antichrist will not be able to destroy it, though he may bring a heavy calamity upon it. Therefore, if you are going to attack us with slaughter in the future as you do now with hatred, we may die in the body, but you will go to Gehenna in your soul. 

Take this from me in passing regarding the "sin unto death"; though it comes from a man who is not your enemy, listen closely to this severe but nonetheless wholesome admonition: The sin of those fallen soldiers was not of this kind. They had sinned only through greed. I admit that this is a capital sin, but it is one committed out of human infirmity, which does not directly oppose divine grace. Zacchaeus and Matthew were both tax collectors, yet they earned the remission of that sin, whereas the Jews who denied the miracles of Christ died in their sins. Those soldiers of Judas Maccabeus sinned through greed; therefore, there was hope for their remission. For this reason, it is written of the survivors: *So they all blessed the just judgment of the Lord, who had made the hidden things manifest,* and so, turning to prayers, they asked that what had been done might be delivered to oblivion. 

Here, so that your effort might seem more credible—for you saw that we were about to say they had repented of their wounds at the very end of life—you forestall us and shut our mouths, saying: "they died without repentance." You certainly did not find this written. You assert what is "not written" here just as easily as you deny what is written elsewhere. But because you saw that the "sin unto death" argument had no weight on its own as to why you should mention it here, you added this: "they died without repentance." Because you add this of your own accord and without a witness, I shall replace it with the same or better faith of my own: they died in a state of repentance.

Or rather, what great forgetfulness of yours is it that you did not name such a person, to our true shame? Yet too often, when a necessary matter must be proven, you lack evidence, unless you have here some more recent author whom you read in secret, but were afraid to bring forward. Indeed, you were right to be afraid; for whichever recent authors you might call upon by name, you would immediately be granting them credit. Finally, you would have to confess that the truth remains sincere in the Church even today. 

However, because this was placed at the end of the chapter, you bring it forth as if, had you found it further back or in the middle, you would not have suspected it to be a forgery just the same. Otherwise, they have produced neither the author of the saying, nor any place where it is missing in the most ancient Latin and Greek copies. This was beyond their sharp-wittedness; there, their rustic effort struck a wall. Therefore, they cannot yet remove the book as if it were <term>apocryphal</term> <note>Books not accepted into the official Canon of Scripture.</note> or not received; they cannot yet remove the verse as if it were a forgery.

For to allow the writings of the ancients to be removed rashly for whatever whim or cause would, in the end, expose them to injury by the most wicked and ignorant alike. ### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE

...your madness, let it prove against us Judas Maccabeus, whose piety and faith God attested from heaven with frequent miracles; for he could not have been accepted by God except on account of his piety. Behold, for your sake, Maccabeus sends silver to Jerusalem as a sacrifice for the sins of the dead, believing it not vain to pray for the dead. <note>The author refers to 2 Maccabees 12:43-45, where Judas Maccabeus sends a collection to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering for fallen soldiers.</note> What further reason do you have to resist, so as to say both that sacrifice for the dead ought not to be made, and that those same people [the Catholics] recently devised this out of greed? Therefore, does not that verse, *"It is a holy and wholesome thought,"* <note>original: "Sancta & salubris". Referring to 2 Maccabees 12:46: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."</note> and the rest of it, agree with the preceding passage according to a related meaning? What objection, then, do you have against it, as if it were a forgery and foreign to this place? Confess your evasion, Waldensian, and do not charge us with violating Scripture—a crime committed only on your side.

Next, to argue for the damnation of those slain soldiers, you bring forward that word of the Apostle John: *"There is a sin unto death,"* <note>original: "Est peccatū ad mortē". From 1 John 5:16. The Waldensians argued that the soldiers died in mortal sin (idolatry/greed) and therefore could not be prayed for.</note> and what follows. Before I speak to you from this passage regarding the present matter, I justly demand an explanation for your treachery: since in the previous chapter, where the intercession of the saints was discussed, you pretended to find no place in the whole Bible from which you thought intercessions were believed, yet now, after something else had to be done and a lie of another kind had to be prepared, you conveniently found it. You lead the Scripture captive to veil a lie—the very text you prohibited when it wanted to come by its own right to testify to the truth against you. 

But let us return to the point: you say these slain men committed a "sin unto death." What then is a "sin unto death" for which we ought not to pray? It is final despair, hatred of a brother, or the attacking of known truth. A sin unto death is that which is not admitted through human frailty, and thus is not purged by the prayer of the righteous. So may God have mercy on me, for I do not lie: *your* sin is unto death, Waldensian, you who—out of your spontaneous hatred toward your neighbor and not having slipped out of ignorance (that is, human frailty)—both stir up and defend a multi-headed, pestilent heresy. Everywhere I confront you, pointing out things you have intentionally passed over, things you have stumbled upon right in front of you and refused to see. I show from these things that a modest and good conscience ought either never to have taken up such errors or finally to have set them aside. 

But you persist in madness; with too great a stake—that is, to the detriment of your own salvation—you exercise hatred against us, and otherwise in vain. The Church which you now attack, you will never destroy; even the Antichrist will not be able to destroy it, though he might be able to bring a heavy calamity upon it. Therefore, if as you now move with hatred, you were once to move against us with slaughter: we die in body, but you will go to Gehenna in soul. Take this from me in passing regarding the "sin unto death"; it comes from a man who was not your enemy, so may you listen attentively to this healthy admonition. 

The sin of those fallen soldiers was not of this kind; they had sinned only out of greed. <note>In 2 Maccabees 12:40, it is discovered that the fallen Jewish soldiers had kept sacred amulets taken from idols, which was forbidden.</note> It is, I confess, a capital sin, but one that is admitted through human infirmity and does not directly oppose divine grace. Zacchaeus and Matthew, both <term>publicans</term> <note>Tax collectors in the New Testament, often associated with greed and collaboration with Rome, yet capable of repentance.</note>, earned remission for that sin, whereas the Jews who denied Christ's miracles died in their sins. Those soldiers of Judas Maccabeus sinned out of greed; therefore there was hope of remission. On account of which it is written of the survivors: *"They all therefore blessed the just judgment of the Lord, who had made manifest the things that were hidden,"* and so turning to prayer they asked that what had been done might be delivered to oblivion. 

Here, so that your attempt might seem more credible—for you saw it was likely that we would say they had performed penance amid their wounds at the end of life—you anticipate us and shut our mouths, saying: *"They died without penance."* Certainly you did not find this written! You assert what is not written here as easily as you deny what *is* written elsewhere. But because you saw that your point about the "sin unto death" was bare by itself and had no appearance of why you should mention it here, you therefore add: *"They died without penance."* Since you add this of your own accord and without a witness, I shall therefore reply with the same or better faith of my own: they died in penance.

### ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

For indeed, God does not punish twice for the same thing. <note>The author invokes a legal and theological principle (*non bis in idipsum*) suggesting that the soldiers' deaths in battle served as a sufficient earthly punishment, allowing for their souls to be purified afterward.</note> Indeed, they sinned out of human frailty; but since they were fighting for the worship of God, the sanctification of the temple, and the keeping of divine laws, their merit carried more weight with the merciful God than their offense. They washed away their sin with their own blood, so that their remaining merits might stay intact. And so I reply to you from my own position: they died with the fruit of repentance. You are without a witness; by what witness will you refute me? You have no other history regarding this matter, and you are so far removed from that century that you cannot know it of yourself. By what witness, then, will you refute me? Finally, so that you may be held as truthful, you send them to Tartarus <note>A classical term for Hell, often used by Renaissance writers.</note>. We, to be held as truthful, send them to heaven; which of us wins out better? Which of us thinks more closely to divine goodness?

Finally, we maintain that they died out of repentance and the hope of pardon, and not out of some drunken or old wives' tale. The surviving army agrees with us on this; so does the war-leader Maccabeus, who, as eyewitnesses of the deed, felt there was a remission for that sin, for which reason they also prayed for the slain. For thus it is written: *And because he considered that those who had fallen asleep with piety had great grace laid up for them, he therefore considered it a holy thing to pray for them that they might be loosed from sins.* <note>A translation of 2 Maccabees 12:45. The author uses this to show that Judas Maccabeus believed the soldiers died "with piety" despite their mistake.</note>

But you must prove it true that they died without repentance. For that to be true, many incredible things would have had to happen—suppose the enemy's attack was so headlong and sudden, so utterly beyond any appearance of imminent death, that they could neither see nor face the inevitable danger. Such an instantaneous death can scarcely happen even to those crushed in their sleep, let alone to those who were engaged in the line of battle and in the midst of death. Therefore, they foresaw the loss of life; even before they lost it from a wound, they committed themselves to God’s mercy.

Granted, they did not foresee it. But they thought themselves safe among the armed ranks—therefore, whether they were killed from afar by a missile or up close by a sword, they must have been killed by a pierced heart, a severed head, or a body cut open. I do not recall any other kind of death that can happen in battle that is so sudden; and that such a momentary necessity happened to each individual or to all of them together is unthinkable. There again, there was time left for them to pray for mercy from God.

You speak the truth: if therefore time of life remained, why did they not cast away their shame? <note>Referring to the "donaria," or amulets taken from the idols of Jamnia, which the soldiers had hidden under their tunics.</note> There are many causes, but I will treat this one out of piety: namely, the just man is the first accuser of himself. Should they have thrown away the things sacrificed to idols? <note>original: "idolothyta". These were the forbidden objects that caused the soldiers' deaths, according to the biblical narrative.</note> What else would they do but add sin to sin? The just desire to be found [faithful] before men, and they would draw God’s goodness into suspicion—as if He left those who fought for piety undefended. It was better to take this shame upon themselves and give glory to God.

But you insist on another point: how were those who survived the wound found dead together afterward? I refer you to the history: because they were first gathered for burial on the day after next. For the Sabbath followed the day of battle, when the victor Maccabeus remained quiet according to his custom. <note>Under Jewish law, no work, including the collection of bodies, could be done on the Sabbath; this delay provided a window where wounded soldiers might have repented before succumbing.</note>

But we have long indulged your freedom, following wherever you call as if we were ignorant, although you have already long since fallen away from the status of the question. When we respond to you quite simply, you think we have forgotten the point; you think you have seized us and led us away. But we yielded willingly, until you had poured out what you had to say, so that you would not complain as if I had not faithfully answered your points. But since we have come to where you called us, you will judge it fair that we reclaim our discourse by our own right. Your wickedness forces us to recall so often what we are actually debating; for you always slip away from it. First you laid snares regarding Purgatory; now you weave traps regarding the slain. Thus, you labor to weaken the business from matters on which the nature of the business does not depend. But you fear to handle the true core of the matter directly, just as a sailor fears a reef. This is what I maintain: there are purgations of souls, and there are releases from guilt after death. You reject this: "they do not exist." Therefore, we inquire: do they exist or do they not? And here we stand; this is the knot for us...

### WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE

Whichever part he solves must be tested; beware that once you are recalled from this point, you do not prevaricate into another so many times. For look at how you have excluded us presently. Whereas you ought to have treated the heart of the question universally, according to the opinion of the ancients and the testimony of the divine scriptures, you leave this behind and turn to the state and person of some private individual. You have ultimately fashioned this person as one whom these things could not benefit. You return from this to the whole cause, as if what you imagine did not benefit a few does not benefit anyone in general. In this, you sin in many ways. First, you inquire into the judgment of God. You take these undeserving men, whom the Book of Maccabees professes to have "received sleep with piety" and to "have excellent grace stored up," and you make them out to be damned based on your sheer whim, just so you might seem to have support for your fiction. In this, you are most justly struck by your own Seneca: <note>original: "De rebus incertis iudicium incertum tene"</note> "Hold an uncertain judgment regarding uncertain things." 

Then, even if you had contended regarding those who are admittedly damned—such as Judas Iscariot, Herod, Caiaphas, and Annas—and you proved that suffrages <note>A term for intercessory prayers, masses, or alms given for the benefit of a soul in Purgatory.</note> for them are in vain, you would not thereby have proven that they are in vain for everyone in general. For what ought not to be done for one specific person does not mean it ought not to be done for the whole kind. For the singular act of any individual is naturally secondary and inferior to that which is done in general; that which is secondary is weaker, so that its own specific deed cannot establish or remove a general rule. Therefore, we shall never judge the state of the universe from the condition of a particular fact. Thus you sin against us presently, Waldensian. 

If you do not yet grasp this, it is like this: You approached the King for a favor and did not obtain it. Going away, you then say the prince is inexorable to everyone. However, you do not speak truly based on your single rejection; another stands right nearby who is entirely blessed by the King’s favors. Do you grasp the fraud of your syllogism <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> now, or not yet? Do you still not surrender? Do you not yet recognize the error? Look, I will use your own sword against you, which you gave me. Since those slain men "received sleep with piety," as the words of the book say, and "have excellent grace stored up," they therefore did not die in mortal sin. Therefore, the suffrages made for them were beneficial. Consequently, in general, suffrages for the dead are beneficial. 

You see you are attacked by your own art. But we grant this to you, for we do not want those word-traps; I only wanted to uncover your fraud. Concerning the purgation of souls, we have previously said many things clearly, and we will say others later with the same faith. Therefore, we have proceeded according to the whole thread of your words above. We find that the books of Maccabees are not Apocryphal <note>The author is defending the inclusion of 2 Maccabees in the Bible, which the Waldensians and later Protestants rejected.</note>, nor rejected by the Church. We find that the verse, "It is therefore a holy and wholesome [thought to pray for the dead]," is not counterfeit. Those word-traps regarding the slain, by which you avoided the cause, we have unraveled and exploded. 

All things remain intact for us again. The faith in the book remains, in which it is written so aptly about suffrages for the dead. The deed remains, which Maccabeus performed entirely according to his own faith, and indeed the faith of his ancestors. We have received intercession for the dead as a safe doctrine. For neither he nor his army conceived this faith for themselves for the first time then; the high priests and priests of the temple would not have admitted a new religion taken up against the faith of their ancestors. But for parents, kinsmen, relations, and all the piously deceased, they learned the funeral office received from the institution of the fathers, the Prophets, and the ancient Church which preceded Christ. 

Let it be said, then, that the memory for the dead is recent and new, unknown to that "innocent age." Let it be said to have been thought up in recent years from the mere greed of priests. Yet we have witnesses against such accusers from the divine books: from the Old Law, the book of Maccabees; from the Gospel, Saint Paul to the Corinthians. But look, they slip back into their accustomed fraud and say, "Nevertheless, nothing stands there about Purgatory." Slowly, little donkey <note>A common Renaissance rhetorical insult used to describe a stubborn or slow-witted opponent.</note>, turn your face back! Where are you going again? Look here! Consider this! Regarding the purgation of souls after death, regarding the funeral rites...

As the remission of their guilt is performed here by the Church, it also prays: "Absolve, O Lord, their souls from every bond of sin; let no torment of death touch them, but let your mercy establish them in the region of peace and light. If there be any faults in them, O Lord, worthy of torment, do Thou graciously grant the forgiveness of Thy leniency." <note>original: "Absolve dñe aīas eorū..." The author quotes a traditional liturgical prayer for the dead.</note> Concerning these matters, we established our discourse from the beginning and found, both from other reasons and from divine law, that there is a remission of guilt after death. Now, what do you have to object against Christian piety regarding <term>suffrages</term> <note>intercessory prayers, masses, or alms offered for the benefit of souls in Purgatory</note> for the dead? Specifically, you claim that there is no mention of "Purgatory" there. 

Listen, you who remain an obstinate heretic regarding Purgatory: leave this for a moment and look this way. The Apostle [Paul] says that "wood, hay, and stubble" perish by fire, yet in such a way that the one whose works are thus purged returns safe from the fire. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:12-15, a cornerstone text for the doctrine of Purgatory.</note> Confess freely to this opinion; give glory to the Apostle and testify that he speaks the truth. Hold onto this then: Judas Maccabeus and his entire army together prayed over the slain so that their sin might be forgotten by God. They arranged for a sacrifice so that whatever remained of the sin of those who had otherwise died fighting for a pious cause might be paid for through the intercession of the faithful. <note>Referring to 2 Maccabees 12:43-46.</note> 

Go then, and believe in this opinion: that it was a holy deed to intercede for the dead so they might be loosed from their sins. Since this is so, into what place—or no place at all—will you believe the Apostle and Judas Maccabeus have put the souls to be purged, while they are detained by God's decree for punishment? Until they receive full remission of sin? For souls, truly, are not in every place at once in the same moment; that belongs to divine power alone. Therefore, they must be in some defined place. They are not in heaven. They are not companions of the demons or of all those eternally damned—that is, those cast into the "outer darkness." And yet, they must have been in some place, as they truly exist, to undergo the <term>Purgation</term> <note>The process of cleansing or purifying a soul</note> which the Apostle and Judas Maccabeus acknowledge. 

Permit us, therefore—for it is without deception in this investigation—if, just as we name a place for the blessed and a place for the damned, we likewise name a place for those to be purged by one certain word? Thus, we shall say: Heaven, Hell, Purgatory. You deny Purgatory? You do not deny the "fraud" of a single little word, but the very meaning of the Apostle and Maccabeus, and indeed the entire matter. For you say it is in no way real because you contend it happens in no place. Thus, insidiously, while you pretend to be dealing with something else by attacking the word "Purgatory," you there strike down, trample, and dissect the conscience of the Apostle, the piety of Judas Maccabeus, the truth of the Scriptures, and the collective Catholic faith on this matter. 

This is your "piety." This faith of yours is truly wicked. May you be so; thus you can never leave this Purgatory <note>A play on words suggesting the opponent's own stubbornness is a kind of prison</note> because if you had deferred to such great witnesses with a pure heart without fraud, you would not make such a business for yourself over a single word. This "Purgatory" would not weary you so sharply. For it follows that if you believed a purgation occurred, you would think it happened not "outside of place" but in some place entirely. Therefore, whatever single place you had conceived of yourself, or heard from another as being believed to be where purgations occur, you ought not to have hesitated, resisted, or finally fled from it. 

But the devil has cauterized you with his own branding iron, so that you no longer wish nor are able to swear by the words of any truth. Hence also comes this: that [Purgatory] would not even exist today unless Thomas Aquinas had thought it up in Hell! <note>The author is quoting his opponent's radical claim that the doctrine of Purgatory was a medieval invention by Aquinas, whom the opponent considers damned.</note> You think that Doctor Heinrich, the Inquisitor of <term>heretical depravity</term>, <note>Likely Heinrich Institoris (c. 1430–1505), a famous inquisitor. "Heretical depravity" was the formal legal term for heresy.</note> has sinned against you; for this, he is in turn punished by St. Thomas. 

But let us hear, I pray, the filth of your defiled mouth. You say Thomas thought this in Hell? Do you not only envy the divine grace and the enjoyment of St. Thomas, but utterly take it away, hoping you might never see Heaven? You accuse God of His own judgment; for either He made more of a saint of this man than was necessary according to your wish, or the blessed seats do not endure your hatred. There is nothing in the fellowship of the saints except peace, tranquility, and mutual charity. You, out of your most burning hatred which seethes against St. Thomas, admit within yourself an example of brotherly envy. It is of that kind which will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the future. God is charity; and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. The devil, by whose envy death entered into the world, is envy itself. And he who remains in envy remains in the devil, and the devil in him. But you sin not only against Saint Thomas, but against all holiness alike.

You undermine the Apostle and the divine scriptures, and you neglect the Apostolic commentators; contrary to what you pretend, you cast them out and call them false. By these words of yours, you defame them. <insert>[ We shall also set forth how the first discoverers thought regarding a second and uncertain purgatory, and how this too is against the faith. ]</insert> You admit that a "second Purgatory" was known to the ancients. I hear with great bitterness that all holiness is so shaken, and that such filthy barbarism speaks so boldly against the most eminent men. But there is an old saying: *Let the shoemaker not go above the boot.* <note>original: "Ne sutor super Ocream." For this reason, we are clearly compelled to set before your sight who our men are, and who yours are.

Our men are those through whom, as Apostles, the Christian cause was advanced, and by whom it was defended against the most savage persecutions of the sword and false doctrine: Dionysius, Polycarp, Ignatius, Justin, Origen, Athanasius, Basil the Great, Didymus, Gregory Nazianzen. <note>A list of the "Greek Fathers," the founding theologians of the early Eastern Church.</note> From the Latins: Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory. <note>The "Latin Fathers" who shaped Western Christianity.</note> Countless others are equally outstanding but less known through smaller works. All of these were nurtured nobly and industriously amidst the service of nurses and attendants; they possessed a dignity of the most distinguished and pure spirit, a generosity of heart, a reverence of countenance, a faithfulness in word and deed, a conscience for what is right, and a constancy in all things. Finally, lest they should desire disgrace, they would blush before themselves sooner than before a judge; they reflected this character of an innocent life from the glory of their families, the virtue of their grandfathers and fathers, and their noble lineages. Such men, instructed by domestic examples and shaped by their models, were sent across the seas with servants and attendants to the most outstanding teachers of every kind of erudition, so that by adding learning to the virtue of their ancestors, they might become perfect and excellent in all things. In their later years, they were held in the highest honor among princes and peoples as necessary and healthful counselors of the state. They practiced the examples of their ancestors in the present work. As for philosophy, they not only held as much as they found before them, but they even illustrated it in many ways. It is an admitted fact that Plato was first understood by his own followers only after they had read our authors. <note>A common claim in medieval and Renaissance apologetics—that pagan philosophers like Plato actually derived their best ideas from Hebrew or Christian tradition.</note> They were famous for their ancestors, memorable for their education, innocent in their religion; many were martyrs, and all are blessed.

You, however, born from profound beggary, not well-born, without ancestors, even without parents—conceived, one might think, from the common rabble—grew up amidst domestic poverty. You were taught at the plow-handle and the stars; <note>An insult implying the opponent was a common field laborer who only learned by looking at the sky while working.</note> you have seen and thought of nothing beyond shoemaker’s ink and filth. Having only this one example of your parents' virtues: if they did not owe a limb to the laws. <note>A dark suggestion that the opponent's parents were criminals who only kept their limbs because they weren't caught.</note> If by some chance you came into a school of letters, you lived on alms collected street by street among monstrous schoolmasters, such as you have in your countryside, deterred by whips; finally, you make yourself "learned" only by wearing a longer tunic. You leave your childhood no better than you entered it, only larger and older; a most vile commoner from the common herd. You are impudent, injurious, with no shame in your brow, and of a shifting faith, driven by hope and fear. I call as witnesses your masters, whom you either try to slander or are tried by; you never stand faithful or true until the fear of prison chains and the dark pit commands your faith. Otherwise, you are slippery, perplexed, and circular; finally, you mix things done and undone as you see fit. You are dutiful toward your master when he is harsh and merciless, yet toward the kind and indulgent, you are rebellious, a scorner, and a deserter. Finally, you never distinguish in your conscience between the just and the unjust, or right and injury.

...you measure out such punishment by the drop.
