Even that **Saint Thomas** [Aquinas], whom you cannot now forget, was born of the sublime and illustrious line of the Counts. For the sake of his desire for the heavenly fatherland, he cast off the pride of his noble birth and his wealth alike, putting on the monastic habit. He excelled under the most learned teacher of his age, whom even the Greeks—which is a most rare example—translated into their own language because of his singular knowledge of many things. Saint Thomas had such a teacher, and was perfected by him; he meditated on the **Law of the Lord** day and night. Given such noble birth, such contempt for the world, and such erudition, why would it have been necessary for him to devise a sacrilegious profit from religion to his own infamy and the ruin of his soul? If he had been greedy by some vice of the mind, would he not have sooner kept his most lawful riches and the splendor of his birth, rather than despising them for Christ’s sake under the **poverty of Saint Dominic**?

The Waldensian, against our will, has compelled us into this discourse, since he holds the honor of churchmen—whether of the recent or the distant past—at so little value. And while we have spoken of the integrity, holiness, and erudition of the Catholics as being lower than they deserve, and have spoken of the "purity" of the Waldensians as even less than it is, it was nonetheless necessary to touch upon these things so that the weakness of the accusation might be known by the unworthiness of the accuser. I have left the rest to a sense of shame, which is required as much by the work as by the speech. Yet often, here and elsewhere, I am accustomed to call these same Waldensians **heretics, forgers, and liars**, or names of that sort. I do this not for the sake of insult, but because they are found to be so from the facts at hand. Therefore, in this place, I shall excuse myself once and for all to any modest mind, and I pray for pardon, lest our action be imputed to ruthlessness rather than to the sin of the Waldensians. For indeed, a **hard wedge** <note>original: "duro illi nodo fuit durus Cuneus adhibendus." A proverb meaning "a hard knot requires a hard wedge"—tough problems require tough solutions.</note> must be applied to that thick-headed Waldensian.

From this, let us recall our speech to its beginning. They say: *"There would not even be a Purgatory today if Thomas 'of the Lamb' had not thought this up in hell."* <note>The opponent likely used "Thomas de agno" as a mocking nickname for Thomas Aquinas, perhaps poking fun at his devotion or a specific title.</note> If you say, Thomas, that he was the first to think this, then either you say this—as you do everything—against your conscience, or you have a poor grasp of chronology. There are only two hundred and fifty years from the time of Saint Thomas. Yet many tombs, as we read from the stones in holy places, belong to men who established **diocesan churches, monasteries, and priesthoods** for the sake of perpetual prayers and memorials to be made for them at the altar; these are older than the century of Saint Thomas. Thomas, who was yet to come, did not persuade these founders to religiously establish such great works at such great expense out of fear of a future Purgatory or hope of a swifter satisfaction. This faith, therefore, depended on an earlier time.

**Saint Gregory the Great** is six hundred and forty years older than Thomas of Aquino. He wrote the *Books of Dialogues*, which are full of examples of the **purgatory of souls**; these books are even more common...

...these things are such that most of you could not have been ignorant of them. But in your eyes, no one is considered **Catholic** unless he is also a heretic. More than two hundred years before Gregory the Great, there were Cyril, Patriarch of Jerusalem; Eusebius of Cremona; and Aurelius Augustine. In those writings which they sent back and forth to one another concerning the passing of the divine **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note>, they recount so many things concerning the **Purgatory of souls**. Most ancient of all—from the very time of the Apostles, a listener to the Saint Apostle Paul and a companion in the preaching of the Gospel, the Apostle to the Gauls himself, Bishop and most happy martyr—the sacred Father **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>The author refers to the writer of the "Corpus Areopagiticum." In the Renaissance, he was still believed to be the Dionysius converted by St. Paul in Acts 17, though modern scholars refer to him as Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>, in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, writes the following regarding the purgation of souls and the expiation of guilt after death:

"Then the venerable prelate approaches and performs a sacred prayer over the dead. In that prayer, he beseeches the divine mercy to forgive all sins committed through human infirmity by the deceased, and to station him in the light and the region of the living, in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in a place from which pain, sadness, and sighing have fled."

Later, explaining this matter more broadly, he discusses many things regarding the **adoration of the saints** and regarding **suffrages for the dead** <term>Suffrages: Intercessory prayers or pious acts performed by the living to benefit the souls of the deceased.</term>—all of which the Waldensian denies as one, as if they had not been observed in Apostolic times. He argues in this manner: 

"But perhaps you will say: 'These things are indeed rightly said by us, but it is uncertain for what reason the prelate prays for divine mercy, asking for forgiveness of sins for the deceased and a lot equal to the saints and most luminous.' For if one receives rewards from divine justice according to the good or evil they did in life, and the deceased has finished his actions in this life, what prayer of a prelate will transfer him to another rest besides that which he earned in response to the life led here?"

"I am not ignorant," he continues, "that according to the divine oracles, a lot is to be rendered to each according to their merits; for the Lord concluded within himself, saying: 'Each one shall bring back the things he did through his body, whether good or evil.' However, sacred tradition teaches us that the prayers of the righteous, even in this life and not only after death, benefit only those who are worthy of them." 

What, after all, did the prayer of Samuel profit **Saul**? <note>Referring to the biblical account where the Prophet Samuel's intercession could not save King Saul from God's rejection due to Saul's own disobedience.</note> How did the intercession of the Prophet help the Hebrew people? For truly, it is just as if someone, while the sun is bestowing its rays upon healthy eyes, were to demand to become a partaker of the solar light while his own eyes were closed. Thus, one is suspended by a superfluous hope for impossible things if he demands the prayers of the saints while casting away the sacred actions that agree with their nature, by no means intending to receive divine gifts and retreating from the most holy commands and benefits. 

Therefore, yielding to the Sacred Scripture, I would say that the prayers of the saints are useful in this life in this way: namely, if anyone, inflamed by a desire for holy gifts and piously inclined to receive them, yet conscious of his own smallness, goes to one of the holy men and prays for him to approach as a helper and intercessor. He will certainly receive a benefit from this, exceeding all comforts; for he will enjoy those most sacred gifts he seeks, as divine mercy receives him, and especially as he embraces a religious knowledge of God, a reverence for the saints, and a laudable desire for the holy petitions he has requested. For it is also sanctioned by divine judgments that divine gifts are bestowed in a most becoming order upon those who are worthy to receive them, through those who are not unworthy to hand them down. If anyone spurns this most holy discipline and, led astray by an unhappy pride, thinks himself worthy of divine familiarity and despises the saints, he shall certainly lack his desire for divine things if he asks for petitions unworthy of God or not sacred...

"For what did the prayer of Samuel profit Saul? How did the prophetic intercession help the people of the Hebrews? For surely it is the same as if someone, while the sun bestows its rays upon healthy eyes, should tear out his own eyes and demand to become a partaker of the solar light. Thus, he who demands the prayers of the saints is suspended by a superfluous hope of the impossible, for he casts away the sacred operations natural to them, by no means intending to receive divine gifts and receding from the most holy and beneficial commands. If anyone should scorn this sacrosanct discipline and, seduced by an unhappy elation, judge himself worthy of divine familiarity and despise the saints, he—certainly if he asks for petitions unworthy of God and not sacred, and lacks a focused desire for divine things—is inconsistent with himself..."

The venerable <term>Bishop</term> <note>Original: "Antistes."</note>, as Scripture says, is the "interpreter of divine judgments" and the "messenger of Almighty God" <note>Original: "angelus omnipotentis dei." The word "angelus" means messenger or envoy.</note>. Divine goodness, through supreme mercy, does not remember the stains that clung to them due to human frailty; for as he says, "no one is clean of stain."

The <term>Pontiff</term> <note>In this context, the Bishop officiating the funeral rite.</note> knows these promises from the holy scriptures; he asks that they be fulfilled and that sacred rewards be granted to those who lived piously. At the same time, he shapes himself to imitate God’s kindness, seeking the gifts of others as if they were his own favors. He is not ignorant that the true promises of the future are clearly demonstrated to those now present. Those things which he requests by sacred right are granted to those who have reached fulfillment in a divine life. For the <term>Pontiff</term>, a preacher of divine justification, would never ask for things he knew were not pleasing to God or things God had not promised to bestow.

Therefore, he does not pray these things for those who died in a profane state <note>Original: "prophanis vita functis," referring to those who died outside the faith or in mortal sin, who were excluded from these prayers.</note>. Not only because he would be abandoning his own proper order and presuming something of the pontifical office without being moved by the Divine Spirit, but also because, praying unworthily, he would not be heard. Thus far the holy Dionysius. <note>The author is quoting from *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* by Dionysius the Areopagite. Now, bring your objection against us if you believe that anything new has been devised concerning these matters out of **greed**—anything not repeated since the Apostolic time. Such things you then cast against ecclesiastical piety, you "angel of Satan," transfiguring yourself into an "angel of light." <note>A biblical metaphor for a deceiver who appears holy.</note> At that time, before we had come to a true confrontation, you wanted to be thought of as truly Apostolic and a true nursling of the ancient Church. From the beginning, you as it were prescribed to our ears the kind of faith we should expect from you: namely, one [ *revealed by the Holy Spirit, guarded in reality by the primitive Church, and certified by virtues, miracles, sincere dogma, and martyrdom* ].

Behold, therefore, your Dionysius! Behold a martyr! Behold sincere dogma! You have him in every way as you defined. But after you come from your promise to the reality of where you should have stood, you follow nothing less. Instead, you resist and fight against him just as you fight against the present Church. You are evil. You are impious, a seducer of the ignorant commoners. You are more harmful through the cunning of the demon than the treacherous race of the Turks has ever been. The Saracen once treated our Gospel with reverence; he walked in its institutions, and many more were going to do so—witness Nicholas of Cusa in the *Sifting of the Koran* <note>Original: "Cribratio Alkoran," a work by the 15th-century cardinal Nicholas of Cusa attempting to find Christian truths within the Quran.</note>—but the Sultan prohibited its reading by an edict. You and the Turk have the same enemy, and you are equally insane in your shared dissent from the apostolic faith. You equally mock Christian institutions and sacred things, kicking them away with your heels as if they were impure profanations. You call us "enemies" and "foes" no less constantly than the Turk does. Yet with the Turk, we often have truces and treaties; often peace is agreed upon for many years. For you, there is no peace with us. Outside, you are entirely occupied in seeking the "harvest of defection." You are entirely in the field, making a profit. You spare no coin in sacred matters, in clothing, or in food; you are entirely focused on seeking the sinews of war. You dig ramparts and ditches; you have constructed several walled towns on steep hills, on plains, and on precipices in just a few years. You urge on the work, whatever you spend there. You do not think it a "spending" to give the smallest coin for divine worship; you think you are prohibited by religion from doing so. But in truth, you prepare the seats and fortifications of war; you rouse them up. Did you take *this* from the primitive church? 

Such are you outwardly and toward the safety of the kingdom. Internally, however, you are a denier of religion, of Holy Scripture, and of the oracle of the Holy Spirit, and a deceiver of apostolic doctrine. With a lying innocence and faith, you lead away every simple soul into the snares of the devil. Now, not content with your own territory, you creep into your neighborhood through your imposture, into the bordering kingdoms of the Hungarians and the Germans. There is no rest from your contagion. As long as they are publicly hallucinating, there can be no truce between you and us, no peace and no treaties—and yet you dare, most wickedly, to charge us with the very crimes you commit. You accuse the Roman Church, just as you have the craftiness to claim many others...

...often deceived by your own. Hey you, thief! Hey you, plunderer of the Christian people, who are those you drag along as captives after your errors? Have you not recently fished these out of the devil’s net <note>Original: "nassa diaboli." A *nassa* is specifically a wicker fish-trap or weel.</note> from among our own? Surely, if you were to steal bodies from a kingdom as you do souls from Christ, you would be making them your own property, holding them captive among the unfaithful, and finally exporting and selling them. You would be held for the crime of man-stealing <note>Original: "plagio." In Roman law, *plagium* was the crime of kidnapping or selling free people as slaves; this is the root of our word "plagiarism."</note>, you would be beaten at the stake, and you would be beheaded. But it is only religion, only the cause of Christ and souls, in which it is permitted to sin with impunity. Indeed, you even accuse us of trickery—so great is the license for your crimes! If we bring back our own—do you not make yourself one of that number of wicked men of whom the Comic Poet <note>Likely the Roman playwright Terence, who was a staple of Renaissance education.</note> said: "They think they are being wronged when they are the ones who committed the injury"? They complain and accuse first. For these reasons, all good men have reported you to the just and the fair for your pestilential conspiracy, for blasphemies against the saints, and for your heresy. From the wicked and unjust, [they reported] the insulting of royal simplicity <note>This likely refers to the king's piety or straightforwardness being mocked or exploited by the heretics.</note> in which a few have interfered with the public good for the sake of the convenience of the fields.

### THE WALDENSIAN,

We must still say this because it is said that these alone go [to heaven] and so forth up to this point: that even if that [prayer] is granted, it is not from books, but by the living faith of a faithful and upright priest, which he offers to God along with his faithful people.

In the present chapter, regarding the matter of <term>satisfaction</term> <note>The performance of acts of penance (like prayer, fasting, or alms) to make amends for the temporal punishment of sin after the "guilt" has been forgiven.</note>, the Waldensians deny the purgation of souls after death. They say it is false, what the Catholic faith believes: that those go to purgatory who, having been prevented by death after their guilt was forgiven, did not satisfy for their demerits. They are convinced that by a single act of absolution, both the guilt and the punishment are remitted. For this, they bring forward from the Gospel the Publican and that Servant whose master took pity on him, released him, and forgave him the debt. I wonder that you have forgotten that Prodigal Son whom the father led into the feast at the very first word. I now warn them of him on my own; if they had found him first, they would have seemed to us ungrateful people to have said something in favor of their error. 

But let us see how these things stand. They deny "satisfaction" where those prevented by death and caught in <term>venial sins</term> <note>Minor sins that do not break a person's relationship with God, as opposed to "mortal" sins which require confession.</note> have not satisfied the counsel of the priest. By right, I ask the Waldensians: what do they think of the survivors? Is the punishment remitted along with the guilt for them too? It will be remitted according to the opinion of those who say: "since God has forgiven the greater [the guilt], why should He not grant the lesser [the punishment]?" It will be remitted according to the suspicion of those who are ignorant of "satisfaction" for washing away stains. Therefore, the entire subject of good works is removed; the whole divine law is overturned. 

But if for those survivors only the guilt is remitted, but they are sent to various punishments according to the counsel of the priest, then there is a different kind of sin in these people and those; a different kind of justice of God; there will be a different kind of the <term>sacrament of penance</term> <note>The ritual of confession and reconciliation.</note> for those living and those about to die. Where then will the equity of God’s judgments be seen? If a sinner from a lazy bed, from embraces and a well-spread table, from bread and provisions—which are hardly left even at death itself—at whose departure the soul first repents and receives remission, has yet done nothing painful for himself to deserve heaven: yet, free from guilt and punishment, he is sent immediately into heaven? To receive which, a manifold sword of grief pierced the soul of the most glorious Virgin Mary beforehand? Which heaven Peter earned from the cross, Paul from the numerous catalogue of his sufferings and finally from the sword? Which all the apostles and martyrs earned through many difficulties with their blood? According to what is written: "If the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" <note>A quote from 1 Peter 4:18.</note> Again: "From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force." <note>A quote from Matthew 11:12.</note> For that reason, the Apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and a "vessel of election," forgetting the past...

...reaches out toward things further off, if in any way he might grasp them. You, lying sluggish through your whole life, think you will grasp [salvation] through pure remission alone without **satisfaction** <term>satisfaction: the Catholic doctrine that a person must perform acts of penance (fasting, prayer, alms) to "satisfy" the debt of temporal punishment remains after the guilt of sin is forgiven</term>. You have done nothing in this world in common with Paul, and yet you wish to be his companion immediately in heaven? It is not fitting. For entirely there awaits you that which we previously cited from Aurelius Augustine—he must first be cleansed by the fire of purgation <note>original: "igne purgationis"</note> because he postponed the fruit of conversion to another world. Concerning these matters, therefore, we must speak more clearly about **satisfaction**, starting from those things which the Waldensians now define. In the first place, we do not deny that sometimes the crime is forgiven so that the penalty is also released. For this reason, we not unwillingly admit the example of the servant in the Gospel. However, regarding the tax collector <note>original: "publicano." Referring to the Parable of the Pharisee and the Publican in Luke 18.</note>, we still have doubts; for the Lord did not say this absolutely, but by comparison: "this man went down to his house justified *rather than* the other." Yet, we know this happens sometimes by privilege, indulgence, and dispensation. We shall admit that this occurs universally and through the direct nature of the thing. Therefore, let them not press us too hard regarding that principle: "If God forgives the greater, He also forgives the lesser." For even in human examples, they perceive that what we say is true: an offense which is owed to the laws is sometimes also released from punishment. Truly, that this should happen *always* and for *everyone* by the nature of the laws, no one contends. Otherwise, we know that a civil crime is not forgiven unless a fine is its companion. Therefore, I shall prove from the present testimonies of the Scriptures that the same is owed even in things which pertain to God—that is, that **satisfaction** follows the guilt. The Apostle writes:
> *Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification.*

And this is the **sanctification** for which we now strive with you: namely, that the virtues of a substitute may punish the vice, such as humility for pride, purity for filth, faith for perfidy—so that each individual virtue may amend the individual vices from the opposite side. Because of this, the Prophet also spoke two things for our justification:
> *Depart from evil, and do good.*

And the Apostle James:
> *What does it profit, my brothers, if someone says he has faith, but does not have works? Can faith save him?*

And a little after:
> *Faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself.*

It is necessary, therefore, for punishment to follow the remission of sin—that is, a purgative work. For this reason, that Samaritan <note>The Good Samaritan in Luke 10.</note> poured oil and wine upon the man wounded among thieves; signifying the gentleness of indulgence by the oil, and the sharpness of **satisfaction** by the wine. For this is the justice of God: that sin be ordered through the due punishment. But if someone has set aside pride but has not taken up humility—and he has not taken it up if he is content with remission alone and denies **satisfaction**—you may say in what state and merit he is. You do not know? I will say it:
> *These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of the creation of God: I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth. Because you say, "I am rich and enriched, and I lack nothing," and you do not know that you are wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.*

So, in another place, the same Prophet says:
> *From now on, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow them.*

What labors, I ask, did they have, that they should "rest from their labors," who neither endured the chastening of the body here for the release of guilt, nor will endure the fire of purgatory after the end of life for **satisfaction**? This business does not have the form you dream of, Waldensian! The prodigal son—I confess—is immediately called to the feast. But this is the "First Remission." Truly, what do you think he must do afterward? I ask for your opinion. You deny **satisfaction**. Perhaps you want him to snore, empty, toward divine grace? I demand a testimony as to why he should do that. For my part, I certainly have many testimonies why he should *not* do so. The elder...

# ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

Indeed, the son comes from the field, and the master sends other sons to work. Regarding these, he says here: "I go, Lord," and did not go; while the other said "I will not go," yet went. He also rebukes the hired laborers because he finds them idle; finally, he teaches that one must be vigilant always and everywhere. Above all, however, the Truth <note>Referring to Jesus Christ as "The Truth."</note> says: "When you have done all things that you ought to have done, say: 'we are unprofitable servants.'" <note>original: "fervi inutiles sumus," quoting Luke 17:10.</note> If those who do everything they ought to do are considered "unprofitable servants," then surely there will be no place for those who do nothing at all. Or if those who do nothing become heirs of the kingdom, then all the holiness [of the saints] has labored in vain to attain this kingdom. But holiness does not labor in vain. For the Apostle <note>Saint Paul.</note> says again: "To those who are at Damascus first, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I announced that they should do penance, and turn to God, performing **works worthy of penance**." <note>original: "digna poenitentiæ opera facientes," quoting Acts 26:20.</note> Truly, he speaks here of the remission of sins, yet he does not stop at that stage; rather, he adds: "performing works worthy of penance." To this we are equally bound, whether we are in health or about to die. 

The Prophet <note>King David in the Psalms.</note> confirms this: "Bless our God, O nations, and make the voice of his praise to be heard. Who has set my soul unto life, and has not suffered my feet to be moved. For you, O God, have proved us; you have tried us by fire, as silver is tried. You brought us into a snare; you laid tribulations on our back; you set men over our heads. We passed through **fire and water**, and you led us out into a place of **refreshment**." <term>refreshment: original "refrigerium," a theological term for the state of comfort or rest for the soul after the trials of purgation.</term>

If God set the soul of the Prophet unto life—this is the grace of remission of which you speak—yet if he also examined him like silver, placed tribulations on his back, and led him through fire and water, this is the **work of purgation**. This is the work of **satisfaction** <term>satisfaction: the performance of penance to pay the debt of temporal punishment due for sin</term> which we affirm and you deny. But why do you struggle against this for so long? Did you not also seem to have described previously the number of things by which the souls of bodies are purged for immortality, as you say? Why was it necessary for you to feel this way if you believed the penalty was granted along with the guilt? Therefore, I judge it to be established that we should no longer deny that a penalty follows the remission of guilt, which washes away that which was contracted from the contagion of sin. Otherwise, that saying of Ezekiel would be addressed to us: "Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose rust is in it, and its rust has not gone out of it." <note>Quoting Ezekiel 24:6.</note>

Afterward, they bring up another example to us: the thief on the cross. I have spoken of this before. I do not deny that such sudden salvation occasionally happens through the singular indulgence and profound mercy of God. But we should not judge the nature of the entire matter based on rare examples that are above nature. We have not previously admitted this from the testimony of the Scriptures, nor do we admit it now. 

But if I have not yet done enough for those of you with circumcised hearts and stiff necks, I wish to say something further regarding the thief. Which "thief" are you showing me? Is it that one from the cross, who was saved from guilt and penalty in one act through the atrocious breaking of his legs and arms? <note>Referring to the *crurifragium*, the practice of breaking the legs of the crucified to hasten death.</note> I pray you never die so "easily" as to think such a torment is a very light thing for paying the debt of sin! 

Yet even so, he would not have been deemed worthy of such a great promise unless Christ the Lord, placed on the cross at that time for the salvation of the human race, had received this first-fruit of his redemption as a gift from God the Father for the consolation of his present Passion. This is just as in famous and imperial cities, where those ordered into exile for an offense may be restored if they cling to the reins of the entering princes and their retinues; it is the law that such people are restored out of honor for illustrious men and reverence for the right of hospitality. Thus, this thief was granted to Christ as he was triumphing and now entering into that glory from mortal life which he had with the Father before the world was made. 

But indeed, we shall move onto something more laborious concerning this thief. Paul the Apostle writes to the Romans: "Where then is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we judge that a man is justified..."

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE

Expounding upon this passage regarding man without the works of the law, Adamantius Origen <note>Adamantius was a common nickname for Origen (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> says: the Apostle states that the justification of faith alone is sufficient, so that a believer is justified even if no work has been completed by him. It is necessary for us, who strive to assert that the writings of the Apostle are a complete whole, to seek out what it means to be justified by faith alone without works. As far as an example is concerned, I believe that thief is sufficient who, when he was crucified with Christ, cried out to Him from the cross: "Lord Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom." No other good work of his is described in the Gospels, but for this faith alone, Jesus said to him: "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." 

But notice that Origen mentions only one example—that of the thief. However, all who are reborn of water and spirit—whether newborn infants or decrepit old men—if they depart from the bath of rebirth <note>original: "lauacro regenerationis," a common theological term for the Sacrament of Baptism.</note> before they have time to earn merit, they are released from guilt and punishment. They are all saved in the blood of Christ through faith alone. 

Consequently, they <note>The Waldensians, whose arguments the author is refuting.</note> cite another point against us from the Apostle Paul: "There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." <note>Romans 8:1.</note> I admit this; neither is that purgatorial fire "unto condemnation" for those who are being purged by it. Or, if they contend that it is "unto condemnation," then the penance we pay while living in this body would also be "unto condemnation," since it is used for the same purpose as Purgatory. And since they provoke us on this point, although it is a matter of a different kind, it is pleasing to dispute a little regarding the understanding of our position. 

There are, therefore, two sacraments: Baptism and Penance. Baptism was ordained not so much to delete the stain implanted in us by our parents <note>Original sin.</note> as for our adoption as sons, for spiritual generation, and for illumination. Even if the deletion of all stains follows these things, for those who are thus cleansed, there is nothing further—provided they do not make that grace void—unto condemnation. For Baptism is a divine birth. 

Just as someone must first be born into life if he is to perform human actions, and he who is an outsider must first be adopted as a son before he can rightfully access our substance as a free child; so too, for someone to know anything of those things handed down by God, he must first reach that divine state of being taken into the adoption of sons. Therefore the Savior said: "Truly, truly I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." And "Truly, truly I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." <note>John 3:3-5.</note> 

We explain it in this way because it often troubles many when they suspect that if some unbeliever competes with or surpasses a Christian in moral uprightness and civil honesty, they might wonder why the conscience of the unbeliever hopes for nothing from heaven. The reason, of course, is that they are not yet reborn through divine birth nor yet received into the rights of children. For even if a father designates one of many as his heir, those who are neglected may compete with the heir in uprightness, yet the first one remains the heir. Likewise, some foreigner might perhaps surpass most citizens in the innocence of his life; yet, unless he has been enrolled into the rights of the city, he is not admitted to the fruits of liberty and the laws; he will always be considered a foreigner. It is in this sense that the Apostle said: "Therefore you are no longer guests and sojourners, but you are citizens of the saints and members of the household of God." <note>Ephesians 2:19.</note> 

Penance, the second sacrament, follows rebirth. It is provided for the remission of sins—understand this as the sins we have committed after losing that first grace. Therefore, it is called the sacrament of reconciliation. Paul does not speak of this <note>in the verse "no condemnation for those in Christ."</note> because those who need it have many things "unto condemnation"—namely, all those things for which they must be reconciled again. This is according to what is written: "Many are called, but few are chosen," and according to the king who ordered the man received at the wedding to be bound hand and foot and cast into the exterior darkness. To this penance, <term>satisfaction</term> <note>Satisfaction refers to the voluntary performance of penance to make amends for the temporal punishment due to sin.</note> follows according to all the testimonies we have previously introduced. If they had used the Apostle correctly against us, the rest would follow from him: therefore, the inability of the penitent is not from the soul, but from the body.

### ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

"Therefore the body ought to be punished, since it no longer lives; the soul ought not to be punished."
Behold the "sharpness" of the Waldensians—not to call it stupidity—worthy of raising new corruptions and, alongside Pelagius <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD) was a monk whose teachings on free will and the denial of original sin were declared heretical.</note>, again denying free will. Indeed, unless I knew that they do not frequent wine taverns, I would believe this was dreamed up by drunks over their cups; yet it smells entirely of the tavern nonetheless. Therefore, some old cobbler <note>original: "veteramentarius," a repairer of old shoes. The author is using a class-based insult to suggest the Waldensian leaders are uneducated tradesmen playing at theology.</note> must have thought this up while at his awl.
Now, if the body is the author of sin and not the soul, then the soul ought not to be sent into purgatory—that is, to pay for the crime of the body. By that same logic, the soul ought not to be sent into Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna. A biblical term for Hell or the place of eternal punishment.</note> for the punishment due to the body; and yet it is certainly sent there, because it is written: "The rich man also died and was buried in Hell." <note>Luke 16:22.</note> Again, if it is because the soul is the architect of a good work—and it is—then if you say <insert>the impossibility of satisfaction in the penitent does not proceed from the soul but from the body, because the spirit is willing</insert>, the body should not then share in the salvation of the soul—that is, in a merit that is not its own. But it does share in it, because it is written: "The body is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it shall rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it shall rise in power; it is sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body." <note>1 Corinthians 15:42-44.</note> And to those thus resurrected, He says: "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." <note>Matthew 25:34.</note>
And by this, the vanity of the Waldensian might be sufficiently exploded. But because he errs so crudely and does not yet understand a matter that is otherwise manifest—namely, from whence sin comes and how it arises in man—I shall confront him even more closely. Let him know that sin is from the soul, but the <term>tinder</term> <note>original: "fomitem" (fomes). In theology, this refers to the "tinder" or "fuel" of sin—the inclination toward evil resulting from original sin.</note> is from the body, of which tinder the Apostle said: "I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind." <note>Romans 7:23.</note> From this, finally, the flesh lusts against the spirit.
Regarding this sentiment of the Apostle, Origen writes thus: "We frequently find in the scriptures, and it has been discussed by us, that man is said to be spirit, soul, and body. But when it says that the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, it undoubtedly places the soul in the middle, which either acquiesces to the desire of the spirit or inclines toward the lusts of the flesh. And if it joins itself to the flesh, it becomes one body with it in its lusts and desires. But if it associates itself with the spirit, it will be one body with it." <note>A reference to Origen's tripartite anthropology, viewing the soul as the seat of free will between the higher spirit and lower flesh.</note> And as Origen declares from what follows: "The spirit is that highest part of the rational portion which was made in the image and likeness of God; this is never deceived." You see, therefore, that sin is from the choice of the soul, which sits as an arbiter between sense and reason; and from this it contracts guilt for itself, on account of which God said through the Prophet: "The soul that sins, it shall die." <note>Ezekiel 18:4.</note> And Ecclesiasticus says: "God from the beginning established man and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added His mandates and precepts. If you wish to keep His mandates, they shall preserve you... He set before you water and fire; stretch forth your hand to whichever you wish. Before man is life and death, good and evil." <note>Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 15:14-18.</note> Moses also frequently and in many places speaks thus: "If a soul shall sin" and "If a soul shall commit a crime." Even the pagans understood this, which makes it all the more indignant that the Waldensian, coming out of the school of Christians, should deny it. Plato, in *The Laws*, says: "It is necessary that the soul be the cause of both virtues and vices."
However, because Saint James said: "Each one is tempted by his own concupiscence <note>original: "concupiscentia," often translated as "lust" or "strong desire," here referring to the internal inclination to sin.</note>, being drawn away and enticed," <note>James 1:14.</note> the unlearned perhaps think that there is no concupiscence except that which is from the flesh. And yet, was not that concupiscence of the devil great, by which he wished to be like God? Hear of his concupiscence and the excellence of his very nature; hear so that you may learn that vice can exist in a soul just as it could fall upon the first angel. Isaiah and Ezekiel write thus regarding him: "How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have fallen down to the earth, you who wounded the nations, who said in your heart: 'I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will sit on the mountain of the covenant...'" <note>Isaiah 14:12-13.</note>

<summary>The author argues against the Waldensian claim that only the body sins, asserting instead that the soul is the primary agent of sin through its free will. Using authorities like Origen, Plato, and Scripture, he demonstrates that the soul must face punishment (including Purgatory) because it chooses to follow the "tinder" of the flesh rather than the spirit.</summary>

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE,

In the sides of the north, I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High. <note>original: "in lateribus aqilonis..." These are the boasts of Lucifer as described in Isaiah 14:13-14, traditionally used to explain the origin of pride.</note> You were the seal of resemblance, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. Every precious stone was your covering: the Sardius, Topaz, and Jasper; the Chrysolite, Onyx, and Beryl; the Sapphire, Carbuncle, and Emerald; gold was the work of your beauty, and your pipes were prepared on the day you were created. <note>A paraphrase of Ezekiel 28:12-14, describing the "King of Tyre," interpreted by the author as the prelapsarian state of the devil.</note> You were an outstretched and protecting Cherub, and I set you on the holy mountain of God; you walked in the midst of the stones of fire, perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you.

Therefore, this angel, so received by God the Creator, was formed from that most sublime particle from which every angelic, incorporeal, and spiritual substance above the heavens was fashioned. Above him, nothing was seen except infinity, eternity, and deity. Yet in him, iniquity was found and the stain of pride was born—in a soul which, so to speak, approaches power by an infinite degree more than [the body], and which was created at the very boundary, the knot of spiritual and corporal things. Below which, whatever you look upon, you encounter nothing but physical things: the heavens and the heavens of heavens, all the stars, the Sun and Moon, the elements, and those things which exist within them.

If such a soul, I say, were in its nature so narrow that it conceived no stain or sin from itself (except what it might draw from the body), why should it deserve purgation by its own guilt or fall into damnation at all? Rather, the soul itself is the cause and the definer of all sin, because of which, by the just judgment of God, even when stripped of the body, it suffers uniquely for the evil it admitted while here in the body. For this reason, guilt is imputed to the mind <note>original: "renū," literally "kidneys/reins," a biblical metaphor for the seat of emotions and intent.</note> in a human being, but not in beasts. 

Otherwise, all corporal passions are given to beasts: to this one pride, to that one cunning or deceit, to others filth and gluttony—we laugh at "the pig from Epicurus's herd." <note>A reference to Horace's *Epistles*, mocking those who live only for physical pleasure.</note> They might feel envy, or as the saying goes, "the crow could feed in silence if it had more of the feast." <note>A reference to Horace, suggesting that greed and noise often go together.</note> There would be much less quarreling and envy—which, meanwhile, is made a mockery in the treachery of the Waldensians. Beasts go to lust indiscriminately; they kill and tear each other apart. Many are now guilty of shedding human blood, yet no one accuses them of murder, nor will they stand at the divine judgment. Yet they would have stood there if—as that Waldensian barbarity philosophizes—sin were merely drawn from the body. The soul would not have stood [for judgment] if it admitted vice not from its own nature but from the body's wickedness.

They add, furthermore, that it would be in contempt of the merit of Christ's passion if satisfaction and purgatory were more powerful than Christ's passion. In this, they mix those things together and have no discernment of the matter or substance. I have said in the preceding sections, regarding the purification of souls, what Baptism and Penance are. I said what both are and of what virtue. I said that **Baptism** is the unique sacrament of the most full purgation, which makes us fit for the eternal promises. I added that by faith alone—that is, the merit of Christ's redemption—is a man saved. Nor did I admit that **Penance** is anything else regarding the purgation of souls than a reconciliation in those whom baptism (that is, true purgation) has preceded, so that penance is nothing but the purification of a relapse. 

Is it so, then? If a man, once reborn, could thereafter stand in that... (if Latinity will grant the word) "impeccability," then the sacrament of penance would be unnecessary. Therefore, if I were to reverse the order and claim that this penance, with its companion "satisfaction," was the primary purgation to the exclusion of baptism, I would be destroying the Scripture and weakening the merit of Christ's redemption—and the Waldensian would rightly blame us. But because he imposes this upon us out of sheer calumny and no truth of the matter—after those things which we said before—there is no need to explain it further with more words. 

They mention afterward some unwritten prayer from books; but what sort of thing that is, or with what intent they say it, we shall see better in that discussion regarding the priesthood.

# ON THE PURGATORY OF SOULS AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

...up to this point: this is what we believe concerning Purgatory, of which the teacher Augustine <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western theology, who discussed the idea of a purifying fire in works like *The City of God*.</note> made mention; and [the opponent] unjustly incites the King’s anger against us.

Regarding what they said previously about the "hindrance of satisfaction"—that it does not proceed from the soul but from the body—they now repeat that same point. They think it is beyond the scope of reason that the soul alone should suffer in Purgatory, since the soul did not sin alone, but rather in partnership with the body. To this "insoluble knot," I certainly respond with that saying from Scripture: *The fool snores at night and speaks sublime things in the morning.* <note>original: "Stultus nocte stertit & mane loquitur sublimia." This is a proverbial expression mocking those who think they are wise after a night's sleep but lack true understanding.</note> For if they thought even a little bit above the level of a peasant and had any wisdom, they would not have fallen into such absurd and remote opinions. They might have caught a scent for themselves of the very things we have disputed to refute them. Or, if they did not catch the scent, they should submit to the judgment of those with better understanding. Enough could have been said in response to this in the previous sections, but since it does not weary them to repeat their errors, let it not weary us to add whatever further can be disputed on this matter.

They say that reason cannot grasp how a soul might suffer without a body. I say: if they think that is something "atrocious," yet it is necessary to grasp the reason from a present example, then reason will certainly grasp another very light matter. All the reprobate <term>reprobate: those destined for damnation</term> who have died since the beginning of the world have had their souls tortured from their first exit. The soul of Cain the murderer has endured in Gehenna <note>original: "gehenna" — a term for Hell or a place of fiery torment.</note> for six thousand, seven hundred, and more years. That rich man at the feast <note>original: "diues ille epulo" — referring to the Parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16.</note> has sustained punishments in his soul for fifteen hundred years—at least from the time the Gospel mentions him—concerning whom the infallible truth, Christ, said:

> The rich man also died and was buried in hell; and in his torment he cried out: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tortured in this flame.

Therefore, take heed: if you believe correctly regarding the damned, what do you hear happens regarding those who must be purified? You cannot dodge it, nor can you deny the fact. You concede it to the damned; you do well. Do you grumble? Beware lest you contend with God and His judgments, for *he who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory.* <note>A paraphrase of Proverbs 25:27, warning against prying too deeply into God's divine mysteries.</note> Finally, if it were beyond reason for a soul to be punished alone for the stain of sin, we would not have been able to say the things we have said so far against you on this matter; nor could a Gentile <note>original: "gentilis homo" — a non-Christian or pagan.</note> have felt the same way against you, because "what is known of God is manifest in them."

Consider Plato, then, in his book on the soul—I bring him up to your shame, that a Gentile surpasses you in the piety of things to be believed. I bring him up to you so that while you fight against a heathen, while you fight against a Gentile, you cannot break through the defense; you cannot burst into your blasphemies against the Prophets, the Law, Christ, the Apostles, and the consensus of the Catholic Church. I cite him from the tradition of Eusebius of Caesarea <note>An early Christian historian (c. 260–339 AD) who often quoted Greek philosophers to show they anticipated Christian truths.</note> from his own book *On the Preparation for the Gospel*, book eleven and again book twelve, so that you may know what a great philosopher felt: he did not feel these things from some dark corner or outside the approval of Catholics. From one place, therefore, both Plato and Eusebius strike you as authors for the sake of one cause. In the book on the soul, Plato writes as follows:

> When the deceased arrive at that place to which they are carried, they are first judged as to who lived justly and who lived otherwise. And if any seem to have lived in a sort of middle way, they climb into their own vehicles and are carried through Acheron <note>original: "Acherunta" — one of the rivers of the underworld in Greek mythology.</note> into the marsh, where they are purified by heavy punishment, and afterward, being set free, they receive honors according to the merit of their good deeds. But those who seem to be unable to be cured because of the magnitude of their sins are all cast into Tartarus, <note>original: "Tartarum" — the deepest abyss of torment in ancient Greek belief.</note> from which they can never exit. Those, however, who are curable, even if they have sinned greatly—as for instance if they did something out of anger against a father or mother and afterward felt repentance, or were contaminated by homicide or some other crime—it is necessary for these to come into Tartarus, but after being tortured for the space of a year, they are cast out by the wave.

Furthermore, in the dialogue titled *Gorgias*, he confesses the same in these words:

### THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK THREE

For if the body had scars from wounds while living, or certain broken bones, or lopped-off limbs, it remains in that same state after death until everything decays. Similarly, it is observed that in the soul—after it has been stripped of the body—all the habits in which it practiced its passions and pursuits remain present. Therefore, when the soul comes before the judge, the judge immediately sees the wounds and scars of injuries which the individual actions of the soul have impressed upon it, even if it were the soul of a great king. He sees all things twisted by falsehood and pride; he recognizes that nothing there is upright because of the license, luxuries, insults, and lack of self-control in that person’s way of living. He perceives the soul to be filled with every kind of foulness, and for this reason, it is rightly cast into the prison of Tartarus <note>Tartarus: In Greek mythology, a deep abyss of torment. Here, the author uses the classical term to describe a place of purification or punishment for the soul.</note> where it is tortured with punishments, so that either the souls themselves may be purged and become better, or others, warned by their example, may be deterred from sinning by the dread of torture. 

Those who have sinned "curably" <term>curable sins</term> <note>These are what theologians call "venial" sins—wrongs that do not completely destroy the relationship with God and can be "healed" through punishment or penance.</note> are purged by pains both here while living and among the dead in the underworld. For it is not otherwise possible for the impressed stains of vices to be wiped away. But for those who have committed the greatest injuries and have sinned incurably, no benefit can ever come to them because they are beyond healing; instead, others are helped by their example. 

He <note>Referring to Plato, whose ideas the author is paraphrasing.</note> then adds something that is most justly said against the Waldensians: "Perhaps these things seem to you like old wives' tales told by some grandmother, and for that reason you despise them." It would not be a wonder for you to despise these things if, by searching diligently, we could find better and truer things than these. But what have you heard here from Plato—who was not a Christian—that is not Christian? Unless you knew he lived before the Coming of Christ, you would believe he had been taught from the Gospel; and yet he conceived this by the natural light <term>natural light</term> <note>The human capacity to discover truths through reason alone, without the help of divine revelation or scripture.</note> alone.

After these things, I will also say something regarding the body. Bodies return into the first seeds of the elements from which they were taken; therefore, the contagions contracted through sin vanish in them, yet not so much so that even the bodies themselves do not eventually pay the penalty. Consider the general fire <note>The "Great Conflagration" or the fire at the end of the world believed to purify all of creation.</note> when heaven and earth shall pass away, and the elements and the entire mass of bodily things shall be purged from the curse to which they were subjected in the sin of the first parent <note>Adam.</note> and the murder by Cain, and from all the abominations with which sinners infected them. 

Now, however, while every creature plays its part, when bodies die through the end of life, since all sense comes only from life, how could bodies now suffer when they are void of sense? How could they suffer when they are reduced back to those invisible, foundational substances? Therefore, corpses cannot suffer, though they can be purged just like other inanimate things. Thus the soul, the partner in sin, is purged; but since the soul is life, and life is sense, it follows that the soul also feels while it is being purged. So it will be with bodies when they are purged. If the body were life of itself—to corner you most strictly—then you assume falsely when you say:

<margin>
It is against reason that the soul alone should suffer and not the body.
</margin>

It would have been proper for you to say: "It is against reason if the soul alone should be *purged* and not the body." But we do not say this. You allege Saint Paul in support of your false assumption, yet you do so neither with a complete testimony nor with his true meaning. You say: "If we endure together, we shall reign together." That passage, if I remember correctly, is from the second epistle to Timothy, where he writes: *If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.* <note>2 Timothy 2:11-13. The author argues that the Waldensians are cherry-picking one phrase to support their idea that the body and soul must always be together in punishment or reward.</note> Four points were set forth; you ignore three and seize upon one. For the remaining points did not allow your meaning to be corrupted, which you present to us as follows: "If we endure together"—meaning by body and soul—"we shall reign together in body and soul." Now, if you have correctly imposed this meaning on the words of the Apostle, apply it also to the related verses and see what comes out: "If we deny Him in body and soul, He will deny us." What will He deny? The body or the soul? Furthermore: "If we do not believe in body and soul, He remains faithful." Who is He? Amen.

...does the faithful body or soul remain? You see the monstrosities of this opinion; indeed, you see the innocence of the cause which you cannot defend except with false testimonies. Return to the Apostle his own meaning, and everything will be consistent from a single perspective, though they will do nothing for your cause. <note>original: "si commortui sumus cum Christo & convivamus cum christo si cum eo sustinebimus & cum eo corregnabimus, Si eum negaverimus, ille Christus negabit nos, si christo non credimus. Christus ille fidelis permanet se ipsum negare non potest"</note> "If we have died with Christ, we shall also live with Him; if we endure with Him, we shall also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He, Christ, will deny us; if we do not believe in Christ, Christ remains faithful; He cannot deny Himself." <note>This is a quotation from 2 Timothy 2:11-13, a key passage used in debates over the nature of salvation and the necessity of suffering or penance.</note>

After this, you come to another massive point: "Those who are found needing to be purged at the final time of the world, just before the arrival of the Judge, cannot be purged in that purgatory." It is as if you are saying that because it will not exist for them in the future, it does not exist for those in the present. This is a very weak argument—as if someone who deserves to be purged then could not have their penalty paid off except through a long period of time. What a foolish opinion! For if someone is found then who requires cleansing, if God in His mercy wishes them to be purged, could He not by His omnipotence purify them with some momentary pain? 

Furthermore, the reasoning of the <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval Christian movement (the Valdensium) that predated the Reformation; they were often criticized by the Catholic Church for rejecting Purgatory and the authority of the priesthood.</note> depends upon this "prevention." <note>In this context, being "prevented" or "overtaken" by the sudden arrival of Judgment Day before one has finished their penance.</note> They ought, therefore, to invalidate Purgatory not only because of the supposed loss to those who are alive then, but for everyone who is ever overtaken throughout the whole course of the Church, according to the example of the foolish virgins whose lamps are extinguished and against whom the door is closed. <note>Reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25, where those unprepared are locked out of the wedding feast.</note> Regarding these people, however, we have no dispute, for we are debating only those who died in the hope of forgiveness.

For just as it is now, so it will be then: those who are overtaken will have been overtaken. To prevent this, the Lord commands us to watch, nor does He say to us in vain: "But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but the Father alone." And just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will be the coming of the Son of Man. Consider: "When they say to you, 'peace and security,' then sudden destruction will come upon them." Since we know, therefore, that we must go to judgment so suddenly, we fear and we grant that there will be no time remaining after death to pay off the debt of guilt. Let us now insist even more that we prepare ourselves through bodily <term>satisfaction</term> <note>Acts of penance or reparation performed to "satisfy" the debt of sin while alive.</note> rather than purgatorial satisfaction for the arrival of the Judge. 

But they add another point that is no less impious than the previous one was frivolous: "that the elect of God will then be cleansed when God appears in fire." If we remember what was said above, they return remarkably against themselves. They said before that those go into purgatory who do not perform satisfaction according to the priest's counsel—and they argued that this was not true because it would be in contempt of the merit of Christ's passion. Now, forgetting their own words, they say the elect of God must be cleansed by the final fire.

Do you not fear, then, Waldensian, that this fire also might be more powerful than Christ's <term>redemption</term>? Or do you now fear and assert a purgation after this life which you previously always denied? Certainly. But let us return to the words. I grant them that statement in two parts: first, because in that general conflagration, both the bodies and the living who are then caught up into the air to meet Christ will be purged there of their venial stains. <note>original: "venialibus eorum maculis"</note>

Thirdly, the idea that all souls needing purgation from the foundation of the world are meanwhile suspended from the paying off of guilt until that final fire comes is manifest insanity. For they think it must be done so that the soul is not punished alone; they think it must be done so that the body and soul can suffer together. However, I have already disputed this matter previously: that this should rather happen for the same reason to the damned than to those being purged, the contrary of which we have shown from Scripture. Furthermore, if the soul is not purged without its companion the body, it is even less damned; nor is the soul saved without its companion the body. I press them with their own scripture which they drummed into us just a little while ago as if it were the Apostle's: "If we endure together here, we shall also reign together." This would apply to the Apostles, the Martyrs, and all the elect of God, who would be kept in some secret place away from the heavens until that day. Nor does that saying of the Apostle to the Corinthians state that...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK THREE
->R 3<-

...which they take up to fortify their error; it looks back to what we have spoken of extensively <gloss>in</gloss> the previous sections. After this, the Waldensian returns to his natural character and brings upon himself the proverb: **“The dog is returned to his own vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.”** <note>A quotation from 2 Peter 2:22, commonly used in polemics to describe those who return to heresy or sin after being corrected.</note> They charge, of course, the greed of priests, as if this doctrine—the **Purgation of souls**—were a mere fabrication. Therefore, if Purgation truly did not exist according to the divine law and the opinion of the ancients, why did you not prove its non-existence from scripture more consistently and clearly? Why was that “truth” of yours so fragile that it could not be defended unless you corrupted some passages and struck out others, assembling a mask for all things—a mere facade under which nothing of substance existed?

Therefore, to touch your raw nerves, it is not the truth of what must be believed that invites you to hold such views. Rather, it is the hatred you once conceived against the clergy that prevents you from thinking rightly. In this regard—though I would excuse no one—I answer you thus: If you expect justice from a tribunal, and if justice is indeed rendered to you, what does it matter to you what the private conscience of the judge might be? You understand the <term>parable</term><note>The author uses a "parable" or analogy here: the moral character of a priest (the judge) does not invalidate the spiritual truth or sacrament (the judgment) he administers.</note>. But we shall dispute more regarding this matter in the treatise on the **priesthood**.

The remaining things you say here against priests are mere trifles, which you had to lie to yourself even to put forward. **Suffrages for the dead** <note>original: "Suffragia pro mortuis"; these are prayers, alms, or Masses offered to benefit the souls in Purgatory.</note> were not devised in any recent time. On the contrary, they were received from the Apostles, as we have shown before. You think wrongly in all matters and against the Apostles concerning the purgation of souls; the learned **Augustine** <note>Likely referring to Augustine of Alfeld, a contemporary polemicist, rather than St. Augustine, given the contemporary address to a King.</note> rightly reported your treachery to **His Royal Majesty**. And would that the **Most Christian King** might finally better provide both for an end to your treachery and for the safety of the kingdom from this pernicious secession.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific debate over Purgatory to the foundational issue of the Waldensian controversy: the authority of the Priesthood and the Church. It marks the beginning of Book Four of the treatise.</meta>

->CONCERNING THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST<-

## ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE 
## CHURCH, BOOK FOUR,

At last, and not without long intervals, we have concluded the discourse on **suffrages** <note>original: "suffragijs"; these are intercessory prayers or good works offered on behalf of the deceased to aid their journey through Purgatory.</note> for the dead. Let no one think that we have been long-winded merely by our own whim or beyond what the matter requires; we certainly took up this necessity from their own actions. It was not because their perfidy—which they have built from nothing but tricks and superficial testimonies—was difficult to refute. For where they move against us openly, I have never been long-winded in striking down their obvious errors, nor have I labored much over them. But where they turn to traps and fight against us from the shadows, where they provoke us and then pretend they have not, there I must first drag their arts into the light and bring to the surface those things they said but wish they hadn't. In such places, the writing grows long.

Look, for instance, how much we had to move, how much we had to say regarding a single carved image <note>original: "sculptili"; likely a reference to the use of icons or religious carvings, which the Waldensians opposed.</note>—which they mentioned as if doing something else—and how much regarding that very brief verse: **"They have not called upon the Lord."** <note>A quote from Psalm 14:4 or 53:4, used here to accuse the Waldensians of lacking true prayer or divine connection.</note> There they trembled with fear where there was no fear! How much we had to repeat regarding a single **Apocryphal** <note>original: "Apocrypho"; referring to non-canonical books which the Waldensians often cited or which were debated during the Reformation era.</note> text! Because they are so indirect and slippery, and hide most of their words in corners, I am made long-winded by their vice.

But with God as my helper, I have overcome. I stand at the finish line, about to emerge after them to vindicate the **priesthood**, to which they now call me from nearby. This is a labor, I say, that is most necessary of all those that come into contention against this **Waldensian**. <note>The author refers to the Waldensians, a medieval movement that preceded the Protestant Reformation and rejected many Roman Catholic doctrines, including the specialized power of the clergy.</note> For this is the priesthood which, having once rejected it for themselves, they became "badly free" from the master of **Apostolic discipline**. Following the desires of their own hearts, despising authority, bold, and self-pleasing, they did not fear to introduce blasphemous sects. 

This is the priesthood which they left—exiting the Church and the "Republic of the Apostles" <note>original: "re publica Apostolorum"; a phrase describing the organized, communal structure of the early Church as a governed body.</note>—with a license that was by no means healthy for them. They now scrape together all sorts of shameful things for themselves, mixing the lawful and the unlawful, the sacred and the profane, without reverence. They think they can "buy" a greater reputation for **innocence** among the common people when they hold views most divergent from Christians. 

Look! Aside from the conscience of the one God, in the remaining matters which they know of the **Apostolic rule**, they differ from us more than any Jew does. And truly, this one thing serves as the greatest argument for witnessing both our innocence and their crime: if the things they feel against us are so impious and so alien to Apostolic institutes (as we have proved from the scriptures thus far and will continue to prove with equal constancy), then our views, by the very nature of the opposite, must be pious and kindred to the Apostolic institutes. 

Or if they deny they are adversaries, let them set aside their contention! Let them concede to our people what they wish to seem to easily concede regarding the **Chalice**. <note>A reference to the "Utraquist" controversy, where some groups demanded the laity receive both the bread and the wine (the chalice) during the Eucharist.</note> However, such fury and such ignorance of themselves would not have driven them into such sacrilegious opinions if they had willed to stand in obedience. Clearly, if the priesthood were once accepted as the master of faith, they would thereafter believe rightly and without scruple concerning the suffrages of the saints, the **purgation of souls**, and the **Sacrament of the Altar**.

For these reasons, the present treatise is easily the most urgent of all, but also the most difficult to use for persuading those once infected by rebellion. This is not because the truths here are "more true" than those discussed previously, but because here the "throat" of the whole **heresy** is being attacked. The very "soul" of their error sits in this "heart." For how shall they not thereafter be judged as wicked traitors of the Apostolic faith and condemned, if they are convicted of being rebels against the power established by God and against the legitimate sacred rites? Therefore, it will be a very laborious task to persuade them, both for these reasons and because, as the Apostle said: **"For it is impossible..."** <note>A reference to Hebrews 6:4, which discusses the difficulty of restoring those who have fallen away from the faith.</note>

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK FOUR,

...is for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have nonetheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance; since they crucify the Son of God again for themselves and hold him up to contempt. <note>The author is quoting Hebrews 6:4–6 to argue that the Waldensians, having once been part of the Church, are now in a state of spiritual peril that is difficult to remedy.</note> 

Another personal and significant difficulty arose for me—whether it was their strategy or an ignorance of how to handle matters, I do not know—because the evidence they usually summon to support their cause is spoken with no single order or fixed place. I had to seek out many things from their **first confession** (which we struck down at the beginning of our work), many from that other one prepared later for the King, and others scattered throughout the present work. These had to be tracked down: some from the beginning, some from the middle, and the rest from the end. 

If I had thought that this scattered body of theirs—which accuses the priesthood without any order—should be gathered from whatever parts I happened to encounter first, the matter would have taken no clear shape. No single line of reasoning could have been established in the speech; as soon as it began, it would have immediately slipped away into something entirely different. Therefore, while I deliberated for some time on what would be best to follow, I finally took the liberty to establish a rule for myself, which I think is fair: to bring each point into a certain order and respond to them, not according to their "calling" <note>The author suggests the Waldensians use terminology or a structure that doesn't match the "nature of the reality" he is defending.</note>, but as the nature of the subject requires.

Thus, with God and His truth, Christ, as the guide of our discourse, I shall proceed against them. As I have been accustomed to do in other sections, I will now also propose at the beginning what specifically we are debating with those Waldensians from the entire mass of their claims regarding the priesthood. 

This is the first point: they condemn the **Apostolic faith** and obedience, as well as ecclesiastical institutions, as human fictions, and they reject them. They say that the legitimate anointing of the priesthood and the **power of the keys** <note>The "power of the keys" refers to the spiritual authority granted to the Church, based on Matthew 16:19, to forgive sins and govern the faithful.</note> are nothing to us; they say these have long since ceased because of our own vices. They commit the priesthood to every filthy member of their flock who rashly usurps it, as if they were acting truly according to the mind of Christ and the Apostles. This is a grave matter, for he who has excluded the priesthood from us has excluded Religion and the Gospel itself. 

Therefore, before all else, we shall look at the vices of priests. We shall see whether they exist or not, or whether they are as great as the Waldensian makes them out to be. While doing so, I will first say this of myself, as one who knows that Gospel saying: 

> "And why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, 'Brother, let me take out the speck from your eye,' when behold, there is a beam in your own eye? You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck from your brother's eye." <note>A famous teaching from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:3–5).</note> 

I also keep before my eyes that word of the Apostle: 

> "But you, why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? Each of us shall give an account of himself to God. Let us therefore no longer judge one another." <note>Quoting Romans 14:10–13.</note> 

I, deferring to the authority of the Gospel and the Apostle, will consider it of little importance to my argument what kind of men the priests are, lest anyone suspect I am writing a panegyric <note>term: panegyric (a speech or text in high praise of someone)</note> here. For the sacred things and promises of the Gospel do not depend upon human infirmity. Rather, I will return to the true nerve of the whole matter, inquiring this: Does religion cease because of the vices of priests? If it were necessary to fail in obedience except in cases of **idolatry** and **heresy**, I see that the state of the kingdom, obedience, and public laws would otherwise be dissolved by right if evil men sometimes presided over them. In those cases, vices harm no one but the individual's own head; the Commonwealth <note>original: "Res pub." or Res publica.</note> remains safe. 

I will demonstrate that it ought to be the same with religion, even amidst the sins of those presiding. For we did not receive the Gospel on the condition that we would believe only if the leaders were going to be good, and not believe if they were going to be evil. This comes from the eternal counsels of God, not from the condition of men, just as the Apostle said in a similar matter: 

> "For what if some of them did not believe? Shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid!" <note>Quoting Romans 3:3.</note>
