# ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

From this pivotal point, after I have shown that the integrity of Apostolic teaching and institution remains unshaken even amidst vices, we shall turn to the third part of our discourse. We will say something regarding the virtues of those **Waldensians** <note>The Waldensians were a medieval spiritual movement that advocated for poverty and lay preaching; they were declared heretical by the Catholic Church for rejecting the authority of the priesthood.</note> and their supposed emulation of the Gospel. It will then be manifest whether from such things as they seize upon, any "heavenly illumination" (as they boast) regarding a holier knowledge of the truth could have come to them. We shall see if the things they hold were truly taken from Apostolic times; for, as I see it now, these claims will be found to be nothing but empty boasting.

Therefore, in the fourth place, I will begin to suggest that **Apostolic obedience** is necessary for them to attain the salvation of their souls. If, by some unexpected good fortune, I persuade them, then I have "gained my brother." <note>original: "lucratus fratrem meum" — a reference to Matthew 18:15.</note> If I fail to persuade them, and they turn a deaf ear to one giving good counsel, I still hope this present speech will not be without fruit despite the great detriment to their salvation. For our Christian commoners will receive this work gratefully; they were perhaps being shaken by the talk of heretics—which *creeps like a malignant cancer of the body* <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:17, comparing heresy to gangrene or cancer.</note>—thinking that those people were saying something true or wise in their insolent boasts against us. Through this work, the Christian people may clearly understand that the arguments by which they reject the Gospel as we hold it are not true, but are mere trifles.

With the matter of our dispute thus placed before the eye, let us now turn to the work. In their **first confession**, under the chapter on the Holy Church, they make this profession against us:

->THE WALDENSIAN,<-

> In this span of time in which we live, all the bitter and sad things that Christ and His Apostles prophesied have come down upon this Church in heaps: namely, that those who are unworthy of ecclesiastical honor rule over it by their own power.

This is the "theme," as it were, of all the sinister things they think about the priesthood. For this reason, we must come to their other statements where they speak of these things openly and by name. In that other confession, they write as follows:

->THE WALDENSIAN,<-

> Furthermore, we wish it to be known to your Magnificence <note>The author is quoting a Waldensian petition likely addressed to a King or high noble.</note> why we long ago deserted the **Roman cohort**. Up to this point, they have not sufficiently cleared themselves before the multitude of the common people by a public satisfaction, and thus we rightly deserted them.

If they wished to bring forward any cause for their dissent and their "new religion," I would have hoped they would bring forth things from prophetic and evangelical predictions or publicly witnessed divine inspiration—which is the only proper way. But regarding this, they say nothing, nor can they say anything. Instead, they took the cause of their "perfidy" <note>The author uses "perfidy" (treachery/faithlessness) to describe the Waldensians' break from the Church.</note> from **scandal**. Specifically, they claim that certain Catholics and schismatics contended among themselves, using the strongest arguments for their strife. In the midst of such great events, [the Waldensians say] we responded with nothing to defend the truth, ourselves, or our reputation. "Thus," they say, "we defected from the religion of those contenders as if it were impure and profane, and we followed a third way for ourselves."

Behold the "crime" of the Catholics! Behold the nursery of a new religion grown from the discord of others! We shall now examine more closely how each of these claims stands. We ought to consider whether they defected for a just or unjust reason—since this will be the heart of the matter—yet they have not touched upon this. But because they drag us into this discussion even against our will, let us look at their reasoning. They remind us of the crimes of certain men, but they do not report these things sincerely. For since two parties were contending there, and vices were being tossed back and forth, they keep a well-behaved silence regarding the **schismatics** and openly publicize only the crimes of the "Roman cohort," as they call it. In that mutual contention, as if the sin belonged only to our side, they attribute the common vice only to our...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

...they labor to push [their views] and afterwards they abandoned the holy Roman fold <note>original: "Romana cohorte"</note> by their own choice. They conceal those very powerful arguments that each side presented; through this concealment—especially by those who everywhere suppress our works—I have come to believe (both because of their silence and my own suspicion) that the arguments regarding the faith belonged to our side. For our people defended the better cause: specifically, the faith guarded since ancient times and **Apostolic obedience**, the very things truth itself is most naturally suited to support.

As for novelty, rebellion, and disobedience: when should such things ever be defended unless by the authority of the Scriptures? What Scripture could **schismatics** <note>Schismatics: individuals or groups who cause a formal division or split within a church, typically over matters of authority or discipline rather than core dogma.</note> possibly use to protect their sin? Disobedience shut the gates of heaven to the first angel <note>A reference to Lucifer’s rebellion against God.</note> and Paradise to the first man; in the same way, it will surely shut the Church to the schismatic. If there is some way to defend disobedience there, I pray that the Devil and our first parent <note>Adam</note> do not discover it; for I fear that, like those rebels, they might try to retract the condemnation that followed them. I have placed those very firm arguments on our side, even against your will. Relying on these, God Himself punishes disobedience. 

Another reason for my suspicion is the fact that the works of our people survive today, having responded to their errors with great learning—not to say most abundantly. I do not see how the schismatics can proceed against them, as they are wise only to themselves. They complain that the whole kingdom was afterwards thrown into turmoil and that slaughter was committed. I admit this happened, but there is no appearance of truth in their attempt to blame the Catholics for it. There was peace and deep happiness as long as one was permitted to be a Catholic. Discord was suddenly stirred up by those factious men rising from among themselves. Finally, no sedition or slaughter was initiated by the Catholics; it is well known that public riots were begun and ended only with the loss and blood of our own people. 

If anyone is to be blamed for the kingdom being in turmoil, let the crime be charged to the schismatics. For it is not the one who suffers the loss, but the one who threatens it as a predator who is liable to the laws. After this, they turn to the **Whore of the Apocalypse** <note>original: "meretricem Apocalypfis." This refers to the "Whore of Babylon" from the Book of Revelation, a figure medieval dissenters often identified with the Roman Church to claim it had become corrupt and "fallen."</note>. I am well aware of this; it is common now in their secret meetings <note>original: "conueticulis"</note> to hurl this accusation at the Church. The **Luciferians** <note>A 4th-century schismatic group who took a very rigorous stance against priests who had wavered in their faith, eventually claiming they were the only "true" church.</note> once did the same thing, denying penance to those who had fallen. But how does this serve to weaken the Church? Is it not a blind accusation?

Hear the words of the **Apocalypse**: *“Come, and I will show you the damnation of the great whore who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication. And those who inhabit the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her prostitution.”* And he took me away in spirit into the desert. And I saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns. And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of the abomination and filthiness of her fornication. And on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: **Babylon the Great, Mother of fornications and abominations of the earth.** 

And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. And I wondered with great admiration when I saw her. And the angel said to me: “Why do you wonder? I will tell you the sacrament of the woman and the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The beast which you saw, was, and is not, and shall come up out of the bottomless pit, and go into destruction. And the inhabitants of the earth (whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world) shall wonder, seeing the beast that was, and is not.” 

And here is the meaning for one who has wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain a short time. And the beast which was and is not, is himself the eighth, and is of the seven, and goes into destruction. And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings, who have not yet received a kingdom, but shall receive power as kings for one hour after the beast. These have one counsel...

In the Scriptures, "fornication" is understood as the sin of idolatry <note>In the Old Testament, prophets often described Israel's worship of false gods as "spiritual adultery" or "fornication."</note>. You sacrificed my sons and gave them up, consecrating them to those idols; and after all your abominations and fornications, you did not remember the days of your youth."

But this matter is manifest, and the books of the Prophets are full of it. I appeal here to the judgment of all who know the current institutions of the Roman See: would you dare to justly thrust the charge of "idolatry" upon it? Does it know anything other than the Most High God, the Creator of heaven and earth, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—three persons in one indivisible essence? Where, then, is this "first fornication" of that prophecy? Where are those "names of blasphemy"? Where is the "cup full of abominations"? If the Church had fashioned for itself anything like idolatry regarding the veneration of saints or images, we have already rejected <note>original: "explodimus," meaning to hiss off stage or completely refute</note> such claims. Cease, therefore, to return to these arguments to concoct a case against us for this "prostitute" until you have examined all our beliefs.

Inquire, then: where is that "fornication" of the Church, which, established by God as the incorruptible judge of faith, has extinguished all fornications and heresies by its own Spirit? Where is that "drunkenness from the blood of the saints"? Whose saints' blood, then, has it shed? Stephen, Lawrence <note>Saint Stephen (the first martyr) and Saint Lawrence (martyred on a gridiron) are central figures of the early Church.</note>, and all the apostles and martyrs were snatched away from the Church itself—as if from a most pious mother—by the hands of others. Today, the Church celebrates their struggles; it invites us to follow them.

How is it "to ascend from the abyss" if it comes from the succession of the Apostle Peter? How does it "fight with the Lamb" when it guards the faith of the Lamb? For whom does the Turk <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire, which in the 16th century was viewed as the primary external threat to Christian Europe.</note> attack? Christ. If even this prostitute has her "mystery" over the Roman See, then, once captured, she has fulfilled that meaning. <meta>This page continues the author's polemic against the Waldensians. Having previously discussed the apocalyptic imagery of Revelation, the author now addresses the proper method of scriptural interpretation and uses the history of the early Church—specifically the Arian heresy—to argue that one must remain loyal to the "first" (original) Church rather than inventing a "third" way or a new sect.</meta>

->## THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR<-

A passage of Holy Scripture must be interpreted so that all things agree with one another in a single line and thread. An interpretation of divine law must be sincere, firm, consistent with other related passages, and constant within itself. If that innate harmony does not agree in all subsequent points as it began from a single part, the interpretation is arbitrary, foreign to Scripture, and false. In this way, all heretics, by pulling small parts out of the rest of the body of the discourse and imposing whatever sense pleases them in the moment, corrupt the Scriptures by a common conspiracy. In this matter, near the end [of our previous discussion] on prayers for the dead regarding that verse, "If we endure, we shall also reign with him" <note>2 Timothy 2:12. The author argues that the Waldensians take verses out of context to deny the efficacy of prayers for the deceased (suffrages).</note>, we showed accurately that the Waldensian has sinned most shamelessly.

Therefore, you should understand this depicted prostitute <note>The "Whore of Babylon" from Revelation, whom the Waldensians identified with the Roman Church.</note> as the sum total of impiety, of all error and disobedience against God and the Church, which the devil and the world exercise. To this sense, all the points of her prophecy fit; so that you do not have to force them, they come willingly and agree in all things. Much could be said about this prostitute, but since we have no confession from the Waldensian on this matter, I fear he might say I am starting a "blind fight" <note>original: "cecam pugnam" — an idiom meaning a fight without a clear target or a futile struggle.</note>.

Finally, I come to the infamy with which the Waldensian marks our people. He calls them "infamous," but does not state from what crime—whether they were thieves, traitors, assassins, murderers, or poisoners. For he who alleges infamy without a defined crime causes it to be suspected of any one or all [crimes]. Far be it, and indeed far is infamy from our priesthood, which no one has ever defamed except out of their own infamy. As for heresy, which I suspect they have mutually charged against each other, this is an old habit: whatever anyone thinks, he wants that to be the decree of God. But no one is justified merely by his own bare opinion.

There were many things available to you from which you could have decided with equity between the two parties in these evils: first, the shaking off of obedience; second, injuries—outrages, plunderings, and killings—from which side they broke out. For without doubt, he who commits a crime is the guilty one. In that case, one ought to grant [favor] to the one who suffered injury according to common laws, and not raise up some "third" thing, just as happens in a kingdom. He who protects the old laws is a just lord; he who introduces new ones to the subversion of the old out of his own lust is a tyrant. If arms are taken up for that reason, whatever you decide for yourself separately, unless you stand by the first [the original laws], you will be held as a deserter of the kingdom and the laws, just like a tyrant.

In the same way, if the unfaithfulness of some has shaken off the old observance and obedience of religion, you ought to have stood by the first [the original faith]. But you deny that you ought to. If you do this by right and the example of the ancestors, then a new institution and some "third" way should have been followed as many times as there were heresies. Arius <note>Arius (c. 256–336) was a priest in Alexandria who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father. This led to the first major schism in the Christian Church.</note> contended with the Church of God over the faith of the Trinity. He argued that the Church of his time believed things that the Apostles did not know. The Church was split—if indeed it is appropriate to call a gathering of the faithless a "church." Arius defamed the Church because of its "non-Apostolic" faith (as he thought). Furthermore, he even charged this most holy Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius was the chief defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> with sorcery and [the severed] arm of a certain Arsenius <note>At the Council of Tyre in 335, Arians accused Athanasius of murdering a bishop named Arsenius and using his hand for magic. Athanasius famously won the argument by bringing the very much alive Arsenius into the room, showing both his hands were intact.</note> through magical incantations. Arius, I say, defamed the churchmen as much as he himself was truly infamous for his sacrileges.

Did the fathers of the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council (325 AD), which established the Nicene Creed and condemned Arianism.</note>, who gathered having been stirred by this contention, defect from the faith of the ancestors because of the scandal born within it? Did they establish some "third" faith for themselves? No—rather, they refuted Arius, sent him into exile, and decreed that the faith of the ancestors should be held as valid once more for the faithful people. Constantine the Great, who was present at that contention and heard that those professing the Christian faith did not agree on the faith—did he, having been offended, fall away to some "third" thing? No. Indeed, he both aided and followed the opinion of the Council. Constantius, his son and heir, through the corruptions of the palace, evilly defected to Arius and in his life...

<meta>This page continues the author's polemical defense of the Catholic Church against the accusations of the Waldensians. # ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE HERETICS]

Julian <note>Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), known as "the Apostate" because he rejected Christianity to return to Roman paganism.</note> accused [the Church] of the most extreme error, having been badly offended by that famous discord and simultaneously deceived by the sophist Libanius. He chose a third path for himself and the Lord of the Church, as he thought; imagining that he was fleeing "fictions," he instead fell into the true fictions and the cult of idols. But he was finally forced to recognize against his will what he had willingly denied; for, wounded by an unknown hand in the parched, dusty, and thirsty plains of Mesopotamia, he recognized the hand of God. Tossing his own blood into the air, he exclaimed: **"You have conquered, O Galilean!"** <note>original: "vicisti galilee." These are the traditional final words of Julian the Apostate, acknowledging Christ’s victory over his attempt to restore paganism.</note> Thus, out of his former scandal <note>In this context, "scandal" means a stumbling block or a cause of offense that leads to a loss of faith.</note>, he called upon Christ; he earned the name "the Deserter" on earth for his impiety, and in Gehenna <note>Hell.</note>, a punishment that shall never end. 

This same end of Julian awaits those who treat the example of the fathers of the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The first ecumenical council (325 AD) which established the core tenets of Christian orthodoxy.</note> with contempt and take scandal over the faith. He says: "I follow the middle-way Catholic." Thus far you have followed us poorly, as we proved in the previous pages; you follow even worse in the matters mentioned above, and I shall show that with the same conscience. You have just now taken scandal regarding a few people, and you invent a "just cause" for why you should depart. But what if the whole world—which will happen in the time of the **Antichrist**—had defamed the entire Church of God? Should one therefore have withdrawn from the **orthodox faith**? Will the Antichrist then detract from the Church in small matters? Not at all; he will not merely invade communion in one or both kinds <note>A reference to the debate over whether the laity should receive both the bread and the wine in the Eucharist.</note>, but will attack the miracles of Christ. In such great matters, the Church will be accused of erring, so that (as it is heard) even the elect could be scandalized by these things, if it were within God’s decree. 

The Savior says, "Woe" to both those who set the scandal and those who suffer from it. For so the Gospel has it: "Woe to the world because of scandals. For it is necessary that scandals come; nevertheless, woe to that man through whom the scandal comes." <note>Matthew 18:7.</note> You have raised a double "woe" for yourself: first, because you have once fallen into error, and second, because you labor to make others—caught in your snares—fall into the same. You thought the honor of a few of ours was damaged, yet you damaged the reputation of all who were not harmed. You ought to have followed the **Rule of Faith** <note>The basic summary of Christian belief used to judge the orthodoxy of a teaching.</note>. But you failed; and who could deny your impiety? You conceived it within yourself before you even had a cause derived from another. But after you began to complain, you seized a cause from whatever occurred nearest to you. 

Am I not speaking the truth? The morals of the present age displeased you; but did **Dionysius** <note>Likely Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian highly regarded in the Middle Ages.</note> displease you? What fault did you find in **Saint Augustine** that you should hold views contrary to his? What infamy did the **Canon of Scripture** bring that you do not receive its testimonies, especially those first ones that prove you wrong? Or have we not caught you laboring in these lies? Ah, it is even too well-confessed. Therefore, you composed, according to your own judgment and adorned as best you could, a sentence of defection for the "King of Defection." 

Allow us also to state, with a true conscience, the cause of your sedition—namely, your evil mind and your evil soul. I shall say it plainly: your soul, ulcerated with the most burning hatred toward us, persuaded you to defect. You breathe out this hatred toward us everywhere. You recount the vices that were objectified back and forth during our contentions in such a way that, as much as the nature of that deed allowed your speech, you wished to say them so that they would be understood only as our faults. Beyond that matter, immediately from the beginning, you blather on about some "Roman cohort" <note>The opponent likely used "Roman cohort" as a derogatory military metaphor for the Catholic clergy.</note>—a word which has its own dignity and grace in military affairs, but here is both irritable and insulting. If you are fair to yourself, why did you not mention the common crimes of the opposing side both aptly and insultingly? But you have proven the proverb true: **"A stutterer understands a stutterer best."** <note>original: "Balbus balbum melius intelligit." A proverb meaning that those with similar flaws or backgrounds find it easier to communicate or sympathize with each other.</note>

-> VALDENSIS, <-

Although we might incline more toward simplicity than toward that sort of prudence, because we understand that simplicity is more secure before God than prudence itself—of which **Roman cunning** <note>original: "Rhomana astucia."</note> provides us enough examples, through which they have often deceived some of our people. If the **Roman See** has any concern for souls and desires to invite many to the purity of faith, this action of the Church... [is] among the Waldensians <note>term: "Waldensis" refers to a member of a medieval ascetic movement often declared heretical for its rejection of Church hierarchy.</note> through pastoral faith and cunning...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

...interprets. However, regarding the power of that word as it is usually understood in the Scriptures, we are not much moved by that quibble. Indeed, we do not begrudge them the name of "cunning" <note>The author is playing with the Latin word *astutia* (cunning/shrewdness). In a biblical context, this can be a virtue of the wise or a vice of the deceitful.</note>, for these members of the Church are devoid of it: **The root of wisdom, to whom has it been revealed? And who has known its cunning?** <note>original: "Radix sapientiæ cui reuelata est & astucias illius quis agnowit." A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 1:6.</note> But if these men turn toward the truth, they make themselves no better than mere deceivers. For they insinuate these wolves in sheep’s clothing into the neighborhood. If they earn a name for these frauds, they will most truly be to us **shifters of skins** <note>original: "versipelles." This term implies a "turncoat" or someone who changes their shape/appearance to deceive, like a werewolf or a chameleon.</note>. I would say no more on this now, but they strive to defame the zeal of the Roman See for instilling piety in the minds of men by such a name—that is, the infamy of "deception." 

Lest I recall what I replied previously in passing regarding the quibble over prayers for the dead, I only ask this now: how many among you were born as Waldensians? You will not be many. From where, then, did you find your present numbers? Clearly, you lead away the deceived from among our people. You have filled **Moravia** with your blasphemies; now you stealthily penetrate into **Silesia**, **Hungary**, **Carinthia**, and **Styria**. While the watchmen of the Lord’s flock act too securely, they think you are merely smoke passing through Moravia. Yet you are present among them, corrupting the good seed that was sown. Secretly and by night, you oversow thorns, tares, thistles, and the sterile oats of pestilential error. Let it be allowed for us to do our duty there without reproach, which on your part you do most wickedly. For what you do, you do in secret, outside the power granted to you, and in the manner of a bandit. 

Our men, by legitimate and commended power, publicly either defend their own teachings or call back what has been corrupted. You preach in **weaving-shops** <note>original: "textrinas." Waldensians were often associated with the weaving trade, and they frequently used workshops as secret meeting places for preaching.</note>; our men do not fear to preach publicly from the **pulpit** <note>original: "suggestu."</note> at your entrance, but rather rise up further against error. In your secret assemblies, if one of our people should intervene—an institution that those with a guilty conscience perform poorly—you abandon your sermon and fall back into another topic that the ears of our people can bear. In all things, you show yourself to Christian simplicity as a deserter of the State; a deserter seeks, tempts, and solicits accomplices for his defection in secret. A just power calls its own people publicly and by edict. 

Suppose you were all born Waldensians. Since, however, you uphold such great errors, you make the Saints no more honorable than demons. Understand me: you reject the honor of the Saints with the same scriptural testimonies by which the cult of demons was condemned. You deny the intercessions of the saints against the most clear testimonies of Scripture, like impure **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus. In medieval polemics, "Epicurean" was a slur for those who denied the immortality of the soul or divine providence.</note>. You deny the purification of souls after death <note>The doctrine of Purgatory.</note>, being worse than the pagans who understood this. You allow no reputation or honesty to ecclesiastical institutions, and you think of the **Sacrament of the Altar** <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> in a coarse and equally impious way. 

It was necessary for Roman piety to take pity on such great errors. Why did Christ descend into man and become human? To dissolve the errors of the human race. Why were the Apostles sent into the world? For the same cause: to open the way of life and light to those walking in darkness. **Peter**, the leader of the believers of the city of Rome, taking pity on the Gauls <note>France.</note>, sent disciples there to preach the faith. **Gregory the Great**, the vicar of the See of Peter, sent evangelists to England. **Boniface** was ordered from this See to Germany. Whoever among the Emperors and Patriarchs of Constantinople wished to think rightly sought the form of right belief from this See of their own accord. Was it "Roman cunning" that shone upon all these, even the most acute Greeks? Rather, as we say more truly, the Roman See considers this custom, received from the Apostles, to be its own by right. Thus, it exercises that custom holily. But how is it a wonder if you traitors cannot bear its face, and so you speak ill of it? You challenge it to follow the examples of its predecessors. Behold the example! But if the See takes it upon itself to instruct your barbarism, it is nonetheless accused of being "cunning"—that is, captious and fraudulent—acting in this way so as to go about seeking whom it may devour, led by human faction...

### ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST...

...thinks as if he attempts nothing else regarding **Valdes** <note>original: "Valdesem." Peter Waldo, the 12th-century founder of the Waldensian movement.</note> than which side might draw more disciples after itself. For if his conscience here sins beyond what is witnessed, it is permitted for you to take it so sinisterly out of pure rancor; truly, this is most unjust. And if you rightly cast aside the censorship of the Roman See <note>The Papacy and the central administration of the Catholic Church.</note> of the present age as craftiness and deception in the same cause, how will you excuse the examples of Christ, the Apostles, and the leaders of the Roman See from earlier times from a similar craftiness? Therefore, let those who would object to tricks and trifles for themselves be the persecutors of your opinion, who would pursue the faith because of perceived tricks and arbitrary inventions. If you are found in our time to have brought back those same fictions and "Roman craftiness," see into what parts you have cast yourselves, following the iniquity of the ancient persecutors.

->THE WALDENSIAN,<-

"Regarding the second part, we make it known," and so forth, up to this place. And to this, he mentions the old and new [authorities], whom we now leave out for the sake of brevity.

The heart of the matter which they seem to call into accusation here is that they despise the **ceremonies** of the Church on the grounds that they lead to the "overthrow of faith" and are a "nursery of **idolatry**" <note>The Waldensians often argued that Catholic rituals, such as the veneration of images or the Host, were forms of idol worship.</note>, a source of **avarice** <term>Greed; specifically the accusation that priests used rituals to extract money from the laity.</term> for bad priests, and a snare for the Christian people, leading to the seduction and ruin of their fortunes. In that "cloud of words" which they use, they seem to me to have alluded to the veneration and patronage of the saints, and the decoration and gifts of the churches. 

But whatever things are done among us according to the faith and institution of the ancients—which nevertheless displease their ill-will—they think it sufficient to accuse such things as being done without a [biblical] name, but against the law of God, and as being a source of evil by chance. Yet, they speak with an open mouth and from a nearby place of infamy, avarice, and whatever lies within itself by confession, hoping to obtain this from the unlearned: that those things estimated by their proximity might be condemned one by the other. 

But if they had wished to act from a conscience of the facts, they ought to have stated each thing by name and assigned the reasons why they accused them, rather than merely insinuating or placing them in bare suspicion. Now, to seem to have accused everything to the wind is, among fair judges, a most weak thing; yet among the unjust and those unlearned in these matters, it is the safest path for an accuser. For instance, whatever you defend, if you begin to become more weightier than your adversary, he yields; he denies that he intended it. So that your innocence may be made safe, he immediately calls you to another point; thus you, the discloser of your own affairs, are tumbled through everything. In the end, he departs so that it remains free for the accuser to say that you have not yet touched upon your most foul crime which he intended. 

For behold, they have found our "inventions" to be for the overthrow of faith, a matter of robbery for the Christian people, and greed for the priests. What then are these things? I desire to hear them by name. And being certain and not despairing of their "goodwill" toward us, if these things are as foul as they accuse, they will surely send them to the page along with the avarice and infamy—those new and old teachers who say they have things to rebuke in us. It is a foolish clemency and earns no gratitude from us if they withhold them; let them be produced! For nowhere will they strike us more sharply. They are wrongly failing their own great cause out of "favor" to us. Whatever they say of such a nature without a witness, we rightly suspect them of lying. 

They reply: "We leave out the writers for the sake of brevity." Pure trifles! For why do they comply with brevity now, when in other matters it was necessary to be brief? Behold, what a long web they weave concerning the **suffrages for the dead** <note>Prayers, alms, and Masses offered for the souls in Purgatory.</note> and the **sacrament of the altar** <note>The Eucharist or the Mass.</note>! Furthermore, they did not write to a preoccupied judge or to royal ears busy with other matters of state, but to all those wishing to know their writings; they composed them similarly at their leisure. In that case, there was no cause for them to follow such importunate brevity. For every speech that follows what is necessary has its just measure; every speech that fails itself in necessary matters is lame and corrupt. On account of this kind of vanity of those Waldensians, unless we enjoyed the conscience of our own affairs, I would say in a brief speech...

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK FOUR

[S ij]

They mention our **Ceremonies**, yet since they do not specify which ones are condemned or on what authority, they are by no means truly condemned. But because we do not blush at our own practices, and since we labor out of conscience rather than a desire for conflict—hoping equally that they might come to a better understanding and that our own people might not be seduced by worse ideas—we voluntarily offer a defense of the faith for which we are accused, putting forward everything that ought to be said on the matter. And although this is difficult for us—for since we have received no specific established charges from them to which we might respond, we are forced to review everything of ours that comes to mind. Thus, it may happen that we speak at greater length about things they care little for, while saying less about the things they most wish to see addressed. But through that conscience which I now hold—having voluntarily come down to face them when I could have remained silent—I believe it is clear to all. I testify that nothing has been passed over voluntarily that I thought would satisfy them significantly. Therefore, if we say less than they desire, this will stem from their own evasiveness, since we have had to rely on our own suspicions to guess what it is that their malice might find fault with in us.

I see, therefore, two categories of charges. One concerns the envy stirred up against us regarding the violation of faith—namely, those which concern the magnificence, decoration, and wealth of the temples. The other concerns the administration of the sacraments and the whole order of the divine office that we observe. I see that these can be accused on two grounds: either because they are against the law of God and the decrees of our ancestors, or because they provide the material for vice in wicked men.

Therefore, regarding the ecclesiastical rites: if they reject them on the latter ground <note>Because they are abused by bad people.</note>, it has not yet been proved that they are against the law of God. Furthermore, the first leaders of religion should not have established these same rites if they were to be judged by the same **Waldensian** <note>original: "valdensis." Referring to the followers of Peter Waldo.</note> reasoning. If they did establish them, then whatever purpose they had in mind, we shall preserve them for that same purpose. For it would be a great injustice if rites that are holy in their own right were condemned because of the vice of a few. If some think this fair, I, in turn, will think it fair that these same rites be preserved for the sake of the innocence of the better men.

Even if the Waldensian entirely rejects all this innocence from us—because he thinks himself good and knows how to use good things well—out of that very confidence, and out of reverence for our ancestors, he ought not to cast away those holy things. He should not prostitute them, but rather preserve what might have been corrupted through the vices of our own people. For indeed, the guilty and the violators of the apostolic sanctions will be found; but ecclesiastical rites are not to be condemned just because they have been an occasion for evil to wicked men.

For what holy thing exists anywhere that the perverse do not wish to use badly? To avoid seeking long examples: for your contempt of the Virgin Mother of God, for your dishonoring of the saints, for your impious opinion on the cleansing of souls <note>A reference to the doctrine of Purgatory, which the Waldensians rejected.</note>, you have abused the **Scriptures** to manufacture heresy. Should we, therefore, say something similar about the Scriptures? That we do not keep them because they are used for the subversion and error of faith? Let us turn the figure of speech back on you. You despise our ecclesiastical rites because of our vices, as you say. Therefore, because of the **Manichean** <note>original: "Manicheum." An ancient dualistic heresy that rejected parts of the Bible; the author argues that by the Waldensian's logic, the Bible should be rejected because heretics use it.</note> and every impurity of heresy, will you also despise the Sacred Scriptures according to this logic of yours? Imagine: "We do not receive them because they existed for the subversion of faith and justice for the Manichean."

You see the horns <note>A "horned syllogism" or dilemma where every path leads to a trap.</note> growing against you from the opposite side; you see the madness of your mind. I will say other things so that you may be clearly caught. You boast of I know not what obstacles to justice. Shall I, therefore, cast away my dead unburied because I know the undertaker will buy a prostitute with my money? An impure word, but the folly of those men provokes me—men who have openly declared, once and again, that the same just treatment should be applied to the priests for similar crimes. We expose the laws and impious things for profit, so they say: the priest-presidents of the **Mosaic Law** <note>original: "Mosayce legis." The religious laws of the Old Testament.</note> abused those same things for **Avarice**. Shall we therefore remove Judaism? Even before Christ himself removed it on his cross...

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR
S ii

They criticize our ceremonies, yet as they neither say which ones nor on what authority they find fault, they say they are by no means refuted. But because we do not blush at our practices and labor for the sake of conscience—striving not for contention but equally for them, that they might perceive better things, and for our own people, that they may not be seduced by worse ones—we offer a reason for the faith for which we are accused. We voluntarily bring forward whatever ought to be said on the matter, even if this is difficult for us. For since we have nothing specific established by them against which we might excuse ourselves, we are compelled to recount everything of ours that can come to memory. Thus, it might happen that we say more about things they least care about, and less about those they most wanted to see treated. But by that conscience which I now hold—after I have voluntarily come down to face them, though I could have kept myself in silence—I believe it is evident to all. I testify that I have passed over nothing voluntarily that I thought would sufficiently satisfy them. Therefore, if anything is said by us that falls short of their desire, this will proceed from their own concealment, since it depended only on our own suspicion to guess what it was that another’s wickedness might hold against us.

I see, therefore, two issues out of two. Everywhere, envy over a "violated faith" is stirred up against us—specifically, concerning the magnificence of temples, their ornamentation, and wealth; and concerning the distribution of the sacraments and everything we observe in the order of the divine office. I see that these can be attacked on two grounds: either because they are against the law of God and the decrees of the elders, or because they are material for vice in evil men.

Regarding the sacred ecclesiastical rites, if they reject them for the latter reason, it has not yet been proven that these same things are done against the law of God. Furthermore, it would follow that the first presiding leaders of religion, for the same Waldensian reason, ought not to have instituted these same sacred things. But if they did institute them, by whatever counsel they were established, by that same counsel they shall be preserved by us. For it would be a great injustice if things that are sacred in their own right were condemned because of the vice of a few. If some think it is fair for this to happen, I, in turn, shall think it fair that these same sacred things be preserved because of the innocence of the better sort. Therefore, whether the Waldensian completely casts out all this innocence from us or not—because he nevertheless thinks himself to be good, and knows how to use good things well for the sake of the good—on account of that confidence, and even out of reverence for the elders, he ought not to cast out those holy things. He should not prostitute them, but preserve them, even if they had collapsed through the vices of our own people. For they would be found guilty as transgressors of the apostolic sanctions. 

But even if sacred ecclesiastical rites have been an occasion for evil to evil men, they shall not be condemned for that reason. For what is holy anywhere that perverse men do not wish to use badly? To avoid seeking long examples: You <note>The author is addressing a hypothetical or specific Waldensian opponent.</note> use the Canonical Scriptures for the sake of contempt for the Virgin Mother of God, for the dishonoring of the saints, for the impious opinion regarding the cleansing of souls <note>original: "purgatione animarum"; referring here to the Waldensian rejection of the doctrine of Purgatory</note>, and for the fashioning of heresy. Shall we then say something similar about the Scriptures? We do not reject them simply because they are used for the subversion and error of faith. Let us turn your own figure of speech back on you. You have despised our sacred ecclesiastical rites because of our "vices," as you say. Therefore, because of the Manichaean <note>An ancient dualistic sect; here used as a label for heretics who misuse Scripture.</note> and every impurity of heresy, will you also despise the Holy Scriptures according to that same sentiment of yours? Suppose we say: "We do not receive them because they have stood for the subversion of faith and justice for the Manichaean." You see the horns of the dilemma growing against you from the opposing side; you see the madness of your mind. 

I will say other things so that you may be clearly caught. You boast of I know not what "impediments to justice." Should I therefore cast away my dead unburied because I know the undertaker <note>original: "libitinarius"; a Roman term for an undertaker, used here to imply someone who profits from death.</note> will use my money to pay for a harlot? It is a foul word, but their folly provokes me, for they have once and again openly proclaimed that the just, equal rights of priests were conceived from similar wickedness. We expose the laws and the impious for the sake of profit; therefore, let them be cast out. The priests presiding over the Mosaic Law abused those same things for greed. Should we have abolished Judaism before Christ himself abolished it on his cross?

->### OF THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS<-

Therefore, if other things which are held as holy are everywhere invaded by the wicked and yet remain valid, our ceremonies shall also remain valid. Behold, the most pleasant, most fragrant, and medicinal flowers may become liable to the spider for collecting venom, yet they do not lose their grace; they are not lacking to the bees for honey, nor to the physician for gathering healthful strength. Therefore, do not wish, O Waldensian, out of anyone's character or greedy art, to mock the holiness of the apostolic rite. 

But if you charge that these ecclesiastical institutions of ours are against the law of God and the decrees of the apostles, we shall henceforth show that all our practices proceed from the law of God, from the apostles themselves, and finally from natural judgment. These include (to repeat a second time): temples and all the sacred furnishings surrounding them; blessed salt and water; the divine office, whether what is sung or what is spoken; the burials and rites of the dead; tithes, offerings, and the foundations of the priesthoods. For we believe that under these, other things which do not come to our memory are also comprised. 

In the beginning, therefore, we confess—and we freely grant this to our adversary, lest he think we flee from a right conscience—that nothing should be assumed in the church of God against the divine law. However, if the law either commands or permits something to be done in ceremonies, and if that thing is performed by a new genius as excellently, as skillfully, and as magnificently as possible, even if this specific manner is not contained in the law, we shall not be said to have invented something against the law, but rather something more becoming. 

For example: David says in the psalm, "praise the Lord with the psaltery and the harp; praise him with the timbrel and choir; praise him with strings and the organ." <note>original: "psaltio & cithara... tỹpano et choro... cordis et orgão" - Psalm 150:3-4</note> Who does not know that the psaltery and harp were simpler then than those found later? The organ of that time was of an unformed sound compared to that most perfect music according to which we use these instruments in our century. Or if another new instrument, which David did not mention, had been used, he would never be blamed for acting against the law of God and the rite of the temple. For those things which are to be done in the service of God must be done according to one's strength; for so it is written: "David played upon the fitted instruments <note>original: "organis armigatis"</note> and danced with all his strength before the Lord." <note>2 Samuel 6:5, 14</note> 

And for this reason, the sacrifice of Cain was rejected by the Lord, because he did not do it with all his strength, but since he had better things, he sacrificed from the viler ones. Thus he is said to have sacrificed rightly—because he gave to the God of heaven and earth—but to have "divided poorly." <note>This refers to a traditional interpretation of Genesis 4, where Cain's sin was not the act of sacrificing, but the poor quality of the portion he chose for God.</note> So if we have any capacity and art to be spent on the divine office, if we do not do it according to our strength, we "divide poorly." I would boldly say to you, Waldensian, that because of your most squalid and most neglected worship of God—not to mention the many other things you do most wickedly—you divide poorly with God. For the prophet says, "Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock and, making a vow, sacrifices a weak thing to the Lord." <note>Malachi 1:14</note>

I mention these things so it may be understood that not everything done *besides* the law is done *against* the law. Likewise, the apostolic institutions—which were simpler because of the condition and persecutions of those saints—if they were later raised to a more venerable form through severity, they will not deserve to be called contrary to the law of God and the decrees of the ancients. For example, if those primitive Christians performed their sacred rites in crypts whenever persecutions pressed upon them, it is permitted to us, in such great prosperity of kingdoms, to elevate temples from those same crypts into the open air. 

But the Waldensian does not admit this beginning: that we have done anything of the sort regarding apostolic rites, but rather charges that the whole form of the present Church is a recent invention and was entirely unknown to those first [apostles]. He contends that those apostles observed nothing except what can be found in the books of the New Law <note>The New Testament</note>. To refute this ignorance of the Waldensian, we respond thus: if we believe that nothing was observed except what is read here, the first Church would have been nothing but a naked thing. You might believe the apostles never performed the sacrifice at the altar; or if you believe it was performed, you might contend that any Christian performed it promiscuously, under no set form, according to how religion moved and invited him by a reputation for holiness. Whether either of these truly did not happen cannot easily be shown from the law; yet, just as their devotion toward God was holy as if from the apostles, so it was not done randomly by everyone and in an undigested manner. This is proven by the commentaries of that time, as well as the perfect fullness of apostolic knowledge from the Holy Spirit. 

Peter the Apostle was the first to rule the See of Antioch; you, O Waldensian, who read the New Law as if they were annals, show from the history of the law how he administered it! Because it is not found, therefore [you say] it ought not to have been done? But certainly it was done, and the holy Ignatius, the successor of the blessed Peter in that place, in his epistles, as well as Eusebius of Caesarea in his *Ecclesiastical History*, most well-attested authors, have left it on record. In the thirty-seventh year after Christ ascended into heaven, the Apostle Paul [was killed] by the sword of Nero...

Having completed his work from Syria to Illyricum <note>Illyricum was a Roman province covering the Balkan Peninsula.</note>, he filled everything with the Gospel. He wrote letters to only a few churches, and even in these, he did not write them as if they were commentaries of his own deeds, but rather he included questions concerning the Law and the Prophets and instructions for living well. Let it be shown to me here, either from the letters or the Acts of the Apostles, what he did among others during such a great span of years. What did he teach? What did he establish through ecclesiastical discipline and Christian rites? If he did nothing there except what the Waldensian teacher finds repeated in the law—remaining quiet for over half the years and doing nothing—then it must be that the Apostle left the churches stripped of order and ceremonies.

But the Waldensian is clearly foolish. For the Apostle, in his second letter to the Thessalonians, openly testifies that not all aspects of the apostolic time were committed to scripture. "Therefore, brothers, stand firm," he says, "and hold to the traditions you have learned, whether by our words or by our letter." <note>Original: *Itaque fratres state, inquit, & tenete traditiones quas didicistis sive per sermones sive per epistolam nostram* (2 Thessalonians 2:15).</note> Behold, the Apostle writes some things, and he establishes others by his personal presence. You, Waldensian, tell us from the texts those things which the Apostle handed down not by letter, but by word of mouth. 

Thus, they did not write everything down. For things that are committed to ink and paper, however they may be guarded, fall into the hands of the unworthy just as the worthy. Therefore, all the more secret things—those without a veil, without figures of speech and signs—they wished to communicate to their most worthy followers, such as Timothy, Titus, Dionysius, Ignatius, and Polycarp, which they handed down through oral reception <term>receptio: the oral passing down of tradition from teacher to student</term> alone. 

The divine Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a theologian whose 5th-century writings on the "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" were considered by medieval scholars to be the work of a direct disciple of St. Paul.</note> is my witness in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. He says: "Our most holy leaders, when they instituted the sacred rites to be performed publicly, did not hand them down through open and exposed meanings, but through more solemn signs." And again: "Those highest and beyond-substantial things they handed down to us partly in writing and partly through unwritten instructions, according to what the sacred laws define." This was not only for the sake of the profane multitude, for whom it is not even lawful to touch the signs themselves. 

Behold, Waldensian—if I may say so in passing—from how many things the sacred father Dionysius comes against you! The apostles did not institute Christian rites with plain meanings. Do you practice these "most plainly"—that is, most profanely and nakedly—as if you were coming straight from a field? It is not right for the profane multitude to touch even the outward signs. Yet you, with your sacrilegious audacity and hands filthy with dung, burst even into the Holy of Holies! And although you possess nothing holy (for as the most filthy swine, you profane everything you touch), you neither revere that which you believe you possess. This corrupted conscience has stirred up in you a guilt for sacred crimes at the altar, like that of Korah <note>Chore/Korah: a biblical figure who led a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16).</note> and his accomplices.

But let us return to our point. We have it from this passage, therefore, that the most holy leaders of the Apostles instituted the sacred rites to be performed publicly in the Church. You, who seek the history of the times in the New Law <note>The "New Law" refers to the New Testament era.</note>: show us where and when they met to establish these things. And yet, it was necessary for them to meet. They ordered many things there through unwritten instructions. Where shall those things which were not written be found? And yet, it was necessary for them to be ordered. 

Do you understand your own trifles? Indeed, you come forth as a "new man" after the passage of so many centuries, prompted by a demon. If your apostolic tradition is from unwritten things, then ours is not! Surely, if one of the two parties—either us or the Waldensian—must be aware of such institutions, will it not be the one that has descended in perpetual succession from that time? Just as it happens in every commonwealth: if a question arises over customs, the judgment is sought from antiquity. For customs usually persevere no less faithfully through oral reception than laws do through writing. 

Therefore, whatever ecclesiastical institutions are not found openly in the canon of the scriptures cannot be accused by this Waldensian novelty of being non-apostolic or of being recently devised fictions of the priests. And having asserted these things for the faith, we return opportunely to our first discourse regarding temples, ornaments, and all the things we proposed. Once again, therefore, we say that ceremonies were sought from the primitive church; some of these still preserve their complete form, while others have been changed according to the conditions of the times into a more solemn but nonetheless consistent custom. I show that this could and should have been done by example. If the Synagogue <note>The author uses "Synagogue" to refer to the Jewish religious system of the Old Testament.</note> had to be content only with the first founder of the law, God would have inspired others in vain after Moses to...

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK FOUR

It was not that they met in profane places until the storm of persecution subsided so that they could build crypts; for the apostles and the first Christians never met in just any profane places, which you <note>The author is addressing a hypothetical or specific Waldensian opponent here.</note> have misunderstood. But it will seem a wonder to you how they could build churches throughout the cities. We have proved from witnesses of those times that there were churches, such that they were not merely crypts, but manifest temples. We know that when the Christian religion first went out into the world, it was thought by the Greek and Latin peoples to be a Jewish institution. This was because it philosophized in the same way regarding the worship of one God, adored the same God, and observed the same books of the Law and the Prophets. Furthermore, our leaders were of that same Law and language and associated closely with the Jews. But they [the Greeks and Romans] believed there were contrary sects regarding questions of the Law; this contention did not much bother the Gentiles, who were accustomed to such disputes in their own gymnasiums, where it was frequent that no two philosophers were thought to feel the same way. 

Celsus the Epicurean <note>original: "Celsus epicureus"; Celsus was actually a 2nd-century Platonic philosopher known for the first comprehensive intellectual attack on Christianity.</note>, a slanderer of the apostolic faith of that time, is my witness that such a study of opinions existed between the external religions of the Jews and Christians. He attacks this contention as if it were childish and unworthy of men; the great and tireless Origen <note>original: "adamantius origenes"; 'Adamantius' was a nickname for Origen meaning 'man of steel' or 'unbreakable' due to his rigorous lifestyle.</note> responds to the trifles of this Celsus. Festus, the procurator of Judea, is also my witness, who said of the Apostle Paul to King Agrippa: "There is a certain man left in bonds by Felix, concerning whom, when the accusers stood up, they brought no accusation of such things as I supposed, but had certain questions against him about their own superstition, and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive." <note>This is a translation of the Latin Vulgate version of Acts 25:14–19.</note> Thus, they thought Christians lived under the Jewish rite. 

At that time, the Jews held privileges from the Macedonian and Roman empires for a shared citizenship throughout all the cities, in which they openly built synagogues. Therefore, whether they were from the Jews or from the Gentiles, Christians had the power under both laws to build a sacred house; and the more powerful Christians dedicated plots on their estates for churches. Yet, I do not assert that Christian temples arose only from Jewish liberty, since Christians were also able to do such a thing by public custom. Even those Egyptian monstrosities <note>A derogatory reference to the various foreign "mystery cults," such as the cult of Isis, which were permitted in Rome.</note> each had their own shrines in Rome, where a judgment was held for every foreign religion. The Father and His Son Christ, with the Holy Spirit, possessed the riches of the Christian cause, which advanced this heaven-commended religion into greatness.

You press me here: "But those temples were simple and small." I do not deny it, but you have not yet said that building temples was against the law of God. You rebuke the magnificence and the towering mass of the temples; you then, from your huts, from your straw-thatched houses—you who lie in the same stable with your beast—having emerged from such filth, would you blame the will of princes and of distinguished cities? You should understand what constraint strikes kings: they build cities, theaters, palaces, basilicas, and all manner of profane things most sumptuously. Indeed, they change the face of the earth with insane structures: they level the seas and cut down steep hills into precipices. They clothe the walls of their lodgings with gold. For one little body that will tomorrow turn to ashes, they pour out their strength in receiving it. 

Among such lusts, should they think they owe nothing worthy of a King to God? Or if a church is built, should it cost less and be humbler than the stalls for cattle? No, for their conscience strikes them, and with King David they say: "Do you not see that I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of God is placed in the midst of skins [tents]?" <note>Referring to 2 Samuel 7:2, where David expresses guilt that his palace is better than God's dwelling.</note> And in another place: "Lord, remember David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord, and vowed a vow to the God of Jacob: I will not enter into the tabernacle of my house, I will not go up into my bed... until I find out a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob." <note>A translation of Psalm 132 (Vulgate 131).</note> 

But the Lord also rebukes your people through the prophet Haggai: "This people says, 'The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built.'" And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: "Is it time for you to dwell in paneled houses <note>original: "domibus laqueatis"; refers to expensive coffered or inlaid ceilings.</note> while this house lies deserted? You looked for much, and behold, it came to little; and when you brought it home, I blew it away. For what cause?' says the Lord of hosts. 'Because my house is deserted, and every one of you runs to his own house.'" <note>A translation of Haggai 1:2–9.</note> 

You hear King David; you hear the prophet. You will begin first from David, then Solomon, and perhaps from Moses before you damn the present works of kings and cities. If you are a rustic and live on three obols <note>original: "triobolo vivis"; a 'triobolus' was a coin of very small value, implying living in extreme poverty.</note>, we do not bind you beyond your means. Keep those most simple rural churches which you find ready; if you wish, celebrate in those smoky huts where you meet. What have you noted in these things that is alien to ancient simplicity? Here, you shall find no cause for complaint on our part.

->## ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS<-

Truly you pretend to be apostolic, yet in your mind you are a heretic. You reveal this in your voice, your face, your gestures, and every external work, and even in your refusal to join in common prayer. We perform the dedications of temples and altars with sacred prayers. This displeases you; therefore, let it displease you! But we certainly took this practice from the primitive Church—listen to the sacred father Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works on the "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> on this matter from the same book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*: "Wherefore the divine law has distributed the testimony of pontifical ordinations, the consecration of the divine ointment, and the consecration of the sacred altar among the offices and virtues of the most reverend pontiffs." 

You, therefore, O Waldensian <note>original: "valdesis"</note>, just as you have no Bishop or anointing, so you do not consecrate altars or priests. You stray from the Church, from the Bishop, from the anointing, and from the priest—in short, from all apostolic discipline. To refute this, even if we did not have Dionysius, we would still understand by the instruction of natural reason that there is a difference between the sacred and the profane. The religion of the Gentiles performed sacred rites in a temple only after it had been dedicated. But let us leave those examples and call upon our own. Moses in the desert sanctifies the tabernacle; Solomon, the son of the migration <note>original: "filium transmigrationis"; this likely refers to the "children of the captivity" or a specific title for Solomon in this context</note>, and the Maccabees consecrate the temple, whether newly built or after it had been profaned. 

Of these things you recognize nothing as apostolic. You know nothing of sacred vestments—which is no surprise, since you know nothing of the whole Catholic faith. In this matter I will not be long, for the facts are manifest and innate judgment prevails. Moses teaches by divine illumination which garments the High Priest, the priest, and the Levite should use. Since the Apostles knew those things were figures of the future and most august sacrifice, would they have approached the sacred rite immediately from the market in profane clothes? And what of that pontifical miter <note>original: "insula," a common medieval spelling for "infula," a liturgical headband or miter.</note> of Saint Sylvester, which Constantine wanted to adorn with gold and gems? Do not believe he invented it from himself. Yet even so, if you saw such a thing worn over profane clothing, you would think it looked like a masked figure <note>original: "larue simile"</note> coming forward. Suppose the later Church received vestments neither from the Old Law nor from the Apostles; even so, you will sweat, O Waldensian, to prove that they were received against divine law.

I come now to the bells <note>original: "campanas"</note>, which are cast at such great expense of bronze. I excuse here the generosity of princes and cities—though I would not excuse it if I had not read in the sacred law of cymbals, trumpets, horns, and various vessels of song by which the whole temple resounded during sacrifice. The Apostles did not know bells, for it is a new invention; and the Christian cause does not depend on these vessels. There are many Christians among the Turks and the Sultan where bells are not permitted. If you begin to benefit from the higher steps and then find them an annoyance to hear because your head is too thick, we grant this to you: never use bells. But because of the work involved, you will have to give a name to a caller or sacristan <term>edituo: a temple warden or sacristan</term> who will be forced to summon you to the church doors.

But let us pass over these and mention other, more serious things: wealth, treasures, garments heavy with gold and gems, and statues of solid gold and silver (or at least gilded) in the temples. I suspect these are most heavily criticized in the writings of those Waldensians. I say what the Waldensian will gladly hear: the severity of the apostolic age did not know these things. However, if through long-standing frugality and the generosity of kings and the votive gifts of the people they have come to such riches, it will never be argued that they were collected or preserved against the law of God. 

Look at the ancient tabernacle in the desert—how much wealth of gold and gems! It was built not out of human ambition but by the command of God. As for the riches of Solomon's temple, I cannot explain them because of their abundance. Do not attribute this to royal pride; God approved the deed and He was dedicated and sanctified there in the darkness <note>Refers to the "thick darkness" or cloud that filled the Temple during its dedication in 1 Kings 8:12.</note> when He descended into the temple. Finally, dedicated gold was always kept in the temple. 

Lest you object that this was done against God's will, look at Antiochus the Illustrious <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note>, Nicanor, and Heliodorus, who were all struck by divine vengeance for their sacrilegious intent toward those sacred treasures. Crassus the triumvir plundered the treasures of the temple and was killed among the Parthians, along with his son and his legions, to the greatest disgrace and detriment of Roman majesty. Constantine—not the Great, but the Constantine from the succession of Emperor Heraclius <note>Refers to Constans II, who plundered Rome in 663 AD and was later assassinated in his bath in Sicily.</note>—plundered the sacred Roman things and, having barely left Sicily, was killed amidst the luxury of the baths. There are innumerable examples showing that dedicated gold was never violated with impunity. But these are enough from all of them; for divine judgments...

### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR
g. 5.

Do they not look at the frequency of the deed itself? But here you might say to me: besides those things which you show in this context to displease you in our works—to which I will respond appropriately below—you could presently object: what value is there in gold retained for sacred things? Would not any sane person be reproached if he buried his riches? At this point, you should know, O Waldensian <note>The Waldensians were a medieval sect that advocated for apostolic poverty and criticized the wealth and corruption of the established Church.</note>, we do not devote it in such a way that it never comes into use, but it is reserved for public and most desperate difficulties. Many famous republics are witnesses to me, which have the wealth of the churches of their city cataloged, and lest any fraud occur regarding them, they review them from the records every year.

The Romans, having gathered that most opulent treasure from the prosperity of Asia, the inheritance of Attalus <note>Attalus III, the last king of Pergamum, who bequeathed his wealthy kingdom to the Roman Republic in 133 BCE.</note>, and the spoils of Cyprus, Corinth, Carthage, and Spain, hid it under an unspoken curse in the Temple of Saturn <note>The Aerarium or Roman public treasury was housed in the Temple of Saturn.</note>, so that they might never unseal it until a "Gallic terror" <note>original: "terror Celticus"—a reference to a Roman law allowing the use of sacred emergency funds only in the event of an invasion by Gauls (Celts).</note> was imminent. Asa, the king of Judah, took the treasures of the house of the Lord to hire a foreign soldier; it was permitted for him to move the sacred money for the sake of the republic without the stain of sacrilege. Nor was he rebuked by the prophet for that, but because he did not trust in the God of Israel.

By this same counsel, we also preserve the wealth of the churches. But in the meantime, it is spent on the splendor and adornment of divine things. They enclose the relics of the saints in gold and gems, and rightly so; for it was permitted even for Moses to enclose the tablets of the testament, the bread of presence, and the rod of Aaron in an Ark fashioned from gold of such great price. Therefore, we think and certainly believe that we are also without sin when we preserve the remains of the friends of God in our most precious things.

And yet these things are inferior to their merits and dignity, whose souls are worthy of heaven; even the relics of the saints will one day be deemed worthy of greater things. Therefore, we would be willing to provide even more, but we are certainly unable to receive and honor the saints more significantly than from this tabernacle <note>meaning the earthly church or the physical body.</note>. In these things, the devotion of our minds, though confined within the narrow limits of earthly things, will have merit in heaven. 

But you, who consider all our things impure, even beyond the authority of Scripture and the elders, suffer from a certain passion toward us, like someone who has conceived a hatred for another: whether the person is just or unjust matters not to him—he is displeased by his words and deeds, his entering and exiting; in short, he is displeased by everything. You hold this attitude toward our religion without any distinction, which is surely a spirit of blasphemy.

But I come to your words: you say our constitutions are causes for the overthrow of the faith, material for idolatry, vain superstition, mortal sin, robberies, and more things which you commemorate there. What "robberies" you name and what "idolatry" I cannot find, or what thought occurred to you, except that you are accustomed to thunder against the wealth of the churches and against images. 

You say, however, that wealth of this kind ought to be spent on the poor and needy. Therefore, just as I hear, it will be considered just in your eyes for the Church to have wealth, but you judge it iniquitous because she does not spend it. If, therefore, they spend it more opportunely than even you can guess, it will be just for the Church to have wealth. That she should not squander what she has rashly or at any time—this both civil prudence teaches and the example of the Gospel suggests. For the Savior did not spend the three hundred denarii on the poor at the first possible moment, as they could have been redeemed from the ointment. Instead, he wished the poor to be helped from other things which were to be taken from elsewhere, but he wanted this ointment prepared for a greater use. 

But look! Just as if Judas were reproaching Christ for forgetting the poor, he put forward a show of mercy and a pretense of piety under the memory of the poor—the same as the Waldensian does toward us today. And in truth, the material of his rebuke was not piety, but profound greed, from which his betrayal followed. Neither does the Waldensian act against us out of the equity of the matter, for he himself does nothing notable either for God or the poor. For if there is one condition of men who brood greedily over their own things, the Waldensian broods; but out of a malice which he nevertheless clothes in a show of piety, he thus rebukes our votive gifts. This does not come from piety toward us, and the betrayal of Christian reverence has followed him. 

But though he may go out from the apostolic college with the traitor Judas, let them burst asunder together <note>A reference to the death of Judas Iscariot as described in Acts 1:18.</note>: the former because of the ointment, the latter because of the wealth. The ointment and the wealth are preserved: the former for burial, the wealth lest, when some most urgent necessity falls, neither the Church nor the poor have the means to assist exhausted affairs. As for those whose wealth he says is a burden to the Christian people, I do not understand what burden the Waldensian is talking about. For whatever gift anyone gives to the sanctuary, he gives it of his own accord. No one does anything there under compulsion. If, however...
