# ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

I possess purple cloth interwoven with gold. I consider it unworthy of my own poor body, but I consider it worthy of the divine altar. Therefore, I give it to the sanctuary. To you, perhaps, I seem to have imposed a burden upon my own resources. But you are mistaken, for I wish to purchase these things only from the smallest and most superfluous funds, whereas I could and should present my very self to God from a gold coin. Why should my conscience not remind me, repeating again and again, that this is true piety? You redeem merit before God from a farthing <note>original: "quadrante" — the smallest Roman coin, often used to signify a widow's mite or a humble offering</note>. Yet you arrange games, banquets, and proud horses from your entire wealth. How much more happily do my fortunes perish for the sake of God than for the sake of luxury?

As for what you call a "burden" to me, I move on to other matters where you might perhaps find this "burden" you speak of. Indulgences and the remissions of sins are transmitted to us. It is again in your power whether you redeem <note>In this context, "redeem" refers to the practice of performing an act of penance or giving an alms to satisfy a spiritual obligation</note> this satisfaction or not. You will seek heaven no less based on your own merit. When life ends—for a parent, a wife, or a son—you "redeem" the gravedigger; you "redeem" the intercession for them at the altar or you do not. It is your own judgment; no one imposes a burden upon you. Do what your conscience and love of neighbor suggest to you in the sight of God.

But how is it that you expect to have a priest for free, when a cobbler does not even pick up his awl to fix a shoe for free? You serve your shop because you wish to live from your shop. Since the priest serves the altar—as the words of Saint Paul say—if he lives from the altar, should he be considered unjust and greedy? <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 9:13: "Do you not know that those who perform the sacred services eat the food of the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the offerings of the altar?"</note> Certainly the priests of the Old Law lived from the altar. And since it remains in your power to do nothing beyond your own means, I do not yet understand what sort of "burden" you suspect is being imposed upon the Christian people by such ceremonies.

You say that these things which are "burdensome" are the very cause of robbery. I do not quite follow the logic of your argument. For I do not know if anyone ever thought it so necessary to contribute to the Church that they decided to plunder for that reason—unless, perhaps, that common proverb has struck you: "the place makes the thief" <note>original: "locus furem facit"</note>. You think that where there are no riches, sacrilege would not be committed. Look at this "sharp wit" of ours! In this way, I might as well say that where there is no innocence, there would be no injury; therefore, let us do away with innocence itself, since it alone makes our attacker a criminal. Cast your possessions away from you, since if they are kept, they are in fear of making someone a thief or a murderer! But this argument falls of its own weight.

Let us proceed to another point, since they say that those ecclesiastical constitutions are the causes of idolatry, of erroneous hope, and of vain superstition—and thus lead to the concealment of mortal sin. Here, no one doubts that they are attacking the veneration of saints and images. Regarding this matter, a specific discourse was held by us earlier; nevertheless, I wish to offer a small reminder here on this subject, lest their present "poison" not be diluted by our present "remedy."

Images of the saints, as Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Church.</note> testifies in the *Preparation for the Gospel*, are things sought after since the very first Church. That woman healed of a flow of blood set up a statue of the Savior cast in bronze <note>Referring to the story of the Haemorrhoissa in Eusebius’s Church History (7.18), who reportedly erected a statue of Jesus in Caesarea Philippi.</note>. And what you might marvel at: the Divinity deigned to ennoble this image with its own miracle. For a plant grew from the ground at its base, and when it had grown high enough to touch the hem of the statue's garment, it was plucked and found useful for many infirmities. The same Eusebius recorded that images of the Apostles Peter and Paul were preserved for memory. If I should come across these by chance, and out of the record of the Church established by them, I should say in congratulation: "The Apostle Peter and Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, they themselves taught us Your law, O Lord"—I ask you, show me from the Scriptures how I have admitted the stain of idolatry or vain superstition into myself.

I will challenge you more precisely: what would you have done if the power were given to you to throw down that image of the Savior? Look—the Divinity honors it with a miracle. See with what "innocence" you are about to violate it? It was once a capital offense to urinate near the statues of princes. Will you utterly destroy the memory of the Savior as if it were the statue of an impure idol? The Turk who captured Constantinople <note>The Fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire occurred in 1453, a recent and traumatic event for the author’s audience.</note> caused a captured crucifix to be carried into the camp and defiled with every kind of mockery. Are you going to follow his example, you who think no less than the Turk regarding "idolatry" and "vain superstition" in Christian institutions?

# WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

...infamous superstitions. When you say that our infamy pertains to the images of the saints: it is much indeed. For remove the infamy from a theft, and you have similarly removed the infamy from the thief. Thus, you call us idolaters only based on some prior crime—namely, because you attack the images of the saints as if they were impious idols. Therefore, we are idolaters in your view. Remove this impious charge and you have freed us from infamy; but you would more readily grant everything to an enemy of the cross of Christ than to a Christian. We, however, observe nothing that would be an impediment to the word of justice, as you lyingly whisper. In our prayers and holy things, you will find nothing alien to the law and the sense of God, nothing of human fiction. You can hardly quibble that these are human institutions that we hold more tenaciously than the precepts of God. These and similar things come from your previous fabrications, as when you were forging treachery from your own mind regarding the veneration of saints and the prayers for the dead <note>original: "suffragijs" — intercessory prayers or works offered on behalf of the souls in purgatory</note>. Those conclusions seemed to follow naturally for you. But after we have tested that discourse from another workshop and struck it again to the dross, whatever you now say regarding idolatry and vain superstition is spoken to the wind or out of ignorance.

But let us descend from this to the ecclesiastical office and whatever is found within it: the canonical hours, the order of the service at the altar, the singing, the blessed salt <note>original: "salbenedictū"</note>, and the water. For you clearly seemed to pluck these things from those words in that sermon on prayers for the dead: [ *What if he also allows this: a prayer not written from books but from the living faith of a faithful and upright priest, which he offers to God with his faithful people?* ] Here, however, you mock the prayer contained in books. You make it manifest that the ecclesiastical office is taken from nowhere else but the New and Old Law, and at the same time, you most maliciously mock every treatment of Sacred Scripture—unless, by your sharp wit, you think it makes a difference whether holy things are treated freely, or if, being commanded by the Church, I act out of a "fiction." 

In truth, when priests pray from books, they act entirely out of obedience and the very nature of holy religion. For if we do not approach a king with requests while unprepared, and if we owe some duty to God for the sake of piety, it will be most fitting for the divine majesty—and to avoid the vice of a stuttering speech in a sudden matter—that it be done in a certain conceived manner. But if the divine service were prescribed in no certain way, and if it permitted the indeterminate lust of anyone, however filthy or unwashed, you would see a most abject and corrupt state of the Church, similar to a gathering of lunatics <note>original: "lymphatorū" — literally "water-maddened," used to describe those in a state of religious frenzy or madness</note>. If you do not yet grasp this in your mind, I will show it more clearly and presently by an example: let everyone place before their eyes their own household affairs; what would they become if they were not managed by a fixed judgment? It would be a thing like insanity if one allowed everything in his home to happen by chance. How much less could the Church, which ought to grow throughout the whole world of brothers, allow its affairs to be handled by chance in such great magnitude? It would no longer be a Church, but a confusion of the devil. 

Therefore, every divine office in the Church is held in an orderly fashion, and is moreover raised to such honest and majestic ceremonies that, just as in the holiness of the believers, so in the order of the sacred rites, our religion has never been nor ever will be anything that surpasses the apostolic institution. For the Church, in its orders, is composed by the holy fathers according to the example of the heavenly hierarchies. The divine Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential early Christian theologian who wrote on the "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy," paralleling the ranks of the Church with the ranks of angels.</note> is my witness. In his *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, he speaks in such a way as to show that the priest must drive away all disordered, incomplete, and confused things from himself, and instead exhibit the beauty, order, and gravity in the proportions of their holy orders. 

Regarding the office: which the written book of the Waldensian mocks, he [Dionysius] says: the most sacred songs and readings of the Scriptures teach the mastery of that perfect life. Behold: both songs, hymns, and psalms—for those are "songs"—and readings. The performance of the priest has maintained the order and gravity of these beauties, not from his own fictions, but from the apostolic rule received until now. Why then do the priests pray? He says: so that they might hold to the reading of the sacred law; so that, finally, they do not approach the altars for the handling of holy things while "naked" or unpurified from whatever profane business. But what is the more urgent cause? Since those who manage temporal things in the Church—whether from poverty or from craftsmen—take care, according to the words of the Apostle, for the things of this world so that nothing is lacking to the external affairs of the Church, let the priests in turn take care that nothing is lacking to the Church in divine matters, so that each status may provide a mutual service to the other, if the matter is to grow in this course of the age...

### ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE ENTIRE CHURCH AGAINST...

...of the body of Christ. It is necessary there to pray for things that are consistent with the divine will, lest if something unworthy be asked, it becomes an insult to the divine majesty. To discern this, however, not everyone is fit. The judgment of such a great matter stood with the holiest fathers, who by the merit of their lives deserved to know these things; it was so that we might pray securely according to their pre-defined law, and not fall into that saying, "You know not what you ask," and also, "You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly," <note>The author is quoting Matthew 20:22 and James 4:3 to argue that spontaneous prayer can be selfish or ignorant, necessitating the pre-written prayers of the Church.</note> as if you were consumed by your own desires. 

Therefore, the leaders of the Christian cause adopted the psalms for every divine office and the administration of the sacraments, as well as all the readings from the Old and New Law. These are found to be observed and ordered to this day, not rashly, but by those who held sacred power. Among them we find Saint James the Apostle and Patriarch of the Jerusalem church (in which the singing of the "Alleluia" <note>original: "cani alleluia"</note> first began); then Basil the Great, the Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; and the Roman Pontiffs Celestine, Gregory the Great, Telesphorus, Gelasius, Pelagius, and Sergius—all emulators of apostolic severity—and finally the most holy Ambrose, Bishop of Milan. 

Now, if these authors of our sacred rites also displease you—you, whom nothing apostolic has pleased thus far—then review even older things: how much divine order the Synagogue <note>The author uses "Synagoga" to refer to the religious assembly of the Old Testament as a precursor to the Church.</note> held in its sacred rites; with what great care David instituted the psalms and the singers of psalms. These things were indeed done by divine inspiration, since the psalms written by those singers and prophets are confirmed to be divine both by the prophets of that time and later by the Gospel and the Apostles. 

With such great authors sought from divinity for our prayers and singing during the divine office—even if it greatly displeases those Waldensians—we both sing and speak from books. Following this, we are reminded of tithes <term>decimas: a tenth part of agricultural produce or income contributed to the church</term> and offerings, lest these too be accused by that Waldensian as being mere fictions of priests. If they do so, they act against the law of nature and the written law, in which the use of tithes was certainly established. Abraham tithed all his substance to God through the priest Melchizedek. In the Law of Moses, God commands tithes of all things, from man to beast, from the field to the gardens. 

And he who denies offerings denies that he owes anything of his possessions to God. Furthermore, concerning spontaneous offerings, God arranged many things for the people of Israel. Whether it be money, or fruit, or abstinence of the body—whatever of your things you finally offer to God—by that very vow you signify that you and your things are owed to God. To the extent that this is pious, it would be equally impious not to recognize God, the giver of life and the Lord of your substance, through both voluntary and mandatory gifts. 

But the Waldensian is harder than all Judaic hardness, for he never looks at the equity of such things from their true origin, but only from their immediate use <note>The author argues the Waldensians focus only on how current priests might misuse money, ignoring the ancient, holy reasons why tithes were established.</note>. Suppose there are some evil men who use such things badly; the sons of Eli did this, yet the sacrifices of the Synagogue were known to be irreproachable in their origin. We rightfully demand that the things of the church be perceived in such a way. For even if they were found to be entirely human inventions (which the Waldensian has not yet shown), they would still be regarded as ecclesiastical ceremonies, and we would certainly observe them for our mutual benefit. For if ancient holiness used them holily, there is no reason why we should not also use them holily. Consider that in other indifferent matters, a frugal man sets before himself the examples of the good to follow, not the bad. But we will dispute this more copiously later.

Now, with a great part of the ecclesiastical institutions having been reviewed by us, I see the last ones remain: Salt and holy water <note>original: "Sal & aquā benedictā"</note>, which those Waldensians certainly mock. I wish to respond to this wickedness with a brief chapter. Salt was adopted because Elisha <note>original: "Heliſeus"</note> healed the unhealthy waters of Jericho with it. Finally, we know it was adopted from the rite of the Tabernacle, concerning which God commanded Moses: "Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt, nor shall you take away the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice; in every offering you shall offer salt." Truly, above...

### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR
**T**

Regarding the water of sprinkling <note>original: "aquā aspsionis"</note>, we have that testament from the Old Law: "A clean man shall gather up the ashes of the heifer and pour them outside the camp in a very pure place, that they may be kept for the multitude of the children of Israel for protection and for the water of sprinkling." <note>The author cites Numbers 19 to provide a biblical precedent for the use of "holy water."</note> These elements are therefore blessed with sacred prayers and the commemoration of the divine works formerly performed through them, along with the invocation of the name of Jesus and the marking of the triumphal cross of Christ. By this certain symbol, wondrous works have always been performed in the Church. Therefore, by the power of the name of Jesus and the sign of the cross, by which the elements of salt and water are bound together <note>The ritual for blessing holy water traditionally involves mixing salt into the water.</note> for the presence of such great things, we sprinkle ourselves with them against human spells, illusions of the devil, terrors of the night, and for the cleansing of venial sins. 

He who disagrees here is impious and a most wicked detractor of the majesty of Jesus’s name and the power of his cross. He considers these things weaker than the ashes of the heifer, about which Moses certainly wrote from the mouth of God, so that they might be for the protection of the children of Israel. We shall settle these matters in order, so that I believe nothing remains of the Church’s ceremonies to which I have not responded for those Waldensians. If they think the response is insufficient, the fault is theirs; for he who accuses vaguely should expect a discretionary defense. Therefore, although we have acted for conscience’s sake, if they still think they are not satisfied, we freely invite them and all their concerns: if they are fair, let them return to us openly. Then it will be clear who is a Waldensian and who is a Christian. 

We take up his other words, in which they claim the Church’s ceremonies are "fictions of priests," used as an occasion for them to hide their greed, conducting a business of sacred things and living in luxury from their robes, buildings, abundance of all things, and ambition. These same things are mentioned in that sermon on Purgatory in these words:

->THE WALDENSIAN,<-

> "But all these confirmers of purgatory send everyone there until those people arose who, through the invention of the word <note>Likely referring to the "invention" or doctrinal formulation of the word "Purgatory."</note>, began to make a profit—first with the living, and then with the dead."

Although I believe there is an abundant response in what I said elsewhere regarding those accusations, since it was necessary to bring those same points here where the case of the priests is discussed, I will repeat similar things for the sake of memory. The whole accusation is truly this: that priests, to earn possessions, promoted that faith concerning the purgatory of souls, believing that by striking such terror into mortals, men would desire to drive that fear away through foundations and offerings to the priesthood. But when the priests saw there would be others who, trusting in themselves, would consider themselves just, the priests met this thought with their greed, saying it was equally for all—living and dead alike—praying without distinction whether we are in a state of grace or not. 

Behold the narrowness of the Waldensians' understanding! For while difficulty concerning faith should be handled piously—"Bringing every intellect into captivity to the obedience of Christ," <note>2 Corinthians 10:5</note> as the Apostle says—they do not wait for such a path. Instead, they seek a cause to mock the truth of the greatest things from the talk of the common crossroads and from the deepest infection of gluttons. For who has not heard at some time, from the most sordid people amidst talk worn thin by levity, that the terrors of hell <term>Gehenna: a term for hell or a place of fiery torment</term> are nothing but the "inventions of priests"? Behold the school of our Waldensians! Behold the "heavenly illumination" from which they rise up against the Church. They say: "These confirmers of purgatory send everyone there where they know they will find profit." But I say that they do not send everyone there from whom they hope for profit.

### ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

For I know that even the most powerful men, who had brought death upon themselves, were unable by any prayer or price to obtain a sacred place <note>original: "sacrum locum"; referring to burial in consecrated ground</note> for themselves, even if their relatives offered a foundation for a perpetual priesthood. But if the Church prays for those who have died regenerated in Christ, in the remission of sins, and in the communion of the sacraments, and does not distinguish between this person or that person for whom it prays, we have shown before and will show now that the Church does this rightly according to the rule handed down by the saints. 

For they <note>the Waldensians</note> say directly that priests make no distinction as to whom they pray for. From this very word, I shall confront these Waldensians: they admit in a certain place that they pray patiently for their persecutors. Do they consider those persecutors worthy of merit, so that they should pray for them, or unworthy? They must consider them unworthy, since they have opposed them with new dogmas, recent inventions against the law of God, heresy, and bloodthirsty cruelty. Therefore, if a choice must be made regarding whom to intercede for before God, they would never pray for those men as enemies of the truth. Thus, because they lied then about praying for their persecutors, they also sinned against the Gospel, which commands that one should pray for one's persecutors. 

But if the sentences of the Gospel are granted, and they pray for us—whom they have made most unworthy of prayer due to "idolatry"—then those who were unworthy become worthy of being prayed for by that very act. You see into what a narrow corner you have been driven! Whether someone shows himself to be worthy or unworthy, he shall be held worthy of a priest's prayer during the divine rites without distinction, just as his own crucifiers were held worthy by Christ, so that he might pray for them. 

Furthermore, as to whether we should first inquire if such a person is in a state of grace or not—and thus worthy or unworthy—it does not belong to a mortal to know. For "who are you to judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls." <note>original: "tu em̄ quis es qui alienū feruum iudicas, domino tm̄ suo ſtat aut cadit"; a quote from Romans 14:4.</note> But you seem to argue that since we do not know if the dead or the living are in grace, then if they are in grace, we pray in vain for the grace they already have; and if they are not in grace, we pray in vain for a grace they are not going to have. 

You move more deeply and more wickedly, Waldensian, than you yourself understand, for this sentiment of yours strikes against the necessity of fate <note>The author accuses the Waldensian view of being a form of fatalism or strict predestination that renders human action useless.</note>. If you are right, then the word which I am about to quote from the Son himself would also be true. Saint James writes: "The prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up." <note>James 5:15.</note> According to your opinion, I would have to inquire and first make a distinction as to whether the sick person is in grace or not so that he might be saved. Therefore, if it is destined that he be saved, I shall pray in vain, because even without my praying he will be saved. If it is destined that he not be saved, I shall pray in vain again, because even with me praying he will not be saved. 

Thus you go against the Apostle, who did not speak from either case but said purely: "The prayer of faith shall save the sick." You go against the Gospel which commands: "Ask and you shall receive," <note>John 16:24.</note> and again, "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do." How will you solve this? You bring back the impious dogma of fate; you impose necessity upon things. You deny the free administration of God and you take away the choice of the will <note>term: "arbitrij electionem"; free will or the power to choose.</note>. 

From this source of most impious error, you have gained strength against the intercessions of the saints and against the suffrages <note>prayers or works of piety</note> for the dead. The simple neighbor thinks that you are instructing them in everything from the middle of the Scriptures, which you lead them around in under the false habit of true faith; yet you actually mangle and tear those Scriptures apart. Although I can hardly believe that you, in your crude understanding, fully and clearly grasp the hidden poison of your present speech according to its internal impiety. But the evil demon, whose instrument you offer yourself to be, brings back through you a blasphemy often tested in other heretics, so that if this small portion of your words—<insert>They do not wish to have a distinction, nor do they judge for whom they ought to pray, whether for the living or the dead</insert>—and the many things that follow should settle in the minds of men and be admitted as true, suddenly that sacrilegious dogma, an enemy to God and man, would be introduced into the world again through you. And all the more powerfully because you are so coarse <note>original: "crassior"; literally 'thicker' or 'duller', suggesting the opponent lacks the education to see the danger of his own ideas.</note>, which makes us less wary of you.

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR #
->T ii<-

...thinking that, on account of your deep rusticity <note>The author uses "rusticity" (rusticitas) as a jab at the Waldensians' lack of formal education, suggesting they are mere unlearned peasants.</note>, such an acute heresy could not have been conceived by you unless it was drawn from the existing testimonies of Holy Scripture. Therefore, you ask what it is we pray for in both cases? Indeed, for the living, if a person is impious, we pray to the divine clemency that he may no longer be impious. If he is pious, we pray that he may be confirmed, so that he may become even more pious. We pray: *Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, preserve the righteous, justify the sinners, and have mercy on all the faithful.* 

For the dead, however, we pray: *Lord Jesus Christ, salvation and liberation of the souls of the faithful, who came not to destroy souls but to save them and to give your life as a ransom for many, we suppliantly implore your immense clemency and ineffable mercy that you might deign to look mercifully upon the souls of the faithful departed who are tortured by the pains of purgatory; and that those who are justly afflicted for their sins may be liberated by your most kind piety.* 

Thus, we ought to pray for both without distinction. You, however, out of excessive ignorance and wickedness, falsely attribute this practice of ours to the "greed of priests." Let us consider another point: possessions had not yet been given to those early teachers of the Church. Therefore, they should have been more likely to invent something by which they might be given. Now, since you say possessions have already been given, what cause was there for them to invent such a thing? For the invention and the terror of purgatory ought to have come *before* the possessions were given, as a reason for giving them. 

Furthermore, consider that Kings and Princes are among those who were persuaded. See what contempt you hold for such high majesty! Do you think that neither by their own sharp minds nor by their friends could they have rebuked such "crass priestly figments"—things unheard of in the age of the Fathers and unknown to Holy Scripture—which you, coming from the plow-handle <note>original: "stiva"; the handle of a plow, used here to mock the opponent's background as a common laborer.</note>, have discovered so clearly? 

But the donations to the churches are most ancient, and there were never lacking, even besides Kings, most powerful Christians: Praetorian Prefects, commanders of the camps, Consuls, Praetors, and also private men and very wealthy women, from whose piety—which in those times was certainly at its greatest—estates were entrusted to the churches. I do not know if you would easily find in the histories of the ancients that those who established dioceses and monasteries exposed the servants of God to beggary or to seeking food by chance. 

But perhaps you think, when you hear of "alms" <term>Alms: charitable donations, usually small coins or food given to the poor.</term> in the deeds of the ancients, that it refers only to something like what you, out of your beggary or stinginess, provide from a small coin or a crumb of bread. Certainly, the most wealthy patrimonies passed into pious uses. Therefore, when Saint Lawrence distributed the treasure of the Augusti <note>original: "thesaurum Philipporum"; likely referring to the Emperor Philip the Arab, whose wealth Lawrence was said to have distributed.</note>, did he provide only for the lame and the weak? Did he not also provide for those burdened by debt and the quiet poverty and need of the heads of families and of the churches? Most certainly. The necessity of these people is not well-relieved by a pittance; rather, he dealt there with *sesterces* and *talents* <note>Ancient units of high-value currency.</note>. 

Away with that poverty which the wise man prayed against as much as he did wealth! <note>A reference to Proverbs 30:8: "Give me neither poverty nor riches."</note> Piety is safe when there is sufficiency; it does not live merely for the day, but has something to set aside for the future. But here you press me, saying that the standard of "sufficiency" for churchmen who have gone out from the world should be more restrained. If you insist on this so as to think the Church is therefore dissolved, you err. For the Church was not established upon poverty, but upon faith and the power of the keys <note>original: "potestate clavium"; the spiritual authority granted to St. Peter and his successors.</note>. 

And Christ our Savior placed it not as a command of God, but as the will of the one doing it, when he said: *If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all you have and give to the poor.* <note>Matthew 19:21.</note> Therefore, whoever is still weaker may retain the riches he has; he has not for that reason "cast off Christ." I speak of those riches which you Waldensians think should be abandoned at the Lord's voice—yet you yourself have not yet abandoned your own fortunes, nor have you even yet obeyed that voice of the Lord. For our fortunes are among "indifferent things" <note>original: "rebus indifferentibus"; things that are neither inherently good nor evil, but depend on their use.</note> which, if we use them well, we are not prohibited from using. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, David, Hezekiah, Josiah, and infinite Kings and Princes of our religion used them and nonetheless reached the state of perfect virtue. This fault alone remains in wealth: if it is possessed with an evil mind for gain and use. In this sense the Savior said: *It is easier for a camel...* <note>A reference to the "eye of a needle" proverb regarding the difficulty of the rich entering heaven.</note>

# ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS] #

...to enter through the eye of a needle <note>A reference to Matthew 19:24: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God."</note> than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. If the Savior had said this in an absolute sense, it would have been necessary for Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Martha, and her brother Lazarus—who certainly listened to the voice of the Lord—to have abandoned their wealth. Even that famous Zacchaeus did not say, "I am leaving all my goods," but rather, "If I have defrauded anyone, I restore it fourfold, and I give half of my goods to the poor." And yet the Lord testifies that salvation had come to him. For these people were not of the sort who allowed the word of the sower to fall among the thorns of the heart and the cares of riches. Instead, they had clothed themselves in a great spirit; even amidst riches, their minds remained sincere in the contemplation of heavenly things.

If there are any among us today who abuse their wealth—whether private or ecclesiastical—for worse ends, I will not say that you are looking for a speck in another’s eye while you yourself carry a beam. <note>A reference to Jesus’s teaching in Matthew 7:3 regarding hypocrisy.</note> I say only this: there is no excuse for our wrongdoing on your part. But when you penetrate from the crime of any individual all the way to those first principles, crying out that the state of the Church has collapsed—there you err. The Church, which is holy in itself, is not defiled by the sins of men, just as a fire, pure in itself, is not stained by the vice of those who handle it badly. Furthermore, Abraham, Nicodemus, Joseph, and all the righteous wealthy men have as much power to preserve the Church as any evil rich men have to overturn it.

You continue your speech, saying: *Neither did they deliver souls from hell.* Clearly, you do not depart from your own malice. Our priests do not deliver souls from the hell of the damned; rather, according to the institution of the Church, they intercede for those to be purified <note>The author is referring to souls in Purgatory.</note> so that they may be absolved more quickly. You think, however—and you labor to persuade us—as if the ancient Doctors of the Church did not believe in delivering souls from a temporary "hell" (Purgatory). But I ask you, when Saint Augustine said, *“Souls were shown in these places and torments,”* <note>original: "anime in his locis & cruciatibus ostense sunt"</note> and when he said, *“This fire, even if it be not eternal, is nevertheless wonderfully severe,”* <note>original: "Hic autem ignis & si eternus non sit, mıro tamẽ modo est grauis"</note> I ask you, Waldensian: did he not mean to deliver those souls whom he said were in torments, especially since he said this fire was not eternal for them?

But you impose all these things—hateful to the ear—upon the priests of the Church: namely, "fictions," "gain," and "avarice." We have exploded these "fictions." We have restored the ceremonies of the Church to their rightful place. If some wicked men use them for gain and greed, I have said before that what is fair by its own right is not made unjust by someone else’s vice. Behold, even the Gospel was preached by some for the sake of a convenient living. The sedentary arts <note>original: "Sellularie artes" — this likely refers to manual trades like weaving or shoemaking, which the Waldensians were famous for practicing while they preached.</note>—which I think are very well known to you—are practiced by many both viciously and with excessive greed, yet no one condemns the arts themselves because of another’s vice.

This, therefore, is your great wickedness, Waldensian: that you take what was holily instituted by holy men and thrust it into the category of "fictions" because of the sin of every wicked person. You take the conscience of ancient holiness, which was most full of God, and because of present behaviors (which nevertheless displease you more than is fair), you encompass them both and make the Church a liar. What evil dizziness is this that drives our kings, our princes, and all the sublimity of genius so far off track that for so many centuries they have not noticed what is congruent with the law of God or even with natural reason? Or do you think they are fanatics to be played with like blind men? Yet fictions and lies are by their nature too weak to defend themselves for very long.

But let us all be foolish together, so that you alone may be wise! Therefore, if the things you call "fictions"—the temples, their decoration and majesty, the divine office within them, the order of ministers, and finally everything in divine worship defined in its own prescribed manner—if these are all "fictions," and if the "Apostolic Church" is that which does none of these things, having no designated place, much less any beauty, measure, or order: then point your finger and show us what church you have left for us! That church escapes human thought. It will be even less than yours, which is certainly nothing. For it will lie mangled like a corpse, with all its members loosened from their order; it will seem more empty than the world will be when all things fall back into that formless confusion.

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK FOUR: THE WALDENSIAN #

Let a faithful man hold whatever is just against those men; nevertheless, they in no way confess their sin and do penance.

Have those rebels—who are truly men of disobedience—now found certain "faithful men" among themselves? But what wonder is it? For any impure assemblies are accustomed to usurp the names of virtues and to impose beautiful-sounding titles upon their own deeds. They are like deserters of a kingdom who bring their standards against their own lord. On their part, you might even dare to call the skill of their plotting "fortitude" and "faith," just as one does in a righteous army. By this cleverness, those fugitives have now found "faithful men" among themselves; and they severely question those whose faith does not yield to Roman authority.

Far be it, and may God turn it away, that while the purity of faith and the incorrupt guardian of the meaning of the Apostles’ Creed <note>The "symbolum apostolorum" refers to the Apostles' Creed, the defining statement of Christian belief.</note> endures, this judgment should perish, or that any foreign opinion should finally prevail against the Roman Church. For as long as this promise of the Savior remains—"I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail" <note>original: "Ego pro te rogaui Petre vt non deficiat fides tua." A quote from Luke 22:32, used here to assert the infallibility of the Papacy (the successors of Peter).</note>—no falsehood shall prevail against it. 

But do you wish to be faithful? Join the common body of the Christian commonwealth. Or rather, do you wish for yourself and others—whom you suggest as your accomplices—to be faithful? Say what you have; what do you believe? Truly, we have heard much regarding this. If you were truthful there, why did you fall short of the testimonies of the Scriptures? Why did you suppress those things that wished to go against you? Why did you pile up other things merely to adorn the surface? Otherwise, truth conquers above all things.

But if you are caught being a trifler, how then can you prevail? You make an example of our iniquity starting from that article of communion. I was afraid that you might even challenge us regarding the veneration of the saints, the prayers for the dead, or the entire faith concerning the Sacrament of the Altar <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>. But here you had to tickle the ear of another, wishing to be their ally, though you certainly agree with them less than you do with us. 

Therefore, out of everything, you have found only the [matter of] communion. From that, you stir up envy—not out of the whole faith regarding it (in which you are certainly uniquely impious), but you thunder loudly against us only concerning its *use*, as if by pretending to be pious in its use, you could not be a heretic in the rest. For if you deserve praise for this reason alone, we shall be much better than you for the same reason. For even if I grant you for the moment that we sin in its use—which we shall discuss shortly—nevertheless, because we believe rightly in the rest according to the will of Scripture and the Fathers, we are more innocent as those who believe well in many things. I wonder at you: you believe nothing rightly in anything, and yet you boast of yourself as innocent based on a single manner of use, and falsely so. 

You later hold out I know not what "commandment of God." I confess and I know that there is a commandment of God regarding its *use*, but as for the *mode* of the use of that sacrament, I do not know if there is a commandment, except that the inestimable and incomprehensible reverence for it demands that it be distributed to the Christian people in the most fitting use, and as far as possible from all danger. 

Let us also grant that the Apostles in the Church offered [communion] under both species <note>Receiving both the bread (the Body) and the wine (the Blood). The Waldensians and Hussites insisted the laity must receive both, whereas the Roman Church had moved to offering only the bread to the laity to avoid spilling the consecrated wine.</note>. But who does not know—and does not observe even in the affairs of the state—that administrations regarding laws are exercised with integrity, attentiveness, and dignity as long as the matter remains in its beginnings and among a few people? But where the commonwealth has now grown immensely, and because of its magnitude, it cannot distinguish by character or dedication every person who handles its rights and laws. Not only the vigorous, circumspect, and diligent push themselves into dispensing the laws, but also the sluggish and remiss. Neither can it be said that the majesty of the laws is unworthy because of the negligence of men; rather, something must be set against it. This is the reason why the later Church changed the earlier rite of communion—even if we grant for now that it was somewhat different. In this, you oppose our own doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," authoritative theologians like Thomas Aquinas.</note> to us; yet no one among us, even outside the doctors, denies [this history]. ->they in no way confess their sin or perform penance.<-

Those rebels have now discovered certain "faithful men" among themselves—men who are, in truth, stubborn and disobedient. But what is there to wonder at? For every impure assembly <note>original: "conciliabula," often used to describe illicit or heretical gatherings</note> is accustomed to usurp the names of virtues and to impose beautiful labels upon their own deeds. Deserters of a kingdom, when they gather their banners against their own lord, dare to call their "dexterity of counsel" by the names of "fortitude" and "faith," just as if they were in a righteous army. By this same ingenuity, those fugitives have now found "faithful men" among themselves, and they demand to know why the Roman authority does not strictly yield to their "faith." 

But far be it—and may God prevent it—that this censure should perish so long as the purity of the faith and the incorrupt guardian of the meaning of the Apostles' Creed endures. May no foreign opinion prevail against the Roman Church, since, as long as this promise of the Savior remains—*I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail* <note>original: "Ego pro te rogaui Petre vt non deficiat fides tua." This refers to Luke 22:32, the biblical basis for the doctrine of Papal infallibility</note>—no falsehood shall triumph over her. 

Do you wish to be "faithful"? Then yield yourself to the common body of the Christian society. Indeed, if you wish yourself and the others whom you introduce as your accomplices to be faithful, say what you have: what do you believe? We have heard much from your side on this: if you were true, why did you fall away from the testimonies of the Scriptures? Why did you suppress those things in you that were willing to go [toward the truth]? Why did you heap up other things only to decorate the surface? Truth, otherwise, conquers all things. If, however, you are caught being a trifler, from where then do you obtain your standing? 

You make an example of our "iniquity" regarding the article of Communion. I was afraid that you might even challenge us regarding the veneration of the saints, or the prayers offered for the dead, or the entire faith concerning the Sacrament of the Altar <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>. But here you had to scratch a stranger's ear <note>A metaphor for seeking an ally or a sympathetic listener</note> whose partner you wish to be; certainly, you agree with such a person less than you do with us. Yet you decorate them with your speech as if we were most opposed to them. 

Therefore, out of everything, you have found only the manner of Communion to complain about. From that, you stir up envy—not from the whole faith concerning it (in which you are certainly uniquely impious), but you thunder against us regarding its *use* alone. You pretend that you are pious because of this one practice, as if you could not be a heretic in all other things! Even if you deserve praise for this reason alone, we would be much better than you for the same reason. For even if we grant for a moment that we err in the "use" (which we shall discuss shortly), because we believe rightly in the rest according to the will of the Scripture and the Fathers, we—believing well in many things—will be more innocent than you, who believe nothing rightly about anything, yet falsely boast that you are innocent because of this one practice. 

You later hold out I know not what "commandment of God." I confess and I know that there is a commandment of God regarding the *use* of it; but regarding the *manner* of the use of that Sacrament, I do not know if there is a commandment, except that the inestimable and incomprehensible reverence for it demands that it be distributed to the Christian people as far as possible from any danger, and in the most decent manner. 

We grant that the Apostles in the Church offered the sacrament under both species <note>original: "sub vtraque specie." This refers to the Utraquist controversy: the Waldensians and later Hussites insisted that the laity must receive both the bread and the wine, whereas the Roman Church at this time restricted the chalice to the clergy to prevent accidental spilling of the "Blood of Christ."</note>. But who does not know—and does not notice even in the business of the state <note>original: "reipub," the republic or commonweal</note>—that administrations concerning the laws are exercised with integrity, attentiveness, and dignity as long as the matter remains in its beginnings and among a few people? But when it grows immensely, and because of its sheer size the law cannot distinguish between those who handle its rights with talent and devotion, there rush into the dispensing of the laws not only the vigorous, circumspect, and diligent, but also the sluggish and negligent. To prevent anything unworthy from happening to the majesty of the laws through human carelessness, some opposition must be set up. 

Let this be your reason why the later Church changed the earlier ritual of Communion (even if we grant for a moment that it was once different). You oppose us in this by citing our own learned men; yet no one among us, even besides the doctors, denies this. You say that they confess in their councils...

# ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE HERETICS]

...communion under both kinds <note>original: "sub utraque specie." This refers to the practice of receiving both the bread and the wine. The Roman Church at this time generally reserved the chalice for the priest alone</note>. You mention the first of their points there, but you are silent about the rest of what they believe—for instance, that the Church, on account of the danger of administering the sacrament in the liquid element of wine (a danger equally to be feared for the one giving and the one receiving), has, for the sake of the highest veneration of the body and blood of Christ, holily and healthfully withheld it. You remember what the Council of Basel <note>A 15th-century council that attempted to address the Hussite wars by granting limited use of the chalice</note> said on that matter. What of this? If it is confessed, as no one denies, that a danger is feared in such a practice from the start—no one who has a worthy reverence for this sacrament would wish it to be administered under both kinds. Nor did the Council of Basel grant this use out of its own free conscience; rather, it yielded to the wickedness of the Hussites, just as the "hardness of the Jews" extorted a "bill of divorce" <note>A reference to Matthew 19:8, where Moses allows divorce due to the people's stubbornness</note> from Moses against the law of nature. You claim that the administration under one kind has not yet been formally decreed. Why then do you contend over something not decreed? Or, more truly: it has indeed been decreed, but you despise this no less than you usually do with other things. Out of the four Great Councils <note>Usually referring to Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon</note>, you recognize only the Council of Nicaea. In this same way, Arius <note>A 4th-century priest whose teachings were condemned at Nicaea</note> withdrew his faith from that very Council of Nicaea by which his blasphemy was condemned, just as all you seditious people do who cast off public and legitimate consent. 

Therefore, communion under one kind has been decreed; the universal consent of the Western Church has subscribed to the decree. And I do not know if its use is not most ancient, repeated from the very first Church: we read in Eusebius of Cremona <note>A disciple of St. Jerome</note> that Saint Jerome, at the end of his life, received communion under only one kind. Furthermore, no one should doubt that this communion was participated in by those about to die in the primitive Church. When Saint James commanded that priests be brought to the sick and that anointing be administered for the remission of sins, he especially commanded the <term>synaxis</term> <note>synaxis: A Greek term for the gathering of the faithful for the Eucharist</note> because of its supreme virtues; for in it there is a singular and peculiar remission of sins, and it creates the deepest union between us and our head, Christ. Therefore, they administered it to those about to die because they would most certainly be purified and prepared to meet their Judge. 

However, it must not be believed at all that they would carry the sacrament of the blood of Christ under the form of wine out to the sick, both because of the risk of spilling and because a liquid substance sloshes and scatters in a vessel. Because of this, many full-scale dangers and inconveniences occur. But they provoke us with the pamphlets of those schismatics—that Hus <note>Jan Hus (c. 1369–1415), the Czech reformer burned at the stake for heresy</note> and Rokyczana <note>Jan Rokycana (c. 1396–1471), a primary theologian of the Hussite Utraquists</note> and similar scholars. These are truly the men who are placed before the judgment of the entire Church! To them, the Christian cause should yield—a cause which never yielded to all of Greece in this matter of its abuse. But I ask, were those schismatics never part of our rite? Perhaps it has been a hundred years since that plague began to be brewed. When did they defect? Namely, when private hatreds against their colleagues at the University of Prague <note>original: "Pragense studium," the Charles University in Prague, a center of Hussite thought</note> began, and when the greedy and the poor conceived of the plundering and robbing of churches. There at last, as if through a crime, lest they be called to punishment, they cast off the Lord. Finally, they never find the causes of their desertion in their own fault, but in the Lord's. Thus they themselves, after the crime or while failing in the crime, put on that "communion" as a cloak for their wickedness. 

After this, they say that we call them "heretics of the chalice," as if by being called erroneous by one name, it remains less of a duty for us to confer with them later—as if we were going to say, "Why should we convict again what has been convicted once?" Unless we turn away from such words, they pretend that they will have such weight against us in their reasoning that we will be entirely shared in their error or entirely despair of our own cause. Clearly, then, those men of the chalice are the most acute of all who have ever moved a contention against the Church! Clearly, the matter of communion is the most acute of all questions that have ever been discussed through the Church! But truly, are you not the worst of all mortals? For you agree with them in nothing regarding the faith: not the saints, nor purgatory, nor the sacrament of the altar, nor its use, nor temples, nor priests—not in any single thing at all, rebellion only excepted.

## THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

...whom you have tried to separate from all those things you have said so bitterly against us—from the graven image <note>original: "sculptili," referring to the use of statues or idols</note> and from the veneration of the sacrament of the altar, and from infamy not yet purged, and from killings—you dissect us indirectly no less than you have dissected us directly. As if you had never thought of or done such things, you distance yourself from them. In this way, then, since you finally come to our errors which you think are never to be overcome, we wish now to inquire into what may be in their cause. Certainly, those little books you mentioned have not come into my hands; if they had, I would not respond to them now, since I have currently undertaken another task regarding you. It would have been useful, however, to have taken some more urgent headings from there so that I might more easily respond to our affairs from an admitted starting point. 

But we will attempt the same by ourselves, lest we leave what we have undertaken in danger. Nor is there lacking even at this time a very learned man who responds learnedly and sharply to these schismatics, as well as to you, Waldensian, and to other Nicolaitans <note>A term often used polemically to describe those who rejected clerical celibacy</note> or Adamites <note>A radical sect that practiced nudism to symbolize a return to the innocence of Adam</note> and all your errors. I hope his labors will soon reach the public ear, so that you may not say we avoid your clever arguments or assert that you are a heretic only out of thin air. 

But I return to the purpose; therefore, as it pertains to the brief and chief point, I will note the present matter under a heading as it seems to me. It must therefore be clear to us from the start what exactly is being criticized regarding the whole matter: is it the whole faith concerning this sacrament, or only its use? Regarding the faith, indeed, I believe we are not accused by them concerning the chalice <note>The wine or cup</note>; which we will also explain by admission in the whole of the fifth book. But your known blasphemies regarding this are equally condemned by both of us. 

We are therefore attacked on the grounds of use alone, which they think we have usurped contrary to the rite of the Lord’s Supper and the Apostles. I have already sprinkled in the reason above why the Church wished to change this; now I will complete the remaining part of the speech attempted then. I would have hoped that if this most divine sacrament were administered in the most fitting way and for the total safety of the Church’s purpose, its piety would merit praise and not the disparagement of error. But since no progress is made from this conscience, but this communion under one species <note>original: "sub una specie." The practice where the laity receives only the bread</note> is continually blamed, it would be necessary that they be blamed as transgressors of the command of God and the Apostles—as if, unless we keep that same manner, we have dissolved the faith and the Gospel concerning this, and because of which the integrity of receiving the sacrament might perish for the Christian people. 

For where these things are safe, for what other reasons will they accuse whatever they accuse concerning us? Thus they hold no command, but a use kept from antiquity. Therefore, perhaps something was lacking for the Christian people from that use? If they show this, it will be because we do not receive the whole Christ <note>The doctrine of "concomitance," asserting Christ is fully present in both the bread and the wine</note>, just as he who went forth from the Virgin raised himself, glorified, into heaven. 

Therefore, when we do it in this way, we would be openly against the Gospel, which says: *Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you* <note>John 6:53</note>. Then the schismatics themselves would believe the worst regarding this sacrament. For if under one species we do not communicate in the body and blood of Christ, it would be because they say the whole Christ is not received—there would then be a separate bloodless body elsewhere, and separately blood poured out from its seat. I ask, in this condition—which is as unworthy as it is impossible—where will the soul be? It is not in bloodless flesh, nor in blood poured out outside the flesh; it would be nowhere. 

And where, I ask, would even the divinity be? For he did not institute separately a third kind of the sacrament over which he would have said, "this is my soul and my divinity." For these reasons, under either species, the whole Christ is received just as equally as under both together: the whole man and true God in one person, with two natures. Because of this, although we receive this most divine sacrament under the species of the solid element of bread, we certainly communicate rightly in the body and blood of Christ according to the will of the Gospel, just as he commanded. Wherefore, we will indeed have in us the promise of his life.

### ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST...

What, then, is lacking for a Christian such that he would run afoul of the Gospel's command? The Gospel says: *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.* <note>John 6:54</note> You say here that a Christian [receiving only the bread] has not shared in the blood, and thus you fall into your earlier difficulties. Indeed, prove from these words, or others like them in that passage, that Communion must occur with the species <note>The outward appearances of bread and wine</note> divided separately, unless you add from your own invention the word "separately." If you were to read it as: "He who eats my flesh *separately* and drinks my blood *separately* has eternal life," then I say: unless you read it thus, you can never compel us regarding **Communion under both kinds**.

Therefore, with the same conscience with which you add that word "separately," we—with much greater justice—strike it out and return to the Gospel its own words: *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.* We confess again that just as **Communion under both kinds** was observed in antiquity for its own reasons, so was it admitted under one kind because Christ the Savior later reduced the Communion of the chalice to that which is under one kind, saying: *He who eats me, even he shall live because of me,* <note>John 6:57</note> and again, *He who eats this bread shall live forever.* <note>John 6:58</note> Therefore, we eat **this bread** under the Roman Church and in obedience to her, certain that because of this obedience of faith—above all disobedience—we shall live forever.

At this point you ask me: "Why then did the Savior speak so expressly, saying, *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood*?" He did so in order that, according to our capacity, He might signify the fullness of refreshment, just as He also says: *My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.* <note>John 6:55</note> Therefore, because Christ suggests the name of the sacrament of His body and blood in both ways—sometimes with the species separated, and sometimes under one kind only—we, for the use of the Christian people, have chosen the latter: *He who eats me, even he shall live because of me,* and *He who eats this bread shall live forever.*

And grant this to our piety: if, for the sake of the majesty of this sacrament which must not be profaned, the Church conceived that practice to be the most secure of all. The blood of Christ was mistreated once, with the perpetual guilt of those who shed it, and it was not yet glorified while it still stood within the boundaries of mortality from which it could suffer such things. But the thought of a **glorified body**—which now overflows with most present divinity—being shed upon the ground from a single drop or even from the whole vessel, escapes the sense of so horrid a crime. If I knew by my own practice that such a thing would happen, I would never approach Communion. I would hope for more mercy in a divine visitation if I had willed a loss on my own part rather than a loss of the blood of Christ. I am certain, however, that my piety cannot suffer in hell, and I hope that I am more pious for such an abstinence than the man who, fearing such a thing, nevertheless attempts it with less reverence, thinking to himself that it is easier for the loss to occur on the part of the sacrament than on his own.

And indeed, it is not for us to merely suspect how many unworthy things happen among the people from this Communion of the chalice; they are laid out before our eyes. Here it is coughed up from the windpipe <note>original: "sinistra arteria," literally 'left artery,' used here to refer to the throat or airway</note>, there it drips, elsewhere it overflows. For all these reasons, let no invincible error be thrust upon the priests. For this rite of **Communion under one kind**—which is neither against the Gospel nor against the power of the sacrament, and thus in no way a defect in the salvation of the Christian people—the Church has received with much greater piety than those who retained the ancient rite in daily fear of violating the sacrament.

Furthermore, if Christ instituted and administered this sacrament under both kinds at that Last Supper, He did this as a priest among priests. Let the priests preserve this for themselves at the altar, forever and inviolate. But what the Savior was going to do for others, you might more easily guess than dare to affirm with truth. For He certainly bypassed the seventy disciples (many or all of whom were then in Jerusalem) and all the women devoted to Him who had ascended together to Jerusalem from Galilee...

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK FOUR,

->P. 5.<-

...just as <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing "Sicut" (Just as) from the previous page</note> she did not admit those incapable of the **priestly character** <note>The "sacramental character" is a theological concept referring to an indelible mark left on the soul by certain sacraments, such as ordination</note> to that place, so that anyone considering this in their mind—even if unwillingly—must confess that the Supper was a **mystery great and secret**. For this reason, we should not run toward it either nakedly or rashly as an example to be taken up. 

Turning from this to certain great killings which you say our people would rather commit than correct their error: we have already satisfied the requirements regarding how many errors were found. Those homicides you mention, I say, did not begin from our side, neither in the second nor the third instance. And it is a related symbol of the Church that she has never initiated slaughter over the faith; rather, she has always suffered the rage of foreign treachery. The **Arian heresy** <note>A 4th-century belief that denied the full divinity of Christ, which led to significant conflict in the early Church</note> most cruelly harassed the Church and Catholic Bishops. That **beast of Constantinople** <note>Likely referring to the Byzantine Emperors or the Eastern Church during periods of schism or iconoclasm</note> has always pursued the Latins with blood and exile. The Church has never mixed provinces with slaughter over such rancid contentions. 

But you now accuse her of being hungry for blood? If a hand is sought by an enemy, should she not even hide it in her bosom? <note>Suggesting the Church acts in self-defense or restraint</note> Digestion of such a crude stomach, O **Waldensian**! For from this alone you cannot feel as a Catholic, or are you now most unjust, since you hang in the power of those who still hold you grasped in their hands, yet leave you in deep peace? You would cast these homicides and the blood of innocents against them? I wish, Waldensian, that you were as innocent as you make yourself out to be; but now you are certainly such that if our men were clear-eyed and prudent enough to guard against the future fire from the first spark, you would have already given cause for your conspiracy to be restrained and forced to return to the common laws. Truly, we shall speak of this in its proper place. 

You have turned from this to **Simony** <note>The act of buying or selling sacred things or church offices, named after Simon Magus</note>; I say, whoever that man is, he shall bear his own judgment. I would only add this: that Simoniacal depravity in its author, **Simon**, stemmed from idolatry. He was a **Samaritan**, and by the superstition of his own race, he worshipped a creature in place of God. Therefore, his heresy was most deadly, having nothing in common with the Christian religion except that he held baptism. The Simoniacal stain of this current time does not fall into such profound impiety. It holds nothing of Simon’s example except that just as he wished to redeem baptism for a price, so these men, corrupted by greed, practice the exchange of sacred things, while in all other matters not wandering from Christian observance. Therefore, much of the weight of the crime is taken away from this Simony; it falls into the category not of idolatry and heresy, but of **greed**. 

Lastly, you bring up **concubinaries** <note>Clergy living with partners despite vows of celibacy</note> and **tax collectors**, and because it is prohibited for any of them to take part in the sacred rites. This was indeed the case, but it was later repealed, if I remember correctly, by the **Council of Constance** <note>A major church council (1414–1418) that settled the Western Schism and addressed clerical reform</note>. I say a completely just punishment was proposed for the sinner, so that he who does not strive to be good out of his own conscience might at least strive to do so out of a sense of shame before others. 

But for you, who act as if you were now just, you turn your face away from your own, you rebuke, you lash out over this. This example is full of danger and was rightly repealed for greater reasons. For now, beyond doubt, you see the **speck in another's eye** while ignoring the **beam in your own**; now with the **Pharisee** you say over the tax collector: *I give thanks to you, God, that I am not like even this tax collector.* <note>original: "gratias ago tibi deus quod non sum velut hic etiam publicanus"</note> Now you judge another's servant; now, as if you were without sin, you cast a stone at another. Lastly, you fall in every part into **evangelical censure**. 

I shall venerate a priest emerging from a **brothel** <note>original: "prostibulo"</note> at the altars of God, thinking to myself that nothing is more subtle than the illumination of God, and repeating to myself that **the spirit blows where it wills**. <note>original: "spiritus ubi vult spirat"; John 3:8</note> In this way, I do not fall into the judgments of the Gospel, and the priest nonetheless "stands or falls to his own master." <note>Romans 14:4</note> Because you dispute regarding manifest sins and think that because of this you may justly damn another, let us see then what constitutes a **manifest and convicted sin**.

### ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]
<meta>catchword: Concerning</meta>

In the second part of this entire discourse, we shall demonstrate our points. These, therefore, are the things regarding the crimes of priests that were discovered from that Waldensian <note>The Waldensians were a medieval Christian movement that advocated for poverty and lay preaching, eventually being declared heretical for rejecting the authority of the Catholic clergy</note>; and certainly, they are not as great in number or in wickedness as what the Waldensian himself has done. Yet, he considers these things with such bitterness that, because of them, he has cast off obedience. And what is more wicked, he thinks that the Church of God has ceased to exist entirely, on account of which they have written these and similar things: 

[
> "Indeed, regarding the evil workers whom we have discovered to be enemies of the Bride <note>A common theological metaphor for the Church is the "Bride of Christ"</note> and of His truth: out of fear of eternal damnation and out of obedience to Christ, how can we fear to be subject to or obey His Church in those matters where they think, speak, and act against the law? And again, we are surely separated from that Catholic faith so that we may freely carry out the prayers and Sacraments ordained by Christ. And again: For which reason our ancestors—I will not note the whole passage, which is very long, but only a few words—being exceedingly desirous of peace and concord, and beholding these evils which then arose from the men of the Church, began to disagree vehemently concerning these very things. And again: But we do not dare to go to the priests who are against us, because we cannot think of them as being in common with us, who would so perform the message of Almighty God through works contrary to the matters of the Christian faith and both the work and the ordination of scripture."]

We hear them running about everywhere so that, whatever pertains either to ecclesiastical ceremonies or the personal morals of each person, they charge that everything is done against the law of God. Yet, he has by no means said from the opposite side or directly which laws are being violated. But we have now strayed into these external matters; now, in this second part of our discourse, we shall closely discuss whether, on account of those crimes—whether they are judged by our judgment or theirs—they have rightly, as they think, defected from the faith and from obedience.

## NEITHER THE STATE OF THE CHURCH CAN BE CORRUPTED
## NOR OBEDIENCE TO THE ORTHODOX FAITH BE DISSOLVED ON ACCOUNT OF THE VICES OF THE LEADERS.

Those Waldensians have established the ultimate cause of their departure from the Catholic faith and obedience in the vices of the leaders of the Christian world. Looking into these vices more accurately and extensively than is right or good, they are going to say that the priesthood, the grace of the sacraments, and—to say it in one word—the entire Church among us has collapsed. 

Meeting this great error from the opposite side, I shall show first that the Church is holy, and then that the Holy Church cannot be corrupted by the personal sin of anyone. We shall apply ourselves especially to this matter because the Waldensian seems to doubt most greatly here. The Church, therefore, is holy because of the sprinkling of the blood of Christ. "For if," says the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews 9:13–14</note>, "the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer being sprinkled, sanctifies the defiled unto the cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" 

But also in that passage to the Ephesians: "Christ loved the Church," he says, "and gave Himself up for her, that He might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, that He might present the Church to Himself in glory, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and unblemished" <note>Ephesians 5:25–27</note>. And the Apostles' Creed says: "I believe in the Holy Catholic Church." Regarding this, Rufinus of Aquileia <note>A 4th-century monk and historian known for his commentary on the Apostles' Creed</note>, a priest, says: "The Holy Church in which there is no spot nor wrinkle of infidelity." And for this reason, the Church is called holy; not, as the Waldensian thinks, because there is nothing of sin to be admitted among its members, who are certainly surrounded by human infirmity. The first Church was holy without dispute, and yet the errors of men were present in her everywhere, which the Apostles frequently rebuke through their Epistles.

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

With these words, Saint John also consoled the believers, saying: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous" <note>original: "aduocatum habemus apud Patrem ihsuhm Christum iustum" — a citation of 1 John 2:1</note>. And He Himself is the propitiation <term>propitiation|An act of atonement or a way to regain favor; here, Christ’s sacrifice which reconciles the sinner with God</term> for our sins. But even in the weakness of her members, that holy Church is conscious of her own state. For this reason, she prays using the words of the Savior: "Forgive us our debts. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil" <note>original: "Dimitte nobis debita nostra... libera nos a malo" — the Lord's Prayer</note>. And as a remedy for her children who labor under various vices, she received the Sacrament of penance and remission; she received the power of binding and loosing. Since, therefore, Christ joined that holy Church to Himself—a Church not to be defiled by the personal vice of any individual—these are the words of the Bridegroom: "What God has joined, let no man separate" <note>Matthew 19:6</note>. For this is a "great Sacrament in Christ and in the Church" <note>Ephesians 5:32</note>, except in the case of fornication.

Now, "fornication"—as we have said in another place when discussing the Prostitute of the Apocalypse <note>The "Whore of Babylon" from the Book of Revelation, often interpreted by medieval commentators as a symbol of spiritual corruption or heresy</note>—is understood only as idolatry, perfidy, and heresy. Therefore, as long as the Church is free from these, she is not repudiated by Christ. Yet the Waldensian <note>Likely referring to Peter Waldo or the movement generally</note> has fabricated such a charge against the Church regarding carved images and Simony <term>Simony|The sin of buying or selling sacred things, such as church offices or sacraments</term>. But we have refuted this false calumny in our previous external arguments.

Even if the Church were to be repudiated by Christ on account of some admitted idolatry or heresy—though we have shown by many points that the Waldensian's view is not the Church's view—the Waldensian would still have no legal right to take the "repudiated" Church for himself. This is because of that same impiety, and because the Savior said again: "He who marries a divorced woman commits adultery" <note>Matthew 5:32</note>.

But why do I mention these things? For the Church remains for eternity, which Christ, that wise Architect, is said to have built upon a rock—that is, upon Christ Himself—on account of her unfailing faith. Nevertheless, rivers, winds, and storms come against her, sometimes from an external enemy and sometimes from domestic vice, but she always triumphs in herself. If she were to fall, as the Waldensian suspects, it would mean she was not holy and did not have a wise Architect—one who, for instance, founded her upon the sand. Such an insult would reach even to the heavenly promises and God Most High!

Finally, we are said to have received a New Testament from God. Now, even according to natural law, testaments and last wills are considered irrevocable. How much more so, then, is the testament of the Gospel? As the Apostle wrote to the Hebrews: "God, wanting to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immobility of His counsel, interposed an oath, so that through two immutable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have a very strong consolation—we who have fled to hold fast to the hope set before us" <note>Hebrews 6:17-18</note>.

Here, the Waldensian will suggest to me: "But the Law of Moses was also called a 'testament,' and its will was not preserved." I do not know if he is so foolish as not to understand this, but if he truly does not know, let him understand that the Old Testament was temporary. It was merely a guardian of childhood <note>A reference to the "pedagogue" or "tutor" in Galatians 3:24</note> until the heir grew into perfection and was admitted into the true testament of the Eternal Gospel, which was to be sealed by the blood of Christ Jesus, the true mediator between God and men.

To this, those epistles of Saint Paul to the Romans, to the Galatians, and to the Hebrews are my witnesses with all their arguments. Here the Apostle finally discusses how, "the priesthood being translated, the law is also translated" <note>Hebrews 7:12; "translated" here means transferred or changed</note>. If, therefore, the priesthood was transferred from the tribe of Levi into Christ—a priesthood that is eternal according to the order of Melchizedek <term>Melchizedek|An Old Testament priest-king who prefigured Christ; unlike the Levites, his priesthood was seen as eternal and superior</term>—and if the priesthood of the Church descends from this priest, Christ, through substitution into the world, then if this is taken from us, both the law and the church...

He contrasts the temporary nature of the Mosaic Law with the irrevocable New Testament priesthood of Christ.</summary>
