# ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

Otherwise, everything we have just established would be undone. But the Waldensians <note>The Waldensians were a medieval Christian movement that practiced voluntary poverty and criticized the perceived corruption of the Catholic clergy, eventually being declared heretical by the Church.</note> shall not succeed to such a great inheritance of the Church and the priesthood, both for other reasons I touched upon above, and because they did not receive this through a continuous succession of ancestors, which began once and for all in Christ the Head. As the experience of facts refutes them—and they themselves do not deny it—they came forth from themselves and first appeared in our own century <note>original: "noſtro primū ſeculo" — the author argues the Waldensians are a "new" innovation without ancient roots</note> without any beginnings in the Church. The next step is for them to say they dropped down from heaven; we shall shake out these trifles more thoroughly in their proper place.

Therefore, I believe it is established by these facts that the Church is holy, "without spot or wrinkle" <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:27, describing the ideal purity of the Church</note>, and because she is holy, she is therefore perpetual. Furthermore, because she is perpetual, she cannot be made reckless by the ignorance of her members or be hindered in her course. It would have been enough to have said this much for our business, but since our Waldensian friend is held obsessed by the arts of the Malignant One <note>A common term for the Devil</note>, and can be dragged rather than led, we have taken up for separate discussion that last part of what we have said—namely, that the sins of the Church’s members do not abolish the Church—which the Waldensian most bitterly refuses to admit.

I see one primary cause why, whether willing or unwilling, he casts himself and others into this opinion—a cause by which he can seem just to many in condemning our people. He reads, especially in the Prophets, that the priests of the Old Law were rebuked for certain sins which he thinks similarly fall upon our people, either in fact or at least by a suspicion of the opinion he has formed about them. Such as that passage:
> Where is my fear, says the Lord of hosts to you, O priests, who despise my name? And you said, "In what have we despised your name?" You offer polluted bread upon my altar, and you say, "In what have we polluted you?" Who is there among you who will shut the doors and kindle my altar for nothing? <note>original: "vbi eſt timor meus dicit dn̄s... panem pollutū" — a citation of Malachi 1:6–10</note>

When he reads such things, he thinks our people are rebuked either in deed or in appearance (because the words seem to fit well), and from that, he wants our people to be thought of as equally rebuked by all the other things said against the Mosaic priesthood <term>Mosaic priesthood|The order of priests established under the Law of Moses in the Old Testament</term>. Therefore, when he sees the rejection of the Old Law and its sacrifice so often threatened in the Scriptures, he tries to force the cessation of the anointing and of our priesthood based on a common and equal footing. Such as:
> I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not receive a gift from your hand. I will send poverty upon you, and I will curse your blessings. <note>original: "Non eſt mihi voluntas in vobis... maledicā benedictionibus veſtris" — Malachi 1:10 and 2:2</note>

But in this matter, the Waldensian plays with others and is himself played with, both quite blindly and most unjustly. For the Old Law and priesthood were destined to cease, but the New Law and its priestly anointing <term>anointing|The sacramental ritual (ordination) that confers the authority of the priesthood</term> were meant to endure forever according to the predictions of all the Prophets. Therefore, if the Waldensian had a conscience that did not even wish to err, he could have distinguished between the two. The Prophets do not allow anyone to be deceived in this, even in this very passage. For when Malachi had said,
> I have no pleasure in you,

he immediately added:
> For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name. <note>original: "Ab ortu em̄ ſolis vſq; ad occaſum... oblatio munda" — Malachi 1:11. Traditionally interpreted by Catholic theologians as a prophecy of the Mass</note>

It is most clearly testified that both things were said of different priests.
> I have no pleasure in you,

And
> from the rising of the sun even to its setting, a pure offering is offered to me.

Thus, the former must have been said of the Jewish priesthood, and the latter of the Church’s priesthood which succeeded that old one. Otherwise, the Waldensians must transfer that first part to us and this latter part to themselves. Therefore, because of the aforementioned reasons of their own infidelity, their rejection of the Church, and the fact that they proceeded without legitimate beginnings—and they certainly have not raised themselves up from the rising to the setting of the sun, but rather mutter their errors in a furtive whisper among neighbors rather than preaching them—for all these reasons they are rightly rejected. Finally, they have dissolved the holy and perpetual Church—I mean that offering of the Apostles and of all holiness which, through the institutions of the Apostles, is spread through the churches in the whole world...

# WALDENSES BOOK FOUR

...this pure offering of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, has been poured out as an atonement for our sins from that time until our own day. He offered and fulfilled it, something which surely no other creature could do. For he himself is with us until the end of the age. This same Christ, who is our sacrifice, spoke through the prophet Jeremiah: *If these laws ever cease to exist before me, says the Lord, then the descendants of Israel shall also cease to be a nation before me for all time.* <note>original: "Si defecerint leges iste corā me... tunc & semen Israel deficiet" — quoting Jeremiah 31:36 to argue for the Church’s permanence</note> 

But the Prophet speaks, as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> testifies in the eighth chapter of the Letter to the Hebrews, concerning the law of the Gospel. "The people of Israel," the Lord says, "regardless of all they have done, I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more." Do you hear this, Waldensian? This applies despite all the sins that the children of Israel might commit. Understand that this refers not to those born according to the flesh, but to those of the promises made to Abraham—as the Apostle writes to the Galatians—and to the faith of his son. For the Lord will not cast off David. 

He said something similar through Zechariah: *In that day, the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem; even the one who stumbles among them on that day shall be like David, and the house of David shall be like God, like the angel of the Lord in his sight.* <note>Reference to Zechariah 12:8</note> What does it mean that God protects those "inhabitants of Jerusalem"? It refers to the Church. For the inhabitants of the earthly Jerusalem were not protected, but rather excluded, on that day of which the Prophet spoke. 

Why is it said that the inhabitants of the Church will be protected just like David? It is because David, even in his adultery, even in the murder of the righteous husband <note>Uriah the Hittite</note>, and even when he took a forbidden census of the people of Israel, always obtained God's mercy and the forgiveness of his sins so that God would not cast him aside. Yet Saul, as King, was held guilty of an eternal offense and was utterly rejected for a single unauthorized sacrifice and the matter of Amalek. <note>The author contrasts David’s enduring favor with Saul’s total rejection (1 Samuel 13 and 15) to show that God preserves the Church despite its flaws.</note>

In this way, God protects His Church in the midst of our ignorance, just as He protected King David. The Church stands forever in the sight of God, like the Angel of the Lord. But that Waldensian, contrary to the meaning of Scripture and of God, rejects and cuts off the Church in the same way that Saul was rejected and his house destroyed. I shall subsequently demonstrate how greatly the Waldensian errs in this, using many examples as they come to mind. In a certain passage of that first confession of theirs, after the Waldensian had set out a specific list of requirements for what priests ought to be, he added:

<insert>
[Whatever cleric is raised to the priesthood by such an ordination, we confess that such an ordination is a sacrament.]
</insert>

These words raise a suspicion in the reader: does he believe that ecclesiastical power and the sacred anointing depend upon the personal merit of the individual? If he thinks this, then we could never truly judge anyone's merits, whether our own or those of others. Even Saint Paul, a "chosen vessel," was uncertain about himself, saying: *I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified.* <note>1 Corinthians 4:4</note> Therefore, the entire Christian faith would waver. For if a man were a priest only as long as he remained in a state of grace, he would cease to be a priest the moment he yielded to temptation. Since he cannot know when he might deserve to be received back into God's grace, he would never know if he were a priest or not. Thus, no one would dare to handle divine matters according to his conscience and authority unless he were clearly and continuously moved by God.

In this way, all Christian works—Baptism, the forgiveness of sins, the Sacrifice of the Altar, the sanctity of marriage and children—indeed, everything that depends on the priesthood, would be considered uncertain and profane by us. This would not be a good provision for the salvation of the faithful by Christ, our author. Moreover, the efficacy of His Passion and Redemption would fluctuate most unworthily based on the merit of another person. Ecclesiastical power, therefore, does not depend on the merits of priests, concerning which they said in another place:

<insert>
[We cannot think of them collectively as fulfilling the message of Almighty God when their works are contrary to the matters of the Christian faith and the decree and ordination of Scripture.]
</insert>

In this, ecclesiastical power does not depend on that <note>The author is refuting the idea that a priest's sinful life nullifies his official power</note>. For if a holy life is added to that most holy power, it adds as much innocence as...

# ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

...thence authority is derived: *Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds so doing; Amen I say to you, he will set him over all his goods.* <note>Quoting Matthew 24:46-47 to illustrate the ideal faithful steward of the Church.</note> But where this occurs less often—and certain unworthy men, not having weighed their own strength but rashly and prematurely, thrust themselves into exercising such great power—they do so at great peril to themselves by usurping the **keys** <term>keys: The "Power of the Keys" refers to the spiritual authority to forgive sins and govern the Church, traditionally held to be granted by Christ to St. Peter.</term> and the administration of the Church with no submission. For it is known that the power and efficacy of the sacraments are poured into the Church by the merit of Christ alone, and by no other mortal, regardless of the merit or demerit of the ministers.

For it was Christ who fixed death to his cross and gave life, from which flowed the power of our salvation. No one shall block its perennial course, just as it is with the sowing of seeds: whether they are scattered by a pure or an impure hand, by a guilty or an innocent one, they achieve no less of the power of nature from the sun and the rain.

We can also bring forth plenty of examples of this from the Scriptures. Of old, the Prophets openly rebuked Kings and Priests themselves for great crimes, yet neither they nor any who believed the prophecy ever believed that the state of the kingdom or the holiness of the **Synagogue** <note>In this context, "Synagogue" refers to the religious assembly and authority of the Old Covenant/Jewish people, which the author uses as a precursor to the Christian Church.</note> was thereby dissolved. Christ himself blamed the priests of the Mosaic law in his own time for their greed, ambition, and for following the traditions of men rather than of God. They commanded tithes even of mint and rue, and they preached that it was better to give a gift to the Temple than to help the poverty of one’s parents. They bought the highest priesthoods with bribes, and they were frequent in sacrileges and blasphemies against Christ. They were the ones who consulted on and authored his death, and to whom Christ said in the very first year of his preaching: *Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up.* At another time he said: *You seek to kill me.*

Nevertheless, Christ granted an acknowledgment of the power of the sacred rites of the Synagogue even to those so criminal, when he said to those ten lepers: *Go, show yourselves to the priests.* <note>Luke 17:14; Christ directs them to the established religious authorities despite his criticisms of those men.</note> And in another place: *The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on the chair of Moses; therefore, observe and do all things whatsoever they tell you, but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do.* <note>Matthew 23:2-3</note>

What does "observe and do whatsoever they tell you" mean, and how does it agree with "do not do according to their works"? It means nothing other than that the authority of the Synagogue—which remained holy from the sprinkling of the **tabernacle** <note>Refers to the original consecration of the Jewish place of worship</note>—was to be followed in the authority they wielded, but their own way of life was not to be followed. It is in this sense that the Savior spoke in another place: *If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it from you; and if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out.* The Savior does not want us to imitate the sin of the one in whom public power is observed.

But you say: "That was then, in that shadow, and the imperfection of the Synagogue; but now a holier law demands holier leaders." I say the same: it does indeed demand them. But when evil men, just like good men, thrust themselves into the care of the Church’s governance, the public power must—for the reasons we stated above—be distinguished from the private condition of each man, and the law ought not to be dissolved because of them.

You have the greatest examples of this from the Gospel. That servant who hid the talent entrusted to him in the earth was certainly evil, for which reason he was condemned; but was he therefore *not* a servant? Did the goods of that man traveling abroad (who is Christ) perish because of it? For in what other "goods" would the rest of the faithful servants have worked? Consider the other "evil servant" whom the Lord set over his household. Although he dispensed his duties poorly, saying, "My Lord is delayed in coming," and began to beat his fellow servants and eat and drink with drunkards—despite such morals, he was still the steward of the Lord's household. The household did not perish; rather, he alone is separated from it and takes his portion with the hypocrites, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Judas was a thief, of whom the Lord said from the very beginning: *And one of you is a devil.* Nevertheless, he received a place and power from Christ among the apostles. And as they were going...

The previous page established that the efficacy of the sacraments depends on Christ’s merit rather than the personal holiness of the priest; here, the author reinforces this by citing biblical figures like Judas and Caiaphas, as well as Stoic philosophy, to argue that the "office" remains sacred even when held by a "wicked" individual.</meta>

-># THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR<-

“Preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received, freely give.” <note>original: "p̄dicāte dicētes quia appropinquabit regnū celorū... gratis accepistis gratis date"; quoting Matthew 10:7-8.</note> His blessing is upon the house he enters, and likewise, a curse is upon the house from which he is barred. Just as the blessing of that disciple whom Jesus loved was effective, so during that same time, the same blessing was present in the one giving a drink to Judas as was in one of the great apostles. For among such great things, there was no lack of merit in Judas when he dispensed the Gospel or performed miracles, specifically because of the legitimate authority transferred into him by Christ—just as it was to the chosen apostles—which he truly received freely above all others. Neither was the administration of the Gospel performed through him weakened, nor did his character excuse anyone from obeying his message. 

Caiaphas—of whom Judas now reminds me in this context—was a murderer in spirit, presiding over the council when the death of the Lord was being discussed. And yet, out of all that wicked council, he alone was inspired because he was the **High Priest** <term>High Priest: The supreme religious leader of the Jewish people; the author argues that the office itself carried prophetic power regardless of the man's personal sin.</term> of that year. He said: “It is expedient for you that one man should die, and that the whole nation should not perish.” <note>original: "Expedit vobis vt vnus moriaꝭ homo, & non tota gens pereat"; quoting John 11:50.</note> Thus, the priestly holiness of even the Synagogue was held in such dignity by the Holy Spirit that a wicked man might prophesy through it. In all these things—whether in the distribution of grace, the preaching of the Word, or the anointing of the priesthood—the office is one thing and the evil merit of the individual is another. The office does not fall from its authority because of the person's malice.

I invite the **Waldensian** <note>The Waldensians (Valdenses) were a medieval movement that often argued that "unworthy" or sinful priests lost their spiritual authority.</note> to consider these examples. From these, let him return to the Apostolic Church and to our priestly anointing, which he has long believed to be overturned by the vices of our men. Let him return, I say, and let him now set aside those laws by which he judges the priestly anointing to be void. He defends his error with no scriptural example or witness. Let him therefore finally follow and understand that our priesthood stands unshaken, derived from Christ as its author. Why should the malice of another man—for which he himself will not have to answer—frighten him away? He should choose to be under even evil priests rather than under none at all, just as he is compelled at times to be subject to tyrannical princes. Should he shake off a cruel master who currently presides by right and public consent? Should he dissolve his obedience? He will see that, to his own great loss and infamy, he has privately destroyed his own master. But this matter of the Church is the work of God, not of men; I say not of men, yet you dissolve the laws and the republic of God. 

Samuel had sons who turned aside after avarice, accepted bribes, and perverted judgment. Therefore, all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah and said to him: “Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways; appoint for us a King to judge us.” <note>referencing 1 Samuel 8:3-5.</note> You hear of this defection, and that they meditated on it not rashly, but because of the crimes of Samuel’s sons. And yet, the Lord was indignant and said to Samuel: “For they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.” <note>1 Samuel 8:7.</note> The Waldensian brings this very same case against the Church, and he falls headlong into those great examples by which God is most provoked. Let him spare, therefore—let him finally spare his own salvation, he who does not spare us. 

Let the Waldensian finally consider that he must carry ecclesiastical discipline with him. Imagine a man wandering in the deepest wilderness, in an unknown and hostile region without hope of safety. If a guide for the journey were unexpectedly offered there—whom he might otherwise mark as being of bad character—he would surely not dwell on the guide's vices, since that guide led him in good faith out of present desperation. Rather, he would judge in his own conscience that he owes the highest gratitude to the leader for the benefit received. 

However, so that the Waldensian might better take this matter to heart, that Stoic, **Epictetus**, shall help me. In the work titled the **Enchiridion** <term>Enchiridion: Ancient Greek for "Manual" or "Handy Book"; a famous work of Stoic philosophy emphasizing what is within our control.</term>, he says that every thing has two handles, by either of which a man may take hold of it: one leading to a good estimation, the other to a bad one. For example: you have a brother. He is greedy, or he is wasteful—there is reason for him to be rightly displeasing. You think you cannot bear him. In "taking up" your brother, leave that handle alone; hold him by the other handle—that he is your brother, he is your own blood, and you have parents in common. Sweetly, from the first...

### CONCERNING THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

...you have grown for years. In that place, you will serve your brother well. In this way, I would turn that Waldensian moral saying back on them. Similarly regarding priests—to speak now only of those who are bad—there are, as it were, **two handles**. <note>The author uses the metaphor of "two handles" (Latin: *ansae*) to describe how one might "grasp" or perceive a priest: either by his personal sins or by his holy office.</note> From the handle on which their vices hang, the priests appear heavy and burdensome; the Waldensian cannot hold onto them and so casts them aside. Let him, therefore, take them up by the other handle: because they are priests; because they handle the **keys of the Church**; <term>Keys of the Church: The authority given to the apostles to "bind and loose" (forgive or retain) sins, traditionally associated with the sacrament of Penance.</term> and because with them is placed that power of binding and loosing which we find nowhere else but in the Church.

Just as **Saint Augustine** writes in his book *On True and False Penance*: "Let the penitent labor to be in the Church and strive for the unity of the Church. For unless the unity of the Church brings aid—unless it completes by its own help what is lacking in the sinner—the soul of the dead shall not be snatched from the hands of the enemy." From this handle—if indeed the Waldensian has a conscience, and if he does not deny the authority of the Scriptures like some **heathen** <note>original: "ethnicus"; used here to mean someone outside the faith or a pagan.</note>—he would easily be able to accept the priesthood. Indeed, he would not even be able to cast it aside.

But as I frequently repeat, I fear that common stubbornness of heretics, who, exalting themselves by mere contention rather than any judgment of the truth, consider themselves to be the true ones if they simply refuse to hear, value, or admit others. I fear the Waldensian is held back by this same vice, preventing him from following better things. It makes me suspicious because he blames our practices with naked words alone, rather than reasons. He does nothing but make noise with words, such as: <insert>“Whoever is a cleric elevated to the priesthood by such an ordination, we profess that such an ordination is the sacrament.”</insert> Therefore, by what scriptural example or by what reason does he profess that this ordination alone, as they define it, is the sacrament? 

If I were to write against them in this way—following only my own sense and saying whatever I pleased, just as they are accustomed to say—I would tell them I have many reasons but cannot explain them all right now for lack of time. I would become a laughingstock to them. Therefore, as long as they receive whatever they believe from their own whims and feelings, it is not those who are scandalized by them who fall, but the Scripture and the Saints who will damn them along with their similar accomplices.

The early Church had those princes, the Apostles; it had their holy successors, pure in faith, enlightened with wisdom, and many of them martyrs. Yet even those times found their own heretics: rebellious, disobedient men, corrupt in mind and sense. What complaint did those heretics have against the leaders of the Church, through which they fell away from Catholic discipline? Today, the **Waldensians** <term>Waldensians: A movement originating in the 12th century that emphasized poverty and lay preaching, often criticizing the wealth and corruption of the institutional Church.</term> pretend it is the bad life of the priests. But does that same life not offend the rest of the Christian world as well? Are they the only ones who judge that the Church has fallen so far that they are right to cast it out along with its members? 

What, then, did the ancient teachers deserve—the pastors of the Church from the time of the Apostles—whom they despise as if they had not felt the rule of faith just as much as any Christian? Therefore, because they do not observe the innocence of the ancients any more than they observe the vices of those today, I do not know what other cause remains for them, except that Gospel saying: “To what then shall I compare the men of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, saying: ‘We piped to you and you did not dance; we wailed and you did not weep.’ For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <note>Quoting the Parable of the Children in the Marketplace from Matthew 11 or Luke 7.</note>

This is fulfilled again today in the Waldensian: he ignores the ancient fathers and openly accuses those who came later. He presents us with censors like **Saint Bernard**, **Francis**, **Petrarch**, and certain others, as if they did not feel the same way! Namely, that they possess riches. These are the words of **Saint Jerome**, <note>original: "vba sũt diui Hiero"; referring to Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> though some may rage against this witness: [they seek riches] under a wealthy devil which they did not have under a poor Christ. ### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

Books are full of those who rebuke the vices of Catholics of every status. Have all those who were displeased by such vices defected from the faith following the example of the Waldensians? The Waldensian stumbles quite perversely in reading our books; he skips over all the better parts. For look: **Saint Bernard** <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a hugely influential Cistercian monk and mystic whom many reformers admired for his criticisms of Church corruption.</note> pleases them now and holds the highest authority among them in those passages where he rebukes priests and exhorts them to a life of innocence.

But where Bernard discusses Christian ceremonies, the sacraments, obedience, the **veneration of the saints**, <term>Veneration of the saints: The practice of honoring holy people and asking for their intercession, which the Waldensians rejected.</term> the purification of souls [Purgatory], the observance of the Church, and priestly unction—it is in these matters that the Waldensian should have followed him. Instead, he suppresses Bernard’s words as if he had found nothing of our faith in them. Conversely, he follows him only in those parts where it seems he might have erred on our side. In this, the Waldensian invites a voluntary damnation upon himself; for if he follows the one who corrects vices, let him also follow Bernard in being obedient to the Church, in which Bernard, living innocently, earned heaven.

Therefore, on that day [of Judgment], the "regeneration" of the Waldensian will be scrutinized—that rebirth through which no one can be saved unless they are born again. This he did not receive in the communion and faith of the saints, but through his own departure, from some **Cerdo**. <note>original: "Cerdone"; likely a reference to Cerdo, a 2nd-century Gnostic heretic, used here as a derogatory label for the founder of a sect.</note> The veneration of the saints will be demanded; of this, he had none. Obedience to the Church will be demanded—that is, the communion and faith of the saints; this, he lost. It will be asked whether Bernard and **Petrarch**, <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet who also wrote scathingly about the corruption of the papal court at Avignon, yet remained within the Church.</note> while they were alive, ever broke their apostolic obedience. If they endured new impieties unknown to the apostolic faith, he will not provide a single jot of proof. It will be asked by which Catholic writers he eventually adopted all those errors; there will be none. Here his tricks will be revealed; here the Waldensian will gape and fall silent. He will scarcely be able to say these final words:

> "Ah Lord, we have called your name upon us; your name stands frequently in our books."

"I say to you," the angry Judge will speak, "even if you prophesied in my name, 
> if you cast out demons, if you performed miracles, nevertheless I do not know you. Depart from me, you cursed ones, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels." <note>A paraphrase of Matthew 7:22-23 and 25:41.</note>

In such great consternation, the Waldensian has forgotten to say one thing: that because of **notorious sins**, <term>Notorious sins: In canon law, "notorious" refers to crimes so public and manifest that they cannot be concealed or legally denied.</term> he thought he could rightly despise our priesthood. This is a favorable accusation and one that could easily win the judgment of the common people. Truly he errs; but how can we explain this in vain to one who is divided and now takes his part with the hypocrites? I wish, however, to explain this same thing to the Christian people, lest they err in the same way he does. 

Therefore, anyone else who is of that opinion—thinking that what he sees, hears, or touches is "notorious" and manifest, and wishing to judge the author of the deed based on that—is deceived and does not rightly understand the word "notorious." For it often happens that, based on a tiny suspicion arising from the senses, one is utterly deceived in judging another's deed. One reads that **Anchorites** <term>Anchorites: Religious recluses who lived in solitary cells to devote themselves to prayer.</term> turned aside to visit harlots. No one seeing this would not have thought they went there out of lust. But they were actually warning the sinful woman to seek a better life; and so they spent the night in wakeful prayer for the salvation of their neighbor. They departed chaste, just as they had entered most chaste. 

**Saint Ambrose**, the Bishop of Milan, at the time he was being requested for the bishop's office, admitted women of suspect reputation into his house in the sight of the city. He did this not out of desire, but because he was striving to offend the minds of the citizens under that appearance, so that he would not be asked to take the bishopric, of which he considered himself unworthy. But even our senses, in which we trust so much and by which we judge, often play tricks on us in manifest things, and one sense corrects another. It is a well-known thing from those deceptive arts [illusions] how crudely they may mock us. 

Therefore, a thing is by no means "notorious" simply because we have perceived it. Even if the senses are not deceived, what we think was done will by no means be manifest; for we err no less regarding the moment than we do regarding the passage of time, because we are continually different people. Just as in a clock, there is not only one wheel which...

...distinguishes the time; thus there is not a single will in man that flows through his whole life. How quickly one moment falls away after another; just as suddenly, desire succeeds desire there. Christ the Savior taught this when his disciples warned him to beware of the Jews who were laying snares for him. He said to them: **"Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."** <note>original: "Nōne duodecim sunt hore diei..." (John 11:9-10). The author uses this to show that a person's moral state can change over time; a sinner yesterday may be in the "light" today.</note> For this reason, I do not judge someone for a deed done yesterday, for which the penitent was recently absolved. Should I accuse him of a debt whose promissory note God has already blotted out?

Consider the great city of **Nineveh**. If one had seen it in its fornications and all its impiety, and had heard what the Prophet **Jonah** was commanded regarding its destruction, who would not have condemned it—both by their own judgment and by the Prophet's oracle? Yet, without you knowing it, the city received a remission of its damnation. The crime, which you thought was <term>Notorious</term> <note>A "notorious" crime in canon law is one so public and evident that it requires no further proof or trial.</note> because of so many signs, completely vanishes from your sight through a sudden indulgence [pardon]. 

Furthermore, if you believe your own senses are certain and you label someone with a "notorious" crime and are not mistaken, how much more is the knowledge of God not mistaken? Therefore, will God judge as suddenly from his knowledge of the first sin as you do from your senses? No. You will find in the Sacred Scriptures, if you weigh them carefully, how evident the proofs are. Just as a judge on a tribunal does not usually pass sentence except upon a convicted and contested crime, so too has God observed the same form of justice.

God did not immediately strike **Cain**, the murderer of his brother, as soon as the voice of his brother’s blood cried out from the earth. Instead, he summoned the murderer to be present. He confronted him with the crime; a defense was required. Only when Cain failed here was he first condemned for his wickedness. 

The descendants of **Noah** built a tower in their pride. God knew the defiance of these men before they even measured the foundations or dug—he knew they were impious before they laid a single stone, and that they deserved punishment. Yet, God did not cast them down from heaven based solely on his foreknowledge. Instead, he inspected the crime in person, and only after the impiety was witnessed did he punish it. It is worthwhile to hear how the Scripture describes this deliberate divine sentence: **"But the Lord came down to see the city and the tower which the sons of Adam were building. And he said, 'Behold, they are one people and they have all one language... Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech.'"** <note>Genesis 11:5-7.</note>

Finally, regarding the sin of the **Sodomites**, Scripture witnesses the same delay in the divine sentence. God said, **"The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is multiplied, and their sin is become exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry that has come to me."** <note>Genesis 18:20-21.</note> Since the Divinity decrees damnation so thoughtfully, shall we say that God was ignorant until he was present through his angels? Rather, Scripture shows that God exercised his judgments so vigilantly for our instruction. This is so that we—who judge not according to such a form but from a precipitous and blind sense—might be rendered inexcusable before God and our neighbor for our rashness. 

**Judas Iscariot** was not convicted in a similar manner, nor was his theft "notorious"; therefore, Christ Jesus justly allowed him to remain in his order. If you had known Judas’s crime as clearly as Christ did, how quickly you would have cast him out from the number of the Apostles by your own judgment—or rather, by what an injustice against the sentence of equity and law! You see your rashness caught in the act of judging; you see that you err; you see that a "manifest" crime does not depend on just anyone’s private sense. Even human laws do not wish for another's reputation to collapse so rashly. Surely, if you saw a garment taken by someone, would you now publicly say that such a person is a thief? Proof is demanded. You would certainly sweat to prove a theft based only on your own perception if the matter is not legally established by others...

### THAT THE WALDENSIAN FAITH IS NOT AN INSPIRATION;
### that it relies neither on a sect from God nor any other legitimate cause, but on seduction and lies alone.

We have rendered an account of the things which the Waldensians have put forward in condemning the Church and our priesthood; we have found that the Church has by no means ceased to exist on our part, as they supposed. Instead, we have found from multiple scriptures and examples that the Priesthood continues today among us inviolate, with the same anointing and power with which it was received from Christ and the apostles. Therefore, someone might think the argument is now complete. And it would have been complete; but because the adversary also has things to say, it will be necessary not only to assert our own rights but also to call the accuser's case into examination. For the Christian state is not so free and open that two parties who do not hold the same views can both stand purely and equally. He has done only half the work who shows his own views to be true, when he ought also to show how the faction of the adversary cannot be true. And this is now the third part of our entire treatise, which we have undertaken to assert regarding the Church and the priesthood. The entire "nerve" <note>The "nerve" or "sinew" (nervus) refers to the central strength or core of their argument.</note> of this Waldensian, from which he thinks himself true, is that he desires to be believed to be divinely inspired; so that if this is once believed, those other things must necessarily be believed: that his faith is true, his church is true, and his priesthood is true. Here, therefore, we turn the argument back upon him: that he is *not* inspired. First, because all the notable changes that are to happen to the Church regarding faith are shown beforehand by the predictions of the prophets; and when they go out into the world at the decreed time, they are illustrated by manifest and divinely performed miracles and take on significant beginnings, so that a person is inexcusable who does not follow such a divine work. None of these things happened concerning this Waldensian. Secondly, because in building up his own affairs in various places, he says and does different things at different times, and shows himself to be a liar. Divine inspiration does not fit with such a thing, since the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, of whom Wisdom said: **"For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw itself from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be rebuked when iniquity comes. For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent and will not acquit a speaker of evil from his lips."** <note>original: "spiritus enim sanctus... non liberabit maledictum a labijs suis" (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4-6).</note> Until we can note all these things one by one from their own present words by confession, we will first deposit this in the conscience of the reader.

# WALDENSIANS BOOK FOUR

...it is not for us to know the times and moments which the Father has placed in his own power <note>A reference to Acts 1:7, where Jesus tells the apostles that the timing of the restoration of the kingdom belongs to God alone.</note>. Therefore, if this "renewal" is now fulfilled, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> defines that time of the **renewal of the church** in his letter to the Romans as that moment when the Jews—having been deluded by the final error of the **Antichrist**—shall be converted to Christ with a great ardor of faith. The surviving Gentiles will follow their conversion; the Christians of that time, emulating the Jews' fervor of faith, will likewise rouse that sluggish and cold spirit by which they have wandered until now, returning to the primitive fervor of the church. Therefore, Waldensian, you must either assign multiple renewals based on the prophecies, or you must leave that single one of the Apostle to be fulfilled at another time. Certainly, the Jew is not yet converted to Christ; he has not yet set aside his expectation of his own Messiah. Because of these things, that **renewal of the church** has certainly not yet happened but is in the future. Finally, that renewal will change nothing regarding ecclesiastical and apostolic institutions—which is exactly what you are doing—just as those **seven thousand men in Israel** <note>1 Kings 19:18. God tells Elijah that 7,000 in Israel have not bowed the knee to the idol Baal.</note>, even though their tribesmen went after the calves of **Jeroboam** <note>Jeroboam I, King of Israel, who set up golden calves at Dan and Bethel to prevent his people from worshiping in Jerusalem.</note>, and although the integrity of the Law and the **Synagogue** was preserved through them in **Ephraim**, they did not invent new ceremonies, nor a new law, nor a new place of worship, nor anything foreign to **Moses** and the institutions of the Temple. Instead, they remained in the line of piety which they had received from their fathers. Thus would I strike down the Waldensian's prophetic prediction, if he thinks he has any such sign concerning himself: that a new progress from an insolent doctrine and ritual might renew the Church within himself.

Next, it is impossible for him to have the authority to transfer the church into himself through present inspiration. But come, let him boast that he is inspired—I do not envy him, provided he boasts truly. Let him show there if he possesses the life, the knowledge, the faith, and the Church which inspired men of old once used; let him use those same things similarly in this time. If those stupendous works, which were accustomed to follow inspired men of old from the presence of a heavenly gift, follow this Waldensian, then let them follow. For we know that men were inspired not just once, nor only in this century: the **Prophets**, then the **Apostles**, and after them innumerable confessors of the faith were suddenly changed into other men by the presence of a divine ray, according to that which is written of **Saul**: "God changed his heart into another" <note>1 Samuel 10:9. When Saul was anointed king, he was said to be "turned into another man" by the Spirit of God.</note>. They became detached from divisible <note>Meaning material or worldly things that can be divided and consumed.</note> things, snatched entirely into the contemplation of heavenly things. There they gathered the fruit of a more secret knowledge, a certainty of prophecy and faith, and a symbol of will and love toward God, from which miracles followed them. They possessed an inexhaustible desire to transfer others to that place where they themselves existed. In this work, they possessed an oblivion of injuries and punishments toward those who resisted them; they possessed a goodness, tranquility, kindness, and grace of life equally for every simplicity of heart. There was one consensus among them all regarding what should be believed and done; so much so that in human disciplines, no two or three students ever emerged from the same teacher at the same time agreeing as much as those men of different places and times agreed across such a great number of books of both Testaments. 

However, in this Waldensian, you find no such related work. He is entirely immersed in those "divisible" <note>Worldly/Material</note> things. He knows nothing beyond making a profit, or increasing his family's estate through farming or craftsmanship. Yet he lies, claiming he has chosen some "narrow way"—sad and mocked. But what of this? Do they not build? Do they not inhabit houses? Do they not plant gardens for pleasure? They exchange warm things for cold, and cooked things for those that ripened on their own; subsisting from the marketplace and their own threshing floor, they live with a wife amidst a crown of children. What then is this "narrow way"—sad and mocked—which could be tolerated by none except the divinely inspired? I certainly thought that whoever said this would be shaggy in his whole body, squalid, thorny, and torn, having emerged from some uncertain forest, sweltering under the open sky...

### CONCERNING THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS

...shivering with cold, wasted by a month-long hunger, poorly fed on herbs and roots, and deserted by every living soul—such a man might speak of a narrow, sad, and mocked path. But now, as for that Waldensian: does he lack for anything? And who throughout Moravia <note>A region in the modern-day Czech Republic where many Waldensian and Hussite groups found refuge.</note> lives more opulently? Even if he were excluded from all of nature's bounty, is God only the God of the wretched? Does piety not also seek heaven from within purple <note>Purple was the color of royalty and high-ranking clergy; the author argues that wealth or status does not inherently prevent holiness.</note> robes? 

He walks more sadly, I confess; we ourselves have seen it, and we have a great number of such people among us. Let our own people also boast of that Waldensian trait—those who love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets so that they may be seen by men. Like "sad hypocrites," they "disfigure their faces" so that they may appear to men to be fasting <note>original: "sicut hypocrite tristes, extermina̅t facies suas vt pareant hominibus ieiuna̅tes." A direct quote from the Latin Vulgate, Matthew 6:16.</note>. 

Truly, as to whether a Waldensian is mocked for his path, I do not know if there is anyone among the wiser men who would hurl such untimely laughter at them. Rather, one should weep for the public stain on the kingdom, the insult to God and the saints, and the misery of the deceivers that awaits such people because of their heresy. I do not know why they call their way "mocked." Perhaps I might believe they have wandered in their speech? For since they go against the canon of the Scriptures, against the ecclesiastical commentators <note>term: "tractatoribus ecclesiasticis" — The Church Fathers and theologians who interpreted the Bible.</note>, and against all ancient holiness—as we have now shown in many matters—and because they revive ancient heresies, they ought to have said they chose an "infamous" path. 

But for the sake of their cause, they avoided their own true description and called it "mocked." And so, if it is permitted to abuse words in this way, and they wish "mocked" to be held as "holy," then any other path—theft, sacrilege, treason, and every legal infamy—will be celebrated as such. 

Or perhaps he judges that "narrow path" or that "mocked" way by his hut, the stench of the stable, a dark tunic, common bread, or a table recklessly prepared? And because he is neglected by others who, relying on their fortune and lineage, live more splendidly and liberally, he takes it poorly—as if peasants and craftsmen <note>term: "Sellularij" — Those who work sitting down, such as cobblers or weavers; used here as a term for common laborers.</note> do not live this way among their own people and ours by their very lot in life. For human law does not promote the man on foot and the man on horseback equally. 

The Waldensians do not go out for wine in public, and this also perhaps seems to them a "narrow and sad path." Certainly, the Tatar <note>original: "Tartarus"</note> stays away from wine because of poverty; the Turk and the Saracen <note>Terms used for Muslims.</note> do not know wine even in private because of their law. Should they, therefore, be considered "inspired" because of their abstinence from wine? But you also have six hundred of our own people who are teetotalers; truly, what does this have to do with piety? 

I might take wine outside because of thirst; you take it at home because of lust. I might sit innocently with my wine, while you, far from wine at home, more carefully meditate on rebellions against God, the saints, the law, and the Church. In that case, I ask, in which sin do they offend more wickedly: in my "drunkenness" or in your "sobriety"? What, then, does naked abstinence from wine matter for piety if you are impious in everything else? What does this matter for innocence of life, if you do not shake down the traveler as a highwayman, but instead pillage sacred things in another place? 

Or is it that you, because you are a Waldensian and a traitor, would do nothing anywhere that public laws could tolerate? On the contrary, you study only how to "buy" a reputation for innocence from the smallest things, while in the gravest matters—those regarding divinity and religion—you are most harmful. Thus, for our benefit, you "strain out the gnat" from your external habit, but from the internal bilge-water of treachery, you plainly "swallow a camel" <note>A reference to Matthew 23:24, where Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for focusing on tiny details of the law while ignoring major moral failures.</note>. 

**Blind Pharisee!** First clean the inside of the cup and the dish, so that the outside may also become clean. Begin, I say, with obedience and true faith; afterward, if you do any of those things that befit a frugal master of a house, all things will be clean for you. 

Because of these behaviors, you are not what you first claimed: "inspired men" withdrawn from worldly things so that, called back to the meditation of heavenly things, you might merit a familiar knowledge of divine matters. For if you have ever separated yourselves from us, you show that you have no greater "knowledge of the mysteries of faith" than what one might get from a six-month school, or from frequent conversation and preaching among our people—or, finally, from the common crossroads. 

Where is that wisdom of yours, so that you might say with Saint Paul (who was truly inspired): *“We speak wisdom among the perfect”*? <note>1 Corinthians 2:6.</note> You, who attack the ecclesiastical commentators without judgment and without shame...

### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR
y 6.

Do you argue that we are superfluous and mendacious <note>Lying or untruthful.</note>, while you, by your commentaries, both reject and provoke the wisdom of the ancients? I call them "commentaries" though you boast they are worthy of inspiration—unless these things we hold in our hands are the only pledges of your professed inspiration. Why then, if they were drawn from the divine, have you been unable to prove them thus far, except by fictions distorted from their true sense, and by things feigned and concealed? You have fashioned testimonies for us based on the appearance of words, not the sense of the Holy Spirit, just as the Tempter-Devil did to Christ. You have used the Scriptures in the same way the Antichrist will use them among the Jews; for he will surely use the veil of the Scriptures to deceive them, since they believe they have life within them. Furthermore, it is a lie to boast of being inspired when one is outside of true inspiration. Therefore, for you to treat the divine Scriptures with sincerity and according to their knowledge and power is as foreign to you as if I were to suddenly attempt to manage your rustic affairs; surely I would not know the names of the tools to call each one correctly, nor the boundaries within which to skillfully manage them. 

With what great unworthiness, then, do you fly suddenly from the manuring of fields and the working of leather <note>original: "de stercoratione de subacto corio." The author is mocking the Waldensians' humble origins as farmers and tanners.</note> to the disputation of the greatest matters! We labor for whole years just to understand the wise men of the world, and we barely reach their meaning. How much more worthy than you were the Apostles to dare and take up such a task? And yet, until they were enlightened by power from on high, they were ignorant of where the deeds and words of Christ pointed—I might say they were ignorant of almost everything. Their successors, the leaders of the Church—most diligent men of the most burning intellects, practiced in every discipline, using vigils, meditations, and prayers before God for knowledge of the Law—have not yet exhausted the mysteries of the faith and the Scriptures in so many thousands of books. 

Yet these Waldensians, inspired from the field, from the cobbler’s shop <term>Sutrina</term>, the tanner’s yard <term>Cerdonica</term>, and the weaver's loom, act as "long-eared ones" <note>original: "Auriti." A mocking reference to asses, implying they are foolish listeners who think they understand deep secrets.</note> among long-eared faces, treating Apostolic decrees as if there were no difficulty in them, as suddenly as they work leather under their hands. But here he refutes them: when they are called out of their workshop by a neighbor to settle a dispute over marking boundaries, they do not decide so lightly as they do upon the Sacred Letters! Finally, they themselves admit no one to the craft of making a shoe who has not learned from a master shoemaker. If this is true among those who sit at benches <note>referring to manual tradesmen</note>, how much more must the divine wisdom, which is known by its own kind, be learned from those who know it? 

But these Waldensians also join that common madness, long ago lamented by the most learned: farmers, masons, smiths of metal and wood, wool-workers, fullers, and others who manufacture various household goods and lowly works cannot be what they desire to be without a teacher. "Physicians practice what belongs to physicians; smiths handle the tools of the smith" <note>original: "Quod medicorum est pmittunt medici, Tractant Fabrilia fabri." A quote from Horace's Epistles (2.1.115-116).</note>. The art of the Scriptures is the only one which everyone everywhere claims for themselves: "learned and unlearned alike, we write poems everywhere" <note>original: "scribimus indocti doctiq3 poemata passim." Another quote from Horace.</note>. The chatty old woman, the doting old man, the wordy sophist—everyone presumes to tear apart and teach this art before they have learned it. 

But they say, "While our hands labor, our mind philosophizes on divine things." But listen here, you Waldensian: "to stand and sip at the same time is not easy to do" <note>original: "Stare simul & sorbere factu haud est facile." A Latin proverb meaning one cannot do two things at once effectively.</note>. You cannot apply your hand and your mind to two different thoughts at once. For if this were so easily reconciled, you would not have been the first to discover it, nor would you be the only one to emerge from such an example. Finally, Christ the Savior proves you a liar, for He most certainly distinguished the active life from the theoretical <note>or contemplative</note> life. "Martha, Martha," He said, "you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her" <note>original: "Martha martha inquit sollicita es. & turbaris erga plurima. porro vnũ est necessariũ Maria optimã partem elegit." A reference to Luke 10:41-42.</note>. Martha was busy with service so that she might receive Christ as a guest with sufficient and honest care for His bodily needs. Thus she is said to be "troubled about many things"—that is, she was anxious, in the sense of the Apostle, and thinking of divided things which belong to the world. Mary, however, was free from this kind of care...

He uses the biblical figures of Martha and Mary to argue that one cannot simultaneously perform manual labor and achieve high spiritual contemplation.</summary>

->### ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS<-

[Mary] sat at the feet of the Lord, a quiet seat. And with her affection gathered within her, she could not help Martha, but being swept up in contemplation, she heard His word. Martha's care was to be left here with the body. Mary's contemplation was not to be taken from her; rather, it was to be perpetuated from this life into the future. Therefore, you, who are entirely consumed in seeking profit, have by no means been enlightened in the contemplation of the law according to the Savior’s decree. 

In testimony of this, you are consistent nowhere. You follow a religion of boasting, certain of nothing either privately or publicly regarding what should be believed. We see you change your beliefs as we change the value of the coin a man holds with new edicts at every rising sun. Behold even your **leaders** <note>original: "Archimandrite" — a high-ranking Eastern church official, here used mockingly for Waldensian leaders</note>, your **high priests** <note>original: "flamines diales" — the high priests of Jupiter in Ancient Rome; the author uses this pagan term to insult them</note> whom you look up to as heirs of the seat of the Apostles Peter and Paul! One of them, as rumor has it, first cast off his monk’s habit, then acted as a priest. From this, he crossed with the same dignity to the schismatics, and from there he fell away to the Waldensians. He has revolved through as many religions as the decades he completed in the year [14]63. I suspect that in the next ten years he will yet walk into a snare. 

But he denies it. Certainly, what he cannot deny is that he was a "priest of the chalice" <note>Likely a reference to the Utraquists or Hussites who insisted on the lay chalice</note> and a parish priest. There, having betrayed his priestly vow, he took a "little woman" <note>original: "muliercula" — a derogatory diminutive for a mistress or wife</note>, whether she be wife or harlot. For a priest loses the right to marriage because of the vow of celibacy he has pledged; yet he took her as a wife **under the bridal veil** <note>original: "sub flammeo"</note>. Grudging those fingers anointed with holy oil to the altars, he began to use that infamous finger—yes, *that* one—to handle greasy robes. He who claims to follow the Holy Spirit—so kind, mild, settled, and placid—shows none of these traits. He is a misanthrope: harsh, rustic, troublesome, unsociable, and devoid of all human character. He shares nothing with humanity except the physical shape.

There is another among them of high rank, a self-styled heir to the "miter of Peter," who cut off his own virility <note>The author is accusing the leader of self-castration</note> against the decrees of the Council of Nicaea <note>The first Council of Nicaea (325 AD) strictly forbade self-castrated men from the clergy</note>, to which they are always appealing. That fool is like a **priest of Cybele** <note>original: "deorum Matris gallus" — the "Galli" were self-castrated priests of the goddess Cybele in antiquity</note> who blocked the running water from the stream but not from the source itself. For just as a smothered fire, because it does not consume itself in flames, glows more heavily within itself, so those who are castrated burn no less with an unquenchable desire and are most lustful for women. But perhaps he was ruptured <note>original: "herniosus" — suffering from a hernia</note> and his intestines fell into the scrotum, and he freed himself from such trouble with this "remedy"; his health might excuse his previous foolishness, or certainly this man’s "continence."

The rest of the accomplices of this "sacred"—I might better say "execrable"—flock yield in honor to him. They defer the highest priestly authority to him for this very reason: so that those among our priests who perhaps disliked celibacy might now decide by their own deed whether a husband or a celibate stands more worthily at the altars, handles the sacraments, and presides over the church. 

Another among them believes that the souls of men are mortal. Therefore, they even add this to their faith and the **Apostles' Creed**. This is a great error in every way. For he who does not believe rightly about the nature of the soul will believe rightly neither of Christ nor the Gospel promises. For Christ is God, and as He is true God, so He is true man, subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh. If rational souls are mortal, then the soul of Christ would also have been mortal. By what part of Himself, then, did Christ descend into hell to lead out those who were bound? With what part of Himself did He come into Paradise with the thief? By what small part of His humanity did He rise again and ascend into heaven? It would no longer be the same Christ who acted who is to judge the world; yet it *will* be the same Christ, for He said: "When the Son of Man comes in His majesty..." Who is the Son of Man if not the son of the Virgin Mary? Truly He consists of a rational soul and human flesh. Furthermore, if the soul is mortal, Christ—having died once on the cross—lives no longer, and much less did He rise again, since the life of the body comes only from the soul. Unless the Waldensian says that in Christ the office...

## THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

...to fill his divinity with a soul. Therefore, he restores again the condemned dogma of **Apollinaris** <note>original: "Apollinaris" — a 4th-century bishop who taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a human soul</note> against the Gospel, where the Savior said: *I lay down my soul so that I may take it up again.* <note>John 10:17; original: "Ego ponã animã meã ut iterũ summã eam"</note> If the Savior takes up his soul again, is it clearly mortal? But if Christ assumes an immortal soul again, why should his divinity fill the place of something present as if it were absent? 

But the Waldensian will say: "I will confess, according to my received opinion, that the soul is immortal in Christ alone, but mortal in all other men." Listen then, you wicked Waldensian: If the soul exists as mortal in the latter and immortal in the former, then Christ did not assume a human nature of the same kind and species as ours. From this part—that is, the soul—by which he would be unlike us, he would not have redeemed man. By what reasoning would he have redeemed man from a dissimilar nature, and by that same nature redeemed a fallen angel? 

But that symbol of a single nature in the humanity of both gave us the power alone to become participants in Christ’s redemption. For this reason, it is said he did not take up angels, as **Saint Paul** says, but *he took up the seed of Abraham*, <note>Hebrews 2:16</note> whence he ought to be made like his brothers in all things. Behold the Apostle, how soberly he philosophizes on this present discourse compared to that Waldensian! 

Furthermore, all the promises of eternal things would become false based on this opinion. And so, *if in this life only*, as the Apostle says to the **Corinthians**, *we are hoping in Christ, we are more miserable than all men.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:19</note> The Law would be voided, as would the Gospel. Christ says: *Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.* <note>Matthew 10:28; "Gehenna" refers to hell</note> The Savior added: *But even the hairs of your head are all numbered.* <note>Matthew 10:30</note> That is to say: if God weighs the hairs in the resurrection and takes them into account—will he not take into account the soul for which Christ died? 

The Apostle writes to the Corinthians: *I have judged to deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.* <note>1 Corinthians 5:5</note> If, according to that man's heresy, the soul is mortal, where will the spirit reside that is to be saved on the day of the Lord?

But the common **Synagogue of the Waldensians** <note>original: "Synagoga valdẽsium" — a derogatory term used by Catholic writers to describe the Waldensian community</note> denies that there is anyone among them who thinks so wickedly. On the contrary, there is indeed such a person, even one who recently swore a horrendous oath regarding a written testament before the judges. Illustrious lords were present for the speech, and it is in their eyes that I write these things. 

There are other Waldensians—or rather, it is their whole "Synagogue"—who believe in only one judgment of God. For while divine judgment is twofold—one proper to each person immediately upon their passing, and the other a universal judgment at the end of the world—the Waldensians understand this in such a way that if someone is judged by either of the two, they do not undergo the other. 

Since, however, the **General Judgment** <term>General Judgment: The final judgment of all humanity at the end of time, as opposed to the "Particular Judgment" of an individual soul at death</term> is coming (at which the Son of Man will sit in his majesty to judge all flesh, with all nature moved from its seat at his coming), and since this is signified as coming by the clearest prophecies, hidden by no veil—the Waldensians escape to this: they confess only this one judgment. And they deny that other judgment which is proper to each individual at this time. 

And that was the very origin and the innermost root of their entire error, which they previously brought forth regarding the **Purgatory of souls**. <term>Purgatory: In Catholic theology, a place of purification for souls before entering heaven; the Waldensians famously rejected its existence</term> But those crafty men disguised it, and they only poured out publicly those things that seemed to follow from this principle. Truly, they themselves used to argue from their secrets in this way: "If God will appear in fire at any time, then the work of each person, of what sort it is, will be tested." And only at the end of the age will God appear in fire; therefore, only at the end of the age will each person's work be tested. Thus, they conclude, the things now believed about Purgatory are fables. 

Behold the serpentine, behold the diabolical cunning! For that reason, as I now recall, they said: <insert>[Here it is noted that the Apostle does not speak in this place about what is to come after death, nor does he record these words for this reason, because at death God will not appear in fire. Again, there at the end, about which the ancient Doctors spoke more harmoniously, that before the Last Judgment, first when God appears in fire...]</insert>

### ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST [THE HERETICS]

...the elect of God will cleanse <unclear/> behold the hiding places of the Waldensians <note>original: "latebre valdesiū"</note>. Who then would have led them by their words into such retreats? Are they not indeed cunning? Do they not know how to hide their mysteries? Against such great treachery of theirs, we shall proceed from the opposite side. Even if I were to remain silent regarding their lies—for they wish to tell us that we should consider them the "ancient doctors" who said the elect of God were to be purged only at the end of the world—they are in truth no more orthodox in his name than those they have led astray. I shall now touch upon the sinews of such a great error. They say that because there is no judgment now, there is no penalty; on the contrary, I say that because there is a penalty now, there is indeed a judgment. I speak this more clearly: if the merit of blessedness and the demerit of damnation are received from God at any time, they are received only by judgment. Since both are received for one's deeds immediately upon being released from the body, it is there that the particular judgment of God finds everyone. 

Indeed, many "blessed" are read about today. **John**, in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, says: *I saw under the altar the souls of those slaughtered for the word of God and for the testimony they held, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" And single white robes were given to each of them.* <note>Revelation 6:9-11; original: "vsq; q dñe sctūs et ver⁹ nō iudicas & nō vīdicas saguinē nīm"</note> Again: *Behold, a Lamb stood on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand having his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads,* and it follows, *These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes; these were purchased from all as the first fruits to God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are without blemish before the throne of God.* <note>Revelation 14:1-5</note> 

But also in another place, Saint John saw a great multitude which no one could number. And speaking in the person of **Christ**, he says: *Do penance. If not, I will come to you quickly and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.* <note>Revelation 2:16</note> If, therefore, we do not do penance at some time, Christ comes "quickly." We do not perform penance except in this life; therefore, quickly after this life, penance performed or not performed will be placed into the examination of divine judgment. Just as it is written: *The rich man also died, and was buried in Hell.* <note>Luke 16:22</note> And regarding another rich man: *Fool, this night they will require your soul from you; then whose will those things be which you have prepared?* <note>Luke 12:20</note> Furthermore, there is a fire in the particular judgment of each person—contrary to what the Waldensians feel—which goes before God for the purging of the good and the torment of the wicked. As the Scripture says: *A fire shall go before him and shall inflame his enemies round about.* <note>Psalm 97:3</note> And **Isaiah**: *The Lord will come in fire, and his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his fury in indignation and his rebuke in a flame of fire.* <note>Isaiah 66:15</note> 

But the Waldensians, deceived by a Jewish fable, think that if this were to happen in the present age, it must happen in the way the Jews expect the **Messiah**—in whirlwind, wind, thunder, and lightning. To suspect such a thing happens at this time is a sign of a very narrow mind. For Christ will by no means come with nature disturbed, as he will on the last day of the world with the elements burning in majesty and all power, but concerning the *effect* of judgment—that each will receive according to their merits—we confess he "comes in fire." Just as a prince who punishes a criminal is said to have come "in fury and with the sword," even though he himself remains most calm in his own mind and among his friends. 

But lest the Waldensians accuse me here of speaking from fabricated suspicion, I will bring forward a witness of our opinion whom I believe the Waldensians will hear willingly, and whom they themselves in another place praise to us as a primary teacher of the Church: **Origen**. In the fourth book of his work *Against Celsus the Philosopher*—that **Celsus**, the Epicurean <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher who wrote the first comprehensive attack on Christianity</note>, used to attack the Catholics with these words: "These things indeed forced them—as they were seized by a false opinion—to affirm that God would descend in the likeness of a torturer carrying fire." Celsus claimed that "it is clear they do not celebrate these things about God either religiously or purely." 

In response, Origen says these words: "He thinks indeed that we do these things to strike terror into the common people, and that we announce words about future punishments which are entirely to be inflicted upon transgressors. But Divine Scripture declares that God is a 'consuming fire' and that rivers of fire proceed before him, and that he himself comes like a refiner's fire and like fuller's soap to refine the people of God as his own. Since, therefore, he is called a 'consuming fire,' we ask what things are to be consumed by it? We indeed affirm that it is wickedness <note>original: "nequiciā"</note> that must be consumed, and the things perpetrated through it, and those things which are figuratively called 'wood, hay, and stubble' <note>original: "ligna fenū et stipła"</note>; God will consume them like a fire. The wicked man, therefore, builds upon the rational foundation subject to the Lord either wood, or hay, or stubble..."

...stubble, which can be demonstrated if the one who wrote it felt quite differently. And it will be clear that the wicked person built upon wood, hay, and stubble, and it will be understood that the fire consists of matter and is tangible. But if the works of the wicked are taken tropologically <note>figuratively or morally</note>—namely as the wood, hay, and stubble—why does it not occur what kind of fire that will be which is to consume them? For it is said: *The fire shall try every man's work, of what sort it is. If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss.* <note>Quoting 1 Corinthians 3:13-15</note> What other work is said to be consumed by fire except all that is done wickedly? Therefore, as we ourselves have handed down, our God is a consuming fire <note>original: "ignis consumens"</note>; and he proceeds no differently than a refining fire <term>refining fire: original "ignis conflantis," referring to a smelter's fire used to purify ore</term> usually does, about to flow into the rational nature which is filled with lead and impure metals, which—so to speak—adulterate the nature of gold or silver. Thus, they likewise say that fire and a river [of fire] precede God to destroy the wickedness that is mixed into the soul from every side. From these things shall I grasp the Waldensians by their own art? When each person's work is tested, it is examined by God the author in the preceding rivers of fire. It is examined suddenly upon each person’s passing [from this life]. 

We show this to be true from the Scriptures, and thus, with the matter now confirmed for both sides, it follows that at each person's death, God—as the judge of the life lived—precedes in the manner of a refining fire. It follows, finally, that you are proven false in claiming that God will only appear in fire at the end of the age. Since, moreover, no purgation of souls is admitted at any other time except then, why should not the one to be saved be saved immediately from death by the present judgment of God, the one to be damned be damned, and the one to be purged be purged? The Waldensians admit many such things, by which men are carried about by every wind of doctrine: men who are lovers of themselves, greedy, puffed up, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, merciless, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, and lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God; having a appearance of piety, but denying its power. "Avoid these," says the Apostle to **Timothy** <note>2 Timothy 3:2-5</note>. For of this sort are they who penetrate houses and lead captive silly women weighed down with sins, who are led away by various desires, always saying [they are learning] and never coming to the knowledge of the truth. But just as **Jannes** and **Mambres** <note>Traditionally identified as the Egyptian sorcerers who opposed Moses</note> resisted **Moses**, so do these resist the truth: men corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall proceed no further, for their folly shall be manifest to all, as was that of the others. 

Let us therefore act consequently according to the promise of the Apostle, so that for those to whom the folly of the Waldensians is not yet sufficiently explored, they may explore it more through manifest lies—under which they cannot possibly be carried by the Holy Spirit as they falsely claim—which we shall gather from their own scripture. I cannot sufficiently remember the sheer number of them, but I have touched upon a great part of such things in the preceding pages; therefore, I shall now assign a few out of all of them which will seem sufficient for judgment. 

And so, first they say of themselves: <insert>as long as they strive to please the divine kindness and emulate His acknowledged will; and again we testify indeed before the living God, who will judge the world in equity, that we have never been found to bark or blather anything heretical or blasphemous against God, nor against the orthodox faith, nor against the Eucharist of the body and blood of Christ, nor finally against the Blessed Virgin, nor the saints of God</insert>. 

From such a conscience of inspiration and certainty of faith, they say in another place to those who doubt: <insert>and we wish to be taught that very thing through human instruction, and we desire to be led from the sacred traditions of the law to a sane sense of the Christian religion, nor surely will his labor toward us seem vain or ungrateful</insert>. Therefore, having called God as a witness to the known truth in such horrific ways, now you nonetheless doubt after the heavenly teacher? You appeal to human instruction? You show that you desire to be taught better and more certain things there? Truly, you do an insult...
