# ON THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST <note>The title likely concludes "against the Waldensians" or "against the heretics," based on the previous page.</note>

The people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play—and they perished at the hand of the destroyer. Korah <note>original: *Chore*; a biblical figure who rebelled against the authority of Moses and Aaron</note> seized the priesthood for himself, and he was swallowed by a gap in the earth. Ananias and his wife Sapphira lied to the Holy Spirit; they fell down suddenly and breathed their last. 
Do you, therefore, demand a miracle here? I am not so much your enemy that—if I truly desire you to remain in your duty and in the public law of religion—I would wish your lack of faith to be set aside because of miracles. Paul the Apostle preaches to Sergius Paulus the proconsul, a prudent man; Elymas the sorcerer <note>original: *Elymas magus*; a magician who opposed Paul in Acts 13</note> resisted him, and Paul struck him with blindness. 
May this miracle happen to you: that you, who seem wise to yourself, may be blind—not seeing the sun for a time—so that you might eventually seek someone to lead you, and not run headlong into the decrees of God. For these are the words of Jude the Apostle, the brother of James: "The angels who did not keep their own principality but abandoned their own dwelling, He has reserved in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day." 
Understand that those who are rebels, and those who are of your faction, likewise defile the flesh, despise lordship, and blaspheme majesty. 

But believe with us that the world is ruled everywhere by a visible power. More than seventy heresies have risen up against the Church of God. By no example, or a very rare one—and even then a public one—will you find that a heretic wishing to disturb the Church was met with a strike from heaven. Rather, like one sleeping, Christ sits at the stern in the little boat <note>A traditional metaphor for the Church as the "Barque of Peter" during a storm</note>; and lest the salvation of the believers suffer harm from the waves, He commands the leaders of the churches to the oars. By their vigilance, patience, and labor, the storms of faithlessness are overcome. Finally, when those of little heart, driven by desperation at the state of things, let the business slip from their hands, they wake Christ to the power of a miracle: "Arise! Why are you afraid, you who do not yet have faith?" 

But even earthly kingdoms have proceeded according to the will of God. Thus, Daniel says: "Blessed be the name of the Lord from age to age, because wisdom and strength are His; He changes the times and the ages, He transfers and establishes kingdoms." Likewise, in another place: "God has numbered your kingdom and finished it; you have been weighed in the scales and found wanting; your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians." <note>A reference to the "writing on the wall" during Belshazzar's feast in the Book of Daniel</note> 
And the Savior says: "You would have no power at all against me, unless it had been given to you from above." For God created this machine of bodily things so that man—not God or angels in his place—might work with freedom of will to attain the glory that is to come to us. 
Nevertheless, God the inspector presides over all these things. Furthermore, He submits His spirits as co-helpers, yet in such a way that the immediate requirements of human actions are fulfilled through the ministry of men. 

From the virtue of such great things, we look back, secondly, to the power and the knot and the bond of things. Therefore, we restore the home to the father; we restore his own people to the lords; we make cities and provinces listen once again to their kings. We recognize the Parish Priests, Bishops, and Patriarchs once more as the arbiters of faith. We arrange all things like members in a body, each in its own place; everything will return to itself in a most sweet covenant. They will stand firm within themselves. 

Otherwise, discord disturbs the smallest of things, while peace maintains the greatest. The human race, I say, lives by means of a few. It is a sense full of heroic majesty: behold, from one father, a house is at peace; many houses are at peace by the counsel of the Republic; many Republics by one Prince; many Princes by one sacred Emperor <note>original: *impio Augusto*; though *impius* usually means "wicked," in this rhetorical context of "heroic majesty" and "peace," it likely refers to the "pious" or "imperial" Augustus, or perhaps "distinguished" (*amplus*), though the transcription reads *impio*</note>. 
This, finally, contains the East and the West, the Christian and the Turk, in a covenant. If these two supreme heads on both sides were unwilling, then even with the world trembling, all things would still collide. 
For just as the soul is the leader of the body, and without it the body lies senseless, so the Prince is the ruler of the world. Thus, outside of him, the circle of the lands grows numb. To be sure, <insert>wicked men</insert> nourish the world, and human arts were at their greatest under the greatest <insert>wicked rulers</insert>. <note>The author argues that even "wicked" or "secular" order is better than the total anarchy proposed by his opponents</note> 
When the king of the bees is dead, the hives are ruined; so too would the world fail if lordship were extinguished.

-># THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR<-

Who else besides a Pighard <note>original: *Pighardū*; a derogatory name for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren, often used by their Catholic opponents</note> is so foolish? And no matter where such a person comes from, he finds a law for himself out of his own whim. Perhaps now the Pighards wish to be seen as accepting the King's Majesty and every power that can exist under kings; however, they still stain the ecclesiastical administration, since for them it is free from danger <note>i.e., they feel safe attacking the Church while pretending to respect the State</note>. I say they wrongly deny it, for the Apostle certainly writes to the Ephesians: "He himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ." <note>Ephesians 4:11–12</note> But he also commands Titus: "That you should appoint priests <term>presbyters; from the Greek 'presbyteros' meaning elder</term> in every city, as I directed you." Likewise, he subsequently mentions the bishop: "For a bishop <term>episcopus; literally 'overseer'</term> must be without crime, as a steward of God, not proud, not hot-tempered," and the many things that follow. First, I will throw this in the Pighard's face for now: If God gave these orders in the Catholic Church and the Apostles instituted them, then those Pighards who do not have these same orders, and indeed deny them, will not themselves be any part of the Catholic Church.

But let us deal with the matter regarding the true head. It is agreed by us, both from the facts themselves and from the present Apostle, who says that the bishop is a steward of God, and that apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers are given for the work of the ministry; I say, it remains attested by these things that God governs everything in this Church through the mediation of human office. Therefore, the common people shall stand by the judgment of the priest, and those priests by the judgment of the bishop. Thus far, the matter remains in harmony. 

But what if the bishops themselves have a dispute among them? Which one there will yield to the other in terms of Authority? We have not yet coordinated them under one head. What if they differ in judgment among themselves concerning "leprosy and non-leprosy" <note>A biblical metaphor for distinguishing between sin and purity, or heresy and orthodoxy</note>, or concerning what to believe and what not to believe? By command, they ought to ascend here to the judge who existed at that time. This "judge of judges," this "bishop of bishops," the Pighard removes from human affairs. Therefore, there stands here an error of the Church just as great regarding bishops without a supreme Patriarch, as the error of the people without a priest, or the error of priests without a bishop would be. 

It would then be necessary for us to run back—even against the will of Scripture—to demand miracles, or it would be necessary to rouse this man, Christ, as if He were a traveler gone abroad. We would need Christ "sleeping in the ship." <note>A reference to Matthew 8:24; the author argues that if there is no earthly head (the Pope), the Church is like a ship in a storm with a sleeping captain</note> But even if the Pighard thinks this ought to be done, the same surely ought to have been done by the people toward Christ. By that same logic, God could have dispensed with invisible presidency for those closest to the people just as well as for that supreme office, so that God should have appointed no orders, no stewards, and no ministries through the Apostles at all. 

Furthermore, in that same passage to the Ephesians, the Apostle immediately adds: "For the building up of the body of Christ." And again to the Corinthians: "For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though they are many, are yet one body, so also is Christ." <note>1 Corinthians 12:12</note> And after many things, concluding, he says: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." If, therefore, there are many members in the Church, but it is not one body, then that body is not perfect without a head. And so those members are understood to be those who visibly perform their stewardship in the Church, according to that saying of the Savior: "If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off; and if your foot causes you to stumble, amputate it; and if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out." <note>Mark 9:43–47</note> For far be it from us to think that those members of the Church Triumphant <term>The 'Church Triumphant' refers to the saints and angels already in heaven</term>, who now reign happily with Christ, could cause any of the faithful to stumble. Far be it that they should be cut off, amputated, or cast out any further, concerning whom it is certainly written: "God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, nor shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away." <note>Revelation 21:4</note> I say again, if these are therefore members of the Church Militant <term>The 'Church Militant' refers to Christians currently living on earth, struggling against sin and temptation</term> still on earth, regarding their bodily exi...

existence, they certainly receive, and the head by which that body is brought to perfection will also be received from bodily existence, so that there may be a fittingness through all the joints of the body related to itself. Now, if this connection of the members of the present Church is not to remain within its own kind in its highest member, then neither will the members nearest to the first remain in that kind. For by whatever reason the Pighard <note>original: *Pighardus*; a derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians</note> fears to confess a vicarious head on earth from Christ, by that same reason another will fear to confess a vicarious eye, vicarious hands, or vicarious feet, following those who in past centuries were the eyes, hands, and feet in the church militant and have now been received into heaven. For in one body, under one head, Christ, to double the remaining members here and there <note>i.e., to have both heavenly and earthly versions of the same roles</note> will seem just as foreign or indeed most alien to the reality as it seems strange to that Pighard to acknowledge a vicarious head for the head, Christ, on earth.

But certainly, just as those who once built the faith from the beginning under the present head, Christ, have been carried into heaven, vicarious laborers have succeeded them and will succeed them in that same order of the Church, "until we all meet," as Paul says, "in the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ." <note>Ephesians 4:13</note> So, with this head, Christ, having been taken up into heaven, a vicarious head succeeding Him in this order will preside over the members. From this, that ecclesiastical hierarchy <term>hierarchia; from Greek, meaning 'sacred rule'</term> stands perfected on earth in its own order, which was instituted by the Apostles according to the pattern of that which they had seen from heavenly secrets, revealed by the Holy Spirit on the mountain; hence Saint John also saw it descending from heaven, having the radiance of God. <note>Revelation 21:10</note>

Therefore, we must next inquire who that supreme Patriarch <note>original: *Patriarcha*; here used to designate the Pope as the "first father" of the faith</note> and vicar of Christ on earth is, who alone received universal power over almost all the churches which we know were instituted either in the times of the Apostles or everywhere on earth afterward—a power as great as we previously described from Deuteronomy. Nor should we fear to confess such a man; we detract nothing from Christ by doing so, and we have other examples of this matter in the Scriptures. Paul says to us: "there is but one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in Him, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things and we through Him." <note>1 Corinthians 8:6</note> Nevertheless, he writes in another place: "I have said, you are gods," <note>Psalm 82:6</note> and again, "the God of gods, the Lord, has spoken," <note>Psalm 50:1</note> and "Give praise to the Lord of lords." <note>Psalm 136:3</note> Thus, we know Christ as the sole head of the Church, yet we confess His vicar on earth as head by a shared power.

Therefore, whatever place was chosen by God and established must have its course perennial alongside the Church, so that we can acknowledge that none of the dioceses which were contemporary with the nascent faith—whether in the remote East, or Greece, or Africa, or the whole world—and later ceased to be, nor any that began everywhere on earth after the age of the Apostles, could have held the general dispensation of the keys and of the Christian state. For either it will be shown from the commentaries of the ancients that the authority of a failed church was transferred into another present one, or, because it is not shown, then the members of the passing Church would have been without a head for some time. 

But we confess that the Roman Church is the one that was aware of the faith as it was born in the Apostles and will be aware of it as it ceases with the world; we acknowledge her as the guardian of the keys, the teacher of the faith, and the port of salvation for the faithful on earth. The remaining churches of which either the Apostles or the primitive disciples were the authors—Jerusalem, Caesarea in Palestine, Antioch, Alexandria, Carthage, and last of all, Constantinople—ceased to be because of disobedience, since they did not want the See of Peter to be the judge of their faith. For if the Roman Church, out of similar ambition, had cast itself out from any other church that held the supreme right, it too would have had to fail from that same fault. For it is against the power of nature for a member cut off from the body to be able to remain in itself; it is against the state of a Commonwealth for those deprived of their head <term>capite diminutos; a Roman legal term referring to a loss of status or civil rights</term> to exercise the force of the laws—which the Apostle also confirms?

y.6.

"Let no one," he says to the Colossians, "seduce you by a voluntary humility and the religion of angels, walking in things he has not seen, puffed up in vain by his fleshly sense, and not holding the head, from which the whole body, being supplied and constructed by joints and bands, grows into its increase." <note>original: *nemo... ad colofenses...* quoting Colossians 2:18-19</note>. But the Roman Church remains whole in itself. It even had the Emperors and Patriarchs of the city of Constantinople—who envied this honor for old Rome—trying to draw this right to themselves. The city of Rome itself has endured as many and as frequent calamities from hostile forces as no other republic ever suffered, so that it could not have lasted to this day by any human help or effort. Yet, through threats, through rebellions, through devastation, fire, and sword, and through the conspiracy of the human race for the destruction of this city, it overcame by heavenly help and remained in its place. And though Greek arrogance <note>referring to the Eastern Orthodox Church's resistance to Papal authority</note> claimed everything for itself according to its own whim and desire, it eventually yielded of its own accord to Roman rights, where the Roman authority never doubted its own power and never gave way. For this house was founded from the very beginning upon the rock <term>petra: the Greek word for rock, used by Jesus as a pun on Peter's name (*Petros*)</term>, from which rock—which is Christ—it received such privileges as no other church deserved. "You are Peter," says the Savior, "and upon this rock I will build my church." <note>original: *Tu es Petrus...* quoting Matthew 16:18</note>

But you say, Pighard <note>original: *Pigharde*; a derogatory label for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians</note>, "He said 'I will build' [in the future] and not 'I build' [in the present]," and you argue whether this refers to a near or remote future, or if it is ever fulfilled at all—yet regarding the perpetual future, it carries the same weight. But listen, Pighard: it is a shameful thing for a grave man to promise and not deliver. God, however, is Truth. If He is going to do something, it is already as good as done by God. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, as Paul says, who was preached among you by us, was not "Yes" and "No," but in Him was "Yes." <note>original: *2 Corinthians 1:19*. The author argues that God's word is eternally present and reliable.</note> In God's eternal counsels, the past and the future are equally present. If He has decreed anything, because that "time" exists in the instant of eternity, it exists surely before it even comes to effect in this elementary machine <note>the physical, created universe</note>, where it first receives the divisions of time. Thus, "I will build" is the same as "I build my mother church." And in truth, this then began to be perfected, for the apostles immediately built the Church of Christ after the sending of the Holy Spirit, and this was not built except upon the rock. That rock was Peter. "And upon this rock I will build my church."

Again, the Savior says in the Gospel according to Luke: "Simon, behold, Satan has desired you all, that he may sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not: and when you are converted, strengthen your brethren." <note>original: *Luke 22:31-32*</note>. He speaks to Peter alone in the hearing of the apostles about what would happen to the whole college, and He prays specifically for Peter that his faith would not fail. Now, if we think this was said regarding the *person* of Peter, then the faith of none of the apostles failed *more* than Peter’s, for he denied Christ. Finally, once converted, he did not "strengthen" any of the apostles as if they were failing. If we understand this as being said to a person, then the one whose faith did *not* fail would be John, who stood under the cross during Christ's passion; he stood by his Master in His torment when the whole world contradicted Him; he took the Virgin Mother into his protection; and he did not tremble before the ferocious Jews. 

Certainly, therefore, this is a deeper prophecy concerning the Universal Church. Satan has sifted everyone; the churches which the apostles personally established have already passed away. But the Roman diocese lasts in perpetual succession from Peter. While the sees of the other Apostles failed in various ways under their successors through heresies, this see of Peter alone remained sincere in the confession of the faith of its founder. Thus, whenever the world, weary of so many errors, finally wishes to return to a true faith, the world may have a teacher from whom it may be taught heavenly piety. This the Roman Church received in its author, Peter, and has kept for all time thereafter, just as one who receives the badge of liberty and nobility from a prince for his people or posterity, guards it. How can you doubt this, Pighard? Because...

### CONCERNING THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST THE WALDENSIANS ###

For it happens that he whose faith is not to fail may nonetheless be converted <note>original: *is cuius non est defectura fides, tamen convertatur*; a reference to Christ’s words to Peter in Luke 22:32</note>; that is to say, the charity of many grows cold, which is the case whenever we sin beneath the level of heresy. It is for this very reason that you desire the present Church to be cast out. We know it, and many things offend you, so that finally you seek to be offended and fall of your own accord. You continually send spies of your own to Rome; they go and return without rest; they bring and bring back reports of deeds done and undone. You penetrate the inner workings of the Christian commonwealth <term>Christian republic: a common Renaissance term for the collective body of all Christian nations</term> and equally destroy them. 

But you, as the wise man says, "Lay not in wait, and seek not impiety in the house of the just, nor lay waste to his rest. For the just man shall fall seven times a day and rise again; but the impious shall fall into evil" <note>quoting Proverbs 24:15-16</note>. Therefore, let the prelates be whatever they might do out of weakness, or whatever you can manufacture against them out of your own impudence; certainly, by the very fact that you think yourself innocent, you are by that same deed guilty. 

> For he who speaks evil of a brother, as James says in his Canonical Epistle, or who judges his brother, speaks evil of the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge <note>quoting James 4:11</note>.

Behold, in a brief word, how the apostle casts you out from your own action and from every divine status. Lawful kingdoms often have tyrants; indeed, God even allows a hypocritical man to reign because of the sins of the people. The world does not always have pure suns. The elements also have their failures; rivers do not always flow pure, but often carry mud. In short, there is nothing human that runs its course everywhere without fault; do not contend that the prelates of our nurturing religion must either be entirely pure or have dissolved the Christian matter. 

Yet, in this ambition and pride, and in this arrogance of affairs, it is a great miracle that although many dare to provoke all sorts of offenses in all sorts of matters, they nevertheless abstain from treachery <note>original: *perfidia*; in this context, it refers to apostasy or heresy—the abandonment of the core faith</note>. In former times, throughout Asia and Greece, the Bishops did not stop at fulfilling mutual enmities within this limit, but even proceeded with hostile minds toward new heresies. The angers of our people stay within this boundary, and in religion, they are even so restrained in their vengeance. They agree. This, I say, is the work of God, not of men. 

Therefore, as long as one sins below the boundary of treachery, God is certainly present there as the arbiter of His religion, and those placed in charge have not fallen from the power of the Church. They manage the Christian commonwealth without any diminishing of the keys <term>the keys: the authority to forgive sins or excommunicate, based on Matthew 16</term>. Yet it will come to pass that they too shall one day return to their due innocence—I believe in that renewal when "all Israel shall be saved" <note>referring to Romans 11:26</note>. They, and the entire Catholic world, will return to that primitive fervor of the Christians; then the Apostolic order, which never failed in faith, having been converted, shall confirm his brothers in the fruitful and universal preaching of the Gospel. 

But let the discourse return to where it departed. This double privilege was therefore given to the blessed Peter: that his faith should not fail, and that the Roman Church should have the mastery of faith. She possesses this prerogative by her own hereditary right above all churches, so that now no one can be saved outside her prefecture and judgment, just as the Savior says again:

> I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven <note>Matthew 16:19</note>.

If indeed we are born and live in sins, we cannot be saved unless we lay these down at the "toll-gate" <note>original: *portorium*; literally a customs office or tax-gate, here used as a metaphor for confession and the Church's authority to remit sins</note> of our earthly migration. If, however, this toll-gate for the paying off of sins is not set up everywhere and in every place, then one must run to where Christ, the Lord of the world, established it. He established it here, where Peter presides at the helm; for He said to Peter:

> I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

Did he not receive that power specifically, rather than in common with the rest of the Apostles? If, therefore, Christ said to them in common and equally:

> Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven,

did Peter receive only as much as all the others received there as part of the group? This power, commended in a single word thus, so that it might never cause suspicion of a higher power, ought to stand. Otherwise, it is in Job: "God speaks..."

<meta>This page continues the defense of the Roman Catholic hierarchy against the Waldensian critique. Having previously discussed the moral conduct of the clergy and the necessity of the Law, the author now focuses on the "Power of the Keys" granted to Saint Peter and how this authority is uniquely transmitted to his successors in the Roman See.</meta>

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR #

He does not repeat this same thing a second time. For if God repeated that same word to Peter individually, "To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven" <note>original: *Tibi dabo claues regni celorū*; Matthew 16:19</note>, then surely what Peter received singularly, he commends as singular. He received it according to a prerogative of power. Therefore, you grant this: that Peter received a principal power above the other apostles; but you deny that he either could or should have transferred that same power to his successors. If there was no cause for God, in ancient times, to promise Peter such power as we now hear of in the Gospel, then you would call Christ the author of a rash and ill-considered act. We would then freely grant you that a "fortuitous" power should not—and perhaps could not—be transmitted to successors. 

However, since Christ is God, His will is no more changeable or weak than His very essence. If He wills something, that willing is as necessary as the fact that He is God; thus, He could never have given this power of the keys to Peter rashly or without necessary cause. Since the Church, running through all of time, is also one body, and one body has one nature, then if it was necessary for the first believers to depend upon Peter as their president—on account of the promise regarding sins and the communion of the Sacraments—it will likewise be necessary for the faithful of all subsequent time, by that same immovable will of God and that immutable nature of the body, to depend upon his successors and presidents at that See where Peter laid down the keys.

We render these reasons for our actions. Thus, we exhibit universal obedience to the pontiffs <term>pontiff: a title for the Pope, derived from the Latin for 'bridge-builder'</term> of that See. We are as unwilling to try to seize heaven outside the awareness of that power as we are unable to do so. Therefore, Kings, forgetting their own majesty, submit themselves to this See; Kings tremble at its censure by divine right, and not out of a "lazy superstition" as you imagine. 

The sublimity of philosophy and of all wisdom dares less by its own faculty; indeed, the arts and inventions of men only confess themselves to be pleasing when they have been received as pure and true according to the Apostolic rule. In absolutely no annals is it recorded that anyone ever denied the supreme power of this See who had not previously denied faith, piety, and both human and divine law. There are, therefore, those who envy its loftiness and disparage its power and authority for wicked reasons. One man, accustomed to seizing the property of others, sees that the Roman pontiffs possess what he himself covets; he therefore considers the Pope's wealth to be unjust. If everything desired by a greedy plunderer is to be deemed "unjust," then no wealth anywhere will ever be considered just. 

Another—and I speak here of many—incited by ambition, has disparaged the general authority of this Roman See because he did not wish to be subject to it, making himself the master of sacred things. This was the disease from which Constantinople suffered, as did Ravenna and, for a time, Milan and those bishops throughout Insubria <note>a region in northern Italy, centered around Milan</note>. But because they were led by pride to desire to be what their predecessors had not been, were they therefore just? For if they were, why do they not today, in their own conscience, desire that which they once claimed was fair and good? Their sin is manifest, and a figure of this very contention appeared in ancient times. 

Christ paid the didrachma <term>didrachma: a two-drachma coin used to pay the Jewish temple tax</term> for Himself and for Peter. Because of this, the other apostles reacted with human frailty and complained loudly: "Who do you think is greater in the kingdom of heaven?" <note>Matthew 18:1</note>. Peter is excused, and the Apostles are checked toward equality: "Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven" <note>Matthew 18:3</note>. Therefore, the sons are free by right; but so that they do not scandalize those who do not know better, they pay the didrachma and thus openly prove themselves to be free. Christ paid the didrachma for Himself and Peter so that He might relieve the sons of the heavenly kingdom from the laws of the world, ensuring there was no accusation of a "false liberty." Unless you wish the didrachma paid there in Peter to be given for you as well, Christ has not yet released you from the law of the world.

The last type of person is the denier of ecclesiastical power—and he is the worst of all—who either invents or follows impious opinions. Now, if the Church were as impious as those who stir up perverse dogmas claim it to be...

->PIGHARD,<-

Now this learned man finishes his scriptural [writing] against ours, in which he placed no probable or just obstacle, and so forth, until the point: "so that by doing penance here, he may obtain grace, and after this, eternal glory."

They mock Doctor Augustine <note>Likely referring to Saint Augustine of Hippo, whose writings were frequently cited by Catholics to combat the "Pighards," or potentially a contemporary Catholic polemicist.</note> as if he accused things he could not disprove; but at the time he was drawn into his confession, he showed that the frauds and trickeries of the Pighards were to be avoided, before anything else had come forth that he could refute by name. The confessions of the Pighards were non-existent, or rather, they were slippery and deceptive. Although many things—and the most certain ones—were known to the common people, just as we all know how clearly a Pighard differs from a Christian, yet if their impiety were spoken of plainly and from common rumor, it would happen that they would not be held to their own writing, so that they could be held to nothing by any wit. They would have denied everything and sworn that those things were not theirs, whatever they were challenged on. Thus, by another's evasion <note>original: *tergiuerfaciõe*; a legalistic term for "shuffling" or avoiding the issue.</note>, our labor would have fallen into vain. For that reason, Doctor Augustine could not more closely disprove the impiety of the Pighards. Grant that he could have disproved it, but surely he ought not have—namely, because those most abandoned men, had they trembled at the adversary's strength right at the beginning, would thereafter have been more cautious for themselves. Now, because he provoked them at first glance and then stood back without calling them closer, the Pighard believed he had the whole adversary [figured out]. Thus, his unadvised rusticity leaped into the open from a new and present work—which we are also writing now—from which the Pighard's impiety is held by his own confession. And today, if someone else were of such sharp wit that, while responding to the treachery of the Pighards, he made himself seem like one declining and fearing to join battle, that feigned timidness would give them audacity. And so today, for the Pighard to be struck as an enemy from afar, he will break out again with much more impure things. Therefore, let the Pighards accuse whatever they please. Our feigned delay is sufficiently consistent with our plan, through which we now hold them most firmly. As for their claim that the Doctor changed the points of their confession, it is a blatant lie, as we shall show more clearly from our fifth book; for they are the very ones who appear as different people from every page. They even say against the same Doctor: "If that man understood that we were speaking contrary to the faith in 그 confession, surely he would not have remained silent." Because Doctor Augustine did not remain silent, they remain just as impious and wicked now as he declared them to be in those letters of his. But they consider those letters to be nothing. Therefore, if they are "correct believers" because Doctor Augustine did not write against them, it follows by the same logic that they are "correct believers" because His Royal Majesty, by his own will, has not yet removed them and their treachery...

...they essentially strive to thrust ignorance of the Christian faith upon both His Royal Majesty and Doctor Augustine equally. For His Royal Majesty would not have suffered the Pighards if he had understood that they speak and feel things contrary to the Christian faith. Look at what a foul suspicion they cast upon His Royal Majesty, as if there were now something in the faith of the Pighards that the most Christian King has received and believed. But how the impiety of the Pighard has been able to remain safe under so pious a Prince until now—whether we have said it before or not yet—we certainly shall not inquire into the Royal councils. Yet I say this: so that they may protect their treachery from such a suspicion, that [defense] is most weak. For everyone will understand, from those things which we have now cited against their errors, that the Pighards are foul and detestable in all their impiety. It is the **charming face of the Scorpion**, while it plans a strike from the sting behind. Indeed, they wish to be and to be held as good—let them begin from their actions. They could never persuade us of true piety better or with less effort than by acting as Christians. For though they may fawn with words, yet nothing is more foreign to the Pighard than the manifestation of virtue.

Then they accuse Doctor Augustine <note>The author, Augustin Käsebrot, refers to himself in the third person. He was a prominent humanist and fierce opponent of the Bohemian Reformation.</note> of inciting His Royal Majesty to take vengeance upon the impious, and they think he is driven by that same spirit which once caused the prophets to be killed. Therefore, our Pighards make themselves out to have the merit of prophets, so that whoever thereafter attacks them is seen as attacking heavenly majesty. But this face of innocence is also a lie; or rather, let them first purge themselves of all the sacrileges for which they have been caught: most wicked traitors of divine worship, corrupters of the sacred canon of the Scriptures, and the [false] initiators of ecclesiastical holiness upon which this Christian state stands. They are mere deceivers of His Royal Majesty and the state of the kingdom—let them purge themselves of such great crimes which I have brought against them in the present work, and only then let them claim for themselves the merit of prophets, so that we might be said to sin against a Pighard with the same crime as one who sins against a Prophet of God. 

But now, because Doctor Augustine cannot endure their treachery, because he contradicts them, and because he desires it to be torn out from the world, his spirit is surely that of the one who says: *The zeal for your house has consumed me* <note>original: "Zelus domus tue comedit me"; a reference to Psalm 69:9, used to justify righteous anger or holy "violence" in defense of the Church.</note>. It is his spirit, I say, which in the Prophet Elijah killed the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves. 

They mention afterwards how the persecutors of good and just men insinuate themselves to princes and strengthen their impious hands. Does the most pious King Wladislaus <note>Wladislaus II (r. 1471–1516), King of Bohemia and Hungary.</note>, then, have impious hands, destined at last to shed blood when the exhorter of the crime approaches? But since they try to frighten the exhorter, Doctor Augustine, with the threat of divine vengeance, then the "impious" hands of the king must be restraining themselves below their own severity. O poisonous serpent! O infector of royal majesty! Thus His Royal Majesty listens to your feigned innocence, to your lying prologues, and to your doubtful epilogues. Thus he allows your arts to remain unharmed so that his majesty may be wounded from a hidden place—not content to have done this once. But this is now the third time that you violate that untainted and sacrosanct majesty. 

Such was that old saying: *they did not call upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear* <note>original: "dominum non inuocauerunt illic trepidauerunt timore ubi non erat timor"; a quote from Psalm 14/53 describing the foolishness of the godless.</note>. Just as they do now regarding the saints and holy women; such was it when you profaned the church; when you cast out our priesthood—so that by your lurking fraud you might cast out just parents, a just wife, and just children from a powerful King and from all Christian people. Now you accuse His Royal Majesty of the crime of persecutors, and claim that nothing is lacking for the perpetration of the crime except an exhorter. It is near, O deadly Pighard, that you may shake me from my purpose, that I may change my speech and appeal to His Royal Majesty—to explain that unless the Pighards are resisted even in small matters, this Royal indulgence will one day bring the greatest ruin to the kingdom and the whole Christian world. For anyone who has become a public enemy of religion rages no less, and perhaps even more, than one who fights for the sake of earthly possession...

### CONCERNING THE PRIESTHOOD AND THE WHOLE CHURCH AGAINST...

...they defend, and all similar things readily agree. Why do they not either compromise or pretend not to see the errors of the Roman Church as easily as they do the errors of others? But such a man cannot be safe under this Lord, nor can he excuse his blasphemies under this censure with impunity. Thus, just as a deserter speaks against every just command, so the Roman authority is disparaged as if the Pighard believed it were itself unjust. That Pighard <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren, or *Unitas Fratrum*, used by their critics to link them to the "Picards," an earlier heretical group.</note> accuses the Roman Church for every possible reason and charges it with crimes, so that he might remain unpunished for a long time. He denies the Apostolic faith so that he may be compelled to stand by no one’s judgment concerning his heresy; he denies Apostolic obedience and has removed the Guardian from himself, so that he may frolic through errors like a **wild ass in the woods**. He makes himself the dispenser of the sacraments and of the merit of Christ’s passion; he strives to enter heaven not through the public port, but by a **secret ford** like a little bandit. Since this Pighard has mocked our obedience, by what great reasons does he defend such childishness? Unless, perhaps, dreams drive him, and just as in a kingdom where—as it is said—**monkeys rule**, they only perform the images of a republic rather than actual affairs; so the Pighard exhibits the image of the Christian thing, but not its power.

->PIGHARD,<-

Now, this learned man finishes his writing of the scriptures against ours, in which he has placed no probable or just obstacle, and so forth, until the point where he says that "here, doing penance, he may obtain grace and after this eternal glory."

They taunt Doctor Augustine <note>The author, Augustin Käsebrot, writing about himself in the third person.</note> as if he had accused things that he could not disprove. But at the time he attacked the confession of the Pighards and showed that their frauds and deceits were to be avoided, nothing else had yet come forward that he could refute by name. The confessions of the Pighards were non-existent—or rather, they were slippery and deceptive. It was common knowledge, as clearly as we all know the Pighard differs from the Christian, yet if their impiety had been spoken of plainly and based only on common rumor, it would have happened—since they were not held to their own written words—that they could not have been pinned down by any wit. They would have denied everything and sworn that those views were not theirs, regardless of the charges brought against them. Thus, through the evasion of others, our labor would have been wasted. For that reason, Doctor Augustine could not disprove the Pighards’ impiety more directly. 

Even if he could have disproved it, he certainly should not have; for those most abandoned men, if they had trembled at the enemy's strength right at the start, would have been more cautious thereafter. But because he provoked them only at first glance and then stood back, without challenging them more closely, the Pighard believed he had the better of his adversary. Thus, their rash ignorance leaped out into the open from this new and present work—the very one we are writing now—in which the Pighard's impiety is caught by his own confession. And today, if someone else were of such sharp wit that, while responding to the Pighards' treachery, he made himself appear similar to one who avoids and fears a direct encounter, that feigned timidity would give them the audacity to strike at him as an enemy. Then the Pighards would break out again from far more impure depths.

Therefore, let the Pighards accuse whatever they please. Our pretense of hesitation is well-founded in strategy, for it is by this that we now hold them most firmly. Furthermore, when they say that the Doctor changed the points of their confession, it is an **open lie**, as we shall show more clearly in our fifth book, because those very men are the ones who produce different versions on every page. They even say against the same Doctor: "If that man understood us to be speaking contrary to the faith in that confession, surely he would not keep silent." Because Doctor Augustine did not remain silent, they remain as impious and wicked now as he declared them to be in those letters of his. But they consider those letters to be nothing. Therefore, if they are "correct believers" simply because Doctor Augustine did not write against them, it follows by the same token that because His Royal Majesty <note>King Wladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary.</note> did not, by his own will, remove them and their treachery, they must be correct believers.

### WALDENSIANS: BOOK FOUR

...they necessarily exist—so that they may now thrust their ignorance of the Christian faith, with a single effort and equally, upon the Royal Majesty and upon Doctor Augustine. For the Royal Majesty would not have tolerated the Pighards <note>A derogatory nickname for the Bohemian Brethren, or *Unitas Fratrum*, used to link them to the heretical Picards of France.</note> if he had understood that they speak and feel things contrary to the Christian faith. Behold the foul suspicion they cast upon the Royal Majesty, as if there were now something in the faith of the Pighards that the most Christian King has accepted and believed! But as to how the Pighards' impiety has been able to remain safe until now under so pious a Prince—whether we have spoken of that before or have not yet done so—we certainly shall not inquire into the King’s private councils. I say only this: that they may protect their treachery from such suspicion, but that defense is very weak. For everyone will understand, from the facts we have just cited against their errors, that the Pighards are foully impious and detestable. 

The charming face of the **Scorpion** meditates on the sting from the tail behind; if they truly wish to be and be held as good men, let them begin with their actions. They could never persuade us of true piety better or with less effort than by acting like Christians. For though they may use flattering words, nothing is further from the Pighard than the display of virtue. Next, they accuse Doctor Augustine of driving the Royal Majesty toward the punishment of the impious, and they think he is driven by that same spirit which once saw to it that the prophets were killed. Therefore, our Pighards make themselves heirs to the merit of the prophets, so that whoever attacks them thereafter is seen as attacking heavenly majesty! 

Truly, even this face of innocence is a lie. Let them first purge themselves of all the sacrileges in which they have been caught: most wicked traitors of divine veneration, corruptors of the holy canon of Scripture, deniers of that ecclesiastical holiness upon which this Christian state stands, and mere colluders against the Royal Majesty and the state of the kingdom. Let them purge themselves of such great crimes which I have brought against them in the present work, and only then let them claim the merit of the prophets, so that we might be guilty of the same sin against a Pighard as we would be against a Prophet of God. 

But now, because Doctor Augustine cannot endure their treachery, because he contradicts them, and because he desires their sect to be uprooted from the earth, he is surely driven by that spirit which says: **"The zeal for your house has consumed me"** <note>original: "Zelus domus tuae comedit me" — a quote from Psalm 69:9, famously applied to Jesus cleansing the Temple.</note>. It is, I say, that same spirit which, through the Prophet Elijah, killed four hundred and fifty **Prophets of Baal** and four hundred prophets of the groves <note>Referring to the biblical contest on Mount Carmel in 1 Kings 18.</note>. 

They mention afterwards how the persecutors of the good and the just insinuate themselves with princes and strengthen their impious hands. Does this mean even the most pious King Wladislaus has "impious hands," destined at last for blood whenever an inciter of crime approaches? But since the King is deterred from the threat of divine vengeance by his counselor, Doctor Augustine, then the "impious hands" of the King must be restraining themselves from their own cruelty! 

O **pernicious serpent**! O infector of royal majesty! Thus may the Royal Majesty listen to your feigned innocence, your lying prologues, and your doubtful epilogues. Thus he allows your arts to remain unharmed so that his Majesty might be wounded from the shadows—not content to have done this once, but this is now the third time you violate his untainted and sacrosanct majesty! Such was that old saying: *they did not call upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear* <note>Psalm 14:4-5</note>. Just as they do now regarding the saints, and such was it when you profaned the Church and cast out our priesthood—so that by your hidden fraud you might cast out righteous parents, a righteous wife, and righteous children from the powerful King, as you would from all Christian people. 

Now you accuse the Royal Majesty of the crime of persecutors; you, who lack nothing for the commission of a crime except someone to urge it! It is almost enough, O deadly Pighard, to shake me from my purpose, to make me change my tone and appeal to the Royal Majesty—explaining that unless the Pighards are resisted even in small matters, this royal indulgence will one day bring the greatest ruin to the kingdom and the whole Christian world. For anyone who has been made a public enemy of religion rages no less, or even more, than one who rages over a dispute for earthly possession...

# ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST

...he has made himself a declared enemy to the kingdom. After this, they threaten divine wrath upon anyone who attempts to trouble them concerning their impiety. Hey there, you public plague, you **Pighard** <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren, intended to link them to the heretical Picard sect.</note>! Since you claim to be such a friend to God, what proof of such great merit do you offer? Are you not the one who, by your treachery, gives us this present labor? Is it so that you might be counted among the number of the saints, and we who persecute you might be counted among the number of the enemies of Christ? 

What so pious do we find on your part? You have put forward prologues cloaked in words of innocence, and deceitful <term>entrances and exits</term> <note>original: "Ingressus egressusq[ue]" — likely referring to the rhetorical structure of their published apologies or their public conduct.</note> of your work. By these tricks alone, you labor to cast a cloud before our eyes; but otherwise, you have stuffed your inner parts full of every filthy sacrilege. And yet you labor so that we might yield in our faith! You even threaten, most wicked one, divine wrath upon all who resist you for such a great crime. 

What would you do if you added miracles, and fulfilled your arrival according to the <term>working of Satan</term> <note>original: "operacionem Sathane" — a reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:9, which describes the coming of the Antichrist with "lying wonders."</note> with all power and signs and lying wonders, and every deception of wickedness for those who are perishing? You most impure man, would you strike down the **Christian confession** for this reason, so that you might be thought of as someone great in virtue and faith? Certainly not! Cease then, you madman! 

For the Christian conscience recognizes the hissings of the most wicked serpent <note>An allusion to the Devil in the Garden of Eden, suggesting the Pighards' words are diabolically inspired.</note> who speaks these things through you. Therefore, it is not deterred by the threat of an angry God; it is too firm for you to shake it with that light spirit of yours. And it holds you—however much you threaten—you, I say, impure, treacherous, sacrilegious, an overturner of divine and human affairs, and detestable in all things; so it names you and pursues you.

### FIFTH BOOK ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST THE PIGHARDS,

Just as one who has crossed a distant and deep sea is more eager to cross the channels of the **Euripus** <note>original: "Euripos" — referring to the Euripus Strait in Greece, famous for its strong and unpredictable currents; here used as a metaphor for difficult passages.</note>, estuaries, and rivers, or to graze the nearby shore, so too, most Reverend Prelate, after the labor of the previous books—which seemed to grow the more I put into them and refused to reach an end—I consider that work completed. I now approach what remains of the work, which we have dedicated to your Episcopal Authority, with renewed vigor. There remains for us that discussion concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. In this matter, the **Pighard** <note>A derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren, a Christian group in the Czech lands that the author considers heretical.</note>, who felt things alien to piety in the earlier sections, now holds views that are even more monstrous.

The causes of his sacrilegious error are readily apparent. One cause is constant for him: he has denied the faith of heavenly things. Because he has conspired to be an enemy of the Church, he chooses to think nothing is pious or pure if it is something he would have to believe in common with us. The second cause, specific to this matter, is that the unspeakable craftsman of errors, the Pighard, perceives that we believe many or even all things regarding this most divine sacrament which exist beyond the capacity of nature and beyond the human comprehension of reason. Thus, he mocks our faith as if it were unthinkable. In place of our beliefs, he offers nothing but common, vulgar ideas, exposed to his own rustic understanding, and he dishonors this most divine sacrament in unworthy ways with mournful sacrileges. He strips the almighty majesty of God of its power. Although we shall speak more regarding this crime of the Pighard in its proper place later, it is not out of place to mention a few things now.

If, therefore, the Pighard admits nothing to be believed concerning sincere faith except what he can grasp, then in that same case, he must either comprehend the infinite and incomprehensible God within his own imagination to believe rightly of God, or, because he does not comprehend God, he will believe in God according to the idols by which he has defined the nature of God within himself. Thus, he is now neither able nor willing to feel and believe rightly concerning the most blessed and incomprehensible Divinity. But he who believes only what he comprehends believes nothing at all. For faith, says **Saint Paul**, "is the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" <note>original: "Eſt ſperandarū ſubſtancia rerum, Argumentū non apparenciū" — a quotation from Hebrews 11:1.</note>. We have heard that faith is the "evidence of things not seen"; therefore, that Pighard who believes only what is apparent to him has surely fallen away from the nature of faith. We should no longer wonder how he could ever fall into such execrable errors; for he interprets the faith of heavenly things not according to its own nature, but according to the narrow confines of his own demented brain. 

Thus, he places boundaries on the omnipotence of God and throws on chains, so that now God cannot do whatever the Pighard cannot grasp the "how" of. But let us refute such profound stupidity with more arguments. In the beginning, God created things of two kinds: Heaven and Earth; the invisible and the visible creature, the incorporeal and the corporeal, **act and potency** <note>original: "actum & potenciā" — technical philosophical terms: "act" refers to the current reality of a thing, while "potency" refers to its potential to change or become something else.</note>, matter and form—all things difficult to apprehend. Nothing of these things would exist if they depended on what the Pighard has managed to perceive.

Furthermore, God has set before both types of creatures two things to be contemplated: Himself and the world. Both are immense—the world according to human estimation and capacity, but He Himself is truly immense and without limit. Only the Angels and all the blessed spirits have the world's immensity beneath them; but they look upon the divine omnipotence with their own eyes. Even through all the ages that have passed and those that will come without end, they cannot yet, nor will they ever be able to, fully conceive of the divine majesty in its innermost parts, to penetrate it, or to drain it to the bottom. This unending immensity grazes the blessed; but if they were to grasp it in its full power, then either God would no longer be immense (having been encompassed by a "measured" thing, that is, a creature whose progress has a limit and an end), or the creature itself would become immense because it had enclosed the infinite within itself.

Aa iiij

<meta>This page continues the polemic against the Bohemian Brethren ("Pighards") regarding the Eucharist. It transitions from the theological argument for God's omnipotence—which the author claims the Pighards limit based on their own physical understanding—to an accusation of hypocrisy in their formal confessions of faith.</meta>

->### ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST THE PIGHARDS<-

Indeed, no creature was ever made who could contain eternity within itself; therefore, God remains forever immense, incomprehensible, and omnipotent to the spiritual creature. He truly **made darkness his hiding place** <note>original: "tenebras latibulum ſuum" — a reference to Psalm 18:11, suggesting that God's essence is hidden from human sight.</note>. This heavenly capacity, the Pighard <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren, used here to suggest they are "Picards" or heretics.</note> attempts to conquer with his earthly mass; he tries to open this hiding place of God, this bosom of divinity. According to him, this is now what God is—this limit and this power which the Pighard has fashioned for himself out of physical measurements. By this meager standard, the Pighard denies the power and truth of the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ.

He speaks from earthly filth; he speaks from the field with rakes and hoes. He, who has not yet grasped the power of nature, presumes to step over heavenly things. He sets a limit to super-heavenly power. Indeed, let us drag down this mad senselessness from that height to which Satan fell into hell when he attempted to ascend, never to be restored. Let the Pighard experiment in this immense world; let him place its vast spaces before his eyes as he is accustomed to look at the fist of his own hand; let him explain the causes of natural things within it. Let him restore to us that knowledge of **Solomon** <note>King Solomon was traditionally credited with a supernatural understanding of all nature.</note> whose loss we suffer; for Solomon **disputed about trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; and he discoursed on beasts, and birds, and creeping things, and fish** <note>original: "diſputauit em̄ ſuper lignis a cedro... vſqƺ ad hyſopum... & piſcib⁹" — a paraphrase of 1 Kings 4:33.</note>.

Let him now restore those labors; for surely nothing of worldly things can be hidden from a man who so easily defines divine omnipotence! But here we hold him: let him perform these tasks from the things nearest to him; let him offer proof from things that are at the very boundary of human limitation. If he is ignorant of these, how can he not be utterly ignorant when it comes to providing a faithful account of the power of heavenly things? Therefore, let the Pighard cease to bark for this reason against men of better faith. Let him cease to aim his trifles about the **sacrament of the altar** <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> at the whole world. Nor should he think that what the senses do not grasp cannot happen; for intellects, just like bodies, have their own limits. 

For behold: what prison, what shackles, what walls, or what rampart, or what lord’s command prevents us from flying up into the open air? It is not because the riverbanks are high everywhere; often the river and its bed end in level sand. What do you object to the fish here, that they do not graze outside the water? **Nature is the goal of things** <note>original: "Natura meta rerū"</note>. Thus, God has given to the intellect inborn limits at which it must remain. Consequently, those who circumscribe God’s omnipotence and the logic of things to be believed out of their own heads are not only ridiculous, but wicked. Thus we have exploded this first approach of the Pighards, from which they think wrongly about the sacrament of the altar. 

And so, with the omnipotence of God asserted once more against their own error—for they have never stood by the truth, yet in this matter they are especially perplexed—they act just as if they were turning something scalding hot in their mouths. They continually change the words coming out of their cheeks. From such beginnings, I say, it will be very easy for us to strike those little thieves for their impiety. And now, we expect nothing but the encounter.

## THE PIGHARD

They falsely argue against us that this confession of ours is not genuine, on the grounds that we write one thing about the sacrament of the body of Christ and believe another... and so on up to this point: *Because he does not hold the right faith*, as we have said in our Latin letters. Such things the Pighards offer us concerning their faith on the sacrament of the altar, yet they do not yet fully see themselves for who they are. But just as in that **Apology** <note>original: "Apologia" — referring to a formal written defense of their faith published by the Bohemian Brethren.</note> of theirs in the past, they had masked their own face and feigned ours by using the words of the Christian faith, so today they say the same things as we do with their tongues, but in spirit and opinion they are very far away. We hold them guilty of such a crime even today by their own fault, since they write all these things for no other reason than to cover themselves so that they might appear just before men.

<meta>This page continues the polemic against the Bohemian Brethren (disparagingly called "Pighards"), focusing on the exact wording of their confession regarding the Eucharist. The author argues that while their formal statements might sound orthodox, their underlying theology is deceptive and fraudulent because they refuse to accept the physical change of substance (transubstantiation) or the adoration of the Host.</meta>

<header>THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE</header>

They appear most cunningly and most vainly; therefore they say: "Standing that bread for his body, he showed it over the bread and said..." If Christ, therefore, took the bread into his venerable hands—as they say again—with what other fingers did he show it over the bread? <note>The author is mocking the Pighards' overly literal or peculiar description of the Last Supper, suggesting they are imagining Christ using extra fingers to point at the bread while holding it.</note> Lest they attribute to God a sermon about fingers, or those bodily gestures which a man avoids when he is even slightly delayed. Truly, what is it that they speak so circumspectly? What does that diligence of words produce in secret? I do not understand, and yet I suspect it is not without fraud. But whatever it may be from which they received so express a representation of that deed—"standing the bread for his body, he showed it over the bread"—they have accused us as if we confess our faith outside the words of the Lord. Certainly, we confess our beliefs from the words of the Lord, whereas those words of theirs exist nowhere in scripture. They are, therefore, far too scrupulous there, and they truly commit a fault in that for which they accuse others. After those things, they propose their faith:

[ Whenever, according to the sense of the Savior and the ordinance of the holy undivided Trinity, a worthy priest makes a prayer with his faithful people and says with that word: **"This is my body,"** and **"This is my blood,"** immediately the bread present is the body of Christ given unto death, and the wine present is his blood poured out for the redemption of sins. ]

Here they play with us again from their usual hiding places, but we have long since exploded those trifles and extorted them from them. Let them no longer require that "ordinance of the holy undivided Trinity," nor that "worthy priest," nor that "faithful people" on their part. <note>The author argues that the validity of the Sacrament depends on the power of Christ's words, not the personal holiness of the priest or the people, which was a major point of contention between Catholics and "heretical" groups like the Waldensians.</note> But I go further into the matter: we confess the same. Wherever a legitimate priest says those words of consecration, immediately the bread present is the body of Christ given unto death, and the wine present is his blood poured out for the redemption of sins. If they, therefore, are pure and manifest in this, why do they still contend? Why do they turn away from us? Why do the Pighards <note>term: Pighardi (Pighards). A derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren or Hussites, often used to link them to the older "Picard" heretics.</note> not confess themselves to be Christians? Certainly, however, they practice a hidden deceit and a fraud. As I have said once before: they deal with us one way, write another, and feel yet another. 

But let us now weigh these things. If what they write is what they also feel—and the bread is, as they say, the present body of Christ and the wine his blood—then do they also confess that a conversion of the substance <note>original: "cōuersionem substancie" — referring to Transubstantiation, the Catholic doctrine that the essence of bread becomes the essence of Christ's body.</note> of the species of bread and wine occurs? And they would become one with us in believing what they say they hold against the foundation of the words of the Lord—in which they do not believe it is contained that *this* becomes *that*. Therefore, although they write this part of the confession and say it with their mouths, they nevertheless feel differently from it in their souls. And we have extracted this first lie from them: that they do not purely and truly accept that phrase, **"This is my body,"** just as they themselves admit regarding those words:

[ For such a confession of faith has no foundation in the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, who spoke no word about the conversion of substance. ]

And later:

[ And that they believed this bread not only to be the body of Christ but also in the proper substance of bread with its own accidents after the consecration. ] <note>term: accidents (accidētib⁹). In scholastic philosophy, "accidents" are the physical properties of a thing (like smell, taste, or color) that remain even if the internal "substance" changes.</note>

But they cannot sincerely believe even this. For it would have followed that they would worship Christ as present, which is the one thing they stubbornly refuse. It would have followed that multiple singular existences would penetrate each other under the *suppositum* <note>term: suppositum. A technical term in logic and theology referring to the individual substance or "person" that underlies properties.</note> of one individual. Furthermore, they said that this has no foundation in the words of the Lord—namely, those in which it is not said "Under these species," nor "in that," nor "together with that is my body." And they say this truly. For containers do not receive into themselves the significance or the demonstration of the things they contain, nor are they spoken of in a direct mode of speaking, but indirectly toward one another. But if Christ spoke in a direct mode—**"This is my body"**—then we Christians rightly confess that now only that, and besides that nothing of a different substance, is under these species. However, the Pighards disapprove of this faith, by which they say...

# ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST <note>The title is incomplete in the original, but the context indicates it is "Against the Pighards" (the Bohemian Brethren).</note>

They claim that our faith has no foundation in the words of the Lord. And yet Christ said, **"This is my Body," "This is my Blood."** There are no metaphors there, no figures or parables. Real things are presented there and pure words; we give a direct sense to direct words without any detours. Therefore, do we not receive our faith from the gospel? Indeed, we believe that Christ is present in the Sacrament by the operation of the divine word just as we believe creation was made when God likewise said, **"Let there be light,"** and light was made. Unless we confess it so, Truth <note>The author uses "Truth" as a title for Christ.</note> spoke falsely; He spoke and it was not done so. Nevertheless, they think this kind of confession does not agree with the gospel because no word is spoken there concerning the "conversion of substance" <term>transubstantiation: the doctrine that the substance of bread and wine changes into the body and blood of Christ</term>. But listen here, you Pighard, stop! These detours belong to the devil. They are handles for one who is seeking a fight for no reason.

Listen to a nearby example of this matter. Moses writes: "The earth was empty and void," and God also said, "Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind, cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their species," and it was done so. Here, if what God said was done, the earth—even if Moses said not a single word about "conversion"—was required to be transformed into a living nature. So it is in our case: because Christ said, **"This is my body,"** so that this thing might become what God said, the substance of the bread passed into the body of Christ.

After this, they contend that the phrase "breaking of bread" was used for the mystery of the Sacrament of the altar. I do not know if they spoke this way specifically in the time of the Apostles, but we have understood that the communion was called a *synaxis* <note>original: "synaxin," from the Greek for "assembly" or "gathering"</note> and a collection, while the "breaking of bread" signified the daily custom of Christ's disciples for the nourishment of the body. This is how Christ is said to have broken five and seven loaves for the five thousand and again the four thousand men; that multitude certainly did not communicate in the body and blood of Christ then. In another place Luke writes: "On the first day of the week, when we had come together to break bread, Paul disputed with them, being about to depart on the morrow," and again, "Ascending and breaking bread and tasting it." He said this concerning bodily nourishment, just as in another place: "Peter went up to the higher parts to pray about the sixth hour, and when he became hungry, he wished to taste [food]."

For this reason, the present passage in the Acts of the Apostles, which the Pighards cite, refers not to the mystery of the sacrament of the altar (as they falsely explain it) but to the shared living of daily necessity. Scripture is a witness to this statement of ours, which adds shortly after in this sense: "In those days, the number of disciples increasing, there arose a murmuring of the Greeks against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily ministry. Then the twelve, calling together the multitude of the disciples, said: 'It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables.'" Here, if the Pighard truly accepts the "breaking of bread" as the communion of the body and blood of Christ, then it would mean the Apostles did not want to minister at the tables because they committed the office of the ministry of the altar—which belonged only to priests—to the deacons.

But let us descend to more recent matters. After they said <insert>[</insert> they believed this bread was not only the body of Christ, but also remained in its own substance of bread along with its accidents after the consecration <insert>]</insert> <note>The "accidents" are the physical properties like taste and smell; the author is accusing them of "consubstantiation"—the belief that bread and Christ's body exist together.</note>, lest they be thought to have fashioned this from their own heads, they saw fit to bring in the Apostle: "As often as you shall eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall announce the death of the Lord until he comes." But how does this confirm the error of the Pighard? Do either the words or the sense agree on both sides? No; but in such a way they impose upon the unlearned common people. But let us uncover the frauds of the most wicked Pighard. Therefore, in only one way, by the word "bread," they corrupt both the sense of the Apostle and the integrity of the true faith.

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE

[...they claim] and wish to argue that the Apostle would never have said "bread" unless material bread truly existed within the same appearances together with the body of Christ. But if the Pighards <note>A derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren, possibly derived from "Picards," a group often associated with the Waldensians.</note> do not impose this sense upon the Apostle's words out of some fallacy and their own lie, then consider this: when Christ said, **"This is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die,"** it would be necessary in this passage as well to understand some other bread outside the nature of Christ, yet coexisting with Him under the same appearances. But what bakers <term>Artoptae: a Greek-derived term for professional bread-bakers</term> baked that bread then? Or under the appearances of what bread was Christ then hiding when He could say—according to the treachery <note>Original: "perfidiam," a common polemic term for lack of orthodox faith.</note> of the Pighard—**"This is the bread descending from heaven"**?

Do you perceive, Christian people, the insanities of the Pighard by which he mocks you from this passage of the Apostle? From this most lying brain he rouses new impieties against us, saying that the existence of a double nature—namely, both the body of Christ and natural bread—is contained under the same appearances of the Sacrament. But the Pighard lies against the Apostle and the Gospel alike. For that bread is the same as the flesh of Christ. For thus the Gospel has it: **"That bread is true which descends from heaven and gives life to the world."** **"I am,"** says Christ, **"the living bread who descended from heaven."** By no diverse nature are this bread and Christ distinguished there; they are one both in nature and in place in this Sacrament, just as He says again, **"The bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world. This is the bread which descended from heaven."** 

From these words, let the most lying Pighard return to us with his treachery and say that they believed this bread was not only the body of Christ, but also bread in its own substance along with its accidents <term>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, the physical properties (like taste, smell, or color) that remain even after the underlying substance has changed</term>. Most vain heretic! If he were truthful in that sense of his, why did he not also cite these Gospel passages against us? But if the Gospel most directly accused such treachery, why did they betray the Gospel so they might remain treacherous? They passed it by and suppressed it as if they had not yet seen it. They corrupted the Apostle for their own treachery, as if he had received the Gospel not in the third heaven but within the Pighard's secret assembly <note>Original: "conciliabulum," used here to suggest an illicit or heretical meeting rather than a true council of the church.</note>. 

But hey, you most wicked Pighard, do you grant so little to conscience? You suppressed the Gospel, you cast out the Apostle from his own meaning, and you corrupted him for your own heresy. That was once your horrendous protestation; thus you held the royal ears with your lie when you wrote:

> "For we testify before the living God, who will judge the world in equity, that we have never been found to assert or babble anything heretical or blasphemous, neither against God, nor against the orthodox faith, nor against the Eucharist of the Body and Blood of Christ, nor finally against the blessed Virgin, nor at all against the saints of God."

Behold, the most impure lies! And from these, do you boast that you are inspired by the Holy Spirit for this present heresy? If we strike out these lies of yours, this most dreadful heresy, you would bring forth against us the threat of divine judgment, saying:

> "that we ought to fear entirely unless we leave you in peace, lest the plague of God come upon us"

and you pray that God, out of His love, may convert such people. Therefore, let Him convert them and make them Pighards! What fruit will there be? Naturally, so that He may have more enemies of the divine name, of the Gospel, of the Apostles, and of all heavenly piety. But let us pursue the rest. As if they had legitimately proved their treachery from Scripture, they then infer another point: **"From this it is manifest that the primitive church held this faith."** Therefore, what witnesses have they called for their treachery? They corrupted the Apostle; they suppressed the Gospel. To whom else do they demand that we stand?
