-># WALDENSIANS, BOOK FIVE #<-

revealed. We also, with great consideration, weight, and at leisure, have read and reread all their writings. We found them to be in no way more innocent; indeed, they were found by us to be the most harmful of all. However, those letters which they sent to everyone I have not yet seen, for they remained in their native language <note>The author refers to the Czech or German vernacular used by the Bohemian Brethren, which he apparently could not read directly.</note>. I believe, however, that just as they did then, so in their present labor they would not wish to omit anything they thought might significantly aid themselves and their cause. But in the present matter, they act with nothing but lies; they believe the same things on both sides, yet have conducted other matters with falsehoods. For perfidy <note>faithlessness or treachery</note> cannot bear to be confirmed by truths. Nothing less do they do than provoke Doctor Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the most influential Western theologian, whom both sides claimed as an authority.</note> to answer them. Therefore, we have answered. And if now we plead our case not before their accomplices, but before all the sincere nobility—those who tremble before the Divinity, the Gospel, the Apostles, and the Christian truth, and who believe that the state of their souls is set toward either eternal happiness or damnation, and not toward distant fables—I shall hope that the conscience of all sincere nobility has been so instructed by our work against the perfidy, sacrileges, and every wicked crime of the Pighard <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren</note> that I might have answered to their great misfortune.

They subjoin: "therefore believing that bread and wine, according to the word of the Savior, is his body and blood, we obey his commands." They do not obey. And it is a true confession if it does not deviate from the words of the Lord. But they say this so coldly that I plainly fear nothing is being shown to us except the bare tips of letters <note>original: "nudos apices," meaning the literal surface of the text without depth or spirit</note>, empty of all power and meaning. Nor is the suspicion groundless, because they immediately add: **"we do not believe him to be personally on earth, nor do we receive those who show this same person to be here, nor do we follow them."** The Pighard speaks well here! And we give that up to his most contaminated sacrifice. 

Finally, they add from the same sentiment: **"But we believe that the bread and wine is the body and blood of Christ in the existence of the blessing <note>original: "in existencia benedictionis." This refers to the Utraquist or Brethren view that Christ is present through the power of the rite rather than a physical change of the bread's substance.</note>, made only for reception, use, and memory."** 

You who feel this now: in which place are you false, Pighard? Previously you said: [**"We believe that after the word is rightly consecrated by the priest, the Bread is immediately the true, natural body of Christ taken from the Virgin Mary, which had to be handed over."**] If the body of Christ which "had to be handed over" is that which is in the Sacrament, then Christ exists in the nature of one person both at the right hand of the Father and in the Sacrament. If, on the other hand, you do not receive the nature of that same person of Christ in heaven and in the sacrament, then with what body did Christ suffer? That body will not now be in the Sacrament. See how these things agree with one another! Or rather, see how they do *not* agree, and how one is refuted by the other, leaving you in the middle as a liar and a waverer. 

You say you believe nothing less than the words of the Savior; therefore, by which of his words, or in what place of the Gospel, did you receive the idea that he is not in the nature of his person in the Sacrament, but only in the "existence of the blessing"? You are surely talking nonsense. You are inventing this, as you do all your things, from your own mind. Christ said, "This is my body." It is a just sentence that everything which is now called the body of Christ should be in the Sacrament. Believe the words of the Savior here; show the faith you promised. But you steal away the full power of the meaning when you snatch away the body, and you make it signify not as much as it ought, but as much as you wanted. You deny the body of Christ, and outside of the Gospel and the Apostles, you substitute I-know-not-what bread "in the existence of the blessing." 

But we shall refute this matter from itself. They take that point about the "person" too crudely, as if, if we confess that person to be in that existence at the right hand of the Father, no power remains for Christ to be able to be according to his own nature in the sacrament as well. Thus they place limits on the omnipotence of Christ, and they believe nothing can happen which they themselves cannot comprehend. Yet, while the rays of the sun subsist in the very source of light, they are nevertheless present in every place in that same substance of theirs by their illustration...

<meta>This page continues the author’s theological assault on the Pighards (the Bohemian Brethren). While the previous page addressed their perceived "perfidy" and "lies" regarding church authority, this page moves into the heart of the sacramental debate: whether Christ is physically or merely spiritually present in the bread and wine of the Altar.</meta>

# ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST [THE PIGHARDS]

They claim that Christ, sitting at the right hand of God, cannot—in his nature as both God and man—be made present here and there in the various places of the mystery of the altar through his glorified body, which is most obedient to God’s omnipotence. Yet concerning this, Wisdom has said: "For power is at your command whenever you desire" <note>original: "Subest enim tibi cum volueris posse." This is a quote from the Book of Wisdom 12:18, emphasizing that God's power is not limited by human logic.</note>. Therefore, I say to these Pighards <note>A derogatory term used by Catholic polemicists for the Bohemian Brethren, or "Unitas Fratrum."</note> exactly what the most holy widow Judith said to her own people: "Who are you to tempt the Lord?" This is not the kind of speech that provokes mercy, but rather one that excites anger and kindles fury. You have set a limit on the Lord’s power, and you have established an end to it based on your own judgment. 

They act as if they perceive all things holily and according to the Scriptures, and as if they have not confessed themselves to be enemies of the words of the Lord and the Gospel; thus they bring against us a charge of "disobedience" based on the Book of Samuel. However, after those facts which we have produced against them from their own writings—concerning their disobedience, rebellion, faithlessness, and the blasphemous war they wage against God—we most justly demand a reckoning. Indeed, those men, enemies to God, choke themselves on this passage from Samuel as if on a bitter pear <note>A metaphor suggesting that the very scripture they use for defense actually causes their own downfall or is "hard to swallow."</note>. Then, since they have said, "We do not believe Him to be personally on earth," yet it was necessary that *something* of Him be in the sacrament, they now state the ways in which Christ is present there: 

<insert>[Furthermore, according to His precepts, we receive Him in His powerful, spiritual majesty and honor Him in faith and obedience. And again: we believe that the bread and wine are the body of Christ in the existence of a blessing.]</insert> 

I do not wish to compare these contradictory feelings and words; rather, we shall weigh the matter itself: what it possesses inwardly by its own power. Therefore, in this mystery of the altar, since the true body of Christ—born of the Virgin, having suffered for us and been crucified—is contained under the appearances of bread and wine, it also signifies that <term>mystical body</term> <note>In traditional theology, the "mystical body" refers to the unity of the whole Church as a community, whereas the "true body" refers to Christ's physical flesh.</note> which is the unity of the Church under Christ the head. Our Pighards acknowledge *only* this mystical body of Christ in the sacrament. They believe the body and blood are received "spiritually" only, in the way that it is received by pious minds and those who receive it worthily according to the merit of invisible grace. 

If, therefore, nothing else is contained or received in the sacrament except this, and they completely turn away from us regarding the word "body," let us hold them to the terms "flesh" and "blood." These words are written in the canon of the Scriptures; they are accepted, as I recall, according to the significance of natural substance, just as in that passage: "The Word was made flesh." Christ, therefore, said: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you" <note>John 6:53</note>. Therefore, whatever force the receiving of His flesh and blood has, so shall we accept His existence in the sacrament and His very word: "This is my body." 

And I marvel that while those Pighards carry on so much regarding this sacrament, they have always been careful to avoid this one word—"flesh"—as if they would be committing a crime by admitting it. They have so diligently shunned it. They have also never cited the Gospel of John from his sixth chapter, where those words are read—"Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man"—as if that passage nowhere existed, or said very little to the point. They would have cited it, I suspect, if they could have snatched any handle for a malevolent contention from which they could impose some distorted meaning upon the truth of the sacrament. Thus, they resist using only the single word: "body." 

But even this word "body" is not so weak that it does not defend itself and its legitimate sense in its own place. For after the phrase "This is my body," it immediately follows: "which is given for you." If, therefore, that which was "given unto death" is the body of Christ in the sacrament, no one is ignorant of what kind of body of Christ is in the sacrament—for that "mystical body" [the Church] was neither "given" [to death] nor did it suffer; only the head, Christ, did so as a part on behalf of all the members. Finally, if only the mystical body of Christ is in the sacrament, and it is received only spiritually and according to invisible grace, then the wicked and all those who receive unworthily...

<meta>This page continues the polemic against the "Pighards" (the Bohemian Brethren), specifically focusing on the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist versus the Pighards' more symbolic or spiritual interpretation. The author argues that even those who do not receive the Sacrament with the right spirit still consume the "reality" of Christ's body, which is why they incur judgment.</meta>

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE

...although they perceive nothing of the Sacrament spiritually, they nonetheless consume the sacrament itself entirely. They claim they are not guilty of the body and blood of Christ; yet, in truth, certain people *are* guilty of His body and blood. For "he who eats unworthily," says the Apostle, "eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord." <note>original: "Nam qui manducat... indigne, iudicium sibi manducat..." A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:29, used here to argue that Christ is physically present even if the recipient is unworthy.</note> Therefore, there is in the sacrament a reality according to the truth of [His] natural existence; because of this, even those who do not remain in the unity of Christ and the Church—and thus do not receive spiritually—nevertheless consume it, and they are made guilty of it: the body of the Lord. Furthermore, they think that in their own way, by believing [only] in the "superior sacrament," <note>This likely refers to the Pighard view that Christ is only present "spiritually" in heaven, rather than physically in the bread.</note> the Scriptures and the Saints offer them no obstacle. On the contrary, by thus corrupting the Scriptures, suppressing them, and twisting them into a different meaning, they allow no defender to stand against their treachery. If they had not so wickedly ignored the Gospel and the Apostles, they could not have fallen into such nefarious errors. Is it therefore because nothing in Divine Scripture concedes anything from a pure and innocent sense to their error, that Scripture is not an impediment to their treachery? On the contrary, it is the greatest impediment.

They add: "If we believed the body of Jesus Christ was in the sacrament just as He sits at the right hand of the Father, we would truly be rebelling against His veneration." <note>The Pighards argued that if Christ were physically in the bread, it would lead to idolatry (venerating bread as God).</note> So now I hear how the Pighards <term>Pighards: a derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren, implying they were followers of the heretical "Picards" from Flanders.</term> might free themselves from the crime of impiety: let the truth of the sacrament pay the price! We would not contend much with a Pighard on that point—he would be treacherous to every whim at his own peril—but because he wounds the Divine Majesty, because he desires whatever he believes to be held as Apostolic, and because he circumvents the simplicity of our people with that [deceit], here we stand firm for our conscience. We show it to be necessary for him to believe not what he wishes, but what the Canon of Scripture and ancient holiness have prescribed according to the Gospel and the divinely commanded faith. Here, then, let either the Scripture yield to the Pighard, or the Pighard yield to the Scripture; which is more just does not require our judgment, as all understand it.

After this, they reject the truth of the sacrament based on the idea that if Christ were there, He would have warned the disciples and the others who believed in Him to worship before they consumed it. I have said before: if the truth of the sacrament were weakened by this, then because we read in no Scripture that the Apostles "adored" Christ [at the Last Supper], then Christ was no more God and man in His nature than He was adored by the Apostles. For if He had been, He would not have neglected His faithful (according to that same Pighard sophistry), but would have manifested to the Apostles that they should adore Him whenever they met Him on the road. They also say: "But He warned them not to commit idolatry." There, the Pighard lies. He gave no warning that veneration should not be offered; and he was so far from guarding against it that He even permitted Himself to be adored. But if the Apostles did not adore Christ while He dwelled with them in the "form of a servant," <note>original: "in forma servi." A reference to Philippians 2:7, describing Christ's humble human existence on Earth.</note> this example of the Apostles is by no means to be followed after the Resurrection and Christ's ascension into heaven.

And thus, regarding that passage of the Gospel: "But I tell you the truth: It is expedient for you that I go; for if I do not go, the Advocate will not come to you," <note>John 16:7.</note> Saint Augustine, in the first book of *On the Trinity*, discussed this passage as follows: "He said this not because of any inequality between the Word of God and the Holy Spirit, but as if the presence of the Son of Man among them were an impediment to the coming of Him who was not inferior, because He did not empty Himself by taking the form of a servant as the Son did. It was necessary, therefore, that the form of a servant be removed from their eyes, for in gazing upon it, they thought that Christ was only what they saw." <note>original: "Sanctus Augustinus libro de trinitate primo... Oportebat ergo vt auferretur ab oculis eorum forma servi." Augustine argues that the disciples' physical sight of Christ's humanity prevented them from perceiving His spiritual divinity.</note> This is also the source of that which He says: "If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I"; that is, "it is necessary for me to go to the Father for this reason: that while you see me thus, and from what you see, you judge that I am less than the Father; and thus, being occupied with the creature and the assumed habit, you do not understand the equality I have with the Father."

### ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST [THE PIGHARDS]

If, therefore, we today adopt that same act of the apostles—of honoring Christ—as our example, then Christ has not yet departed from us, nor has the Advocate <note>The Holy Spirit.</note> yet arrived. Even today He still says to us as the rising Savior: *Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.* <note>original: "Noli me tangere nondum enim ascendi ad Patrem meum." A quote from John 20:17.</note> For "touch," as Augustine says elsewhere, is like an ending of knowledge; therefore, He did not want the focus of a devoted heart to end in Him in such a way that He was thought of only as that which could be seen. For this reason, those who believe must follow the later examples of the Apostles, not the first ones, so that we might "sanctify the Lord Christ," as Peter says in his Epistle, "in our hearts," <note>1 Peter 3:15.</note> and so that "every knee should bow to Him," as the Apostle Paul says, "of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. And every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father." <note>Philippians 2:10–11.</note> Wherever that glory is, even in the Sacrament, Christ does not depart from it, nor does He fall away from it—just as the angel Raphael did not leave his blessed state and divine enjoyment while he was leading the younger Tobias on his journey and bringing him back. <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit, used here as an analogy for how Christ can be physically present on an altar without leaving His divine state in heaven.</note>

->PIGHARDVS,<-
<note>The author uses "Pighard" as a derogatory label for the Bohemian Brethren, a pre-Reformation Christian movement.</note>

Although we replied that we do not believe or think as he does, but rather as the words of faith demonstrate, and so on until that point. To conclude briefly, we teach in such a way that, by God’s help, we do not fear the snares that "clever hunter" <note>A sarcastic reference to the Pighard leader or theologian.</note> has set for us—as if before the eyes of birds—claiming that we must confess "two Christs."

Regarding those final remarks of the previous section, where they reproach us for our obedience to the Roman Pontiff: since we have responded more fully to this matter at the end of the fourth book, we rightly pass over it now. Ultimately, these claims are mere trifles, because we certainly confess our Christian faith based on a higher reason, and not because of the will of any particular Pope. We recognize and observe no one as the author of the Apostolic faith after the Savior and His Apostles, but we do recognize them as its defenders, judges, and stewards. In the same way, even in the smallest republic, we place the "sinews" of civil harmony and the judgment of the laws themselves in the hands of a single public magistrate. Therefore, let us hasten on to other matters which are served to us by the "synagogue of the devil" <note>A harsh polemical reference to Revelation 3:9.</note> regarding the Sacrament of faith from the "cup of Babylon." <note>Revelation 17:4.</note> He commends his own faith again, as he is accustomed to doing everywhere, as if he had derived it from the words of the Lord, the sense of the Apostle, and the rule of the primitive Church; yet he calls all these things into "faith" in word only, while in fact he wickedly overturns all of them in the present matter. Truly, we have often exposed those trifles before, and we have refuted their present evasions, for these Pighards play with us as if we were common peasants and they were traveling poison-sellers <note>term: "circulatores venenarij" (traveling poison-sellers). These were quack doctors or charlatans who sold fake medicines at fairs.</note> who claim all doctors as their witnesses in name only, yet are unable to cite any specific one from a specific place to support their deceptive antidotes—just as the peasant folk do not know any better. The people expect results from them, but they will never hear the promised truth.

Therefore, they first say that they confess only one Christ—wicked men!—as if it followed that if we confess the truth of the Sacrament, we no longer have one Lord, but rather as many Christs as there are places where the mysteries of the altar are celebrated. But as to how the same Christ is one in heaven and in the Sacrament: we shall explain this hereafter, to the measure of our ability, when they begin to question us concerning our faith. For now, we shall press them only on their own claims. They say Christ is in the Sacrament with His natural body; yet this is now contrary to his [the Pighard's] other claim, "Nor does He descend corporally with His body." He contradicts himself. We do not accept those who show that the same person is here [in one way] while they follow another [logic]. But come now: if Christ is in the Sacrament with His natural body, this natural body must follow His own person; and since the person of Christ is one, the unity of the individual follows the unity of the person.

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE

From this, therefore, in His natural body, Christ is one in heaven and in the Sacrament. Or, if we consider what they said previously—suppose we do not accept those who show the same person to be here—they say: If they believe this is true, and yet His natural body is in the Sacrament, this body will also bring its own person with it; therefore, Christ would exist from a person of double existence, in heaven and in the Sacrament. And because a multiplication of the person follows from the number of individuals, there would also be multiple Christs. Truly, they excuse themselves from this contradiction through some other existence I know not of, which they neither state explicitly, nor can or should we interpret it without their permission, unless they mean that which they once said: <note>The author is attacking the logic of the Brethren, who argued that physical presence in many places at once would imply multiple versions of Jesus.</note>

[We receive Him in His powerful spiritual majesty; and again, that the bread and wine are the body and blood of Christ in the existence of a blessing made only for reception, use, and memory.]

Therefore, if they understand Christ to exist in the Sacrament only as a sign of invisible grace, or only in His mystical body, even in this present place—since these things relate nothing of the natural body of Christ—they will then think of another existence of Christ in the Sacrament. Furthermore, they mention a certain spiritual flesh of Christ, both in this place and also later from these words: [We say that He is also present with spiritual flesh; and again: He cannot be received bodily by the souls of the faithful, but only spiritually, because He said: *The Spirit is the one who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.*] <note>original: "Spiritus est qui viuificat Caro non prodest quicq;" - A quote from John 6:63, often used by reformers to argue against the physical eating of Christ's flesh.</note>

If they say this now, just as the Apostle defined the nature of the righteous after the resurrection of the flesh—*It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body* <note>1 Corinthians 15:44. original: "Seminatur corpus animale surget corpus spiritale."</note>—they certainly speak well. And they can correctly call it not only spiritual flesh but even, according to the words of Saint Jerome, divine flesh; finally, they correctly receive the scripture: *The Spirit is the one who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.* But this spiritual flesh establishes nothing different in person and individual, but is the same in number and substance with the natural body, as Job confirms: *I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see and not another, and my eyes shall behold Him and not another.* <note>Job 19:25–27.</note>

But if, however, they speak of a certain spiritual flesh of Christ in the same way that angels are spirits, then they oppose both the Apostle and Job; finally, they break the confession of the rising Christ. Christ our Savior teaches the truth of His nature in which He rose to the Apostles, saying: *See my hands and feet, that it is I myself. Handle and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have.* <note>Luke 24:39.</note> Therefore, if they do not stand with us regarding the first opinion, let them no longer lie in wait for us regarding the latter sense concerning that spiritual flesh against the truth of the Scriptures.

For we receive in the Sacrament that natural flesh, taken from the Virgin, which suffered and died—that same flesh made spiritual in the Resurrection according to the sense of the Apostle Paul, into whose wounds from the nails and the spear the Apostle Thomas placed his hand, and which the wicked who pierced Him shall one day see; that same natural and spiritual flesh of Christ we receive in the Sacrament. As to whether His nature is multiplied in it—that, we agree with the Pighard <note>term: Pighardus. A common pejorative term for the Bohemian Brethren, who the author is debating.</note>. But as to the claim that because it is not divided into different subjects, it is therefore not in the Sacrament according to the truth of its nature—that, on the other hand, we deny against the Pighard, and we contend that he should not wish to cast shackles upon God's omnipotence. Rather, let him perpetually consider with himself that God does many things, even those which exist presently before our eyes, but how He has done them, men have not yet comprehended.

The author uses biblical analogies, such as the appearance of the Trinity to Abraham and the gathering of manna, to explain how Christ can be physically present in many places at once in the Eucharist without being "divided."</meta>

### ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST [THE PICARDS]

...the Trinity appeared to Abraham in the form of three men, and yet the one God is not divided into three natures but remained within Himself, and remains forever an indivisible God. God rained manna in the desert, and the children of Israel gathered it, some more and some less, and they measured it; and each one’s portion matched the measure of a Gomer <note>original: "Gomoret," an ancient Hebrew unit of volume used for dry goods like manna</note>. Neither he who had gathered more had extra, nor did he who had prepared less find he had too little. Instead, each individual gathered according to what they were able to eat. From these facts and examples set before the senses, let the Pighardi <term>Pighardi: A term for the "Picards" or Bohemian Brethren, a proto-Protestant group whose views on the Eucharist the author is attacking.</term> learn not to deny the omnipotence of God regarding His other hidden works. For just as it was then, so it is here and there and in the most diverse places: in the Sacrament, Christ is one and the same and undivided. Thus, wherever Christ is consecrated in the mystery of the altar, He is neither more extended in many places nor more contracted in few. Let them judge these things by these nearby examples, lest—because we attribute all highest and greatest things to God—they call us impious, while they themselves, who strip these same powers from God, actually confine God to the narrow limits of an earthly body. From the root of that same impiety they also attach the claim that He cannot be "bodily lifted up." Therefore, just as the Jews and those disciples who "went back" <note>A reference to John 6:66, where followers left Jesus after his teaching on the Bread of Life</note> were offended, so are the Pighardi scandalized by the Sacrament and say, "this is a hard saying, and who can hear it?" <note>original: "durus est hic sermo, & quis potest eum audire," quoting John 6:60</note> Truly, after those things we have now explained regarding the spiritual flesh of Christ, there will be no need at all to thrust such a coarse confession upon us, unless they wish to misrepresent everything and, beyond their own guilt, turn things for the worse so as to strike a stupor into the unlearned common folk regarding our confession.

Therefore, can a glorified body not be lifted? Certainly it can; for it is not "heavy" in the way that the heavens of heavens are not heavy, or as it was not heavy when He once ascended above all angelic, incorporeal excellence. Conversely, it is not "light" in the way that air, fire, and ether are light, since they are fixed by God in definite places and do not fly off into the extremes. Again, it is neither heavy nor light because it has been sublimated beyond the passions of corruptible matter. While He Himself remains unmoved at the right hand of the Father <note>original: "ad dexteram Patris," a standard creedal phrase</note>, He can just as well be "lifted" and "placed" in the Sacrament as the unmoved Divinity nevertheless "walked in Paradise in the breeze after midday" <note>A reference to God in the Garden of Eden, Genesis 3:8</note>, or departed from His host Abraham toward Sodom. Yet they invoke the divine Scriptures to support their perfidy, and they are both numerous and wordy in a matter that is both confessed and manifest. They desire that others believe the Gospel is denied by us as much as they seem to labor to uphold it themselves—which was not at all necessary. For even if we felt something contrary to the Gospel, it would have been enough for them to refute the opposing error with only one, or at most a second, sentence which they might bring forth regarding its true power; for in such matters, it is not the number of arguments but divine authority that prevails. Indeed, we agree with the Pighardi concerning Christ’s ascension into heaven. From our own viewpoint also comes Aurelius Augustine <note>original: "Aurelius Augustinus," the influential early Christian theologian St. Augustine</note>. Only at the end, when they conclude not the truth from the true Scriptures but their own suspicions, is where they diverge. There, so that we might not even be contrary to them, the Pighardi themselves depart in a different direction from their own previous opinion. For they deny that Christ is in the Sacrament in His body by which He ascended into heaven—and yet that is the very body by which He was born of the Virgin, suffered, and died. Since they have said so many times before that what was "given unto death" is present in the Sacrament after the words of consecration, they now deny that the same body of Christ offered unto death is in the Sacrament, for the reason that He ascended into heaven. If, therefore, Christ has departed so completely that He left nothing of Himself to us, I fear that according to that logic they will also be forced to understand the verse: "I came forth from the Father and came into the world..." <note>A reference to John 16:28, implying that if "leaving" means a total physical absence, then his "coming" must be interpreted in a similarly limited way</note>

"Again, I leave the world and go to the Father" <note>original: "Iterum relinquo mundum & vado ad Patrem"</note>. If we were to say that when He came from the Father and entered the womb of the Virgin, He descended into the world in such a way that, in the meantime, no part of Him remained in heaven, then I say: If this phrase "I leave the world and go to the Father"—and other Scriptures which the Picards <term>Picards: A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), who held a more symbolic view of the Eucharist.</term> bring against us with the same meaning—were taken as they suggest, they would leave us with nothing by which Christ could have both ascended to the Father and yet remained, and still remain, with His Church. Certainly, therefore, what they desire to be understood by everyone against us would then be understood by everyone and toward all; so that even their own claim—"He is nevertheless here spiritually and powerfully"—could not rightly be admitted by them as blessed in truth. 

Should the Apostolic Church be considered inferior to the ancient Synagogue, which certainly always had God present among them above the mercy seat between the Cherubim? If these men, following those scriptures, wish their own interpretation to remain secure, they must by the same right admit our interpretation as well: that while all the scriptures testifying that Christ has ascended remain true, He nevertheless did not abandon the Church, just as He did not then abandon the Father when He descended into the world and the womb of the Virgin. Therefore, let them not be burdened by accepting these scriptures from us, not from such a headlong interpretation, but from a more moderate one. 

Truly, therefore, Christ ascended into the heavens and removed His visible presence from the eyes of the faithful, so that henceforth, regarding His human form, He might be seen as visible in only one place at the right hand of the Father. However, His truth and divinity are in all pious minds; and the **true nature of His body**, concealed under the <term>Sacramental species: The outward appearances of bread and wine that remain after the substance has changed.</term> species of the Sacrament, is with us on every altar wherever this mystery is celebrated. Just as He said so that He might be with us: "I am with you always, even to the end of the age" <note>original: "Ego vobiscum sum vsq; cõsumationem seculi"</note>, and "This is my body" <note>original: "Et hoc est corpus meum"</note>. 

Therefore, let us in no way deny Christ in the Sacrament of the altar under the protection of the Scriptures, even though He is said to have gone away into heaven in human form and visible presence. However, during this dispute, a wonder seizes me: how they have found so many passages for the ascension of Christ into heaven, yet they could never be reminded by the Gospel of John regarding the body of Christ (which they might even once or rashly admit to be flesh in the sacrament). I also marvel at those tricks—how they have now brought forth **Aurelius Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, a central Church Father frequently cited by both Catholics and Reformers.</note> to support the ascension of Christ, yet they never wished to encounter the same author regarding the belief in the truth and veneration of the Sacrament. 

Hey there, Picard! Perhaps you did not read that passage from which you copied this saying of Saint Augustine in its original context? For I have a probable conjecture that you did not read it in its proper place—and where you did read it, I will not say now on purpose, until perhaps you return to us from some other writing. In that place, then, from which you then transferred that passage of Saint Augustine: did you not also read other things by this doctor, such as this: *“Just as through the Holy Spirit the flesh of Christ is created without sexual union, so through the same Spirit, from the substance of bread and wine, the same body and blood of Christ is consecrated.”* And again: *“In the species of bread and wine which we see, we honor invisible things, that is, the flesh and blood. We do not value these two species in the same way as we valued them before the consecration; for we faithfully confess that before the consecration it is bread and wine which nature formed, but after the consecration it is truly the flesh and blood of Christ which the blessing has consecrated.”* 

I ask: why did you not follow these things as well, so that you too might put on the faith of Saint Augustine regarding the Sacrament? But you are merely a slanderer, a denier and overturner of the faith of the Apostles; and neither the Gospel, nor the Apostles, nor all the holiness of those through whom [the truth comes] have any weight with you.

Let us hear, I pray, the blasphemies which the Picards bring in here. If they had only said: "At no other time was Christ in different places at one moment, and so He will not be today either," and if they had remained silent as to whether He *could* or *could not* do so, it would have been more forgivable for them, even if that were also false. For the Divine power <note>original: "Diuina enim potencia"</note> is measured by no spaces between the boundaries from which movement begins and where it ends; rather, in that extended space itself, according to the non-extended point of space, it fills all things from the highest point of heaven to the lowest parts of the earth, and exists everywhere present in the most extended world. Cc iiij

[...they wanted] therefore to receive him into the ship, and immediately the ship was at the land to which they were going. <note>Refers to the miracle in John 6:21, where the ship instantly reaches its destination.</note> Here, why should I argue further about the power of Christ’s body, when the ship itself, through a dimensionless point, was nevertheless at both ends of its course—that is, in distant places—at the same moment? Thus the Picards <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren, a pre-Reformation Christian movement in Bohemia.</note> sin in both ways: they say Christ did not do things which He certainly did, and they say He could not have done the things He did not do. This is an admitted blasphemy against the Most High God. Finally, the one does not follow from the other—for instance, "Christ did not do it, therefore He could not do it." For what else should we expect to follow from that Picard argument, except that God could not have made this heaven and the things within it any larger in space or fuller with more things, simply because He did not do so? They assume this current measure was sufficient for the world’s purpose. 

For God—according to His supreme nature, if I may put it that way—since there is no end to His virtue, never has done nor will do anything that exhausts His power <note>The author is explaining that God's infinite potential (potentia) is never fully spent by His finite actions (actus).</note>. Instead, He works according to a measure that is sufficient for the creature, according to the condition in which it was created. Just as in human affairs—if it be permitted to compare these small things to the immense majesty of God—no one always strives to the absolute limit of their strength. Neither do the most powerful Kings want or grant everything, nor do they exercise their full authority over everything; they apply only as much measure as is sufficient for the business at hand. 

Thus, it is false in itself to say: "Christ was not in different places at once, therefore He could not be." It is like saying that because He did not descend from the cross when challenged, it was because He was unable to descend. But what does Christ respond to such a blasphemous suspicion from the Picard? 

> "Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and He will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen this way?" <note>original: "An putas quia non possum rogare Patrem meum..." from Matthew 26:53-54</note> 

I say, it had to happen this way so that Christ would perform whatever miracles He did, not merely to show off His divine power, but to fulfill the prophetic predictions—yet not without divine power. He was able, however, had He not wished to fulfill the Scriptures, to do far greater and more frequent things, just as He did. Regarding what He said to the Apostles:

> "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father." <note>original: "Amen Amen dico vobis..." from John 14:12</note>

Certainly, whatever greater things the Apostles did, Christ also did, since they performed them by calling upon His name. As He had also predicted:

> "Without me you can do nothing." <note>original: "Sine me nihil potestis facere" from John 15:5</note>

There is no reason, therefore, why we should dictate a limit to the power of Christ based only on the things He actually did. He did not allow such a limit to be set for Himself—nor even for His faithful—since He says again without any exception:

> "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it." <note>original: "Quodcunq; pecieritis..." from John 14:13-14</note>

And again in another place:

> "Have faith in God. Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours." <note>original: "Habete fidem Dei..." from Mark 11:22-24</note>

Christ said this to those believing in Him. But if He Himself is the head of the believers, how much more excellent is He than those who participate in Him? He possesses a more perfect power for performing miracles, so that whatever is spoken is done according to His will.

Because if He said from this sign, "This is my Body which will be given for you," surely out of reverence for Christ, holding to this, let us believe that the Body of Christ is there. Let us leave the Picard <note>A derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren.</note> to his suspicion regarding whether or not Christ is in one or several different places at the same moment. For unless Christ had known this to be within His power, He would not have left that statement behind: "This is my body." But we have said enough and more than enough about this admitted blasphemy. Therefore, let us drive out the Picard from here as far as possible, like a rabid dog with that insanity of his: the idea that whatever Christ was able to do, He did all of it, and what He did not do, He was not able to do.

But let us pursue more similar points. They say, therefore, from this place: <insert>⌜We ought not to worship Him in the blessing of the Sacrament, which takes place and ought to take place in His personal existence while He exists at the right hand of God⌟</insert> Since we have, with better reasoning, driven out that sacrilegious suspicion of theirs—namely, that Christ cannot be in different places—therefore, by that same effort of ours, what they now decree about not worshiping the Sacrament falls into ruin. 

And I should like them to say: for what reason do they worship Christ? Is it because He remains above at the right hand of the Father, as they have alleged, because no one here honors the Father in a creature but in heaven, saying, "Our Father who art in heaven"? Therefore, the adoration of Christ would be judged not by His divine nature but by the dignity of the location. Thus the Picards would hardly be able to excuse themselves if they do not worship the powers closest to God with equal honor, since these also inhabit the heavens. If, however, they adore Christ because of the majesty of His divine nature, why do they change the adoration due to His divinity based on the condition of the location? As if, long ago when Christ was born, the manger <note>original: "incunabula," literally swaddling clothes or cradle.</note> stood in the way so that He should not have been adored, while now the place at the right hand of the Father is an advantage so that He must be adored? 

O blind contention! Is adoration then chosen for the location rather than the divinity? But as we have frequently shown up to this point: Christ is in the Sacrament according to the truth of His nature, and nothing foreign happens to Christ’s nature regarding location wherever He may be. Therefore, the presence of Christ will be adored equally in the Sacrament as in heaven. Although the Picards commit such nefarious acts against heavenly piety everywhere, they still fear—such is the boldness of their brow <note>An idiom meaning "shamelessness."</note>—that they might not be understood in their sacrilege. 

But they repeat the same things over and over, and they play again with false similarities the same games they previously played with us concerning the false sense of the Scriptures. Since the Picards said they accept a certain "spiritual" presence of Christ in the Sacrament, lest they be thought to have suddenly invented that alone, they impose that spiritual presence also onto the person of John the Baptist—as distortedly and corruptly as they previously gathered the Scriptures into the same meaning. They say, however: "We do not make a comparison, nor do we set them as one; we have his example in John the Baptist." 

I, however, was expecting that the Scripture would not make a comparison, nor place the true nature of Christ in the Sacrament. But it is those Picards who do not compare or set them as one; so we should not wonder if they perceive nothing correctly, since they invent everything not according to the will of the Scriptures but according to their own lust. And let us be of a secure mind, because the things we argue to the contrary are argued not against the Divine Scriptures, but against the Picard. Now then, if Christ is in the Sacrament in the same way that John is Elijah <note>Refers to Matthew 11:14, where Jesus says John the Baptist "is" Elijah. The author argues this is a metaphor of "grace," whereas the Eucharist is a literal reality.</note>, then nothing will be more foreign to Christ than the Sacrament. For John was not Elijah, just as they remained distinct from each other in time, place, parents, manner of death, and finally, their entire nature. But John was called "Elijah" because of the equality of grace.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that they impose some sort of "spiritual" quality on John the Baptist—I know not what—we laugh at this for its foreignness of phrasing and because it is not so used among the interpreters of Scripture; yet we do not permit them to impose that same "spiritual" quality upon the Sacrament of the altar, unless they accept it according to the sense of the Apostle which we have shown. For as for the idea that it is only a sign of invisible grace, and the mystical Body of Christ—and that these things alone, and besides these nothing of the nature of Christ, exist in the Sacrament—this is so far from a true confession that those things [the bread and wine] are not *This body of Christ*, which, as He said, *is delivered for us unto death.* <note>original: "Est pro nobis traditum in mortē," a reference to the Words of Institution in the Mass/Luke 22:19.</note> Therefore, this body of Christ delivered unto death, this His blood poured out in redemption for many—this nature of the body and blood in this person of Christ is in the Sacrament. Then, like a perennial fountain, there follow (as individual streams) that invisible grace and, finally, that assumption into the mystical body of Christ in all who receive worthily. These are the only things that the Picards now wish to confess in the Sacrament. 

Whether this faithlessness—which has hitherto lain rejected in such great matters and scriptures—can prevail <unclear>for</unclear> the Picards with their distorted and never-fitting arguments, we care very little. For we do not care what they themselves feel outside of the <unclear>scriptures</unclear>, since they leave it free for us to neither approve nor believe anything outside of scripture. Therefore, regarding what they now propose to us concerning a fabricated comparison—*This is the body of Christ*, and again, *This is not the body of Christ*—we judge that it pertains nothing to us. Rather, we set before them from the Gospel: *This is my body*; *I am the living bread who descended from heaven*; *My flesh is truly food.* <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meū / Ego sum panis viuus... / Caro mea vere est cibus." Citations from the Gospels of Matthew and John.</note> And we remain so firmly in this confession against the Picard, and we perpetually believe this to be the Sacrament, because these things are said with a single and perpetual meaning. Because the Picards depart from this, and because they seek out foreign and far-fetched diversions for their faithlessness outside of the proper places for this matter, they testify to their own depravity; for they receive nothing to be believed on behalf of the Gospel, but only out of their own malevolence. 

Nor do they stop, though beaten back by one crime. But as if thunderstruck and out of their minds, they heap crime upon crime. Thus, barely catching their breath—indeed, suddenly rising up against us with one spirit from another outrage—they seize upon the resisting Apostle in excuse of their faithlessness, and with certain words brought to the surface based on a false sense, they hallucinate at us. ### ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST [THE HERETICS]

they ate—to use the Picards’ <note>A derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren, a proto-Protestant group the author is attacking.</note> own words—nor did they drink the Body and blood of Christ corporally. Does it follow then that now the body and blood of Christ are received in the sacrament not corporally, but spiritually? Here, we hold entirely and by their own confession the Picards’ decree concerning the faith of the Sacrament. Nor in any other place was he so far removed from his own sense; for this reason, I previously explained that word "spiritual" in many senses, so that whether he thought this or that, he might not slip away, and might know by what standard the truth of the Scriptures would make his claim either just or unjust. 

Now, we have no such doubt about the Picard, for he says "with full cheeks" <note>A Latin idiom, *plenis buccis*, meaning to speak loudly, boldly, or boastfully.</note> and quite plainly: that only a sign and figure of invisible grace is contained in this Sacrament, just according to the manner that the fathers in the desert ate of the same spiritual food and drank of the same spiritual drink, who certainly had nothing of the Sacrament except the shadow. Therefore, the Picards are resuscitating the Synagogue <note>In medieval theology, "the Synagogue" often referred to the Old Testament legal system, which was seen as a "shadow" of the "truth" found in the Christian Gospel.</note>, from which they might slander the truth of the Gospel. In this, the Picard betrays his wickedness even more by adding help to his error. 

To shake off this error, we will seek nothing from afar; indeed, they destroy themselves with the contrary scriptures which they voluntarily offer here. Either this: because the law had only a shadow of the good things to come, and not the true image itself <note>A reference to Hebrews 10:1, contrasting Old Testament "shadows" with New Testament "realities."</note>, the Gospel will therefore possess those good things, according to the sense of the Apostle <note>Saint Paul.</note>, in full truth. This, I say, the Scripture asserts so that the comparison does not falter, lest the Sacraments of the Gospel be weakened by the shadow of the Synagogue. 

Another point also: *The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.* <note>original: "lex per Moysen data est. gracia & veritas per ihsum Christum facta est." From John 1:17.</note> This also points to the same conclusion. For if—as the Picards say—those fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink not corporally but in a figure, it follows that everything happened to them in a figure, and not in true reality or complete power. But because the figure has passed away and the truth has been made through Jesus Christ, truth must therefore exist in our Sacrament, and no likeness of shadow or figure remains. 

Furthermore, since the law given through Moses was void of grace—as the Apostle says to the Romans, because *by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him,* <note>Romans 3:20.</note> but rather *the law works wrath,* <note>Romans 4:15.</note> and as he says again to the Hebrews, *the law brought nothing to perfection* <note>Hebrews 7:19.</note>—but grace was made through Jesus Christ, then the Sacraments of each Testament will not be of equal power. Therefore, let the latter not be judged by the former, nor let the virtues of present things be placed in the shadow of those that came before. Finally, nothing opposes this error more powerfully than the Gospel of John, from its sixth chapter, which the Picards everywhere avoid so vehemently, as if it were a magical incantation or a serpent. There it is read:

> This is the bread that came down from heaven; not as your fathers ate manna and are dead. He who eats this bread shall live forever. <note>original: "Hic est panis qui de celo descendit..." John 6:58.</note>

What could have been said more clearly than this Gospel against the treachery of the Picard? I wonder if they still draw breath, or if these lost men will return from this and say: "In the Sacrament today, Christ is not present according to the truth of his nature, just as the fathers ate and drank of him not in a corporal nature but in a spiritual and figurative way." And they shall hear us oppose them with a different sense:

> This is the bread that came down from heaven. Not as your fathers ate the Manna and are dead.

Most treacherous heretics, I speak to you! You who kick the truth of the Gospel out of the way and pierce it with diabolical arrows! What reason did you have to suppress this most obvious passage, which is on everyone’s lips? Perhaps it did not serve your purpose. Therefore, you should correct that treachery of yours according to its meaning, and then it would serve your purpose. But there is no...

# BOOK FIVE ON THE WALDENSIANS

[...with your] diabolical devices <note>original: *canterijs*, likely referring here to the logical "props" or "frames" used by the heretics to support their arguments</note> in concord with holiness and all pure faith. Neither God, nor Christ, nor the Apostles, nor all the saints are considered friends in whatever places they prove your treachery. You go as most wicked deserters against all things, only so that you may protect your impiety and your stance against God.

->THE PICARD,<-

*But he himself, along with others who feel as he does, must entirely fear those traps—confessing, namely, that Christ is personally on earth just as he sits at the right hand of the Father, and so forth, up to that point. Here it will be necessary to show faith in Christ the Lord.*

This place now demands that we explain ourselves against the Picards, who mock our faith regarding the Sacrament as impiously as they do shamelessly. We shall show that we by no means "divide Christ" (as they think), even if we confess him to be in the Sacrament according to the truth of his nature, by which he also sits at the right hand of the Father. Truly, as to the claim that we seduce the faithful by this confession: here either the Picards do not understand our faith, or they deliberately slander it. For Christ, just as he is in the Sacrament, is so received by the minds of the worthy through his presence. This is because all true things befit Christ, who is Truth itself, and who said: *This is my body*, and *my flesh is truly food* <note>John 6:55</note>. This occurs both according to the truth of his nature and according to the increase of invisible grace—which grace is followed by that spiritual adoption into the mystical body of Christ.

To those Picards, we offer St. Augustine as a witness to this faith of ours. In his book *On the Remedy of Penance*, he speaks thus: 
> How is Christ to be eaten? He himself says: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him." If he remains in me and I in him, then he drinks. But he who remains in me, and I not in him—even if he receives the Sacrament—he acquires great torment.

St. Augustine thus confesses a twofold receiving of the Sacrament. One is where the "thing" <term>The "thing" (res) of the sacrament refers to the actual reality or grace it contains, distinguished from the outward sign.</term> or the Sacrament of the body and blood of Christ is received alone, as in the one who receives unworthily and to his own torment. He understood the other receiving of the Sacrament to be spiritual: that where, along with the Sacrament, the grace of the Sacrament is received at the same time—as in the one who truly remains in Christ and Christ in him.

Likewise, as Aurelius Augustine says again in *On the Sacraments of the Faithful*: 
> No one should doubt that each person becomes a partaker of the body and blood of the Lord when they are made a member of Christ. Nor is one alienated from the fellowship of that bread and cup, even if they depart from this world established in the unity of Christ’s body before they eat that bread and drink that cup; for such a person is not deprived of the benefit of that Sacrament when they are found to possess that which the Sacrament signifies.

All the books of the Catholics are full of this confession. Therefore, the Picards lie wickedly when they claim we lead the faithful away from believing in the spiritual receiving of the Sacrament—which is the only fruit we confess to be found there! So much so, that we say those who do not receive grace along with the sacrament become "guilty of the body and blood of the Lord" <note>1 Corinthians 11:27</note> according to the meaning of the Apostle. This Christian confession is as true as the lies which the Picards previously directed against this faith were pure. After all this, they wish to appear to ask the teacher Augustine for pardon, if they have questioned him on anything. They speak now to his ungodly [opponent]; for certainly, if they had ever wished to act or speak according to Augustine's judgment alone, they would have long ago ceased their thundering of such horrific impiety and intolerable blasphemies. But they treat us so with their jeers—they who, as they do everywhere, are now presently going to do everything according to their own lust, beyond any hope of pardon.

### ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST THE PICARDS

They ask, however, if we confess Christ to be in the sacrament according to the truth of his nature, why we do not adore Christ in man <note>referring to the believer in whom Christ dwells</note> just as we do in heaven and in the sacrament. They think it is especially necessary for us to adore him there, or else we have denied the truth of the sacrament. It is a small thing for them to bring this into question regarding only the sacrament of the body of Christ; for just as God the Son dwells in pious minds, so similarly the Father and the Holy Spirit dwell there, as it is written:
> If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him. <note>John 14:23</note>
And in the Acts of the Apostles:
> And it sat upon each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit. <note>Acts 2:3-4</note>

Therefore, we shall not change the point of the argument <note>original: *non nodum mutabimus*, literally "we shall not change the knot"</note>, and the Picards shall remain stuck in their own snares. If the Picards confess that the Divinity dwells in pious minds, why do they not also adore the Divinity in man? Whatever the heretical Picards find to explain this for themselves, they have found the same for us; therefore, let them cease to impose this upon us. Either Christ ought to be adored in man just as much as in the sacrament, or—as they think—Christ ought not to be adored in the sacrament just as he is not adored in man. Thus we respond to the Picard regarding his own wickedness.

But since I promised from the beginning of the present book that I would provide an account, according to the measure of our talent, of what is demanded by those Picards regarding the faith of the Sacrament, I will now fulfill this promise. I shall confute those sophistries of the Picard a little more severely. From this, the matter of the adoration of saints must be repeated again—an adoration for which they today so justly rebuke us if we did not show it, yet which they once so wickedly accused us of because we *do* show it. The things we are about to say here could have come under discussion then as well, but I thought they should be deferred to a more convenient place—if perhaps (as has now happened) the necessity should arise to penetrate two wedges of the enemy's troops with a single defense. Therefore, God has always been adored in his saints, both in angels and in men. To testify to this matter, a few examples out of many will suffice for us.

In Joshua we read:
> When Joshua was in the field of the city of Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and saw a man standing against him, holding a drawn sword. He went to him and said, "Are you one of ours or of our adversaries?" Who responded, "Not so, but I am the prince of the host of the Lord, and now I come." Joshua fell face down upon the earth and, adoring, said: "What does my Lord speak to his servant?" <note>Joshua 5:13-14</note>

Furthermore, in Daniel:
> Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and adored Daniel, and commanded that victims and incense be sacrificed to him. <note>Daniel 2:46</note>

And as to why he did this, the King himself gives the reason for his action to the Prophet, saying:
> Truly your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings. <note>Daniel 2:47</note>

Angels and other men perfected by virtue permitted this to be done to them, not because they were ignorant or wished to violate the Scripture to the injury of God which says:
> You shall adore the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve. <note>Matthew 4:10; Deuteronomy 6:13</note>

But rather, they were deferring this honor to God who was present within them.

But here the Picards rise up: Why then are these examples of Scripture not accepted everywhere? Of course, the reminder of our own fragility is more present to us, and true humility thinks it much holier for itself to claim nothing, but rather to venerate it in another and to prevent what another was going to do toward it. Thus, one withdraws from a greater virtue, and the awareness of human weakness does not allow that veneration—which is full of danger—to grow into a daily custom. Therefore, when a certain Cornelius had fallen at the feet of Peter and desired to venerate that divine quality which he sensed in him, Peter did not allow it, but raised him up saying:
> Arise, I myself am also a man. <note>Acts 10:25-26</note>

We read similarly in the Apocalypse:
> And I fell at his feet to adore him, and he said to me: "See that you do not do it; I am your fellow servant, and of your brothers." <note>Revelation 19:10</note>

# THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE

...having the testimony of Jesus. Does anyone dare to contend that the Apostle <note>Referring to St. John the Evangelist in the Book of Revelation</note>—who was then conversing within the secrets of the divinity—had forgotten that commandment, "You shall adore the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve," and intentionally wished to fall into forbidden adoration and something close to idolatry? I do not believe even a Picard <note>original: *Pighardū*; a member of the Bohemian Brethren</note> is so profoundly insane as to suspect such an atrocious crime of so great an Apostle. Rather, because of the greatness of the revelations, John beheld the presence of the divinity in the messenger <note>original: *angelo*</note>, and wished to bow down fully before that dwelling place of the divine.

Why, then, was he prohibited from such a holy intention? It was because the Apostle stood in the same place as the angel on the holy mountain, in order that he might come to know the divine secrets. For this reason, those secrets had been revealed to the angel, and thus each was offering the other that same veneration. Finally, the angel, most humbly refusing it, said: "See that you do not do this, for I am nothing better than your fellow servant and the servant of your brothers." This is the sole reason why mortals do not adore one another. 

But the time is coming when He will deliver us from this body of death; then, those of us who remain in the body may rightly, following the previous examples, cry out to those most holy dwellings of the divinity and adore the holy souls in heaven for the very reason that God dwells in them—just as it is written: *And I will walk in them.* <note>Leviticus 26:12 or 2 Corinthians 6:16</note> Furthermore, we even venerate their bodies on earth, which are the hostels of such a happy soul in which God dwells. Nor do we only do this, but we also confess our negligences to all those same blessed spirits:

> I, an unworthy sinner, confess to merciful God and to all his saints that I have sinned in my life. Therefore, I beseech all the saints to pray to God for me, a sinner.

And according to this example, Christ our Savior says that the Prodigal Son accused himself, saying: *Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.* <note>Luke 15:21</note> For he did not confess to the physical elements or the literal sky, but to the holy angels; and he confessed to the angels first, for whom there is such great joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance. Through the angels, God knows everything about us, just as it is written: *When you prayed with tears, and buried the dead, and left your dinner and hid the dead man in your house by day, and buried him by night, I offered your prayer to the Lord.* <note>The angel Raphael speaking to Tobit; Tobit 12:12</note>

There is another reason why men were not always adored. Since the Church has always run its course among the enemies of true religion, if they had ever permitted such a thing to be done—which was otherwise just and holy by its own right—no one could have persuaded those "dogs" <note>A term often used for pagans or scoffers of the faith</note> that Christians were not possessed by the same folly of idolatry for which they criticized others. Thus, because of external wickedness, the Church kept its practices within a quiet conscience. For mortals, in their disparagement, think it a torment to themselves to teach anything beyond their own minds regarding equity and truth, as judged by the reality of the matter. 

This necessity—caused sometimes by the stubbornness of men and sometimes by other reasons—is often so grave that it holds sway not only over human laws but even over divine ones. Thus, the hardness of the Jews extorted the bill of divorce from Moses, even though from the beginning it was not so, but two were to be in one flesh in a perpetual covenant. Similarly, the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint; the Greek translators of the Hebrew Bible</note> kept silent about the weightiest and most hidden matters in their interpretation of the Law because of the stubbornness of King Ptolemy, who had been schooled in the teachings of Plato and would have reacted harshly had he heard that God is one in essence but three in persons. Likewise, the Apostles retained circumcision and the observance of the Law for a time, which Paul nevertheless regarded differently elsewhere, doing so only that he might "win Christ." Similarly, our ancestors did not introduce images of the saints into the church for a certain time, because they would have undergone great slander due to the ignorance of the matter—both among Jews who did not understand images, and among Gentiles who were raving after idols to the point of insulting God. Thus our leaders became "Jews to the Jews and Greeks to the Greeks" at that time, so that they might win everyone, just as it is written: *The Apostles and the elder brothers to the brothers from the Gentiles who are in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: Greetings.* <note>Acts 15:23</note>

...and after other things: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell." <note>A quotation of the Decree of the Council of Jerusalem from Acts 15:28–29</note> And again: "You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law," and after other things: "Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law." <note>A quotation from Acts 21:20–24, where James advises the Apostle Paul on Jewish customs</note>

All these things, however, were changed later in a time of greater freedom, after the Church was able to exercise authority against outsiders. The bill of divorce was rejected; the Seventy <note>The "LXX" or Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> were corrected according to the Hebrew truth. Circumcision and ceremonies among Christians utterly ceased. Images also, after idolatry fell into oblivion, were restored—I say *restored*. 

For Saint Jerome is a witness in his book of *Hebrew Questions* on that passage, explaining: "He himself began to call upon the name of the Lord." <note>Genesis 4:26</note> Even the first mortals worshipped the true God under an image. And since we have entered so strictly into this discourse on the images of the saints, I wish by the same effort to treat a brief and indeed supplemental place—one which I shall wonder at enough if the Picards <note>original: *Pighardi*; a term used for the Bohemian Brethren, whom the author considers heretical</note> did not know, or if they do know it. But for whatever purpose they have kept it in reserve, they will hold it in vain, for we now provoke it into the open of our own accord. 

It is a passage from the Letter of Blessed Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem, and these are his words: "I found there a veil hanging at the doors of the same church, dyed and painted and having an image of Christ or some saint—for I do not quite remember whose image it was. When, therefore, I had seen this image of a man hanging in the Church of Christ against the authority of the Scriptures, I tore it, and rather gave counsel to the keepers of that place that they should wrap a poor dead man in it and carry him out." And a little later: "And I pray that you command the priests of that place to receive the veil from the bearer which has been sent by us, and henceforth to command that in the Church of Christ such veils, which come against our religion, should not be hung." 

This passage might seem to have provided material to the detractors <note>The "calumniators" or those who attack Church traditions</note> of the Christian religion, and they direct it at us as if this were the entirety of what the ancients felt concerning the veneration of images. If, therefore, Epiphanius said and felt this according to a decree of the Church, he must be heard; for "he who will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector." <note>Matthew 18:17</note> But if he believed such a thing only from his private conscience, then it remained free to believe something different from him by public consensus—just as the use of images truly was at that time, as we testify even from this present letter of Epiphanius. 

But the Picards say, "So there were images, but by no one who then believed sincerely." Prove it! On the contrary, they were approved even by the holy confessors. For Cyril, also Bishop of Jerusalem, in that book given to Saint Augustine concerning the miracles of Saint Jerome, most consistently mentions his image. Moreover, Saint Jerome scourged himself before a crucifix. Nor were they ignorant of Epiphanius’s letter, since Jerome himself translated it from Greek into Latin. As for Cyril, he was the Bishop of the same city as that John to whom it was written; so even if he did not know it by Epiphanius’s reputation nor from the recent translation and friendship of Jerome, he would nevertheless have found it in the commentaries of the daily acts of that church. For these reasons, Saint Epiphanius felt this way privately. Because at that time idolatry had been only recently cast down, he feared lest the scar of pagan superstition, <unclear>scarcely</unclear> well closed, might break open into a new wound from the memory of images.

# THE WALDENSIANS, BOOK FIVE,

Thus, he disapproved of them [images] not because of the fault of the images themselves, but out of fear of scandal <note>The author is likely referring to Saint Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403 AD), who famously tore down a church curtain depicting an image. The author argues this was a local, pastoral decision to prevent new converts from reverting to pagan-style idolatry, not a universal ban.</note>. He thought to himself what the Apostle once said in a similar fear: *Wherefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble.* <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 8:13.</note> The Apostle removes meat—which is permitted by everyone’s confession—not because of the fault of the meat, but because of the occasion, if it might cause a stumbling-block for the weak. But give faith to the Apostle, for when the weak are no longer struck in their conscience, the Apostle will return to the first table without scruple. 

And today, since pagan madness is equally detested and ignored by us, and since everyone knows to what extent the images of the saints are to be venerated, therefore—with the pardon of Saint Epiphanius and by the decree of the universal Church—images of the Crucified and of the saints are piously and religiously displayed to the Christian people as an example for a holier life. 

But let us return at last to the words of the Picard <note>The "Picards" (Pighardi) was a derogatory term often used for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians.</note>. They quote Scripture to us: *He who eats this bread shall live forever.* <note>John 6:58.</note> Most wicked men! Now, after the matter has come beyond dispute, they bring forward the Gospel of John from its sixth chapter; truly they did so then so that they might not remain perpetually in the word "Body." And they wanted to exchange the same with the flesh, because they would devise some spiritual existence, I know not what, outside the nature of Christ; and they would falsely invent a figurative receiving of the sacrament from the shadow of the Old Testament. They certainly did not want to find or cite the Gospel there. And the common people think that those Picards recall the Gospel, the Apostles, and all ancient holiness to faith and life; whereas they are surely the only ones of all who are the professed enemies of the Gospel, the Apostles, and all ancient holiness in faith and life. 

If, however, as they say last, Christ were divided from himself in the Sacrament—to say this is as far from us as we vehemently contend, against that heretical Picard, that Christ at the right hand of the Father and the sacrament are not divided.

->THE PICARD,<-

And where he holds and mentions the transformation of the bread and wine, and the rest, up until that point: *one soul once created unites and unifies and gives life to those bodies together.*

From this point, the Picards deny the truth of the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ and the nature of the transformation <note>The Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation, where the "substance" of bread and wine changes into the body and blood of Christ.</note>. They seek the matter itself in this way: Whether the species <note>The "species" refers to the outward appearances—taste, smell, shape—of bread and wine that remain after the change.</note> of the Sacrament are transformed into the whole Christ or not the whole Christ? 

We say, meanwhile, that those species of bread and wine pass—the wine into the blood and the bread into the body of Christ—and therefore under those species of bread and wine is the true and whole Christ according to His full nature. I say this so that I might more quickly free the Christian confession from those monsters which they impose upon us from the other side of the question: namely, that we confess a body without blood, and blood without a body, and finally both without Christ in the sacrament. 

We certainly do not value these trifles at a straw <note>original: "pro flocco," literally "for a tuft of wool."</note>. Truly, we stand by the first principles. But as for whether those species of bread and wine are transformed also into the soul and divinity of Christ, and thus the Creator is made from the creature—whether the Picard says that knowingly or unknowingly, he certainly interprets our confession both falsely and violently. For since Christ did not say "this is my soul" and "this is my divinity," it is just as wicked to confess that in this transubstantiation either the soul or the divinity is "made." 

Since, therefore, nothing proper to the Sacrament is transformed into the soul and divinity, what else shall there be through which we may rightly confess Christ in the sacrament as true God and man? This is it: for just as in generation a particle of the human body is transformed into the body alone, and what is made from it is a man subsisting in a rational soul and human flesh—even though the rational soul does not come from the transmission <note>original: "ex traduce," referring to the "traducian" theory that souls are inherited from parents like the body.</note> of the body—and just as Christ took only flesh and blood and the rest of His bodily nature from the transmission of the Virgin's body,
