...and after other matters: *it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication. By keeping yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.* <note>Acts 15:28–29. These were the requirements of the "Apostolic Decree," intended to help Jewish and Gentile Christians live together.</note> And again: *You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealots for the law.* And after other matters: *Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow; take them and sanctify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads, and all will know that what they have heard about you is false, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law.* <note>Acts 21:20–24. This passage describes Saint Paul following Jewish ritual laws to appease Jewish Christians in Jerusalem.</note> All of these things, however, were changed later in a time of greater liberty, after the Church was able to exercise authority against outsiders. The bill of divorce was rejected; the **Seventy** <note>original: "lxx." Refers to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> were corrected according to the **Hebrew Truth** <note>original: "veritatem Hebraicam." This refers to Saint Jerome’s project of translating the Bible directly from Hebrew rather than relying on the Greek Septuagint.</note>. Circumcision and ceremonies among Christians utterly ceased. 

**Images**, too, were restored once idolatry fell into oblivion—I say restored, because Saint Jerome is a witness in his book *Hebrew Questions* <note>*Hebraicarum Quaestionum in Genesim*</note>, explaining that passage: *He began to call upon the name of the Lord.* <note>Genesis 4:26.</note> He explains that the first mortals also worshipped the true God under an image. And since we have entered so strictly into this discourse regarding the images of the saints, I wish by this same work to treat a brief and indeed supplementary point, which I would be quite surprised if the **Picards** <note>original: "Pighardi." A derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians.</note> did not know—or if they do know it, with whatever counsel they have kept it in reserve, they shall hold it in vain, for we now provoke it into the open of our own accord. 

It is a passage from the **Letter of Blessed Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem**, and these are his very words: 
*I found there a veil hanging at the doors of the same Church, dyed and painted, and having an image of Christ or of some saint—for I do not quite remember whose image it was. When, therefore, I had seen this image of a man hanging in the Church of Christ against the authority of the Scriptures, I tore it, and moreover gave counsel to the keepers of that place that they should wrap a poor dead man in it and carry him out.* 
And a little later: 
*And I pray that you bid the priests of that place to accept the veil from the bearer which has been sent by us, and henceforth to command that in the Church of Christ such veils, which come against our religion, should not be hung.* 

This passage may seem to have given material to the detractors of the Christian religion, and they direct it against us as if this were the sum total of what the ancients felt regarding the veneration of images. If, therefore, **Epiphanius** said and felt this by a decree of the Church, he ought to be heard; for he who will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector. But if he believed such a thing only out of **private conscience**, then it remained free to believe differently from him by public consent—just as there truly was a use of images at that time, which we witness even from this present letter of Epiphanius. 

But the Picards say: "So there were images, but by no one who then believed sincerely." **Prove it!** On the contrary, they were approved even by the holy confessors. For **Cyril**, who was also Bishop of Jerusalem, in that book given to Father Augustine concerning the miracles of Saint Jerome, mentions his image most constantly. <note>The author is likely referring to a late medieval pseudepigraphal letter attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem.</note> Moreover, Saint Jerome scourged himself before a crucifix. Nor were they ignorant of the letter of Epiphanius, since Jerome himself translated it from Greek into Latin. Furthermore, Cyril was the bishop of the same city as that John to whom it was written; so even if he did not know it by the fame of Epiphanius, nor from the recent translation and his familiarity with Jerome, he would nevertheless have found it in the commentaries of the daily acts of that church. 

For these reasons, Saint Epiphanius felt this way **privately**. Because at that time idolatry had been only recently cast down, he feared lest the **scar of pagan superstition**, which had only recently and barely healed over, might break open into a new wound from the memory of images.

Thus, he disapproved of them [the images] not because of a fault in the images themselves but from a fear of causing a scandal; <note>The author is likely referring to Epiphanius of Salamis, a 4th-century bishop known for opposing images to prevent a return to pagan idolatry.</note> he thought within himself what the Apostle had once said in a similar fear: *Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble.* <note>original: "Qua p̃pter si esca scãdalizat fratrẽ meũ non manducabo carnẽ in eternũ ne fratrem meum scandalizem." But if, as they say at the end, Christ were divided from himself in the Sacrament—to say this is as far from us as we vehemently contend against that heretical Picard, so that Christ is not divided between the right hand of the Father and the Sacrament.

And where he holds and mentions the transmutation of the bread and wine, and the rest, up to that point: *a single soul once created might unite and make one and give life to those bodies together.*

But nevertheless, that symbol of the formed body also drew a rational soul from elsewhere, beyond the fact that a small portion of the Virgin's body was transformed into a soul. And this is now the true man, subsisting in a rational soul and human flesh: Christ God, without any part of a creature passing into the Creator; and so the true God and man, Jesus Christ, is born of the Virgin. In the same way, the <term>species</term> <note>The outward appearances of bread and wine—such as taste, color, and smell—which remain after the substance has changed.</note> of the Sacrament are transformed into the body and blood of Christ alone. Yet, in the Sacrament, according to the symbol of his body and blood, the whole and entire Christ is present—true God and true man—without the species of the sacrament being transformed into the rational soul or the divinity itself. 

Finally, because Christ died once and was then a body without blood, and blood without a body, and both were without a soul, and the soul was without both; but now that he has risen, he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him. Since his body and blood are in the Sacrament, that vital portion of the soul is necessarily there as well, due to Christ’s immortality. His divinity is also there, because once he assumed human nature, he never laid it down; Christ remains God and man for ever and ever. 

This is the reason why the soul and divinity enter the Sacrament. It is far different, he says, from those "monstrosities" which the Picard <note>original: "pighardus" — a derogatory term for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren, likely derived from "Picards."</note> lyingly claims follow from our confession. For a sound and composed mind does not shrink from this Christian faith, but confesses it as pure and true from its own conscience. No one except a Picard and his disturbed brain could have thought up those monstrosities to defame the Catholic faith. I am not surprised if the Picard is such a man, since he says and does all these things out of mere malevolence, impiety, and wicked contention. As a certain wise man said: *He who seeks the law shall be filled by it; and he who acts deceitfully shall be scandalized by it.* <note>A paraphrase of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 32:19.</note>

After this, they raise doubts about the water that is put into the chalice. These wicked men call it "water" so that if they had called it a "tiny drop" (which it is), the reason would have immediately been apparent: because it is diffused and lost in more than a six-hundredth part of the wine, it passes into the wine itself and becomes one body with it, just as we learn from daily examples. For even a small drop of wine lost in a greater abundance of water loses its flavor and nature in turn. Yet they say the whole idea is impossible. I agree with them on this: those monsters which this Picard puts forward can truly never happen, and we Christians do not stand by them. However, the things we confess are so similar to the sacrament—things done once and done daily in generation—that we can demonstrate them using present examples. 

In the next section, the Picards reject the truth of the Sacrament for another reason: because Christ’s flesh was formed once by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin. They act as if, according to our faith, the flesh of Christ were being made again, neither by its author the Holy Spirit, nor in its own "chamber" of the Virgin’s womb. If the Picards did not fabricate such horrors—dreadful to hear—concerning the Apostolic faith out of their own malevolence just to shock the common people, but instead stuck to our actual confession (confuting it only if it were found to be impious), we would hear fewer of the Picard's blasphemies, and the dispute regarding the Christian faith would be more direct. Even now, they falsely charge Christian innocence as if the body of Christ were always being produced or generated anew whenever and wherever it is consecrated in the Sacrament. No Christian believes this. If one believes that Christ is present according to his nature in the sacrament wherever it is consecrated, it does not follow that he is made anew by someone other than the Holy Spirit (namely, the priest), nor in any place other than the Virgin’s womb (namely, in the species of bread and wine). For there is no other author of this transformation than the Holy Spirit.

God is the Trinity; the Priest approaches only as a minister who brings out into the open that which the Divinity performs in an incomprehensible manner. This is just as it happens in all miracles, which are certainly performed by God alone, yet produced through a human being into a visible effect. This, then, is the first point about which the <term>Picards</term> <note>original: "Pighardi." A derogatory term used for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren, often associating them with the "Beghards" or suggesting they originated in Picardy.</note> lie concerning our faith: they falsely claim we attribute that <term>transmutation</term> <note>The change of the substance of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ.</note> to a foreign author [the priest]. 

Furthermore, nothing new happens to the nature of Christ in that transformation. Therefore, they should not speak truly against us as if Christ were "made" in some way, as he was in the womb of the Virgin. For to begin to be made or to exist from another and in another are properties belonging to individual things, from which follows a diversity of one existence and then another within an individual. If, therefore, Christ were made "from another" (such as the priest) and thus "in another" (such as the <term>species</term> <note>The outward appearances of bread and wine.</note> of the Sacrament), he would consequently be made diverse from himself in nature and in number. 

Christian confession recoils from this! Truly, just as no new existence was created for the Divinity when it appeared to Abraham in the form of three men, or when it came to Sodom in the form of two; and just as the Holy Spirit was not made from somewhere else than from the Father and the Son when he appeared like a dove, or when he sat upon the Apostles in tongues of fire—rather, something new was made only in those *assumed* things which previously were not what they were said to be. All those transformations occurred at a single point and only within the creature. 

Following these examples, in the Sacrament there is no new existence of Christ's nature made from elsewhere, as was done once in the womb of the Virgin. Instead, it is the creature of bread and wine—these alone—which after the consecration become the body and blood of Christ by a new existence. That same creature which was not the body of the Lord yesterday is so today, and that which was not today will be so tomorrow, according to the nature of the previous example. 

For when God is said to move or not move, or to be present visibly through an assumed form (who was not present the day before and would not be the next day), this does not refer to his Divinity—for of Himself God says:

> **"I am who I am,"** <note>Exodus 3:14</note>

But those changes were limited to the creature. Likewise, in the Sacrament, "being" or "not being," "being lifted up" or "being set down," and similar changes do not apply to the nature of Christ. For He himself remains unmoved and unfailing upon his throne at the right hand of the majesty of the Father. Rather, all these things consist in the Sacrament—that is, in the species of bread and wine. 

If the Picard does not grasp this and cannot believe it, let him at least not reproach the Christian who has made his senses captive in obedience to faith for thinking of it. Rather, let him pity his own lot and weep over the damnation rushing toward him, into whose ear the wise man daily says:

> **"Do not be wiser than is necessary, lest you be dazed,"** <note>Ecclesiastes 7:16</note>

and again,

> **"Just as eating too much honey is not good for a person, so he who is a searcher of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory."** <note>Proverbs 25:27</note>

But these perverse men say again—hear their heresies: our teachings are certainly consistent with Scripture and the examples of Scripture, the Prophets, the Apostles, and even the Gospel. However, we have not heard these blasphemies which the Picards speak here. They do not carry the flavor of the Prophets and Apostles; rather, a foul-smelling and sulfurous smoke from the flames of Gehenna has passed through them. They claim that for the truth of our confession to follow, we would be making God do something "greater than the Incarnation of the Word." First, we are never afraid to confess this, since God is always doing something new, just as he said through Isaiah:

> **"I am the Lord and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil."** <note>Isaiah 45:7</note>

The present tense signifies perpetuity and unfailing action, as in that other passage:

> **"My Father is working until now, and I am working,"** <note>John 5:17</note>

Therefore, God does new things daily, even if he does greater things than the [Incarnation] of the Word...

# ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST [THE PICARDS]

Those <term>Picards</term> <note>original: "Pighardi." A term for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren, used here as a label for heretics.</note> do not speak rightly when they compare the Sacrament to the Incarnation. For in God’s <term>omnipotence</term> <note>His all-powerful nature.</note>, one act is not greater than another, nor is one more laborious than the rest. Rather, by his word, he calls whatever he wishes into existence, and those things come forth promptly and without difficulty. Furthermore—and here I am not speaking of the Picard's monstrous inventions, but of what we have just reported regarding the Sacrament of the Altar—all things are minor compared to God’s omnipotence. For while the Divinity appears in one specific place within a creature, it is nevertheless everywhere and fills all things. 

In the Sacrament of the Altar, Christ is present as his body and blood both here and there, and in the most diverse places simultaneously; he himself remains undivided and <term>unextended</term> <note>Meaning he does not take up physical space in the way a normal body does, occupying "inches" or "feet."</note>. Finally, they claim that we believe those "multiplied bodies" in the Sacrament are united and brought to life by a single soul—as if we would suddenly confess to every lie their evil-mindedness imposes on us! Thus they now fabricate stories against us, saying there are as many bodies or "many Christs" in the Sacrament as there happen to be <term>species</term> <note>The outward appearances of the bread and the wine (the "accidents") that remain after the substance has changed.</note> consecrated in the mystery of the altar. 

That Picard, defiled by every filth of error, ought first to have proven that we said Christ is "multiplied" in the Sacrament. We do not say this, as we have professed regarding many other matters nearby and abroad. We say that only the Sacrament itself is multiplied in the forms of bread and wine; however, in all of them, there is one body and one blood, a completely single and undivided existence of Christ. 

This is just as it was among the twelve Apostles: there were twelve small pieces which each individual received, yet the body and blood of Christ were not multiplied there to match the number of the pieces. For this reason, Christ did not say: "Those things which you each receive are my bodies," but rather: "This (which you all receive as one) is my body." And "This is my blood." 

Likewise, when a thousand, or two, or three, or fifteen thousand people or more participate in this most divine Sacrament, the nature of Christ is not multiplied into that number. Nor does the priest say anything over any number of the species of bread and wine other than that word preordained by God: "This is my body. This is my blood." 

Only that most dismal heretic, that Picard, I say—only he is of such a calloused conscience that he does not fear to blaspheme with his own inventions outside the faith of the Gospel, speaking of "this body and that body." These are the words of our heretic: "that many bodies, multiplied across some thousands of places, are united by a single soul created once." 

Listen now, you contaminated heretic: whatever is multiplied there, whatever becomes and then ceases to be, whatever is lifted up and set down, or received and elevated—all of that is effected and completed only in the realm of the <term>creature</term> <note>The physical, created elements of bread and wine, rather than Christ's eternal nature.</note>. If the Picard does not yet grasp this, let him blame the slowness of his own brain. But let him also set a guard over his mouth. For the Apostolic faith is not of such a nature that it is subject to the senses. Indeed, faith is nothing if the senses themselves can experience it. 

Nevertheless, we wish to offer a small bit of understanding—not for this most ungrateful Picard, who is capable of despising our words as much as the Gospel, but for the Christian people. We do this so they do not think we are speaking of monsters, and so they do not render themselves vulnerable to being harmed by the great poison of the Picard’s words. Beyond the examples given above, we can draw from the traces of natural things: 

The <term>rational soul</term> <note>original: "anima racionalis." The human soul, which medieval philosophers argued was present in every part of the body simultaneously.</note> remains whole in the whole body and whole in every individual part of the body, yet it is not multiplied, because it stays at the indivisible point of its own nature, being a spirit. The extremities of the body move, yet the soul sits unmoved in its own seat. So too, Christ is present, whole, here and there and in the most diverse places in the Sacrament; he does not "spread out" from his distinct nature or from the place where he sits at the right hand of the Father. Any man, being himself undivided in place and form, remains...

D iiij

...in many mirrors he represents his own form most fully. Images of him are made there in the mirrors which were not there shortly before; those that were there cease again; they move, they stop, they are lifted and set down, and finally, they are multiplied. Yet all these changes happen only on the side of the mirrors, for the man himself remains undivided; he does not begin to be or not be according to the images, nor finally does he suffer anything at all of what happens to the mirror images. 

And Christ—God and man—himself unmoved in place and nature while existing at the right hand of the Father, communicates his nature to the many <term>species</term> <note>The outward appearances of the bread and wine, which remain even after the "substance" changes.</note> of the Sacrament as wholly as he does truly. There the species of bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ which were not there yesterday; they will be there tomorrow when they are not here today; they are lifted up, set down, and multiplied throughout the places of the entire Christian world. Christ himself, however, is neither then "made" nor "not made"; he is not moved, not stopped, not lifted, not set down; his person is not multiplied at all, nor does he receive any part of the change. Instead, all those transformations are limited to one side: the created elements of bread and wine.

But we are far too bold when we compare divine miracles to shadows and then confine them within the narrow limits of earthly things. Instead, let us rebuke our own rashness and yield to God his own omnipotence, for it is more fitting for mortals to leave the reasoning of his works to God. As he said through <term>Isaiah</term>: "My secret is my own, my secret is my own" <note>original: "secretum meum mihi." A quote from Isaiah 24:16, often used in medieval theology to signify that certain divine mysteries are hidden from human reason.</note>.

## THE PICARD <note>original: "Pighardus." A derogatory term for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren, suggesting they were followers of a "Picard" heresy.</note>,

These things and many others come from the fact that they have devised a "substantial transformation" of this kind. That doctor who holds this view will be obligated to explain it according to the rule of faith, and so forth up to that place. For now, we do not intend to say more about these things because we have written enough on this in those public letters which we gave to everyone.

First, they say that we devised that transformation of the Sacrament into the body and blood of Christ so that we might magnify the faith of this Sacrament beyond the boundaries of human intelligence. What fruit was there in this, and what pleasure did the Church have in it? Perhaps, as they once said about <term>purgatory</term>, did we devise this too out of the hope of profit <note>The author is refuting the common Protestant/Waldensian claim that the Catholic Church invented doctrines like Purgatory or Transubstantiation simply to make money from the laity.</note>, as the Picard's accusation claims? But I would like the Picards to tell me: since the blood of generation grows into a new man, and since they grow warm when they were previously cold—let the Picards say, and say clearly: when in the beginning God produced all things from unformed matter into manifest existence according to their kinds, did not a "middle transformation" <note>original: "transmutacio media." The philosophical concept of a process of change between a starting point and a finishing point.</note> intervene so that all these things might be what they previously were not? 

Although the Picards may see their "horns" growing here <note>A metaphor for becoming aggressive or stubborn in argument.</note> and see their own logic excluded by the contrary sense, they will never be so twisted in their brains as to dare anything unless they confess these things were made with a "middle transformation" intervening. Or if they deny it, then nature will never mature an offspring from the humor of generation, and the Picards themselves, once cold, will remain cold forever after. Finally, Moses would have been a liar, and nothing at all would have been made that God said should be made. And for us, when God said, "This is my body, this is my blood" <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meum, Hic est sanguis meus."</note>, so that we might not deny the power of the Lord's words nor negate the fact of what God said should be done, it was necessary to confess that it was done by a middle transformation. Therefore, we did not conceive of some transformation by our own license, as the Picard falsely accuses, nor did we impose this meaning on the Lord's words from our own sense; rather, because it was so from the beginning: "This is my body, this is my blood."

# ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST [THE WALDENSIANS]

...regarding the Incarnation, those Pighards <note>A polemical term for the Picards or Bohemian Brethren, a pre-Reformation Christian group often accused of heresy regarding the Eucharist.</note> do not speak correctly. For in the omnipotence of God, one thing is not greater than another, nor is one task more laborious than another. Rather, by His word, whatever He calls into existence comes forth promptly and without difficulty. And finally, I am not speaking of the monstrous ideas of Pighard, but of those things we have just reported concerning the Sacrament of the altar. In the face of God's omnipotence, all these things are lesser, since the Divinity—though appearing in some specific place within a creature—is nevertheless everywhere and fills all things. 

Christ, however, is present in the Sacrament of the altar as His own body and blood; He is both here and there, and in the most diverse places simultaneously, yet He Himself remains undivided and without spatial extension <note>original: "in extensus"; meaning He does not take up physical space in the way a normal body does.</note>. 

Lastly, they claim that those multiplied bodies in the Sacrament are united and animated by a single soul—as if we would suddenly confess whatever lies Pighard’s malevolence imposes upon us! Thus they now invent stories against us, claiming there are as many bodies or as many "Christs" in the Sacrament as there are <term>species</term> <note>The outward appearances of bread and wine (taste, color, shape) that remain after the substance has changed.</note> of the Sacrament happening to be consecrated in the mystery of the altar. 

That Pighard, defiled by every filth of error, ought first to have proven that we say Christ is "multiplied" in the Sacrament. We do not say this, as we have already professed many times regarding things both near and far. We say that only the Sacrament itself is multiplied in the forms of the bread and wine. However, in all of them, there is one body and one blood, and entirely one undivided existence of Christ. 

Just as among the twelve Apostles there were twelve small portions which each individual received, yet the body and blood of Christ were not multiplied there to match the number of those portions. For this reason, He did not say, "The things you each receive are my bodies," but rather that which you all receive as one: **This is my body. And this is my blood.** 

So too, when a thousand, two, three, fifteen, or even more thousands of people participate in this most divine Sacrament, the nature of Christ is not multiplied into that number. Nor does the priest say anything other than that word predefined by God over any number of the <term>species</term> of bread and wine: **This is my body. This is my blood.** 

It is only that Pighard—that most deadly heretic, I say—it is only he, with a conscience so callous, who has not shrunk from blaspheming his own fiction outside the faith of the Gospel, speaking of "these and those bodies." These are the words of our heretic: *“Let one soul, created once, unite bodies multiplied across several thousand places.”* 

Listen still, you contaminated heretic: whatever is multiplied there, whatever becomes and again ceases to be, whatever is lifted up and set down, received and raised—all of that, from its beginning, pertains only to the created element and is fulfilled in it. If Pighard does not yet grasp this, let him blame the slowness of his own brain. But let him also set a guard over his mouth; for the Apostolic faith is not of such a nature as to be subject to the physical senses. Indeed, there is no faith where the sense itself begins to provide the proof. 

Nevertheless, we wish to offer a small amount of understanding—not to this most ungrateful Pighard, who can despise our words just as he does the Gospel—but to the Christian people. We do this so they do not think we are speaking of monsters, and to prevent them from making themselves vulnerable to the injury of such poisonous words from Pighard. Beyond the previous examples, we wish to draw from the traces of natural things. 

The **rational soul** <note>The human soul, capable of reason.</note> remains whole in the whole body and whole in every individual part of the body, yet from the indivisible point of its nature—since it is spirit—it is not multiplied. The extremities of the body move, yet the soul sits unmoved in its own seat. And Christ, whole here and there, present in the Sacrament in most diverse places at once, is not spread out or thinned from His own distinct nature, by which He sits at the right hand of the Father. Whatever man he may be, he remains undivided from himself in place and form...

### THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE

...so that we might confess without deceit, there followed the additional point of change <note>Latin: *transmutatio*, referring to the change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ.</note>, for which reason the Picards <note>The "Pighardi" or Picards were a term often used for the Waldensians or the Bohemian Brethren, who held views on the Eucharist that the author considers heretical.</note> are all the more to be openly accused of wickedness. For beginning from the consequences, they turn back against the first principles. They decide from their own heads that there is no change; from that, they twist the words of the Lord and deny their power. They cast these words away as mere trifles, and finally, in order to retain such trifles, it follows for them that the whole of what God said is not in the Sacrament, but rather certain vanishing figures which the Picards substitute for the <term>species</term> <note>The outward appearances (taste, smell, color) of the bread and wine.</note> of the Sacrament, which they could not even make consistent with themselves. 

Lest the Gospel be revealed, they have suppressed it in appropriate places; yet they themselves have everywhere resorted to us with ambiguous words, slippery meanings, and perpetual lies. By such evil arts of theirs, the Picards accuse us regarding "substantial change," since they have no basis in Scripture by which they might rightly deny it. They invent some other "change," I know not what, outside of all substance, though they equally lack scriptural support for that as they did for the former. For nothing other than substance is changed into the body of Christ, nor do the works of God everywhere terminate in anything other than substance. Therefore, whatever change in the Sacrament either we or they confess, we must necessarily confess it to terminate in substance—unless the Picards admit that no change at all occurs in the Sacrament. And if this is so, the species of bread and wine would be the same after as they were before the consecration; therefore, the words of the Lord would be empty of all power, and the apostolic mysteries would be mere mockeries—a most foul impiety that falls back upon its author, the Picard. 

Yet these most worthless men demand a reason for our faith. Behold the reason, which they shall find refutes them regarding things so certain and established, and which we in turn confirm against the heresy of the Picards. They turn from this to other trifles, saying: "This body of Christ in the Sacrament is either mortal or glorified." I say: "Glorified." They reply: "It will also be this [mortal], since it first becomes so at the words of consecration." <insert>[Christ with his body and blood is in the dwelling of blessing, just as he is at the right hand of God]</insert> I will respond here to the Picards regarding their own impudence: let them say in another place whatever they finally think the body and blood of Christ to be; since, however, they believe that it first comes to be in the species of bread and wine after the words of consecration, then that body of Christ at the right hand of God will also be "mortal" in the Sacrament. Or, by whatever reasoning they might free themselves from calling it mortal, by that same reasoning they have freed both us and our faith from confessing anything mortal in the Sacrament. 

Truly, we expect nothing from the reasoning of the Picards, since we are truthful of ourselves—or rather, from the Scriptures we give the reason for apostolic piety. The Picards, however, are liars of their own making. Therefore, we first say this: because that which becomes and does not become the body and blood of Christ in the Sacrament is not called "mortal." For "mortal" is only that which has had a beginning by being born. The Sacrament, however, is neither born nor not born. Therefore, if they wished to strike the ears of the people with some serious voice, they ought to say: "It will be temporal," because it is blessed and consecrated by these words. But they limit that "becoming temporal" and "ceasing to be," and "not being" and "becoming then," and many similar things—without injury to Christ the Savior—only to the creature of bread and wine, as we have explained more fully in another place. 

For this reason, let the Picards abstain from those portents: "Christ will yet die," "His blood will be shed anew," or that "they shall make other words of consecration." With those or other words, they will achieve nothing. For the Picards invent all those things out of their own stomach, and to the offense of the apostolic faith, they compose them all to the horror of those listening. # THE WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE

[If] the Apostles had continued this sacrament of the body and blood of Christ until the **Great Friday** <note>Good Friday (Latin: *magna sexta feria*).</note>, Christ would have been in that same body of his both alive and dead at once, glorified and mortal. 

O Christian people, those most filthy **Picards** <note>A derogatory term for the Waldensians or Bohemian Brethren.</note>—if they had not condemned the Christian faith based on their own inventions and not from their own insanity—you would not hear such unthinkable blasphemies as you have heard from us while we took up the Catholic faith to assert its innocence and purity against those **"tailed beasts"** <note>original: *caudatas bestias*. A medieval insult for heretics, often depicted as monstrous or animalistic.</note>. 

But they say: [ "If the Apostles had indeed retained anything of the sacrament, such inconsistencies—namely, being alive and dead, glorified and mortal, here and there in his own person and in the sacrament of Christ's nature—would have occurred." ] From this, they attack the truth of the sacrament more deeply. [They argue:] "So that such inconsistencies concerning Christ's person would not happen, Christ was not present in the sacrament according to his own nature." 

I would not know how to free the Christian confession from such a tight knot here, unless the Picards had left me this: that the Apostles reserved nothing of the sacrament <note>The author points out that because the Apostles didn't actually keep a host from the Last Supper until the Crucifixion, the "contradiction" never happened.</note>. Therefore, just as they say from things they have made up themselves, "If they had reserved it, contrary things would have happened to Christ here and there; which, lest they happen, Christ was not in the sacrament." 

Thus we say much more truly from the present history of the Gospel and from the facts themselves: because the Apostles reserved nothing, therefore contrary things did not happen to the nature of Christ. Therefore, no such unthinkable things shall prevent the truth of Christ's nature from being in the sacrament. 

Finally, what kind of <term>sophism</term> <note>A clever but fallacious argument used to deceive.</note> do the Picards now use against us? So that what is not, nor ought to have been or happened by divine will, they imagine that as a temporary condition as if it were so, and by that they destroy something else which truly is. Indeed, this kind of **"knot in a bulrush"** <note>original: *scirpi genus*. A Latin proverb (*nodum in scirpo quaerere*) for looking for a problem or difficulty where there is none.</note> is most vain in itself; for things are asserted and affirmed from actual things, while only ghosts and empty phantoms fight or agree with things that are not. 

Or, if the "shape-shifting" Picard thinks one should philosophize from faith and the Gospel in this way, let us then be purged of the reasoning of similar sophisms by several more manifest examples, and we will understand how many monsters come forth. 

If the **Canaanite** had repented of his crimes upon the departure of the [Israelite] sons from Egypt, he ought then to have been cast out of his land and not cast out. Cast out indeed because of the sons of Israel, to whom the land was promised; but not cast out because of the repentance he performed. But this contradiction—which not even God, by his total omnipotence (these are the words of the Picard), will make—implies therefore that the sons of Israel did not depart from Egypt. 

It was near that **Absalom** had followed the counsel of Ahithophel, and would have captured **David** his father, weary from the journey. If he had been followed, when would **Solomon** have come to the kingdom? There, therefore, lest that coming and simultaneously not coming to the kingdom should require God to do both equally—which the Picard denies he can do—God would never have promised David concerning Solomon: "Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne." 

If the **Virgin Mary**, then when the conception of the Savior was being announced, had suffered something such as Moses said at the "Waters of Contradiction" <note>Meribah (Numbers 20), where Moses doubted.</note>: could not God make a man from an inviolate virgin alone, unless God chooses the mother whom he is about to choose? My virginity is devoted; that "other" will of the virgin would have prevented God from coming into the flesh—just as in a later time Christ did not perform many miracles in his own country because of their unbelief. Since therefore God—according to the Picard's own confession—would not, by all his omnipotence, make God to be both incarnate and not incarnate, therefore Christ would not have been incarnate. 

If **Judas Iscariot** had repented at Christ's warning; if the Jews and their princes had been pricked in heart; if **Pilate**, by Roman power, had snatched away and released Christ (as Paul was later snatched away and released), Christ would be sacrificed and not sacrificed. Sacrificed by divine ordinance; not sacrificed by human compunction and conscience. 

But because God, by his total omnipotence (as the Picards say), will not do contrary things to the same object, Christ would not be delivered into the hands of the impious, nor would he suffer at all. We have laid bare this pattern of argument from which the Picards deny the truth of the sacrament. Therefore, what is lacking in our examples? Why did we assemble such discordant monsters, so foreign to piety—that is, things not related to themselves?

### ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST...

When the discussion began: If the Canaanite woman had repented. If Absalom had followed the counsel of Ahithophel <note>Ahithophel was a counselor to King David who betrayed him to join the rebellion of David's son, Absalom. The author is using "what if" historical scenarios to show how logic can be misapplied.</note>. If the Virgin had hesitated. If the Jews had been moved to remorse. These points should not have been followed by the conclusions we made to expose the deception of the Picard; rather, they followed from the power of a just judgment. The Canaanite did not repent. The counsel of Ahithophel did not prevail. The Virgin did not hesitate. The Jews were not moved to remorse. Those contentious Picards, when they began the discussion, "If the disciples had continued [the sacrament] into the **Great Friday**" <note>original: *magnam sextam feriae*. This refers to Good Friday, the day of the Crucifixion.</note>—they themselves should not have tried to extort from this the idea that the Apostles did not have the faith that Christ was in the sacrament. Instead, they should have let the discussion lead here: that the disciples did not actually retain any of the sacrament the following day. Thus, by the actual deed of the Apostles, the matter would have been freed from all contradiction. For how could Christ be both living and dead, glorified and mortal, in his one body?

Now, therefore, since we have dragged those **little foxes**, the Picards, out of their burrows <note>original: *ex Cuniculis fuis vulpeculas illas Pighardos extraximus*. Tunnels or burrows (*cuniculi*) and foxes (*vulpeculas*) were common metaphors in the Middle Ages for heretics hiding in the "vines" of the Church.</note>, and we are now out of danger from those deceptions, I want them to play against us again with those same frauds. For this purpose, we allow that crafty Picard his sophistry for a time. Let him think, then, regarding his empty and nowhere-appearing fiction: "If the Apostles had continued..." What then? Would the heavens have fallen? Or would God not have had a way for all things to remain safe for Himself? For certainly, when the Divinity appeared to the holy fathers in a created form, He walked, He stood, He sat, He spoke, and again He was silent; yet in His absolute nature, He did none of these things, for God is the same and unchangeable. There, therefore, contrary things occurred at the same moment. 

Following this example of omnipotence: if the Apostles had also retained [the host], Christ in the Sacrament would have been glorified, not suffering, not dead, even while in His absolute person He was suffering, dying, and rising. Let the Picard return from this miracle of God's omnipotence and say: "God, out of all His omnipotence, will not do it." Because of such a rash statement <note>original: *temerariam vocem*</note> from the Picard, we must necessarily inquire what exactly it is that is "impossible" for God, and whether there is indeed something that God simply cannot do. 

Therefore, in human affairs, something is said to be "impossible" which is beyond our capacity, just as making ourselves live forever is beyond our nature and our arts. Whatever humans cannot do, therefore, arises from a **defect of power** <note>original: *defectu virtutis*</note>. If we attribute this also to God—that there is now something He cannot do because of its difficulty—then that thing would be more sublime than God and more powerful than God’s omnipotence. However, since God is immeasurable in His entire nature—immeasurable in justice, goodness, and truth, immeasurable in omnipotence and power—if there were still something He could not do because of the difficulty of the task, that thing would also be "immeasurable above the immeasurable," which is unthinkable. 

Therefore, what we mean when we say "God cannot do" something is different from what we mean when we say a human or any creature "cannot do" something. For this "inability" that we attribute to God actually signifies the efficacy of divine power; it is as truly the fullest omnipotence of God as God is truly omnipotent. For example: a human **can** "not-live" (can die), but God **cannot** "not-live." A human can err and fall into worse things; God can do neither. Therefore, God cannot do anything from the whole universe that is against the fullness of the divine essence. Just as a human can attempt a thing and yet achieve nothing, God cannot "create" and "do" in such a way that the thing does not result. He cannot, therefore, do a "nothing-thing" <note>original: *non rem*. Meaning God cannot act in a way that is futile or results in nothingness.</note>, because then the divine operation would be frustrated and vanish into nothing, which does not happen in the nature of God because of the fullness of His omnipotence. Therefore, that "inability" is spoken of in divine and human matters according to one or another **power of the word** <note>original: *vocis poteftatem*. # WALDENSIANS: BOOK FIVE #

...a lack of power. The **Picards** <note>The "Picards" was a common, often derogatory, name for the Bohemian Brethren, whom the author associates with the Waldensians.</note> claim that God, out of the totality of His omnipotence, cannot make one and the same thing both living and dead, or both glorified and mortal. They argue these states cannot be brought about even though they do not contradict the fullness of divine action. For "dead" is nothing other than the entry of different forms into the original matter; while "mortal" is that which still remains within the boundary to which birth runs out. Both, therefore, truly exist within the realm of being, and we have shown previously that it is only "non-being" that God cannot create. If, therefore, God were unable to do those things—as the Picard opinion holds—this would imply a weakness in the divine power, which is impious even to think or say, and is contrary to the faith of all the Scriptures.

For God never restricted the power of His miraculous works in His saints, and certainly not in **Christ**, and least of all in Himself. **Moses** afflicted the Egyptians in astounding ways; he led the people of God through the dry bed of the sea; he struck a torrent of water from a parched rock. **Joshua** made the sun stand still. **Elijah** shut the heavens and opened them again for rain. **Isaiah** cast his hand upon the daily rotation and called back the falling day by a reverse course for ten hours <note>This refers to the miracle of the sun's shadow moving backward on the sundial of Ahaz as a sign for King Hezekiah.</note>. All of these were able to change the face of nature through the power of miracles—and shall we place a limit on the omnipotence of **Christ** as God, when He Himself has not yet set a limit for mortals, but rather permits much greater things for the human race?

For indeed, Christ Jesus said: *If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes* <note>original: "Si potes credere, omnia poffibilia funt credēti"</note>. He said *all things*, excluding no works from following those who believe. Thus, that presumption is entirely foolish which says "Christ cannot do this" or "God cannot do that." On the contrary, Christ is the **seal of the wonder-working prophets**, and He Himself fills the world with miracles; yet as long as He was in the flesh, He did nothing unique that exceeded the examples of the prophets and Apostles. Shall we not then honor Christ above His companions with some sovereign power which He alone, after God, possesses without the example of the saints?

Certainly, this will now be found in what He said: **"This is my body; This is my blood."** Just as God, appearing of old to the holy fathers, was moved within a creature <note>This refers to "theophanies," such as God appearing in the burning bush or a pillar of cloud.</note>, yet in Himself was not truly moved, and nature obeyed God even in contrary things; so Christ in the **Sacrament** <term>Sacrament: here specifically the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term> may become present under the appearances of bread and wine—appearing, disappearing, being lifted up, being placed down, being consumed, or being reserved—while He Himself, in His absolute person, receives within Himself no suffering or corruption of matter at all. We have no doubt concerning this power of Christ, since Christ is in God and God is in Christ. Therefore, whatever we contend Christ "cannot do" would be to say that God in Christ cannot do it. If the Picard, due to the sluggishness of his brain, does not grasp such difficult matters, let him not deny the omnipotence of God based on his own limitations. There are many other miracles of divine works that he does not grasp—for instance, where would this visible world be if it were created at the moment the Picard suspects it would come into being out of nothing?

Next, they ask: *When* does that transformation of the appearances of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ take place according to our faith? It is a very ill-advised struggle for the Picard to demand from an opponent the cause of an event when he himself suffers from the same difficulty. If he does not give a reason, he is the first to be unfair; if he does give one, he will have answered for his opponent as well. They ask us about the **moment of transformation** of the sacramental species into the body and blood of Christ. Unless we can point to the exact instant, they intend to use our silence to deny the truth of the sacrament. But do they not say themselves in their own **Apology** <note>original: *Apologia*. This likely refers to the *Confessio Fidei* or a similar defense of faith published by the Bohemian Brethren.</note>: <insert>⌜</insert> "Wherever a worthy priest, with a faithful people, acting according to the mind of Christ and the intention of the Church, performs the ordained prayer with words of this kind, namely: **This is my body; This is my blood**, he has testified; and immediately the bread present is the body of Christ offered for us unto death, and the wine likewise present is..."

->### CONCERNING THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST THE HERETICS ###<-

"...his blood shed for the remission of sins" <note>original: "sanguis eius effusus in peccatorum remissionem"</note>. Furthermore, in the confession of faith which they claim to make before tribunals, they appear to hold this same opinion. Let us seek there, by the same right, an answer from the **Picard** <note>The "Picards" or "Pighardi" were names given to the Bohemian Brethren, whom the author considers heretical for their views on the Eucharist.</note>. If he does not think it fitting to point to the beginning or the end, or even the middle of the words, then where does he place his faith regarding that **transformation** <term>transmutatio: the change of the bread and wine into the Body and Blood of Christ</term> of the appearances of bread and wine into the Body and Blood? For if something is to be there by virtue of the words of consecration that was not there before, it must have happened at some specific moment of those words; let them, therefore, assign whatever moment they wish. We shall assign the same, and from their own mouths we shall solve the question for our own faith. Truly, they allow us neither a beginning, nor an end, nor any moment at all during which the transformation occurs. Therefore, that which they say cannot be granted for the sake of weakening our confession, they must also deny for themselves. Thus, let us speak no longer of mere suspicion but of a witnessed faith: the Picard believes that the sacrament is nothing but the bare appearances of bread and wine, and nothing more.

But let us, I pray, leave behind as quickly as possible such horrible blasphemies of the Picards, who cast such sacrilegious ravings against the words of the Lord and the truth of the sacrament. Instead of that place where they demand to know the "moments" of transformation, let us rather free ourselves with a Catholic defense. Let the wicked Picard say, first of all: who works the Sacrament in the appearances of bread and wine—God or man? Surely, it is God.

Therefore, it is not the beginnings or the ends of human words that effect the sacrament. Let that impure man say again: Does God work through time or in an instant? Surely in an instant, since "by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth" <note>A reference to Psalm 33:6</note>. Moreover, the Word of the Father and the Holy Spirit are extended neither by time nor by any quantity at all, but are one undivided and immense essence.

Therefore, whatever miracles are called forth to happen through the ministry of a human voice, although those voices are subject to spans of time, the divine power is not bound to these vocal articulations. Rather, in an indivisible moment, it performs whatever miracle it performs according to the power of the words.

But here the Picards demand that this "instant" of transformation be given to them under the Lord's words: "This is my body. This is my blood." I say: God knows the instant of that prayer. Otherwise, no mortal can assign an instant out of time or a point out of space, since a continuous thing is caused by an infinite flow of indivisible parts; if any part of it were assigned, it would be a finite part of the infinite itself. Therefore, because we do not yet assign the specific moment of transformation, the Picards want to deny the power and truth of the sacrament. Certainly, however, they deny it wrongly. For is this the only miracle among all those that are called forth by a temporal voice? Not at all. Indeed, there are infinite others. **Jesus Christ**, holding the hand of the girl, said to her: "Maiden, arise" <note>original: "Puella surge"</note>, and immediately the girl arose and walked. Again, He cried out with a loud voice: "Lazarus, come out" <note>original: "Lazare veni foras"</note>, and immediately he who had been dead came forth. The Apostles **Peter** and **John** said to the lame man: "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk," and instantly his feet and ankles were made strong, and leaping up, he stood and walked.

Here, in turn, I meet those most clever men who have willingly turned away so as not to see the light of the Lord's face which is sealed upon Christians. I ask those Picards: Did the effect of these present miracles follow the beginning of the words, or the end, or both? The Picard, by his own sophistry, denies us both. Therefore, if it followed neither the beginning nor the end of the words, it must not have happened at all! But the Scriptures convict that lie of the Picard, since at these words the present powers occurred—which no one but a pagan denies. In whatever moment of the words those transformations into new things came forth, it is in a similar moment of the Lord's words: "This is my body."

<header>WALDENSES BOOK FIVE</header>

"This is my blood" <note>original: "Hic est sanguis meus"</note>. The **species** <term>species: the outward appearances of bread and wine, such as color, taste, and smell, which remain after the substance has changed</term> of bread and wine become the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord. Therefore, whether we fail to perceive it due to the poverty of our senses or whether we can identify that exact moment, the change is real in itself, just as it has been in all miracles. Even if no mortal could designate the exact moment then, or if one cannot designate it today, it does not mean those powers failed to take effect. It is mere nonsense that the **Picards** <note>The "Pighardi" or Picards were a reformist group, often identified with the Bohemian Brethren, who rejected the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence.</note> labor to weaken the truth of divine matters with such deceptive evasions. 

We shall attempt, however, to see if anything can be proposed regarding this "instant." Therefore, that instant of divine work does not fall at the very beginning of the Lord’s words, "This is my body; This is my blood." If the words of consecration, when spoken, could attain that indivisible point of time which the incomprehensible Word of the Father attained when God created heaven and earth, then the beginning of the action would be its end, and both would equally be the moment of divine operation—and it would be pointless to ask whether the **transmutation** <term>transmutatio: the change of the bread's substance into the Body of Christ</term> of the sacramental species happened at the beginning or the end. 

But because the physical condition is bound to time, and words follow one another in intervals of time, the beginning and the end cannot occur simultaneously. Only the prayer occupies time; truly, the power within the words remains in its own "indivisible moment" by which the Divinity always operates. Therefore, let the Picard not attempt to use the slowness of the human voice to cause injury or insult to divine works. For God acts in His own way without hindrance. While the words are being voiced, they provide the intellectual understanding of what is meant to happen; however, once perfected, at that same moment, they signify the full truth of their meaning and the reality of the fact. Thus, at the end of the words of consecration, that **transubstantiation** <term>transubstantiatio: the doctrine that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the Body and Blood of Christ</term> occurs entirely, just as other miracles are known to have been completed at the end of the words spoken to perform them. For this reason, we know the Scripture used specific terms like "immediately," "at once," or "instantly," which testify to the swift effect following the commanded miracles.

The Picards then ask: what did Christ point to when he said, "This is" and "Here is"? These Picards, because they demand a physical gesture, attribute to God that manner of speaking and pointing with fingers which even well-mannered men despise. But let them attribute it, out of their rustic ignorance. Truly, where do they find this in Scripture? The Picards otherwise wish to be seen as neither willing nor able to feel or say anything outside of the Scriptures. Yet this "pointing finger" is a fiction unique to their own Synagogue. 

For recently, when some of our people were holding certain Picards strictly to the meaning of the Lord’s words "This is my body" regarding the truth of the sacrament, they mockingly evaded the Catholic position by claiming that when Christ spoke these words, he pointed his finger at himself. Behold the cleverness of the Picard! As if the most important thing for Christ to do at that Supper was to show that he was himself! As if the Apostles did not know this was Christ, or that this was his body! And if they had been ignorant of Christ, why would he not have pointed his finger to his chest? That would have been a better way to show his own body. 

Furthermore, what did he point to when he said, "This is my blood"? For his finger was not the blood of Christ, just as it was not his body, but only a small part of him. Then, if he had pointed to his body and blood in his own person, why, when speaking of his body, did he first take bread, bless it, break it, give it to his disciples and say:

> Take and eat, this is my body.

And when speaking of the blood, he first took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying:

> Drink from this, all of you, for this is my blood of the new testament.

Certainly, therefore, that which they ate and drank is the Body and the Blood of the Lord. He did not point to his finger, but to the **sacrament**. However, there was no need to refute such manifest insanity of the Picards so laboriously, since it was neither becoming nor necessary for Christ to point to anything with a physical gesture. The demonstration was not made with fingers, but by the power of the Word.

<meta>catchword: signs</meta>

...represented. Nevertheless, the **Picards** <note>original: "Pighardi"; a derogatory term for the Bohemian Brethren, who rejected the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence.</note> ask: while one part of that demonstration is being spoken and the other part is yet to be said, what is the truth of that demonstration in the meantime? Is it over the body of Christ, or over the **species** <term>species: the outward appearances of bread and wine—like taste, color, and smell—that remain after the substance has changed</term> of the sacrament?

The Picards would be right to ask this if that **transubstantiation** <term>transubstantiation: the change of the whole substance of bread into the Body of Christ and wine into the Blood</term> occurred in successive moments just as the words are pronounced. If it happened that way, I would say that as long as the prayer and the demonstration itself are being voiced, they possess the truth of their meaning **in the process of becoming** <term>in fieri: a Latin philosophical term for a thing while it is still being made or changing</term>; and finally, when they are perfected, in that specific moment they have the effect of their meaning in a **completed state** <term>in facto esse: a thing in its finished, final state</term>. 

But these transubstantiations do not happen in the way they are spoken—in successive intervals of time—but are instead perfected in one single, indivisible instant. Therefore, the Picards wrongly entrap both us and the sacrament based on that physical speech. Rather, they ought to have disputed over the power of the prayer. For the power of the prayer is fulfilled so suddenly that it is the very act of the "word of the instant," in which no moment can be assigned where what is now was not already there, and what will be was not yet present; instead, these things coincide in one and the same present point of time. In that one moment, the species of bread and wine are the body and blood of Christ.

Therefore, regarding the "demonstration" that the Picards question, nothing of it is "in the process of becoming," but all of it is in the "completed state." The Picards also mock the ecclesiastical writers, claiming they labor so hard over this question that they are in a tight spot wherever they turn. But even if they were indeed in a tight spot, would the truth of the Sacrament be any less consistent in itself? Is it not fitting for mortals to refrain from doubting the **Secrets of the Divine** <note>original: "Archana diuinorum"</note>? Indeed it is fitting; God is altogether more sublime, and His works are more sublime than our thoughts. Yet, even on this point, our writers do not doubt. 

The Picards are clearly lying against our people. They assert reasons regarding the present matter, some closer to the truth than others; but who would reproach a mortal intellect for this? Is faith established on the decrees of mortals, such that it might be rightly despised when we do not know the reason for its perception? Or did it not proceed from divine truth? Certainly it did. Divine truth is not made void by human ignorance, and we do not impose earthly darkness upon heaven. 

But as I said, the Picards lie. For the ecclesiastical writers free themselves from this point quite learnedly. As proof of this, and so that they may recognize this lie in the face of the present facts, I shall produce what **Thomas Aquinas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the highly influential Dominican friar and theologian whose "Summa Theologica" defined much of the Catholic understanding of the Eucharist.</note> left written on this matter. In his fourth writing, he speaks in this manner:

"Those things which are in the voice are proportioned to those which are in the soul. The conception of the soul exists in two ways. In one way, as a representation of a thing only, as it is in cognitions received from things; in that case, the truth of the conception presupposes the entity of the thing as its own measure. Words uttered only for the sake of significance relate to this mode of conception. In another way, the conception of the soul is not representative of a thing, but rather **pre-figurative** <note>original: "praesignativa"</note>, like a productive model, as is evident in practical science, which is the cause of the thing. And the truth of this conception does not presuppose the entity of the thing but precedes it naturally as a cause, even if they are simultaneous in time. 

The aforementioned words [of consecration] relate to this second mode, because they are both significative and causative of that which is signified. Whence the truth and significance of that speech naturally precedes the entity of the thing which it signifies and does not presuppose it, although it is simultaneous with it in time, just as a proper cause is with its proper effect. But because the significance and truth of the speech—which is simultaneous in time with transubstantiation—arises from the combined meanings of the parts uttered successively, it is therefore necessary that the word uttered last completes the significance of the speech... and simultaneously with the significance, the entity of the thing comes to be. Consequently, the meanings of the first parts precede the transubstantiation, which indeed does not happen successively but in the final instant through the now-perfected significance of the speech."

Thus, therefore, this pronoun "This" <note>The "Hoc" in "Hoc est enim corpus meum" (For this is my body).</note> does not demonstrate the **end-point** <term>terminum ad quem: the final state or destination of a change</term> of the Transubstantiation determinately, because already with the signs...

# THE FIFTH BOOK ON THE WALDENSES

...the signification of the speech would presuppose the entity of the thing signified and would not be its cause; nor, likewise, does it demonstrate the "term from which" <term>term from which: (Latin: *terminus a quo*) the starting point of a change; in this case, the bread</term> in a determinate way. This is because its signification would hinder the truth of the whole speech's meaning, since the "term from which" does not remain in the final instant of the speaking. It remains, therefore, that it demonstrates that which is common to both terms indeterminately. Just as in formal changes the "subject" or "matter" is common to both terms, while the terms are distinguished by accidental or substantial forms, so too in **transubstantiation**, the common elements are the **sensible accidents** <term>sensible accidents: the physical properties of a thing (like color, shape, or taste) that can be perceived by the senses</term> which remain, while the diversity lies in the subject. Hence the sense is: "This, contained under these **species** <term>species: the outward appearance of the bread and wine that remains after the substance has changed</term>, is my body." And for this reason, the pronoun "this" is used in a pure sense.

Let the most lying **Picards** <note>original: "Pighardi"; a derogatory name for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians</note> take up this passage of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval theologian whose work defined the Catholic understanding of the Eucharist</note> into their hands and let them say that our people are trapped wherever they turn. It would indeed be a narrow place for our people if they were false; but since they are true, they are therefore free, and the truth has set them free. The "narrow place" truly belongs to the Picards, who have suppressed and denied all true things which, if they were brought forward, would refute them. 

After this, they provoke this most holy and undefiled sacrament with a notable and even atrocious insult using these words of theirs: <insert>[And they state more: that here nothing is broken, nothing is seen, nothing is heard, it does not smell, and it is unpleasant...]</insert> Clearly, that insane Picard "Butcher" <note>original: "lanius"; the author is playing on the name or profession of an opponent, likely Jan Kalenec or a similar figure, by calling him a butcher</note> from his "Slaughterhouse" <note>original: "de Macello suo"; a pun on the opponent's origin or name, implying he treats the holy sacrament like raw meat</note> dreams of the tools of gluttony. And like the Jews who rebelled against God, he says: "Our soul now feels nausea over this most light food" <note>A reference to Numbers 21:5, where the Israelites complained about the Manna in the desert</note>. 

Go away, you stinking dog, to your ruin with that palate of yours! Seek out taverns for yourself; there, examine the meats in the pots. But leave to the most divine sacrament its own heavenly nature. Once Christ was cut and sacrificed <note>original: "sectus... et dilectus"</note>; now he is not broken into pieces for you. He is whole wherever he is—whole in the whole, and whole in the smallest particle. You do not see anything of him; you do not hear him; you do not grasp him; he does not smell. He does not appear at all to your most contaminated senses. For these "first things" have passed away; Christ laid these aside along with his mortality. For those things are related to earthly matters and affect only corruptible matter. They have no right in heavenly things; therefore, they are as far from this glorified body of Christ as it is exalted above them, as far as heaven is distant from the earth. 

Therefore, since the mere substance of bread and wine passes into the body and blood of Christ, the sacrament is rendered subject to none of the accidents. Instead, those accidents remain—either in the "quantity" which stood at the closest degree to the substance, or sustained in the surrounding space. Nevertheless, it is not as you, Picard, blaspheme: that there is no "taste" in the sacrament. For Christ is the sacrament, and he *does* taste and breathe a spiritual sense and a heavenly odor and grace and every delight to the soul; and, as Wisdom said, "it has in itself the sweetness of every taste." 

In this way, although we confess all the most worthy things concerning this sacrament, and although the wicked Picards devise all the most contemptible things about the same—finally denying its very truth—yet, forgetting their own sacrileges, they dare to call our most pure faith into envy and contempt, saying: "Is *this* the Christian faith?" 

I say to you: you lie, wicked Picard! That is not the faith which you, from your ulcerated stomach, have thrust out as some monster. Rather, that is the Christian faith which we, having struck out your fictions, have restored to its place. We are never ashamed of this Christian faith; the divine Scriptures teach it, and they preserve it, pouring it into all pure minds that believe in God. But the Picard has another faith, and lest it slip away from him, he has both suppressed and corrupted the Holy Scriptures. He has harmed the divinity of Christ in unspeakable ways: by his "carved image," by his prophecy about the Antichrist, by his focus on "breaking" and "smell" and "taste," and finally by his display of figures that exist nowhere—again treating it as a sign to be contradicted. From such great sacrileges, his own ulcerated tongue nonetheless cries out loudly against our faith, and from the middle of it all, he points a finger <note>original: "ungue ostendit"; literally "shows with a nail," a gesture of mockery</note> saying: "This is the Christian faith."

# ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AGAINST
### THE ERRORS OF THE PICARDS

I say it is a truth which no one can be saved unless they believe it faithfully and firmly. It has displeased no one throughout their entire life, nor has it been attacked by any, nor have any wished it overturned who were not also enemies of God: the Neros, the Domitians, the Diocletians, the Turks, the Saracens, the Tartars, and last of all, the precursors of the Antichrist, the **Picards** <note>original: "Pighardi"; a derogatory term used by Catholic polemicists for the Bohemian Brethren or Waldensians</note>. It follows now that I should speak finally of these **Picards** who dissect the virtue and truth of the sacrament. They ask whether the words of consecration which the priests speak are said according to the form and power of the speech, or only as a bare voice. They intend this so that in neither way are they uttered correctly; and if they are not uttered correctly, they effect nothing of the Sacrament. Thus, they wish the Christian faith to not rightly believe that the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ exists under the **species** <term>species: the outward physical appearances (color, taste, smell) of bread and wine that remain after the substance has changed</term> of bread and wine. From this imprudence, the Picard often slips, attempting to tie knots for his adversary; yet if he should finish them, he himself would be the first caught. For unless he thinks the sacrament is absolutely nothing, if he believes anything of the Sacrament exists through the words of consecration, those words—whether used by a Picard butcher, or a meat-seller, or any filthy bench-worker—would have had their own power and would have been spoken in one way or the other. Therefore, our priests also speak those same words in one form or the other. 

But because they presently contend that those words cannot be spoken by our priests in either way, what they want accepted among us, they have first accepted from their own opinion: that they should confess the mystery of the altar to be nothing but "bare creature," bread and wine. Thus, Christ would have spoken in vain over those species to his disciples: **Take and eat, this is my body. Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the new testament which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins** <note>original Latin: "Accipite et comedite, hoc est corpus meum. Bibite ex hoc omnes. hic est enim sanguis meus novi testamenti qui pro multis effundetur in remissionem peccatorum"</note>. But those are the customary blasphemies of the Picard, and let them be gone. As he who is in filth becomes even filthier, we shall instead attempt a solution of this kind based on Christian piety. Therefore, the priests speak these words of consecration according to the form of the words and the power of the meaning; for by speech—to use the words of **Saint Ambrose** <note>Ambrose of Milan (c. 340–397), an influential Church Father</note>—this sacrament is produced. The speech of Christ changes the creature, and thus from bread comes the body of Christ, and the wine mixed with water in the chalice becomes blood by the consecration of the heavenly word. 

The priest, therefore, speaks the words of consecration **in the person of Christ** <note>original: "ex persona christi"; the theological concept that the priest acts as a representative or "mask" of Christ during the sacraments</note>. Of whose person he is the minister and representative, he maintains the demonstration in the words. Just as it is with court secretaries: when they set forth words from the mouth of a prince in edicts and record them in bronze, the command and power represented by those words belong not to them, but to the principal person. So in the mystery, both the word and the power are spoken through the priest representing the person of Christ; yet he himself transforms nothing, but it is the power of Christ, who first spoke these words, that acts. 

Afterward, they reproach us regarding ecclesiastical learning and say: "These questions are yours, and from your beehives" <note>a metaphor suggesting that scholastic theology is overly complex, crowded, and perhaps stings like a bee</note>. They would have done well to abstain from this reproach, for no other religion has been carried forward with equal learning, nor have any other writers been held as friends of God for their holiness of life. I confess, ecclesiastical writers dispute over matters of faith, not toward the creation of faith—as **Saint Eustachius** or **Bonaventure** <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a major Franciscan theologian and Doctor of the Church</note> say—but for its nourishment, lest anyone through ignorance believe something foreign to the faith. Thus our men dispute so that they might remain most pious. The Picards scrutinize the faith so that they might be most treacherous. Either our men here establish questions, or they leave those Picard refutations in the midst of the common people, so the Picard thinks he cannot find the heads of the questions in our works. It might seem, therefore, that the Christian faith denies what is in the Gospel while confessing all sorts of portents whose ends and beginnings it does not know. Here, if the Picards wished to be pure and candid, and not study only malicious contention, they ought to have accepted whatever was true in our writings—whether asserted through simple or absolute reasoning—out of reverence for truth and their own conscience. If things were false, it was necessary for them, for the sake of truth and conscience, to reject the false.

He condemns the "Picards" (Waldensians) for reducing the Eucharist to mere bread and wine and defends scholastic theology against their mockery.</summary>
